Visitors who already have an account **are excluded from the denominator**: existing customers visit the website regularly and can't sign up again, and they drag the conversion rate down. They're separated by login status or by the known-user flag in analytics.
The numerator and the denominator **are counted in the same** unit. Signups are counted once per visitor; otherwise, one person who registered two accounts counts twice in the numerator.
A visitor **is assigned to the period** by the date of their first visit, and the signup is assigned to that visit's cohort. Otherwise a person who came in March and signed up in April lands in different months in the numerator and the denominator.
**The denominator is limited to visitors to pages** where signing up is possible: if you count all traffic, including the blog and help center, the number measures the blog's share of traffic rather than how well the form works.
53.example:
Unique visitors to pages with signup in March: 26,900
Of those, with an existing account: 2,900 (not in the denominator)
Visitors without an account: 24,000
Sessions in March: 61,000 (not in the denominator)
Signed up: 800

Signup Conversion Rate = 800 / 24,000 × 100 = **3.3%**

Dividing by sessions gives 1.3%: that's conversion per session rather than per visitor.
53.importance: **It determines** how much traffic you need to buy to reach the planned user base, and it directly drives the cost per signup. Even a small drop after a signup form update is caught here faster than in any other metric: changes to an input field or password requirements show up the same day.
53.not_needed: **Skip it on** websites without signup: brochure sites, landing pages with an inquiry form, catalogs without customer accounts, and sites where the sales team grants access after negotiations.
53.essence_note: the more visitors create an account, the less each new user costs

54.name: Average Session Duration
54.formula: Total Duration of All Sessions / Number of Sessions
54.description: The average duration of one session. Calculated as the total session duration divided by the number of sessions.
54.nuances:
**Numbers from different systems** shouldn't be compared with each other: a system that calculates duration from the time between actions records a duration of zero for a single-pageview session, while GA4 counts the time the tab was active, so such a session still gets a nonzero duration. Even with identical user behavior, the numbers diverge noticeably.
**Decide** whether bounced sessions are included in the calculation. Zero-length single-pageview sessions pull the average down, and the higher the bounce rate, the stronger the pull; calculated over engaged sessions, the number reflects actual reading time.
**An open tab** the user never came back to is cut off by the inactivity timeout and doesn't inflate the duration.
54.example:
Sessions in the month: 40,000
Total duration: 3,040,000 seconds

Average Session Duration = 3,040,000 / 40,000 = 76 seconds = **1 min 16 sec**

Over engaged sessions (22,800), the same total gives 133 seconds: zero-length bounced sessions pulled the average down by almost half.
54.importance: **It answers the question** of whether people read the content or skim it. A sharp increase isn't always good: it also happens when someone can't find what they need and wanders from section to section, so read an increase alongside the conversion rate.
54.not_needed: **Skip it on websites** where the goal is a quick answer: reference pages, schedules, order status. A long session there means the person didn't find what they needed.
54.essence_note: a session that's too short means the person found nothing, and one that's too long means they're wandering from section to section

55.name: Page Load Time
55.formula: Total Load Time of All Pages / Number of Page Loads
55.description: The average time from when a page starts opening to when it's fully rendered and ready to use.
55.nuances:
**The arithmetic mean is heavily** pulled up by occasional loads that take tens of seconds. The median and the 75th percentile give a stable picture, while the mean shows how long people waited in total.
**The moment loading ends** is defined in different ways: when the visible part is fully rendered, when DOMContentLoaded fires, or when all resources have loaded, including images and scripts. On the same page, the heavier the images and scripts, the further apart these moments are.
**The calculation includes only loads** where the tag had time to fire: a user who left before the page finished loading doesn't make it into the calculation, and slow cases are systematically undercounted.
55.example:
Page loads in the week: 86,000
Total load time: 137,600 seconds

Page Load Time = 137,600 / 86,000 = **1.6 seconds**

The median for the same data is 1.1 seconds. The gap comes from a tail of 4% of loads that take longer than 8 seconds.
55.importance: It directly affects **whether users get** to the content. Every extra second spent loading the above-the-fold content loses part of the traffic before people see the offer, and this loss doesn't show up in any conversion metric: people simply never appear in the funnel.
55.not_needed: Skip it when you track speed with Core Web Vitals: those metrics **are based on real** visits and a percentile, while the average load time hides slow loads behind fast ones.
55.synonyms: Average Page Load Time, Page Speed, Site Speed
55.essence_note: a slow page loses people before they see the offer

56.name: Pages per Session
56.description: The average number of pages viewed per session. Repeat views of the same page are counted.
56.nuances:
Going back to a page already viewed **counts as a new pageview**, so going back and forth between a product page and a list raises pages per session with no real increase in interest.
If moving between sections doesn't reload the page, the tag counts only the initial page load, and pages per session on such a website stays around one no matter how much the person viewed. **It's measured there** only when the developer sends an event on every navigation.
Loading more of a feed as the user scrolls and reloading the page also produce separate pageviews if an event is set up for them. On long feeds, the more loads fit into one screen of scrolling, the **more this decision changes** pages per session.
The minimum value of the metric is one: a session with no pageviews **isn't recorded**.
56.example:
Pageviews in the month: 120,000
Sessions: 40,000

Pages per Session = 120,000 / 40,000 = **3.0 pages**

Excluding bounced sessions leaves 102,800 pageviews over 22,800 sessions, or 4.5 pages: single-page visits pull the average down.
56.importance: **It shows** whether the website structure leads people beyond the first page. A drop with stable traffic usually comes down to navigation or catalog search: people don't find the next step and leave from the same page they landed on.
56.not_needed: **Skip it on** single-page websites: landing pages and brochure sites, where there's nowhere to go and pages per session is always one.
56.synonyms: Pages per Visit, Views per Session, Page Depth
56.essence_note: one page per session means the person went no further, and browsing dozens of pages means they can't find what they need

57.name: Bounce Rate
57.description: The share of sessions in which the user left without showing interest in the website.
57.nuances:
Systems define a bounce differently, and their numbers can't be compared directly. Some systems count a bounce when a session had one pageview, lasted less than 15 seconds and triggered no event flagged as non-bounce. In GA4, a bounce **is any session** that didn't qualify as engaged, that is, a session shorter than 10 seconds with no second pageview and no key event.
**Any event** sent automatically a few seconds after a page opens pushes the bounce rate down to near zero: the system sees activity in sessions where the person has already left.
**Single-page websites have** an inherently high bounce rate: there's no second page to view, and the result depends entirely on the time threshold.
57.example:
Sessions in the month: 40,000
Of those, single-page sessions under 15 seconds: 17,200

Bounce Rate = 17,200 / 40,000 × 100 = **43%**

After a scroll event that fires at 10 seconds was added, the bounce rate fell to 6%. People's behavior stayed the same, and only the criterion changed.
57.importance: **The first sign** that the expectation set by an ad or a search snippet didn't match the page content. A jump in the bounce rate after ads are replaced or a page title is edited points to a broken promise before orders reflect it.
57.essence_note: these are people who came and left right away, and the money to acquire them has already been spent

58.name: Sessions per User
58.description: The average number of sessions per user during the period.
58.nuances:
Both values **are taken over the same** window. Over a month the value is higher than over a week for purely mechanical reasons: a user has time to come back more often but still counts once in the denominator.
**The inactivity timeout setting** changes the numerator: a longer timeout merges adjacent visits, and the value drops with no change in people's behavior.
**Clearing cookies and** visiting from different devices inflate the denominator, so the real return frequency is higher than the calculated one.
58.example:
Sessions in the month: 40,000
Unique users: 24,000

Sessions per User = 40,000 / 24,000 = **1.7**

Over a week, the same website has 9,400 sessions from 7,800 users, or 1.2: the window is shorter, leaving less time for return visits.
58.importance: **It answers** whether the website gives people a reason to come back, and shows what exactly drove traffic growth: new people or existing users visiting more often. A value close to one with a large ad budget means the money is buying one-time users.
58.not_needed: **Skip it on** websites built for a one-time task: submitting an inquiry, a one-off purchase, looking up information. A return visit isn't expected, and the average tells you nothing.
58.synonyms: Sessions per Visitor, Visits per Visitor
58.essence_note: the more often people come back, the less you need to pay for new ones

59.name: Website Sessions
59.description: The number of sessions on the website during the period. A session starts with the first pageview and ends when the user stops interacting with the website.
59.nuances:
A session closes after an inactivity timeout: in GA4 it's 30 minutes by default, and the value **can be changed in the settings**. A longer timeout merges adjacent visits into one session and lowers the number; a shorter one splits them.
One user can have **several sessions** in a period, so there are never fewer sessions than users.
In some analytics systems, a session that starts before midnight and continues past it is **split into two**.
59.example:
Sessions in the month recorded by the tag: 240,000
In addition, bot sessions: 12,000 (not counted: filtered out by the tag)

Website Sessions = **240,000**
59.importance: **The baseline volume of demand** for the website, which almost every other metric is tied to. A drop shows up before orders fall and gives you time to find the cause: dropping out of search results, a paused ad campaign, a broken tag.
59.not_needed: Skip it when you have **no website of your own** and sell only through third-party platforms.
59.essence_note: the more sessions, the more people see the offer

60.name: Signups
60.description: The number of completed signups on the website during the period. A signup counts when the account has been created and is available to the user.
60.nuances:
**Decide** when a signup counts: at form submission or at email or phone confirmation. Some people are lost between these points, and the entire count depends on the moment you choose.
Signups **are counted once per** visitor.
**Resubmitting the form** after a validation error shouldn't create a second signup; otherwise, the count grows with no real users behind it.
**Internal and test accounts created by the team and contractors are removed** from the count: with low traffic, they make up a noticeable share.
In B2B, an employee signing up within an existing account **doesn't count** as a new signup: the unit here is the company account, the same unit as in customer retention and CAC. The number of employees within an account is counted separately: a customer with ten seats and one with a thousand each count as one signup, and the difference between them shows only in seats and MRR.
60.example:
Signup form submissions in the month: 1,460
Of those, duplicates after a validation error: 240 (not counted)
Didn't confirm their email: 118 (not counted)
Team test accounts: 22 (not counted)

Signups = 1,460 − 240 − 118 − 22 = **1,080**
60.importance: **The direct result of the website's work** on acquisition and on bringing people into the base that messaging campaigns and sales then work with. It's used to check actuals against the plan for new users and to calculate whether the cost per signup fits the product's economics.
60.not_needed: **Skip it on** websites without a customer account: landing pages, brochure sites, catalogs where an inquiry is sent through a form without creating an account.
60.essence_note: every account is a person you can keep working with through messaging campaigns and sales

61.name: Sessions with Cart Additions
61.description: The number of sessions in which at least one product was added to the cart. The main result of the middle of the funnel: the shopper has shown intent to buy but hasn't paid yet.
61.nuances:
Unit of count: a session. A session with four additions **counts once**: the addition events themselves go into the numerator of [[Adds to Cart per Session→voronki_prodazh_h4/dobavleniya_v_korzinu_na_sessiyu]].
Adding three units of the same product means one session and **one addition**: the quantity doesn't affect the count.
**Changing the quantity in** the cart or adding the same product again doesn't create new sessions.
**Removing a product from** the cart doesn't take the session out of the count.
61.example:
Sessions in the month: 50,000
Sessions with a cart addition: 5,500
Add-to-cart events in these sessions: 9,350 (they count toward Adds to Cart per Session, not here)
Sessions where a product was later removed from the cart: 900 (stay in the count)

Sessions with Cart Additions = **5,500 sessions**
61.importance: **This is the point** where browsing turns into purchase intent, and the basis for every step after the cart. Without it, you can't tell apart two different problems: users not reaching the cart, and users reaching it but not paying. The first is fixed with the storefront and prices, the second with delivery and payment, and the two fixes cost very different amounts.
61.not_needed: **Skip it in** a one-click purchase model, where the cart isn't a step and the order is placed right from the product page.
61.essence_note: this is the last step before checkout

62.name: Sessions with Wishlist Additions
62.description: The number of sessions in which at least one product was added to the wishlist. Counts sessions rather than products: a session with five additions counts once.
62.nuances:
**Unit of count**: a session, as throughout the funnel. Counting unique users gives a different, smaller number that doesn't line up with the other metrics on the map.
If the wishlist is available only to logged-in users, only their sessions get into the count: a guest sees the button, but clicking it opens the login form. The metric is then capped by the share of logged-in sessions, so read its trend alongside that share: growth can reflect either increased interest in products or more frequent **logins**.
Removing an item from the wishlist **doesn't cancel the addition**: the session has already been counted.
Adding the same product again after removing it within one session doesn't affect the count: the session **counts once**.
Saves from a product list and from the product page **count the same**: where the button is doesn't matter.
62.example:
Sessions in the month: 50,000
Sessions where “Add to wishlist” was clicked at least once: 3,100
Of those, with an addition on the product page: 2,300; only in product lists: 800
Total addition events in these sessions: 7,400 (not used for this metric)

Sessions with Wishlist Additions = **3,100 sessions**
62.importance: **It captures demand** that didn't turn into an order right away: a wishlist most often means “too expensive today” or “waiting for my size.” You decide whether to launch price-drop and back-in-stock reminders based on the size of this base. Without it, deferred demand isn't visible at all and is treated as lost.
62.not_needed: **Skip it** when the storefront has no wishlist.
62.essence_note: a saved product is often bought later

63.name: Add-to-Wishlist Rate
63.description: The share of all sessions in which a product was added to the wishlist. Shows how often a session ends with a saved product.
63.nuances:
The numerator and denominator **are measured in sessions**: the numerator is the same quantity that [[Sessions with Wishlist Additions→voronki_prodazh_h4/dobavlenie_v_izbrannoe]] counts.
**Denominator**: all sessions in the period, including those with no product views. The share among sessions that viewed a product page is the [[View-to-Wishlist Rate→voronki_prodazh_h4/konversiya_iz_kartochki_v_izbrannoe]], and its value is always higher.
A session with several additions goes into the numerator **once**: the share can't exceed 100%.
63.example:
Sessions in the month: 50,000
Sessions with a wishlist addition: 3,100

Add-to-Wishlist Rate = 3,100 / 50,000 × 100 = **6.2%**
63.importance: **It gives a figure you can compare across** periods and traffic sources: the absolute number of additions grows with traffic, while the share shows whether behavior has changed. It tells you whether a new channel brings people who are ready to choose or just random users.
63.not_needed: **Skip it where** the storefront has no wishlist.
63.essence_note: the more sessions end with a saved item, the more deferred demand builds up

64.name: Add-to-Cart Rate
64.description: The share of all sessions in which a product was added to the cart. The main conversion rate from a site visit to a cart addition.
64.nuances:
The numerator and denominator **are measured in sessions**: the numerator is the same quantity that [[Sessions with Cart Additions→voronki_prodazh_h4/dobavlenie_v_korzinu]] counts.
**Denominator**: all sessions in the period, including sessions without product views. The share among sessions that viewed a product page is the [[View-to-Cart Rate→voronki_prodazh_h4/konversiya_iz_kartochki_v_korzinu]], and its value is always higher.
A session with several additions goes into the numerator **once**: the share can't exceed 100%.
64.example:
Sessions in the month: 50,000
Sessions with a cart addition: 5,500

Add-to-Cart Rate = 5,500 / 50,000 × 100 = **11%**

Putting add-to-cart events (9,350) in the numerator gives 18.7%: that's events divided by sessions, and the number is no longer a conversion rate.
64.importance: **The main summary indicator of** whether the storefront works: it reacts to price, availability, site speed and traffic quality earlier than the Ecommerce Conversion Rate, and it isn't muddied by payment and delivery problems. When it drops, those factors are where you start.
64.not_needed: Skip it with **one-click purchases** that have no cart step.
64.synonyms: Cart Addition Rate, Added to Cart Rate
64.essence_note: the more sessions reach the cart, the more orders you get from the same traffic

65.name: Share of New Users
65.description: The share of users who came to the website for the first time during the period, out of all users in the period. A user counts as new if the analytics system hasn't seen their browser identifier before.
65.nuances:
New-user status **is determined by the browser identifier** rather than by the person: clearing cookies, incognito mode and switching from a phone to a laptop turn an existing user into a new one, and the share is inflated.
The denominator **is the number of unique** users for the period rather than the sum of new and returning users by day: when days are added up, the same person is counted several times.
65.example:
Unique users in the month: 24,000
Of those, with a first session: 9,000

Share of New Users = 9,000 / 24,000 × 100 = **37.5%**

Adding up new users by day gives 11,400 and a share of 47.5%: a person who visited for the first time on the 3rd and again on the 20th was counted as new twice.
65.importance: **It shows the balance between** acquisition and retention. If the share grows with flat traffic, the audience keeps turning over but people don't stick around, and the money goes into buying the same people again and again. If the share falls, the website depends on its existing audience, and any churn from it hits revenue right away.
65.not_needed: **It adds little** for websites built for a one-time task: submitting an inquiry, buying insurance, buying major appliances. There, almost all users are new by the nature of the product, and the share stays near 100% on its own.
65.synonyms: New User Rate, Percentage of New Visitors
65.essence_note: a share that's too low means the website depends on its existing audience, and one that's too high means people come and don't stay

66.name: New Users
66.formula: Number of users with a first session in the period
66.description: The number of users who opened the website for the first time during the period. A first visit is identified by a browser identifier that hasn't appeared in the data before.
66.nuances:
New-user status is tied to the browser rather than the person: the same user on a phone and on a laptop **counts as two new users**.
**Clearing cookies and** incognito mode turn an existing user back into a new one, and the number is inflated by an amount that depends on the audience's habits.
The number for a quarter is lower than the sum of three months: a user who first came in January and came again in February is new **once** in the quarterly view but appears twice in the monthly ones.
66.example:
Unique users in the month: 24,000
Of those, already seen before: 15,000

New Users = 24,000 − 15,000 = **9,000**

Sum of new users across the three months of the quarter: 27,400. For the quarter as a whole, there are 22,100 new users: 5,300 people were counted as new more than once.
66.importance: **The only measure of the inflow** of new people: without it, you can't tell whether growth in sessions comes from new people or from the same people visiting more often. Awareness campaigns that have no direct sales are evaluated against it.
66.essence_note: this is the inflow of new people, without which the website runs only on the audience it already has

67.name: Website Users
67.description: The number of unique website users during the period. Each person counts once, regardless of the number of sessions.
67.nuances:
Users **are identified by the browser identifier** rather than by the person: visits from a phone and from a laptop count as two users, and clearing cookies has the same effect.
The number can't be summed across days and months: a user who visited on Monday and on Wednesday **is counted twice** in the sum of daily counts but once in the weekly view. The value for a period is always taken from the report for that whole period.
**When users log in on the website**, systems can merge a person's devices by user ID, and then the user count drops as cross-device duplicates are removed.
67.example:
Sessions in the month: 40,000
Unique users: **24,000**

Sum of unique users across 30 days: 38,600. The difference from 24,000 comes from people who visited on more than one day of the month.
67.importance: The denominator for acquisition cost and reach calculations, and the only metric on the map that answers the question "How many people?" **Without it, growth in sessions** can't be broken down into an inflow of people and more frequent visits, and the ad budget gets allocated blindly.
67.synonyms: Total Users, Unique Visitors, Unique Users
67.essence_note: these are real people, the ones who turn into inquiries and purchases

68.name: Products Viewed per Session
68.formula: Sum of Unique Product Pages Viewed per Session / Sessions with Product Page Views
68.description: The average number of different product pages opened per session. Shows how many options a user compares before choosing.
68.nuances:
Unique product pages **are counted within each** session separately, and the per-session numbers are added up: opening the same product page again in a session doesn't add one, but the same product opened in another session counts again.
If you take unique product pages **for the whole period** instead, the numerator becomes the number of different catalog products that were opened at all. You can't divide it by sessions: it answers a different question, what part of the assortment users came across.
**Denominator**: sessions with a product page view rather than all sessions. Divided by all traffic, the average falls below one and no longer shows how many products a user compares.
68.example:
Sessions with a product page view: 15,600
Sum of unique product pages across these sessions: 40,600

Products Viewed per Session = 40,600 / 15,600 = **2.6**

Dividing by all 50,000 sessions gives 0.81: this mixes in traffic that never reached products, so it no longer shows how many products a user compares.
68.importance: **It helps diagnose the listings**: a value around one means users come for a specific product and don't compare options, while many product pages per session mean they can't find the right product and keep going through options. The two cases lead to different decisions about what to fix: recommendations or search relevance.
68.not_needed: Skip it for a **narrow assortment** where there's nothing to choose from: with about ten products, the number of products viewed is capped by the size of the catalog.
68.synonyms: Product Views per Session, Items Viewed per Session
68.essence_note: when there are few views, the user found nothing to choose from; when there are many, they can't make up their mind

69.name: Returning Users
69.description: The number of users who had a session during the period that wasn't their first visit to the website.
69.nuances:
A user **counts as returning** if the system has already seen their browser identifier. That identifier is stored for a limited time: Safari keeps cookies set by a tracking script for no longer than 7 days, so a person who comes back after two weeks is counted as a new user. How often this happens depends on which browsers the website's audience uses.
One user counts **once** in a period, no matter how many sessions they had. The metric counts people rather than visits.
**The number of returning users for** a quarter is higher than the sum of three months: a person who visited in January and came back in March is returning in the quarterly view but is listed as new in both monthly views.
69.example:
Unique users in the month: 24,000
Of those, with a first session: 9,000

Returning Users = 24,000 − 9,000 = **15,000**

These 15,000 people had 31,000 sessions: one person with eight visits counts once here.
69.importance: It shows whether the website builds up an audience or starts from zero every month. This is the audience that messaging campaigns and retargeting work with: until it grows, any revenue growth rests **only on buying** new traffic and stops when the budget does.
69.essence_note: a returning user already knows the website and buys more readily, and there's no need to acquire them again

70.name: View-to-Cart Rate
70.formula: (Sessions with a Cart Addition from the Product Page / Sessions with Product Page Views) × 100
70.description: The share of sessions with a product page view in which the product was added to the cart. The main metric for the quality of the product page itself.
70.nuances:
The numerator includes **only additions from** the product page. Quick add from a product list, the wishlist or a recommendations block puts sessions in the numerator without a product page view in the denominator and inflates the result, even to values above 100%.
**Both quantities are measured in sessions**: a session with several additions counts once.
Opening the same product page again within a session **doesn't increase the denominator**.
70.example:
Sessions with a product page view: 15,600
Sessions with a cart addition from the product page: 5,930
Sessions with a quick add from a product list without opening the product page: 2,460 (not in the calculation)

View-to-Cart Rate = 5,930 / 15,600 × 100 = **38%**

Taking all 8,390 sessions with a cart addition gives 54%: the numerator includes sessions the denominator doesn't.
70.importance: **Better than any other** metric, it answers whether the product page sells: traffic and category effects are already filtered out, leaving photos, description, price, availability and delivery terms. This is the metric used to compare products with each other and to find items that everyone views and nobody buys.
70.not_needed: **Skip it where** most cart additions, as counted in [[Sessions with Cart Additions→voronki_prodazh_h4/dobavlenie_v_korzinu]], happen from the list and the product page is rarely opened: the numerator would be a small, unrepresentative part of demand.
70.synonyms: Cart-to-View Rate, Product Page Conversion Rate
70.essence_note: the product page exists precisely so that the product gets added to the cart

71.name: View-to-Wishlist Rate
71.formula: (Sessions with a Wishlist Addition from the Product Page / Sessions with Product Page Views) × 100
71.description: The share of sessions with a product page view in which the product was saved to the wishlist. Shows which outcome is more common after studying the product page: saving or leaving.
71.nuances:
The numerator includes **only additions** made on the product page itself. Additions with the button in product lists, search results and the recommendations block would get into the numerator without a product page view in the denominator, and the share would exceed 100%.
Both quantities are measured in sessions: a session with three saves **counts once**.
Opening the same product page again within a session **doesn't increase the denominator**.
71.example:
Sessions with a product page view: 15,600
Total sessions with a wishlist addition: 3,100
Of those, with an addition on the product page itself: 2,300
With additions only via the button in product lists, without opening the product page: 800 (not in the calculation)

View-to-Wishlist Rate = 2,300 / 15,600 × 100 = **15%**

Taking all 3,100 sessions with a wishlist addition gives 20%: the numerator would include sessions where the product page wasn't opened.
71.importance: **Read it together with** the View-to-Cart Rate: if there are many wishlist saves and few cart additions, the shopper liked the product but was stopped by the price or the delivery time. The page and the price call for different fixes, and without telling them apart, a store starts reworking the product page when the issue was the price.
71.not_needed: Skip it when the wishlist button is **only in product lists** and isn't on the product page.
71.essence_note: the more often a product page leads to a save, the more deferred demand you can follow up on with a reminder

72.name: Time on Product Page
72.formula: Total Time on Product Pages / Product Page Views
72.description: How much time, on average, a user spends on one product page. Indirectly shows whether the page has enough information to make a choice.
72.nuances:
**Denominator**: product page views rather than sessions. With sessions, the time on several product pages adds up, and the metric grows with the number of pages opened rather than with interest in the product; the two can't be separated afterward.
The time on the last page of a session usually isn't measured: if a product page ended the session, its time is zero, while the view itself stays in the denominator and pulls the average down. **This is solved either by excluding** such views from both the numerator and the denominator or by calculating time from scroll and click events on the product page.
**A tab** left open produces extreme outliers: abnormally long views are cut off at an upper limit.
If you need time per session rather than per product page, the denominator **is sessions with** a product page view: that's a different quantity, and it also depends on how many products the user compares.
72.example:
Product page views in the month: 40,600
Total time on product pages: 1,294,800 seconds

Time on Product Page = 1,294,800 / 40,600 = **32 seconds**

Dividing by 15,600 sessions with a product page view gives 83 seconds: that's time per session, which adds up the time on every product page opened.
72.importance: It helps diagnose a questionable product page: a short time combined with low conversion to the cart usually means the person didn't find the size, materials or delivery time and left. Time by itself is neither good nor bad; read it **only alongside** the View-to-Cart Rate.
72.not_needed: **Skip it where** decisions are made instantly: for everyday goods, a long viewing time says more about hesitation than about interest.
72.synonyms: Product Page Dwell Time, Average Time on Product Page
72.essence_note: when a product page is closed right away, the product didn't interest the user; when it's read for a long time, the description and photos don't answer their questions

73.name: Cost per User
73.description: The average marketing spend per acquired user.
73.nuances:
The denominator **has to match** the numerator: if the spend includes only advertising, only users who came through paid placements are counted. Dividing the ad budget by all users, including organic ones, understates the cost and makes traffic look cheap.
**Decide what goes into the spend**: only placement payments, or also agency work, creative production and team salaries. If what goes into the spend isn't fixed, numbers from different months can't be compared.
73.example:
Ad spend for the month: $25,050
Sessions from paid sources: 16,700
Users who came through paid placements: 12,900

Cost per User = $25,050 / 12,900 = **$1.94**

Dividing by all 24,000 website users gives $1.04: the denominator then includes people you didn't pay for.
73.importance: The threshold that revenue per user is checked against: **as soon as the acquisition cost** overtakes that revenue, every new dollar spent on advertising loses money. It's also used to compare sources with each other when audience quality is the same.
73.not_needed: **Skip it** when there's no paid traffic at all and all traffic comes from search, recommendations and direct visits.
73.synonyms: Cost per Visitor, Cost per Unique Visitor
73.essence_note: every dollar spent on acquisition is subtracted from what the user will bring in

74.name: Total App Installs
74.description: The number of app installs during the period, paid and organic combined.
74.nuances:
The download itself can't be tracked: the analytics code lives inside the app, and nothing runs it before the first launch. That's why reports **count the first launch** as the install, and all ad platforms and trackers count exactly that.
Downloads are visible **only to the stores themselves**, which show them in a separate report in their consoles. That number is always higher: some people download the app and never open it. Don't mix the two sources in one report: they count different events.
**The unit here is the install** rather than the person: one user with a phone and a tablet gives two installs, and deleting and reinstalling the app can add a third.
**A reinstall with the same** account on the same device usually isn't included in the number.
74.example:
Attribution tracker data for March: 11,200 installs, meaning first launches
Store console data for the same month: 14,100 downloads
Reinstalls on the same device: 640 (not counted by the store)

Total App Installs = **11,200**

The difference of 2,900 is downloads by people who never opened the app. Ad reports don't include them: there, an install and a first launch are the same event.
74.importance: It sets the upper limit for the whole funnel: there can never be more users than installs, and any dip here eventually shows up in revenue. Store downloads, tracked **separately** from first launches, show whether people are lost before the first screen.
74.essence_note: without an install, a person can't become a user

75.name: Cost per Install (CPI)
75.description: How much one app install from advertising costs on average.
75.nuances:
The denominator includes **only [[Paid Installs→voronki_prodazh_h4/platnye_ustanovki]]**: dividing spend by all installs, organic included, artificially lowers the cost, and the more organic installs there are, the stronger the effect.
Spend and installs **cover the same** window, and an install is assigned to the date of the ad click rather than the date of the install itself. Otherwise spend at the end of the month is divided by installs that arrive at the start of the next one.
Spend **includes platform fees** and contractor payments: without them, the cost comes out lower than the actual one, and the decision to scale is based on an understated cost.
Widening the attribution window increases paid installs and lowers the cost, even though **the same amount** was spent.
75.example:
Ad spend for March: $23,400 including fees
[[Paid Installs→voronki_prodazh_h4/platnye_ustanovki]]: 6,500
[[Organic Installs→voronki_prodazh_h4/ogranicheskie_ustanovki]]: 4,700 (not in the denominator)

Cost per Install (CPI) = 23,400 / 6,500 = **$3.60**

Dividing by all 11,200 installs gives $2.09: that's the acquisition cost including free traffic rather than the price of a paid install.
75.importance: This is the first point where you can see **whether the unit economics work**: the cost per install is compared with the money a user will bring in over their lifetime in the app, and you decide whether to scale the channel or shut it down. A mistake here means budget spent on traffic that will never pay off.
75.not_needed: **Skip it** when the app isn't promoted through paid channels.
75.essence_note: every dollar paid for an install comes out of what the user will bring in

76.name: Average App Rating
76.formula: Sum of Ratings / Number of Ratings
76.description: The average of all user ratings of the app in the app store.
76.nuances:
Stores show a cumulative rating over the app's entire lifetime, and it's slow to move: with 50,000 old ratings, a hundred new five-star ratings barely shift the number. To see the reaction to a release, calculate the average of the period's ratings **separately**.
**A rating is tied to** an app version and stays in the overall number after an update, so the average mixes ratings of a product that no longer exists with ratings of the current one.
Ratings without text **are included** just like ratings that come with a review: there are more of them, and they determine the result.
76.example:
All-time ratings: 52,400; sum of scores: 231,100
All-time average = 231,100 / 52,400 = **4.41**

Ratings in March: 3,200; sum of scores: 12,160
March average = 12,160 / 3,200 = **3.80**

The cumulative rating holds at 4.4, even though users rated the March release noticeably lower.
76.importance: **The rating sits right next** to the install button and directly affects conversion from the store listing: the lower it is, the more each install costs, because some people leave without downloading. Stores also factor it into rankings, so a drop hits twice: conversion and impressions in store search.
76.not_needed: **Skip it for** apps outside the stores and for internal corporate builds, where users have no choice.
76.essence_note: a low rating sits next to the install button and cuts conversion from the store listing

77.name: App Reviews
77.description: The number of reviews with text that users left in the app store during the period.
77.nuances:
Reviews with text and ratings without text **are counted separately**: leaving a rating is easier than writing text, so there are more ratings than reviews, and mixing them inflates the review count.
An edited review still counts as one review, but its date **changes to the date** of the edit, so it moves to another period.
**Reviews deleted by the store or** the developer drop out of the count, so last month's value shrinks over time.
77.example:
Ratings in the store for March: 3,200
Of those, with review text: 214
Deleted as spam: 9

App Reviews = 214 − 9 = **205**
77.importance: **The volume of reviews determines how quickly** the average rating responds to changes: with ten or so reviews a month, a single wave of negative ones drags the rating down for a long time. It's used to decide whether it's time to add a rating prompt to the app.
77.not_needed: **Skip it for apps** distributed outside the stores: corporate builds, internal distribution, preinstalled apps.
77.essence_note: the more reviews, the more stable the rating and the higher the app ranks in store search

78.name: Paid Installs
78.formula: Number of installs attributed to paid sources
78.description: The number of app installs attributed to paid ad campaigns.
78.nuances:
**Set an attribution window**: how many days after a click or an impression an install is still credited to the ad. Widening the window from one day to a week noticeably increases paid installs at the same spend.
Each install goes to one source: when campaigns overlap, **the last click counts**; otherwise paid installs added up across sources would exceed the total number of installs.
78.example:
Installs in March: 11,200
Ad clicks followed by an install within 7 days: 6,500
Of those, installs preceded by a click on an ad from another campaign: 340 (credited to the last click)

Paid Installs = **6,500**

With a 1-day attribution window, the same number would be 5,100, and the remaining 1,400 would count as organic.
78.importance: **It's the denominator of Cost per Install (CPI)**, and the entire ad payback analysis depends on it. Inflated attribution makes traffic look cheaper on paper and pushes you to raise the budget where it doesn't work.
78.not_needed: **Skip it** when the app isn't promoted through paid channels and all traffic comes from the store and the company's own channels.
78.essence_note: these are the installs you buy, and the more of them at the same price, the faster the audience grows

79.name: Organic Installs
79.description: The number of app installs that aren't attributed to any paid campaign.
79.nuances:
Organic installs **are defined as the remainder**: everything that couldn't be attributed to a paid campaign ends up here, so lost attribution inflates organic installs and at the same time understates [[Paid Installs→voronki_prodazh_h4/platnye_ustanovki]].
**Some organic installs are driven by advertising**: a person saw a banner and installed the app through store search two days later. Such installs are classified as organic, so when ads are turned off, organic installs drop along with paid ones.
The store **usually doesn't count a reinstall** on the same device as a new install, while an install by the same person on a second device does count.
79.example:
Installs in March: 11,200
Attributed to paid campaigns: 6,500

Organic Installs = 11,200 − 6,500 = **4,700**

After ads were turned off in April, organic installs fell to 3,100: part of the organic volume had been a delayed effect of paid traffic.
79.importance: It answers whether the product grows on its own or **only while you pay** for traffic. The share of organic installs determines how well the business would survive a pause in ad spending.
79.not_needed: **Skip it** when there are no installs without paid promotion: all new installs come from campaigns, and organic installs are zero.
79.essence_note: these installs aren't paid for with advertising, so they lower the average acquisition cost

80.name: Push Notification Opt-Ins
80.formula: Users with push notifications enabled as of the snapshot date
80.description: The number of users who have the store's push notifications turned on as of the snapshot date. The size of the base the store can reach directly with a message.
80.nuances:
**The count is taken as of** the date rather than from permissions granted during the period: this is an accumulated base, so compare it between snapshot dates rather than adding it up across months.
**Two different things are subtracted** from the base, and they're detected in different ways. The app detects a revoked permission directly: the status is requested from the system at launch and updated in analytics. Deleting the app isn't tracked directly: it's detected indirectly, when the messaging service stops delivering messages to the token, so such users drop out of the base with a delay and only after the next send.
**Tokens** that haven't received a successful delivery in more than a few weeks are removed from the base: the permission is still on record, but notifications no longer reach the user.
A user subscribed on both a phone and a browser has **two subscriptions** but counts as one user: the unit of count is the user; otherwise users with multiple subscriptions inflate the count.
80.example:
Permissions on May 1: 19,400
New ones granted in May: 2,900
Users who revoked permission (detected from the status at launch): 900
Tokens with delivery failures: 400

Push Notification Opt-Ins on May 31 = 19,400 + 2,900 − 900 − 400 = **21,000 users**

Across months, you can add up new opt-ins like the 2,900 but not balances like the 19,400: this metric is a balance rather than a flow.
80.importance: **The size of the base determines** how to bring a customer back: through your own free channel or by buying traffic. A stagnant base with a growing audience means the permission request is shown at the wrong time or not at all, and every month the store permanently loses part of its future reach. Because undeliverable tokens are removed with a delay, the actual reach is always slightly lower than the base figure.
80.not_needed: **Skip it** when push notifications aren't set up and communication goes through email or messaging apps.
80.essence_note: every user who allows push notifications can be brought back to the app for free

81.name: Push Notification Opt-In Rate
81.formula: (Users with Push Notifications Enabled / Users Who Can Technically Receive Push Notifications) × 100
81.description: The share of users who have the store's push notifications turned on. Shows what part of the audience the store can reach with a message without spending on advertising.
81.nuances:
Denominator: **only users on** devices and browsers that support push notifications. If you include all users, those who were never shown the permission request pull the rate down.
In the app, push support **can be checked directly**; on the web, it's inferred from the browser and device: some browsers don't support push notifications, so the denominator is less precise here.
**It's calculated as of** the snapshot date: the numerator counts users with notifications enabled on that date rather than permissions granted during the period. The numerator comes from [[Push Notification Opt-Ins→voronki_prodazh_h4/pushi_razresheny]] and inherits its limitation: users who deleted the app drop out of the base with a delay, only once delivery starts failing.
81.example:
Users in the month: 120,000
Of those, on devices that support push notifications: 84,000
Users with push notifications enabled as of the snapshot date: 21,000

Push Notification Opt-In Rate = 21,000 / 84,000 × 100 = **25%**

Dividing by all 120,000 gives 17.5%: users who were never shown the request pull the rate down.
81.importance: **It sets the maximum reach of the free channel** for bringing customers back: with a small opted-in base, a push campaign won't be enough for either abandoned-cart recovery or a sale, and the budget has to go to paid traffic. A drop after a release most likely means the permission request itself broke or became too intrusive.
81.not_needed: **Skip it** when bringing customers back relies on email and messaging apps, and push notifications aren't set up.
81.synonyms: Push Opt-In Rate, Push Permission Rate
81.essence_note: a push notification can bring a person back to the app for free

82.name: App DAU
82.formula: Number of unique active users per day
82.description: The number of unique users who were active in the app during a calendar day. For periods longer than a day, the average daily value is shown.
82.nuances:
Activity **is defined explicitly**: opening the app, or opening it plus a key action. The second option gives a smaller number: it filters out accidental launches and background opens from push notifications. How much smaller depends on how often the app is opened without a purpose.
**The same** definition of activity is used for the daily, weekly and monthly figures; otherwise they don't line up.
A user **counts once** regardless of the number of sessions during the day.
**Day boundaries are set in** one time zone for all days: shifting the boundary moves evening activity into the next day and breaks the comparison between days.
Reports for a month or a quarter show the average daily value for the period rather than a single day's number. Only daily values are averaged with each other: you can't add up days to get a weekly or monthly figure, because the same person **is counted once for each day** they were active.
82.example:
Unique users who opened the app on March 14: 21,400
Of those, completed a key action: 18,950
Total sessions for the day: 47,300

DAU for March 14 based on the key action = **18,950**

Sessions don't go into DAU: a user with three visits still counts as one.
DAU for March as a whole = sum of daily values 612,000 / 31 days = 19,742 per day on average.
82.importance: **It reacts faster than any other** metric: a broken release, a server outage or a traffic source being turned off shows up the same day, while revenue dips only later.
82.not_needed: **Skip it in** apps with an infrequent usage pattern, where opening the app once a month is normal: insurance, tax filing, seasonal services. There, the daily number is noisy and tells you nothing.
82.essence_note: the more people open the app every day, the stronger the habit

83.name: App MAU
83.formula: Number of unique active users per month
83.description: The number of unique users who were active in the app at least once during the month. For periods longer than a month, the average monthly value is shown.
83.nuances:
Activity **is defined the same way** as in the daily and weekly figures.
**A user** who was active 20 days in a row counts as one, so the sum of daily values for the month is higher than the monthly number, and you can't get MAU by adding up daily values.
**Window length changes** the result mechanically: over 30 days the number is larger than over 28, so February is compared with February, or you switch to a rolling window of fixed length.
The yearly figure is the average of the monthly values rather than the number of unique users for the year. The latter **is calculated separately and** is always higher, because it includes everyone who was active in any month of the year, while each month includes only some of them.
83.example:
Unique active users in March: 96,300
Sum of daily values for March: 612,000

App MAU = **96,300**

612,000 is the number of user-days rather than MAU: one person is counted once for each day they were active.
83.importance: **It defines the size of the active audience** you can reach: monetization potential, the cost of messaging campaigns and infrastructure load are all estimated from it. Growing installs alongside flat MAU mean new users are replacing those who left rather than adding to the audience.
83.not_needed: **Skip it in** apps with an infrequent usage pattern: insurance, tax filing, services for a one-off task. Opening the app once every few months is normal there.
83.essence_note: this is the size of the app's active audience

84.name: App Stickiness
84.description: The ratio of the daily audience to the monthly one. Shows how many days a month a typical user opens the app.
84.nuances:
Both numbers **are based on the same** definition of activity; otherwise the ratio is meaningless.
The numerator **is the average daily** value for the same month as the denominator: the value for a single arbitrary day jumps around because of weekends and messaging campaigns.
**Month length changes** the result mechanically: February has a floor of 1/28 and March 1/31, so months of different lengths are compared with a caveat, or you switch to a rolling 28-day window.
The maximum is 100%, reached **only if every** user was active on every day of the month.
84.example:
Sum of daily values for March: 612,000
Average daily value = 612,000 / 31 = 19,742
Unique active users in March: 96,300

App Stickiness = 19,742 / 96,300 × 100 = **20.5%**

So a typical user opens the app on about 6 days out of 31. You can't take a single day's DAU instead of the average: weekends and messaging campaigns cause noticeable jumps.
84.importance: **It distinguishes an app** people use out of habit from one they open once a month when they need to. Audience growth with falling stickiness means the inflow of new users is masking the loss of habit among existing ones, and this will later show up in revenue.
84.not_needed: **Skip it where** the use case doesn't call for daily use: submitting utility meter readings, buying insurance, tax services. A low value is normal there rather than a problem.
84.essence_note: the more often a person opens the app, the less likely they are to delete it

85.name: Engaged Sessions
85.description: The number of sessions in which the user showed interest in the website: spent meaningful time on it or viewed more than one page.
85.nuances:
**The engagement threshold differs** between systems. Some systems count a session as non-bounce if it had more than one pageview, lasted longer than 15 seconds, or triggered an event flagged as non-bounce. GA4 counts a session as engaged if it lasts 10 seconds or longer, has at least two pageviews, or includes a key event.
In GA4, the threshold is set manually anywhere from 10 to 60 seconds, and changing it affects the count **only for new** data, without recalculating past periods.
85.example:
Sessions in the month: 40,000
Of those, single-page sessions under 15 seconds: 17,200

Engaged Sessions = 40,000 − 17,200 = **22,800**

An 8-second session with two pageviews counts here too: one of the two criteria is enough.
85.importance: It filters accidental visits out of traffic and shows the real size of the audience the website has reached. If total sessions grow while engaged sessions stay flat, the growth is hollow: people arrive and leave without seeing a single screen **in full**.
85.essence_note: these are sessions in which the person actually looked at the website rather than closing it right away

86.name: Key Events per Session
86.description: The average number of key events per session.
86.nuances:
The numerator **is counted the same way** as [[Key Events→voronki_prodazh_h4/dostignutye_celi]]: all key events, not the number of sessions with at least one key event. One session with three key events adds three to the numerator, so with many micro-conversions the value can go above 1.
**The denominator includes** all sessions, including those without key events: the metric shows the yield of all traffic rather than only of sessions that converted.
The set of key events **is fixed**: adding micro-conversions raises the value sharply, and comparison with past periods becomes meaningless.
86.example:
Key events in March: 685
Sessions: 16,000

Key Events per Session = 685 / 16,000 = **0.043**
86.importance: **It shows the yield per unit** of traffic and doesn't depend on traffic volume, so a drop here while traffic grows points straight to the quality of the traffic you buy rather than to seasonality. It works for quick checks of site changes: it responds early, when absolute numbers don't show anything yet.
86.not_needed: **Skip it** when the site has only one key event: the value duplicates the conversion rate and carries no information of its own.
86.synonyms: Conversions per Session, Goal Completions per Session
86.essence_note: the more actions per session, the more useful the site is for the person and for the company

87.name: Weekly Active Users (WAU)
87.formula: Number of unique active users per week
87.description: The number of unique users who were active in the app at least once during the week. For periods longer than a week, the average weekly value is shown.
87.nuances:
Activity **is defined the same way** as in the daily and monthly figures.
**Week boundaries stay** the same from period to period: a week starting Monday and a week starting Sunday give different numbers, because they split weekends differently, and activity in consumer apps is usually higher on weekends.
**A user** who was active on all seven days counts as one.
Reports for a quarter or a year show the average weekly value. Only weekly values are averaged with each other: daily values **don't add up** to a weekly one, and weekly values don't turn into a monthly one, because the unique users in different windows overlap.
87.example:
Unique active users from March 9 to 15: 48,700
Sum of daily values for these seven days: 132,500

WAU = **48,700**
87.importance: **It smooths out the difference between** weekdays and weekends that makes the daily number jump, while still reacting faster than the monthly figure. Churn shows up in it earlier than in MAU.
87.not_needed: Skip it where usage is daily: for messaging apps and feeds, the weekly number almost **matches the monthly one** and adds nothing.
87.essence_note: this is the week's active audience, and churn shows up in it earlier than in the monthly one

88.name: Peak Concurrent Users (PCU)
88.description: The highest number of users in the app at the same time during the selected period.
88.nuances:
**The result depends on** how often you measure: with a reading every five minutes, a short spike is missed; with a reading every second, the peak comes out higher. Keep the frequency the same; otherwise values from different periods can't be compared.
**Decide** what counts as being present at a given moment: an active connection, an open screen, or a session with activity in the last few minutes. The last option counts users as present for longer and inflates the peak.
**The window length changes** the result by itself: the wider the window, the higher the peak, because it takes in more readings. A monthly maximum is always at least as high as a daily one, and you can't compare the two: fix the window and state it next to the value.
88.example:
Concurrent user readings on March 14, once a minute
The maximum came at 8:47 p.m.: 4,830 users
Second-highest reading, at 8:46 p.m.: 4,790

PCU for March 14 = **4,830**

With readings every 10 minutes, the 8:47 p.m. peak wouldn't have been captured, and PCU would have come out lower.
88.importance: **This number is the basis** for planning server capacity and licenses: infrastructure is built for the peak rather than the average, because outages happen exactly at maximum load, when the losses are most visible.
88.not_needed: **Skip it in** apps without a persistent connection, where sessions are short and each user acts alone: sending documents, paying bills, one-off requests. The idea of simultaneous presence doesn't apply there.
88.essence_note: the more users the product handles at once, the larger the audience it serves at its busiest hour

89.name: Average Concurrent Users (ACU)
89.formula: Sum(Concurrent Users at Measurement Points) / Number of Measurement Points
89.description: The average number of users in the app at the same time during the selected period.
89.nuances:
The sum **includes all measurement points**, even nighttime ones with zero activity: if you count only active hours, the average comes out higher and no longer matches the load over the whole day.
**Readings are taken** at equal intervals; otherwise hours with more frequent readings get more weight and the average shifts.
Presence at a given moment **is defined the same way** as for the peak value; otherwise the average and the peak can't be compared.
89.example:
Readings once a minute on March 14: 1,440 points
Sum of values across all points: 2,246,400
Of those, night readings with near-zero values: 480 points

ACU = 2,246,400 / 1,440 = **1,560**

Excluding the night and dividing by 960 points gives 2,340: that's the average daytime load rather than the average for the whole day.
89.importance: **Together with the peak** value, it shows how uneven the load is. The more the peak exceeds the average, the larger the part of the day when paid capacity sits idle: a direct argument for autoscaling instead of permanent servers sized for the peak. If the peak and the average are close, the load is even, and there's no reason to complicate the infrastructure.
89.not_needed: **Skip it in** apps without a persistent connection and without a notion of simultaneous presence.
89.essence_note: the higher the average number of concurrent users, the less paid capacity sits idle

90.name: Share of Paying App Users
90.description: The share of users who paid at least once among all app users.
90.nuances:
The numerator and the denominator **are taken from the same** user base: if paying users are counted over the entire lifetime and all users over a month, the share can exceed 100%.
**A user with** several purchases counts as one in the numerator.
**Decide** what to do with refunds and canceled subscriptions: if a user got a refund and is still counted as paying, the share is inflated; if they're removed, the numbers for past periods change retroactively.
90.example:
Users in March: 42,000
Paid at least once in March: 1,386
Two of them made two purchases each (counted as two users)

Share of Paying App Users = 1,386 / 42,000 × 100 = **3.3%**
90.importance: **It determines** what revenue rests on: revenue growth with an unchanged share of paying users means the same people are paying, more and more often, and that runs into a ceiling. Without it, it's easy to mistake audience growth for monetization growth.
90.not_needed: **Skip it in** apps without direct payments from users: ad-supported apps, internal corporate apps, free banking and government service apps.
90.essence_note: the more paying users among all users, the more money the same audience brings in

92.name: App Time to Value
92.formula: Sum of First-Launch-to-Activation Times for All Activated Users / Number of Activated Users
92.description: How much time passes on average from the first app launch to activation, among users who activated.
92.nuances:
The calculation **includes only activated** users: those who never got there have no time to measure, and you can't assign them a placeholder value.
**Because of this, the metric improves** when the product gets worse: if slower users drop off and never activate, the average falls even though there are fewer activated users.
**The distribution is heavily skewed**: some users activate much later than the rest. A few such users pull the mean up, so the median is more reliable.
**The activation event is the same** as in the count of activated users.
92.example:
Activated in March: 5 users
Time to activation: 2 min, 3 min, 4 min, 6 min, 400 min

Mean = (2 + 3 + 4 + 6 + 400) / 5 = **83 min**
Median = **4 min**

The mean is driven by one user out of five; the median shows the typical case.
92.importance: **It shows** where exactly users get stuck in onboarding: if activation takes days rather than minutes, the person leaves the app and comes back later, and the app usually loses such users. Shortening this time directly raises the Activation Rate.
92.not_needed: **Skip it** if activation is technically instant and happens on the first screen.
92.synonyms: Time to First Value, Time to Activation
92.essence_note: the longer a person goes without getting value, the higher the chance they won't come back

93.name: App Opens
93.description: How many times the app was opened during the period. One user can generate several opens a day.
93.nuances:
**Decide** what counts as an open: any time the app comes to the foreground, or only a launch after it was closed. Under the first option, returning from the background a minute later creates a new open: in apps that people often minimize and bring back, the number grows with no change in behavior.
**Opens from push notifications** and from links are usually counted, so a spike after a messaging campaign doesn't mean interest has grown.
**The unit here is the open** rather than the user: the same audience coming in more often raises the number without the audience growing.
93.example:
Opens in March: 340,000
Unique users in March: 96,300
Opens triggered by push notifications: 62,000

App Opens = **340,000**

That's 3.5 opens per user on average, and almost one in five of them was triggered by a messaging campaign rather than the user's own intent.
93.importance: **It shows how often people turn to** the app: the more often a person opens it, the stronger the habit and the harder it is for them to switch to a competitor. A sharp rise in opens without a rise in time spent in the app usually means people come in and don't find what they need.
93.essence_note: the more often people open the app, the stronger the habit of using it

94.name: Key Events per User
94.description: The average number of key events per user.
94.nuances:
The numerator **is counted the same way** as [[Key Events→voronki_prodazh_h4/dostignutye_celi]]. The denominator counts unique users, not sessions: one person can visit five times in a month but counts once in the denominator.
Users are identified by device and browser. One person on a phone and a computer **counts as two**, and the longer the path to purchase, the more the metric is understated.
94.example:
Key events in March: 685
Users: 12,000
Sessions: 16,000

Key Events per User = 685 / 12,000 = **0.057**

Dividing by sessions would give 0.043: that's a different metric, [[Key Events per Session→voronki_prodazh_h4/celey_na_vizit]].
94.importance: The gap between this and the per-session figure shows how many visits a person needs before acting. If the two numbers almost **match**, users decide in one session, and there's no point investing in bringing them back. If key events per user are noticeably higher, repeat touches work, and retargeting pays off.
94.not_needed: **Skip it where** users can't be told apart: without analytics that identifies users, the denominator will equal sessions.
94.synonyms: Conversions per User, Goal Completions per User
94.essence_note: the more actions one person takes, the more you get out of the same acquisition effort

95.name: Key Events
95.description: The number of key events recorded in the period. Actions are counted rather than people: one user can complete a key event several times, and each completion counts.
95.nuances:
**The analytics settings determine** whether a repeat of the same key event within one session is counted.
**A double click on** the inquiry button gives two key events when every event is counted and one when each key event counts once per session.
**The set of key events must be fixed**: adding micro-conversions such as scrolls or phone clicks raises the number sharply, and month-over-month trends become unreadable.
95.example:
Form submissions in March: 380
Phone number clicks: 210
Price list downloads: 95
Scrolls to 75% of the page: 4,100 (not in the key event set)

Key Events = 380 + 210 + 95 = **685**
95.importance: An overall measure of demand that shows whether the site's output is growing. Without it, ad evaluation rests **only on revenue**, which arrives with a delay, and in the meantime you can burn the budget on a campaign that has stopped bringing in inquiries.
95.not_needed: **Skip it** if the site has no forms or other trackable actions: a storefront with a phone number in the header and no call tracking won't record anything.
95.essence_note: these are the actions the site was built for

96.name: Sessions with Product Page Views
96.formula: Sessions with a product page view
96.description: The number of sessions in which a product page was opened. Counts sessions rather than product pages: a session with ten product page views counts once.
96.nuances:
Unit of count: a session. The number of product pages opened is higher and **isn't counted** as a separate metric on the map: it goes into the denominator of Time on Product Page and Interactions per Product Page View; counted as unique pages per session, it also goes into the numerator of [[Products Viewed per Session→voronki_prodazh_h4/prosmotrennyh_tovarov_za_sessiyu]].
Viewing the same product page again within a session doesn't increase the count. Opening a product page from any source **counts the same**: from a product list, search, the wishlist, a messaging campaign or a direct link.
A quick view in a pop-up over the product list **counts as a product page view** if it shows the same photos and specifications.
96.example:
Sessions in the month: 50,000
Sessions with a product list view: 34,000
Of those, with a product page view: 12,300
Sessions with a product page opened from a direct link, a messaging campaign or the wishlist, without a product list: 3,300

Sessions with Product Page Views = 12,300 + 3,300 = **15,600 sessions**

Product page views in these sessions: 40,600 (not in the count: sessions are counted, not product pages).
96.importance: **The core count for the middle of the funnel**: it serves as the denominator for conversion rates from the product page and separates sessions where people were choosing a product from sessions where they just browsed. Without it, a drop in sales can't be broken down into “less interest in products” and “interest is there, but people don't buy.”
96.not_needed: **Skip it where** there's no separate product page: quick view and adding to the cart, as counted in [[Sessions with Cart Additions→voronki_prodazh_h4/dobavlenie_v_korzinu]], happen right in the product list.
96.synonyms: Product Detail Views, Product Page Sessions
96.essence_note: until the product page is opened, the product won't be chosen

97.name: Sessions with Product List Views
97.formula: Sessions with a product list view
97.description: The number of sessions in which at least one product list was opened. Counts sessions rather than product list page views.
97.nuances:
Unit of count: a session. A session that goes through ten categories **counts once**.
Product lists **include category pages**, search results and the product collection on the homepage.
The “Similar products” and “Frequently bought together” blocks on a product page **aren't included**: they're part of the product page, and including them inflates the number of sessions with a product list.
The same set of lists is used for product list clicks and impressions. If the homepage collection **counts as a product list** here but not in product clicks, the conversion rate between these steps becomes inconsistent.
97.example:
Sessions in the month: 50,000
Sessions with a category page opened: 29,000
Sessions with search results only, no categories: 3,800
Sessions with the homepage collection only: 1,200
Total sessions with at least one list (no double counting): 34,000
Sessions where only the “Similar products” block on a product page was seen: 1,500 (not counted)

Sessions with Product List Views = **34,000 sessions**
97.importance: **It's the starting count for the whole** product-browsing part of the funnel and shows how much traffic actually reaches the assortment. If it drops while traffic is stable, the way in is broken: the menu, the homepage or ad landing pages. Every later step will drop with it.
97.not_needed: **Skip it** when ads lead straight to product pages: users don't go through the product list as a separate step.
97.essence_note: choosing a product starts with the catalog

98.name: Paying App Users
98.formula: Number of unique users with at least one successful payment
98.description: The number of unique users who made at least one payment in the app during the period: a purchase, a subscription or a top-up.
98.nuances:
**A user with five** purchases counts as one: the metric counts people rather than transactions.
Only completed payments count: failed attempts and subscriptions canceled before the charge **aren't counted**.
**A subscription auto-renewal counts** as a payment, so a subscriber remains a paying user every month without doing anything. If auto-renewals aren't counted, the number drops to users with new purchases only.
**A trial period without** a charge isn't included: a user becomes a paying user on the day of the first charge.
98.example:
Successful payments in March: 2,140
Of those, subscription auto-renewals: 1,020
Unique users behind these payments: 1,386
Started a trial period without a charge: 470 (not counted)

Paying App Users = **1,386**
98.importance: **It separates revenue growth driven by** new payers from growth driven by larger purchases from existing ones: these are different situations that call for different actions. The number of paying users determines how stable revenue is, because a broad base survives losing a large customer and a narrow one doesn't.
98.not_needed: **Skip it for** ad-monetized apps and apps where payment happens outside the app.
98.essence_note: they are the ones who bring in the money

99.name: Activated App Users
99.formula: Number of unique users who completed the activation event
99.description: The number of unique users who reached activation: the first action after which a person gets the promised value from the app.
99.nuances:
One activation event is chosen and **fixed**: the first order, the first saved schedule, the first money transfer. It must be an action after which a person gets the promised value, rather than just accessing the product: signing up and opening the app don't count as activation; otherwise the share of activated users among registered ones would always be close to 100%. Both the number and all the rates calculated from it depend on the choice of event.
A user counts **once**, at their first activation: repeat logins don't add users to the count.
**Users are counted** rather than devices: one person who installed the app on a phone and a tablet counts as one if they signed in with the same account.
99.example:
Signed up in March: 8,400
Of those, placed a first order (the activation event): 3,108
Logged in again in March after activating in February: 1,240 (not counted)

Activated App Users = **3,108**
99.importance: **It answers the question** of how many people actually needed the app, rather than how many downloaded it. The gap between installs and activated users shows how much of the acquisition effort was wasted: the person never reached value and most likely won't come back. The same number is the base for retention and repeat-action rates: calculating them from installs makes no sense, because a person who got no value has no reason to come back.
99.not_needed: **Skip it where** value is available from the first screen and there is no activation step.
99.essence_note: these are the people who got value from the app, and only they come back

100.name: Time Between Sessions
100.formula: Sum of Intervals Between Consecutive Sessions / Number of Intervals
100.description: The average time between two consecutive sessions of the same user. Shows how often people come back to the website.
100.nuances:
The denominator **is the number of intervals** rather than users: a person with three sessions has two intervals, and a person with one session has none and drops out of the calculation entirely.
**The length of the observation window** caps the result: over a month, the interval can't possibly exceed 30 days, so an audience that rarely comes back looks more loyal than it is.
**A user** who clears cookies gets cut off from their past sessions, and their interval doesn't make it into the calculation.
100.example:
Users with two or more sessions in the quarter: 6,400
Intervals between their sessions: 15,200
Sum of intervals: 288,800 days

Time Between Sessions = 288,800 / 15,200 = **19 days**

Dividing by the 6,400 users gives 45 days: that's the sum of intervals per user rather than the interval between sessions.
100.importance: **It sets the frequency** at which it makes sense to remind people about the website with messaging campaigns and retargeting. If emails go out once a week and people come back once every three weeks, most touches are wasted and drive up unsubscribes.
100.not_needed: **It adds little** for websites built for a one-time task: applying to a college, buying major appliances, getting insurance. A return visit isn't expected there by the nature of the product.
100.synonyms: Time Between Visits, Days Between Visits
100.essence_note: the less often a person comes back, the weaker their connection to the website

101.name: Share of Single-Session Website Users
101.description: The share of users who visited the website exactly once during the period and didn't come back.
101.nuances:
**It's calculated within a single** period from the number of sessions per user: users with one session go into the numerator, those with two or more don't. No second observation window is needed.
**The period length sets the result**: over a week, the share of users who don't return is always higher than over a month, because a short window simply leaves no room for a return. The period is fixed and not changed between comparisons.
Users are identified by browser, so someone who comes back from another device or after clearing cookies is counted as having visited **once**. The real share is always lower than the calculated one.
You can calculate it for the whole audience or **separately** for new users: for everyone, the result is diluted by the loyal audience you already have; for new users, you can see whether the website retains them.
101.example:
Unique users in the month: 24,000
Of those, with one session: 16,800
With two or more: 7,200

Share of Single-Session Website Users = 16,800 / 24,000 × 100 = **70%**

Among the month's new users (9,000), 7,650 had one session, a share of 85%: newcomers come back noticeably less often than established users.
101.importance: **It answers** whether it makes sense to invest in retention or whether it's cheaper to keep buying traffic. A high share with expensive acquisition means every dollar spent on ads brings a one-time visit, and the model can't count on return visits to pay off.
101.not_needed: **Skip it on websites** that aren't built for return visits: one-time inquiries, reference pages, promos for a single event.
101.synonyms: Non-Returning User Rate, One-Time Visitor Rate
101.essence_note: these are people who came once and didn't come back, so they have to be acquired all over again

102.name: Engaged Sessions per User
102.description: The average number of engaged sessions per user during the period.
102.nuances:
