The denominator includes all users in the period, including those who had no engaged sessions. If you keep **only users with** an engaged session, the value goes up and no longer reflects the whole audience.
**The engagement threshold in** the numerator changes the result directly: the looser the non-bounce criterion, the higher the value for the same behavior.
Both values **are taken over the same** window and aren't added up by day: a user who visited on three different days in a week counts three times in the daily views instead of once.
102.example:
Engaged sessions in the month: 22,800
Unique users: 24,000

Engaged Sessions per User = 22,800 / 24,000 = **0.95**

Counting all sessions, there are 1.7 per user. The gap comes entirely from visits that ended within seconds: 17,200 of 40,000 sessions.
102.importance: It separates audience quality from audience size. A value around one means the average user genuinely engaged with the website **once** in the month, and this drives the decision on where to invest: in new touchpoints with the same audience or in expanding reach.
102.not_needed: **Skip it on** websites built for a one-time task: return visits aren't expected there, and the average stays around one regardless of the website's quality.
102.essence_note: the more often a person genuinely engages with the website, the stronger their connection to it

103.name: Average Engagement Time per Session
103.description: The average length of active engagement with the site per session.
103.nuances:
**A tab counts as active** when it's open and visible on screen. A minimized window or a background tab doesn't count, so the value is always lower than the elapsed duration of the session.
The inactivity timeout after which a session ends **is set in the analytics settings** and is usually 30 minutes.
**Changing the timeout shifts** both the number of sessions and the time, so periods with different settings can't be compared.
**The denominator includes** all sessions, including those where the person left right away: their zero time pulls the average down.
103.example:
Sessions in March: 16,000
Total engagement time: 12,800 minutes

Average Engagement Time per Session = 12,800 / 16,000 = **0.8 minutes (48 seconds)**
103.importance: **It separates real traffic** from fake traffic: bots and incentivized clicks show engagement time close to zero with a normal number of sessions. A sharp drop after a new campaign launches is a signal to check the source before the monthly budget is spent.
103.not_needed: **Skip it** if the analytics tag doesn't record engagement events: then the number reflects the intervals between pageviews rather than real engagement.
103.synonyms: Average Engagement Time, Engaged Time per Session
103.essence_note: short engagement means the offer isn't being read, and very long engagement means the person can't find what they need

104.name: Total Key Event Value
104.formula: Sum of the values of all key events
104.description: The total monetary value of all key events in the period. Each key event is assigned a value in advance, and the metric adds up the values of every key event recorded.
104.nuances:
A key event's value **is set manually and** is typically calculated as the average profit per deal multiplied by the conversion rate from that key event to a sale.
**If you put in** the full deal value, the metric turns into a fantasy where every inquiry equals a purchase.
**Values are revised when** conversion rates or prices change: with outdated numbers, the total no longer matches real money but still looks credible.
Key events with zero value add nothing to the total, although they **do count** toward Key Events, so the numbers for these two metrics will differ.
When nested key events are summed, value is double-counted: if both the inquiry and the “Thank you for your inquiry” page view have a value, one action **is counted twice**.
104.example:
Form submissions in March: 380, value $60
Phone number clicks: 210, value $30
Price list downloads: 95, value $0

Total Key Event Value = 380 × 60 + 210 × 30 + 95 × 0 = **$29,100**
104.importance: **It shows the return on advertising** before deals close, which with a long sales cycle is the only way to manage bids in real time. The cost of a mistake is that ad platforms learn from these values: by overstating the value of a cheap key event, the company gets a campaign optimized for useless actions.
104.not_needed: **Skip it with** a short sales cycle, where the sale is visible right away and its actual amount can be used.
104.essence_note: this estimates the monetary value of on-site actions

105.name: Sessions with Product List Clicks
105.formula: Sessions with a product click in a product list
105.description: How many sessions got as far as choosing a specific product: sessions in which at least one product in a list was clicked. Like the other funnel steps, it's counted in sessions rather than in the clicks themselves.
105.nuances:
**Unit of count**: a session. The clicks themselves make up the numerator of [[Product List CTR→voronki_prodazh_h4/ctr_tovarov_v_kataloge]], and there are more of them: a user may click on several products in one session.
**A repeat click on** the same product doesn't count the session again.
A click on a product in the “Similar products” block on a product page **doesn't count**: that isn't a product list. The definition of a product list is the same as in Sessions with Product List Views.
105.example:
Sessions in the month: 50,000
Sessions with a product list view: 34,000
Sessions where at least one product was clicked: 12,000

Sessions with Product List Clicks = **12,000**

Total product clicks in these sessions: 96,000. This is a different quantity: the numerator of Product List CTR.
105.importance: **It separates those** who browsed the product list from those who chose a specific product, and serves as the denominator for the step from a click to the product page. If there are many sessions with a product list and few with a click, the problem is in the listings themselves: the assortment, the order or the prices rather than the traffic.
105.not_needed: **Skip it** if the product page opens right in the list as a pop-up and there's no separate click-through.
105.synonyms: Product List Clicks, Items Clicked in List
105.essence_note: a product click marks the transition from browsing to choosing a product

106.name: Product List Impressions
106.formula: Number of product impressions in lists
106.description: The total number of product impressions in lists. Counts how many times products were seen in the catalog, search and collections rather than how many product pages were opened.
106.nuances:
**An impression counts** when the product tile appears on screen. If you count all products on the page, including those users didn't scroll to, the number grows sharply and no longer lines up with clicks.
**One product** shown in three different lists gives three impressions.
A repeat impression of the same product when returning to the catalog **counts again**: identical impressions aren't merged.
**The quantity is event-based**: it counts neither sessions nor unique products.
106.example:
Sessions with a product list view: 34,000
Times a product appeared on screen: 2,400,000
Times a product was rendered on a page but not scrolled to: 1,700,000 (not counted)

Product List Impressions = **2,400,000**
106.importance: **The denominator for Product List CTR** and a measure of how much attention each item gets. The distribution of impressions across products shows whether the catalog keeps showing the same things: if most impressions go to a small number of items, the rest of the assortment doesn't sell because nobody saw it rather than because it's bad.
106.not_needed: Skip it for a catalog that fits on a couple of screens: there, an impression **is the same as opening** the page, and the metric just mirrors traffic.
106.synonyms: Product Impressions, Items Viewed in List
106.essence_note: the more products a shopper sees, the higher the chance they find the one they want

107.name: Product List CTR
107.formula: (Product Clicks in Lists / Product Impressions in Lists) × 100
107.description: The share of product impressions in lists that ended with a click. Shows how well the product tile in the catalog draws attention: photo, price, name.
107.nuances:
Both quantities are events rather than sessions. A session with three clicks puts three clicks in the numerator. An impression **counts only for a product** that actually appeared on screen.
If you count **all products on the page**, including those at the bottom that users didn't scroll to, the rate comes out far lower.
**One product** shown in three different lists gives three impressions.
Repeat clicks on the same product within a session **each count**: the quantity is event-based.
107.example:
Product impressions in lists in the month: 2,400,000
Product clicks in lists: 96,000

Product List CTR = 96,000 / 2,400,000 × 100 = **4%**

Putting sessions with a click (12,000) in the numerator gives 0.5%: the units of the numerator and denominator don't match.
107.importance: **It tells you** whether to change the sort order of the listings, the preview photos and the way the price is shown. A low CTR with high product list traffic means the wrong products get to the top of the listings, and rearranging products is cheaper than buying more traffic.
107.not_needed: **Skip it where** the listings can't be rearranged: if the order of products is fixed and the previews come from an external catalog, knowing the CTR doesn't change anything.
107.synonyms: Item List Click-Through Rate, Product Listing CTR
107.essence_note: the more often products in a list get clicked, the better the photos, prices and listing order work

108.name: Adds to Cart per Session
108.description: The average number of cart additions per session. Calculated over all traffic, including sessions without a single addition.
108.nuances:
**The numerator counts addition events** rather than sessions with an addition: substituting sessions turns the average into a share.
Denominator: all sessions in the period. If you take **only sessions with** a product view, the average goes up and no longer fits the funnel as a whole.
Adding three units of the same product **counts as one addition**: events are counted, not product units.
108.example:
Sessions in the month: 50,000
Add-to-cart events: 9,350
Sessions with a cart addition: 5,500

Adds to Cart per Session = 9,350 / 50,000 = **0.19**

Within sessions with a cart addition, the average is different: 9,350 / 5,500 = **1.7 products**
108.importance: An early indicator of Average Order Value (AOV): changes in basket size **show up here earlier** than in paid orders. It's used to check whether recommendations and bundles work: if the “Frequently bought together” block was moved higher on the page and the average didn't move, the block doesn't work.
108.not_needed: Skip it in categories where people buy one item at a time, such as appliances or furniture: there, the average **doesn't change with the store's actions**.
108.synonyms: Cart Additions per Session, Add-to-Carts per Session
108.essence_note: the more products are added per session, the larger the order will be

109.name: Adds to Wishlist per Session
109.description: The average number of wishlist additions per session. Calculated over all traffic, including sessions where the wishlist wasn't used.
109.nuances:
The numerator counts the **addition events themselves** rather than sessions with an addition: dividing sessions by sessions gives a share rather than an average, and the name and the unit no longer match.
Denominator: all sessions in the period, not **only sessions with** a wishlist addition. This way the metric can be compared with Adds to Cart per Session, which has the same base.
Removals from the wishlist **aren't subtracted** from the numerator: what's counted is the act of saving, not what remains on the list.
109.example:
Sessions in the month: 50,000
Wishlist addition events: 7,400
Sessions with at least one addition: 3,100

Adds to Wishlist per Session = 7,400 / 50,000 = **0.15**

Dividing 3,100 / 50,000 gives 6.2%: that's the [[Add-to-Wishlist Rate→voronki_prodazh_h4/konversiya_v_dobavlenie_v_izbrannoe]], a different metric.
109.importance: It shows how many products a person saves per session: the Add-to-Wishlist Rate counts sessions and doesn't distinguish someone who saved one item from someone who saved five. Growth in the average with an unchanged rate means the same people use the wishlist but put more into it, and messaging campaigns about saved items have more products to feature. The metric doesn't show the size of the accumulated lists: removals **aren't subtracted** from the numerator, so it's the flow of additions over the period rather than what remains.
109.not_needed: **Skip it** when only a small part of the audience uses the wishlist: an average that's only hundredths of an addition per session is noisy and doesn't show changes.
109.essence_note: the more products a person saves, the more reasons they have to come back

110.name: Unique Products Shown per Product List Session
110.formula: Sum of Unique Products Shown in Product Lists per Session / Sessions with Product List Views
110.description: The average number of different products a user sees in product lists per session. Shows how much of the assortment a session covers.
110.nuances:
The numerator counts different products rather than impressions: a product seen in three lists during a session **counts once**. The total number of impressions without this deduplication is counted by [[Product List Impressions→voronki_prodazh_h4/prosmotry_tovarov_v_kataloge]], and it's noticeably larger.
Unique products **are counted within each** session separately, and the per-session numbers are added up: the same product in another session counts again.
Denominator: sessions with a product list view rather than all sessions. Sessions without a product list view had no products shown in lists at all, and such sessions **only pull the average down**.
A product **counts as seen** when it appears on screen, as in Product List Impressions.
110.example:
Sessions with a product list view: 34,000
Sum of different products across these sessions: 1,496,000
Total product impressions, including repeats: 2,400,000

Unique Products Shown per Product List Session = 1,496,000 / 34,000 = **44 products**

Using [[Product List Impressions→voronki_prodazh_h4/prosmotry_tovarov_v_kataloge]] as the numerator would give 2,400,000 / 34,000 = 70.6: the same products would be counted several times.
110.importance: **It shows** how much of the assortment a user manages to cover before choosing or leaving. If users see many products but rarely open product pages, the listings don't match what the user is looking for and they scroll in vain: that's an argument for changing sorting and filters rather than expanding the catalog.
110.not_needed: Skip it for a catalog that fits on a couple of screens: there, the average runs up against the size of the assortment and **doesn't change**.
110.essence_note: when there are few impressions, the catalog doesn't reveal the assortment; when there are many, the person keeps scrolling and doesn't find what they need

111.name: New Customers
111.formula: Number of customers whose first purchase ever falls in the period
111.description: The number of customers whose first purchase ever fell in the period.
111.nuances:
The first purchase is determined over **the full purchase history** rather than the chosen window: a customer who bought two years ago and came back during the period isn't counted as new.
A customer is counted **once**, no matter how many orders they placed within the period.
The start date of the purchase history **is set explicitly**: if the database was cleaned up or the system changed, customers from before the migration date look new, and the number swells in the first month after the transfer.
**Identification** is by loyalty card, phone number or customer account. Purchases without a card aren't included in this number, and the same person who got a second card is counted as new again: without merging by phone number, the inflow is overstated.
A new customer whose **only purchase was fully returned** is excluded: the store didn't actually gain a customer.
111.example:
Unique cardholders with a purchase in March: 4,850
Of those, with purchases before March 1: 3,600
First purchase ever: 1,250
Fully returned it: 50

[[New Customers→crm/novye_klienty]] = 1,250 − 50 = **1,200**

New customers can't be identified from the 5,500 anonymous receipts in March: these receipts count toward neither new nor repeat customers.
111.importance: A direct measure of whether acquisition works, and the denominator of [[New Customer Acquisition Cost→crm/stoimost_privlecheniya_novogo_klienta_ca]]: **an error here distorts CAC** and every calculation of ad payback. The inflow of new customers reacts to changes in marketing **earlier than revenue**, so a decline shows up before revenue sags.
111.not_needed: Skip it where **purchases can't be tied to a customer**: in physical stores without a loyalty program or in online stores with guest checkout. Without identification, an order can't be assigned to either new or repeat customers.
111.essence_note: this is the inflow without which the base only shrinks

112.name: New Customer Acquisition Cost
112.formula: Acquisition Costs for the Period / New Customers for the Period
112.description: How much it costs on average to acquire one customer who first bought during the period.
112.nuances:
Costs include everything spent **to win the first purchase**: ad placements, creative production, marketing work, the new customer discount and the cost of bonus points awarded when a card is issued. Counting only ad buying understates CAC, especially in retail with a new customer discount.
Retention costs **aren't part of CAC**: messaging campaigns and bonus points for existing customers belong to [[Customer Retention Cost→crm/stoimost_uderzhaniya_klienta]].
**The denominator is the same** as [[New Customers→crm/novye_klienty]]: customers with their first purchase ever, rather than everyone who signed up for a card.
**The lag between spending and purchase** shifts the figure: with a decision cycle of several weeks, March ads bring in customers in April, and dividing month by month produces jumps. Costs are assigned to the month they were spent in and compared using a rolling quarterly average, or calculated by cohort if the customer's source is known.
Costs that can't be attributed to acquisition separately from general marketing (storefront rent, signage, mall foot traffic) are allocated **by a chosen rule** or left out entirely, but the same way in every period: changing the rule moves CAC more than actual marketing performance does.
112.example:
Costs for March: advertising $18,000, marketing work $6,000, new customer discounts $11,800, welcome bonus points $1,200
Total: $37,000
[[New Customers→crm/novye_klienty]]: 1,200

CAC = 37,000 / 1,200 = **$30.83**

Advertising alone would give $15: the new customer discount and marketing work are real costs too.
112.importance:
Comparing CAC with first-order revenue answers the most practical question: **does a customer's acquisition pay off right away**, or does it stay in the red for a while. Growing CAC with an unchanged budget means **the channel has burned out**, and this shows up before revenue falls.
Without an honest CAC, the decision to scale advertising is made on a number where **part of the costs is missing**.
112.not_needed: Skip it when customers come **without paid acquisition**: mall foot traffic, word of mouth, a partner channel with no payment per customer. Calculating CAC from zero costs is meaningless.
112.essence_note: every acquisition dollar is subtracted from what the customer will bring in

113.name: First-Visit Purchase Rate
113.formula: (New Users Who Bought on Their First Visit / New Users for the Period) × 100
113.description: The share of new website or app users who bought during their first visit.
113.nuances:
The denominator is **users rather than customers**: if you divide by [[New Customers→crm/novye_klienty]], the denominator by definition consists only of people who bought, and the result no longer describes users.
Decide what counts as **the same visit**: one session or one day. A purchase the same evening after a morning visit goes into the numerator with a one-day threshold and doesn't with a one-session threshold, and the longer the decision cycle, the bigger the difference.
**Whether a user is new** is determined the same way as everywhere else on the map: by device ID or by login. Clearing cookies or visiting from another device creates a new user, so the share of purchases on the first visit is overstated.
113.example:
[[New Users→voronki_prodazh_h4/novye_posetiteli]] on the website in March: 9,400
Of those, placed an order during the same visit: 1,128
Bought later, on a following visit: 72

First-Visit Purchase Rate = 1,128 / 9,400 × 100 = **12%**

Dividing 1,128 by the 1,200 new customers gives 94%: that's the share of new customers who bought right away rather than the share of users.
113.importance:
It answers whether **the storefront sells on its own** or a person needs to leave and think it over. A low percentage with high traffic means the acquisition money has been spent, and the decision is postponed to a second visit that may never happen.
It's used to decide whether **tools to bring people back** are needed: a follow-up messaging campaign, a first-order discount, a callback.
113.not_needed:
Skip it **offline**: a door counter gives visits rather than people, there's no way to link someone who walked in to a purchase, and someone who left without buying can't be identified at all.
It doesn't fit products that **require a measurement or project approval**, where the process rules out a purchase on the first visit.
113.essence_note: buying right away means you don't have to pay extra for ads to bring the person back

114.name: New Customer Rate
114.description: The share of customers who first bought in this period among everyone who bought during the period.
114.nuances:
A new customer goes into both the numerator and **the denominator**: [[Active Customers→crm/aktivnye_klienty]] for the period are [[New Customers→crm/novye_klienty]] plus [[Repeat Customers→crm/povtornye_klienty]], so the share can't exceed 100%, and together with [[Repeat Customer Rate→crm/povtornyh_klientov]] it gives exactly 100%.
Newness is determined over **the whole history** rather than the chosen window: a customer who bought three years ago and came back doesn't go into the numerator.
**Anonymous receipts** without a loyalty card **drop out of both parts of the fraction**, but they distort the result unevenly: a shopper without a card more often looks new on every visit, and over a long horizon the share of new customers is overstated.
114.example:
Bought in March (identified by card): 4,800 customers
Of those, first purchase ever: 1,200
Bought before: 3,600

New Customer Rate = 1,200 / 4,800 × 100 = **25%**

Anonymous receipts in March: 5,100: they go into neither the numerator nor the denominator.
114.importance:
It shows who the customer base is made of: people who came for the first time or those who come back. **A persistently high share** means the customer base isn't building up: people come once, and sales volume rests on a constant inflow of new customers.
A sharp drop in the share with the same number of shoppers is **an early signal** that acquisition channels have stopped bringing people in.
114.not_needed: Skip it for one-time purchases, where repeat buying isn't expected given the nature of the product: wedding services, window installation, children's products for a specific age. There, **every customer is new**, and the share is always close to 100%.
114.synonyms: New Customer Percentage, New Customer Share
114.essence_note: without an inflow of new customers, the base ages, and when almost all shoppers are new, the company retains no one and pays for every sale again

115.name: New Customer Revenue
115.formula: Revenue from all orders placed during the period by customers who first bought in that period
115.description: Revenue from all orders of customers who first bought during the period.
115.nuances:
**All of a newcomer's orders** in the period count, rather than only the first: if a customer first bought during the period and placed two more orders, all three go here. A customer is assigned to the new or repeat group once, and all their orders for the period follow them.
Returns are subtracted from the period **the order itself belongs to**, rather than from the period of the return: otherwise new customer revenue for a closed period stays overstated forever.
Only **identified purchases**: an anonymous receipt can't be assigned to either new or repeat customers, so the sum of new and repeat customer revenue is less than the store's total revenue.
**The window length changes the makeup of the groups**: the longer the period, the more customers fall into the new group, because more first purchases fall within the window.
115.example:
Customers with a first purchase in March: 1,200
Their first orders at list prices: $84,000
New customer discount: $12,000
Returns on these orders: $3,600
Second and third orders by the same customers in March: $10,800

New Customer Revenue = 84,000 − 12,000 − 3,600 + 10,800 = **$79,200**

Counting only first orders gives $68,400: that's revenue from first purchases rather than revenue from new customers.
115.importance:
It shows how much money **the inflow of new people** brought in over the period. Comparing it with acquisition costs for the same month answers whether advertising pays for itself within the period or the business runs a cash deficit until the customer starts buying more.
If new customer revenue grows while total revenue doesn't, **new customers are plugging the hole** left by departing old ones.
115.not_needed: Skip it where **purchases can't be tied to a customer**: offline without a loyalty program, in an online store with guest checkout. Without identification, an order can't be assigned to either new or repeat customers.
115.essence_note: this is money from people who weren't in the base before

116.name: Time to First Purchase
116.formula: Σ(Date of 1st Purchase − Date of First Visit) / Number of Customers Who Made a First Purchase
116.description: How much time passes on average from a customer's first online contact with the company to their first purchase.
116.nuances:
The count starts from **the first recorded contact**: the first session on the website, installing the app, signing up ([[Signups→voronki_prodazh_h4/registracii]]), subscribing to a mailing list. One starting point is chosen and doesn't change between periods.
Only **customers who bought** are in the denominator: those who came and didn't buy have no interval. The metric measures how long the path takes for those who made it, while the share who made it is counted by [[Signup-to-Purchase Conversion Rate→crm/konversiya_iz_registracii_v_pokupku]].
The calculation is based on **the first-visit cohort**: if you take everyone who bought in a month, the average includes people who first visited years ago, and the figure swells.
If the first visit is recorded only for logged-in users but a purchase is possible without logging in, some intervals come out **negative or zero**: such records are discarded; otherwise, the average is understated.
116.example:
Cohort: 1,000 people who first visited the website in January
Bought within six months: 210
Sum of intervals from first visit to first purchase: 2,730 days

Time to First Purchase = 2,730 / 210 = **13 days**

The 790 who didn't buy don't go into the denominator: with them included, the metric would start measuring conversion too.
116.importance:
It shows **how long people deliberate** before buying and sets the horizon over which it makes sense to judge ad payback at all. If the typical path is 13 days and a channel's payback is judged by the first week, part of the result stays outside the report, and **channels that work get switched off too early**.
It's also used to decide **on what day** to send a browse abandonment reminder email.
116.not_needed: Skip it **offline**: a loyalty card is issued at the register at the moment of purchase, so the first contact and the purchase coincide in time, and everyone's interval comes out zero. A door counter doesn't help here: it can't tell that the same person came in. It's also not needed where the nature of demand means a purchase happens **at the moment of first contact**: impulse goods, checkout-counter items.
116.synonyms: Days to First Purchase, Time to Convert
116.essence_note: until a person buys, the money to acquire them has already been spent

117.name: New Customer AOV
117.formula: New Customer Revenue / New Customer Orders
117.description: The average order value of customers who first bought during the period.
117.nuances:
**All of a newcomer's orders** in the period count, rather than only the first: the numerator and the denominator match what [[New Customer Revenue→crm/vyruchka_s_novyh_klientov]] and [[New Customer Orders→crm/zakazy_novyh_klientov]] give.
**The new customer discount is subtracted**: the amount the customer actually paid is taken.
**Fully returned orders are excluded** from both parts of the fraction.
**The window length changes the makeup of the groups**: the longer the period, the more customers fall into the new group, because more first purchases fall within the window.
117.example:
[[New Customer Revenue→crm/vyruchka_s_novyh_klientov]] for March: $79,200
[[New Customer Orders→crm/zakazy_novyh_klientov]]: 1,375

New Customer AOV = 79,200 / 1,375 = **$57.60**

At list prices, without the new customer discount, it would be $66.33: the gap is the price of acquisition.
117.importance:
It shows the order value new customers come in with, and together with [[New Customer Acquisition Cost→crm/stoimost_privlecheniya_novogo_klienta_ca]] answers whether **acquiring new customers pays off** within the period.
A drop in newcomers' order value with a stable number of newcomers means acquisition is bringing in **a lower-spending audience**: the same number of people, but less money from them, and the ad budget needs to be reconsidered before this shows up in revenue.
117.not_needed: Skip it where **purchases can't be tied to a customer**: offline without a loyalty program, in an online store with guest checkout. Without identification, an order can't be assigned to either new or repeat customers.
117.essence_note: the bigger the first order, the sooner acquisition costs are recovered

118.name: New Customer Orders
118.formula: Total number of orders for the period from customers who first bought in this period
118.description: The total number of orders from customers who first bought during the period.
118.nuances:
A customer counts as new if their **first purchase ever** falls in the period. A customer who bought a year ago and came back during the period doesn't go here.
**All of their orders in the period** count, rather than only the first: three orders by a newcomer in the period give 3, while [[New Customers→crm/novye_klienty]] counts that person once. That's why there are always at least as many new customer orders as new customers.
**A fully returned order is excluded**; otherwise, the average order value is calculated on money that doesn't exist.
Orders **without a loyalty card** can't be assigned to new customers, so the number is always lower than the real inflow of shoppers.
**The window length changes the makeup of the groups**: the longer the period, the more customers fall into the new group, because more first purchases fall within the window.
118.example:
Customers with a first purchase in March: 1,200
Their first orders: 1,200
Second and third orders by the same customers in March: 190
Fully returned: 15

New Customer Orders = 1,200 + 190 − 15 = **1,375**

Meanwhile, [[New Customers→crm/novye_klienty]] is 1,200: 1,200 people placed 1,375 orders.
118.importance:
It measures **the return on acquisition** in orders: how many purchases marketing brought in over the month, unaffected by swings in order value.
When ad spend grows and the number of first orders stays flat, it means **traffic has become more expensive** rather than customer behavior having changed, and the decision here is different: change the channel rather than the storefront.
118.not_needed: Skip it where **purchases can't be tied to a customer**: offline without a loyalty program, in an online store with guest checkout. Without identification, an order can't be assigned to either new or repeat customers.
118.essence_note: these purchases begin the relationship with a customer

119.name: Signup-to-Purchase Conversion Rate
119.formula: (Customers Who Signed Up in the Period and Made a First Purchase / Signups in the Period) × 100
119.description: The share of people who signed up and went on to make a first purchase.
119.nuances:
The numerator and the denominator cover **the same people**: the cohort of people who signed up in the period is counted, and a purchase counts whenever it happens. A customer who signed up in January and bought in March goes into the January cohort: assigning them to March means dividing one month's buyers by another month's signups and getting a share that can exceed 100%.
A cohort needs **time to mature**: the share for a recent month is always lower than the final one, so an observation window is fixed (30 or 90 days), and cohorts are compared only over the same window.
Signups created **at checkout** **are excluded from the calculation**: there, the account is created for the current purchase, conversion is 100% by definition, and such records dilute the real figure. The metric is calculated for those who signed up separately from a purchase.
119.example:
[[Signups→voronki_prodazh_h4/registracii]] on the website and in the app in January: 3,400
Of those, with placeholder addresses and duplicate phone numbers: 340 (excluded)
Cohort base: 3,060
Bought within 90 days: 673

Signup-to-Purchase Conversion Rate = 673 / 3,060 × 100 = **22%**

Calculating March purchases against March signups gives a different figure: the numerator would include people who signed up in January and February.
119.importance:
It separates **interest from money**: people left their contact details, but not all of them pay, and the gap shows where the path breaks. A falling conversion rate with a growing number of signups usually means **traffic quality has dropped** rather than that the website is broken.
It's also used to estimate **how much revenue** the accumulated subscriber base can bring in before investing in messaging campaigns.
119.not_needed: Skip it when **it's technically impossible to sign up before purchasing**: one-step checkout without creating an account, sales without customer accounts.
119.essence_note: a signup without a purchase brings in no money

120.name: Active Customers
120.formula: Number of unique customers with purchases in the period
120.description: The number of unique customers who bought at least once during the period. It's the sum of new and repeat customers.
120.nuances:
A customer is counted **once** regardless of the number of purchases: five receipts from one person give one active customer.
Active simply means **bought within the chosen window**; there's no separate status behind the word. The length of the window changes the number mechanically: there are more active customers over a year than over a month, so only windows of the same length can be compared.
Only **identified purchases** count: a receipt with a loyalty card, an order placed in a customer account, a purchase where the customer gave a phone number. Anonymous receipts don't go into the number, so active customers are always fewer than the real number of shoppers. When revenue or orders are divided by this number, the numerator is filtered the same way: it includes only what identified customers brought in.
A fully returned order **doesn't create activity**: if a customer's only purchase in the period was returned, the customer is excluded from the count; otherwise, revenue per customer drops for no reason.
One person with two cards is counted **twice** until the cards are merged by phone number, and the number of active customers ends up overstated.
120.example:
Receipts in March: 12,400
With a loyalty card: 6,900
Unique cardholders among them: 4,850
Fully returned their only purchase: 50

[[Active Customers→crm/aktivnye_klienty]] = 4,850 − 50 = **4,800**

The remaining 5,500 anonymous receipts aren't included: there's no way to know how many people are behind them.
120.importance:
**The denominator** for half the metrics on this map: revenue per customer, the shares of new and repeat customers, [[Customer Churn Rate→crm/ottok_klientov]]. An error in it carries over to all the derived metrics at once.
A falling number of active customers with flat revenue means sales rest on **the growing spend of a few customers** rather than on an inflow of new ones, and such revenue drops off fast.
120.not_needed:
Skip it where **purchases can't be tied to a customer**: offline without a loyalty program, in an online store with guest checkout.
When most receipts are anonymous, the metric covers **only the shoppers who showed a card** rather than all shoppers.
120.essence_note: it's customers who buy that bring in money, rather than everyone who has ever bought

121.name: Orders per Customer
121.formula: Orders for the Period / Active Customers for the Period
121.description: How many orders there are on average per customer who bought during the period.
121.nuances:
The denominator is the period's [[Active Customers→crm/aktivnye_klienty]] rather than **everyone who has ever bought**: dividing by all of them lowers the result, and it no longer measures purchase frequency.
The numerator includes only orders of identified **customers from the denominator**: if you take all the store's receipts, anonymous ones included, and keep cardholders in the denominator, the average doubles where half of purchases are made without a card.
**An order equals a receipt**: one payment by one person at one time. An online order split into two shipments remains one order.
**Fully returned orders** are subtracted from the numerator, and customers left with no other orders, from the denominator.
**The length of the period changes the result** mechanically: there are more orders per customer over a year than over a month.
121.example:
Orders with loyalty cards in March: 6,850
[[Active Customers→crm/aktivnye_klienty]]: 4,800
Fully returned orders: 50 (subtracted, along with their customers, who had no other orders)

Orders per Customer = (6,850 − 50) / 4,800 = **1.42**

Taking all 12,400 store receipts as the numerator gives 2.58: anonymous receipts are in the numerator, but anonymous shoppers aren't in the denominator.
121.importance: It shows whether customers buy from you **just once** or come back within the period. A value around 1 means the base rests on one-time buyers: repeat sales will have to be built from scratch rather than nudged along.
121.not_needed: Skip it where **purchases can't be tied to a customer**: in physical stores without a loyalty program or in online stores with guest checkout. When most receipts are anonymous, the metric describes only cardholders.
121.synonyms: Purchase Frequency, Average Orders per Customer
121.essence_note: the more often one person buys, the more they bring in over the same period

122.name: Average Revenue per Customer (ARPC)
122.formula: Revenue from Identified Customers for the Period / Active Customers for the Period
122.description: How much revenue one customer who bought during the period brings in on average.
122.nuances:
**The numerator includes only** the revenue of customers in the denominator. The store's total revenue includes anonymous receipts, while the denominator includes only cardholders: when half of purchases are made without a card, such a division doubles the result.
**Returns are subtracted**, and [[Points Redeemed→programma_loyalnosti/ispolzovannye_bonusy]] reduce the amount.
**It differs from [[Average Order Value (AOV)→zakazy/sredniy_chek_aov]] in the denominator**: AOV divides revenue by orders, and this metric divides it by customers. They match only when every customer bought exactly once, and at a frequency of 1.4 orders per customer, revenue per customer is 40% higher than the average order value.
**The length of the period changes the result** mechanically: revenue per customer is higher over a year than over a month, so only windows of the same length are compared.
122.example:
Revenue from loyalty card purchases in March: $571,200
Returns and [[Points Redeemed→programma_loyalnosti/ispolzovannye_bonusy]] already subtracted
[[Active Customers→crm/aktivnye_klienty]]: 4,800

ARPC = 571,200 / 4,800 = **$119**

Taking all the store's revenue, anonymous receipts included, gives a higher result: the numerator includes purchases by people who aren't in the denominator.
122.importance:
It shows the value of one person to the business over the period and serves as **a quick substitute** for [[Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)→crm/pozhiznennaya_cennost_klienta_ltv]] where there's no long history to calculate it from.
Comparing customer groups shows where to direct retention efforts: a growing base with **falling revenue per customer** means acquisition is bringing in a lower-spending audience, and total revenue will catch up with this decline later.
122.not_needed: Skip it where **purchases can't be tied to a customer**: offline without a loyalty program, in an online store with guest checkout. When most receipts are anonymous, the metric describes only cardholders.
122.synonyms: Revenue per Customer, Average Spend per Customer
122.essence_note: the more one customer brings in, the fewer customers you need for the same revenue

123.name: Units per Customer
123.formula: Units Sold for the Period / Active Customers for the Period
123.description: How many units of goods one customer buys on average during the period.
123.nuances:
**Units are counted, rather than distinct products**: three identical T-shirts are three units rather than one line item. Counting distinct products understates the result in categories where people stock up.
**The denominator is the same** as in [[Orders per Customer→crm/zakazov_na_klienta]]: the period's [[Active Customers→crm/aktivnye_klienty]] rather than the whole base.
The numerator includes only units from orders of **identified customers**: you can't divide the store's total sales by cardholders, because anonymous purchases raise the average with no change in behavior.
**Returned units are subtracted**: in apparel and footwear, where customers try items on at home, noticeably fewer units may be kept than shipped.
Decide how to count **bundles** and buy-one-get-one-free promotions: by the number of units actually taken home or by the number paid for. Units taken home describe consumption more accurately, but the result grows with promo depth; units paid for give a steadier comparison across periods but understate the real volume. One rule is fixed for all periods.
123.example:
Units sold with loyalty cards in March: 15,400
Returned: 1,900
Of the units sold, 700 went out as the free second unit in a buy-one-get-one-free promotion
[[Active Customers→crm/aktivnye_klienty]]: 4,800

By units taken home = (15,400 − 1,900) / 4,800 = **2.81**
By units paid for = (15,400 − 1,900 − 700) / 4,800 = **2.67**

A 5% difference when free promo units make up 5% of volume: the deeper the promotion, the further apart the two methods are.
123.importance:
It shows **whether merchandising and upselling work**: order value can grow because of price increases while the number of units bought stays flat, and then there's no real sales growth.
Comparing it with [[Orders per Customer→crm/zakazov_na_klienta]] separates two different growth scenarios: a customer **comes back more often** or **buys more per visit**, and they call for opposite decisions.
123.not_needed: Skip it when the product is by nature **bought one at a time** and there's no other option: large appliances, cars, a subscription to a single service.
123.synonyms: Items per Customer, Average Units per Customer
123.essence_note: the more units one person buys, the more revenue from the same customer

124.name: Total Customers
124.formula: Number of unique customers with at least one purchase over the whole history
124.description: The number of unique customers who bought at least once over the company's whole history.
124.nuances:
**Set the date** from which history is kept: when a database is transferred, some old customers get lost, and the number falls because of the migration rather than because of churn.
Customers who fully returned all their purchases **are excluded from the base**: no purchase took place.
The number **only grows** and can't decrease: customers who left years ago are still counted in it. To assess the live base, look at active customers for the period; this metric measures accumulated reach.
**Duplicate cards and phone numbers** inflate the base more and more as it grows: without periodic merging, the gap with the real number of people keeps widening.
124.example:
Customer records in the CRM: 412,000
Of those, with no purchases (signed up without ordering): 78,000 (not counted)
Duplicates by phone number: 31,000
Fully returned all their purchases: 3,000

Total Customers = 412,000 − 78,000 − 31,000 − 3,000 = **300,000**
124.importance:
**It sets the ceiling on what** reactivation can bring back: if 300,000 people have ever bought and 5,000 are active per month, the gap is the pool you can work with. It serves as the denominator for estimating loyalty program penetration, and the churned customers counted in [[Customer Churn Rate→crm/ottok_klientov]] come from this base.
Without this number, messaging campaigns are planned **blindly**, and the cost per contact is calculated for the wrong audience.
124.not_needed:
Skip it where **repeat purchases aren't expected**: wedding services, window installation, products for a child of a specific age. The base there only grows and shows the company's age rather than who you can work with: there's no one to reactivate.
Also skip it where **customers can't be identified**: without a card or a customer account, receipts can't be matched to unique customers.
124.essence_note: the more people have bought at least once, the larger the base you can reach out to again

125.name: Customer Lifespan
125.formula: Σ(Date of Last Purchase − Date of First Purchase) / Number of Customers with Two or More Purchases
125.description: How much time passes on average from a customer's first purchase to their last.
125.nuances:
Customers with a single purchase **aren't included in the calculation**: their lifespan is zero and drags the average toward zero, and the more one-time buyers there are in the base, the stronger the effect.
Only customers who **have already stopped buying** count, that is, those with no purchases for longer than the window in [[Lost Customers→crm/poteryannye_klienty]]. For active customers, the last purchase hasn't happened yet, and including them systematically understates the lifespan: the younger the base, the bigger the understatement.
**A young base** gives a result that's understated by design: the lifespan can't exceed the age of the base itself, and in the first years of operation the metric hits this ceiling.
**Purchases missed because of anonymous** receipts shorten the observed interval: a purchase without a card doesn't update the last purchase date, and the customer looks like they left earlier than they did.
125.example:
Customers with ≥2 purchases and no purchases for more than 6 months: 8,000
Sum of intervals from first to last purchase: 4,320,000 days

Customer Lifespan = 4,320,000 / 8,000 = **540 days (18 months)**

Adding 6,000 customers with one purchase and a lifespan of 0 gives 309 days: the figure then describes a mix of the lifespan and the share of one-time buyers rather than the lifespan.
125.importance: It sets the horizon over which it makes sense to count the money a customer brings in at all. The trend in lifespan across cohorts shows whether **relationships with customers are getting longer** or customers are passing through the business ever faster.
125.not_needed: Skip it for a base **younger than a couple of typical purchase cycles**: the metric will hit the age of the base and show its age rather than customer behavior.
125.essence_note: the longer a person buys, the more one acquisition brings in

126.name: Repeat Customers
126.formula: Number of active customers in the period who had at least one purchase before the period started
126.description: The number of customers who bought during the period and had purchases before it started. Together with new customers, they make up all active customers in the period.
126.nuances:
**Any past purchase** counts, however long ago: a customer who bought once three years ago is a repeat customer. You can't restrict the purchase history to the previous period; otherwise, repeat and new customers together stop adding up to all active customers, and some customers fall into neither group.
A customer who first bought within the period and bought twice **remains new**: they had no purchases before the period started. All their orders in this period also count as new customers' orders.
A customer is counted **once** regardless of the number of purchases in the period.
**Identification** is by card or phone number: unidentified purchases don't reveal a customer's earlier purchases, so someone with a purchase history looks new.
126.example:
[[Active Customers→crm/aktivnye_klienty]] in March: 4,800
Of those, first purchase ever in March: 1,200

[[Repeat Customers→crm/povtornye_klienty]] = 4,800 − 1,200 = **3,600**

Of the 1,200 new customers, 180 bought twice in March: they remain new and aren't included in this number.
126.importance:
It's **the active core of the customer base** that revenue rests on, and the denominator of [[Customer Retention Cost→crm/stoimost_uderzhaniya_klienta]].
A shrinking number of repeat customers with a growing inflow of new ones means the base is **turning over**: people come and don't return, while total revenue looks stable for a while.
126.not_needed:
Skip it for **one-time purchases**, where repeat buying isn't expected given the nature of the product: wedding services, window installation. There are no repeat customers there by definition.
Also skip it where **purchases can't be tied to a customer**: without identification, an order can't be assigned to either new or repeat customers.
126.essence_note: the more customers buy again, the more revenue in the period

127.name: Lost Customers
127.formula: Customers who bought before and made no purchases during the inactivity window
127.description: The number of customers who bought before but didn't make a single purchase during the chosen inactivity window.
127.nuances:
The base includes customers who bought in the period **before the inactivity window** rather than everyone over the whole history: otherwise everyone who ever bought once ends up among the lost, and the number grows with the age of the base.
The inactivity window **is set explicitly and doesn't change** between periods: when you switch from 3 months to 6, the number of lost customers drops with no change in customer behavior. As a guideline: the typical interval between purchases multiplied by two or three.
A customer with **a single purchase** made years ago isn't counted as lost: they're classified as a one-time buyer; otherwise, every promo buyer from a past season inflates churn.
A customer who comes back after being counted as lost **doesn't rewrite the calculation retroactively**: they enter new calculations as reactivated; otherwise, past reports keep changing.
Purchases **without a card** can't be linked to the customer, so some shoppers are counted as lost while they keep coming to the store: the higher the share of anonymous receipts, the more churn is overstated.
127.example:
Customers with purchases in the first half of 2025: 12,000
Inactivity window: 6 months
Of those, bought at least once in the second half: 9,600
Made no purchases: 2,400

[[Lost Customers→crm/poteryannye_klienty]] = **2,400**

With a 3-month window, there would be 4,100: the same behavior, a different number.
127.importance:
It gives **a list of people for reactivation**: without it, messaging campaigns go to the whole base, including those who bought yesterday, and the cost per contact goes up with nothing to show for it.
The number of customers lost in a period, compared with the number of [[New Customers→crm/novye_klienty]], answers the main question about the base: **is it growing, or losing customers** faster than it gains them.
127.not_needed: Skip it with **a long purchase cycle**, where a year without a purchase is normal, and with a one-time sales model, where a repeat purchase isn't expected.
127.essence_note: their acquisition has already been paid for, and there will be no more purchases from them

128.name: Customer Base Growth Rate
128.formula: ((Active Customers for the Period − Active Customers for the Previous Comparable Period) / Active Customers for the Previous Comparable Period) × 100
128.description: By what percentage the number of active customers changed compared with the previous period.
128.nuances:
It's calculated on **[[Active Customers→crm/aktivnye_klienty]]** rather than everyone who has ever bought: that number can only grow, so the rate based on it is always positive and says nothing about changes.
Comparison periods are **of the same length**: month with month, quarter with quarter. Comparing a 31-day month with February gives a 10% difference that has nothing to do with customers.
For a seasonal business, compare with **the same period last year** rather than the previous one: January after December will show a slump, and it means nothing.
The result is made up of **two flows at once**: new customers came, and some previous ones left. Zero growth can mean either stagnation or a complete turnover of the base: [[New Customers→crm/novye_klienty]] and [[Customer Churn Rate→crm/ottok_klientov]] show what actually happened.
128.example:
[[Active Customers→crm/aktivnye_klienty]] in February: 4,400
Active customers in March: 4,800

Customer Base Growth Rate = (4,800 − 4,400) / 4,400 × 100 = **9.1%**

Behind it: 1,200 new customers came in, and 800 previous ones stopped buying. The increase of 400 people is the difference between two flows rather than the number of new customers.
128.importance:
It's the first place to see **whether the business grows through more customers or higher prices**: revenue can grow with a shrinking base thanks to price increases, and that's a dead end, which will become clear later.
Comparing the growth rate of the base with the growth rate of revenue immediately shows **which of the two sources is working**.
128.not_needed: Skip it where **customers can't be identified**: without a card or a customer account, receipts can't be matched to unique customers, and growth of the base can't be told apart from growth in the number of purchases.
128.synonyms: Customer Growth Rate, Active Customer Growth Rate
128.essence_note: a growing base means growing revenue at the same average order value

129.name: Repeat Customer Rate
129.description: The share of customers who bought before the period started among everyone who bought during the period.
129.nuances:
Repeat status is determined over **the whole purchase history** rather than the previous period: a customer who bought once three years ago and came back now is a repeat customer.
A second purchase within the same period **doesn't make a customer a repeat customer**: they didn't buy before the period started, so they remain new. The share of those who came back within the window is counted by [[Repeat Purchase Rate→crm/koefficient_uderzhaniya]], and the two numbers don't match.
Together with [[New Customer Rate→crm/novyh_klientov]], it gives 100%: the two metrics **are kept together** to see the mix of new and repeat customers in the period at a glance, but it's enough to calculate one.
129.example:
[[Active Customers→crm/aktivnye_klienty]] in March: 4,800
Of those, bought before March 1: 3,600
First purchase ever in March: 1,200

Repeat Customer Rate = 3,600 / 4,800 × 100 = **75%**

Of the 1,200 new customers, 180 bought twice in March: they don't count as repeat customers; they count toward the Repeat Purchase Rate (customers with 2+ purchases within the period).
129.importance:
It shows what share of shoppers come back, and it's used to judge **how stable the base is**. A growing share means the base sustains itself from one period to the next. A falling share means retention isn't working, and sales volume will have to be propped up by new acquisition.
This metric is used to decide whether to invest in **a loyalty program** or in new traffic channels.
129.not_needed: Skip it for one-time purchases, where repeat buying isn't expected given the nature of the product: wedding services, window installation, children's products for a specific age. There, **every customer is new**, and the share of repeat customers is always close to zero.
129.essence_note: without repeat customers, the company pays for every sale again, and when nearly all buyers are existing customers, the inflow has dried up and the base isn't growing

130.name: Repeat Purchase Rate
130.formula: (Customers with ≥2 Purchases in the Period / Active Customers for the Period) × 100
130.description: The share of customers who bought more than once within the period among everyone who bought during the period.
130.nuances:
Both purchases must **fall within the period**: purchases before it started don't count, and a customer with a ten-year history who bought once in the period doesn't go into the numerator. That's how the metric differs from [[Repeat Customer Rate→crm/povtornyh_klientov]], where any past purchase is enough, and the two numbers differ.
**The window length changes the result** mechanically: the longer the window, the more customers make two purchases within it. The window is chosen based on the typical interval between purchases, and only windows of the same length are compared.
Two orders placed on the same day count as **one purchase**: otherwise a purchase split into parts raises the metric with no change in behavior.
Only **identified purchases** count: a customer who bought twice, but once without a card, looks like a one-time buyer, and the rate is understated.
130.example:
[[Active Customers→crm/aktivnye_klienty]] for the quarter: 9,500
Of those, bought twice or more within the quarter: 2,470
Of those, twice on the same day: 120 (merged, counted as one purchase, dropped out of the numerator)

Repeat Purchase Rate = (2,470 − 120) / 9,500 × 100 = **24.7%**

[[Repeat Customer Rate→crm/povtornyh_klientov]] for the same quarter = 75%: there, any past purchase is enough.
130.importance:
It's the only metric on the map that shows **customers coming back within a manageable horizon**: purchase history can't tell you whether this quarter's promotions work, but this metric can. It's used to decide whether to extend the loyalty program and whether a specific campaign to bring customers back worked.
Without it, growth in the share of [[Repeat Customers→crm/povtornye_klienty]] is easy to mistake for retention success, when it's simply **customers acquired over the years**.
130.not_needed:
Skip it for **one-time purchase** products, where a repeat purchase isn't expected given the nature of demand: wedding services, window installation, products for a child of a specific age. No window will capture a repeat purchase there.
Also skip it where **purchases can't be tied to a customer**: without identification, two purchases by the same person can't be matched.
130.essence_note: a second purchase comes with no acquisition costs

131.name: Customer Churn Rate
131.formula: (Lost Customers / Active Customers in the Previous Comparable Period) × 100
131.description: The share of customers who stopped buying, relative to the number who bought in the previous period.
131.nuances:
The denominator is the previous period's [[Active Customers→crm/aktivnye_klienty]] rather than **everyone who has ever bought**: dividing by all of them mixes in those who left years ago and gives a percentage that never grows.
The inactivity window after which a customer counts as lost and the comparison period **must be consistent**: you can't calculate monthly churn with a six-month inactivity window, because the numerator then describes a completely different stretch of time.
The inactivity window is chosen based on **the typical interval between purchases** rather than the calendar: it's shorter for groceries than for apparel, and longer still for furniture. Too short a window records an ordinary pause as churn; too long a window shows churn long after the customer actually stopped coming.
Customers with a single purchase in the previous period can account for most of the churn: they're counted **separately from churned regular customers**; otherwise, the drop-off of one-time promo buyers looks like a loyalty crisis.
131.example:
[[Active Customers→crm/aktivnye_klienty]] in the first half of 2025: 12,000
Of those, made no purchases in the next 6 months: 2,400

Customer Churn Rate = 2,400 / 12,000 × 100 = **20%**

Of the 2,400 who left, 1,700 had exactly one purchase: 700 regular customers left, or 5.8%.
131.importance: It sets how many new customers you need to bring in just **to keep the base from shrinking**: with 20% churn per half-year, acquisition below this level means the business slowly contracts while revenue still grows on paper. The churn trend is the earliest way to see that something has changed in the product or service: customers **stop coming** before it shows up in the sales report.
131.not_needed: Skip it where a repeat purchase **isn't built into the model** or the interval between purchases is measured in years: the customer hasn't left; they just haven't come back yet.
131.essence_note: every customer who leaves is revenue that will have to be replaced through new acquisition

132.name: Revenue Churn Rate
132.formula: (Revenue from Lost Customers in the Previous Comparable Period / Total Revenue for the Previous Comparable Period) × 100
132.description: What share of the previous period's revenue came from customers who stopped buying. It shows the size of the loss in money rather than in the number of customers.
132.nuances:
**The actual revenue of churned** customers is used, rather than the average revenue per active customer. Multiplying the number of lost customers by the average for active customers gives a hypothetical amount: if those who leave bought less often and spent less than average, this calculation overstates the losses.
Both numbers are taken for **the same** past period: how much these customers brought in while they were still buying. You can't divide the previous period's revenue by the current period's revenue: if the company grows, churn will be artificially understated.
A customer is counted as lost using **the same inactivity window** as in [[Lost Customers→crm/poteryannye_klienty]]: if the churn window is longer than the comparison period, the numerator and the denominator describe different stretches of time, and the metric stops adding up.
**The metric doesn't account for the revenue** these customers would have brought in as they grew: it answers how much money there was and is now gone, rather than how much there could have been.
132.example:
Customers who bought in the first half of 2025: 12,000
Their revenue for that half-year: $4,800,000
Of those, made no purchases in the next 6 months: 2,400
Revenue of these 2,400 in the first half: $528,000

Revenue Churn Rate = 528,000 / 4,800,000 × 100 = **11%**

Using the average: 2,400 × $400 = $960,000, or 20%. Churned customers spent $220 each rather than $400, and the figure is almost doubled.
132.importance:
Customer churn and revenue churn diverge the most where **the most valuable customers leave**: you can lose 5% of customers and 20% of revenue, and a customer count won't show it.
This metric shows **exactly whom the company is losing** and determines whether reactivation is worth its cost: it's cheaper to stop trying to retain 100 customers who brought in $20 each.
132.not_needed: Skip it where **an absence of purchases doesn't mean the customer left**: seasonal demand, products with a purchase cycle of several years. The customer will come back, but the metric has already written their revenue off as lost.
132.essence_note: this is money the base used to bring in and stopped bringing in

133.name: Customer Retention Cost
133.formula: Retention Costs for the Period / Repeat Customers for the Period
133.description: How much is spent on average per customer who bought before the period started.
133.nuances:
Costs include **everything aimed at existing** customers: messaging campaigns and push notifications, loyalty card discounts, the cost of [[Points Redeemed→programma_loyalnosti/ispolzovannye_bonusy]], cashback programs, the retention specialist's work and the CRM platform subscription. **Limiting it to direct costs** of messaging campaigns understates the figure, and the bigger the share of discounts and points, the bigger the understatement.
The new customer discount and welcome bonus points **don't go here**: they belong to [[New Customer Acquisition Cost→crm/stoimost_privlecheniya_novogo_klienta_ca]]. Double counting the same discount in CAC and in retention cost is most likely in programs where the card is issued at the first purchase.
Points are counted at **the moment of redemption** rather than when they're awarded: points awarded and not spent cost no money, and counting them when awarded overstates costs by the amount of unredeemed liabilities.
Costs and customers are taken for **the same period**. The denominator is repeat customers, that is, those who bought before the period started: using all active customers understates retention cost, and using customers with ≥2 purchases within the window overstates it.
133.example:
Costs for March: messaging campaigns $2,400, [[Points Redeemed→programma_loyalnosti/ispolzovannye_bonusy]] $18,000, loyalty card discounts $9,000, specialist's work $3,600
Total: $33,000
[[Repeat Customers→crm/povtornye_klienty]]: 3,600

Customer Retention Cost = 33,000 / 3,600 = **$9.17**

Messaging campaigns alone would give $0.67: 82% of the money goes into discounts and points.
133.importance: Comparing it with CAC answers which is cheaper: **bringing back an existing customer or bringing in a new one**. Comparing retention cost with revenue per customer shows whether the loyalty program eats up **the return it generates**: it's easy to hand out discounts so that a retained customer brings in less than their retention costs, and this isn't visible in total revenue.
133.not_needed: Skip it when **there's no targeted spending on retention**: without a loyalty program, messaging campaigns and personal discounts, the numerator is zero.
133.synonyms: Retention Cost per Customer, Cost to Retain
133.essence_note: the cheaper retention is, the more you keep from repeat purchases

134.name: Repeat Customer Revenue
134.formula: Revenue for the period from orders placed by customers who bought before the period started
134.description: Revenue from orders placed by customers who bought before the period started.
134.nuances:
**All of a repeat customer's orders** in the period count: they're a repeat customer from the moment the period starts, so their first order within the window is also included.
Orders from customers who first bought within the period **are excluded entirely**, including their second and third orders: such a customer is counted as new, and all their revenue for the period counts as new customer revenue.
**The window length changes the makeup of the groups**: the longer the period, the more customers fall into the new group, because more first purchases fall within the window.
134.example:
Orders in March from customers who bought before March 1: 8,900 orders worth $534,000
[[Points Redeemed→programma_loyalnosti/ispolzovannye_bonusy]]: $18,000
Returns: $24,000
Second and third orders by March newcomers: $10,800 (not counted: these customers are new)

Repeat Customer Revenue = 534,000 − 18,000 − 24,000 = **$492,000**

Together with [[New Customer Revenue→crm/vyruchka_s_novyh_klientov]], that's $571,200: all revenue from identified purchases.
134.importance:
It's the part of revenue that **rests on the customer base you've already built**, and its share is used to judge how stable the business is. When repeat customer revenue stands still while the base grows, customers are still on the books but buy less and less often, and later this will surface as a drop in total revenue.
It's also used to calculate how much the company can afford to spend on **retention and reactivation**.
134.not_needed:
Skip it for **one-time purchases**, where repeat buying isn't expected given the nature of the product: wedding services, window installation. There are no repeat customers there by definition.
Also skip it where **purchases can't be tied to a customer**: without identification, an order can't be assigned to either new or repeat customers.
134.essence_note: this money comes in with no acquisition costs

135.name: Time to Second Purchase
135.formula: Σ(Date of 2nd Purchase − Date of 1st Purchase) / Number of Customers Who Made a Second Purchase
135.description: How much time passes on average between the first and second purchase for customers who bought a second time.
135.nuances:
Only the interval from **the first purchase to the second** is taken, regardless of how many purchases the customer made afterward. A customer with five purchases adds one interval to the sum.
Customers who haven't bought a second time yet **aren't included in the calculation**: this estimates how fast those who came back did so, rather than the share who came back. The metric is systematically optimistic because it doesn't see those who never came back, so it's read together with the share of customers who made a second purchase.
The denominator is customers with **two or more purchases** over all time, rather than the period's [[Repeat Customers→crm/povtornye_klienty]]: the latter are determined by a purchase before the period started and include those whose second purchase happened years ago.
**The median is more stable than the mean**: a few customers who came back after a very long break pull the mean up.
135.example:
Cohort: 500 customers with a first purchase in January
Bought a second time over the past 6 months: 180
Sum of intervals between the 1st and 2nd purchase: 8,100 days

Time to Second Purchase = 8,100 / 180 = **45 days**

The other 320 customers weren't included: counting them as zero would give 16 days, and that's not the time it takes to come back.
135.importance: It sets the moment when it makes sense to **follow up with the customer** through a messaging campaign or a reminder: sending on day 20 when the typical return is on day 45 means reaching out before the product has run out. This number is used to set up triggered communications and to decide after how many days without a purchase a customer is considered to be lapsing. Without it, **the reactivation window is chosen at random**, and part of the messaging budget goes to people who were going to come back anyway.
135.not_needed: Skip it where a repeat purchase **isn't part of the model**: large one-time services, products for a specific event.
135.synonyms: Time to Second Order, Days to Second Purchase
135.essence_note: the longer the pause, the higher the chance there won't be a second purchase at all

136.name: Repeat Customer AOV
136.formula: Revenue from Repeat Customers' Orders for the Period / Number of Repeat Customers' Orders for the Period
136.description: The average order value of customers who bought before the period started.
136.nuances:
**All of a repeat customer's orders** in the period count: the customer is a repeat customer from the moment the period starts.
Orders from customers who first bought within the period **aren't included**: the numerator and the denominator cover the same orders that [[Repeat Customer Orders→crm/zakazy_povtornyh_klientov]] counts.
**Returns and [[Points Redeemed→programma_loyalnosti/ispolzovannye_bonusy]] are subtracted** from the numerator. In loyalty programs where points are actively redeemed, repeat customers' order value ends up lower than new customers' precisely because of the points rather than because of behavior.
**Fully returned orders are excluded** from both parts of the fraction.
**The window length changes the makeup of the groups**: the longer the period, the more customers fall into the new group, because more first purchases fall within the window.
136.example:
[[Repeat Customer Orders→crm/zakazy_povtornyh_klientov]] for March: 5,425
Their revenue: $492,000
Returns and [[Points Redeemed→programma_loyalnosti/ispolzovannye_bonusy]] already subtracted

Repeat Customer AOV = 492,000 / 5,425 = **$90.69**

[[New Customer AOV→crm/sredniy_chek_novyh_klientov]]: $57.60. The difference of about $33 is the value of bringing a customer back.
136.importance: Comparing it with [[New Customer AOV→crm/sredniy_chek_novyh_klientov]] shows whether **trust is growing**: if the repeat order value isn't higher than the first, the loyalty program retains people but doesn't increase their purchases, and the investment in it doesn't pay off.
136.not_needed:
Skip it for **one-time purchases**, where repeat buying isn't expected given the nature of the product: wedding services, window installation. There are no repeat customers there by definition.
Also skip it where **purchases can't be tied to a customer**: without identification, an order can't be assigned to either new or repeat customers.
136.essence_note: with the same number of repeat orders, a larger order value means more money

137.name: Repeat Customer Orders
137.formula: Number of orders for the period from customers who bought before the period started
137.description: The number of orders for the period from customers who bought before the period started.
137.nuances:
Repeat status is determined **at the start of the period**: a customer who bought before it started is a repeat customer from their very first order within the window.
Orders from customers who first bought within the period **don't go here**, including their second and third orders: such a customer is new, and all their orders count as new customers' orders. Together with [[New Customer Orders→crm/zakazy_novyh_klientov]], this gives all identified orders for the period with no overlap.
**Fully returned orders are subtracted.**
**Anonymous receipts aren't classified**, so the sum of new and repeat customers' orders is less than the total number of receipts.
**The window length changes the makeup of the groups**: the longer the period, the more customers fall into the new group, because more first purchases fall within the window.
137.example:
Orders with cards in March: 6,850
[[New Customer Orders→crm/zakazy_novyh_klientov]] (first and subsequent): 1,390
Fully returned orders of repeat customers: 35

Repeat Customer Orders = 6,850 − 1,390 − 35 = **5,425**

Together with [[New Customer Orders→crm/zakazy_novyh_klientov]], that's 6,800: all identified orders in March, net of returns.
137.importance: It gives the volume of purchases that rests on the customer base you've already built, and serves as a natural basis for estimating the load on the warehouse and logistics: repeat customers' orders are forecast more accurately than the flow of new ones. A decline with a stable number of repeat customers means people are still in the database on paper but **order less often**, and this shows up before revenue sags.
137.not_needed:
Skip it for **one-time purchases**, where repeat buying isn't expected given the nature of the product: wedding services, window installation. There are no repeat customers there by definition.
And where **purchases can't be tied to a customer**: without identification, an order can't be assigned to either new or repeat customers.
137.essence_note: these orders don't require paying for acquisition

138.name: Cart Abandonment Rate
138.description: The share of carts with products for which an order was never placed.
138.nuances:
The denominator is carts with at least one product added; the numerator **follows the same** waiting-period rule as the absolute number of abandoned carts.
Carts whose waiting period hasn't expired yet **are excluded from both** the numerator and the denominator: otherwise the percentage for the last day comes out inflated.
**Empty carts** that were opened and closed without adding a product don't go into the denominator.
138.example:
Carts with products added in the week: 4,200
Carts still active: 340 (excluded from both parts)
Orders placed: 1,260
Abandoned: 2,600

Cart Abandonment Rate = 2,600 / (4,200 − 340) × 100 = **67%**
138.importance: It turns [[Abandoned Carts→oformlenie_zakaza/broshennye_korziny]] from a count into a share, which makes them comparable across periods: the absolute number grows with traffic, the share doesn't. It's the basis for estimating the potential for abandoned cart recovery through email and whether such flows pay off. Each store has its own level, which depends on what **counts as a cart and** when a cart is considered abandoned, so track changes against the store's own history: a sudden jump means something specific has broken.
138.not_needed: **Skip it where** there's no cart as such: one-click purchases, services sold through a request form, orders placed through a sales rep.
138.essence_note: the more carts are abandoned, the more orders are lost at the last step

139.name: Sessions with Cart Views
139.formula: Number of sessions with a cart view
139.description: The number of sessions in which the shopper opened the cart.
139.nuances:
Several cart opens within one session **count as one view**: shoppers go back to the cart several times per session, and without merging the opens the number is inflated.
Opening a slide-out cart panel **counts as a view** if the shopper can go to checkout from it.
Whether to count opening an empty cart **is a separate decision**. If you include it, accidental clicks on the cart icon are counted too, and the [[Cart-to-Checkout Rate→oformlenie_zakaza/konversiya_v_nachalo_chekauta]] comes out lower than it really is.
139.example:
Cart open events in the month: 27,600
Unique sessions with a cart open: 16,900
Of those, sessions with an empty cart: 2,100 (not counted)

Sessions with Cart Views = 16,900 − 2,100 = **14,800**
139.importance: **The denominator for the Cart-to-Checkout Rate** and the point where interest in the product ends and the purchase decision begins. The gap between cart additions and cart views shows how many people leave without ever looking at the total. A counting error here throws off the whole lower part of the funnel.
