139.not_needed: **Skip it** when there's no cart: one-click purchases, service requests.
139.essence_note: checkout starts with an open cart

140.name: Order Placement Rate
140.formula:
Multi-step checkout: (Placed Orders / Payment Method Selections) × 100
One-page checkout: (Placed Orders / Sessions with Checkout Starts) × 100
140.description: The share of checkouts with a selected payment method that resulted in a placed order.
140.nuances:
The formula depends on how the checkout is built. In a **multi-step** checkout, where screens follow one another, the denominator is the count at the previous step, and the metric shows the loss at this particular transition. In a **one-page** checkout, where all fields are on one screen, steps aren't tracked as separate events: the denominator is started checkouts, and the numerator is sessions where the relevant section is completed. The second version answers a different question: “how many got to this part of the form at all” rather than “how many were lost at the transition.”
The versions aren't mixed or compared with each other: with one-page counting, the product of the step conversion rates won't give the Checkout Conversion Rate, because all the shares **are calculated from the same** base.
In the one-page version, this conversion rate **is identical to the Checkout Conversion Rate**: the order is the last step, so the metric is no longer a separate measure.
Both payment method selections and placed orders **are counted by checkout session**, so the numerator can't exceed the denominator.
**An order goes into** the numerator when checkout is confirmed rather than when the money arrives: otherwise the metric mixes drop-off in the form with bank declines.
**Repeated attempts within** one session after a failed payment count as one order.
140.example:
Multi-step checkout

Checkouts with a payment method selected: 5,120
Of those, order confirmed: 4,300
Of the confirmed orders, paid successfully: 3,960 (doesn't affect the calculation)

Order Placement Rate = 4,300 / 5,120 × 100 = **84%**
140.importance: **The last step of the funnel**, and losses here are the most expensive: the shopper has already chosen products, entered their details and selected a payment method, which means they've made the decision to buy. Whatever stops them here lies in the form itself rather than in the price or assortment, so a drop is a reason to look at session recordings and error logs rather than change the offer. Gains at this step come without additional traffic spend: you've already paid for these shoppers and brought them to the end of the form.
140.not_needed: **Skip it** when confirmation and payment are merged into one step and there's no separate order placement.
140.essence_note: this is the last step, where the cart turns into money

141.name: Payment Method Selections
141.formula: Number of completed payment method selection steps
141.description: The number of checkouts in which the shopper selected a payment method and completed this step.
141.nuances:
**Each checkout session** counts once, even if the shopper switched between payment options several times.
A payment method preselected by default counts when the shopper moves on to the next screen: without this rule, the selection **is recorded for everyone**, and the step no longer separates those who got through from those who left.
The event **is recorded at the time** of selection rather than when the money arrives: a failed payment doesn't cancel the step.
141.example:
Checkouts where the payment screen was opened: 5,400
Checkouts where the shopper confirmed a selection and moved to the next step: 5,120
Switches between payment methods: 1,800 (don't increase the count)

Payment Method Selections = **5,120**
141.importance: **The second-to-last point of the funnel** and the denominator of the Order Placement Rate. The difference between this number and the number of orders shows how many people drop off with a payment method already selected, and that's the most frustrating and most fixable loss in checkout.
141.not_needed: **Skip it when** only one payment method is available: there's no separate selection step.
141.synonyms: Add Payment Info, Payment Info Added
141.essence_note: a selected payment method means there's one step left before the money

142.name: Contact Info Completions
142.formula: Number of completed contact information steps
142.description: The number of checkouts in which the shopper filled in their contact details and moved past this step.
142.nuances:
**The step counts** when the shopper successfully advances to the next step rather than when they type characters into a field.
**Each checkout session** counts once, even if the shopper went back and edited their details.
**Logged-in shoppers with** automatically filled details are counted if the form accepted the details and the step was completed.
142.example:
Started checkouts: 9,500
Checkouts that completed the contact details step: 7,410
Sessions where the details were edited twice: 340 (counted once)

Contact Info Completions = **7,410**
142.importance: **The absolute number is needed** as the denominator for the next funnel steps and as an estimate of how many contacts can be collected in a month. It shows how many people get far enough that they can be brought back with an email or a call, even if no order was placed.
142.not_needed: **Skip it** when contact details are part of a single form submitted with one button rather than a separate step.
142.essence_note: filled-in details mean the person is serious about placing the order

143.name: Sessions with Checkout Starts
143.formula: Number of sessions with a checkout start
143.description: The number of sessions in which the shopper started checkout.
143.nuances:
**Decide** what counts as the start: a click on the button that leads to checkout or the loading of the first form screen. Counted by clicks, the number is higher and shows the intent to place an order; counted by loads, it's lower and shows those who actually reached the form. The difference between them is the loss at the transition itself, and it also changes every checkout conversion rate, so make the choice once and keep it the same in every metric on the map.
**Each session counts as** one started checkout, even if the shopper left the form and came back to it several times.
Returning to checkout the next day **counts as a new checkout**: one shopper's sessions aren't stitched together, so the total of started checkouts is always higher than the number of people.
143.example:
Clicks on the “Checkout” button: 10,200
First form screen loads: 9,800
Returns to the form within the same session: 300 (not counted)

Sessions with Checkout Starts = 9,800 − 300 = **9,500**
143.importance: **The point that splits** the funnel in two: everything above it is about interest in the product, everything below it is about the form. It serves as the denominator for all checkout conversion rates, so a different definition of the start throws off half the map. The absolute number tells you whether there's enough volume for an A/B test of the form: with few checkouts a month, a test won't reach significance in a reasonable time.
143.essence_note: a started checkout is one step away from an order

144.name: Average Cart Value
144.formula: Total Value of Items in All Carts / Carts with Products
144.description: The average value of items in a cart, regardless of whether it led to an order.
144.nuances:
**The denominator is carts** with at least one product: empty carts pull the average toward zero.
The value **is fixed at the moment** of the cart's last change rather than at current prices.
A cart **counts once** regardless of how many times the shopper changed its contents.
Amounts **are recorded as** the shopper sees them on the storefront: the metric describes behavior in the cart and is compared with the price tags on the site.
144.example:
Carts with products in the month: 18,200
Total value of items: $2,184,000 at storefront prices
Empty carts: 2,100 (not counted)

Average Cart Value = 2,184,000 / 18,200 = **$120**
144.importance:
It shows how much shoppers put in the cart with the intent to buy, before some carts drop out at checkout and payment. It reacts earlier than revenue: carts shrink or grow right away, while in revenue it shows up **only after orders are paid**.
Read it together with the average order value. If the cart is noticeably larger than the average order, small purchases reach payment more often and large ones stall: check the shipping cost, the availability of installment plans and the payment methods for large amounts. If the cart and the average order are close, checkout lets carts of any size through **equally well**, and the work should focus on what shoppers put in the cart rather than on the form. If the cart is smaller than the average order, shoppers are adding to the order during checkout itself, or most sales bypass the cart through one-click purchases.
144.not_needed: **Skip it where** the cart isn't used and an order is placed for a single product right away.
144.synonyms: Average Basket Value, Average Cart Size
144.essence_note: the more a shopper adds to the cart, the larger the order will be

145.name: Abandoned Carts
145.description: The number of carts that had a product added but never turned into an order.
145.nuances:
A cart **counts as abandoned** once the waiting period since the last action in it has expired; the store sets the length of that period. Until it runs out, the cart stays active and isn't counted, so the figure for the last day is always understated.
A cart **counts once** regardless of the number of products and payment attempts.
**If the cart is saved** in the account and the shopper comes back to it a week later and places an order, it leaves the abandoned count.
145.example:
Carts created in the week: 4,200
Orders placed from them: 1,260
Carts with the last action less than 24 hours ago: 340 (still active, not counted)

Abandoned Carts = 4,200 − 1,260 − 340 = **2,600**
145.importance: **This is the volume of demand** from shoppers who were ready to buy and stopped one step short of payment. It's the starting point for estimating how many people it even makes sense to bring back with emails and push notifications, and whether this flow is worth investing in. Without this number, abandoned cart recovery is launched blind, often to an audience too small for the messaging campaign to pay off.
145.not_needed: **Skip it where** there's no cart as such: one-click purchases, services sold through a request form, orders placed via a messaging app.
145.essence_note: the product has been chosen but no money has come in, and all the acquisition costs have already been incurred

146.name: Average Abandoned Cart Value
146.formula: Total Value of Items in Abandoned Carts / Abandoned Carts
146.description: The average value of items in one abandoned cart.
146.nuances:
The value **is based on the prices** in effect when the cart was counted as abandoned: if you recalculate at current prices, the amounts will change after every promotion.
Both parts **are calculated from the same** set of carts, with the same waiting period as in the count of abandoned carts.
**Decide** whether the amount includes shipping and whether the promo code discount is subtracted. Calculated from the value of items without shipping, the average abandoned cart value is comparable with the average order value; otherwise the comparison loses its meaning.
Amounts **are based on storefront prices**, as with the Average Cart Value: both metrics describe shopper behavior and are compared with each other.
146.example:
Abandoned carts in the week: 2,600
Total value of items in them: $286,000 at storefront prices
Shipping cost: not included

Average Abandoned Cart Value = 286,000 / 2,600 = **$110**
146.importance:
**It determines** how much one recovered shopper is worth, and so which recovery channel to use: a call from an agent won't pay off for a cheap cart but will for an expensive one.
**Read it together** with the Average Cart Value. If the carts counted in [[Abandoned Carts→oformlenie_zakaza/broshennye_korziny]] are noticeably more expensive than average, the size of the total is what stops shoppers: check the shipping cost, whether installment plans are available, and whether shoppers trust the payment process. If they're cheaper than average, shoppers are abandoning impulse purchases whose total is comparable to the shipping cost, and the fix lies in the free shipping threshold. If the amounts are close, the drop-off isn't about money, and the cause lies in the checkout form itself.
146.not_needed: **Skip it when** there's no cart or traffic is low: with only a few abandoned carts, one large cart drives the average.
146.essence_note: the abandoned cart value alone doesn't tell you whether things are good or bad: expensive abandoned carts are big losses, while cheap ones mean small purchases don't turn into orders

147.name: Cart Actions per Session
147.formula: Cart Actions / Sessions with the Cart Opened
147.description: How many actions, on average, a shopper takes in the cart per session: additions, removals, quantity changes, promo code applications.
147.nuances:
**Define the list of events** that count as actions in advance. If scrolling or hovering is included, the average grows and stops being comparable from month to month: the list of events changes rather than shopper behavior.
**The denominator is sessions** where the cart was opened at least once, rather than all site sessions.
Automatic system actions (price recalculation, auto-applied loyalty points) **don't go into the numerator**.
147.example:
Sessions with the cart opened in the month: 18,400
Product additions: 26,100
Product removals: 9,800
Quantity changes: 7,300
Promo code applications: 2,200

Cart Actions per Session = (26,100 + 9,800 + 7,300 + 2,200) / 18,400 = **2.5**
147.importance: **The number of actions shows** how easy it is for a shopper to put together the right set of products. An increase means the shopper has to keep redoing things in the cart: remove a product, add it back, change quantities, try codes. The metric catches this before conversion drops and points to which session recordings to watch. On its own, it doesn't say what exactly gets in the way: break it down to see which actions increased.
147.not_needed: **Skip it when** traffic is low: with few sessions a month, a handful of active shoppers makes the average jump.
147.essence_note: few actions mean the cart isn't being reviewed; too many mean the person is getting confused and putting off the order

148.name: Cart View Rate
148.formula: (Sessions with Cart Views / Sessions with Cart Additions) × 100
148.description: The share of sessions with a product added to the cart in which the shopper then opened the cart itself.
148.nuances:
Both cart additions and cart views **are counted by session**: a shopper who added several products in one session counts as one addition rather than several; otherwise the denominator swells and the result comes out lower than it really is.
Opening a slide-out cart panel **counts as a view just like** a separate cart page, if the shopper can go to checkout from it.
**Sessions** where the cart opened automatically right after a product was added are kept separate from sessions where the shopper opened the cart deliberately: with auto-open, the metric hits 100% and loses its meaning.
148.example:
Sessions with a product added to the cart: 21,300
Of those, sessions with the cart opened, as counted in [[Sessions with Cart Views→oformlenie_zakaza/prosmotr_korziny]]: 14,800
Total add-to-cart events: 38,700 (not the denominator)

Cart View Rate = 14,800 / 21,300 × 100 = **69%**
148.importance: **The gap between adding** to the cart and opening it shows how many people use the cart as a save-for-later list: they add something and leave to think it over. This share is used to decide whether a separate wishlist is needed and whether to send reminders about what's in the cart. Without it, everyone who added a product is wrongly treated as ready to buy, and the revenue forecast is inflated.
148.not_needed: **Skip it where** the cart opens automatically whenever a product is added and there's no way to stay on the product list page.
148.essence_note: a shopper won't place an order without opening the cart

149.name: Average Cart View Duration
149.formula: Total Cart View Time / Cart Views
149.description: How much time, on average, a shopper spends in the cart per view.
149.nuances:
The numerator and denominator **are calculated from the same** set of views: if time is summed over all cart opens while the denominator counts sessions, the average is inflated.
The measurement method determines whether the last view in a session is included in the calculation. Where duration **is calculated as the time until** the next event, the last view has no next event to measure against, so such views are either excluded from both the numerator and the denominator or left in the denominator with zero, and then the average is understated. Systems that track tab activity give a time for the last view too, and the issue goes away.
The upper cutoff **is set in advance**: a single tab left open for a long time skews the average for the whole sample.
149.example:
Measured as the time until the next event

Cart views with measured time: 11,200
Total time: 504,000 seconds
Last views in a session with no measured duration: 3,600 (excluded from both parts)
Views longer than the upper cutoff: 90 (capped at the cutoff)

Average Cart View Duration = 504,000 / 11,200 = **45 seconds**

Keeping the same 3,600 views in the denominator with zero time gives 34 seconds: the difference comes entirely from the counting rule rather than from shopper behavior.
149.importance: **Lingering in** the cart means the person is doing the math: comparing the total, looking for shipping terms, trying to figure out the delivery time. The metric shows where the page itself lacks information, and it's used to check whether a change helped. Too short a time is a signal too: someone opened the cart, saw the total and closed it right away.
149.not_needed: **Skip it** when the cart opens as a slide-out panel over the product list: time on it is measured inaccurately because the page doesn't reload.
149.synonyms: Time in Cart, Time on Cart Page
149.essence_note: too short means the cart was closed without really looking at it; too long means the person is hesitating and doing the math

150.name: Placed Orders
150.description: The number of orders that shoppers successfully placed and submitted for processing.
150.nuances:
An order **counts as placed at** the moment checkout is confirmed rather than when the money arrives. With payment on delivery, the order counts right away.
An order **counts as one regardless** of how many items it contains.
**Cancellations don't reduce the count**, even if the order was canceled the same day. Placement is an event that has already happened; cancellation comes after it and has its own metric on the Orders map. If you subtract cancellations here, the number stops matching the checkout funnel: the shopper completed checkout, but the order is missing from the count.
Test orders and duplicates from clicking the button again **are excluded**.
150.example:
Successful checkout confirmations in March: 3,180
Test orders: 12 (not counted)
Duplicates from repeated clicks: 28 (not counted)
Unpaid orders with online payment: 240 (counted, checkout is complete)
Canceled the same day: 95 (counted, the order was placed)

Placed Orders = 3,180 − 12 − 28 = **3,140**
150.importance: **This is the basis** for half the map: the average order value, [[Cost per Placed Order→oformlenie_zakaza/stoimost_zakaza]] and all the checkout conversion rates are calculated from it. An error here distorts all the other numbers, and nothing in them reveals it. Warehouse workload, packaging purchases and courier shifts are planned from the absolute number of orders.
150.essence_note: warehouse work starts with this request, even though the money comes in one step later

151.name: Payment Method Selection Rate
151.formula:
Multi-step checkout: (Payment Method Selections / Contact Info Completions) × 100
One-page checkout: (Payment Method Selections / Sessions with Checkout Starts) × 100
151.description: The share of checkouts where the shopper got as far as selecting a payment method, among those where they filled in their contact details.
151.nuances:
The formula depends on how the checkout is built. In a **multi-step** checkout, where screens follow one another, the denominator is the count at the previous step, and the metric shows the loss at this particular transition. In a **one-page** checkout, where all fields are on one screen, steps aren't tracked as separate events: the denominator is started checkouts, and the numerator is sessions where the relevant section is completed. The second version answers a different question: “how many got to this part of the form at all” rather than “how many were lost at the transition.”
The versions aren't mixed or compared with each other: with one-page counting, the product of the step conversion rates won't give the Checkout Conversion Rate, because all the shares **are calculated from the same** base.
Both contact info completion and payment selection **are counted by checkout session**: each session counts once, even if the shopper went back and changed their choice.
If the payment method is preselected by default and requires no action, the step **is recorded when the shopper moves on** from the payment screen; otherwise the conversion rate will be close to 100% and the step will tell you nothing.
151.example:
Multi-step checkout

Checkouts with contact details completed: 7,410
Of those, reached payment method selection: 5,120

Payment Method Selection Rate = 5,120 / 7,410 × 100 = **69%**

In a one-page checkout, the same 5,120 would be divided by 9,500 started checkouts and give 54%: a different base and a different question.
151.importance: **It shows** how many shoppers don't get to payment after already leaving their details: these are people who, on paper, agreed to buy and still left. A drop here means something on the way from contact details to payment is putting people off, and it's this part of the form that needs examining rather than the cart or product prices.
151.not_needed: **Skip it when** only one payment method is available: there's nothing to choose from, and the transition becomes a formality.
151.essence_note: a shopper who doesn't get to payment won't pay for the order

152.name: Contact Info Completion Rate
152.formula: (Contact Info Completions / Sessions with Checkout Starts) × 100
152.description: The share of checkouts where the shopper filled in their contact details, among all started checkouts.
152.nuances:
**The formula is the same for** any checkout design: this is the first step of checkout, and its denominator is started checkouts in both the multi-step and the one-page version.
Both started checkouts and completed contact details **are counted by checkout session**, so the numerator doesn't exceed the denominator.
Completion **is recorded when the shopper successfully** advances to the next step, and in a one-page checkout, when the block's fields are accepted without errors: otherwise the numerator will include people who started typing and gave up.
Logged-in shoppers with prefilled details **count as completions** if the form accepted the details without edits.
152.example:
Started checkouts in the month: 9,500
Checkouts where contact details were accepted and the step completed: 7,410
Checkouts where details were entered but the step wasn't completed: 620 (not counted)

Contact Info Completion Rate = 7,410 / 9,500 × 100 = **78%**
152.importance: **The first step of checkout** is where mandatory registration, an SMS code requirement and requests for unnecessary data come to the surface. This metric is used to decide whether to enable guest checkout. A drop at the first step means the money spent on all the traffic further up the funnel was wasted.
152.not_needed: **Skip it** when contact details are collected after payment or pulled from the account without a separate step.
152.essence_note: an order can't be placed without contact details

153.name: Promo Codes Applied
153.description: The number of promo code applications at checkout: the shopper entered a code and applied it. It's counted at the checkout stage, before payment.
153.nuances:
The event **is recorded when a code is applied**, whether it worked or was rejected. Success is used to break the metric down rather than as a condition for being counted: that way you see both the demand for discounts and the share of codes that didn't work.
An application **counts as successful** if the shopper got the promised benefit. The benefit doesn't always change the item total: a code can give free shipping, a gift or a sample, and such applications count the same as a price discount.
Swapping one code for another within one checkout **counts as one application**: otherwise trying code after code inflates the number.
**The metric counts events** rather than money: Orders with Promo Code and Discounts on their own maps show how many discounts were actually given and their total value.
153.example:
Code applications in the month: 3,400
Of those, swaps to another code in the same checkout: 880 (counted once per checkout)

Promo Codes Applied = 3,400 − 880 = **2,520**

Broken down by success: 2,090 worked, 430 were rejected. Rejected applications stay in the total, and they show which codes don't work on the intended products.
153.importance: **It shows demand for discounts**: how many times shoppers try to apply a code at all. The number is compared with the number of codes sent out to judge the return on a promotion and avoid rerunning it when it doesn't pay off. Broken down by success, the same number reveals technical problems: codes that don't work on the intended products, or conditions the messaging campaign didn't mention. The signal comes right away, before it's known how many of these checkouts will turn into orders.
153.not_needed: **Skip it** when there are no promo codes and the price is the same for all shoppers.
153.essence_note: a promo code is often the very reason to complete the order

154.name: Share of Checkouts with Promo Code
154.formula: (Checkouts with a Promo Code Applied / Sessions with Checkout Starts) × 100
154.description: The share of started checkouts in which the shopper applied a promo code. It's counted by checkouts rather than orders: the checkout may not have reached payment.
154.nuances:
The base is checkouts rather than orders: a promo code applied in a checkout the shopper abandoned **counts here the same** as one applied in a checkout that ended in an order. The share of orders with a promo code is calculated separately, on the Orders map, and one can't stand in for the other.
**The numerator includes** checkouts where a code was applied, whether it worked or was rejected: success is tracked as a breakdown, as in Promo Codes Applied. For this metric, a checkout where the shopper wanted a discount and didn't get it is just as much a sign of demand for discounts.
A checkout with a promo code **counts once**, even if the shopper entered several codes in a row or swapped one for another.
154.example:
Started checkouts in the month: 9,500
Checkouts with a code applied: 2,380
Of those, reached order placement: 1,520 (doesn't affect the calculation)

Share of Checkouts with Promo Code = 2,380 / 9,500 × 100 = **25%**

Broken down by success: the code worked in 2,090 checkouts and was rejected in 290. The second group shows how many shoppers counted on a discount and didn't get it.
154.importance: **This percentage shows** what share of purchases doesn't happen at all without a discount, and the decision to expand or wind down promo campaigns depends on it. If the share grows while the number of orders doesn't, the codes have leaked to coupon sites: people who would have bought anyway get the discount, and margin drops with nothing to show for it.
154.not_needed: **Skip it** when there are no promo codes at all or the price is always the same for everyone.
154.synonyms: Promo Code Usage Rate, Coupon Usage Rate
154.essence_note: a promo code nudges shoppers toward an order, but if it shows up in almost every checkout, the company is giving discounts to people who would have bought anyway

155.name: Cost per Placed Order
155.description: The average marketing spend per placed order.
155.nuances:
**Define** in advance what goes into spend: only paid ad placements, or also agency fees, team salaries and creative production. The broader set gives a noticeably higher number, yet both versions go by the same name, so lock in the set and state it next to the result.
Spend and orders **are measured over the same** period. With a long decision cycle, some of a month's orders come from the previous month's advertising, and over short windows the number jumps.
Orders **count as one regardless** of the number of items.
**Decide** whether organic orders stay in the denominator. If they do, the metric shows the overall cost of an order for the business; if not, the efficiency of paid channels. Both versions make sense, but they answer different questions and go by the same name, so lock in the choice and state it next to the result.
155.example:
Marketing spend in March: $68,800
Orders placed: 4,300
Of those, organic: 1,500 (stay in the denominator)

Cost per Placed Order = 68,800 / 4,300 = **$16**

Excluding organic orders gives $24.57: that's the cost per order from paid channels, a separate version that shouldn't be swapped in for this one.
155.importance: **Comparing it with the margin** per order shows whether the store makes money on advertising or loses money on every purchase. This number sets the bid ceiling in auction-based channels and the budget for the next month. A mistake in what goes into spend keeps you buying unprofitable traffic for a long time, because the report looks fine all the while.
155.not_needed: **Skip it** when there's no paid traffic and orders come from organic traffic, repeat purchases and word of mouth.
155.essence_note: the more it costs to get a shopper to place an order, the less of the order's margin is left

156.name: Required Checkout Fields
156.formula: Number of required fields in the checkout form
156.description: How many fields a shopper must fill in to get through checkout from the first screen to the confirm button.
156.nuances:
**Only required fields count**: those without which the form won't submit. Optional ones (order notes, middle name) aren't counted.
Fields the system fills in automatically for a logged-in shopper **aren't counted**: guests and registered shoppers have different numbers of fields, and each number is recorded separately.
Consent checkboxes and SMS code verification **count as fields** if the form can't be submitted without them.
156.example:
Name, phone, email: 3
Street address, apartment, city, ZIP code: 4
Delivery method selection: 1
Payment method selection: 1
Consent to data processing: 1
Order notes: 0 (optional, not counted)

Required Checkout Fields = **10**
156.importance: Every required field costs some orders, so form length explains what a button redesign doesn't. **Shorter doesn't mean** better, though: data removed from the form doesn't disappear; it has to be collected later by phone or email, where some orders are lost as well. On top of that, orders can't be delivered without an address, and the share of fake orders grows without confirmation. The point of measuring is to make deliberate tradeoffs: for every field, it should be clear what it adds and what it costs. Without this number, the form grows on its own as each department asks to add just one more field.
156.not_needed: **Skip it** when checkout doesn't go through a form: voice orders, orders via messages, one-click purchases with saved details.
156.synonyms: Checkout Form Length, Checkout Form Fields
156.essence_note: without the necessary data an order can't be fulfilled, while every extra field loses some shoppers

157.name: Cart-to-Checkout Rate
157.formula: (Sessions with Checkout Starts / Sessions with Cart Views) × 100
157.description: The share of cart views after which the shopper started checkout.
157.nuances:
Both cart views and started checkouts **are counted by session**: a shopper who went to the cart several times in one session and opened the checkout form twice counts as one view and one checkout.
The start of checkout is either a click on the checkout button or the loading of the first form screen, the same as in [[Sessions with Checkout Starts→oformlenie_zakaza/chekaut_nachat]]. If you use the screen load, losses at the transition (errors, slow loading) are reflected in this conversion rate and lower it. If you use the click, they drop out of sight completely, because the next funnel step **is calculated from** those who clicked.
One-click purchases that bypass the cart **are excluded from both** sides of the calculation.
157.example:
Sessions with a cart view in the month: 14,800
Clicks on the “Checkout” button: 10,200
First form screen loads: 9,800, including 300 returns to the form in the same session

Cart-to-Checkout Rate = 9,500 / 14,800 × 100 = **64%**

The gap between 10,200 clicks and 9,800 loads is 400 sessions lost to a technical error at the transition: the form didn't open.
157.importance: **This is where the shopper first sees** the total and decides whether to buy at all. A drop in this conversion rate means something in the cart is putting people off: an unexpected shipping cost, an unavailable product, mandatory registration up front. This transition gives the fastest gain in orders from existing traffic, because these shoppers have already shown purchase intent.
157.not_needed: **Skip it** when the cart is skipped and checkout starts right from the product page.
157.essence_note: until checkout starts, there will be no order

158.name: Checkout Conversion Rate
158.description: The share of started checkouts that ended with a placed order.
158.nuances:
Both started checkouts and placed orders **are counted by checkout session**: the start and the completion must belong to the same session.
**If a shopper abandons** checkout and comes back the next day, that's two started checkouts and one order: the metric understates the real end-to-end result.
**An order counts** when checkout is confirmed, as in the step-by-step checkout conversion rates.
The product of the step conversion rates **matches this** metric only in a multi-step checkout. In a one-page checkout, the step conversion rates use the same denominator and can't be multiplied together: there, this metric is the only one that describes the form as a whole.
158.example:
Started checkouts in the month: 9,500
Orders placed: 4,300

Checkout Conversion Rate = 4,300 / 9,500 × 100 = **45%**

The product of the step conversion rates gives the same number: 78% × 69% × 84% ≈ 45%.
158.importance:
A single number that shows the overall state of the checkout form and whether it's worth reworking. It's what you compare before and after any checkout change. Read it **only together with** the step conversion rates: the total may not move when one step drops and another grows, and then the metric shows nothing even though a lot has changed inside the form. The reverse also holds: a step can improve while the completion rate falls, if drop-off shifts to a later checkout step.
**Compare it with** the store's own history rather than with other stores' numbers: the level depends on what counts as the start of checkout, and for another store that may be a different event.
158.not_needed: **Skip it for** one-click purchases and orders placed via messages: checkout isn't split into a start and a completion, and there's no step between them.
158.essence_note: at this step the person has already decided to buy, and everyone who leaves is a lost order

159.name: Average Selling Price (ASP)
159.description: The average price at which one unit of goods sells.
159.nuances:
Revenue **is taken after discounts** and net of returns: this is the money actually received.
GMV can't be used here: it's based on prices before discounts, and the average price comes out inflated. The denominator **matches the number** of units sold: returns are subtracted from both parts; otherwise the price is distorted.
Goods sold by the piece and by weight **are calculated separately**: dividing dollars by the sum of units and pounds gives a number that isn't the price of anything.
The metric **changes with both** prices and the sales mix: a shift in demand toward the cheaper tier lowers the average price while price tags stay the same.
159.example:
Revenue from goods sold by the piece in March: $416,000
Goods sold by the piece: 12,400 units (net of returns)

Average price = 416,000 / 12,400 = **$33.55**

Goods sold by weight, calculated separately: $47,880 for 7,600 lb = $6.30 per lb

Using GMV of $496,000 instead of revenue gives $40: that's the price before discounts rather than the actual price.
159.importance: It breaks revenue growth down **into two causes**: selling at higher prices or selling more. If revenue grows while the average price falls, discounts and cheaper products are propping up volume, and margin quietly shrinks. The average price is also needed to calculate average order value from the number of units per order.
159.not_needed: Skip it for a **highly diverse assortment** without a breakdown by category: an average price across a nail and a machine tool describes neither.
159.synonyms: Average Unit Price, Average Price per Unit
159.essence_note: the higher the price a unit sells for, the more money the same sale brings

160.name: Units Sold
160.description: How many units of goods were sold during the period.
160.nuances:
Returns **are subtracted**: the metric counts the volume that actually stayed with customers; otherwise it diverges from revenue, which has returns subtracted.
Goods sold by the piece and by weight **aren't added together**: pounds and pieces are different units, and a combined total makes no sense.
Items sold by weight **are counted on a separate line** in pounds, or converted to pieces using the pack size if it's fixed.
Write-offs, spoilage, transfers between stores and items issued to employees **aren't included** in sales.
A product **is assigned to the period** by the date of sale to the customer.
160.example:
Goods sold by the piece in March: 12,620 units
Returned: 220 units
Written off and spoiled: 140 units (not counted)
Sold by weight: 7,600 lb (on a separate line)

Units sold = 12,620 − 220 = **12,400 units** and **7,600 lb**

Adding pieces and pounds together gives 20,000 “units”: a number with no meaning behind it.
160.importance: The physical volume of sales, independent of prices and discounts: when revenue grows while units stay flat, the growth is entirely price-driven and will hit a ceiling. This number **is the basis for the average price**, the average unit cost and sales per product, so a discrepancy in the rules for counting it distorts the whole map.
160.synonyms: Quantity Sold, Unit Sales, Sales Volume
160.essence_note: in units, demand shows up without the price distortion built into revenue

161.name: Line Items per Order
161.formula: Product Lines in Paid Orders Not Returned in Full / [[Paid Orders→vyruchka/oplachennye_zakazy]] Not Returned in Full
161.description: How many different products one order contains on average.
161.nuances:
**Unique products are counted** in an order rather than units: five identical bottles in an order are one product. Units in the numerator give [[Units per Order→assortiment/srednee_kolichestvo_edinic_v_zakaze]], a different number with a different meaning.
A product **is counted as an order line**, that is, as an SKU: two pack sizes of one item are two products, and two sizes of one model are also two. An extra size ordered to try on drops out of the calculation when it's returned.
Lines of one SKU in an order **count as one line**: the register and the accounting system often split an SKU into separate lines, one per unit-level tracking code, or by price in a “buy one, get one” promotion, including a zero-price line.
Shipping, packaging and service fee lines **don't go into the numerator**: there's no product in them.
**The orders are the same** as in [[Average Order Value (AOV)→zakazy/sredniy_chek_aov]]: paid, excluding canceled, refused or unclaimed, and fully returned orders. A product that was returned in full from an order is also removed from the numerator, while a partially returned one stays. Otherwise basket breadth and order value are calculated from different orders. Return receipts aren't counted as separate orders: they're used only to remove lines and orders returned in full.
An order is the cart the customer checked out: if the system splits it into orders by warehouse, there are more orders with fewer products in each.
An order is counted **by the order date**. The monthly number becomes final after the return window closes and the last orders are delivered: if one line item from an order is returned, breadth goes down; if a single-item order is returned in full, it goes up.
161.example:
Canceled, refused or unclaimed, and fully returned orders for the month: 320 (neither they nor their lines are counted)
Paid orders in the calculation: 4,800
Lines in them, excluding products returned in full: 8,640
Total units of goods in them: 12,000, or 2.5 units per order (a different quantity)

Line items per order = 8,640 / 4,800 = **1.8 line items**

The difference from units per order shows that customers buy several units of the same product at a time. For goods sold by the piece: 1.8 line items × 1.39 units per line = 2.5 units per order.

Counting the shipping line, which appears in every order, gives 13,440 / 4,800 = 2.8: every order gets an extra line item.
161.importance: Basket breadth: it grows with recommendations, merchandising and bundles, while units per order grow with “buy one, get one free” promotions. When [[Average Order Value (AOV)→zakazy/sredniy_chek_aov]] rises **only because of** price while the number of products stays flat, customers haven't started buying more distinct products, and the growth rests on price: price increases or a shift toward more expensive items. The difference between this metric and Units per Order shows what exactly worked in a promotion.
161.not_needed: Skip it when selling single expensive items: an order **almost always has one line item**. Also skip it for marketplace data: the seller sees shipments rather than the customer's cart, and on some marketplaces each unit ships as a separate order.
161.essence_note: the more distinct products people buy at once, the higher the order value without discounts

162.name: Average Unit Cost
162.formula: Cost of Goods Sold / Units Sold
162.description: How much one unit of goods sold costs the company on average.
162.nuances:
Cost **is taken as of** the time of sale, using the company's inventory costing method: FIFO and weighted average give different numbers when purchase prices fluctuate, and the method can't change within the comparison period.
**Using the current purchase price** instead of the cost of goods sold breaks comparability with revenue for the same period.
The cost **includes direct costs** of shipping goods to the warehouse and customs duties: without them, the markup looks higher than it really is.
Overhead, salaries and rent aren't allocated. The denominator **matches the number** of units sold: returns are subtracted, goods sold by the piece and by weight are counted separately, and the cost per pound and per unit aren't averaged together.
162.example:
Cost of goods sold by the piece in March: $173,600
Goods sold by the piece: 12,400 units (net of returns)

Average unit cost = 173,600 / 12,400 = **$14 per unit**

Goods sold by weight are calculated separately: $34,200 for 7,600 lb = $4.50 per lb.
162.importance: **The basis for pricing** and for negotiations with suppliers: a rising average unit cost with unchanged selling prices eats into margin, and revenue won't show it. Comparing the trends in unit cost and average price shows whether the company manages to pass higher purchase costs through to its prices or absorbs them out of its own profit.
162.not_needed: Skip it in **consignment selling** and in marketplace models where the seller doesn't buy the goods: the goods aren't purchased, so the seller has no cost of goods.
162.synonyms: Cost per Unit, Average Cost per Unit
162.essence_note: the less a unit costs, the more the company keeps from selling it

163.name: Gross Merchandise Value (GMV)
163.description: The value of all goods sold at base prices, before discounts and returns.
163.nuances:
**Use the item's base price** from the accounting system at the time of sale, rather than the final line amount on the receipt: the receipt already has the discount subtracted, and using it gives revenue rather than gross merchandise value.
Returns **aren't subtracted**: that's what sets it apart from revenue, which goes into [[Average Selling Price (ASP)→assortiment/srednyaya_cena_tovara]] with discounts and returns already subtracted.
163.example:
Goods sold by the piece in March: 12,620 units (returns not subtracted)
Total at base prices: $496,000
Discounts given: $62,000 (not subtracted)
Returned: $18,000, or 220 units (not subtracted)

GMV = **$496,000**

Revenue for the same March = 496,000 − 62,000 − 18,000 = $416,000: two different numbers that are easy to confuse. GMV shows sales volume, and revenue shows the money the company receives.

Metrics calculated after returns have a different denominator: 12,620 − 220 = 12,400 units.
163.importance: **It shows sales potential before** discounts and returns cut into it. The gap between GMV and revenue is the cost of the promotion policy in dollars: if it grows, sales depend on discounts, and volume will drop off once the discounts end. This gap is used to decide whether to reduce promotion depth.
163.not_needed: **Skip it where** there are no discounts and goods sell at list price: GMV will match revenue, and revenue is the more useful of the two.
163.essence_note: this is the value of goods sold, and its growth at unchanged prices means more sales

164.name: Average Product Rating
164.formula:
Per product: Σ Product Ratings / Number of Product Ratings
Across the assortment: Σ Average Product Ratings / Number of Products with Ratings
164.description: The average rating customers give to products.
164.nuances:
Across the assortment, **it's the average of** per-product averages rather than the average of all ratings pooled together: in the second case, a few popular products with thousands of reviews outweigh the rest of the assortment, and the rating no longer describes a typical product.
**Decide on the calculation window**. The cumulative rating is what the shopper sees on the product page. A rating based only on ratings from the period shows how the product is perceived now, and it's needed when something about the product has changed: the cumulative rating moves slowly, old ratings outweigh new ones, and it can't tell you whether things got better.
Products without ratings **aren't included** in the denominator: they have no average to average.
**It's measured in scale points** rather than as a count.
164.example:
Product A: 1,200 ratings, average 4.8
Product B: 12 ratings, average 3.5
Product C: 40 ratings, average 4.2

Assortment average = (4.8 + 3.5 + 4.2) / 3 = **4.2 points**

Pooling all 1,252 ratings together gives 4.77: Product A's rating almost entirely determined the result.
164.importance: **The rating drives both** catalog sorting and the shopper's decision at the moment of choice, so a drop hits conversion before it hits revenue. The average of averages catches problem items that get lost in the pooled number: while the flagship holds 4.8, ten products rated 3.2 rack up returns and complaints, and the overall figure doesn't show it. The metric is used to decide which products to stop promoting and for which ones to change suppliers.
164.not_needed: **Skip it where** ratings aren't collected, and in B2B supply.
164.synonyms: Average Star Rating, Average Review Rating
164.essence_note: the lower the ratings across the assortment, the harder it is to sell it as a whole

165.name: Average Units Sold per Product
165.formula: Units Sold / Number of Active Products
165.description: How many units sell per product on average.
165.nuances:
**Denominator**: [[Active Products→assortiment/aktivnye_tovary]], that is, products that sold during the period: dividing by the whole assortment makes the metric fall simply because the assortment expands, and sales growth gets masked by new product launches.
The share of items with no sales is tracked separately. Goods sold by the piece and by weight **are calculated separately**: pounds and pieces can't be added together in the numerator, and an average over a mix of the two makes no sense.
A product **is counted at the** product level: sales of all variants roll up to the product.
**Returns are subtracted from the numerator**, as in Units Sold.
165.example:
Goods sold by the piece in March: 12,400 units (net of returns)
Active products sold by the piece: 2,480

Sales per product = 12,400 / 2,480 = **5 units**

Items sold by weight are calculated separately: 7,600 lb across 250 active products = 30.4 lb per item

Dividing by all 4,200 products in the assortment gives 3 units: the number falls when new products launch, even if sales don't change.
165.importance: **It shows how much a typical item sells** and answers whether to widen the assortment or deepen it. When sales per item fall as the number of products grows, the new products split existing demand instead of bringing their own: revenue stays flat while warehouse space, purchase volumes and shelf space grow. The same number goes into calculating the minimum purchase quantity.
165.not_needed: **Skip it with** an assortment of categories that differ widely in price and turnover: a single average across consumables and major appliances describes neither.
165.synonyms: Sales per SKU, Units per SKU
165.essence_note: the more a single item sells, the fewer items you need to carry for the same revenue

166.name: Customer Penetration Rate by Product
166.formula: (Customers Who Bought the Product / All Customers) × 100
166.description: The share of customers who bought a specific product.
166.nuances:
**Denominator**: customers who made a purchase during the period, the same as in the map's other customer metrics: the whole base, including inactive customers, understates the share, and the older the company, the more it does.
A customer **counts once**, however many times they bought the product: that's the difference from the share of orders with the product, where the same customer can account for several orders. It's calculated for each product separately.
Receipts **without customer identification** go into neither the numerator nor the denominator.
166.example:
Customers with purchases in March: 8,400
Bought the product at least once: 588 customers
Orders with this product: 940 (some bought it more than once)

Customer penetration = 588 / 8,400 × 100 = **7%**

Using 940 orders instead of 588 people gives 11%: repeat purchases are counted as different customers.
166.importance: **It separates two different cases**: many people buy the product once, or a few buy it regularly. A small share of customers combined with a high share of orders means a narrow core of loyal buyers, and spending on broad-audience advertising for such a product makes no sense. The metric also shows potential: if a tenth of the customer base knows the product, the other nine-tenths haven't tried it yet.
166.not_needed: **Skip it in brick-and-mortar** retail without a loyalty program: customers can't be told apart.
166.essence_note: the larger the share of customers who buy this item, the broader its demand

167.name: Assortment Share per Customer
167.formula: (Average Unique Products per Customer / Total Products) × 100
167.description: What share of the assortment one customer buys on average.
167.nuances:
Average unique products per customer **is calculated as the sum** of each customer's unique product count divided by the number of customers: without averaging across customers, you get one buyer's share of the assortment rather than the average.
Customers who bought during the period and products available for sale in it **come from the same** window: a customer couldn't have bought a product that wasn't in the assortment.
A product **is counted at the** product level; repeat purchases of the same product count once.
The larger the assortment, the smaller the numbers come out. To make the metric readable, it's calculated by category: the share of categories a customer bought something from gives larger, readable numbers and shows whether the customer moves around the whole catalog or stays in one corner. The category level **is the same** as in [[Total Categories→assortiment/kolichestvo_kategoriy]].
167.example:
By product
Products for sale in March: 4,200
Customers with purchases: 8,400
Sum of each customer's unique product count: 26,040

Average unique products per customer = 26,040 / 8,400 = 3.1
Penetration = 3.1 / 4,200 × 100 = **0.07%**

By category
Categories in the catalog: 186
Sum of each customer's unique category count: 20,160

Average categories per customer = 20,160 / 8,400 = 2.4
Penetration = 2.4 / 186 × 100 = **1.3%**

The same purchases, but by category the metric is readable: you can see that a customer shops in two of the catalog's 186 categories.

Calculating for a single customer who bought 12 products: 12 / 4,200 = 0.29%: that's their personal share rather than the average across the base.
167.importance: **It shows** how narrowly customers shop across the assortment: a customer may only ever see a small slice of the range and keep buying the same things. This is a direct argument for recommendations and cross-selling: growth in the metric means the customer has widened their basket rather than buying familiar items more often. When it falls, check navigation and search results first rather than purchasing.
167.not_needed: **Skip it where** customers aren't identified, and with a narrow assortment: with ten or so items, a customer buys a noticeable share of the assortment, and the metric adds nothing beyond Average Order Value (AOV).
167.essence_note: the bigger the part of the assortment one customer buys, the more they bring in with no acquisition cost

168.name: Cross-Sell Index
168.formula: (Orders with Both Products / Orders with At Least One of Them) × 100
168.alt_formula: (Orders with Both Products / Orders with the Base Product) × 100
168.description: How often two products are bought together. It's calculated either symmetrically, across all orders that include at least one product of the pair, or from a chosen base product: what share of its purchases came with the second product.
168.nuances:
The pair of products or categories **is set before the calculation**; the metric isn't calculated as a single number for the whole assortment. The level of comparison is the same on both sides: product with product or category with category; a pair of a product and a category gives parts that can't be compared.
Unit of count: the **whole** order (receipt); the number of units inside doesn't matter.
Symmetric version: the denominator is orders with at least one product of the pair. It shows the strength of the link within the pair as a single number and has no direction. The denominator **is calculated as a union** rather than a sum: an order with both products counts once; otherwise the denominator is inflated and the index understated. For a pair of products with very different popularity, this index is always low: the popular product dominates the denominator, and the link gets lost in it.
**The base-product version**: the denominator is orders with the base product. It answers what share of the base product's purchases came with the second product, and gives two different numbers: with the rare product as the base, you see that almost every purchase of it comes with the main one; with the popular product as the base, that it's more often bought without the other one. Make the base product the one whose buyers you need the answer about.
168.example:
Pair: coffee machine and capsules
Orders with the coffee machine: 420
Orders with capsules: 1,860
Orders with both: 310

Symmetric: orders with at least one = 420 + 1,860 − 310 = 1,970
Index = 310 / 1,970 × 100 = **16%**

From the coffee machine: 310 / 420 × 100 = **74%**, most coffee machine orders include capsules
From capsules: 310 / 1,860 × 100 = **17%**, capsules are more often bought on their own

Three numbers about one pair answer different questions: whether to bundle the products, whether to add capsules to the coffee machine, whether to offer the coffee machine to capsule buyers.

Adding 420 + 1,860 = 2,280 in the symmetric version without subtracting the overlap gives 14%: understated.
168.importance: **It determines** what to put in recommendations and bundles: a pair with a high index is already bought together, and a bundle works for it, while a pair with a low index needs an explanation of why the products go together. The direction suggests who to show the recommendation to: if almost every purchase of one product comes with the second while the reverse doesn't hold, the offer should go to those who bought the second. It's also an argument against delisting a C item: a product can bring in almost no revenue on its own yet drive sales of an expensive item.
168.not_needed: Skip it for an assortment of **a single category** of interchangeable products: they're bought instead of each other rather than together.
168.synonyms: Product Affinity, Co-Purchase Rate, Attach Rate
168.essence_note: the more often products are bought together, the higher the order value with no spending on new customers

169.name: Share of Positive Reviews
169.description: The share of positive reviews among all reviews received.
169.nuances:
Reviews **with 4 or 5** stars count as positive, on the same scale as in the Share of Negative Reviews: 1–2 negative, 3 neutral, 4–5 positive. Because of the neutral middle, the shares of positive and negative reviews don't add up to 100%: the remainder is the 3-star ratings.
Reviews without a rating **aren't counted**.
**Decide on the calculation window**: the share for all-time reviews describes what the shopper sees on the product page today, and the share for the period describes the mix of recent reviews. A review is assigned to a period based on its publication date.
169.example:
Reviews with a rating in March: 1,240
4–5 stars: 1,004
3 stars: 87
1–2 stars: 149

Share of positive reviews = 1,004 / 1,240 × 100 = **81%**

81% + 12% negative = 93%, and the missing 7% are neutral ratings.
169.importance: **It keeps the product's rating up**, and the rating drives both catalog sorting and the shopper's decision at the moment of choice: a drop pushes the product down in search results and cuts conversion. The trend shows whether a change of supplier or improved packaging worked: complaints go away before sales recover.
169.not_needed: Skip it when there are only a handful of reviews: the share **changes with each** new one and says nothing about the product.
169.essence_note: the higher the share of good reviews, the more readily people buy

170.name: Share of Negative Reviews
170.description: The share of negative reviews among all reviews received.
170.nuances:
Reviews **with 1 or 2** stars count as negative; 3 stars are neutral.
Reviews without a rating, **with text only**, aren't counted: classifying them as negative by their text means mixing manual labeling into a numeric metric.
**Decide on the calculation window**: the share for all-time reviews describes what the shopper sees on the product page today, and the share for the period describes the mix of recent reviews. A review is assigned to a period based on its publication date. Reviews removed by moderation drop out of both parts.
170.example:
Reviews with a rating in March: 1,240
Of those, 1–2 stars: 149
3 stars: 87 (neutral, not in the numerator)
Reviews without a rating, text only: 60 (not counted at all)

Share of negative reviews = 149 / 1,240 × 100 = **12%**
170.importance: **The first signal that** something went wrong with the product or delivery: negative reviews come in before sales drop and returns pile up. A growing share for a specific product means it's time to stop promoting the item and take it up with the supplier before the rating drags the whole category down.
170.not_needed: **Skip it** when there are only a handful of reviews: with ten or so opinions, each new review makes the share jump.
170.essence_note: a negative review scares off the next customers and drags the product's rating down

171.name: Reviews per Customer
171.formula: Number of Reviews / Number of Customers
171.description: How many reviews there are per customer on average. Like the Share of Customers with Reviews, it's calculated either per period, for the cohort of customers who bought during the period, or cumulatively, across the whole customer base.
171.nuances:
**Use the same calculation version** as the one chosen for the Share of Customers with Reviews; otherwise the two metrics can no longer be read together. Period-based: customers who bought during the period and all reviews from that cohort, regardless of publication date. Cumulative: the entire customer base to date and all its reviews.
In the period-based version, **a cohort is required**: if the numerator is taken by publication date and the denominator by purchase date, the two sets drift apart. The most recent period is always undercounted, since reviews for it are still coming in.
The denominator includes all customers rather than **only those who wrote** reviews: dividing by authors gives the average number of reviews per active author rather than per customer.
Purchases **without customer identification** go into neither part.
171.example:
Period-based, for the March cohort
Bought in March and identified: 8,400 customers
Reviews from them: 402 (some published in April)
Left at least one review: 336 customers

Reviews per customer = 402 / 8,400 = **0.05**

Cumulative
Customers in the base to date: 96,000
Reviews from them: 12,200

Reviews per customer = 12,200 / 96,000 = **0.13**

Dividing 402 by the 336 customers who wrote reviews gives 1.2: that's author activity rather than coverage of the customer base.
171.importance: Together with the Share of Customers with Reviews, it **shows how reviews are spread across customers**: if the share of customers who write is low and reviews per customer are high, all the content comes from a small group of people, and it doesn't reflect what customers think. The metric is used to judge whether a review incentive program brings in new authors or just boosts activity among the same people.
171.not_needed: **Skip it where** customers can't be identified: anonymous receipts give no denominator.
171.essence_note: the more reviews each customer writes, the cheaper it is to fill product pages with content

172.name: Reviews per Product
172.formula: Number of Reviews / Number of Products Available for Sale
172.description: How many reviews one product has accumulated on average.
172.nuances:
**Decide on the calculation window**. Reviews accumulated to date show how convincing the product page looks now: those are what the shopper sees on it. Reviews for a chosen period show the current flow of reviews and the reaction to changes, such as a new supplier, improved packaging or a rewritten product page; the cumulative number hides that kind of reaction.
Denominator: all products for sale rather than **only products with** reviews. Dividing by products with reviews gives the depth of coverage on products that already have reviews, and assortment coverage stays out of view.
A product **is counted at the same** level as in [[Total Products→assortiment/obschee_kolichestvo_tovarov]]. Reviews of variants that aren't split out as separate products go to the parent product.
**In the cumulative version**, the metric grows over time on its own: an older product has more reviews simply because it's been on sale longer, and new products pull the average down.
172.example:
Products for sale: 4,200
Reviews accumulated on them: 8,900
Products with at least one review: 1,176

Reviews per product = 8,900 / 4,200 = **2.1**

Dividing by the 1,176 products with reviews gives 7.6: that's the density on products that have reviews rather than across the assortment.
172.importance: **Average review density determines** how convincing a typical product page looks. For a product with one or two reviews, a single complaint wrecks the rating, so the rating is unstable and shoppers don't trust it. Together with the Share of Products with Reviews, it shows what's missing: coverage of the assortment or depth on products that already have reviews.
172.synonyms: Average Review Count, Reviews per Item
172.essence_note: the more reviews an item has, the more trust it gets and the higher it ranks in search results

173.name: Total Products
173.formula: Number of Unique Catalog Products Available for Sale
173.description: How many unique products the assortment contains.
173.nuances:
**Decide** which variants count as separate products and which stay part of one product. The test is whether customers choose between them as they would between different products. Sizes of one model usually stay one product, while colors, volumes, flavors and configurations are counted separately. The decision is made once and applies to the whole map: all the shares and averages that divide by this number depend on it.
The level **doesn't change between periods**: comparing at different levels makes assortment growth come from a rule change rather than from purchasing.
Archived and discontinued items **aren't included**; otherwise the number grows with the catalog's history rather than with the assortment.
**It's counted as of a date** rather than for a period: products are added and delisted during a period, so there's no single number for it. To evaluate a period, take the value at its end.
173.example:
Catalog as of March 31: 5,100 products
Of those, archived and discontinued: 900

If variants aren't split out: 5,100 − 900 = **4,200 products**

If colors and volumes count as separate products and sizes don't: **6,800**
If every variant counts separately, including sizes: **11,400**

All the map's shares and averages divide by the chosen number, so it's fixed before the other metrics are calculated.
173.importance: It's the denominator for almost all the shares and averages on this map: the Share of Active Products, reviews per product and sales per product **are calculated from it**. That's why an inconsistent rule (with or without the archive, products or SKUs) breaks half the map rather than one metric. On its own, the number shows how bloated the assortment is relative to what actually sells.
173.synonyms: Product Count, Assortment Size, Catalog Size
173.essence_note: the wider the choice, the better the chance the customer finds what they need and buys here

174.name: Share of Class A Products
174.description: The share of products that fall into class A by contribution to revenue.
174.nuances:
ABC is built on revenue for the period: products are sorted by revenue in descending order, **the cumulative share is calculated**, and class A is the products that fall within the first 80% of cumulative revenue, B from 80% to 95%, and C the remaining 5%.
Products with zero sales in the period **aren't classified and are excluded** from the denominator: otherwise the share of A falls because the tail of non-selling items grows rather than because sales concentrate.
**The denominator is the same** for the shares of A, B and C, so the three shares add up to 100%.
ABC **is calculated for the company** as a whole: a breakdown by store gives a different class composition, and the results can't be added up.
**The period is at least a quarter**: within a week, a random large order pushes a product that rarely sells into A.
174.example:
Products with sales for the quarter: 2,400
Revenue for the quarter: $1,200,000
Sort by revenue in descending order and add up the cumulative share
The first 80% of revenue ($960,000) is reached at the 312th product

Share of class A products = 312 / 2,400 × 100 = **13%**

Products with no sales (300 products) aren't in the denominator.
174.importance: **It shows** how many items carry the bulk of revenue and determines which items can't be allowed to go out of stock. If 80% of the money comes from 13% of the assortment, safety stock and the buyer's attention go to those items first, and the rest get whatever resources are left. Mistakes here cost the most: a stockout on a single A item hits revenue harder than delisting many C items.
174.not_needed: **Skip it with** an assortment of up to a few dozen items: class A is visible there from a simple list sorted by revenue.
174.synonyms: Share of A Items, Class A SKU Share
174.essence_note: the more items make a significant contribution to revenue, the less revenue depends on a few products

175.name: Share of Class B Products
175.description: The share of products that fall into class B by contribution to revenue.
175.nuances: The boundaries are the same as in the Share of Class A Products: class B is the products that fall between 80% and 95% of cumulative revenue. Denominator: products with sales in the period; items with zero revenue **aren't classified**.
175.example:
Products with sales for the quarter: 2,400
Products in the cumulative 80–95% revenue range: 528

Share of class B products = 528 / 2,400 × 100 = **22%**
175.importance: **A growth pipeline** and at the same time a source of future losses: some of these items grow into A, and some slide into C. Movement between B and A shows whether the promotion of new products works, and movement from B to C shows which items it's time to delist before they settle into dead stock.
175.not_needed: **Skip it with** an assortment of up to a few dozen items.
175.synonyms: Share of B Items, Class B SKU Share
175.essence_note: when the middle shrinks, there's nowhere for new leaders to come from, and when it grows, the assortment is made up of average performers with no clear leaders

176.name: Share of Class C Products
176.description: The share of products that fall into class C by contribution to revenue.
176.nuances:
Class C is the products that fall within the last 5% of cumulative revenue; the boundaries **match those of** the Share of Class A Products and the Share of Class B Products.
Products with zero sales don't fall into C: they're outside the classification and are excluded from the denominator. They're counted **separately** as inactive products; otherwise the share of C is inflated by items that never sold.
The three shares **add up to 100% by construction**.
176.example:
Products with sales for the quarter: 2,400
Class A: 312, class B: 528
Class C = 2,400 − 312 − 528 = 1,560

Share of class C products = 1,560 / 2,400 × 100 = **65%**

13% + 22% + 65% = 100%

Another 300 products never sold: they're inactive products rather than class C.
176.importance: **It measures the length of the tail** that costs money: each C item takes up warehouse space and requires purchasing and stock counts while bringing in pennies. It's used to decide what to cut at the next assortment review. Cutting everything indiscriminately is a mistake: some C items bring in traffic and complete the basket, so before delisting, an item is checked for cross-selling.
176.not_needed: **Skip it with** an assortment of up to a few dozen items.
176.synonyms: Share of C Items, Long-Tail Share
176.essence_note: the tail ties up money and shelf space while bringing in almost no revenue

177.name: Active Products
177.formula: Number of Products with Sales in the Period
177.description: The number of products that sold at least once during the period.
177.nuances:
A product **is assigned to the period** by the date of sale to the customer (receipt, shipment to the customer) rather than by the order date or the date it arrived at the warehouse.
**Decide** whether a return cancels activity. If returns aren't taken into account, the product stays active based on the sale, and the number doesn't change retroactively; if they are, a product whose only unit sold was returned drops out of the active count. Items issued to employees, spoilage and internal transfers don't count as sales either way.
**Decide on the calculation level**: for the company, a product is active if it sold anywhere; for a store, only if it sold in that store.
**The longer the period**, the more active products, so periods of different length aren't compared with each other.
177.example:
Products for sale in March: 4,200
Sold at least once: 2,730
Of those, 18 items were sold and fully returned
Issued to employees: 44 items with no sales (not counted)

Active products = **2,730**

If a return cancels activity, the same data gives 2,730 − 18 = 2,712.
177.importance: The absolute number of items that sell, **the anchor for the whole assessment** of assortment efficiency: average sales per product and the share of active products are calculated from it. When the assortment expands while this number stays flat, the expansion goes into dead stock and tied-up cash.
177.not_needed: Skip it for an **assortment of ten or so items**: which products sold is visible there from a simple list.
177.essence_note: the items that sell are the productive part of the assortment

178.name: Share of Active Products
178.description: The share of products in the assortment that sold at least once during the period.
178.nuances:
Denominator: products available for sale during the period; archived and discontinued items **are excluded**; otherwise the share falls because of the size of the archive rather than sales.
The numerator **is calculated the same way** as the [[Active Products→assortiment/aktivnye_tovary]] metric: that's where you decide whether a return cancels activity, at what level a product counts as active (company or store) and what counts as a product. The denominator uses the same unit; otherwise the share doesn't add up.
**The longer the period**, the higher the share, so periods of different length aren't compared with each other.
178.example:
Products available for sale in March: 4,200
Archived products in the catalog: 900 (not in the denominator)
Sold at least once: 2,730

Share of active products = 2,730 / 4,200 × 100 = **65%**

Using the whole catalog of 5,100 gives 54%: the difference comes entirely from the archive.
178.importance: **It shows** what part of the assortment actually works and what part just takes up shelf space and working capital. A large share of items with no sales means money is tied up in goods that don't turn over, and there's no room left for best sellers. It's used to decide what to delist at the next assortment review.
178.not_needed: Skip it for an **assortment of ten or so items**: the products with no sales are visible there in a simple list, without a percentage.
178.essence_note: an item without a single sale ties up money and space

179.name: Share of Customers with Reviews
179.description: The share of customers who have left at least one review.
179.nuances:
The metric **has two calculation versions**, and they answer different questions. Period-based: customers who bought during the period and reviews from that same cohort, regardless of when the review was published. Cumulative: the entire customer base to date and all its reviews; this share is tracked over time to see whether it grows or stays flat.
In the period-based version, **a cohort is required**: reviews come in with a lag, and if the numerator is taken by publication date and the denominator by purchase date, the two sets drift apart. The most recent period is always undercounted, since reviews for it are still coming in.
A customer with five reviews **counts once**.
Purchases **without customer identification** (no loyalty card, no account) go into neither the numerator nor the denominator.
179.example:
Period-based, for the March cohort
Bought in March and identified: 8,400 customers
Of those, left a review of their March purchase: 336 (some reviews published in April)
Total reviews from them: 402 (a customer could write several)

Share of customers with reviews = 336 / 8,400 × 100 = **4%**

Cumulative
Customers in the base to date: 96,000
Of those, left a review at least once: 7,680

Share of customers with reviews = 7,680 / 96,000 × 100 = **8%**

Dividing 402 reviews by 8,400 gives 4.8%: that's reviews per customer rather than the share of customers who wrote one.
179.importance: It shows how many people all product ratings depend on. When the share is low, the opinion of many customers is shaped by a few, and any wave of unhappy customers or fake reviews shifts the picture **as a whole**. It's also the basis for decisions on review incentives: points for a review, reminders, contests.
179.not_needed: **Skip it in brick-and-mortar** retail without a loyalty program: the shopper is anonymous, and there's no way to link them to a review.
179.essence_note: the more customers write reviews, the more convincing the product page is for future shoppers

180.name: Basket Penetration Rate by Product
180.description: The share of orders that include a specific product.
180.nuances:
**It's calculated for each** product separately, and the metric has no single number for the whole assortment. Denominator: orders from stores and channels where the product was part of the assortment. If the product was never stocked in half the stores, including their orders turns the metric into a measure of distribution breadth rather than popularity.
**Periods when the product was** out of stock aren't cut from the denominator: they're exactly the lost sales.
Unit of count: the **whole** order. The number of units of the product in an order doesn't matter: three units in one receipt count as one order.
A product **is counted at the** product level: buying any variant counts toward the product.
180.example:
The product is stocked in 12 of 17 stores
Orders in these 12 stores in March: 46,000
Orders containing the product: 3,220
Orders in the other 5 stores: 19,000 (not in the denominator)

Basket penetration = 3,220 / 46,000 × 100 = **7%**

Counting from all 65,000 orders in the chain gives 5%: the metric penalizes the product for not being stocked.
180.importance: It answers how much demand there is for a product across purchases, rather than **only in absolute** units: an item can sell few units yet show up in many orders, and delisting it will break up the basket customers are used to. The trend catches a product being displaced by a new one before it shows up in revenue. It's used to decide what goes in the checkout area and in cart recommendations.
180.not_needed: Skip it for **one-off large deals**: with few orders a month, the percentage is unstable, and a single sale makes it jump.
180.essence_note: the more often an item ends up in orders, the more it supports sales
