181.name: Share of Products with Reviews
181.description: The share of products that have at least one review.
181.nuances:
**Decide on the calculation window**: all-time reviews show assortment coverage as of today, and reviews for the period show how many products got their first review during that period.
A product **is counted at the same** level as in [[Total Products→assortiment/obschee_kolichestvo_tovarov]]. Reviews of variants that aren't split out as separate products count toward the parent product: one review is enough for a model in five sizes to enter the numerator.
**Denominator**: products available for sale during the period. Archived items won't get any more reviews, and they pull the share down.
181.example:
Products for sale: 4,200
Of those, with at least one review: 1,176
Total reviews: 8,900 (we count products, not reviews)

Share of products with reviews = 1,176 / 4,200 × 100 = **28%**

Counting each variant as a separate SKU (11,400 items) gives 10%: the same coverage in a different unit.
181.importance: A product page **without reviews converts worse**: shoppers don't want to be the first to take the risk. The share shows what part of the assortment sells without social proof and determines where to direct review collection first. If the uncovered products turn out to be best sellers, revenue is lost exactly where it matters most.
181.not_needed: **Skip it in B2B** supply and wherever reviews aren't collected at all: the numerator is always zero.
181.essence_note: a product page without reviews loses to the one next to it even at the same price

182.name: Assortment Growth Rate
182.formula: ((Products at End of Period − Products at Start of Period) / Products at Start of Period) × 100
182.description: The percentage change in the number of products in the assortment over the period.
182.nuances:
Both dates **use the same** product counting rule: catalog products available for sale, excluding the archive.
Switching levels (products or SKUs) between the two dates gives a meaningless percentage. **It's calculated from the counts** at the period boundaries, so products launched and delisted within the period don't show up in the result: when items are frequently launched and delisted, zero growth can hide a complete turnover of the assortment.
**Separately**, look at the number of items launched and delisted during the period.
182.example:
Products for sale on January 1: 3,800
Products for sale on March 31: 4,200

Growth rate = (4,200 − 3,800) / 3,800 × 100 = **+10.5%**

During the quarter, 900 products were launched and 500 delisted: the net gain is the same +400, while a fifth of the assortment was replaced, and the percentage doesn't show it.
182.importance: **When the assortment expands** faster than revenue, the gap between the two growth rates shows what breadth costs: the same money is spread across more items, inventory grows and sales per product fall. If the assortment grew 10% and revenue 2%, the new items brought in no customers and only tied up warehouse space and working capital.
182.not_needed: Skip it with a **fixed assortment**: the percentage is always close to zero.
182.synonyms: SKU Growth Rate, Catalog Growth Rate
182.essence_note: a shelf that's refreshed more often gives regular customers a reason to come back

183.name: Share of Seasonal Products
183.description: The share of the assortment whose sales are concentrated in a particular season.
183.nuances:
Seasonality **is calculated from** sales history rather than set by a checkbox on the product page: a manual flag gives a number that depends on who set it.
The threshold **is set in advance and** is the same for the whole assortment: take the share of annual revenue that comes from the three consecutive months with the highest sales and compare it with the 25% an even spread would give. For example, the threshold can be set at twice that, 50%. It can be moved, but shares of seasonal products calculated with different thresholds can't be compared.
A product needs at least two years of history: with one year, a peak can't be told apart from a one-off spike, such as a promotion or a large contract. A product **counts as seasonal** if its peak fell on the same months in both years. New products without such history drop out of both parts.
If seasonality differs by region, a product **counts as seasonal** when the condition is met for the company as a whole; otherwise the same product would land in both groups at once.
183.example:
Threshold: more than 50% of annual revenue comes from three consecutive months (even spread: 25%)
Products with at least two years of sales history: 3,800
Meet the condition in both years, with the peak in the same months: 646 products

Share of seasonal products = 646 / 3,800 × 100 = **17%**

Example for one product: patio furniture, annual revenue $80,000, of which $52,000 came in May–July. Peak share = 52,000 / 80,000 × 100 = 65%, above the threshold, so the product is seasonal.

New products without two years of history (400 products) are excluded from both the numerator and the denominator.
183.importance: **It sets** what share of the purchasing budget can't be planned from an average month. If a fifth of the assortment is seasonal, a flat purchasing plan is sure to bring overstock after the peak and a shortage before it. The metric also explains revenue dips that would otherwise be blamed on the sales team.
183.not_needed: **Skip it for an assortment** where seasonality clearly applies to everything or to nothing: a holiday decorations seller always has 100%, a fastener supplier close to zero.
183.synonyms: Seasonal SKU Share, Seasonal Assortment Share
183.essence_note: without seasonal items, the company misses the demand peak, and when there are too many, warehouse space and money sit idle in the off-season

184.name: Average Product Lifespan
184.formula: Σ(Delisting Date − Launch Date) / Number of Delisted Products
184.description: How long a product stays in the assortment on average, from launch to delisting.
184.nuances:
**It's calculated only for** products that have been delisted: for products still on sale the lifespan isn't over yet, and cutting it off at “today” understates the average, and the younger the assortment, the more it does.
The start **is the date** the product became available for sale, and the end is the date it was taken off sale or archived, rather than the date of the last sale: a product can go without sales for a long time while staying in the assortment.
A product **is counted at the** product level: delisting a single size doesn't end the product's lifespan.
The metric depends **on the company's age**: a young company can't have long lifespans, and the average is capped by how long the company has existed.
184.example:
Products delisted in the year: 640
Total time from launch to delisting: 486,400 days

Lifespan = 486,400 / 640 = **760 days (about 2 years)**

Adding the 4,200 products on sale and cutting their time off at today's date brings the average down to 430 days: their lifespan simply hasn't ended.
184.importance: **It sets the payback horizon for investment** in a product: building the product page, the photo shoot and the first purchase order have to pay off within the time the item stays in the assortment; otherwise launching new products loses money. A shorter lifespan means the assortment turns over faster, and one-off costs of launches and clearance sales go up.
184.not_needed: **Skip it in** businesses with a permanent assortment where items stay for decades: there are almost no delistings, so there's nothing to calculate from.
184.synonyms: Product Lifetime, Average Time in Assortment
184.essence_note: the longer an item sells, the more fully the investment in its launch and photo shoot pays off

185.name: Engagements per Review
185.formula: (Likes + Comments + Helpful Votes) / Number of Reviews
185.description: How many reactions one review collects on average: likes, comments and helpful votes.
185.nuances:
Denominator: all reviews for the period, including those nobody reacted to. Dividing **only by reviews** with reactions turns the metric into the average number of reactions per popular review.
**Numerator**: all reactions these reviews have collected as of the calculation date, regardless of when each reaction came. If you take reactions for the period, recent reviews don't have time to collect them, and the metric drops.
Recent reviews need **time to collect** reactions, so the calculation is done with a lag: for example, for reviews published no later than two weeks before the measurement date.
185.example:
Reviews published in February: 1,100
Likes on them: 3,400
Comments: 260
“Helpful” votes: 1,640

Engagement = (3,400 + 260 + 1,640) / 1,100 = **4.8 reactions per review**

Dividing only by the 620 reviews that got at least one reaction gives 8.5: that's the average for reviews that got noticed rather than engagement.
185.importance: **It shows** whether reviews get read at all or just sit there as dead weight. A review with reactions rises in the list on the product page and is among the first a shopper sees, so growing engagement lifts conversion with the same number of reviews. A drop with the same number of reviews means the content has become perfunctory: short reviews that just say “all good” don't collect reactions.
185.not_needed: **Skip it in brick-and-mortar** retail and on platforms without reactions: there's nowhere to like a review or mark it as helpful, so the numerator is always zero.
185.essence_note: reactions to a review move it up the list, and more customers read it

186.name: In-Stock Rate
186.formula: (Time the Product Was in Stock / Total Time in the Period) × 100
186.description: The share of time a product was available to customers.
186.nuances:
A product **counts as available when** stock is above zero; no higher threshold is set, since any other boundary would be arbitrary.
With **daily stock snapshots**, a day counts as available if there was stock at the time of the snapshot: the less often stock is captured, the more the metric is inflated, and short stockouts within a day aren't visible.
The denominator includes only the time when the product was supposed to be on sale: the time before it entered the assortment and after it was delisted **isn't counted**.
If the product is stored in several warehouses, **decide on the calculation level**. Product-warehouse pairs show exactly where the product was out of stock; at the company level, where availability means being in stock anywhere, local stockouts aren't visible.
186.example:
A product in March (31 days), 17 warehouses
Total product-days in the period: 17 × 31 = 527
Product-days with stock above zero: 401

In-stock rate = 401 / 527 × 100 = **76%**

Calculating at the company level (in stock anywhere) gives 100%, and the stockouts at five warehouses aren't visible.
186.importance: Every percentage point of unavailability for a best seller means **lost sales** that will never show up in a report: the customer didn't see the product and left. The metric is used to decide where to raise safety stock and how often to replenish stores. For class A items, unavailability costs the most, so they're checked first.
186.not_needed: Skip it for **special-order sales** and project-based supply: there's no stock by design, and the product is always available.
186.essence_note: while a product is out of stock, nobody can buy it

187.name: Repurchase Cycle
187.formula: Σ Intervals Between Consecutive Purchases of the Product / Number of Intervals
187.description: How much time passes on average between two purchases of the same product by the same customer.
187.nuances:
The denominator is **the number of intervals** rather than purchases: a customer with four purchases of a product has three intervals.
**Dividing by the number** of purchases understates the average interval, and the shorter the series, the bigger the error.
All intervals across all customers **go into a single** calculation: averaging first within each customer and then across customers gives a different result, where an occasional buyer with one interval weighs as much as a regular with twenty.
Customers with a single purchase of the product create no intervals and **aren't included** in the calculation: they haven't made a repeat purchase yet.
**It's calculated for each** product separately: the repurchase cycles for coffee and for a vacuum cleaner have nothing in common.
**The metric is limited by the window length**: with a quarterly calculation, intervals longer than three months don't make it into the sample, and the result comes out shorter than the real one.
187.example:
Product: coffee machine capsules, calculation window: one year
Customers who bought the product more than once: 1,240
Total purchases by them: 5,200
Intervals = 5,200 − 1,240 = 3,960
Total of the intervals: 138,600 days

Repurchase cycle = 138,600 / 3,960 = **35 days**

Dividing by 5,200 purchases gives 27 days: the interval is understated by about a quarter because of an off-by-one error.
187.importance: **It sets the moment** when it's time to remind the customer about the product: an email on day 30 with a 35-day cycle arrives before the person goes to buy from a competitor. The same interval determines after how many days of silence to count the customer as churned for this item, and how much stock to replenish stores with for predictable repeat demand. A lengthening cycle with an unchanged number of buyers is an early sign that people have started buying the product elsewhere.
187.not_needed: Skip it for **one-time purchase** products: furniture, major appliances and tools are bought rarely, and the interval doesn't describe behavior. Also skip it where customers can't be identified.
187.synonyms: Time Between Purchases, Repurchase Interval, Replenishment Cycle
187.essence_note: this is the interval between purchases, and the longer it is, the less a customer brings in over the same time

188.name: Share of Reviews with Photos
188.description: The share of reviews to which the customer attached photos.
188.nuances:
**Unit of count**: the review; two photos in one review count as one rather than two.
The share **overlaps** with the Share of Reviews with Video: a review with both attachments counts in both.
**Decide on the calculation window**: the share for all-time reviews describes what the shopper sees on the product page today, and the share for the period describes the mix of recent reviews. A review is assigned to a period based on its publication date.
188.example:
Reviews in March: 1,240
With photos: 285
Total photos attached: 611 (we count reviews, not files)

Share of reviews with photos = 285 / 1,240 × 100 = **23%**
188.importance: Customer photos work as free product page content and noticeably raise add-to-cart conversion, especially in apparel and furniture. A low share means the product page relies **only on studio shots**, which shoppers trust less. The metric is used to decide whether to launch rewards for photos and in which categories.
188.not_needed: **Skip it where** photos can't be attached to a review: the review form has no file upload, so there's nothing to attach.
188.synonyms: Photo Review Rate, Share of Photo Reviews
188.essence_note: a customer photo shows the product as it is and reduces returns

189.name: Purchase-to-Review Time
189.formula: Σ(Review Date − Purchase Date) / Number of Reviews Linked to a Purchase
189.description: How much time passes on average from buying a product to publishing a review of it.
189.nuances:
**Take the most recent purchase** of the product by the customer before the review date: with repeat purchases, counting from the first one stretches the interval and distorts the average.
Reviews not linked to a receipt don't go into the calculation and **are excluded from the denominator**. It's measured in days: hours give false precision for a distribution this spread out.
**The calculation is based on reviews** published during the period: if you select by purchase date, recent purchases haven't had time to produce a review yet, and the average is understated.
189.example:
Reviews in March linked to a receipt: 940
Reviews not linked: 180 (excluded)
Total time from purchase to review: 11,280 days

Time to review = 11,280 / 940 = **12 days**

If a customer bought the product three times and you count from the first purchase, the interval grows to 90 days and pulls the average up.
189.importance: **It sets** when to send a review request: an email sent a day before the typical time arrives when the impression has formed but hasn't faded yet. A reminder sent too early collects reviews of the delivery rather than the product. The metric also shows how long to wait for the first reviews of a new product before promoting it.
189.not_needed: **Skip it where** a review can't be linked to a purchase: without the link, there's nothing to build the numerator from.
189.essence_note: a review that comes too soon is written before the product has been used, and one that comes too late no longer helps the product page

190.name: Average Number of Variants per Product
190.formula: Number of SKUs / Number of Catalog Products
190.description: How many variants (color, size, volume) there are per product on average.
190.nuances:
A product without variants **counts as one** variant: its SKU is the product itself. Counting such products as zero pulls the average below one, and it can no longer be read as “variants per product.”
Denominator: all products for sale rather than **only those** with more than one variant: otherwise the metric reflects depth only for multi-variant items rather than across the assortment.
A variant **is a separate stock** item with its own inventory balance: an attribute that doesn't affect inventory tracking isn't a separate variant.
Archived variants and discontinued sizes **aren't counted**.
190.example:
Products for sale: 4,200
SKUs for sale: 11,400
Of the products, 2,900 have no variants (each counts as 1 SKU)

Variants per product = 11,400 / 4,200 = **2.7**

Counting products without variants as 0 and dividing only by the 1,300 multi-variant products gives 6.5: that's the depth for products with a size range.
190.importance: **Each variant means** a separate stock balance, a separate purchase and a separate line in the stock count, while the storefront still shows one product page. A growing average number of variants means warehouse space and working capital grow faster than the breadth the customer sees. The metric is used to decide where to cut the size range and color options: when sales go to a few popular variants, the rest sit in stock until markdown.
190.not_needed: **Skip it where** products have no variants by nature: food, services, single items without a size range.
190.synonyms: SKUs per Product, Variants per Product
190.essence_note: with too few variants, the customer can't find their size or color, and with too many, each model drags along extra stock

191.name: Total Categories
191.formula: Number of Unique Categories at the Chosen Hierarchy Level
191.description: How many product categories the assortment covers.
191.nuances:
The level **is fixed before the calculation**: the same catalog has a different number of level 1 and level 2 categories, and those numbers can't be compared with each other.
A category **counts as covered** if it has at least one product for sale. Categories that exist in the catalog but are empty aren't counted; otherwise the metric reflects work on the classification rather than the assortment.
**It's counted as of a date** rather than for a period: a category whose last product was delisted mid-month no longer counts at the end of the period.
191.example:
Catalog: 14 level 1 categories, with 240 level 2 categories inside them
We count at level 2
Categories with at least one product for sale: 186
Categories without products: 54 (not counted)

Total categories = **186**

At level 1, the same catalog gives 14: a different level, a different number.
191.importance: **It shows the breadth of the offering and** how far the company stretches across lines of business. A growing number of categories with flat revenue means purchasing and shelf space are spread thin: each category has only a few items, and in none of them does the customer find a real choice. The metric is used to decide whether to deepen existing categories or open new ones.
191.not_needed: Skip it in a **single-category business**: the number is always one.
191.essence_note: each new category is a new reason to come and a new audience

192.name: Time to First Sale
192.formula: Σ(First Sale Date − Date Added to Catalog) / Number of New Products That Reached a First Sale
192.description: How much time passes on average from a product's appearance in the catalog to its first sale.
192.nuances:
The set of products **is fixed by the date** they were added to the catalog: take the products added during the period and look at their first sale date, even if it came after the end of the period. Selecting by first sale date gives a different sample and a different number.
The start **is the date** the product became available to buy (stock arrived and the product went on sale), rather than the date the product page was created: a product page can sit without stock for a long time, and that time has nothing to do with how fast the product takes off.
Products that never sold **are excluded** from the denominator: there's nothing to put in the numerator for them. They're counted separately as the share of new products with no sales; otherwise the average looks good no matter how many launches fail.
**The calculation leaves a buffer** before the current date (for example, it covers only new products older than three months); otherwise recent products that haven't reached a first sale yet drop out of the denominator and understate the time.
192.example:
Products that became available for sale in December: 320
Sold at least once by the time of calculation: 284
Never sold: 36 (not in the denominator, counted separately)
Total time to first sale: 5,396 days

Time to first sale = 5,396 / 284 = **19 days**

Separately: 36 / 320 × 100 = 11% of new products never sold.
192.importance: **It shows** how long money sits idle in a new product between the purchase and the first dollar of revenue. If the time grows, new products are being put on sale without a product page, photos or promotion, and they just sit until a customer happens to find them. The metric is used to decide how much stock to buy for a launch and when to turn on paid promotion: before the typical time or after it.
192.not_needed: Skip it when new product launches are rare: a couple of items a year doesn't give an average, so each launch is reviewed **separately**.
192.synonyms: Time to First Purchase, Days to First Sale
192.essence_note: until a new product sells for the first time, the money for it is already spent and sitting in the warehouse

193.name: Seasonality Index
193.formula: Month's Sales / Average Monthly Sales for the Year
193.description: The ratio of a month's sales to average monthly sales for the year. It's calculated for each month separately, and the values hover around one: 1.8 means people buy almost twice as much as usual in that month, and 0.6 means a little over half as much.
193.nuances:
The index **is calculated for each** month separately, and there's no single number per product: the result is a set of twelve coefficients, the seasonality profile.
Sales **are taken in units** rather than money: otherwise price changes and discount policy get mixed into seasonality.
You need at least **two to three years** of history: each month's sales are summed across all years and divided by the average monthly sales over the same span. With one year, a one-off spike, a promotion or a stockout enters the profile as seasonality.
Months when the product was out of stock **are excluded** from the calculation: zero sales because of a stockout understate that month's index and show a drop in demand where there was a drop in supply.
The index **is calculated for a group** of similar products rather than a single product when sales are sparse: with occasional sales, random orders make the coefficient jump around.
The indices for the twelve months add up to twelve: if they **don't add up**, different sets of months went into the calculation.
193.example:
Annual sales of the product: 24,000 units
Average monthly sales = 24,000 / 12 = 2,000 units

December: 5,600 units
December index = 5,600 / 2,000 = **2.8**

July: 900 units
July index = 900 / 2,000 = **0.45**

Application: December forecast before seasonal adjustment, 2,200 units × 2.8 = 6,160 units to purchase.
193.importance: It gives the multiplier applied to the forecast to get the purchase quantity for a specific month. Without it, the company buys to average monthly sales, is guaranteed to hit the peak with a stockout, and then sits on leftover stock headed for markdown. The profile is also used to decide which items to keep year-round and which to bring in **only for the season**, and when to start clearing out stock: right after a month with a high index, demand drops and full price is no longer achievable.
193.not_needed: Skip it for products **without sales history** of at least a year: there's nothing to build a profile from.
193.essence_note: steady demand is easier to staff and stock for, while strong seasonality brings a revenue peak, and between peaks money and warehouse space sit idle

194.name: Average Gross Margin Rate per Product
194.formula: Σ over products ((Product Price − Product Cost) / Product Price) / Number of Products with Sales × 100
194.description: The average gross margin of a product in the assortment.
194.nuances:
Margin **is calculated for each** product and then averaged across products: plugging the average price and average cost into one formula gives the margin of the whole portfolio, where expensive items carry more weight, and that's a different number.
Products with no sales in the period are left out: they have no actual selling price. The price **is the actual one**, net of discounts: the same basis as in [[Average Selling Price (ASP)→assortiment/srednyaya_cena_tovara]].
The cost **is the same** as in [[Average Unit Cost→assortiment/srednyaya_sebestoimost_tovara]]: the purchase cost at the time of sale plus direct costs of shipping to the warehouse, with no overhead allocated.
194.example:
Product A: price $2, cost $0.80, margin 60%
Product B: price $100, cost $90, margin 10%
Product C: price $6, cost $2.40, margin 60%

Average margin per product = (60 + 10 + 60) / 3 = **43%**

Using averages instead: average price (2 + 100 + 6) / 3 = $36, average cost $31.07, margin 13.7%. The expensive low-margin product skewed the result: this is portfolio margin rather than the average across products.
194.importance: It shows the margin of a typical item in the assortment rather than **only the flagships**. Portfolio margin hides a situation where all the earnings rest on a couple of products and the rest of the assortment just breaks even: expanding such an assortment means growing sales without profit. The metric is used to decide which items get repriced, which get sourced from another supplier and which get delisted.
194.not_needed: **Skip it where** cost isn't tracked by item: consignment selling, services, a single markup on everything.
194.synonyms: Average Product Margin, Average Margin per Item
194.essence_note: the more an item earns on each sale, the more worthwhile it is to keep it in the assortment

195.name: Share of Reviews with Video
195.description: The share of reviews to which the customer attached a video.
195.nuances:
**Unit of count**: the review rather than the file; three videos in one review count as one in the numerator.
A review with both photos and video is counted in both this metric and the Share of Reviews with Photos: these two shares overlap and **don't add up to a share** of reviews with media.
**Decide on the calculation window**: the share for all-time reviews describes what the shopper sees on the product page today, and the share for the period describes the mix of recent reviews. A review is assigned to a period based on its publication date.
195.example:
Reviews in March: 1,240
With video: 62
Of those, 41 also have photos (also counted in the share with photos)

Share of reviews with video = 62 / 1,240 × 100 = **5%**
195.importance: **Video handles objections** that text doesn't: how an item fits, what color it really is, how a mechanism works. The share shows whether incentives for video reviews pay off and whether product pages have material that can be used in promotion. If it's close to zero, shoppers are buying blind, and some of the disappointed buyers end up returning items for not meeting expectations.
195.not_needed: **Skip it where** video can't be attached to a review: the review form has no file upload, so there's nothing to attach.
195.synonyms: Video Review Rate, Share of Video Reviews
195.essence_note: video in a review is more persuasive than text and answers some questions before purchase

196.name: Time Between Orders
196.description: The average time between two consecutive orders by the same customer.
196.nuances:
Customers with one order **aren't included**: they have no interval. Leaving them out makes the number noticeably more optimistic than the actual behavior of the customer base.
**It's calculated over all** pairs of consecutive orders rather than just the first two: otherwise the average captures only the start of the customer lifetime, when purchases come more often.
196.example:
Customer A: orders on March 1, March 20, April 5 = intervals of 19 and 16 days
Customer B: orders on March 3, March 28 = interval of 25 days
Customer C: one order on March 10 (excluded)

Time Between Orders = (19 + 16 + 25) / 3 = **20 days**
196.importance: **It sets the normal purchase rhythm** that churn is measured against: if a typical customer comes back every 20 days, 60 days of silence means they've left, and there's no point in waiting any longer. The same rhythm sets the timing of messaging campaigns: an email that comes too early is annoying, and one that comes too late arrives after the customer has already satisfied their need.
196.not_needed: **Skip it where** repeat purchases are rare: most customers have one order and no interval, and the average describes only the few who do come back.
196.essence_note: the less often a customer comes back, the less they bring in over the same time

197.name: Share of Orders with Promo Code
197.description: The share of paid orders in which the customer applied a promo code.
197.nuances:
Unit of count: an order rather than a coupon. An order with two promo codes **counts once**.
**Only paid** orders count: a code entered in the cart or at checkout on an order that was never paid isn't included. How often promo codes are entered during checkout is measured by a separate metric, the Share of Checkouts with Promo Code: the gap between the two shows how often discounted orders fall through before payment.
**Decide** whether free shipping codes go into the numerator: they don't change the product total, but the customer gets a benefit, and the waived shipping fee is included in discount spend. If you leave them out, the share will diverge from [[Promo Code Discount Spend→zakazy/zatraty_na_predostavlenie_skidok]], where they're included.
197.example:
Paid orders in the month: 4,800
Orders with a promo code: 1,344

Share of Orders with Promo Code = 1,344 / 4,800 × 100 = **28%**
197.importance: It answers the question of whether people buy from you **without a discount**. There's no benchmark for this share: it depends on how often you send out codes yourself, so compare it with your own history. The warning sign is the movement rather than the level: if the share grows while [[Revenue→vyruchka/vyruchka]] stays flat, discounts are replacing regular sales, and full price has stopped working.
197.not_needed: Skip it when **promo codes aren't used** at all and everyone pays the same price.
197.synonyms: Coupon Usage Rate, Promo Code Usage Rate
197.essence_note: the more orders go out at a discount, the less money is left from the same sales volume

198.name: Average Order Value (AOV)
198.description: The average value of one paid order.
198.nuances:
**[[Sales Returns→finansy/vozvraty]] are subtracted** from revenue, and a partially returned order stays in the denominator. A fully returned order is removed from both parts.
**Decide** whether the AOV includes shipping. The shipping fee is part of [[Online Revenue→spravochnik/vyruchka_onlayn]], so the formula includes it in the AOV as well. Excluding it stops the AOV from rising when carrier rates change and makes it comparable across periods, but then it no longer matches revenue divided by orders. Make the decision once and don't change it afterward.
The numerator and denominator **are calculated using the same** orders for the same period; otherwise the result is meaningless.
198.example:
Revenue for the month: $360,000
Paid orders: 4,800

AOV = 360,000 / 4,800 = **$75**

It also breaks down into two factors: average unit price $30 × 2.5 units per order = $75. An order has 1.8 line items on average: customers buy several units of the same product.
198.importance: **One of the two factors** in revenue, and the cheaper one to increase: more orders require acquisition spend, while the AOV can be raised with the same audience through assortment changes, upselling and the [[Free Shipping Threshold→zakazy/porog_besplatnoy_dostavki]]. A drop while the order count grows means discounts and cheap items are canceling out that growth: [[Online Revenue→spravochnik/vyruchka_onlayn]] is flat, while the warehouse and delivery workload has grown.
198.synonyms: Average Order Size, Average Basket Value
198.essence_note: with the same number of orders, a higher AOV directly means more money

199.name: Time from First Visit to First Paid Order
199.formula: Total Time from First Visit to Payment / Number of First Orders
199.description: The average time from a user's first visit to the website to their first payment.
199.nuances:
**It's calculated only for** customers who made a purchase. Those who visited and didn't buy aren't included, so the number describes the buyer's path rather than all users.
**Accuracy depends on whether** you recognize the customer across visits. For logged-in users, visits from different devices are merged into one profile, and the first visit is identified correctly. For anonymous users, visit data lives in the browser for a limited time and is lost when they switch devices or clear their browser data: a customer who first visited from a phone a year ago and bought from a laptop is counted with a short time to purchase and pulls the average down.
**Because of this, the metric** is capped by a chosen observation window: with a 30-day window, purchases with a longer cycle simply don't make it into the calculation, and the average will be noticeably lower than the real one.
199.example:
First orders in the month: 900
Total time from first visit to payment: 10,800 days

Time from First Visit to First Paid Order = 10,800 / 900 = **12 days**

With a cycle like this, a weekly campaign report will show only some of the orders the campaign eventually brings in.
199.importance: **It sets the horizon** over which advertising can be meaningfully evaluated: if the cycle is longer than the reporting period, a campaign looks unprofitable right up until the delayed orders come in. The same number determines the length of the nurture email sequence and the window for retargeting.
199.not_needed: Skip it in **impulse-buy categories**, where the purchase happens on the first visit: the number never exceeds a single visit and won't inform any decision.
199.synonyms: Time to Purchase, Time to Convert
199.essence_note: the longer the path to the first purchase, the more the customer costs

200.name: Ecommerce Conversion Rate
200.description: The share of sessions in which an order was paid.
200.nuances:
Orders come either from the order database or from web analytics events, and the numbers differ: analytics doesn't see orders without tracking and loses some to blockers, while the database shows all of them. A numerator from the database over the same denominator gives a higher conversion rate, so the source is chosen **once** and kept the same across periods.
Blockers cut **tracked sessions as well**: the denominator is understated, so with orders from the database the conversion rate is inflated on both counts.
**An order is credited to the session** in which the payment went through rather than the one where the customer built the cart: with payment by invoice or deferred payment, it ends up in the conversion rate of a different day, sometimes a different month.
200.importance: Brings traffic and sales together **into one number**: traffic growth without growth in this number means ad money is going into useless traffic. It's also used to evaluate changes to the website, because the effect shows up here earlier than in revenue. A drop with steady traffic usually points to something broken in checkout or to an influx of users who don't need your product.
200.not_needed: Skip it when **orders come in outside the website**: by phone, in messaging apps, through a sales manager. The denominator doesn't cover these orders, and the number will be arbitrary.
200.synonyms: Online Store Conversion Rate, Purchase Conversion Rate
200.essence_note: the more sessions end with a payment, the less each order costs

201.name: Paid Orders
201.description: The number of orders for which payment went through.
201.nuances:
An order is assigned to the period **by its placement date**: a payment that arrives at the start of the next month counts toward the month of the order.
Partially paid orders count as paid **once the first payment is received** if their goods are being shipped: waiting for full payment undercounts orders that have already gone out to the customer.
**Orders** that were paid and then canceled with a refund are removed from the count.
201.example:
Website Sessions: 240,000
Ecommerce Conversion Rate: 2.0%
Orders placed: 5,000, of which 200 were canceled and not paid

Paid Orders = 2.0% of 240,000 = **4,800**
201.importance: **The base number** in the denominator of half the metrics on this map: [[Average Order Value (AOV)→zakazy/sredniy_chek_aov]], [[Cost per Order (CPO)→zakazy/stoimost_zakaza]], [[Average Shipping Fee→zakazy/srednyaya_stoimost_dostavki]]. An error in it distorts all derived metrics at once and isn't visible in them, so the first thing to check is whether its payment count matches accounting. The trend in paid orders shows whether the business is growing through the number of purchases or through price.
201.essence_note: these are the orders that bring in the money

202.name: Order Payment Rate
202.description: The share of placed orders for which payment went through.
202.nuances:
An order is assigned to the period **by its placement date**, and its payment counts toward the same period even if it came later.
**You can't count payments by** their own date: the numerator would then include orders from past periods. The latest period is always undercounted: some orders from the last days will still be paid, so use the final rate once late payments for the period have come in.
Canceled orders **stay in the denominator**: they were placed and not paid, and excluding them inflates the rate.
202.example:
Orders placed in March: 6,000
Of those, paid in March: 4,300
Paid in the first days of April: 200 (assigned to March)
Canceled: 750 (stay in the denominator)

Order Payment Rate = 4,500 / 6,000 × 100 = **75%**
202.importance: Measures the last step of the funnel, where the customer has already decided and is left alone with the payment form. Losses here are the most expensive: the ads that brought these people in have already been paid for, and products have been reserved for them. A dip points to a specific cause: a payment method that stopped working, a delivery time that surfaced **only at the last** step, or an unexpected shipping cost in the total.
202.not_needed: Skip it with **payment on delivery**: delivery separates placement and payment, and the metric measures refusals at delivery rather than checkout.
202.essence_note: a placed but unpaid order brings in no money

203.name: Time to Payment
203.formula: Total Time to Payment / Number of Orders
203.description: The average time from the start of checkout to successful payment.
203.nuances:
The denominator includes **only [[Paid Orders→zakazy/oplachennye_zakazy]]**: unpaid orders have no time to payment, and adding them to the base drags the average down to the point of meaninglessness.
Orders with deferred payment pull the average up sharply. They're counted **separately** from orders paid within one session; otherwise a handful of invoices paid much later outweigh many quick payments.
Because of this skew, the average is usually read alongside **the median**: it shows the time within which a typical customer completes payment.
203.example:
Orders paid during the day: 500
Total time to payment: 62,500 seconds

Time to Payment = 62,500 / 500 = **125 seconds**

Of those, 490 orders were paid within 90 seconds and 10 much later: the median will be about 80 seconds.
203.importance: Every extra minute at this stage loses some payments: the customer has already clicked "Buy," and everything after that works **only against the sale**. A longer time points to something specific that's broken: the form has unnecessary fields, the gateway is slow to respond, the verification code doesn't arrive. The payment rate shows this only after customers have already left.
203.not_needed: Skip it with **payment on delivery**: delivery stands between checkout and payment, and the time measures delivery rather than checkout.
203.essence_note: the longer a person spends checking out, the higher the chance they'll change their mind

204.name: Unpaid Orders
204.description: The number of orders placed in the period for which payment never went through.
204.nuances:
**Set the waiting period** after which an order is considered unpaid. Until it expires, the order sits in an intermediate status, and counting too early inflates the number.
Orders canceled by the customer or the company before payment **aren't included** here: they're in [[Canceled Orders→zakazy/otmenennye_zakazy]]. This metric includes orders abandoned without payment and closed when the waiting period expired.
An order that was paid and then canceled with a refund **doesn't count** as unpaid.
204.example:
Orders placed in March: 6,000
Paid (including payments that came in early April): 4,500
Canceled by the customer or the company before payment: 750 (counted as canceled)
Waiting for payment, still within the waiting period: 40 (not counted yet)

Unpaid Orders = 6,000 − 4,500 − 750 − 40 = **710**

Paid, canceled, unpaid and still pending orders add up to placed orders: 4,500 + 750 + 710 + 40 = 6,000.
204.importance: **Money stuck at the last step, measured in orders**: behind each such order is a customer who chose a product and couldn't pay or changed their mind. The list of these orders is a ready-made audience for reminder emails, and its size shows how much revenue can be recovered without acquiring anyone new. A sharp jump within a day usually means a technical failure in payments.
204.not_needed: Skip it with payment on delivery: an order is always unpaid until it's delivered, and the count **equals the total number of** orders.
204.essence_note: the work on these orders is done, but the money hasn't come in

205.name: Cost per Order (CPO)
205.description: The average marketing spend to acquire one paid order.
205.nuances:
Spend includes **all acquisition costs**: ad budgets, platform commissions, contractor fees and the marketing team's salaries.
Counting **only ad platform budgets** understates the cost per order.
Spend and orders **are counted for the same** period. This doesn't capture the delayed effect of advertising: orders from a campaign keep coming after it ends, so over a short window the number is inflated.
Orders from repeat purchases stay in the denominator even though they cost less to acquire: the metric describes the average order rather than **only new ones**.
205.example:
Marketing spend for March: $78,750
Including advertising: $60,000; platform commissions: $8,750; contractor fees and team salaries: $10,000
Paid orders: 4,500

Cost per Order (CPO) = 78,750 / 4,500 = **$17.50**

Counting only advertising gives $13.33, and the cost per order would look about 24% lower.

Compared with margin: with an AOV of $75 and a 35% margin, an order leaves $26.25, of which $17.50 goes to acquisition.
205.importance: **The only number** you can put next to the order margin to see what the company keeps after acquisition. It's used to turn off campaigns and to decide whether increasing the budget makes sense. Growth with flat sales means the cheapest demand has already been captured and each additional order costs more than the one before.
205.not_needed: **Skip it** when sales come without paid acquisition: the numerator is zero.
205.synonyms: Cost per Purchase, Cost per Sale
205.essence_note: every dollar spent on acquisition comes out of the order's profit

206.name: Orders with Promo Code
206.formula: Number of orders with a promo code
206.description: The number of orders in which the customer applied a promo code.
206.nuances:
**The count includes [[Paid Orders→zakazy/oplachennye_zakazy]]** placed in the period. Canceled ones don't count: their discount never happened.
An order with several promo codes **counts once**.
206.example:
Orders with a promo code placed in March: 1,340
Of those, canceled: 80 (excluded)
Orders with two promo codes: 45 (counted as 45 orders, not 90)

Orders with Promo Code = **1,260**
206.importance: **Gives the scale of the coupon program** as an order count: without it, the percentage is easy to misread, because 30% can stand for 60 orders or for 6,000. The absolute number is needed to weigh discounts against lost margin and to see whether the program is worth the hassle of issuing and monitoring codes.
206.not_needed: **Skip it** when promo codes aren't used at all.
206.synonyms: Orders with Discount Code, Coupon Orders
206.essence_note: the promo code led to paid orders, some of which wouldn't have happened otherwise

207.name: Average Promo Code Lifespan
207.formula: Sum of Validity Periods of All Promo Codes / Number of Promo Codes
207.description: The average validity period of a promo code, from launch to expiration.
207.nuances:
**The stated validity period is counted** rather than the time until the redemption limit actually runs out.
Codes with no end date aren't included: they have no validity period, and plugging in any placeholder number makes the average arbitrary. Their number is tracked **separately**.
207.example:
Promo codes in the quarter: 40
Of those, with no end date: 6 (excluded)
Base: 34 codes
Total validity period: 714 days

Average Promo Code Lifespan = 714 / 34 = **21 days**
207.importance: **A short lifespan pushes** the customer to decide, while a long one turns the discount into the new price and teaches customers to wait. A long average lifespan means promotions overlap and the storefront effectively never shows full price. This number is used to decide what the promotion really is: a tool for boosting sales in a given week or a permanent discount under another name.
207.not_needed: Skip it with **open-ended codes**: there's nothing to measure.
207.synonyms: Average Coupon Duration, Average Promo Code Validity
207.essence_note: the longer a code lives, the more people manage to use it instead of buying at the regular price

208.name: Average Share of Orders with Promo Code per Customer
208.formula: Average across customers: (Orders with Promo Code / All of the Customer's Orders) × 100
208.description: The average share of orders with a promo code per customer. It differs from the overall share of orders with a promo code in that every customer carries the same weight, regardless of how many orders they placed.
208.nuances:
Customers with one order give **only 0**% or 100% and shift the average toward the extremes. The base usually includes only customers with at least two orders: the metric is about the habit of buying at a discount, and one purchase doesn't show a habit.
The denominator for each customer **includes only paid** orders; otherwise abandoned and canceled orders dilute the share.
208.example:
Customer A: 10 orders, 2 with a promo code = 20%
Customer B: 4 orders, 4 with a promo code = 100%
Customer C: 6 orders, 3 with a promo code = 50%

Average Share of Orders with Promo Code per Customer = (20 + 100 + 50) / 3 = **57%**

Pooling all orders together gives 9 / 20 × 100 = 45%: that's the share of orders rather than the average customer's habit.
208.importance: **Picks out the core group of customers** who buy only with coupons. The overall Share of Orders with Promo Code hides this group: a few large customers who buy often without a discount outweigh many coupon hunters. This number determines who should get a promo code campaign and for whom it would just be a gift paid for out of margin.
208.not_needed: **Skip it in** a business with one-time purchases, where repeat orders are rare: most customers have a denominator of one.
208.essence_note: a customer who buys only with promo codes brings in less on every order

209.name: Payment Failure Rate
209.description: The share of payment attempts that ended in a decline. All declines count: insufficient funds, a decline by the bank, a payment gateway timeout, a data entry error.
209.nuances:
**Unit of count**: an attempt rather than an order. One order with four attempts gives four entries in the denominator and three in the numerator if it went through on the fourth try: the metric is about how often the gateway rejects a request, and whether the order came back is measured by the Payment Recovery Rate.
Incomplete attempts, where the customer opened the payment form and left without submitting their details, aren't in the base: the payment system gave no response, and this **doesn't count** as a decline.
209.example:
Payment attempts in the month: 12,400
Successful: 10,900
Bank and gateway declines: 1,500
Payment forms opened and abandoned: 2,100 (excluded)

Payment Failure Rate = 1,500 / 12,400 × 100 = **12%**
209.importance: The first metric to react when the payment gateway breaks or the acquirer changes: the drop in revenue becomes visible **only later**, while the spike in errors shows up much sooner. A consistently high rate means some customers who are ready to pay are unable to, and money is lost to technical problems rather than to price or assortment.
209.not_needed: Skip it with invoice payment or payment on delivery: online payment attempts **aren't recorded**.
209.synonyms: Payment Decline Rate, Failed Payment Rate
209.essence_note: every failed attempt is an order that may not happen at all

210.name: Payment Recovery Rate
210.formula: (Recovered Orders / Orders with a Failed Payment) × 100
210.description: The share of orders with a failed payment for which payment eventually went through. Any later successful payment for the same order counts as a recovery: a repeat attempt by the customer, an automatic retry, or payment via a link in an email.
210.nuances:
**Unit of count**: an order rather than a payment attempt. A customer whose card payment failed three times and went through on the fourth try counts as one order and one recovery rather than three failures against one success: the metric answers whether the order was recovered rather than how many times the customer stumbled along the way.
Failed attempts themselves are measured by **a related metric**, the Payment Failure Rate: that one is about the technical health of payments, and this one is about saved orders.
**Set the window** within which a payment counts as recovered. For example, use a window of 7 days from the decline: beyond the window, customers more often come back through new ads, and the credit for those ads would go to the payment recovery flow.
**Orders** rejected by the anti-fraud system are excluded from the denominator: they can't be recovered, and they push the rate down.
An order is assigned to the period **by its placement date** rather than its recovery date: the recovery comes after the decline, and counting by recovery date would put February orders into the March rate. Because of this, the latest period is undercounted until the window closes.
210.example:
Orders with a failed payment placed in March: 1,250
Of those, rejected by the anti-fraud system: 60 (excluded)
Base: 1,190
Paid later within 7 days: 440
Paid on day 12: 35 (outside the window, excluded)

Payment Recovery Rate = 440 / 1,190 × 100 = **37%**

The customer paid for one of these orders on the fourth attempt: it enters the calculation as one recovered order rather than three failures against one success.
210.importance: **It determines** how much revenue is recovered from customers who have already decided to buy, with no ad spend. A slump in the rate means the payment recovery flow isn't working: the customer didn't get the email, the link expired, or retries aren't set up. Each percentage point here is 1% of the orders with a failed payment, revenue that would otherwise simply be lost at the last step.
210.not_needed: Skip it when payment is **only in cash or** by transfer on delivery: there's no such event as a failed payment.
210.synonyms: Failed Payment Recovery Rate, Recovered Payment Rate
210.essence_note: every recovered payment is an order that had already been lost

211.name: Promo Code Discount Spend
211.description: The total discounts given to customers through promo codes and coupons for the period.
211.nuances:
Discounts **are counted for orders** placed in the period. For canceled orders, the discount is removed: the company lost no money.
**When an item is returned**, the discount on it is subtracted too; otherwise promo costs stay attached to a sale that no longer exists.
Discounts and revenue **are calculated under the same** rules: mixing different bases overstates the losses.
Free shipping from a promo code **is counted at the rate** the customer didn't pay rather than at the company's shipping cost. A discount is money not received, while the company pays the carrier its cost in any case, and that cost is already counted in shipping expenses: including it here would put the same money into two metrics.
211.example:
Promo code discounts for March: $27,500
Free shipping from promo codes, 255 orders at the $7.60 rate: $1,938
Discounts on canceled orders: $2,000 (subtracted)
Discounts on returned items: $1,450 (subtracted)

Promo Code Discount Spend = 27,500 + 1,938 − 2,000 − 1,450 = **$25,988**

The company's cost for these deliveries is lower than the rate, but the calculation uses the rate: the company didn't collect $7.60 per order from the customer.
211.importance: **Expresses promotions as the money** the company didn't receive: a discount doesn't show up as an expense line, so the loss stays invisible. Still, not all of it is lost profit: some discounted orders wouldn't have happened without the discount. Payback is calculated from the profit on additional sales rather than from sales volume: at a one-third margin, each dollar of discount needs about three dollars of new sales.
211.not_needed: **Skip it** when promo codes and coupons aren't used at all and everyone pays the same price.
211.essence_note: a discount given comes straight out of the order's profit

212.name: Active Promo Codes
212.description: The number of public promo codes active on the selected date or active at least once during the period.
212.nuances:
**Public codes are counted**: those handed out on the website, in messaging campaigns or through partners, which work for anyone. Personal codes issued in bulk, one per customer, don't count: there are so many of them that they swamp all the others, and the number starts describing the size of the campaign rather than the company's promo policy. The size of a personal campaign is measured by the number of emails sent.
**Pick a date or a period to fit the question**. On a date, you see how many discounts are active right now: a practical figure for checking whether a code has been forgotten. For a period, count the unique codes that were active for at least one day, and that answers a different question: how many promotions ran in March in total.
You can't add up daily values in either case: a code that worked the whole month would enter the sum thirty times. For a period, each code **counts once**, however many days it was active.
**A code counts as active** if it hasn't expired and hasn't used up its redemption limit. A code with days left but its limit used up no longer works and doesn't count.
212.example:
Promo codes not yet expired as of April 1: 64
Of those, with the redemption limit used up: 11 (excluded)
Personal codes from messaging campaigns: 3,200 (excluded)

Active Promo Codes as of April 1 = **53**

In March, 78 codes were active: some of them ended before April 1, so the count for the period is higher than on the selected date.
212.importance: **It shows** how many discounts are running at once and catches codes forgotten after a promotion ended: they keep working and end up on coupon aggregator sites. The longer the list, the higher the chance that two codes stack in one order and give a bigger discount than intended.
212.not_needed: **Skip it with one** or two permanent codes: you can keep the list in your head.
212.essence_note: the more codes are active at once, the more often a buyer finds a discount where it isn't needed

213.name: Average Share of Discounted Items per Order
213.formula: Average across all orders: (Discounted Items in the Order / All Items in the Order) × 100
213.description: The average share of discounted items in an order. Calculated for each order separately, then averaged.
213.nuances:
**It's counted by line items** rather than units: two identical discounted units make one line item.
**Define** what counts as a discount: only promotions and promo codes, or loyalty program discounts as well. Regular customers with their own personal discount can outweigh the whole effect of promotions.
Single-item orders give **only 0**% or 100% and pull the average toward the extremes.
213.example:
Order 1: 4 items, 2 discounted = 50%
Order 2: 3 items, 3 discounted = 100%
Order 3: 5 items, 1 discounted = 20%

Average Share of Discounted Items per Order = (50 + 100 + 20) / 3 = **57%**
213.importance: It shows how much of an order actually sells at full price. The Share of Orders with Promo Code records **only whether** a code was used, while this metric shows the depth of discounting: an order may count as "with a promo code" with a discount on one item out of seven, or it may consist entirely of promotional items. A high share means the product range sells only on promotion, and sales will stall without it.
213.not_needed: **Skip it** when orders almost always contain a single item: the metric collapses into the share of orders with a discount.
213.synonyms: Discounted Item Share, Promotional Item Share
213.essence_note: the more line items sell at a discount, the less product sells at full price

214.name: Average Shipping Share of Order Value
214.description: The average share of order value that goes to the shipping fee. Calculated for each order separately, then averaged.
214.nuances:
The calculation includes **only orders with** paid shipping. Free ones give zero and pull the average down, turning the metric into a mix of two different questions: how much shipping costs and how often it's free.
**The numerator is the amount** the customer paid rather than the company's shipping cost.
**Low-value orders** have large shipping shares and noticeably push the average up.
214.example:
Order 1: shipping $6 on a $30 order = 20%
Order 2: shipping $3.50 on a $70 order = 5%
Order 3: shipping $8 on a $40 order = 20%
Order 4: shipping $0 on a $100 order (excluded)

Average Shipping Share of Order Value = (20 + 5 + 20) / 3 = **15%**
214.importance: **It shows** how much shipping costs those who did pay for it: they were willing to pay the product price, but the cart total turned out noticeably higher. This share is used to set the [[Free Shipping Threshold→zakazy/porog_besplatnoy_dostavki]] and to decide which rates to show by default. The metric doesn't capture people whom shipping scared off: they never got as far as a placed order, and you find them through abandoned carts.
214.not_needed: Skip it with **free shipping** on all orders or when local pickup is the only delivery method.
214.synonyms: Shipping Cost as % of Order Value, Shipping-to-Order Value Ratio
214.essence_note: too large a share scares customers away from ordering, and too small a share means we're shipping at our own expense

215.name: Share of Orders with Free Shipping
215.description: The share of paid orders shipped to the customer with no shipping fee.
215.nuances:
The numerator includes all orders where the customer didn't pay for shipping: both those above the threshold and those that got free shipping through a promotion, a promo code or loyalty program status. Counting **only orders above the threshold** understates the real burden on logistics.
Local pickup orders **are left out of the base**: they don't involve shipping, and they dilute the metric.
215.example:
Paid orders in the month: 4,500
Of those, local pickup: 700 (excluded)
Base: 3,800
Free because of the order amount threshold: 1,340
Free because of a promo code: 255

Share of Orders with Free Shipping = (1,340 + 255) / 3,800 × 100 = **42%**
215.importance: It shows how much of its shipping the company pays for itself. A high share means the [[Free Shipping Threshold→zakazy/porog_besplatnoy_dostavki]] is set low and small orders also qualify for free shipping, which then eats up their entire margin. A low share means almost everyone pays for shipping, and that's when to look at abandoned carts: the metric itself captures **only those** who did place an order.
215.not_needed: **Skip it** when shipping is always free or always paid: the share equals 100% or zero and doesn't change any decisions.
215.essence_note: the company pays for every free delivery out of its margin

216.name: Average Shipping Fee
216.formula: Shipping Fees Paid by Customers / Number of Paid Orders
216.description: The average amount a customer pays for shipping per order.
216.nuances:
Orders with free shipping stay in the denominator: the metric shows how much the company collects for shipping on average across all orders, and without them the number describes **only orders with paid shipping**.
**What's counted is the customer's fee** rather than the company's shipping cost: these are different amounts, and swapping one for the other turns the metric into a cost metric.
Local pickup **isn't in the base**: it doesn't involve shipping.
216.example:
Paid orders in March: 4,500
Of those, local pickup: 700 (excluded)
Base: 3,800
Collected from customers for shipping: $16,758

Average Shipping Fee = 16,758 / 3,800 = **$4.41**

Counting only the 2,205 paid deliveries gives $7.60: that's the average rate rather than the average fee per order.
216.importance: **It shows** how much of the shipping cost the customer pays and how much the company absorbs. The gap between this amount and the actual shipping cost is the true cost of free shipping. It's used to decide whether to raise shipping rates: a higher average fee with the same number of orders adds to margin right away, and a drop in the payment rate will show that customers didn't accept it.
216.not_needed: Skip it with **free shipping** on all orders or when local pickup is the only delivery method.
216.synonyms: Average Shipping Charge, Shipping Revenue per Order
216.essence_note: the fee should cover shipping costs, but one that's too high scares the buyer off at the last step

217.name: Canceled Orders
217.description: The number of placed orders canceled before they were handed over to the customer. The cancellation can come from either the customer or the company.
217.nuances:
An order is assigned to the period **by its placement date** rather than its cancellation date: otherwise the count combines cancellations of orders placed in different months. The latest period is undercounted: some orders from the last days will still be canceled.
Returns after delivery **don't count** as cancellations: the order was delivered.
**An order abandoned without** payment and closed by the system when the waiting period expires is usually classified as unpaid rather than canceled: counting it as a cancellation inflates the count, and the count no longer stands for lost sales.
217.example:
Orders placed in March: 6,000
Canceled by the customer: 540
Canceled by the company because the product was out of stock: 210
Closed by the system for nonpayment: 710 (classified as unpaid rather than canceled)
Returns after delivery: 180 (excluded, the product was received)

Canceled Orders = 540 + 210 = **750**
217.importance: **Every cancellation** initiated by the company costs more than a sale that didn't happen: the product was promised and not shipped, and the customer remembers that. Going through the cancellation reasons points to specific failures, most often a mismatch between the stock shown on the storefront and the actual stock in the warehouse. Without the absolute number, there's nothing to weigh the cancellation rate against: 12% of 6,000 orders and 12% of 60 call for different responses.
217.essence_note: a canceled order costs both the revenue and the work already put into it

218.name: Order Cancellation Rate
218.description: The share of placed orders canceled before they were handed over to the customer. The cancellation can come from either the customer or the company.
218.nuances:
An order is assigned to the period **by its placement date** rather than its cancellation date. Otherwise the rate combines cancellations of orders placed in different months, and a spike in cancellations of past sales looks like a problem with current ones.
Because of this, the latest period is undercounted: orders from the last days still have time to be canceled. Read the final number once the window in which **most cancellations happen** has passed.
[[Sales Returns→finansy/vozvraty]] after delivery **don't count** as cancellations: the order arrived and was paid for.
[[Abandoned Carts→oformlenie_zakaza/broshennye_korziny]] don't go into the denominator: **an order counts as placed** when the customer has confirmed and submitted it.
218.example:
Orders placed in the month: 5,000
Of those, canceled by the customer: 140
Canceled by the company because the product was out of stock: 60
Returns after delivery: 180 (excluded)

Order Cancellation Rate = (140 + 60) / 5,000 × 100 = **4%**
218.importance: **Bridges the gap between what** was sold on the storefront and what actually got delivered. A rising rate usually comes down to one of two causes: the storefront shows products that aren't in the warehouse, or the delivery time on the product page differs from what the customer sees at checkout. Without this metric, revenue targets are built on orders, some of which won't make it to shipment.
218.not_needed: Skip it where ordering and handover are **one event**: digital goods with instant access have no gap between placement and handover, and nothing to cancel within it.
218.essence_note: a canceled order takes away revenue after the work on it is already done

219.name: Average Discount Rate
219.formula: Sum of Stated Discount Percentages across Promotions / Number of Promotions
219.description: The average size of the discount across active promotions, expressed as a percentage.
219.nuances:
**The calculation uses the stated terms** of promotions rather than the discounts actually applied: the metric describes the offer rather than what customers used.
Discounts set as a dollar amount are converted into a percentage of the product price; otherwise they'd have to be dropped, and the average would describe **only some of the promotions**.
**It's a simple average**, not weighted by the number of uses: a rare 70% promotion weighs as much as a widely used 5% one and noticeably pulls the number up.
219.example:
Promotions at 10%, 15%, 20%, 5%
A $6-off promotion at an average item price of $30 = 20%

Average Discount Rate = (10 + 15 + 20 + 5 + 20) / 5 = **14%**
219.importance: Keeps **discount depth** in view: promotions are added one at a time and each seems reasonable, while the average level creeps toward the point beyond which customers no longer take the full price seriously. This number is used to check promotions against margin: an average discount above the margin means some promotions sell products at a loss.
219.not_needed: Skip it under a **single discount policy** with one discount rate.
219.synonyms: Average Discount Depth, Average Discount Percentage
219.essence_note: every percentage point of discount is margin given away

220.name: Average Order Value with Promo Code
220.formula: Revenue from Orders with Promo Code / Number of Orders with Promo Code
220.description: The average value of an order in which a promo code was applied.
220.nuances:
Revenue **is measured after discounts**: what counts is the amount the customer actually paid; otherwise the metric can't be compared with the regular AOV.
The base **is calculated under the same** rules as [[Average Order Value (AOV)→zakazy/sredniy_chek_aov]]: net of returns and with the same decision on whether to include shipping.
220.example:
Orders with a promo code in March: 1,260
Revenue from them after discounts: $99,540

Average Order Value with Promo Code = 99,540 / 1,260 = **$79**

The overall AOV is $75: the promo code raises the order value, which means customers fill up the cart to qualify for the discount.
220.importance: **The only way to understand** what a promo code does to the cart: whether it increases order value or just discounts what customers would have bought anyway. If the discounted order value is lower than usual, the promotion is spinning its wheels and gives away margin without changing behavior. It's also the basis for deciding on a minimum order amount for using the code.
220.not_needed: **Skip it** when promo codes aren't used at all.
220.essence_note: the bigger the discounted order, the more likely the promo code increased the order value rather than just discounted it

221.name: Free Shipping Threshold
221.description: The minimum order amount at which the customer gets free shipping.
221.nuances:
**Define** which amount the threshold applies to: before the discount or after. An $80 order with a 20% promo code becomes $64, and this decision determines whether it qualifies for free shipping.
**Decide** whether the shipping cost itself counts toward the threshold. Usually it doesn't: otherwise the order reaches the threshold on the shipping fee rather than on the products.
221.example:
AOV: $75
Shipping cost to the company: $7
Order margin: 35%
Order amount whose margin covers $7: 7 / 0.35 = $20

The threshold is set above the AOV so that it pushes customers to spend more: **$80**

With a $20 threshold, most orders would ship free, and the company would give shipping away to people who would have paid for it.
221.importance: **One of the few levers** that raise the AOV through a single decision, with no budget or development work. A threshold below the AOV gives shipping away to people who would have bought anyway and cuts margin with no return. One that's too high drives customers away: the customer sees an unreachable amount and abandons the cart.
221.not_needed: **Skip it** when shipping is always free or always paid: there is no threshold.
221.synonyms: Free Shipping Minimum, Minimum Order for Free Shipping
221.essence_note: a low threshold makes the company subsidize small orders, and a high one scares the buyer off at the last step

222.name: Upsell Acceptance Rate
222.description: The share of upsell offer impressions after which the customer bought a higher-priced version of the product.
222.nuances:
**An offer counts as accepted** if it leads to a paid order. Clicking the higher-priced version and then not paying doesn't count as an upsell.
**Set a window between** the impression and the purchase. Usually only a purchase within the same session counts: if the customer came back for the higher-priced version a week later, the upsell offer no longer had anything to do with it.
Repeat impressions of the same offer to the same customer within a session **count as one impression**; otherwise page scrolling inflates the denominator.
222.example:
Upsell offer impressions in the month: 18,000
Clicked the higher-priced version: 2,700
Of those, completed payment in the same session: 1,440

Upsell Acceptance Rate = 1,440 / 18,000 × 100 = **8%**

Using clicks would give 15%: that's interest in the offer rather than the result of the upsell.
222.importance: **It's used to decide** whether to keep the block offering the higher-priced version on the page: the block takes the best spot and competes for attention with the buy button. If the rate stays near zero, the offer gets in the way of the main purchase flow and lowers conversion more than it adds to the order value. Growth in the rate raises the AOV without requiring any acquisition spending.
222.not_needed: **Skip it** when products have no higher-priced versions: with an assortment of one-off items, there's nothing to offer.
222.synonyms: Upsell Take Rate, Upsell Conversion Rate
222.essence_note: the customer buys a higher-priced version, and revenue grows without a new buyer

223.name: Cross-Sell Rate
223.description: The share of paid orders that include an additional product from a cross-sell offer.
223.nuances:
The numerator **is counted in orders** rather than added products: three accessories in one order make one successful cross-sell.
**A product counts as additional** if it was added from the recommendations block; any other second item in the cart doesn't count. Otherwise every two-item order ends up in the numerator, and the metric turns into the share of multi-item orders.
223.example:
Paid orders in the month: 4,500
Orders with two or more items: 1,800
Of those, with a product added from the recommendations block: 630

Cross-Sell Rate = 630 / 4,500 × 100 = **14%**
223.importance: **It shows** whether recommendations work as a salesperson or just take up space on the page. The added order value here costs less than any other kind of growth: the customer is already placing an order, so there's no need to pay to acquire them a second time. If the rate hasn't moved for months, the recommendation set was put together mechanically and misses what the customer actually needs along with the purchase.
223.not_needed: **Skip it** when products don't go together and there's nothing to cross-sell.
223.synonyms: Cross-Sell Conversion Rate, Cross-Sell Success Rate
223.essence_note: an additional product raises the order value without acquisition costs

224.name: Brand Alignment Score
224.formula: (Sum of Factor Scores) / Number of Factors
224.description: The average score of how well an influencer fits the brand across a set of chosen factors. Scale from 0 to 5.
224.nuances:
**The set of factors and** their wording are the same for all influencers being scored: adding a factor for one person makes the scores incomparable.
**If factors are weighted**, the formula uses the weighted average score, and the weights add up to one.
**Each factor is scored** against levels described in advance: without descriptions, two employees' scores for the same influencer diverge, and the result depends on who filled in the form.
A deal-breaker factor sets the **whole score** to zero rather than lowering the average: an influencer involved in a public scandal shouldn't qualify thanks to high scores on the other factors.
224.example:
Audience match by age and gender: 5
Content topic: 4
Tone and language: 3
Past ads for competitors: 4
Reputational risks: 4

Brand Alignment Score = (5 + 4 + 3 + 4 + 4) / 5 = **4.0**
224.importance: **It turns a debate about taste** into comparable numbers: when two people on the team argue whether an influencer is “right for us,” the discussion goes factor by factor rather than by gut feeling. Without formal selection, a campaign gets built from familiar names, and the budget goes to an audience that doesn't buy the product.
224.not_needed: **Skip it for** mass placements with micro-influencers, where hundreds of accounts are selected and scoring each one costs more than the placement itself.
224.synonyms: Brand Fit Score, Influencer Fit Score
224.essence_note: the better an influencer fits the brand, the higher the chance that their audience will buy

225.name: Influencer Selection Success Rate
225.description: What share of the influencers who received an offer agreed to collaborate.
225.nuances:
The denominator **matches the number** in Contacted Influencers, and the numerator matches Collaborating Influencers: both count people, not messages or placements.
Agreement **means a signed contract**, as in Collaborating Influencers: until then, either side can back out, and counting such replies as agreement inflates the rate.
Both values **are assigned to the period by the date** the offer was sent: an agreement that comes three weeks later is assigned to the period when the offer went out; otherwise, one month's outreach is divided by another month's responses.
**Offers** with no reply yet stay in the denominator: silence is a refusal.
225.example:
Offers sent: 10
Signed a contract: 6
Expressed interest but didn't sign a contract: 2 (not counted)
Didn't reply: 2

Influencer Selection Success Rate = 6 / 10 × 100 = **60%**
225.importance: **It tests the brand's offer itself**: when the rate is low, it's the offer that isn't working rather than the list of influencers, and it's the fee, the terms and the first email that need reworking. It's used to calculate how many contacts are needed to get the required number of placements, and without it the recruitment plan is guesswork.
225.not_needed: **Skip it when** working through an agency or a marketplace, where an intermediary runs the negotiations and the brand doesn't see refusals.
225.synonyms: Influencer Acceptance Rate, Outreach Acceptance Rate
225.essence_note: the more often influencers agree, the less time goes into negotiations for the same number of placements

226.name: Contacted Influencers
226.description: How many influencers were sent a collaboration offer.
226.nuances:
**Influencers are counted**, not messages: repeat emails and reminders to one person count as one offer.
**An offer is assigned to the period** by the date it was first sent.
**Mass mailings to** a contact list without personalization don't count unless someone actively works them: otherwise the count is inflated and the Influencer Selection Success Rate falls for reasons unrelated to the actual outreach.
226.example:
Emails and messages sent: 14
Of those, repeat reminders to the same people: 4 (not counted)

Contacted Influencers = **10 influencers**
