226.importance: It sets the top of the recruitment funnel: if there aren't enough agreements, first check whether enough offers were sent at all, and **only then rewrite** the offer itself. It's the denominator for the Influencer Selection Success Rate, so inflating it after the fact makes the second metric meaningless too.
226.not_needed: **Skip it for** inbound inquiries, when influencers come to the brand themselves, and when working through an agency that handles the negotiations itself.
226.essence_note: the more influencers you reach out to, the more agreements you get

227.name: Collaborating Influencers
227.description: How many influencers signed a contract to take part in a campaign. They count once the agreement is made, whether or not the post came out.
227.nuances:
Agreement **means a signed contract**: interest expressed in messages and discussion of terms don't count, because either side can back out until the contract is signed.
**An influencer** who terminated the contract before publication is removed from the count: the campaign with them didn't happen. One who didn't terminate the contract but didn't publish the content stays: the failure shows up in the difference from the number of published pieces.
One influencer with several accounts **counts once**.
227.example:
Offers sent: 10
Agreed: 7
Backed out after the cost estimate was approved: 1 (not counted)
One influencer runs two accounts: counted as one

Collaborating Influencers = **6**
227.importance: It sets the scale of the campaign and the workload of the manager who reviews content and tracks deadlines. A shortfall against the target shows up here earlier than in other metrics: if two out of ten agreed, reach **will fall short, and the budget** will have to be moved to another channel.
227.not_needed: **Skip it for** a one-off placement with one influencer: the number is always one.
227.essence_note: with too few influencers, the result depends on one person; with too many, the manager can't keep up with reviews and oversight

228.name: Average Followers of Contacted Influencers
228.description: How many followers, on average, the influencers the brand contacted have.
228.nuances:
The follower count **is taken as of the date** of contact, not the calculation date: a growing account's count can change noticeably in between.
An influencer with several accounts **counts once**, with the main account's followers; otherwise, the average gets diluted by second and third platforms.
**Large accounts skew the average** upward: with a spread from 5,000 to 1,000,000 followers, the average describes an influencer who doesn't exist, and the median shows the typical value.
228.example:
Influencers contacted: 10
Total followers: 1,240,000
Of those, one account has: 800,000

Average = 1,240,000 / 10 = **124,000 followers**

The median for the same ten: 42,000. The gap shows that the base consists of small accounts and one large one.
228.importance: **It describes** who the brand is trying to make deals with in the first place, and explains the gap between the reach target and the result. If the average falls from period to period, large influencers have stopped responding, and rewording the email alone won't fix that: it takes a different budget.
228.not_needed: **Skip it on** platforms without a public follower count, and on platforms where the audience is measured in views rather than followers.
228.synonyms: Average Follower Count, Average Audience Size
228.essence_note: small influencers give a cheap contact but you need many of them, while large ones are expensive and engage their audience less

229.name: Influencer Marketing Spend
229.formula: Sum of all costs of placements with influencers
229.description: How much money was spent on working with influencers in the period.
229.nuances:
Spend **includes the full cost** of placements: the cash fee, the cost and shipping of products given as barter, payment for content production, the agency or influencer marketplace commission.
Spend **is assigned to the date** of publication, not the date of the money transfer: a prepayment for a January post sent in December goes to January; otherwise, spend doesn't match the results of placements.
Money for content that never came out is assigned to the period when **the agreed publication deadline passed**, as in [[Wasted Budget→rabota_s_inflyuenserami/poteri_byudzheta]]: such content has no publication date, and otherwise this money would never be included in spend.
The in-house manager's salary **isn't included** in spend: it's a fixed team cost that doesn't depend on the number of placements.
229.example:
Cash fees: $9,000
Products given as barter, at cost: $1,600
Video filming: $800
Platform commission: $600
These amounts include money for two pieces that didn't come out or were deleted early: $1,840 (counted)
Prepayment for a post next month: $2,400 (not counted)

Influencer Marketing Spend = 9,000 + 1,600 + 800 + 600 = **$12,000**
229.importance: The basis for all return calculations: without a single cost total, neither the cost per contact nor the return **can be calculated**. Understating it by leaving out barter and production makes the channel look free, and money keeps going into it without a comparison with paid advertising.
229.not_needed: **Skip it for** barter placements where the product has no cash value assigned: no cash is spent.
229.synonyms: Influencer Marketing Budget, Total Influencer Spend, Influencer Marketing Costs
229.essence_note: every dollar spent on placements is subtracted from what the channel brings in

230.name: Influencer Content Pieces Created
230.description: How many pieces influencers produced and submitted as part of a campaign.
230.nuances:
Unit of count: one standalone piece submitted to the brand. A series of Stories from one script **counts as one** piece if it was submitted as a whole.
**A piece is assigned to the period** by the date it was submitted for review, not the date work on it started.
Drafts and interim versions of one piece **count once**: revisions don't create a new unit.
Pieces rejected at review **are included in the count**: the work was done and paid for.
230.example:
Pieces submitted in the month: 8
Of those, with two rounds of revisions: 2 (each counted once)
Rejected outright: 1 (counted)
In progress, not submitted: 3 (not counted)

Influencer Content Pieces Created = **8**
230.importance: **Content Approval Rate is calculated from it**, and it's compared with published content: the gap between these two numbers is the amount of paid work that never reached the audience. It's also used to plan the workload of the review team, because each piece requires a round of revisions.
230.not_needed: **Skip it when** placing ready-made brand creatives, where the influencer doesn't produce anything.
230.essence_note: this is the content the brand got for its budget

231.name: Influencer Content Pieces Published
231.description: How many pieces influencers actually published.
231.nuances:
The unit of count is the same as in Influencer Content Pieces Created: one standalone piece. A series of Stories from one script **counts as one** piece.
**A piece is assigned to the period** by its publication date, not the date it was submitted to the brand.
**Pieces deleted before the agreed** end of the placement period are removed from the count: their results can't be collected.
Re-posting the same piece as a pinned post or in another format **doesn't count** again.
231.example:
Pieces that went live in the month: 7
Of those, deleted on the second day under a 30-day agreement: 1 (not counted)
Piece duplicated as a pinned post: not counted again

Influencer Content Pieces Published = **6**
231.importance: **The denominator for** Engagements per Post and a check against payments: a mismatch with the number of approved invoices means the brand paid for something that didn't happen. The difference from created content shows the amount of work that went to waste.
231.not_needed: **Skip it for** product gifting with no obligation to post: the content comes out at the influencer's discretion, there's no agreed quantity, and there's nothing to check the actual number against.
231.synonyms: Published Influencer Posts, Influencer Posts Published
231.essence_note: until a piece is published, it brings in neither reach nor sales

232.name: Content Approval Rate
232.description: What share of the content created by influencers passed the brand's review and was cleared for publication.
232.nuances:
The unit of count is the same as in Influencer Content Pieces Created and Influencer Content Pieces Published: one standalone piece ready to go live. A series of five Stories from one script **counts as one** piece if it was submitted and reviewed as a whole.
A piece approved after revisions **counts as approved**: revisions don't cancel the result.
The numerator and denominator **are assigned to the period by the date** the piece was submitted, not the approval date; otherwise, pieces submitted at the end of the period and approved later drop out of the calculation.
232.example:
Pieces created: 8
Approved right away: 5
Approved after revisions: 2
Rejected outright: 1

Content Approval Rate = (5 + 2) / 8 × 100 = **87.5%**
232.importance: **It shows the quality of the brief earlier** than placement results do: a low rate points to the brief rather than the influencers, so rewrite the requirements instead of changing contractors. Every rejected piece has been paid for, so a drop in the rate turns directly into lost money.
232.not_needed: **Skip it** when the brand doesn't review content and gives the influencer full freedom, and when placing ready-made brand creatives, where there's nothing to review.
232.synonyms: Content Acceptance Rate, Creative Approval Rate
232.essence_note: every rejected piece has already been paid for and never reached the audience

233.name: Influencer Link Clicks
233.description: How many clicks were made on influencers' tracked links.
233.nuances:
**The unit of count is the same** as in Influencer CTR: a click, not a unique user. Three clicks by the same person count as three clicks.
Clicks that the site identifies as technical duplicates within one session don't count: otherwise the number **diverges from sessions** in site analytics. No one filters out bots for you here: influencer traffic doesn't pass through an ad account's invalid-click filtering and comes in raw, so bots have to be removed on your side.
**Clicks are counted on** links with the tags issued for the placement. Visits from search or from users typing the address directly aren't included.
233.example:
Clicks on influencers' tagged links: 10,200
Bots filtered out: 400 (not counted)
Repeat clicks by one user within a minute: 200 (not counted)

Influencer Link Clicks = **9,600**
233.importance: The first signal of how a placement is doing: clicks come in soon after the post goes live, while orders are still far off, and they show whether it's worth buying more distribution. **Without this number, there's no** denominator for the order conversion rate, and a drop in sales can't be told apart from a drop in interest in the post itself.
233.not_needed: **Skip it on platforms** where links in posts aren't allowed, and for offline activations with influencers.
233.essence_note: every click is a person the placement brought to the site

234.name: Influencer CTR
234.description: The share of content impressions that end in a link click.
234.nuances:
**Denominator**: impressions, the same as in Influencer CPM. Calculating from reach gives a higher percentage because reach is smaller than impressions.
Clicks include only clicks on tracked links with a tag. Visits from search or from users typing the address manually **aren't captured**, so actual interest in the post is higher than the calculated CTR shows.
Clicks **are the same** as in [[Influencer Link Clicks→rabota_s_inflyuenserami/kliki_po_ssylkam_inflyuenserov]], with the same handling of repeat clicks.
234.example:
Impressions: 480,000
Link clicks: 10,200
Of those, bots and duplicates: 600 (not counted)

Influencer CTR = 9,600 / 480,000 × 100 = **2.0%**

Calculated from a reach of 300,000, it would be 3.2%: clicks as a share of people who saw the post rather than of impressions.
234.importance: **It separates two causes** of a weak result: if there are many impressions and no clicks, the problem is the post itself and its call to action rather than the audience size. It helps decide whether to keep the link in the profile bio or require it in the content itself, because the link's placement determines whether someone who watched to the end sees it at all.
234.not_needed: **Skip it** when links aren't available on the platform and sales go through a promo code, and for brand campaigns that don't lead to the site.
234.synonyms: Influencer Click-Through Rate, Influencer Link CTR
234.essence_note: the more impressions end in a click, the better the post works

235.name: Engagements per Post
235.formula: Total Engagements / Number of Published Pieces
235.description: How many engagements a published piece of content receives on average.
235.nuances:
**The set of actions in** the numerator is the same as in Influencer Content Engagement: likes, comments, shares, saves, without views.
The denominator **matches the count in** Influencer Content Pieces Published, not the count of created pieces: unpublished content receives no engagements.
**Engagements are captured over** the same period after the post for all content, for example, 7 days; otherwise, older placements look stronger than recent ones just because they've been up longer.
The result **is an absolute count** and isn't adjusted for audience size: a piece by a large influencer tends to get more engagements than one by a small influencer.
235.example:
Engagements over 7 days after the posts: 24,000
Pieces published: 6

Engagements per Post = 24,000 / 6 = **4,000 engagements per piece**

Dividing by the 8 pieces created gives 3,000: two of them weren't published and couldn't get any reactions.
235.importance: It makes campaigns with different numbers of placements comparable: a campaign of two posts and a campaign of twenty are compared by average engagements per piece rather than by total likes. A drop in the average while the number of posts grows means the brand has taken on weak influencers, and the overall growth rests **only on volume**.
235.not_needed: **Skip it on** platforms with hidden reactions, where engagement counts are unavailable.
235.synonyms: Average Engagements per Post, Average Engagement per Post
235.essence_note: the more reactions a piece gets, the more it has hooked the audience

236.name: Influencer Content Engagement
236.description: How many engagements influencer content generated in total: likes, comments, shares and saves.
236.nuances:
The set of actions **is fixed in advance and** doesn't change between calculations: adding saves and shares to likes and comments noticeably increases the result with no change in the content itself, so the set of engagements is fixed and stated next to the number.
Views **aren't included** in engagements: a view is a passive contact, and it's already counted in impressions.
**Engagements are captured over** a fixed period after the post, for example, 7 days; otherwise, older content keeps getting engagements and the number grows retroactively.
**The influencer's own comments** and the brand's replies are removed from the count.
236.example:
Likes: 18,400
Comments: 2,100
Of those, by the influencer and the brand: 100 (not counted)
Shares: 1,300
Saves: 2,300

Influencer Content Engagement = 18,400 + 2,000 + 1,300 + 2,300 = **24,000 engagements**
236.importance: **It shows** whether the content hooked the audience before sales data comes in. A post with large reach and a hundred likes means people scrolled past it, and it's time to rewrite the next brief rather than buy more reach.
236.not_needed: **Skip it on platforms** where reactions are hidden or turned off, and in private mailing lists and channels without public reactions.
236.essence_note: reactions show that people saw the content and it struck a chord rather than being scrolled past

237.name: Influencer Impressions
237.description: How many times influencer content was shown to users. Three views of a post by the same person count as three impressions.
237.nuances:
**Impressions and reach** are different quantities and can't be added into one number: reach counts unique people and doesn't add up across posts, because the same followers see several pieces in a row.
The data source **is fixed in advance**. There's no way to verify screenshots of statistics from an influencer, so where a placement runs through an influencer marketplace or the brand's ad account, the numbers are taken from there: they come directly from the platform. Impressions from an ad account and impressions from screenshots can't be mixed in one report, because their reliability differs.
**Impressions are captured over** a fixed period after the post, the same for all placements: Stories get their impressions faster, while videos and posts keep getting them for longer, and without a common window recent placements look weaker than older ones.
237.example:
Pieces published: 6
Impressions over 7 days after each post: 480,000
Reach for the same pieces: 300,000 unique people

Influencer Impressions = **480,000**

Adding up the reach of six posts into 300,000 “people” doesn't work: the audiences overlap, so there are fewer actual people.
237.importance: **The denominator for** Influencer CPM and Influencer CTR, so an error here spoils both metrics at once. Checking promised impressions against actual ones settles whether the agreement was met: the influencer promised 100,000, delivered 40,000, and the next fee is negotiated from the 40,000.
237.not_needed: Skip it on platforms that report **only reach without** impression counts, and for offline formats with influencers.
237.synonyms: Influencer Content Impressions, Sponsored Post Impressions
237.essence_note: without an impression, nobody sees the content

238.name: Influencer CPM
238.description: The cost per thousand impressions of influencer content. It's calculated from impressions rather than reach: one person can see a post several times, so there are always at least as many impressions as people.
238.nuances:
Costs **include the full cost** of a placement: the fee, the cost of products given as barter, and content production if the brand paid for filming or editing.
Impressions **come from the platform analytics** that the influencer gives you access to. If there's no access and the platform reports only reach, the metric can't be calculated: substituting reach for impressions inflates the cost per thousand contacts.
**Stories and posts** stay live for different lengths of time, so impressions are captured over a fixed period after the post (for example, 7 days); otherwise, recent content keeps adding impressions after the calculation.
238.example:
Placement costs: $12,000
Impressions over 7 days: 480,000

Influencer CPM = 12,000 / 480,000 × 1,000 = **$25**

Substituting a reach of 300,000 for impressions gives $40: that's the cost per thousand people rather than per thousand impressions.
238.importance: It lets you compare the cost per contact with the cost of buying ads directly and see whether an influencer costs more than display advertising. **Without it, the placement price** is discussed in absolute dollars, and an influencer with a $6,000 fee looks more expensive than one charging $1,000, even if the first influencer's cost per contact is one-third as much.
238.not_needed: **Skip it for** barter placements where the product has no cash value assigned, and when working with micro-influencers in private communities, where the platform doesn't report impression statistics.
238.synonyms: Influencer Cost per Mille, Influencer Cost per Thousand Impressions
238.essence_note: the cheaper a thousand contacts, the more reach the same budget buys

239.name: Influencer Campaign ROI
239.formula: (Gross Profit from Promo Code Orders − [[Influencer Marketing Spend→rabota_s_inflyuenserami/byudzhet_na_inflyuens_marketing]]) / Influencer Marketing Spend × 100
239.description: The return on investment in influencer marketing: how much was earned on top of what was spent, per dollar invested.
239.nuances:
The numerator uses **gross profit rather than revenue**: revenue from orders net of returned and canceled ones, as in [[Revenue from Influencer Promo Codes→rabota_s_inflyuenserami/vyruchka_po_promokodam_inflyuenserov]], minus the cost of goods sold in these orders. Revenue-based ROI is overstated by the full cost of goods.
The cost of goods is calculated **from the products in these orders** rather than estimated from the average [[Gross Margin→finansy/rentabelnost_valovoy_pribyli]]: promo code orders come with a discount, and their margin is below average.
Costs **include the full cost** of a placement: fees, the cost of products given as barter, payment for content production, the agency or platform commission.
Sales are tracked using both promo codes and UTM tags. An order that appears in both sources **is counted once**.
**Some purchases go untracked**: a person saw the post, looked it up in search and bought without a code and without a click, so a calculation based on promo codes and tags gives a lower bound.
Promo code orders keep coming in after the placement ends, so **a window is set**: how long after the post a purchase can still be attributed to this campaign. The window is the same for all placements; otherwise, campaign returns can't be compared. A short window understates the return, and a long one takes in purchases that happened for other reasons.
239.example:
Campaign costs: $12,000
Revenue from promo codes and tags: $37,000
Returns: $3,000
Cost of goods sold, excluding returned goods: $20,400

Net revenue = 37,000 − 3,000 = $34,000
Gross profit = 34,000 − 20,400 = $13,600
Influencer Campaign ROI = (13,600 − 12,000) / 12,000 × 100 = **13%**

Calculated from revenue, it would be (34,000 − 12,000) / 12,000 × 100 = 183%: the cost of goods sold isn't subtracted from it.
239.importance: **It determines** whether to keep working with influencers and what budget to plan for the next period. Without it, decisions on repeat placements are based on like counts and reach, and money keeps going where there are no sales.
239.not_needed: **Skip it for** awareness campaigns around a brand launch and for products with a long consideration period, where the purchase happens long after the post and falls outside the attribution window.
239.essence_note: the more profit each dollar of placement spend brings in, the more profitable the channel

240.name: Average Cost per Collaboration
240.formula: Total Placement Costs / Number of Influencers
240.description: How much one collaboration with an influencer costs on average.
240.nuances:
The numerator **matches Influencer Marketing Spend**: it includes the fee, the cost of products given as barter, payment for content production and the platform commission.
The denominator includes **only influencers** who received payment. Counting those who agreed but never got as far as a placement would pull the average down.
An influencer with several placements in the period **counts once**: otherwise it's the average cost per post rather than per collaboration.
240.example:
Total placement costs: $12,000
Influencers who were paid: 6
One of them had two placements: counted as one

Average Cost per Collaboration = 12,000 / 6 = **$2,000**
240.importance: **A benchmark for negotiations** and planning: knowing the average price, it's easy to calculate how many placements next quarter's budget will buy. A sharp rise in the average with the same reach means the brand has started overpaying for a name, and that's a reason to rebuild the list.
240.not_needed: **Skip it for** barter where the product has no cash value assigned and for payment as a percentage of sales, where there's no fixed cost of a collaboration.
240.synonyms: Average Influencer Fee, Cost per Integration
240.essence_note: the cheaper one placement is, the more of them the same budget buys

241.name: Orders with Influencer Promo Codes
241.formula: Number of orders with influencer promo codes
241.description: How many orders were placed using influencer promo codes.
241.nuances:
**The unit of count is the same** as in Revenue from Influencer Promo Codes: a placed order, not a customer. Two purchases by the same person using the same code count as two orders.
Returned and canceled orders **are subtracted**.
**Orders are counted within** the window after the post, the same one as in Revenue from Influencer Promo Codes: otherwise the order count and the revenue cover different sets of orders.
Orders placed without a promo code by people who came from the post aren't included: the code tracks **only people** who entered it.
241.example:
Orders with promo codes in the month: 780
Canceled before shipping: 25 (not counted)
Returned after delivery: 60 (not counted)
Placed after the 30-day window ended: 45 (not counted)

Orders with Influencer Promo Codes = **650**
241.importance: **It gives the denominator for calculating** the cost per order and the average order value of the channel, so without it you can't calculate the acquisition cost of influencer marketing. The distribution of orders by day after the post shows how long a placement's effect lasts: for some influencers it fades quickly, for others it lasts longer thanks to a pinned post and shares. This is where you decide how long the window should be and when to finalize the campaign results.
241.not_needed: **Skip it** when the brand doesn't give influencers personal codes, and in models without a checkout, where customers pay by subscription through a third-party store.
241.synonyms: Influencer Code Redemptions, Influencer Coupon Orders
241.essence_note: these are confirmed purchases that came from specific influencers

242.name: Unpublished Influencer Content
242.description: How many of the pieces created never went live.
242.nuances:
**The unit of count is the same** as in Influencer Content Pieces Created and Influencer Content Pieces Published: one standalone piece.
A piece **counts as unpublished** once the agreed publication deadline has passed. Until then it isn't counted; otherwise, everything in progress on the calculation date ends up in losses.
Pieces rejected at review **are included**: they were created and paid for but didn't come out.
242.example:
Pieces created: 8
Published: 6
Rejected at review: 1
Approved, but the influencer didn't publish on time: 1
In progress, publication deadline not yet reached: 0

Unpublished Influencer Content = **2**
242.importance: **A direct input for** calculating lost money: each piece was paid for but produced no results. Growth in this number means the problem is in how the process is organized, and the fix is to set deadlines in the contract rather than replace influencers.
242.not_needed: **Skip it when** payment is made upon publication, so unpublished content isn't paid for, and when working with ready-made brand creatives.
242.essence_note: this content has been paid for but never reached the audience

243.name: Wasted Budget
243.formula: Sum of costs for unused content
243.description: How much money went to content that was never published.
243.nuances:
Costs **are based on the amounts actually** paid out. If the money for an unpublished piece was withheld or refunded, there's no loss.
Losses **include the full cost** of the placement for that piece: the fee, the cost of products given as barter, payment for production.
Losses **are assigned to the period** when the agreed publication deadline passed, not to the payment date.
It covers the same pieces as Unpublished Influencer Content, **only in dollars**.
243.example:
Unpublished pieces: 2
Rejected piece, fee paid: $900
Product given as barter to this influencer: $240
Piece not published on time, 50% prepayment: $700
Second half of the fee withheld: $700 (not counted, the money wasn't paid out)

Wasted Budget = 900 + 240 + 700 = **$1,840**
243.importance: **It shows the cost of a weak review process** in dollars and gives grounds to rewrite payment terms: the larger the losses as a share of the budget, the faster a switch to payment after publication pays off. Without this number, failed placements are discussed as an organizational nuisance rather than as an expense line.
243.not_needed: **Skip it when** payment is made in full after publication, and for barter where the product isn't handed over before the content comes out.
243.essence_note: this is money spent on content that never came out and produced no results

244.name: Collaboration Success Rate
244.description: The share of collaborations that took place and met goals set in advance. A collaboration means a published post: an agreement under which the content never came out isn't counted.
244.nuances:
The success criterion **is fixed before launch** and is the same for all collaborations in the calculation: typically a sales target or a cost-per-contact target. Judging after the fact, with the threshold picked to fit the result, turns the metric into a restatement of the results.
Agreements with no published content **are excluded entirely**: there was no collaboration and nothing to evaluate. Losses on such failed agreements are counted separately, through the spending that wasn't recovered.
Only completed collaborations go into the denominator: content whose measurement window hasn't ended yet **isn't included**.
244.example:
Agreements for the period: 6
Of those, the post fell through: 1 (not counted)
Collaborations that took place: 5

Success threshold: cost per acquired order no higher than $20
Met it: 4
Didn't meet it: 1

Collaboration Success Rate = 4 / 5 × 100 = **80%**
244.importance: It answers whether the channel works overall or whether the results come from a few lucky placements. Two strong collaborations out of ten give a decent total ROI, but such a campaign can't be repeated: eight of the ten paid placements lost money, and you can see that **only here**.
244.not_needed: **Skip it for** one-off placements and when working with two or three influencers, where a single result moves the rate by tens of percentage points on such a small base.
244.synonyms: Influencer Success Rate, Campaign Success Rate
244.essence_note: the more placements reach their goal, the more predictable the campaign result

245.name: Revenue from Influencer Promo Codes
245.formula: Sum of revenue from orders with influencer promo codes
245.description: How much revenue came from orders placed with influencer promo codes.
245.nuances:
The amount **is calculated after applying** the promo code discount: that's what the customer actually paid.
Returned and canceled orders **are subtracted**.
A promo code counts **only people** who enter it in the cart. Purchases by people who saw the post and bought without the code aren't included, so the number is always lower than the channel's actual contribution.
An order with an influencer promo code still counts here even if the visit came from another ad: people can get the code **only from the post**.
**Orders are counted within** a window after the post that is the same for all placements: a code stays valid longer than the placement itself, and without a common window, campaigns with different code validity periods can't be compared.
245.example:
Orders with promo codes in the month: 780
Order total after discount: $38,000
Returns: $3,000
Orders outside the 30-day window: $2,000 (not counted)

Revenue from Influencer Promo Codes = 38,000 − 3,000 − 2,000 = **$33,000**
245.importance: It's the only revenue you can attribute to a specific placement, so it's the basis for negotiating repeat deals and a switch to a percentage-of-sales fee. Without this number, you have **only reach** to show for a campaign, and price talks with the influencer rest on the influencer's own statistics.
245.not_needed: Skip it when the brand doesn't issue promo codes and relies **only on UTM tags**, and for sales on marketplaces, where outside promo codes can't be applied at checkout.
245.synonyms: Influencer Coupon Revenue, Discount Code Sales
245.essence_note: this is revenue you can attribute to a specific placement

246.name: Influencer Engagement Rate
246.formula: (Total Engagements / Number of Posts) / Number of Followers × 100
246.description: How actively an influencer's audience reacts to their posts: the average number of engagements per post as a percentage of the follower count.
246.nuances:
**Calculation base**: followers, not reach. The same engagements divided by reach give a different number, usually a higher one, because a post's reach is smaller than the follower count.
**It's calculated over the most recent** posts, with the same number of posts for every influencer, for example 9–12: otherwise one influencer's sample may include a viral post and another's may not.
Sponsored and organic posts **are included together**: without sponsored posts, you can't see how the audience reacts to advertising.
The follower count **is taken as of the date** of calculation, not the date of the oldest post in the sample.
246.example:
Followers: 120,000
Engagements on the last 10 posts: 43,200

Average per post = 43,200 / 10 = 4,320
Influencer Engagement Rate = 4,320 / 120,000 × 100 = **3.6%**

Dividing the same engagements by a post's reach (45,000) gives 9.6%: that's the share of people who reacted among those who saw the post, and it answers a different question. That metric isn't on the map, and it can't stand in for the engagement rate: reach changes from post to post, while the follower count doesn't.
246.importance: **The main filter when** selecting an influencer before a deal: an account with inflated follower numbers gets almost no reactions to its posts, and the money would pay for reach with no real audience behind it. It helps negotiate the price when an influencer asks for a fee based on follower count: comparing the engagement rate among influencers of similar size shows what exactly you're paying for.
246.not_needed: **Skip it on** platforms without publicly available post metrics and when working with private communities where the follower count isn't public.
246.synonyms: Engagement Rate by Followers, Profile Engagement Rate, Audience Engagement Rate
246.essence_note: an account with inflated follower numbers gets almost no reactions, so the money pays for reach with no real audience behind it

247.name: Net Promoter Score (NPS)
247.description: The difference between the share of people willing to recommend the company and the share of those who don't recommend it. Customers answer a question about their willingness to recommend on a scale from 0 to 10.
247.nuances:
The group boundaries are standard: 9–10 promoters, 7–8 passives, 0–6 detractors. Passives **don't enter** either numerator but stay in the denominator of both shares, so you can't drop them from the base.
Both shares **are calculated from the number** of people who responded, not the number surveyed.
**The result falls in** the range from −100 to +100 and is written as a number without a percent sign.
**Survey responses come** more readily from people with strong feelings, so with a low response rate the result shifts toward the ends of the scale.
247.importance: The only metric on the map that shows how customers feel about the company as a whole rather than about their last conversation with an agent. It's used to decide whether to invest in retention or in acquisition: with a negative value, new customers leave faster than they arrive, and advertising **only speeds up the loss**.
247.essence_note: this is how much the people who bring in new customers outweigh those who talk others out of buying

248.name: Customer Satisfaction Score (CSAT)
248.description: The share of positive ratings among all ratings customers gave after contacting support. The rating is for a specific ticket, right after it's closed.
248.nuances:
Ratings of **4 and 5** on a five-point scale count as positive; the middle rating of 3 doesn't go into the numerator.
Denominator: **only the responses received**. Dividing by all tickets gives the share of tickets with a positive response rather than the satisfaction score. Show the response rate next to the score: the lower it is, the more the result leans toward people who had a reason to speak up.
**Unit of count**: a rating per ticket, not per customer. A customer who contacted support five times and rated each conversation gives five ratings.
**When you ask for the rating** changes the result. Right after closing, people rate their impression of the conversation; a few days later, whether the problem was actually solved.
248.example:
Closed tickets with a rating request: 3,780
Rated: 605
Of those, rated 4–5: 502
Rated 3: 41 (not in the numerator)

CSAT = 502 / 605 × 100 = **83%**

Dividing by all 3,780 gives 13%: that's the share of tickets with a positive rating rather than the satisfaction score.
248.importance: Customers primarily rate whether their issue was resolved, so the score is used to judge the quality of solutions and the team's work, and to decide whether to change scripts. Read it together with the Repeat Contact Rate: a high CSAT with a high repeat rate means the customer thought the issue was resolved when they rated it and then came back, so the solution was incomplete or temporary. **On its own**, without the Repeat Contact Rate, the metric shows the impression of the conversation rather than its outcome.
248.not_needed: **Skip it** when only a handful of customers leave a rating: with few responses, one review moves the percentage as much as a real change in the quality of work, and you can't tell one from the other.
248.essence_note: a customer happy with the solution comes back instead of writing a public review

249.name: Ticket Volume
249.description: How many tickets came into support during the period. Each registered customer request counts once.
249.nuances:
A ticket **is assigned to the period** by its creation date.
**Decide** what to do when a customer writes several times in a row about the same question: merging those messages into one ticket reflects the work more accurately, while counting them separately inflates the volume with follow-ups to the same question.
Spam and test tickets **are excluded** from the count.
Tickets answered only by the bot **count the same as** the rest.
249.example:
Tickets created in March: 4,460
Spam and tests: 180 (not counted)
Duplicates from one customer on the same question, merged into one: 80

Ticket Volume = 4,460 − 180 − 80 = **4,200**
249.importance: The starting point for planning shifts and hiring: workload, cost and the forecast **are calculated from it**. A sharp jump means a failure in the product or a process rather than a surge of interest, and support learns about it before other departments: people come in with the same problem before monitoring notices it.
249.essence_note: every ticket is a question someone couldn't solve on their own, and time the team spent on it

250.name: Average Resolution Time
250.description: How much time passes on average from when a ticket is created to when it's closed. Unlike active handling time, it includes waiting in the queue and pauses between messages.
250.nuances:
**Decide** whether to count time in business hours or calendar hours. Calendar hours show the time as the customer experiences it and include nights and weekends; business hours show the team's work and make results comparable across shifts. A ticket created Friday evening and closed Monday morning takes 65 calendar hours or 2 business hours.
**Does the timer pause** while waiting for the customer's reply? With a pause, the metric shows support's work; without one, it shows the real time for the customer, and the more complex the case, the bigger the difference.
**Only closed tickets count**, so stuck tickets don't hurt the average, and a growing queue doesn't show in it.
**The average is sensitive to the tail**: a few very long cases raise it more than many quick closures lower it. The median is more stable.
250.example:
Resolved tickets: 3,780
Total time from creation to closing in business hours: 68,040

Average Resolution Time = 68,040 / 3,780 = **18 business hours**

In calendar hours, the same set gives 41 hours: the whole difference comes from nights and weekends.
250.importance: **This is the time** a customer means when they say “it took too long,” and it drives decisions on shift size and night coverage. Read it together with Average Time from First Response to Resolution: the gap between them is the time the ticket just sits in the queue. If an agent's actual work takes minutes and closing takes hours, hiring won't change anything; look at how tickets are distributed and how the queue is prioritized.
250.synonyms: Full Resolution Time, Time to Resolution
250.essence_note: the whole time, the customer is left with an unresolved issue

251.name: Ticket Resolution Rate
251.description: The share of tickets where the customer got a resolution. The rest are either still in progress or closed without a resolution.
251.nuances:
The denominator is all tickets for the period, **closed or not**. Stuck and unresolved tickets stay in it on purpose: the metric shows what share of incoming issues were resolved, and a growing queue should hurt the percentage. Calculated using only closed tickets, the number would show how well tickets were closed, and it could be kept high simply by not answering some customers.
The numerator **follows the same rule** as [[Resolved Tickets→podderzhka_klientov/reshennye_obrascheniya]]: closed with an actual answer, excluding tickets closed after a timeout or canceled by the customer.
Tickets **are assigned to the period** by creation date, not closing date. Otherwise the percentage drops mechanically at the end of the month: fresh tickets are still in progress but already in the denominator.
**Decide** what to do with tickets created at the end of the period and resolved after it closed. If you recalculate the metric retroactively, the monthly number keeps growing after the month is over; if you don't, the last days of the month always look like a failure.
251.example:
Tickets created in March: 4,200
Of those, resolved: 3,780
Closed after a timeout with no reply from the customer: 190 (not resolved)
Still in progress on April 1: 230

Ticket Resolution Rate = 3,780 / 4,200 × 100 = **90%**
251.importance: It shows whether support is keeping up with incoming tickets at all. A falling percentage with unchanged response times means the queue is building up and some customers leave without an answer, and it will show up in churn **only later**.
251.essence_note: every unresolved ticket is a customer left without an answer

252.name: Average First Response Time (FRT)
252.formula: Total Time to First Response / Ticket Volume
252.description: How long a customer waits on average from contacting support to the agent's first response.
252.nuances:
An auto-reply like “we've received your request” **doesn't count** as a response: the clock stops at the first substantive message from a person or the bot that addresses the question.
Wait time **is counted in business** hours if support has set operating hours: otherwise tickets that come in after hours rack up a whole night of waiting even though the agent replied in the first minutes of the shift. For 24/7 support, the time is in calendar hours.
**Tickets** that got no response at all drop out of the average: they have no first-response timestamp, so the wait can't be calculated.
The number of such tickets is tracked **separately**: the more there are, the better the average looks, and a customer who got no answer at all is sure to leave with a negative impression. They're counted in Unresolved Tickets, and that's the number to look at next to the average wait.
**The metric covers the first** half of the customer's path: the wait until the first response plus the resolution time after it give the full time to close the ticket.
252.example:
Tickets with a response: 4,010
Total wait in business minutes: 30,075
Auto-replies confirming receipt don't count as a response

Average First Response Time (FRT) = 30,075 / 4,010 = **7.5 minutes**
252.importance: **The first** thing a customer feels, and the main source of abandoned conversations: until there's a response, the person doesn't know whether anyone has seen them at all, and they either open a repeat ticket or write a review. Staffing within the day is planned by this number rather than by total monthly volume: a gap usually occurs at specific hours and is invisible in the monthly average.
252.synonyms: First Reply Time, Time to First Response
252.essence_note: until there's a response, the person doesn't even know whether their question has been picked up

253.name: Repeat Contact Rate
253.description: The share of tickets where the customer came back about an issue that had already been closed. Shows how often an issue is closed on paper without being actually resolved.
253.nuances:
**Set the window** in which a new ticket counts as a repeat: 7 days catches incomplete work on a specific case; 30 days also captures systemic problems, but new unrelated questions along with them.
A repeat **is a ticket on** the same topic rather than any later ticket: a regular customer with a new question every week shouldn't land in the numerator.
**Decide** whether the third and fourth tickets on the same issue go into the numerator. Counting each one lets a single hard case inflate the metric; counting only the second understates the scale of the problem.
The numerator and denominator **come from the same** set of tickets for the period; otherwise the share goes beyond reasonable limits.
253.example:
Tickets in the month: 4,200
Of those, the customer had already contacted support about this question in the past 14 days: 546
New questions from the same customers: 310 (not counted)

Repeat Contact Rate = 546 / 4,200 × 100 = **13%**
253.importance: **The most expensive number to ignore** is this one: every repeat ticket is paid for a second time, and the customer loses trust in the meantime. Growth in repeats with a steady response speed means agents are closing tickets without solving the problem.
253.not_needed: **Skip it where** tickets come in anonymously: a new ticket can't be linked to a past one, so a repeat can't be told apart from a new one.
253.essence_note: a repeat ticket means the first answer didn't resolve the question, and the time was spent twice

254.name: Average Time from First Response to Resolution
254.formula: Total Time from First Response to Close / Resolved Tickets
254.description: How much time passes on average from the agent's first response to the ticket being closed. Together with Average First Response Time (FRT), it adds up to the full time to close: the wait covers everything up to the first response, and this metric covers everything after it.
254.nuances:
The clock starts at the agent's first substantive response and runs until the ticket is closed. Everything in between **counts in full**: messages back and forth, pauses between messages, waiting for the customer's reply, handoffs to another department. For the customer it's one continuous wait for a resolution, and splitting it into “working” and “not working” makes no sense.
**Wrap-up time after** the conversation ends, such as notes and requests to other departments, falls into the interval if it happens before the ticket is closed.
The time scale **is the same** as in Average First Response Time (FRT) and Average Resolution Time: business hours for support with set operating hours, calendar hours for 24/7 support.
Denominator: resolved tickets, the same set as in the Ticket Resolution Rate numerator; otherwise the average **is calculated over different** sets.
**The average is sensitive to the tail**: a few tickets that dragged on for weeks raise it more than many quick ones lower it. The median is more stable.
254.example:
Resolved tickets: 3,780
Total time from first response to closing: 67,568 business hours

Average Time from First Response to Resolution = 67,568 / 3,780 = **17.9 business hours**

It ties out with its neighbors on the map: 7.5 minutes of Average First Response Time (FRT) plus 17.9 hours from this metric give the 18 hours of Average Resolution Time.
254.importance: It shows how long the customer waits after the conversation has already started. This is where you see what prevents the issue from being resolved: approvals from other departments, waiting on a supplier, bouncing between tiers. The wait for the first response is fixed by shift scheduling, while this time shrinks **only with broader agent permissions** and simpler procedures, so the two metrics are looked at separately and fixed in different ways.
254.not_needed: **Skip it** when tickets are closed with a single reply and the time after the first message is close to zero: the metric adds nothing beyond the first response time.
254.essence_note: the longer a question takes to resolve, the more it costs and the less satisfied the customer is

255.name: SLA Target Time
255.description: The maximum response or resolution time the company promises the customer. It's set by the company and isn't calculated from data.
255.nuances:
**Set separate targets for** the first response and the full resolution: with one number for both stages, a fast first response covers up a long wait for the resolution, and there's nothing left to control.
State whether the target is measured in business or calendar hours, and **apply the same rule in every** metric checked against it. 24/7 support counts calendar hours; support with set operating hours counts business hours.
**Set the target based on** the actual distribution of resolution times rather than the desired one: a threshold the team rarely meets soon stops being taken seriously.
**The promise to the customer in** the contract and the internal target differ: the internal one is usually stricter, to leave a buffer before obligations are breached.
255.example:
Support works 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., seven days a week
Promise to customers in the terms of service: first response within 4 business hours
Internal target for the team: 2 business hours
Full resolution: 24 business hours

SLA Target Time = **4 business hours for the first response, 24 business hours for resolution**
255.importance: **SLA compliance and overrun are calculated** from this number, so any shift in it changes reporting across the whole map with no change in the work. A threshold set too loose creates the appearance that all is well; one set too tight turns breaches into background noise that people stop reacting to.
255.not_needed: **Don't set it** for support with no time commitments: there's no promise to the customer, so there's nothing to record.
255.essence_note: a target that's too lenient allows slow answers, and one that's too strict isn't met and stops meaning anything

256.name: Forecast Error Rate
256.formula:
((Actual − Forecast) / Forecast) × 100
For the average error over several periods: (Σ |Actual − Forecast| / Σ Forecast) × 100
256.description: How far the actual number of tickets deviated from the forecast. The sign shows which way the forecast missed: a minus sign means fewer tickets came in than expected; a plus sign means more.
256.nuances:
For a single period, the error **retains its sign**: the action depends on it. A shortfall means paid shifts where agents sit idle; an excess means a queue and broken promises, and these call for different decisions.
**When averaging over several** periods, errors are taken as absolute values: otherwise one month's overshoot cancels out another's undershoot, and the annual accuracy comes out perfect despite misses every month. Two values are shown side by side: the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) and the direction in which the model misses more often.
The denominator **is chosen once** and doesn't change. Dividing by the forecast shows how wrong the model was; dividing by the actual shows how big the error is relative to the real load; the bigger the miss, the more the two numbers diverge.
The evaluation granularity **matches the granularity** of planning: an accurate monthly forecast with daily misses won't save the shift schedule, because errors within the month cancel each other out.
256.example:
Forecast for April: 5,148 tickets
Actual: 4,630

Forecast Error Rate = (4,630 − 5,148) / 5,148 × 100 = **−10%**

The minus means a shortfall: fewer tickets came in than the schedule planned for, and some paid shifts sat idle. With the same miss in the other direction, the decision would be the opposite: bringing in extra people.
Over a quarter, the average error is calculated in absolute values: January +8%, February −11%, March −10% give an average error of 9.7%, rather than −4.3%.
256.importance: **It determines** whether shifts can be planned by the model or whether you need a reserve of people in case of a miss. When the error is comparable to the reserve you already keep, the forecast is no good for scheduling: keeping backup agents for it costs more than fixing the model. A consistent sign of the error points to systematic bias: the model regularly underestimates or overestimates volume, and that's fixed with an adjustment rather than a reserve of people.
256.not_needed: **Skip it where** no ticket forecast is built.
256.essence_note: shifts are set by the forecast: too low and people can't handle the volume, too high and extra hours get paid for

257.name: Tickets per Customer
257.description: How many times, on average, one customer contacted support during the period.
257.nuances:
Both values **are taken for the same** period and under the same customer identification rule: if the numerator includes tickets from unidentified senders and the denominator only recognized customers, the average is inflated.
**Growth in this metric more often** means customers coming back with unresolved questions than higher customer activity: to tell one from the other, look at the Repeat Contact Rate.
257.example:
Tickets in the month: 4,200
Unique customers: 3,100

Tickets per Customer = 4,200 / 3,100 = **1.4**
257.importance: **It shows** how much support one customer consumes, and converts into dollars via [[Cost per Ticket→podderzhka_klientov/stoimost_obrascheniya]]. Growth with an unchanged customer base means the problem is systemic: customers come back with the same thing, and hiring agents won't fix it.
257.not_needed: **Skip it** when tickets come in anonymously: there's no denominator.
257.essence_note: the more often one person contacts support, the more difficulty they have using the product on their own

258.name: Cost per Ticket
258.description: How much it costs the company to handle one ticket.
258.nuances:
Costs and tickets **cover the same** period: dividing a month of costs by a quarter of tickets gives a meaningless number.
**The denominator includes** all tickets, including those closed by the bot. Leaving them out inflates the cost and makes automation look pointless on paper: the more the bot closes, the more expensive each ticket looks.
The cost base **stays the same** as in Total Support Cost: changing it between periods makes the trend unreadable.
258.example:
Support costs for the month: $252,000
Tickets in the same month: 4,200

Cost per Ticket = 252,000 / 4,200 = **$60**

Without the tickets closed by the bot, the denominator drops to 3,150 and the cost rises to $80 with the same spend.
258.importance: **It turns any process improvement** into money: cut repeat tickets by a thousand a year, multiply by this number, and you see right away whether the effort pays off. The business case for a bot or a knowledge base is built on it too.
258.not_needed: Skip it when support is handled by employees of other departments between their own tasks: support costs aren't **tracked separately**, so there's no numerator.
258.synonyms: Cost per Contact, Cost per Case
258.essence_note: every ticket is paid for with agent time and comes out of profit

259.name: Support-Driven Revenue
259.description: Revenue from orders that customers placed after talking to support.
259.nuances:
The amount **is calculated at the selling prices** the customer sees.
**The amount includes orders** placed within a ticket, the same set as in [[Converted Tickets→podderzhka_klientov/obrascheniya_zavershivshiesya_pokupkoy]].
Canceled and returned orders **are subtracted from the amount**: this metric counts money, and a returned order leaves the company with none. That's why the count in Converted Tickets and the number of orders included in this amount differ: the first records orders being placed, the second the money received.
**Decide** whether the amount includes the whole order or only the item that was discussed. The whole order credits support with what the customer put in the cart on their own; a single item gives a lower but defensible number.
259.example:
Orders placed in tickets in the month: 240
Order value at selling prices: $52,800
Of those, canceled and returned: 24 orders worth $5,640

Support-Driven Revenue = 52,800 − 5,640 = **$47,160**

Converted Tickets still shows all 240: it counts orders placed rather than money.
259.importance: **Set next to** Total Support Cost, it shows whether the department pays for itself. Companies that don't track this amount cut support first in a crisis and find a revenue gap later, when it's hard to connect the two.
259.not_needed: **Skip it** when agents don't take part in sales and can't place orders.
259.essence_note: this is money that support brings in rather than spends

260.name: Resolved Tickets
260.description: How many tickets were closed with an actual answer to the customer's question.
260.nuances:
Tickets closed after a timeout because the customer stopped replying **don't count as resolved**: the system shows a status, but there's no resolution.
Tickets where the customer's request was denied for a valid reason **count as resolved**: the issue is settled, even if the customer didn't like the answer.
A ticket **is assigned to the period** by its creation date, the same as in Ticket Volume. Counting by closing date mixes requests from different months into one.
**A ticket** that comes back stays in the resolved count from the first time and adds a second ticket to the volume.
260.example:
Tickets created in March: 4,200
Closed with an actual answer: 3,780
Of those, requests denied for a valid reason: 310 (counted)
Closed after a timeout with no reply from the customer: 190 (not counted)

Resolved Tickets = **3,780**
260.importance: **It's the basis for the share** of resolved tickets and the denominator for resolution times. Widening the definition to timeout closures improves both the resolution rate and SLA compliance at once, while not a single customer gets an answer. This number needs watching precisely because that swap is so easy.
260.essence_note: every resolved ticket is a customer left with an answer

261.name: Forecasted Ticket Volume
261.formula: Base version: Tickets in the Same Period Last Year × Customer Base Growth + Adjustment for Planned Events
261.description: The expected number of tickets for a future period. Built from ticket history with adjustments for seasonality and planned events.
261.nuances:
**The basic formula** works when volume grows along with the customer base and seasonality repeats from year to year. Workforce management systems and statistical models are more accurate: they break the series into trend, weekly and intraday cycles and account for several factors at once. The choice depends on whether you have such a tool and enough history: on a short series, a complex model loses to a simple one.
**The history is cleaned of anomalies**: an outage or a mass messaging campaign causes a spike, and the model will carry it into the next period as normal load.
The forecast granularity **depends on the task**: a monthly forecast doesn't help build a shift schedule; for that you need a daily forecast, or better, an hourly one.
Planned promotions, sales and launches are added to the base forecast **separately**: history alone can't predict them.
**The forecast is built on** incoming tickets, not handled ones; otherwise the model learns the team's capacity instead of demand.
261.example:
Tickets in April last year: 3,600
Customer base growth year over year: +18%
Base forecast = 3,600 × 1.18 = 4,248
Sale on April 20–24: +900 based on past launches
Spike from a payment outage in April last year: 400 (removed from history)

Forecast for April = 4,248 + 900 = **5,148 tickets**
261.importance: **The shift schedule** and the decision on temporary hiring are built on this number weeks before the load arrives. Underestimating in peak season means a queue on the most profitable days; overestimating means paid shifts where agents sit idle.
261.not_needed: **Skip it with** a small, steady ticket flow: shifts are planned without a model, and on small numbers the forecast is noisier than the flow itself.
261.essence_note: this is the expected load on support, and the lower it is, the fewer people you need to keep on shifts

262.name: Ticket Conversion Rate
262.description: The share of closed tickets during which an order was placed. Shows to what extent support works as a sales channel.
262.nuances:
The numerator is the same as in [[Converted Tickets→podderzhka_klientov/obrascheniya_zavershivshiesya_pokupkoy]]: tickets with an order placed within the ticket. Canceled and returned orders **aren't subtracted** from it: the order was placed.
**The denominator is all** closed tickets for the period, including those where no purchase was discussed: the share shows what part of support's work leads to a sale at all.
A ticket counts **once**, even if the customer placed several orders during the conversation.
**Read the metric by** contact reason: in pre-purchase consultations the share is high by design, in delivery questions it's close to zero, and the overall number depends on the ticket mix at least as much as on agents' sales skills.
262.example:
Closed tickets in the month: 1,800
Tickets with an order placed during the conversation: 240

Ticket Conversion Rate = 240 / 1,800 × 100 = **13.3%**

By contact reason: 34% in pre-purchase consultations, 1% in delivery status questions.
262.importance: **It's the basis** for deciding whether to let support place orders and whether to train agents to sell. The Contact Reason breakdown shows where this makes sense at all: growing sales is worth it where the customer already came with a question about what to choose, rather than where they're trying to find out where their package is.
262.not_needed: **Skip it** when agents can't place orders: the numerator is always zero.
262.synonyms: Support Conversion Rate, Support-to-Sale Conversion Rate
262.essence_note: a ticket turns into an order, and support brings in money as well as spending it

263.name: Automated Resolutions
263.formula: Number of tickets resolved by automation
263.description: The number of tickets closed by automation without an agent's involvement.
263.nuances:
Count **only the tickets** where an agent never joined: handing the conversation to a person after the bot answers takes the ticket out of this count.
Tickets where the bot only collected details and passed them to an agent **don't count as automated** resolutions, even if the customer didn't write anything else.
263.example:
Bot conversations in the month: 1,430
Closed by the bot, no agent joined: 1,050
Bot collected details and handed off to an agent: 380 (not counted)

Automated Resolutions = **1,050**
263.importance: **It grounds the conversation** about investing in the bot: this one number converts into agent hours saved through the cost of handling a ticket. Without it, automation decisions are made without data, and companies either overpay for flows nobody uses or cut what works.
263.not_needed: **Skip it** while support is fully manual.
263.essence_note: these tickets are closed without any agent time

264.name: Automated Resolution Rate
264.description: The share of tickets closed by automation without an agent getting involved. This includes bot answers, template auto-replies and self-service within the conversation.
264.nuances:
A ticket **counts as automatically resolved** only if no agent stepped in at any point: if the bot answered and the conversation then went to a person, the ticket counts as handled manually.
**Decide** what to do with abandoned conversations where the bot answered and the customer simply left without confirming the resolution. Counting them as automated resolutions inflates the metric by including everyone the bot didn't help. The strict option: count only conversations with explicit confirmation or with no repeat ticket within a few days.
**The denominator includes** all registered tickets, including those the bot didn't try to handle at all.
264.example:
Tickets in the month: 4,200
Closed by the bot without an agent: 1,050
Bot answered, then handed off to an agent: 380 (not in the numerator)

Automated Resolution Rate = 1,050 / 4,200 × 100 = **25%**
264.importance: **It determines** how many people a shift needs and whether the bot pays off. If the share grows and repeat tickets grow along with it, automation is putting off issues instead of resolving them: the customer will come back, already irritated, and handling the second ticket will cost more than the first.
264.not_needed: **Skip it** while support has neither a bot nor auto-replies: the numerator is always zero.
264.essence_note: automation resolves an issue without an agent and almost for free, but when the share is too high, people get stuck with the bot where they need a human

265.name: Unresolved Tickets
265.description: How many tickets were left without a resolution at the end of the period. This includes both open tickets in progress and tickets the customer abandoned before getting an answer.
265.nuances:
**Count the tickets** created in the period and unresolved on its last day. Tickets on their first day of normal handling and tickets stuck since last quarter end up in one number unless you split them by age.
Tickets closed after a timeout without an actual answer **count as unresolved**: formally they're closed, but the problem remains.
**Splitting tickets abandoned by the customer** from open tickets in progress changes what the number means: the first point to slow responses, the second to a shortage of people.
265.example:
Tickets created in March: 4,200
Resolved: 3,780
Open and in progress on April 1: 230
Closed after a timeout with no reply from the customer: 190

Unresolved Tickets = 230 + 190 = **420**
265.importance: A growing queue shows up here earlier than in average times: the average **is calculated from closed tickets** and doesn't show stuck tickets at all. Each such ticket is likely to come back as a repeat ticket or turn into a public review.
265.not_needed: **Skip it in support teams** where every ticket is closed the same day: no open tickets remain at the end of the period.
265.essence_note: these are customers left without an answer, who will come back with a repeat ticket or leave a review

266.name: Ticket SLA Compliance Rate
266.description: The share of tickets resolved within the promised time. Calculated from resolved tickets.
266.nuances:
The threshold **is the same** as the one set in [[SLA Target Time→podderzhka_klientov/celevoe_vremya_obsluzhivaniya_sla]]. For 24/7 support, time is counted in calendar hours, so the choice of hours doesn't come up. For support with set operating hours, elapsed time is measured on the same basis as the threshold: otherwise nights and weekends end up in the resolution time, and every evening ticket becomes a breach.
**The denominator is limited to resolved tickets**, so stuck tickets don't hurt the percentage. A ticket that is in its third week of being open breaches the SLA but won't enter the calculation until it's closed. If that matters, unresolved tickets past the target are added to the denominator as breaches.
**Decide** whether the clock stops while waiting for the customer's reply. With a pause, the metric reflects support's work; without one, the real time for the customer.
266.example:
Resolved tickets: 3,780
Within 24 business hours: 3,250
Over the target: 530

Ticket SLA Compliance Rate = 3,250 / 3,780 × 100 = **86%**

Without pausing the timer while waiting for the customer, only 2,900 meet the SLA, and the number drops to 77%.
266.importance: **Commitments to customers and contract penalties are tied to it**, so it's the first to go into reports. Read it together with Average Resolution Time: if the compliance rate holds steady while resolution time grows, the threshold is too loose and the metric no longer keeps anything in check. It works the same way in reverse: a dip in the rate with unchanged time means the rule for counting time changed, and the time spent on the work did not.
266.not_needed: **Skip it** when there's no promised response time in contracts or in internal rules.
266.essence_note: the customer was promised a response time and notices every breach

267.name: Average Ticket SLA Overrun Rate
267.formula: (Average SLA Overrun on Breached Tickets / SLA) × 100
267.description: How far, on average, a breached ticket goes past the promised time, as a percentage of that time. It's calculated only on tickets that exceeded the SLA and shows how severe breaches are rather than how often they happen.
267.nuances:
The base **includes only tickets** that went past the promised time. Tickets that met it are left out: their spare time offsets the overrun, and the metric starts showing the average time across all tickets instead of the size of the breach.
**Read the metric together** with Ticket SLA Compliance Rate: this one shows how far breaches go past the promise, that one how often they happen. Each one alone is misleading: the compliance rate can hold at an acceptable level while every breach takes several times the promised time.
The overrun and the threshold **are taken in the same** units and under the same accounting rule: if the SLA is set in business hours, time is counted in business hours too; otherwise nights and weekends end up in the overrun.
Unresolved tickets don't enter the calculation, even though many of them have already breached the target: the more stuck tickets there are, the better the overrun looks. They're counted **separately**, in Unresolved Tickets.
**The average hides the tail**: a few tickets stuck for a long time raise the result more than many small delays lower it. Look at the longest breach of the period alongside it.
267.example:
SLA for resolution: 24 business hours
Resolved tickets: 3,780, of which 530 went over the target
Total overrun on them: 4,770 business hours

Average overrun = 4,770 / 530 = 9 business hours
Average Ticket SLA Overrun Rate = 9 / 24 × 100 = **38%**

A breached ticket is resolved in 33 hours on average instead of the promised 24. Dividing the same overrun by all 3,780 resolved tickets gives 5%, and that number doesn't show the severity of the breach.
267.importance: **It answers the question** of how far a breached ticket goes past the promised time. The compliance rate can hold at an acceptable level, but if each breach takes several times the promised time, the customer comes back with another ticket and then writes a public review. Without this number, you see how many breaches there are but not how severe they are, and the analysis starts with the wrong tickets.
267.not_needed: **Skip it** until the target time is set: without the denominator, the formula doesn't work.
267.essence_note: the further a response goes past the promised time, the more noticeable the breach is to the customer

268.name: Interactions per Ticket
268.description: How many messages a ticket takes on average before it's closed. Messages from both sides of the conversation count.
268.nuances:
**Decide** what counts as an interaction: each message or one agent turn as a whole. Three messages an agent sends in a row in a single turn count as either 3 or 1, and the numbers become incomparable.
Automatic notifications like “your request has been received” **don't count**: they inflate the numerator without reflecting any work.
The numerator and denominator **come from the same** set of tickets: messages only from the tickets that made it into the denominator; otherwise the average is calculated over different sets.
268.example:
Resolved tickets: 3,780
Messages in those tickets: 13,986
Of those, auto-notifications: 3,780 (not counted)

Interactions per Ticket = (13,986 − 3,780) / 3,780 = **2.7**

Leaving auto-notifications in the numerator gives 3.7: each ticket gets an extra interaction the agent never made.
268.importance: **It shows earlier than other metrics** where an agent lacks information: growth means agents have to ask customers for information again because the needed data is in neither their profile nor the guidelines. Every extra message adds to resolution time and [[Cost per Ticket→podderzhka_klientov/stoimost_obrascheniya]].
268.not_needed: **Skip it in** phone support, where the whole conversation happens in one call and there's nothing to break into separate interactions.
268.synonyms: Messages per Ticket, Touches per Ticket
268.essence_note: every extra message costs agent time and keeps the customer waiting

269.name: Converted Tickets
269.formula: Number of tickets with a purchase
269.description: How many tickets ended with an order placed within the ticket itself: the agent helped put the order together, placed it for the customer or sent a payment link in the conversation.
269.nuances:
**An order counts** if it was placed within the ticket itself. Purchases the customer made later on their own can't be attributed to the agent's work, so they don't count.
The link **is recorded in the system**: the order was created by the agent, placed via a link from the conversation or attached to the ticket manually. If the system has no such link, the metric isn't calculated: it can't be inferred from purchase timing.
A ticket counts **once**, regardless of how many orders were placed in the conversation.
Canceling or returning an order doesn't reduce the count: the agent did their job, and what happens to the order afterward **is tracked in its own** metrics.
269.example:
Closed tickets in the month: 1,800
Tickets with an order placed within the ticket: 240
Of those, later canceled or returned: 24 (counted: the order was placed)

Converted Tickets = **240**
269.importance: **It moves support from the cost line** to the revenue line, based on orders that wouldn't have happened without an agent: purchases placed right in the conversation rather than “sometime later.” Without this count, the budget discussion comes down to how much support costs, and any cut looks profitable.
269.not_needed: **Skip it** when agents can't place orders: there's no technical way to place a purchase within a ticket.
269.synonyms: Support Conversions, Tickets Converted to Sales
269.essence_note: these are orders that wouldn't exist without a conversation with support

270.name: Customers Contacting Support
270.formula: Number of customers who contacted support
270.description: How many distinct customers contacted support during the period. A customer counts once, regardless of how many tickets they opened.
270.nuances:
A customer is identified by a stable attribute: phone number, account or email. If a person writes from different addresses, they **get counted several times**, and the number of unique customers is inflated.
**Decide** whether to include tickets from people who aren't in the customer base: those who write before becoming customers, or contact support outside their own account or about someone else's contract. With them, the metric shows the load from everyone who contacts support; without them, only from current customers, and in periods with an influx of new people, the difference is noticeable.
270.example:
Tickets in the month: 4,200
Unique customers among them: 3,100
Of those, contacted from different email addresses and recognized as one: 40

Customers Contacting Support = **3,100**
270.importance: **It serves as the denominator for the load** per customer and lets you compare the number of customers contacting support with the active customer base. If the share of the whole base contacting support is high, the cause is usually the product itself or how it's explained rather than support: people come to find out things that should be clear without a conversation.
270.not_needed: **Skip it where** tickets come in anonymously and there's no way to link them to a customer.
270.essence_note: each customer who reached out is a person who couldn't manage something on their own

271.name: Total Support Cost
271.description: How much it costs to run support for the period. Made up of labor, services and the overhead attributable to the department.
271.nuances:
The total **includes salaries with** payroll taxes rather than take-home pay alone: without the taxes, costs are understated by the full amount of mandatory payments for employees, and that's a noticeable part of what the team costs rather than a minor correction.
Payments to contractors and outsourcers **are included on par with** in-house staff costs.
Licenses for the ticketing system, telephony and the bot **belong here too**.
**Decide** whether to allocate shared costs like rent and equipment to support. With allocation, the number can be compared with the department's revenue; without it, it's only good for comparing periods with each other.
271.example:
Salaries with payroll taxes: $205,000
Contractors on the night queue: $25,200
Licenses for the ticketing system and telephony: $7,800
Share of rent and workstations: $14,000

Total Support Cost = **$252,000**
271.importance: **The numerator for Cost per Ticket** and the second half of the conversation about whether the department pays for itself. Understating what goes into costs makes support look cheaper than it is, and the decision on automation keeps getting put off.
271.not_needed: Skip it when support is handled by employees of other departments between their own tasks: their salaries **belong to other** functions, and support costs can't be separated out.
271.essence_note: the cost of running support comes out of profit

272.name: Number of Agents
272.description: How many support employees are on the team at the end of the period.
272.nuances:
**Decide** whether to count people or FTEs. Two half-time agents count as either 2 agents or 1 FTE, and every per-person calculation will differ by a factor of two.
Contractors and outsourced staff **are included** if they handle tickets: leaving them out inflates the workload per agent and understates [[Cost per Ticket→podderzhka_klientov/stoimost_obrascheniya]].
**Managers and trainers** who don't take tickets aren't counted.
272.example:
Agents on staff at the end of the month: 41
Contractors handling the night queue: 7
Team lead and trainer: 2 (not counted)

Number of Agents = **48**
272.importance: **The basis for calculating** payroll and the denominator for workload. An error in this number carries over into every per-agent metric at once, and the hiring decision is based on a distorted picture.
