272.not_needed: **Skip it** when support is handled by employees of other departments between their own tasks: there's no separate team, so there's nobody to count.
272.essence_note: too few agents and the queue grows while customers wait; too many and paid staff sit idle

273.name: Average Active Agents
273.formula: Sum of Active Agents Across Intervals / Number of Intervals
273.description: How many agents, on average, were on duty at the same time. Calculated across time intervals within the period.
273.nuances:
**The interval length shapes** the whole picture: hourly intervals show dips at lunch and at shift changes, while daily ones average them out of sight.
The calculation **uses the intervals** when support is open: including night hours in an average on a 24-hour scale cuts the result in half if support is closed at night.
An agent **counts as active** when available to take tickets: agents on breaks or in training are excluded from the count for that interval; otherwise the average doesn't match the real capacity.
273.example:
Support is open 12 hours a day, 22 working days
Hourly intervals: 264
Sum of agents on duty across all intervals: 4,488

Average Active Agents = 4,488 / 264 = **17**

There are 24 people on duty at peak hours and 9 at lunch: the average hides this.
273.importance: **Comparing this number** with hourly ticket volume shows exactly where you're short of people. Planning by the total number of agents instead of this number gives you a fully staffed team and still a queue every day at the same time.
273.not_needed: **Skip it in support teams** where the schedule is fixed and everyone works the same shift: the average equals the headcount.
273.essence_note: too few people on duty and waits grow; too many and the shift is paid for with no work to fill it

274.name: Agent Satisfaction Rate
274.description: The share of positive ratings among those who responded to the support team's internal survey.
274.nuances:
**Denominator**: employees who responded, not the whole staff. With low participation, the result is skewed: unhappy people either stay quiet for fear of consequences or respond more actively than the rest.
The threshold for a positive rating **is set once** and kept constant across surveys: moving the boundary from 4–5 to 3–5 raises the result at once with no change in sentiment.
**Anonymity directly affects** the number: named responses give systematically higher ratings.
274.example:
Agents on staff: 48
Responded to the survey: 39
Gave 4–5: 27

Agent Satisfaction Rate = 27 / 39 × 100 = **69%**
274.importance: **It warns of resignations** before they show up in Employee Turnover Rate. An agent leaving costs a mentor's time and a dip in response speed while the new hire gets up to speed, so a drop in this number is cheaper to catch early.
274.not_needed: **Skip it in** a support team of two or three people: anonymity can't be preserved, and the survey turns into a conversation.
274.synonyms: Agent Satisfaction Score (ASAT), Support Team Satisfaction
274.essence_note: satisfied agents stay longer and give customers better answers

275.name: Agent Utilization Rate
275.description: What part of paid working time agents spend directly on tickets. The rest goes to breaks, training and idle time.
275.nuances:
**Available time** is paid working time minus lunch and approved breaks. If you don't subtract them, the denominator includes time when the agent wasn't supposed to be working, and utilization comes out lower than it really is with the same work.
Active time **includes all work** on a ticket: the conversation, the messages and wrap-up after the conversation ends. Counting only talk time understates utilization and pushes the team toward unnecessary hiring.
275.example:
Team's paid time for the month: 6,720 hours
Lunches and breaks: 840 hours
Available time = 5,880 hours
Work on tickets, including wrap-up: 4,410 hours

Agent Utilization Rate = 4,410 / 5,880 × 100 = **75%**
275.importance: **Hiring and overtime decisions are tied to it.** Both extremes are bad: with high utilization there's no reserve for a spike, and any failure on the product side drags down response speed; with low utilization, you pay for idle shifts. Pick a working range that fits your seasonality and manage to it.
275.not_needed: **Skip it where** agents combine support with other work: there's no way to split time between tasks.
275.essence_note: low utilization means paid time goes to waste, and high utilization means agents have no buffer for a spike in tickets

276.name: Tickets per Agent
276.formula: Ticket Volume / Number of Active Agents
276.description: How many tickets there are, on average, per working agent during the period.
276.nuances:
**The denominator includes agents** who actually handled tickets during the period: including people on vacation and new hires in training understates the workload and hides overwork for everyone else.
Agents who worked part of the period **count as a fraction**: an agent who started mid-month counts as 0.5; otherwise the team's workload is understated.
The numerator **is based on tickets** received in the period, not resolved ones: with a growing queue, these numbers diverge and the workload is underestimated.
276.example:
Tickets in the month: 4,200
Agents in total: 48
Of those, worked the full month: 44
Started mid-month: 1 (counted as 0.5)
On vacation all month: 3 (not counted)

Tickets per Agent = 4,200 / 44.5 = **94**
276.importance: **This number** is the basis for setting workload targets and assigning shifts. If it grows while resolution time holds, agents are closing tickets faster at the expense of quality, and that will show up in repeat tickets later.
276.not_needed: **Skip it** when support is handled by employees of other departments between their own tasks: there's no clear agent count for the denominator, and the workload can't be judged from it.
276.synonyms: Tickets Handled per Agent, Agent Workload
276.essence_note: few tickets per person means underutilization; many means answer quality will start to drop

277.name: Order Processing Accuracy Rate
277.description: The share of orders that passed verification and confirmation without discrepancies. The error surfaces during processing but is made earlier: the order was accepted for an item that isn't in the warehouse.
277.nuances:
The denominator **matches the number** of orders processed during the period.
An order **counts as incorrect** if it was accepted for an item that isn't actually there: the storefront showed stock, but the check didn't confirm it. Processing is the first stage where the order is checked against actual stock, so the error is found here, although it was made when the order was accepted.
**The metric measures the quality** of stock data rather than the work of the people doing the checks. The reviewer has no influence here: they see the same thing the storefront showed.
**Picking errors**, packing and delivery errors don't go here: those stages have their own work and their own accuracy metrics.
**An order counts** as incorrect regardless of how things ended: the customer waited for incoming stock, the item was replaced or the order was canceled. Otherwise the metric shows how well the situation was salvaged rather than the quality of stock data.
277.example:
Processed in the month: 6,200 orders

Item found out of stock during the check: 137 orders
Of those, waited for incoming stock: 104, canceled: 33 (all 137 counted)

Order Processing Accuracy Rate = (6,200 − 137) / 6,200 × 100 = **97.8%**

Counting only the canceled ones gives 99.5%: the stock discrepancy stays invisible, even though the customer waited longer than promised.
277.importance: **It shows** how much you can trust the stock levels on the storefront. Each discrepancy is an order the customer has already paid for and is waiting for, but the warehouse can't fulfill: next comes either waiting for stock beyond the promised time or a cancellation and refund. A drop in the metric means you need to fix how stock levels sync with the storefront rather than how the shift works: the people doing the checks see exactly what the customer saw.
277.not_needed: **Skip it for** made-to-order or sourced-to-order sales and for a storefront without stock levels, where availability is confirmed after the order is placed: there's no source for a discrepancy, and waiting for the item is part of the process rather than an error.
277.essence_note: an error at this step leads to re-picking and a delay

278.name: Order Processing Time
278.formula: Total Processing Time / Number of Processed Orders
278.description: The average time it takes to process an order, from arrival to confirmation for picking. It covers checking the order, stock availability and payment.
278.nuances:
**It's measured in business** or calendar hours. Business hours show how much of people's time the order actually took and are suitable for calculating shift workload. Calendar hours show how long the order waited from the customer's point of view, and they always come out higher by the amount of non-working time.
**You can't mix the two within** one average: orders that arrive on weekends will pull the result up.
**An order is counted by** the date processing was completed.
Orders canceled before confirmation **are excluded** from the calculation: their processing was cut short and gives an artificially short interval.
**The average hides the tail**: a few orders stuck waiting for incoming stock raise the result more than many fast ones lower it. How much more depends on how far the tail extends.
278.example:
Processed in the week: 1,200 orders
Total processing time: 2,640 business hours
Canceled before confirmation: 45 (not counted)

Order Processing Time = 2,640 / 1,200 = **2.2 business hours**

In calendar hours, the same orders average 5.1 hours: the whole difference built up over nights and weekends.
278.importance: **It determines** how many people to assign to order verification and whether an automated stock check is needed. A rising average at an unchanged order volume means the incoming queue is building up, and the delays will then reach picking and shipping.
278.not_needed: **Skip it** when a paid order goes to picking automatically without a manual check: there's nothing to process, and the interval is zero.
278.synonyms: Order Handling Time, Order Verification Time
278.essence_note: until an order is confirmed, it isn't picked and doesn't ship

279.name: Processed Orders
279.description: The number of orders that passed verification and were confirmed for picking during the period.
279.nuances:
An order **is counted by the date** processing was completed. When counted by arrival date, the number for the period keeps changing after the period closes.
Orders canceled before confirmation **don't count as processed**.
An order sent back for rework and confirmed on the second attempt **is counted once**.
**A cancellation or return** after confirmation doesn't reduce the count: the work was done.
279.example:
Received in the month: 6,425 orders
Confirmed for picking: 6,200
Canceled before confirmation: 80 (not counted)
Still in the queue at month end: 145 (not counted)
Of the confirmed orders, later canceled by the customer: 52 (counted, since processing took place)

Processed Orders = **6,200**
279.importance: **It shows** whether the warehouse is keeping up with incoming orders. The gap between incoming and processed orders is work stuck at the entry point: while the gap holds steady, the warehouse is keeping up; if it grows week after week, the queue is building up, and the delays will then reach picking and shipping. The signal comes before deadlines start to slip, so you can add people to the shift in advance. All the percentages and averages on the map rely on this number as well.
279.essence_note: until an order is processed, it won't go out to the customer

280.name: Pick Accuracy Rate
280.description: The share of orders picked without errors: the right product, the right quantity, nothing missing and nothing extra.
280.nuances:
The denominator **matches the number** of orders picked during the period.
An order with any number of line-item errors **counts as one incorrect order**. Counting by line item gives a different, higher accuracy: one mixed-up item out of twenty is a 5% error rate by line items and a 100% error rate by order.
**Errors** found during the check before packing are counted: without them, the metric shows the quality of the check rather than the quality of picking.
Errors the customer discovers after shipping **are assigned to the period** in which the order was picked. Assigning them to the complaint date mixes the work of different months.
280.example:
Picked in the month: 6,020 orders
Errors found during the check: 74
Errors discovered by customers: 22
Total picking errors: 96

Pick Accuracy Rate = (6,020 − 96) / 6,020 × 100 = **98.4%**

Counting only customer complaints would give 99.6%: three quarters of the errors would go unseen.
280.importance: **A picking error turns into a return**, a reshipment and apologies, and costs more than the picking itself. A drop in the percentage shows where to fix things: confusion in bin locations, no scanning during picking, or not enough training on new items.
280.not_needed: **Skip it when** you ship single-line orders of identical products: there's nothing to mix up.
280.essence_note: an incorrectly picked order leads to a return and a support ticket

281.name: Pick Time
281.formula: Total Picking Time / Number of Picked Orders
281.description: The average time it takes to pick one order, from accepting the picking task to handing the order over to packing.
281.nuances:
**Read the average together** with the average number of line items per order: without it, it's unclear whether pickers got slower or simply got larger orders.
**Decide** whether the interval includes waiting for the task in the queue. Counted from the moment the order is queued, the metric also reflects how busy the warehouse is; counted from the moment the picker accepts the task, it shows the picker's net working time.
**It's measured in** working hours: time between shifts has nothing to do with picking.
Orders picked in parts because of missing stock have a pause inside the interval, and you **decide** whether to count the wait until the stock arrives.
281.example:
Picked in the shift: 340 orders
Total picking time: 91 hours
Partially picked, waiting for incoming stock: 8 (not counted)

Pick Time = 91 / 340 = **0.27 hours, about 16 minutes**
281.importance: **Shift staffing calculations rest** on it: knowing the order volume and the average time, you calculate how many pickers to put on for the peak. A small error in this number gets multiplied by the whole order volume and turns into a staff shortage during a sale, and delays hit the warehouse faster than an extra shift can be brought in.
281.not_needed: **Skip it for** dropshipping and cross-docking: the order isn't picked from shelves, and goods go straight from the supplier. Also skip it where picking isn't separated from packing: if one person picks and immediately packs the order at their own station, there's no timestamp between the stages and nothing to measure them separately with. In that case, the combined time for picking and packing is counted as one number.
281.essence_note: the longer picking takes, the fewer orders get through the warehouse per shift

282.name: Units Picked per Hour
282.formula: Total Units Picked / (Number of Pickers × Hours Worked)
282.description: How many units of product are picked per labor hour. It counts product units rather than orders.
282.nuances:
The denominator uses paid working hours, including idle time and breaks within the shift. If you take **only active** picking time, the rate is overstated and can't be used to plan a shift.
Employees working on receiving or inventory counts are excluded from the denominator **along with** their hours; otherwise the rate falls with no change in the pickers' work.
Read the metric together with the average number of distinct line items per order. Identical items **are taken from the same** bin in one go, while different ones require walking the warehouse, so without this second number it's unclear whether pickers got faster or simply got simpler orders.
With automated picking, there are no labor hours in the denominator, and the metric is calculated per hour of line operation or per shift **as a whole**. That's the throughput of the area rather than an employee's output: it's used to look at equipment utilization and downtime, and it can't be compared with people's output before automation because the denominators differ.
282.example:
Units picked in the shift: 4,200
Pickers on the shift: 6
Shift: 8 hours
One picker spent 3 hours receiving a delivery (subtracted)

Labor hours = 6 × 8 − 3 = 45
Units Picked per Hour = 4,200 / 45 = **93 units per hour**
282.importance: It's **the standard rate** used to calculate whether the current shift can handle the forecasted order volume. Understating it leads to overstaffing and extra payroll; overstating it leads to missed deadlines at the very first peak. The same number is used to evaluate the payoff from rearranging racks and introducing handheld scanners.
282.not_needed: **Skip it where** picking isn't separated from packing: one person's hours are split between the stages arbitrarily, and the output figure is essentially made up. Also skip it for dropshipping and cross-docking: there's nothing to pick from the shelves.
282.essence_note: the more units a person picks per hour, the cheaper picking is

283.name: Picked Orders
283.description: The number of orders whose items have been fully picked and handed over to packing.
283.nuances:
An order **is counted by the date** picking was completed.
Partially picked orders waiting for a missing item **aren't counted until fully** completed; otherwise the same order goes into the count twice.
An order picked and then **canceled before shipping** isn't removed from the count: picking took place and used warehouse resources.
Re-picking after a picking error **isn't counted** as a new order.
283.example:
Picking completed in the month: 6,020 orders
Partially picked, waiting for incoming stock: 95 (not counted)
Picked and canceled before shipping: 40 (counted)
Re-picked after an error: 62 (not counted again)

Picked Orders = **6,020**
283.importance: **It gives the actual volume of work** in the picking area, which labor costs and productivity are calculated from. The gap between processed and picked orders shows how many confirmed orders didn't make it to picking because of missing stock, and that's a signal to review safety stock.
283.not_needed: **Skip it for cross-docking** and dropshipping: there's no picking from shelves.
283.essence_note: the more orders are picked, the more will go out to customers in the same shift

284.name: Packing Accuracy Rate
284.description: The share of orders packed without errors: the right packaging, documents included, the correct label applied.
284.nuances:
The denominator **matches the number** of orders packed during the period.
**Define the list of packing errors**: a mixed-up label, missing documents, unsuitable packaging, a box damaged during packing and a product damaged during packing. The rate itself depends on how long the list is, so the list is fixed and not changed afterward: if it's expanded in the middle of the year, the metric drops because of the new counting rule, yet it looks like the area is failing.
Product damage **is included here as** one type of error and is also counted separately in the Packing Damage Rate: the narrow metric tracks materials and fragile categories, the broad one tracks how well the packing area works as a whole. The overlap is normal, but you can't add the two metrics together.
A dented box with an intact product **belongs here** and doesn't go into the Packing Damage Rate: that metric counts damage to the product itself.
An order with several errors **counts as one incorrect order**.
**Errors** fixed before handover to the carrier are counted.
284.example:
Packed in the month: 5,930 orders

Wrong label: 29
Documents missing: 41
Product damaged during packing: 34
Box dented, product intact: 61
Orders with two errors at once: 6

Incorrect orders = 29 + 41 + 34 + 61 − 6 = 159
Packing Accuracy Rate = (5,930 − 159) / 5,930 × 100 = **97.3%**

The same 34 cases of product damage give 0.6% on their own in the Packing Damage Rate: a dented box doesn't count there, because the customer will receive the product intact.
284.importance: **A mixed-up label means an order** that went to someone else: a second delivery, a bad experience for two customers and a dispute with the carrier. Such errors may be few in number, but each one costs more than many minor slips, so the percentage is watched even when it looks healthy.
284.not_needed: **Skip it when** goods ship in the manufacturer's packaging without repacking.
284.essence_note: a packing error ends in a damaged product or a missing item

285.name: Pack Time
285.formula: Total Packing Time / Number of Packed Orders
285.description: The average time it takes to pack one order, from receiving the picked order until it's ready to ship.
285.nuances:
It's measured in working hours or minutes: breaks between shifts **aren't included** in packing.
**Decide** whether the interval includes inserting documents, applying the label and weighing. For orders that are quick to pack, these operations take a noticeable part of the time, and excluding them puts the number out of line with the station's actual workload.
An order that doesn't fit in one box and ships as several parcels **counts as one order** but takes as much time as several. The higher the share of such orders, the higher the average, even though packers work at the same speed.
285.example:
Packed in the shift: 420 orders
Total packing time: 63 hours
Of those, shipped as several parcels: 30 orders, 11 hours

Pack Time = 63 / 420 = **0.15 hours, about 9 minutes**

For single-box orders only: 52 / 390 = 0.13 hours, about 8 minutes.
285.importance: **It sets the throughput of the packing area** and the number of stations to open for the peak. Packing can become the bottleneck: pickers can be added to the floor, while a packing station takes up space and needs materials at hand.
285.not_needed: **Skip it** when goods ship in the manufacturer's packaging without repacking. Also skip it where packing isn't separated from picking: one person picks and packs the order in one go, the system has no boundary between the stages, and time is measured for both stages at once.
285.essence_note: every extra minute of packing means fewer orders shipped per shift

286.name: Packing Damage Rate
286.description: The share of orders in which the product was damaged during packing. It counts damage found before handover to the carrier.
286.nuances:
**Decide** what counts as damage: only damage to the product itself, or also a dented box with intact contents. The second option gives a noticeably higher percentage: dented packaging is more common than product damage, and how much more common depends on how fragile the category is and on the shipping method.
An order **is counted once**, even if several items are damaged.
**Damage** the customer finds on delivery doesn't go into this metric: there, it's unknown who caused it, the warehouse or the carrier.
286.example:
Packed in the month: 5,930 orders
Product damaged during packing: 34 orders
Outer box dented, product intact: 61 orders (not counted, per company decision)
Customer reported breakage on delivery: 12 (not counted)

Packing Damage Rate = 34 / 5,930 × 100 = **0.6%**
286.importance: **This number drives** the choice of packing materials and the decision to repack fragile categories. With each damaged order, you pay twice: for the written-off product and for repeat picking and shipping. So even a small rise in the rate shows up in costs, and at high order volume it turns into a constant queue of re-picks that the shift handles instead of new orders.
286.not_needed: **Skip it** when goods ship in the manufacturer's packaging without being opened or repacked: the warehouse does nothing to them.
286.essence_note: anything damaged during packing has to be re-picked and written off before it even ships

287.name: Orders Packed per Hour
287.formula: Number of Packed Orders / Total Packing Time
287.description: How many orders are packed per hour of work.
287.nuances:
The denominator **is in labor hours** rather than hours the area is open: three packers on an eight-hour shift give 24 labor hours, and without this the rate is overstated threefold.
The denominator **includes all paid hours**, including waiting for orders from picking. Otherwise the metric shows how fast people pack at the station rather than the area's throughput.
Multi-parcel shipments **count as one order** but take as much time as several: a growing share of them lowers the rate with no drop in the quality of work.
287.example:
Packed in the shift: 420 orders
Packers: 3 on an 8-hour shift
Labor hours: 24

Orders Packed per Hour = 420 / 24 = **17.5 orders per hour**

Dividing by the 8 hours the area is open gives 52.5: that's the throughput of the whole area rather than of one person.
287.importance: **It's what you rely on** when deciding whether to open an extra packing station before the seasonal peak. A dip at the same order volume points to a shortage of materials at hand or a change in the order mix, and it needs to be sorted out before the peak rather than in the middle of it.
287.not_needed: **Skip it when** goods ship in the manufacturer's packaging without repacking. Also skip it where packing isn't separated from picking: one employee's hours can't be split between the two stages, and the area's rate would be the result of dividing them up on paper rather than a measurement.
287.essence_note: the faster orders are packed, the more of them ship in the same shift

288.name: Packing Material Cost per Order
288.formula: Total Packing Material Costs / Number of Packed Orders
288.description: The average cost of packing materials per order.
288.nuances:
Costs **are based on materials used** during the period rather than materials purchased. With a large box purchase once a quarter, basing costs on purchases gives a spike in one month and a dip in the next two.
**Define which materials are included**: boxes, void fill, tape, labels, stretch wrap. Small items like tape and labels add up to a noticeable part of the total at high order volume, and excluding them understates the result.
An order that ships as several parcels **counts as one** but uses materials for each box: a growing share of such orders raises the cost without the materials themselves getting more expensive.
288.example:
Materials used in the month: boxes $6,200, void fill $1,480, tape and labels $720
Total: $8,400
Orders packed: 5,930

Packing Material Cost per Order = 8,400 / 5,930 = **$1.42 per order**

Boxes alone would give $1.05: the other supplies add another third on top.
288.importance: It's the first cost item to cut when working on fulfillment cost, because materials **can be changed without restructuring** processes. Introducing boxes sized for a typical order or switching to poly mailers noticeably lowers this number, and the result shows up as soon as the new materials are in use.
288.not_needed: **Skip it when** goods ship in the manufacturer's packaging: there are no materials of your own.
288.synonyms: Packaging Cost per Order, Packing Supplies Cost per Order
288.essence_note: packaging comes out of the margin on every order

289.name: Labor Cost per Order Packed
289.formula: Total Packer Labor Costs / Number of Packed Orders
289.description: The average cost of packer labor per packed order.
289.nuances:
Costs **include the full cost** of labor with payroll taxes and bonuses, the same as in picking: otherwise the picking and packing figures aren't comparable.
The cost of packing materials **isn't included** here; it's a separate cost item. Mixing them double-counts costs when the metrics are added together.
If the same employee **both picks and packs**, their pay is split between the stages by hours worked. Assigning the whole amount to one stage distorts both numbers at once.
289.example:
Packer payroll with payroll taxes for the month: $15,600
Two of the packers also pick, and 60% of their time goes to packing: we allocate $4,680 of their $7,800
Packing labor costs: $12,480
Orders packed: 5,930

Labor Cost per Order Packed = 12,480 / 5,930 = **$2.10 per order**
289.importance: **Together with the cost** of materials, it gives the full cost of packing an order, and decisions on semi-automated packing lines are made based on that amount. Comparing it with the labor cost of picking shows which stage is more expensive and where it makes more sense to invest first.
289.not_needed: **Skip it when** goods ship in the manufacturer's packaging and when the warehouse is outsourced with a per-order fee. Also skip it where packing isn't separated from picking: one person's pay is split between the stages arbitrarily, and instead of two numbers you take the combined labor cost of picking and packing.
289.essence_note: the cost of packing comes out of the profit on every order

290.name: Packed Orders
290.description: The number of orders fully packed and ready to be handed over to the carrier.
290.nuances:
An order **is counted by the date** packing was completed rather than the ship date: an order packed on the last day of the month goes into that month, even if the truck comes the next day.
An order packed in several boxes **is counted once**.
Repacking after an error **isn't counted** again.
**An order packed and then** canceled isn't removed from the count: the materials were used and the work was done.
290.example:
Packing completed in the month: 5,930 orders
Shipped the same month: 5,800
Packed on the 31st, ships April 1: 130 (counted in March)
Repacked after an error: 47 (not counted again)

Packed Orders = **5,930**
290.importance: **It gives the actual volume of work** in the packing area, over which materials and labor costs are spread. The gap between packed and shipped orders shows how many finished orders pile up waiting for the truck, and if it grows, the bottleneck is the carrier's pickup schedule rather than staffing.
290.not_needed: **Skip it when** goods ship in the manufacturer's packaging without repacking: the count simply duplicates the number of shipped orders and adds nothing of its own.
290.essence_note: a packed order can go to the carrier today rather than tomorrow

291.name: Pack-to-Ship Time
291.formula: Total Time from Packing to Shipping / Number of Orders
291.description: How long, on average, an order waits from the end of packing to handover to the carrier.
291.nuances:
The denominator **includes only orders** that have already shipped: orders packed and sitting in the shipping area at the time of calculation have an incomplete interval and understate the average.
The time between packing and shipping **depends on the carrier's truck schedule**, so calendar hours give a truer picture here than business hours: an order packed after the last pickup waits for the next run, and the customer experiences this wait just as much as the time spent picking.
**Decide** what counts as the moment of shipping: the physical handover of the boxes or the acceptance scan in the carrier's system. The gap between these two moments is more noticeable the larger the shipment and the later the carrier completes acceptance.
291.example:
Shipped in the week: 1,400 orders
Total wait from packing to handover: 8,960 hours
Packed but still in the shipping area: 130 (not counted)

Pack-to-Ship Time = 8,960 / 1,400 = **6.4 hours**
291.importance: **This number shows** how much time an order loses after the warehouse has finished its work. If the wait for the truck is comparable to picking and packing time combined, the issue is the number of pickups per day rather than the pickers, and the right decision is an extra run rather than adding people to the shift.
291.not_needed: **Skip it for customer pickup**: the order doesn't wait for a truck; it sits at the pickup point until the customer comes, and that wait belongs to a different metric.
291.essence_note: while the order waits to be handed to the carrier, the customer's delivery clock is already running

292.name: Shipped Orders
292.description: The number of orders handed over to a carrier during the period.
292.nuances:
An order **is counted by the date** it was actually handed over to the carrier rather than the date it was ready to ship. Orders that are packed and waiting for the truck go into the next period.
An order shipped in several parcels **is counted once**.
For an add-on to the same order shipped as a separate parcel, **decide whether to count it as a second** shipped order or as part of the first. This determines whether the count reconciles with the number of picked orders.
292.example:
Handed over to carriers in March: 5,800 orders
Packed, to be picked up by the truck on April 1: 130 (not counted)
Shipped in two parcels: 45 orders (counted as 45)

Shipped Orders = **5,800**
292.importance: **It marks the point where** the warehouse's responsibility ends and the carrier's begins: it's used to determine who is to blame for a late delivery. Carrier invoice reconciliation relies on the same number, and a mismatch with the carrier's acceptance record means lost or duplicated shipments.
292.not_needed: **Skip it for customer pickup**: the order is handed to the customer instead of a carrier.
292.essence_note: the delivery clock starts at shipping, and the more orders go out, the more customers get them on time

293.name: Order Fulfillment Time
293.formula: Total Fulfillment Time / Number of Orders
293.description: The average time from an order's arrival to its handover to the carrier. It includes processing, picking, packing and waiting for the truck.
293.nuances:
The base **includes only orders** that have reached shipping: unfinished ones cut the interval short and understate the average, while those stuck waiting for incoming stock overstate it when they finally ship.
The time basis **is the same** as in the processing SLA. Counting in calendar hours gives the time the customer sees, and the promise on the storefront is built on it. Counting in business hours shows how fast the warehouse itself works and isn't suitable for promises to the customer.
An order **is assigned to the period** by its ship date: then the period closes right away and isn't recalculated. If orders are assigned by arrival date, the month's result keeps changing after the month ends until the last order ships, and the most problematic orders are the ones that wait the longest.
The metric is always at least the sum of the stage metrics: each stage metric counts only its own work and stops the clock when the order moves on. The time an order waits in a queue between stages doesn't go into any of them, while here it **is part of the interval** in full. The difference between this metric and the sum of the stages is the time spent waiting in queues.
293.example:
Shipped in the month: 5,800 orders
Total time from arrival to shipping: 156,600 calendar hours

Order Fulfillment Time = 156,600 / 5,800 = **27 hours**

The operations themselves take less than a third of that time. The order spends the rest in queues between stages: you can't add up the stage averages and get 27 hours, since they're calculated on different bases and on different time scales.
293.importance: This is the only number on the map that **matches what** the customer experiences. Stage metrics can all be green while the total fulfillment time is longer than their sum, because the order sits in queues between stages. The promise on the storefront is built on this number, and any gap translates directly into support tickets.
293.not_needed: **Skip it for** dropshipping and cross-docking, when goods from the supplier go out to the customer the same day without being stored: the order has no path of its own through the warehouse, and there's nothing to measure.
293.essence_note: the longer an order takes to get through the warehouse, the later it reaches the customer

294.name: Fulfillment Cost per Order
294.formula: Total Fulfillment Costs / Number of Orders
294.description: How much it costs on average to take one order through the warehouse: picking, packing, materials and related expenses.
294.nuances:
**Define the cost items** included. The narrow set is picker and packer labor plus materials. The broad set adds warehouse rent, equipment depreciation and a share of administrative expenses, and the more the warehouse itself costs, the more this raises the result. Without a list of cost items, figures for different periods aren't comparable.
**Fixed costs are divided** by the actual order volume, so in the slow season the cost per order rises on its own, with no decline in performance.
The denominator **matches the base of processed orders**: orders canceled before picking incur almost no costs and are excluded, while orders picked and then canceled are included because money was spent on them.
Shipping costs **aren't included** in this metric: that's payment to the carrier rather than fulfillment.
294.example:
Warehouse costs for the month: labor $44,400, materials $8,400, rent and equipment $18,500
Total: $71,300
Orders processed: 6,200

Fulfillment Cost per Order = 71,300 / 6,200 = **$11.50 per order**

Without rent and equipment, it comes to $8.52: the same work with a different set of costs.
294.importance: It **feeds directly into the order margin** and into setting the minimum order value for free shipping. If fulfillment eats up the entire markup on an average order, every such order loses money, and the free shipping threshold needs to go up. The same number is used to calculate the payback of automation: the investment makes sense as long as the savings per order cover the cost of the equipment over its service life.
294.not_needed: **Skip it when** you use a fulfillment provider that charges per operation: the provider bills at its own rates, and the seller has no need to break the bill down into picking, packing and materials.
294.synonyms: Cost per Order Fulfilled, Order Handling Cost
294.essence_note: every dollar spent on fulfillment comes out of the order's profit

295.name: Perfect Order Rate
295.description: The share of orders that went through the whole process without errors: picked correctly, undamaged, with complete documents and shipped on time.
295.nuances:
**Define the set of conditions** for a perfect order. The classic set is correct contents, an undamaged product, complete documents and an on-time shipment. Each added condition lowers the percentage, so once the set is defined, it stays unchanged. If a condition is added or removed in the middle of the year, the series breaks: the metric drops because of the new counting rule, yet it looks like the warehouse is doing worse. When the set is revised, past periods are recalculated too; otherwise there's nothing to compare with.
An order that fails two conditions at once is subtracted **once**.
An order counts as perfect **only if it passes** every stage without errors, so the shares are multiplied rather than averaged: three stages at 98% accuracy give 0.98 × 0.98 × 0.98, or about 94%. The overall rate is never higher than any stage's accuracy, and the more stages in the set, the wider the gap, even if the quality of work at each stage hasn't changed. You can't compare this number with stage accuracies directly.
Errors found after shipping **are assigned to the period** in which the order shipped, so the figures for past months can still change.
295.example:
Shipped in the month: 5,800 orders

Of those, with a picking error: 92
Damaged during packing: 33
Shipped late: 290
Orders in two categories at once: 18

Orders with errors = 92 + 33 + 290 − 18 = 397
Perfect orders = 5,800 − 397 = 5,403
Perfect Order Rate = 5,403 / 5,800 × 100 = **93.2%**

All four numbers come from the same set of shipped orders. You can't count errors against each stage's own base: picking, packing and processing have bases of different sizes, and shares taken from them don't add up.
295.importance: It brings the quality of all stages into one number: the customer doesn't care at which stage the mistake happened and just sees one order that went wrong. The gap between the stage accuracies and the overall rate shows whether many orders fail for several reasons at once and whether to fix the process **as a whole** rather than a single area.
295.not_needed: **Skip it** when the set of perfect-order conditions isn't defined: it's unclear which criteria an order must meet to count as error-free, and the number will mean something different in every report. The metric also loses its meaning where there's only one stage: it reduces to that stage's own accuracy and adds nothing.
295.synonyms: Perfect Order Index, Perfect Order Percentage
295.essence_note: an order without a single error won't come back, won't generate a support ticket and won't hurt the customer relationship

296.name: Order Processing SLA Target Time
296.description: The target time within which an order must be processed. It's set by the company and isn't calculated from actuals.
296.nuances:
The target **is set on the same** basis used to measure the actual time: in business hours according to the warehouse schedule or in calendar hours. Business hours reflect the actual workload of staff but require keeping a shift calendar. Calendar hours are easier to calculate and clearer to the customer, but any order that arrives on Friday evening uses up part of the target over the weekend while nothing happens to it.
**Define the starting point**: the moment of payment, the moment the order comes in or the moment it enters the warehouse queue. Between payment and entering the queue, time is spent on checks and confirmation, and at high order volume this difference affects the result.
**A separate target for oversized items**, pre-orders and consolidated orders changes the distribution of breaches: with a single target for everything, complex items consistently miss it.
296.example:
The warehouse is open 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., seven days a week
Starting point: a paid order enters the queue
Target: 12 business hours until handover to the carrier

Order Processing SLA Target Time = **12 business hours**

On a calendar basis, the same threshold gives 24 hours: an order that arrives at 8 p.m. is processed by 8 p.m. the next day.
296.importance: **It's the reference point for** all on-time metrics: without it, you can calculate neither the breach rate nor the overrun. A target set too short keeps reports permanently in the red and dulls the response to real failures; one set too long hides slow work behind numbers that are green only on paper.
296.not_needed: **Don't set it** when picking is planned around a specific ship date from the delivery schedule: there, the truck schedule dictates the deadline rather than a per-order target.
296.synonyms: Order Processing SLA, Handling Time Target
296.essence_note: a target that's too loose permits slow work, while one that's too strict is missed all the time and stops meaning anything

297.name: Orders Outside SLA
297.formula: Number of orders that breached the SLA
297.description: The number of orders whose processing exceeded the target time.
297.nuances:
**An order enters** the count on the date its processing is completed.
Orders still in progress that have already exceeded the target time **aren't included**, so the figure for the current day is always incomplete.
An order **is counted once**, even if the target was breached at several stages.
Orders canceled before processing started **don't count as breaches**: there was no processing.
The target and the actual time **are measured on the same** basis, business hours or calendar hours; otherwise every order placed in the evening ends up among the breaches.
297.example:
Processed in the month: 6,200 orders
Took longer than 24 hours: 310
Still in progress and already late: 24 (go into the next period)
Canceled before processing started: 80 (not counted)

Orders Outside SLA = **310**
297.importance: **The absolute number shows** the real stakes that the percentage hides: the same breach rate at different companies means a different number of people whose orders didn't arrive on time. Every broken promise is a potential support ticket and review, and it's the count rather than the rate that's used to estimate the support workload and the compensation budget.
297.not_needed: **Skip it** when the processing target isn't set: there's nothing to breach.
297.essence_note: for these orders, the promise to the customer has been broken

298.name: Orders Within SLA
298.formula: Number of orders that met the SLA
298.description: The number of orders whose processing stayed within the target time.
298.nuances:
**The base is the same** as for breaches: orders that completed processing during the period.
**Orders within the target and orders that breached it** add up to the whole base; there shouldn't be a third category.
**An order processed exactly** at the target time counts here.
**Orders** still in progress don't go into either count.
298.example:
Processed in the month: 6,200 orders
Within 24 hours: 5,890
Breached: 310
Still in progress: 145 (not counted)

Orders Within SLA = **5,890**

Check: 5,890 + 310 = 6,200, so the counts reconcile.
298.importance: It shows the number of commitments met, while the percentage shows **only their share**. This number is used to calculate shift output and bonuses for volume completed, to plan warehouse capacity for the season and to report to the client or the marketplace on whether promised times were met. The same compliance rate at different order volumes means a completely different amount of work, and it's this count that matters when discussing resources.
298.not_needed: **Skip it** when the processing target isn't set: without a promised time, there's no basis for splitting orders into those within the target and those that breached it.
298.essence_note: these are the orders for which the promise was kept

299.name: Order Processing SLA Compliance Rate
299.description: The share of orders whose processing stayed within the target time. The complement of the breach rate.
299.nuances:
The base **includes orders** that completed processing during the period. Orders canceled before processing started aren't included: there was no processing. Orders still in progress go into neither the numerator nor the denominator, so the percentage for the current day is always incomplete.
Separately, **decide** which period an order is assigned to. If it's assigned by the date processing was completed, the period closes right away and isn't recalculated: this answers how the warehouse performed during the month. If it's assigned by arrival date, the month's result keeps updating after the month ends, with the hardest orders added last, but a spike in workload shows up in full and isn't spread across two periods. The choice is made once and applied the same way to the counts of orders within the target and orders that breached it; otherwise the three metrics stop reconciling with each other.
An order processed exactly at the target time **counts as within the target**.
If the target is set in business hours but the actual time is measured in calendar time, the percentage drops on every order that arrives in the evening or before a weekend: both values **are measured on the same** basis.
299.example:
Processed in the month: 6,200 orders
Within the 24-hour target: 5,890
Breached: 310

Order Processing SLA Compliance Rate = 5,890 / 6,200 × 100 = **95%**
299.importance: **It's used to decide** what time to promise customers on the storefront. If actual compliance is 88% and the website promises same-day shipping, one in eight customers gets a broken promise and contacts support. The promised time can safely be brought in line with what the warehouse consistently achieves.
299.not_needed: **Skip it** when the processing target isn't set: without a promised time, there's nothing to compare the actual time with.
299.essence_note: the customer was promised a time, and every breach is a broken promise

300.name: Average Order Processing SLA Overrun Rate
300.formula: (Average Overrun of Late Orders / Target Time) × 100
300.description: How far, on average, a late order goes past the target, as a percentage of the target. It's calculated only on orders that breached the target and shows how large the overrun is rather than how often it happens.
300.nuances:
The base **includes only orders** that exceeded the target. Orders completed on time aren't included: their zero or negative deviations dilute the average and turn the metric into the warehouse's average time buffer instead of the size of the overrun.
**The metric answers the question** of how badly the warehouse misses the deadline, while the SLA compliance rate and the number of breaches answer how often. On its own, each of the three is misleading.
Time **is counted either in** business hours according to the warehouse schedule or in calendar hours. With calendar hours, an order that arrives on Friday evening picks up the weekend hours, and the overrun grows with no real delay in work. With business hours, you need a calendar of shifts and holidays; otherwise weekend hours get counted as working time. The target uses the same basis as the actual time.
Orders canceled before processing started **aren't included**: they have neither an actual time nor a target.
**The average hides the tail**: a few orders stuck for a week raise the result more than ten one-hour overruns lower it.
300.example:
Orders for the week: 500
Target: 24 hours per order
Late: 40 orders
Total overrun for these orders: 360 hours

Average overrun = 360 / 40 = 9 hours
Average Order Processing SLA Overrun Rate = 9 / 24 × 100 = **37.5%**

A late order goes past the target by 9 hours on average: instead of one day, the customer waits almost a day and a half. If you spread the same overrun across all 500 orders and divide by the target, you get 3%, and that number doesn't show how large the overrun is.
300.importance: **It answers the question** of how badly the warehouse misses the deadline when it does. The breach rate may look tolerable, but if every breach stretches the time to several times the promise, the customer leaves and writes a review. Without this number, you see how many problems there are but not how severe they are, and the analysis starts with the wrong orders.
300.not_needed: **Skip it** when the processing target isn't defined numerically by stage and the system doesn't record actual timestamps: there's no baseline to measure the overrun against.
300.essence_note: the further past the target an order runs, the more the customer notices the delay

301.name: Labor Cost per Order Picked
301.formula: Total Picker Labor Costs / Number of Picked Orders
301.description: The average cost of picker labor per picked order.
301.nuances:
Costs **include the full cost** of labor: base pay or piece-rate pay, bonuses, payroll taxes and pay for contract workers. Counting only base pay understates the result by the full amount of payroll taxes and bonuses, and that's a noticeable part of the shift cost rather than a minor adjustment.
Paid hours **are counted in full**, including idle time: a picker's time waiting for tasks is paid, and its cost is still spread across orders.
Hours pickers worked on receiving or inventory counts come out of the calculation **along with** the pay for them; otherwise someone else's work ends up in the cost of picking.
The denominator **matches the number** of picked orders, including those picked and later canceled.
301.example:
Picker payroll for the month: $28,000
Payroll taxes: $2,800
Total: $30,800
Minus pay for hours spent on receiving: $2,000
Picking labor costs: $28,800
Orders picked: 6,020

Labor Cost per Order Picked = 28,800 / 6,020 = **$4.78 per order**
301.importance: It's the largest variable part of fulfillment cost and the basis for calculating the payback of investments in bin location systems, handheld scanners or batch picking. A rise at the same order volume means the shift costs more but does **the same amount** of work: either overtime or an inflated headcount.
301.not_needed: Skip it for cross-docking and dropshipping, and when the warehouse is outsourced with a per-order fee: picker labor isn't a separate cost item. Also skip it where picking isn't separated from packing: one person's pay can be split between the stages **only by rough estimate**, and both numbers become arbitrary. In that case, the combined labor cost of picking and packing is counted.
301.essence_note: the more expensive picking is, the less is left over from each order

302.name: Stuck Order Value
302.description: The total value of orders stuck in processing that haven't reached shipping.
302.nuances:
**Set the threshold** after which an order counts as stuck: usually it's exceeding the processing target. Without a threshold, the total will include every order moving normally through the process right now.
**Decide** whether to value orders at purchase cost or at selling prices. Purchase cost shows the company's tied-up cash; selling prices show revenue at risk. The two differ by the full markup, and you can't mix them in one report.
The metric is measured at a point in time rather than over a period: it's a snapshot of the queue on a specific date, and it **changes every day**.
**Orders** stuck because they're unpaid are separated from those stuck through the warehouse's fault: the warehouse can't clear the first group.
302.example:
Orders in processing longer than the target as of Monday morning: 145
Of those, waiting for the customer's payment: 60 worth $9,600 (counted separately)
Waiting for incoming stock or a free picker: 85
Their value at selling prices: $17,800

Stuck Order Value = **$17,800**
302.importance: It turns the queue from units into money and so determines what to clear first: fifty low-value orders or three high-value ones. Without this total, the queue is cleared in order of arrival, and a large order gets **as much attention** as a $20 order.
302.not_needed: **Skip it** when orders are processed the same day and no queue actually builds up.
302.synonyms: Aged Backlog Value, Stalled Order Value
302.essence_note: these are paid orders that aren't moving and aren't bringing in money

306.name: Active Loyalty Members
306.description: The number of program members who performed the action chosen as the activity criterion during the period: a purchase with the card, a points redemption or another interaction with the program.
306.nuances:
The activity criterion is chosen to fit the program and isn't changed afterward. A narrow set covers purchases with the card and points redemptions: then the metric is about money and comparable with sales. A broad set adds earning points without a purchase, logging in to the program app and opening an email: then it's about attention to the program rather than revenue, and the number is noticeably higher. Both versions make sense but answer different questions, and periods can be compared **only within one of them**.
The metric is periodic: a member is counted in every period in which they were active. Becoming active for the first time, through a first purchase or a first redemption, **isn't counted** here: that's a different event, and the map doesn't measure it.
A member **is counted once** regardless of the number of purchases in the period.
A purchase made without **presenting the card isn't counted**: it isn't linked to the member.
306.example:
Activity criterion: a purchase with the card or a points redemption

Purchases with loyalty cards in March: 14,200
Unique members who made them: 8,700
Redeemed points but didn't buy (exchange for a gift): 400
Logged in to the app but didn't buy or redeem points: 15,700 (not counted under this criterion)

Active Loyalty Members = 8,700 + 400 = **9,100**

With a broad criterion, where an app login also counts as activity, it would be 9,100 + 15,700 = 24,800: the same program, a different question.
306.importance: **This is the program's working base**, used to plan the points budget and the reach of messaging campaigns. Planning on the whole registered base overstates the expected response, and promotional campaigns consistently fall short of plan.
306.essence_note: these are the people who actually come back to buy

307.name: Points Redemption Rate
307.description: The share of earned points that members eventually redeemed.
307.nuances:
The numerator and the denominator **are taken from the same** earning cohort: redeemed points are matched to the period in which they were earned. Dividing a period's redemptions by the points earned in the same period gives a meaningless number, because points redeemed in a period were mostly earned in earlier months.
**The cohort must be observed** for longer than the points validity period; otherwise some points have neither expired nor been spent yet, and the share comes out understated.
307.example:
Earned in the second quarter of last year: 6,200,000 points
Validity period: 12 months
Redeemed from this cohort over the whole period: 3,900,000
Expired: 2,300,000

Points Redemption Rate = 3,900,000 / 6,200,000 × 100 = **63%**
307.importance: **The main indicator of whether** points work as a reason to come back. Low redemption means earned points remain an outstanding liability to customers and don't bring repeat purchases, while high redemption calls for a margin check: every point redeemed reduces revenue from the order.
307.not_needed: Skip it for programs without points, where the program gives a loyalty card discount, elevated status or access to a service: there's nothing to earn or redeem. **It also doesn't apply** to programs where points never expire and redemption has no limits: the share tends toward 100% anyway, and the only difference is when the member gets around to spending.
307.essence_note: unused points don't bring purchases, and points redeemed in full mean everyone gets the discount indiscriminately

308.name: Points Earned
308.description: The total number of points earned by members during the period.
308.nuances:
**All types of points earned count**: for purchases, signup, reviews, promotions and support compensation.
Points canceled when an item is returned or voided when a profile is blocked **are subtracted from the points earned** in the period when the cancellation happened.
Delayed points that become available a few days after a purchase **are assigned to the date** of the purchase; otherwise, at month boundaries, points earned become misaligned with sales.
308.example:
Earned for purchases in March: 11,400,000 points
For signups: 975,000
For reviews and promotions: 900,000
Canceled on returns: 340,000

Points Earned = 11,400,000 + 975,000 + 900,000 − 340,000 = **12,935,000**
308.importance: Every point earned creates a liability to the customer that sooner or later turns into a discount or expires. By tracking **only redemptions**, the company sees the cost after the fact and discovers the accumulated points overhang when there's nothing left to cover it.
308.not_needed: **Skip it for** programs without points, where the program gives a loyalty card discount, elevated status or access to a service: there's nothing to earn or redeem.
308.essence_note: stingy awards don't bring customers back, and generous ones build up a liability that will have to be paid in real money

309.name: Points Redeemed
309.description: The total number of points members redeemed during the period.
309.nuances:
Points restored to the account after an order cancellation or an item return **are subtracted from the total** of the period when the return happened.
Expired points **aren't included** in redemptions: they're a separate value, and adding them overstates members' apparent activity.
**Voiding points when** a profile is blocked isn't a redemption either.
309.example:
Redeemed in March: 3,100,000 points
Returned to accounts because of item returns: 180,000
Expired: 420,000 (not counted)

Points Redeemed = 3,100,000 − 180,000 = **2,920,000**
309.importance: **This is the program's actual spend** in points: redemption is what turns earned points into a discount and into a reduction in revenue. Planning the budget by points earned instead of points redeemed overstates the spend, since some of the points will never be used.
309.not_needed: **Skip it for** programs without points, where the program gives a loyalty card discount, elevated status or access to a service: there's nothing to earn or redeem.
309.essence_note: until points are redeemed, the program doesn't affect purchases, and each redemption is money the company doesn't collect on an order

310.name: Points Expiration Rate
310.description: The share of earned points that expired at the end of their validity period.
310.nuances:
The numerator and the denominator **are taken from the same** earning cohort: expired points are divided by the points earned in the period they came from rather than by points earned in the period when they expired. With a short validity period, the shift is small, and the longer the period, the more it distorts the result.
Manually voiding points when an account is closed or blocked **isn't included** in the numerator: only expiration at the end of the validity period counts.
310.example:
Earned in March of last year: 1,400,000 points
Validity period: 12 months
Expired in March of this year from this cohort: 490,000
Voided manually when profiles were blocked: 12,000 (not counted)

Points Expiration Rate = 490,000 / 1,400,000 × 100 = **35%**
310.importance: **It shows** how much of the promised benefit customers never received. A high share looks good for the budget, but it means points don't motivate people to come back, and at the same time it builds up risk: when expiration rules are relaxed, liabilities surge all at once.
310.not_needed: Skip it for programs without points, where the program gives a loyalty card discount, elevated status or access to a service: there's nothing to earn or redeem. **It also doesn't apply** where points never expire: there's nothing to expire.
310.essence_note: expired points save money, but frequent expiration devalues the program in members' eyes

311.name: Repeat Redemption Rate
311.formula: (Members with Repeat Redemptions / Members with Redemptions) × 100
311.description: The share of members who redeemed points more than once, out of all members who redeemed points during the period.
311.nuances:
**The denominator is limited to those** who redeemed at all: dividing by the whole registered base mixes two different problems, no first redemption and no second one, and makes the number meaningless.
Redemptions on one order **count as one** event regardless of the number of transactions.
**The result depends on** the window length: over a month, fewer members have time to redeem again than over a year. The window should be noticeably longer than the usual interval between purchases.
311.example:
Members who redeemed points in the year: 18,000
Of those, redeemed twice or more: 7,900
Total registered in the base: 84,000

Repeat Redemption Rate = 7,900 / 18,000 × 100 = **44%**

Dividing by all 84,000 gives 9%: that's the share of the whole base that redeems repeatedly rather than the repeat redemption rate.
311.importance: **It separates one-time interest in** points from the habit of using them. As long as repeat redemptions are rare, the program gives a discount on one purchase and doesn't create the repeat business it was launched for.
311.not_needed: Skip it for programs without points, where the program gives a loyalty card discount, elevated status or access to a service: there's nothing to earn or redeem. **It also doesn't apply** to programs where points are redeemed automatically: repeat redemption happens on its own and says nothing about the member's habit.
311.essence_note: a member who redeemed points twice came back to the store again

312.name: Time to First Redemption
312.formula: Total Time to First Redemption / Number of Members Who Redeemed
312.description: The average time from joining the program to the first points redemption among members who redeemed at least once.
312.nuances:
The calculation **includes only members** who have actually redeemed: those who never redeemed have no time to first redemption and aren't in the denominator.
**The clock starts at** the enrollment date rather than the first points earned; otherwise the gap between joining and the first purchase drops out of the result, and the number is understated.
**The result depends on** how far back the observation window goes: if you take members who enrolled in the last three months, all long waits are cut off by construction, and the average comes out shorter than it really is.
312.example:
Enrolled a year ago: 5,000 members
Redeemed points at least once in the year: 1,800
Their total time to first redemption: 79,200 days

Time to First Redemption = 79,200 / 1,800 = **44 days**

Dividing by all 5,000 gives 16 days: it mixes in members who didn't redeem and no longer measures the time to redemption.
312.importance:
**It sets the time** after which it makes sense to remind members of their balance: if the typical first redemption happens after a month and a half, an email on day two is wasted, and one in month three is too late.
You can't use it directly to check the expiration period: the metric **is calculated only from** members who redeemed, while those whose points expired don't enter it, so the average looks better than reality. The expiration period works as a ceiling: the shorter it is, the more the distribution is cut off. To see whether the program lets the benefit expire too early, read this number together with the share of members who redeemed at all and the share of expired points.
312.not_needed: Skip it for programs without points, where the program gives a loyalty card discount, elevated status or access to a service: there's nothing to earn or redeem. **It also doesn't apply** to programs where points are redeemed automatically at the next purchase: the member doesn't choose when to redeem, and the time until then says nothing about their behavior.
312.essence_note: while points sit unused, they haven't brought the customer back to the store

313.name: Loyalty Member Spend Increase
313.formula: Average Spend After − Average Spend Before
313.description: How much a customer's average spend grew after joining the program compared with the period before joining.
313.nuances:
The before and after windows are equal in length and **are anchored to the enrollment date** of each member rather than to calendar boundaries: otherwise the comparison picks up different seasons.
The calculation includes **only members** who made purchases before enrolling. Those who signed up at their first purchase have no baseline for comparison, and including them counts all their spend as an increase from zero.
Spend **is net of** returns.
**Part of the increase comes from the fact** that people join the program during a surge of interest in the brand, when their spend is already higher than usual. Comparing with a comparable group of non-members separates the program's contribution from this effect.
313.example:
Members with purchases before enrolling: 6,400
Average spend over the 6 months before: $182
Average spend over the 6 months after: $247

Loyalty Member Spend Increase = 247 − 182 = **$65**

For a comparable group of non-members, spend grew by $19 over the same six months: the program's contribution is closer to $46.
313.importance: The numerator for calculating program ROI and the only answer to whether the program changes customer behavior or simply hands out a discount to people who were buying anyway. **Without this number, the points budget** is defended by growth in the number of members, which brings in no money by itself.
313.not_needed: Skip it for programs where enrollment happens **only at the moment** of the first purchase: there's no “before” period.
313.synonyms: Incremental Member Spend, Member Spend Lift
313.essence_note: this is the lift the program was set up to deliver

314.name: AOV with Points Redemption
314.formula: Revenue from Orders with Points Redemption / Orders with Points Redemption
314.description: The average order value among orders in which points were redeemed.
314.nuances:
Revenue **is counted as the money actually** received, net of the amount paid with points: including that amount turns the metric into the order size at list prices rather than the money that came in.
Canceled and unclaimed orders **are excluded from both** the numerator and the denominator.
314.example:
Orders with points redeemed, at list prices: $391,000
Paid with points: $29,200
Orders with points redeemed: 2,300

AOV with Points Redemption = (391,000 − 29,200) / 2,300 = **$157.30**

At list prices, it comes to $170: that's the cart value rather than the money received.
314.importance: **Comparing it with the regular** AOV answers whether points add to the cart or simply make it cheaper. When the order value with points turns out lower than the regular one, the program works as a discount on a habitual purchase, and its economics stop adding up.
314.not_needed: Skip it for programs without points, where the program gives a loyalty card discount, elevated status or access to a service: there's nothing to earn or redeem. **It also doesn't apply** to programs where points can't be used to pay for an order: there are no orders with points redeemed, so there's nothing to average.
314.synonyms: Average Spend per Redemption, Redemption AOV
314.essence_note: the bigger the order with points, the more points grow the cart rather than make it cheaper

315.name: Time to First Purchase Post-Enrollment
315.formula: Total Time to First Purchase / Number of New Members Who Made a Purchase
315.description: The average time from joining the program to the first purchase among members who enrolled during the period and went on to make a purchase.
315.nuances:
The denominator **includes only members** who actually made a purchase: the others have no time to first purchase, and including them understates the average.
If enrollment happens at the register at the moment of purchase, such members contribute zero days and pull the average down. They're counted **separately** from those who enrolled before buying; otherwise the result depends on the share of enrollments made at the register rather than on the program.
The result **changes with the length** of the observation window: the shorter the window after enrollment, the fewer long waits make it into the calculation.
315.example:
Enrolled in January, not at the register: 2,100 members
Made a purchase within six months: 1,300
Total time to first purchase: 27,300 days

Time to First Purchase Post-Enrollment = 27,300 / 1,300 = **21 days**
315.importance: **It determines** when to start the onboarding email series for new members and on which day to send a reminder about welcome points. A long time to first purchase means joining the program isn't tied to a reason to buy, and the welcome bonus is wasted.
315.not_needed: **Skip it** when members join the program only at the moment of purchase: the time is always zero.
315.synonyms: Time to First Purchase After Signup
315.essence_note: the longer a member goes without buying, the higher the chance they never start

316.name: Points Earned per Order
316.formula: Points Earned for Purchases / Number of Members' Orders
316.description: The average number of points earned per program member's order during the period.
316.nuances:
The numerator includes **only points earned for** purchases: welcome points and points for reviews aren't tied to orders and inflate the average.
**The denominator is limited to orders** from program members that are eligible for earning. Dividing by all orders mixes members with other customers and understates the result.
316.example:
Earned for purchases in March: 11,400,000 points
Program members' orders in March: 8,900
Orders without a loyalty card: 3,500 (not counted)

[[Points Earned→programma_loyalnosti/nachislennye_bonusy]] per order = 11,400,000 / 8,900 = **1,281 points**
316.importance: **It turns an abstract earn rate** into a value the customer understands and shows whether one order earns enough to buy anything at all. When an order earns less than the redemption minimum, points don't feel like a benefit, and the program doesn't affect the customer's choice.
316.not_needed: Skip it for programs without points, where the program gives a loyalty card discount, elevated status or access to a service: there's nothing to earn or redeem. **It also doesn't apply** to programs with a fixed earn percentage: the average per order mirrors the average order value and carries no information of its own.
316.essence_note: with small awards there's no reason to come back, and with large ones the liability grows faster than the program pays off

317.name: Active Member Rate
317.description: The share of program members who were active during the period, out of all registered members at the end of the period. Each program defines what counts as activity.
317.nuances:
The activity criterion **is the same** as in [[Active Loyalty Members→programma_loyalnosti/aktivnye_uchastniki_programmy]]; otherwise the share and the count measure different people. The broader the criterion, the higher the share: with a narrow set it's about purchases, with a broad one it's about attention to the program.
The denominator **is cumulative over** the program's whole lifetime rather than limited to the period's signups: the base holds more registrations than there are active members, and swapping the denominator gives a number that looks like a new-member conversion rate.
Blocked and deleted profiles **are excluded from the denominator**; otherwise the share falls as junk records pile up in the base.
317.example:
Program members as of March 31: 84,000 (blocked profiles and duplicates already excluded)
Bought or redeemed points in March: 9,100

Active Member Rate = 9,100 / 84,000 × 100 = **10.8%**

Dividing only by the 3,400 who enrolled in March gives 268%: the numerator and the denominator come from different sets.
317.importance: It answers whether the program works or has just accumulated a base of cards. With a low share, spending on points and communications is spread across people who are **only on the books**, and any program economics calculated on the whole base turn out to be fiction.
317.essence_note: the program earns money only from those who use it

318.name: Points Redeemed per Order
318.formula: Points Redeemed in Orders / Orders with Points Redemption
318.description: The average number of points redeemed in one order with points redemption.
318.nuances:
**The numerator is limited to redemptions** within orders: exchanging points for gifts and gift certificates outside an order inflates the average.
Both values **are counted net of** canceled orders and returns with points restored; otherwise the numerator and the denominator are based on different sets of orders.
318.example:
Points redeemed in March: 3,130,000
Of those, exchanged for gifts and gift certificates without an order: 210,000 (not counted)
Orders with points redeemed: 2,300

Points Redeemed per Order = (3,130,000 − 210,000) / 2,300 = **1,270 points**
318.importance: **It translates** directly into the size of the discount the program gives on an average order, and it's compared with the average points earned per order: if noticeably more is redeemed than earned per order, the pool of accumulated points is spent faster than it's replenished.
318.not_needed: Skip it for programs without points, where the program gives a loyalty card discount, elevated status or access to a service: there's nothing to earn or redeem. **It also doesn't apply** to programs where points can't be used to pay for an order: points go toward gifts or services, and no points are redeemed per order.
318.essence_note: points need to noticeably lower the bill or they don't motivate members, but every dollar paid in points is revenue not received

319.name: Average Points Balance
319.formula: Points Balance of Active Members / Active Loyalty Members
319.description: The average number of unused points in one active member's account as of a date.
319.nuances:
The balance **is taken as of a specific** date rather than for a period: it's a stock rather than a flow.
The balance **excludes points in** blocked accounts: the member can't redeem them, and they aren't part of the available balance.
**The denominator is limited to active members**. Dividing by the whole registered base gives a noticeably smaller number and creates the impression that there are hardly any accumulated points.
319.example:
Points balance in active members' accounts as of March 31: 41,000,000
In blocked accounts: 900,000 (excluded)
Expired but not yet written off: 600,000 (excluded)
Active members: 9,100

Average Points Balance = (41,000,000 − 900,000 − 600,000) / 9,100 = **4,341 points**
319.importance: **The average balance shows** what discount is already in the hands of people who will definitely come back. A sharp rise means points accumulate faster than they're spent and may one day be redeemed all at once: money is set aside for this, and the per-order redemption cap is checked.
319.not_needed: Skip it for programs without points, where the program gives a loyalty card discount, elevated status or access to a service: there's nothing to earn or redeem. **It also doesn't apply** to programs where points are redeemed automatically at the next purchase: balances don't build up in accounts, and the average balance stays near zero.
319.synonyms: Average Outstanding Points, Average Points per Member
319.essence_note: an empty account doesn't bring a customer back, and a large balance is a liability the company has accumulated

320.name: Member Growth Rate
320.description: The growth rate of the number of program members over the period compared with an earlier comparable period.
320.nuances:
Both counts **follow the same** rule: either both include blocked and deleted profiles, or both exclude them. Changing the rule between the two dates gives negative growth despite a real inflow.
Cleaning duplicates and inactive profiles out of the base shows up in the metric as a drop, even though the inflow of signups hasn't changed. Such one-time profile removals **are recorded separately**; otherwise the number is misread.
320.example:
Members as of March 31 of last year: 71,000
Members as of March 31 of this year: 84,000
Duplicates removed from the base in the year: 4,000

Member Growth Rate = (84,000 − 71,000) / 71,000 × 100 = **18%**
Without the cleanup, growth would have been 24%
320.importance: **It shows** whether the program is being replenished or living off its old base. Slowing inflow with stable sales means new customers pass the program by, and over time all loyalty revenue will depend on an aging group of members.
