The result depends on how the system measures time. Where duration **is calculated as the time** between events, the last page of a session gets zero: there's no next event, and the average is understated, most of all for pages where people end their session. Where active-tab time is counted, the final page counts too, and the number comes out noticeably higher.
Tracking scrolling and other on-page events extends the measured time, so turning it on raises the number with no change in people's behavior. Periods before and after can be compared **only with a caveat**.
**Tabs** left open stop being counted at the inactivity timeout: with a default timeout of 30 minutes, a tab abandoned overnight adds exactly those 30 minutes to the total rather than eight hours.
362.example:
Content pageviews in the month: 24,500
Total time on these pages: 29,400 minutes

Time on Content Page = 29,400 / 24,500 = **1.2 minutes**

Pageviews that were the last in their session: 9,100. If the system assigns them zero, they drag the average down: the other 15,400 pageviews give 1.9 minutes.
362.importance: **It shows** whether people read a piece to the end or leave before scrolling. When the average time on long articles is very short, the problem is usually a mismatch between the headline's promise and the content rather than the text itself: people come for one thing, see another and leave.
362.not_needed: **Skip it for pieces** where the answer is meant to be instant: reference tables, calculators, pages with a single number. There, leaving quickly means the person found what they were looking for.
362.synonyms: Average Time on Page, Time on Page
362.essence_note: too little means the piece isn't being read, too much means it's dense and hard to follow

363.name: Content Ideation Time
363.formula: Total Ideation Time / Number of Ideas
363.description: How much time, on average, goes into coming up with one topic. Calculated for ideas recorded in the period.
363.nuances:
**An idea counts** when it's written down and phrased clearly enough to be assigned as a task.
**Offhand remarks at** a meeting don't count; otherwise the denominator swells and the time per idea drops artificially.
**Rejected ideas stay** in the denominator: time was spent on them, and without them the metric shows the hit rate rather than the speed of coming up with ideas.
363.example:
Two 3-hour meetings, 4 participants
Effort: 3 × 4 × 2 = 24 hours
Topics recorded and clearly defined: 30
Of those, rejected during topic selection: 12 (stay in the denominator)

Content Ideation Time = 24 / 30 = **0.8 hours per idea**
363.importance: **It answers the question** of where the pipeline is stuck: in ideation or in production. If the time per idea is comparable to the time spent on the piece itself, the problem is a lack of topic sources, and hiring authors won't solve it.
363.not_needed: **Skip it where** topics come ready-made from product, sales or search demand: there's no ideation stage.
363.essence_note: the longer it takes to come up with a topic, the fewer pieces come out with the same team

364.name: Share of Content-Driven Sales
364.description: What share of all sales came from people who interacted with content. Shows content's contribution to total sales.
364.nuances:
The numerator and denominator **are counted in the same** unit: both as a number of sales or both in dollars; otherwise the percentage is meaningless.
You choose an attribution model, and it changes the result substantially: last-click attribution gives content **only the sales** where a piece was the final touchpoint, while spreading credit across all touchpoints makes the share grow.
**Set an attribution window** beyond which a link to content isn't counted. Content works slowly, and a 30-day window cuts off some of the purchases it actually drove.
364.example:
All sales for the quarter: 1,240 totaling $1,860,000
Content-driven sales, last click: 96
Sales where content was any touchpoint within a 90-day window: 214

Last click = 96 / 1,240 × 100 = **7.7%**
Any touchpoint = 214 / 1,240 × 100 = **17.3%**

On the same sales, the two models differ by more than a factor of two, so the model is fixed before the calculation.
364.importance: **It's the basis** for deciding how much money to give content next year. Without this number, content is defended with reach and likes; such arguments lose out next to direct advertising, and its budget is cut first.
364.not_needed: **Skip it** when deals take a long time and close offline, and the CRM has no touchpoint data: you'd have to guess the numerator.
364.synonyms: Content Influence on Sales, Content Contribution to Sales
364.essence_note: the bigger the share of sales that comes from readers, the better content pays off

365.name: Content-Driven Leads
365.description: The number of leads from people who interacted with content. A lead is counted on the date it came in.
365.nuances:
**Define** what counts as a lead: any submitted contact or one that passed a qualification check. The figures differ widely, and without a single definition, comparing periods is meaningless.
A lead **is attributed to content** by the attribution model: last-click attribution credits only those who came directly from a content page, while counting all touchpoints adds those who read content earlier and submitted an inquiry later from a different source.
**Set a window** beyond which an interaction with content no longer counts: content's path to an inquiry is longer than advertising's, and a short window cuts off a noticeable share.
**Duplicates from one person** who submitted several inquiries are merged into one lead.
365.example:
Inquiries with a content tag in the month: 210
Duplicates from the same people: 24 (merged)
Inquiries from people who had read content earlier, within a 90-day window: 68

Last click = 210 − 24 = **186**
All touchpoints = 186 + 68 = 254
365.importance: **It translates reading into a figure** sales understands and makes content comparable with other sources of inquiries. Until content leads are tagged, they dissolve into direct and search traffic, and content marketing looks like a cost line with no results.
365.not_needed: **Skip it in** retail and ecommerce, where people buy right away and there's no lead stage.
365.essence_note: these are inquiries you didn't pay for with advertising

366.name: Content Output per Creator
366.description: How many pieces, on average, one author produces in the period. Only published pieces count, and only authors who had at least one piece published in the period.
366.nuances:
The denominator **is taken from the number** of authors with publications in the period rather than from the staffing plan: people on vacation and new hires without a first piece would lower the average without having anything to do with productivity.
**A co-authored piece** is credited to its authors in fractions; otherwise the sum across all authors exceeds the number of pieces published.
Authors' workloads differ, and without accounting for that, the number is misleading: averaging across a mix of staff and freelance authors makes sense **only after converting** to full-time equivalents.
366.example:
Published in the month: 25 pieces
Authors with publications: 8, of whom 5 on staff and 3 freelance
Co-authored pieces: 4 (each split in half)

Content Output per Creator = 25 / 8 = **3.1**

Freelance authors produced 6 of the 25 pieces: staff authors average 3.8 pieces each, versus 2 for freelancers.
366.importance: **It's the basis for calculating** how many authors you need for next period's plan. A mistake here is costly in both directions: too few people derail the calendar, too many means paying salaries for idle time.
366.not_needed: Skip it when one person runs content: the denominator equals one, and the metric repeats the number of publications. Also skip it when a piece is made **entirely** by a team of an editor, a designer and a producer: you can't assign a single author, and the denominator becomes arbitrary.
366.essence_note: the more pieces one author produces, the cheaper each one is

367.name: Content Pipeline Volume
367.description: How many pieces are in production right now: being written, illustrated, reviewed. Counted at a specific point in time.
367.nuances:
**Set where work begins and ends**: at which stage a piece counts as started and at which it leaves the count. Typically the start is assigning an author and the exit is publication, and a piece awaiting approval remains in production.
**Pieces on hold are excluded** from the count; otherwise they keep the number inflated indefinitely and create the appearance of a full workload.
367.example:
At the end of the week:
Being written: 9
In illustration: 4
In review: 6
Ready, waiting for a publication date: 3
On hold pending a product decision: 5 (not counted)

Content Pipeline Volume = 9 + 4 + 6 + 3 = **22**
367.importance: **The number of concurrent tasks** directly determines how long each one takes to come out: a team of four authors with twenty pieces in production publishes everything more slowly than with eight, with the same output for the quarter. The metric catches overload before it turns into missed deadlines.
367.not_needed: **Skip it when** pieces are produced one at a time: there's always one task in production, and the number shows nothing.
367.essence_note: too few pieces in production: the publishing schedule will fall apart; too many: the team spreads itself thin and everything moves slowly

368.name: Content Production Backlog
368.formula: Number of tasks in the backlog
368.description: How many approved topics are waiting their turn to go into production. Counted at a specific point in time rather than over a period.
368.nuances:
The count includes **only selected and** clearly defined topics. If everything goes into the backlog, the number shows the size of a dumping ground rather than a reserve of work.
Pieces taken into production leave the backlog; otherwise one topic **counts twice**. Topics that have sat idle for a long time are most often no longer relevant, and regular cleanup of them changes the number more than new topics coming in.
368.example:
Topics on the idea list: 120
Of those, selected and clearly defined: 43
Moved into production this week: 7 (leave the backlog)
Sitting idle for more than six months: 9 (written off during cleanup)

Content Production Backlog = 43 − 7 − 9 = **27**
368.importance: **It shows** how many weeks of work the team has lined up. An empty backlog means publishing is about to stall: authors will run out of topics before anyone notices it in the release calendar.
368.not_needed: **Skip it where** topics go into production as they come up, without a queue: there's no backlog list.
368.essence_note: an empty backlog leaves the team without work, and a bloated one means topics go stale before they're published

369.name: Content Costs
369.description: All the money spent on creating and promoting content pieces in the period.
369.nuances:
Salaries of the in-house team **are included in expenses**; otherwise freelance production looks more expensive than in-house simply because its invoices are visible, while salaries sit on a separate line.
The cost of people who work on content part-time **is included in proportion** to their time rather than in full.
Subscriptions to services, stock libraries and licenses are allocated over the period of use rather than as a lump sum in the month of payment: an annual subscription booked **entirely** to January distorts month-to-month comparisons.
**You decide** whether paid promotion of finished pieces is included. If it is, the metric shows the full cost of getting an audience; if not, only production.
369.example:
For the month:
Editorial team salaries with payroll taxes: $42,000
Designer, spending 40% of their time on content: 8,500 × 0.4 = $3,400
Freelance authors, per invoices: $6,000
Annual stock subscription of $3,600: 3,600 / 12 = $300
Promoting publications: $4,500

Content Costs = **$56,200**
369.importance: **Without it you can't calculate** either the cost per piece or the return on investment: it's the basis for every economic calculation in content marketing. As long as expenses are scattered across different budget lines, content looks free, and any comparison with paid channels is skewed.
369.not_needed: **Skip it** when one person makes content as part of their regular salary and no money is spent on promotion: there are no separate content expenses.
369.essence_note: every dollar spent on content is subtracted from what it brings in

370.name: Content Publishing Frequency
370.description: How many pieces are published per unit of time.
370.nuances:
The window length **is set and stated** with the number: three pieces a week and three a month mean very different workloads.
The numerator includes new publications by release date; updates to old pieces **aren't counted**, as in Content Pieces Published.
A piece posted on several platforms **counts once**; otherwise frequency grows from distribution without any growth in production.
**Unevenness within the window** isn't visible in the average: eight pieces released over two days give the same monthly frequency as a steady pace of one every four days.
370.example:
New pieces published in the month: 25
Old pieces updated: 12 (not counted)
Placements on other platforms: 22 (not counted)

Content Publishing Frequency = 25 / 4 = **6.3 pieces per week**

Of those, 11 came out in the last week of the month: the average frequency doesn't show this.
370.importance: **The publishing pace affects** reach more than the quality of any single piece: platform algorithms and search crawlers adjust to regularity, and after a pause it takes time to get impressions back to their previous level. It also translates directly into team workload, so resource planning starts with it.
370.not_needed: **Skip it when** publishing around news hooks: pieces come out unevenly, and the average for the period doesn't describe any single month.
370.synonyms: Publishing Cadence, Posting Frequency, Content Cadence
370.essence_note: infrequent publishing doesn't retain the audience, and overly frequent publishing hurts quality with the same team

371.name: Content Referral Traffic
371.description: The number of sessions that came to content pages via links from other sites.
371.nuances:
Clicks from search and from ads **don't count** as referral traffic: analytics systems treat them as separate sources.
**Clicks from messaging apps** and other apps often lose their source attribution and end up in direct traffic, so referral traffic is understated in practice.
Your own sites and subdomains **are excluded from the sources**; otherwise internal clicks count as visits from outside.
A session **is counted by the rules** of the analytics system with an inactivity timeout, 30 minutes by default in GA4: one person can generate several sessions in a day.
371.example:
Sessions on content pages in the month: 9,800
From search: 5,900
Direct traffic: 1,800
From your second domain: 340 (excluded)
From external sites: 1,760

Content Referral Traffic = **1,760**
371.importance: **It shows** whether a piece lives beyond your own platform: people link to it, quote it, share it on forums. This traffic comes without paying per click and doesn't disappear when ads are turned off, so its share determines how resilient content marketing is to budget cuts.
371.not_needed: Skip it when content lives **only on external** platforms: there's nothing on your site for users to land on, and no [[Referring Pages to Content→kontent_marketing/vneshnie_ssylki]] point to it.
371.essence_note: these are sessions from links on other sites that you didn't pay for

372.name: Share of Unpublished Content
372.description: The share of completed pieces that aren't published: ready, but waiting in the publishing queue.
372.nuances:
A piece **counts as ready** when it has gone through all production stages and review: all it needs is a release date. A piece awaiting approval isn't ready yet; it's still in production.
**The metric is a snapshot on a date** rather than accumulated over a period: it's what's left in the publishing queue, and adding up days would count the same pieces many times.
The denominator includes all completed content: both what was published in the period and what's sitting ready. Dividing **only by what's waiting** always gives 100% and makes no sense.
**Pieces** postponed indefinitely or no longer relevant are taken out of the queue; otherwise they keep the share inflated for as long as they sit there and create the appearance of a reserve.
372.example:
At the end of the month:
Pieces completed in the month: 26
Of those, published: 21
Ready and waiting for a release date: 5
Postponed indefinitely after a change in priorities: 4 (taken out of the queue)

Share of Unpublished Content = 5 / 26 × 100 = **19%**
372.importance: **It shows the stock of ready pieces** before publishing: with it, the editorial team gets through an author's illness or a missed delivery; without it, any delay immediately becomes a gap in the content calendar. Too large a share means the opposite: pieces are made faster than they're published, and some of them will go stale before they come out.
372.not_needed: **Skip it when** pieces are published as soon as they're ready: a piece comes out on the day it's submitted, and there's no publishing queue.
372.essence_note: a ready but unpublished piece is already paid for, but a reserve is needed so there are no gaps in the publishing schedule

373.name: Content Review Time
373.formula: Total Review Time / Number of Pieces Reviewed
373.description: How much time, on average, goes into reviewing one piece before publication. Calculated for pieces reviewed in the period.
373.nuances:
**You decide** whether to count calendar time from submission for review to the review decision or the reviewer's actual working time: the first shows how long a piece sits in the queue, the second how much the editing itself costs.
Repeat reviews after edits are added to the time for one piece and **aren't counted as separate units**; otherwise difficult pieces with three rounds of edits look fast to review.
373.example:
Pieces reviewed in the month: 18
Total reviewer time: 27 hours
Of that, on 3 pieces with repeat rounds: 11 hours

Content Review Time = 27 / 18 = **1.5 hours per piece**
373.importance: **It's what you look at** when deciding whether you need a dedicated editor or can leave review to the authors. A growing review time more often signals that drafts come in unpolished than that the editor is strict: it's cheaper to fix the brief up front than to edit at the end.
373.not_needed: **Skip it where** the author publishes without approval: there's no review stage.
373.essence_note: review delays a piece's release, while the author's work is already paid for

374.name: Content Update Frequency
374.description: How many updates to old pieces there are per unit of time.
374.nuances:
The window length **is fixed**; otherwise there's nothing to compare the number with: two updates a week and two a month differ fourfold.
**An update means the same** as in Content Pieces Updated: a change in content rather than typo fixes and image replacements.
374.example:
Content updates in the quarter: 38
Period: 3 months

Content Update Frequency = 38 / 3 = **12.7 updates per month**

With an archive of 340 pieces, this pace means a full update cycle takes about two years.
374.importance: Comparing the update pace with the size of the archive shows how many years it takes the team to go through it **in full**. If this period is longer than your data stays current, some pieces are guaranteed to be outdated, and you'll find out from reader complaints or from slipping search rankings.
374.not_needed: **Skip it for** fast-turnaround content tied to its release date: it isn't updated.
374.synonyms: Content Refresh Rate, Content Refresh Cadence
374.essence_note: infrequent updates push old pieces out of search, and overly frequent ones mean the team rewrites instead of producing new content

375.name: Content Production Velocity
375.description: How many pieces the team gets ready for publication per unit of time.
375.nuances:
The window length **is set and fixed**: weekly and monthly figures differ by a multiple, and without the unit stated, the result can't be read.
A piece is counted on its completion date rather than its publication date: a piece prepared in March and published in April **belongs to March**. Otherwise the metric repeats the publishing frequency and loses its meaning.
Pieces of different lengths **count the same**, so velocity is easy to raise by splitting topics into short posts.
375.example:
Ready for publication over 4 weeks: 26 pieces
Of those, published in the same month: 21
Waiting for a release date: 5 (included in the calculation)

Content Production Velocity = 26 / 4 = **6.5 pieces per week**
375.importance: **It's used to check** whether the team can deliver the plan before things start slipping. If production velocity is lower than the publishing frequency, the stock of ready pieces gets used up, and eventually publishing stops.
375.not_needed: **Skip it where** topics are taken on as they come up, without a plan: production velocity then reflects the flow of tasks rather than the team's work.
375.essence_note: the faster the team gets pieces ready, the more of them come out with the same team

376.name: Referring Pages to Content
376.description: The number of working links from other sites to your content. Counted by the number of referring pages at the time of the check.
376.nuances:
**You choose the unit of count**: either the link or the referring domain, and the figures can be far apart: one site with a sitewide footer link gives a link from each of its pages but only one domain.
Links with the nofollow attribute **are counted separately from** regular ones: they don't pass link equity, yet they bring real people.
A link **counts as active** while the referring page is available and the link is still on it. The metric is cumulative and needs rechecking: some links disappear along with their pages.
Links from other sites you own **are excluded**; otherwise the metric counts links you placed yourself.
376.example:
Links to blog content found: 1,460
Of those, from your own sites: 210 (excluded)
Referring pages unavailable: 95 (excluded)
Remaining: 1,155, of which nofollow: 380

Referring Pages to Content = **1,155**, including 775 that pass link equity
Referring domains total only 142
376.importance: **It determines** whether content rises in search without spending on ads. Links build up slowly and can hardly be bought without risking search penalties, so a drop in their number predicts a decline in search traffic in advance, which the traffic itself will show only later.
376.not_needed: **Skip it** when content lives inside closed platforms and messaging apps: there are no links from external sites there.
376.essence_note: every link from another site brings people and lifts content in search

377.name: Newsletter Signup Rate
377.description: What share of people who read content signed up. Calculated per user rather than per pageview: a person who opened three pieces in one session counts once in the denominator.
377.nuances:
The denominator also includes readers who are already subscribed: they can't sign up again, yet they visit the section more often than others because the newsletter brings them there. Because of this, the conversion rate is understated, and the larger the list, the bigger the gap. They can be excluded **only if the user** is recognized: by login or by a click from a tagged email. Then a second figure is calculated alongside, for new readers, and it answers whether the signup form works.
**The numerator is limited to signups** made on content pages: signups from other parts of the site credited to content inflate the conversion rate.
**Whether to count by button click** or by address confirmation is the company's decision, but the choice is fixed: some people who click never open the email with the link, and the two figures differ noticeably.
A user **is identified by browser**, so one person on a phone and a laptop counts as two users in the denominator.
**A signup is credited to the session** in which it happened, even though the person may have first come to the content much earlier.
377.example:
Content section users in the month: 8,200
Of those, recognized as current subscribers: 2,400
Clicked the signup button: 264
Confirmed their address via email: 189

By click = 264 / 8,200 × 100 = **3.2%**
By confirmation = 189 / 8,200 × 100 = **2.3%**

If you remove those already subscribed from the denominator, the confirmation-based rate is 189 / 5,800 = 3.3%: the same people and the same form, and the difference comes entirely from the calculation base.
377.importance: **It determines** what traffic turns into: one-time reading or an audience you can reach again without paying for each impression. When the conversion rate is low, traffic growth barely adds to the subscriber list, and it makes more sense to invest in the signup form rather than in new traffic.
377.not_needed: **Skip it** when there's no newsletter, or signups are collected on platforms that don't share this data rather than on the site.
377.synonyms: Newsletter Conversion Rate, Subscriber Conversion Rate, Email Opt-In Rate
377.essence_note: a signup turns a casual reader into part of an audience you can come back to

378.name: Content Pieces Published
378.description: The number of pieces published in the period. A piece is counted on its publication date.
378.nuances:
**The unit of count is a finished piece**, regardless of length: a short post and a long read each count as one.
A piece posted on several platforms **counts once**. Counting by placements is also acceptable, but then the number measures distribution rather than output, and it can't be compared with production metrics.
Updated old pieces **aren't included** in the number published; they're counted separately. A piece split into parts and released as a series counts once for each published part.
378.example:
Published in the month:
Articles: 14
Videos: 8
Series of 3 parts: 3 units
Cross-posted to other platforms: 22 placements (not counted)
Old pieces updated: 12 (not counted)

Content Pieces Published = 14 + 8 + 3 = **25**
378.importance: **The base figure for all of content marketing**: costs, reach and views are divided by it, so an error here distorts all derived metrics at once. It's also the first to show a break in the publishing pace, which on algorithm-driven platforms causes reach to drop even for good pieces.
378.essence_note: until a piece is published, it brings in neither traffic nor leads

379.name: Share of Evergreen Content
379.description: The share of pieces whose content doesn't go out of date and won't need rewriting in the future.
379.nuances:
What makes a piece evergreen is its topic rather than its freshness: an explanation of a principle, a breakdown of a concept or a guide to choosing something stays accurate for a long time. A piece tied to prices, service versions, legislation or the product range **isn't considered** evergreen, even if everything in it is accurate today.
**Hence the main difference** from being up to date: an evergreen piece that has become outdated doesn't drop out of the numerator. It lost relevance through an error or oversight rather than because its topic requires regular updates.
The flag **is set once** at publication and stored with the piece: determining it anew at each calculation means getting different numbers depending on the reviewer's mood.
**Deleted and hidden** pieces drop out of both parts of the formula; otherwise the archive fills up with dead pages and the evergreen share falls for no reason.
**The base is chosen to fit the question**. Across the whole archive, you see the makeup of the accumulated library; across the period's releases, you see what the editorial team produces now. The numbers diverge if the mix of topics has changed.
379.example:
Across the whole archive:
Pieces published and available: 340
Of those, evergreen by topic: 224
Tied to prices, versions and the product range: 116
Removed from the site last quarter: 25 (not included)

Share of Evergreen Content = 224 / 340 × 100 = **66%**

Of the evergreen pieces, 18 are currently outdated through oversight: they stay in the numerator because their topic doesn't require updating; the specific text does.
379.importance: It shows what part of the archive works without investment and what part requires constant upkeep simply because of its topic. This share determines how much editorial effort will go into keeping content current rather than creating new pieces: a library of price and version reviews ties up the **entire** team, even when there are no new publications.
379.not_needed: **Skip it for** fast-turnaround content: news items, promo posts and event coverage are by design never evergreen, and the share is always zero.
379.synonyms: Evergreen Content Ratio, % of Evergreen Content
379.essence_note: such a piece brings in traffic for a long time and doesn't need to be redone

380.name: Content ROI
380.formula: ((Gross Profit from Content − Content Costs) / Content Costs) × 100
380.description: How much gross profit the company earns per dollar spent on content, beyond the dollar itself.
380.nuances:
The numerator is **gross profit rather than revenue**: revenue from content minus the cost of the goods sold through it, as in [[Gross Profit→finansy/valovaya_pribyl]]. Based on revenue, the result is overstated by the full cost of goods and doesn't show whether content actually paid off: in retail with a 20% markup, a 50% return calculated on revenue means a loss.
Revenue from content **is determined by the same** attribution model as content-driven sales; otherwise this metric contradicts the one next to it.
The numerator and denominator **cover the same** period, but content keeps bringing in revenue long after publication: as a result, new pieces look unprofitable, and in a quarter where growth came from last year's publications, the ROI is overstated.
380.example:
[[Content Costs→kontent_marketing/zatraty_na_kontent]] for the quarter: $168,600
Revenue from content: $390,000
Gross profit on this revenue at a 35% margin: $136,500

Content ROI = (136,500 − 168,600) / 168,600 × 100 = **−19%**

Based on revenue, it would be (390,000 − 168,600) / 168,600 × 100 = 131%: content looks profitable, even though it didn't pay off for the quarter.
380.importance: **It determines the budget for** the next year: with a positive number, the discussion is about expansion; with a negative one, about cuts. Calculating it on revenue instead of profit is more dangerous than not calculating it at all: the team gets confirmation that everything is fine and increases spending on a channel that loses money.
380.not_needed: **Skip it** when content is produced for brand awareness, hiring or credibility in the market, and no sales are expected from it: there will be no revenue in the numerator, and a negative number will lead to the wrong decision.
380.synonyms: Return on Content, Content Marketing ROI
380.essence_note: the higher the return per dollar invested in content, the more profitable the channel

381.name: Content Pages per Session
381.description: How many pages are opened, on average, in one session in the content section. One person can visit several times a day, and each session counts separately.
381.nuances:
**Define** what goes into the numerator: only content pages or all site pages opened in the session. The second option credits content with clicks to the catalog and cart and inflates pages per session.
**A session ends after inactivity**, in GA4 after 30 minutes by default. A person who comes back to reading in the evening gives two shallow sessions instead of one deep one.
**That's why the denominator is chosen** to fit the question: sessions answer how many pieces a person opens in one session, and users over a chosen window answer how much they read in total, coming back several times. The first is about ease of navigation within a session, the second about whether the person has become a regular reader. The per-user figure is never lower, and the window is stated with it: the numbers for a month and for a week differ.
**Page refreshes and** going back count as new pageviews, so pieces split across several pages mechanically show more pages per session.
381.example:
Sessions in the content section in the month: 9,800
Content pageviews in these sessions: 16,660
Users in the same month: 8,200

Per session = 16,660 / 9,800 = **1.7 pages**
Per user for the month = 16,660 / 8,200 = 2.0 pages

If you count all site pages in these sessions (24,500), the per-session figure comes out at 2.5: the increase comes from the catalog and cart rather than reading.
381.importance: **It shows** whether pieces work together. About one page per session means each piece stands on its own: a person reads what they came for from search and leaves, and internal links and recommendation widgets aren't doing their job.
381.not_needed: **Skip it for** single-page pieces and landing pages, where by design there's nowhere to go.
381.synonyms: Pages per Session, Pages per Visit
381.essence_note: the more pieces people read per session, the more engaged they become

382.name: Visual Content Pieces
382.description: The number of visual pieces released: videos, infographics, illustrations, presentations. Counted on publication.
382.nuances:
**The unit of count is a finished piece** rather than a file: a series of eight slides published as one post counts as one unit.
Illustrations inside a text article **aren't counted** separately; they're part of the article. If an image was made as a standalone piece and published separately, it counts.
A piece posted on several platforms **counts once**: the metric is about production rather than placement.
382.example:
Released in the month:
Videos: 6
Infographics: 4
Carousel of 10 slides: 1
Illustrations inside articles: 23 (not counted)
Video cross-posted on three platforms: counted once

Visual Content Pieces = 6 + 4 + 1 = **11**
382.importance: **It shows** whether design and production capacity keeps up with the editorial team's requests. If the number stays flat while the number of publications grows, visuals have become a bottleneck: text pieces come out with generic stock images, and pieces become less recognizable.
382.not_needed: **Skip it for** text formats without visuals: newsletters, columns, reference pieces where no illustrations are made.
382.synonyms: Visual Assets Produced, Visual Content Output
382.essence_note: visual pieces attract more attention and shares than text

383.name: Likes
383.description: The number of likes on content pieces for the period.
383.nuances:
Removed likes **are subtracted**: platforms report the current count rather than the total number of clicks over time.
Likes are assigned to a period by the piece's publication date: the platform reports the accumulated count for a post rather than the dates of individual clicks. Counting by click date is possible **only with an event-level** export.
On platforms with different kinds of reactions, **you decide** whether to add them into one number or count only the classic like: adding them changes the result noticeably and makes platforms with different sets of buttons incomparable.
383.example:
Likes as of the end of the month: 3,850
Of those, on pieces from earlier periods: 900 (assigned to their own periods)
Other reactions (fire, heart): 620 (not counted in this metric)

Likes = 3,850 − 900 = **2,950**
383.importance: **The cheapest signal of response**: people give it without thinking, so it quickly shows whether a topic landed. You can't rely on it for decisions about money, since a like doesn't commit anyone to anything, but as a first indicator it reacts earlier than other metrics.
383.not_needed: **Skip it on** platforms without reactions and for newsletters.
383.essence_note: this is the simplest sign that a piece resonated with the audience

384.name: Comments
384.description: The number of comments on content pieces for the period.
384.nuances:
Team replies **are counted separately from** audience comments; otherwise active moderation raises the number by itself.
**Deleted spam is subtracted**, and on platforms with open comments, spam makes up a noticeable share.
Replies within threads **count the same as** top-level comments, so one heated discussion can produce more comments than the rest of the month.
Reactions are assigned to a period by the piece's publication date: platform stats show the post and the accumulated reaction count for it, without the dates of individual reactions. Counting by the date of the action itself is possible **only where** event-level data exists: comments in your own database, an API export. That view answers a different question: audience activity in the period regardless of the age of the posts.
**When counting by publication** date, the figure for a recent period is finalized with a delay: pieces keep gathering discussion after the month ends.
384.example:
Pieces published in the month: 25
Comments on them at the time of the snapshot: 405
Of those, replies from the editorial team: 180 (counted separately)
Deleted as spam: 55

Comments = 405 − 180 − 55 = **170**

A month later, the same pieces will show more: the discussion continues, and the March figure is finalized in April.
384.importance: **Comments show** whether a piece struck a nerve or went unnoticed: people like on autopilot, but a comment takes time. Comments are also where objections and questions come from, which later become topics for new pieces and talking points for sales.
384.not_needed: **Skip it where** comments are closed or the platform doesn't support them.
384.essence_note: a comment is the most costly reaction: the person spent time writing it

385.name: Number of Content-Driven Sales
385.description: The number of sales to people who interacted with content, or their total dollar value. A sale is counted on its payment date.
385.nuances:
It's counted as a number of sales or in dollars, and these are different answers: the number shows how many people content led to a purchase, dollars show how much it brought in. The measure must match the one used to calculate **the share of sales** from content, or the percentage won't add up.
The attribution model affects the result more than any other choice: last-click attribution credits **only purchases made directly** from a content page, while counting all touchpoints adds people who read content well before the purchase.
The attribution window **is set separately**. People read content long before they decide, and a 30-day window cuts off some of the purchases.
Returns and canceled orders **are subtracted** if total sales are counted the same way; otherwise the share of content-driven sales comes out inflated.
A sale **is defined by payment** or by a signed contract, the same way as for total sales.
385.example:
Paid orders with a content tag for the quarter: 108 totaling $172,000
Returns and cancellations: 12 orders totaling $19,000 (subtracted)
Purchases by people who read content within 90 days before the order: 118

Last click = 108 − 12 = **96 sales** totaling $153,000
All touchpoints = 214 sales

Both figures are calculated on the same orders: if the share of content-driven sales is calculated in dollars, the numerator is $153,000 rather than 96.
385.importance: It's the only way content can prove in financial terms that it pays off. Without this number, content marketing is discussed in terms of views and likes, and when the budget is cut, that discussion always ends **the same way**.
385.not_needed: **Skip it** when deals close offline without closed-loop analytics: there's no way to link a purchase back to a piece of content, and any number here would be made up.
385.essence_note: these are purchases by people brought in by content rather than by ads

386.name: Content Creators
386.formula: Number of authors with ≥1 published piece
386.description: How many people had at least one piece published in the period.
386.nuances:
The count **is based on actual** publication rather than the number of people on the team: an author who spent the whole period writing a piece that wasn't published isn't counted.
Co-authors **are each counted**, so the sum of authors across all pieces will be greater than the number of pieces. Staff and freelance authors are counted together: the metric is about how many people took part in production, regardless of worker type.
386.example:
Published in the month: 25 pieces
Authors with publications: 5 on staff and 3 freelance
Author who spent the whole month writing a long read without publishing it: 1 (not counted)

Content Creators = 5 + 3 = **8**
386.importance: **It shows** how many people publishing depends on. When all the content is produced by two people, content marketing becomes fragile: if one leaves, the plan is cut in half, and replacing them takes time because a new author needs to be brought up to speed on the product.
386.not_needed: **Skip it** when all content is made by one person: the count is always one.
386.essence_note: too few authors: the channel depends on one person and stops if they leave; too many: each writes little and the cost of coordination grows

387.name: Content Pieces Updated
387.description: The number of previously published pieces that were reworked in the period.
387.nuances:
**An update means a change in content**: new figures, rewritten sections, replacement of outdated facts. Fixing typos, replacing an image and redoing the layout don't count.
**A significance threshold is set**, and the number depends on it directly: without a threshold, any edit to the text gets counted, and the metric stops distinguishing a substantive revision from a cosmetic edit.
An update **is assigned to the date** of the edit rather than the date the piece was first published.
387.example:
Changes to published pieces in the quarter: 96
Of those, typo fixes and image replacements: 58 (not counted)
Reworked sections and updated data: 38

Content Pieces Updated = **38**
387.importance: **Updating an old piece** usually brings more traffic per hour invested than writing a new one from scratch: the page already has search rankings and links. If the number stays at zero, all the team's capacity goes into new publications, and the accumulated archive slowly loses value.
387.not_needed: **Skip it for** time-sensitive, fast-turnaround content: news and promo posts aren't updated.
387.essence_note: an updated piece brings in traffic again without the cost of a new one

388.name: Newsletter Signups
388.description: The number of new newsletter signups for the period.
388.nuances:
Signups **are counted at the same** step as in the signup rate: either everyone who clicked the button or only those who confirmed their address. A mismatch between the two metrics on the map makes them incomparable.
Unsubscribes for the period **aren't subtracted**: the metric is about inflow rather than the size of the list. If you subtract them, it will show zero when unsubscribes match signups, even though there was inflow.
388.example:
Clicked the signup button in the month: 264
Confirmed their address: 189
Unsubscribed in the month: 40 (not subtracted)

Newsletter Signups = **189**
388.importance: A newsletter remains the only channel where access to the audience doesn't depend on someone else's algorithms and isn't paid for per impression. The inflow of subscribers determines whether this asset is growing or shrinking because of unsubscribes, and that becomes visible **only when compared** with churn.
388.synonyms: New Subscribers, Email Sign-Ups, Newsletter Subscriptions
388.essence_note: each subscriber is a person you can reach without paying per impression

389.name: Referral Conversion Rate
389.formula: (Referrals with a First Purchase / Total Referrals) × 100
389.description: The share of referrals who went on to make a first purchase. Shows what share of signups from invitations turn into customers.
389.nuances:
The denominator **matches the count** in Referrals: signups from invitations rather than invitations sent.
A referral **is assigned to the period** by its signup date, and the purchase is attributed to that period even if it happened later. For a recent period, the rate is understated: part of the cohort hasn't bought yet.
A purchase **counts as completed when** payment is received: an order placed and abandoned before payment doesn't count as a conversion.
**[[Fraudulent Referrals→referalnaya_programma/moshennicheskie_referaly]] stay** in the denominator: removing them raises the conversion rate but hides the volume of fraud.
389.example:
Referrals in the quarter: 900
Of those, bought within 90 days: 540
Placed an order without paying: 45 (not counted)

Referral Conversion Rate = 540 / 900 × 100 = **60%**

Removing the 72 fraudulent referrals from the denominator gives 65%: the conversion rate is higher, and the fraud problem disappears from the report.
389.importance: **It separates an acquisition failure** from a product or pricing failure: if invitations are accepted but no purchases follow, people came for the bonus and didn't find anything to buy. This rate is used to decide whether to give the invitee the reward right away or tie it to the first order. It also translates signups into money: without it, a flow of referrals looks like a success even when only one in ten buys.
389.not_needed: **Skip it** when the program's qualifying action is the signup itself: no purchase is expected from the referral, so there's no conversion to measure.
389.synonyms: Referral-to-Customer Conversion Rate, Referral Purchase Rate
389.essence_note: someone who came through an invitation becomes a customer only after their first purchase

390.name: Referrals
390.formula: Number of signups from referral invitations
390.description: The number of people who signed up through a referral invitation.
390.nuances:
**It's counted per person** rather than per invitation: one person may have been sent five links, but there's still one signup.
A referral **is assigned to the period** by its signup date rather than the date the invitation was sent.
A signup with the email or phone number of a current customer **doesn't count** as a referral: it's an existing customer rather than a newly acquired person.
Signups flagged as fraudulent **are included in the count**: subtracting them hides the volume of fraud, and for a clean number there's the separate Fraudulent Referrals count.
390.example:
Signups via referral links in the quarter: 972
Of those, flagged as fraudulent: 72 (included in the count)
Matched the email or phone number of a current customer: 72 (not counted)
Came through five invitations from different people: counted once

Referrals = 972 − 72 = **900**
390.importance: It's the volume the program brings in at the entry point and the denominator for the purchase conversion rate and the fraud rate. Its trend **is the first to change**: a decline shows up in signups before revenue drops. If invitations are counted here instead of people, all the derived percentages on the map will be off.
390.essence_note: every signup from an invitation is a potential customer with no ad spend

391.name: Referral Revenue
391.formula: Sum of revenue from referred customers
391.description: Revenue from customers who came through the referral program.
391.nuances:
Returns **are subtracted from the total** of the period in which the original sale took place.
**You decide** how long a customer's purchases count as referral purchases: only the first purchase or all purchases over a chosen period of the customer's lifetime. Counting only the first purchase understates the figure and doesn't show whether the program pays off; counting over the full lifetime makes it grow with every period and impossible to compare between windows of different length.
**A discount** the invitee received as a reward reduces revenue: a sale with a $10 discount brings in $10 less revenue, so also counting that amount as a program cost means counting it twice.
391.example:
Referred customers acquired in the quarter: 540
Their purchases over the 12 months after acquisition: $89,100
Returns: $2,700

Referral Revenue = 89,100 − 2,700 = **$86,400**

Counting only this cohort's first purchases would give $37,800.
391.importance: **This is the top line** the program exists for: all payouts are compared against it to see whether the channel pulls its weight compared with advertising. Falling revenue with a steady number of referrals means the program has started bringing in low-spending customers who chase the bonus. Without it, the discussion of the program comes down to the number of signups, while the business needs money.
391.essence_note: it's money that came in without ad spend

392.name: Referral Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)
392.formula: Program Costs / Number of Referred Customers
392.description: How much one person acquired through the program costs, counting only people who completed the qualifying action: a first purchase, a subscription signup, an account activation, that is, the outcome the program was launched for.
392.nuances:
The denominator **counts people** who completed the qualifying action rather than signups: signups in the denominator understate acquisition cost, and the fewer referrals complete that action, the larger the gap.
**The reward is usually credited** after the referral's qualifying action, so costs and referred customers in a recent period diverge: the numerator lags behind. A payout should be assigned to the period of the action it was credited for rather than to the date the money was transferred.
Costs **include both sides** of the reward, to the referrer and to the invitee: they're separate line items; counting only one understates acquisition cost, and the more generous the invitee reward, the larger the gap.
Rewards already paid for **[[Fraudulent Referrals→referalnaya_programma/moshennicheskie_referaly]]** stay in the numerator, while the fraudulent referrals themselves don't go into the denominator: their extra cost falls on genuine referred customers.
392.example:
Qualifying action: first purchase
Program costs for the quarter: $32,400
Of those, rewards to referrers: $16,200
Rewards to invitees: $10,800
Platform and moderation: $5,400
Referred customers who made a first purchase: 540

Referral Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) = 32,400 / 540 = **$60**

Dividing by 900 signups gives $36: that's the cost per signup rather than per acquired customer.
392.importance: **This is the number** paid channels are compared against, and it's used to decide whether to raise the reward. As long as a referred customer costs less than one from advertising and behaves no worse, it makes sense to scale the program. A mistake here is costly either way: an understated CAC pushes you to hand out bonuses generously, and an overstated one makes you cut a channel that is actually the cheapest.
392.not_needed: **Skip it** when invitations aren't rewarded with money: people invite others for status, a higher program tier or early access. There are no costs besides the platform, so there's nothing to compare acquisition cost with.
392.synonyms: Referral CAC, Cost per Referred Customer
392.essence_note: the less a referred person costs, the more profitable the program is compared with advertising

393.name: Referral Average Order Value (AOV)
393.formula: Referral Revenue / Number of Orders from Referred Customers
393.description: The average order value of customers acquired through the referral program.
393.nuances:
Both values **cover the same** customer cohort and the same window: revenue over the 12 months after acquisition is divided by orders from the same period.
**Canceled and returned** orders are removed from both the numerator and the denominator: left in the order count, they understate the AOV.
**The discount from a welcome** reward reduces the value of the first order, so a cohort with a large share of newcomers has a lower AOV: comparing periods makes sense when the share of first orders is the same.
393.example:
Revenue from referred customers: $86,400
Paid orders: 1,694
Of those, canceled or returned: 74 (removed from both the numerator and the denominator)

AOV = 86,400 / (1,694 − 74) = 86,400 / 1,620 = **$53.33**

For this cohort's first orders, the AOV is $70 net of the $10 welcome discount: a newcomer's cart is actually worth about $80, and the reward eats up an eighth of it.
393.importance: **It answers the question** of who the program brings in: buyers with normal-sized orders or bonus hunters who order just enough to qualify. An AOV below the average across the whole base means the reward should be tied to the order amount; otherwise people will pick the cheapest items to get the discount. This number turns the reward into a percentage of the order value and shows how large a reward you can afford.
393.not_needed: Skip it when every purchase is the same, at a fixed price: a single-plan subscription, a course with one price. There the AOV equals the price and **doesn't change**.
393.essence_note: the more a referred customer spends, the sooner the reward paid for them is earned back

394.name: Referral Participation Rate
394.description: The share of customers who brought in at least one referral. It counts people rather than invitations.
394.nuances:
A participant **is a customer** whose invitation led to at least one signup, that is, defined the same way as in Referrers. Sending invitations that produced no signups doesn't create participation: otherwise the metric measures intent rather than results.
**The denominator uses** [[Active Customers→crm/aktivnye_klienty]] for the same period as the numerator: the whole base since launch includes people who left long ago, and the rate falls mechanically as the company ages.
A participant is counted **once** regardless of how many referrals they brought in.
394.example:
Customers with a purchase in the quarter: 8,000
Sent at least one invitation: 1,400
Of those, brought in at least one referral: 640

Participation rate = 640 / 8,000 × 100 = **8%**

Calculated against the whole base over five years (40,000), it comes out at 1.6%: a number about the company's age rather than the program.
394.importance: **It shows** where the program's bottleneck is: in reach or in invitations that don't work. Low participation with a healthy invitation acceptance rate means people simply don't know about the program, and the fix is reminders in the post-delivery email and a section in the customer account. Without this rate, it's easy to keep polishing the invitation text when the problem is that only a handful of people ever get to it.
394.not_needed: **Skip it** when an invitation isn't tied to a specific customer: the program runs on one shared public link, nobody knows who exactly brought in a referral, and there's nowhere to get the numerator from.
394.synonyms: Referral Program Participation Rate, Advocate Rate
394.essence_note: the more customers bring in friends, the less you need to pay for advertising

395.name: Referral Churn Rate
395.description: The share of customers acquired through the referral program who stopped using the product.
395.nuances:
**It's calculated for referred customers**, that is, those who completed the qualifying action, rather than for all referrals who signed up: someone who didn't complete the qualifying action never became a customer and can't churn.
A customer **counts as lost** after showing no activity for longer than the typical interval between uses of the product: purchases, visits, renewals. The company sets the threshold itself and keeps it the same in all periods: moving it changes churn more than actual customer behavior does. For the same reason, churn isn't compared between companies.
For subscriptions, churn **is based on unpaid** renewals, and the threshold there is set by the subscription term itself rather than chosen.
**The denominator is a cohort of referred customers** whose observation window has already ended. Customers acquired within the current window simply haven't had time to stay inactive long enough to count as lost, so they understate churn.
395.example:
Referred customers in the cohort: 540
Typical interval between purchases: 60 days
Churn threshold: 120 days without purchases
Haven't bought for more than 120 days: 216

Referral Churn Rate = 216 / 540 × 100 = **40%**

With a 90-day threshold, it would be 58%: the difference lies entirely in the chosen threshold.
395.importance: **It answers** whether the program brings in customers or one-time bonus hunters. If churn among referred customers is noticeably higher than among the rest, the reward should be moved further along the customer journey, or the terms for referrers should change so that they invite people who actually need the product. Until this rate is tracked, the program looks profitable judged by CAC and quietly fills the base with people who won't come back.
395.not_needed: **Skip it where** the purchase is a one-time event by nature: large appliances, furniture, a training course. No repeat purchase is expected, and any rate will be close to 100%.
395.synonyms: Referred Customer Churn Rate, Referral Attrition Rate
395.essence_note: a referral who leaves doesn't earn back the reward paid for them

396.name: Referral Program ROI
396.formula: (Gross Profit from Referral Purchases − Program Costs) / Program Costs × 100
396.description: How much the program returns per dollar invested. Shows the return on spending on rewards and on running the program.
396.nuances:
The numerator uses **gross profit rather than revenue**: [[Referral Revenue→referalnaya_programma/vyruchka_ot_referalov]] minus the cost of goods sold to referrals, as in [[Gross Profit→finansy/valovaya_pribyl]]. Calculated on revenue, ROI is overstated by the full cost of the goods.
Gross profit and costs **cover the same** cohort: if the numerator has purchases by customers acquired in the quarter, the denominator has the costs of acquiring exactly those customers rather than all payouts made during the period.
**The reward comes after** the referral's first purchase, so in a recent period some costs haven't been accrued yet and ROI looks inflated.
**You decide** whether to count gross profit only from the first purchase or over the full [[Customer Lifespan→crm/srok_zhizni_klienta]]: on the first purchase, the program may look unprofitable; over the lifespan, the return is visible, but the result depends on the chosen horizon, and the horizon is kept the same between periods.
396.example:
Revenue from customers acquired in the quarter: $86,400
Cost of goods sold to them: $51,840
Program costs for the same cohort: $32,400

Gross profit = 86,400 − 51,840 = $34,560
ROI = (34,560 − 32,400) / 32,400 × 100 = **7%**

Using revenue, ROI would be (86,400 − 32,400) / 32,400 × 100 = 167%: the cost of goods sold hasn't been subtracted from it.
For these customers' first purchases only, gross profit is $15,120 on revenue of $37,800, and ROI comes out at −53%: the program doesn't pay off on the first purchase.
396.importance: **It answers the question** of whether the program is worth the money and how high the reward can go before the program goes into the red. A negative value with a healthy flow of referrals means gross profit over the chosen horizon doesn't cover the rewards: either the horizon is shorter than the payback period, or rewards are paid for signups rather than purchases. Without this number, the program lives on as a cost that nobody defends and that gets cut first when the budget shrinks.
396.not_needed: **Skip it** when the program is kept as a condition for entering the market on equal terms with competitors: you can't drop it, so its return isn't weighed against its costs.
396.synonyms: Referral ROI, Referral Program Return on Investment
396.essence_note: the higher the return per dollar invested, the more profitable the program

397.name: Referrers
397.formula: Number of unique referrers with at least one referral
397.description: The number of customers who brought in at least one referral. It counts people rather than invitations.
397.nuances:
A referrer **is counted once** regardless of how many referrals they brought in.
**A referrer is someone** whose invitation led to a signup: sending invitations that produced no signups doesn't count.
A referrer **is assigned to the period** by the signup date of the referral they brought in. A person who brought in referrals in two quarters is counted in both, so quarters can't be added up: the annual number is calculated separately, counting each person once.
**Referrals** flagged as fraudulent don't create a referrer: otherwise fraudsters get counted alongside genuine referrers.
397.example:
Customers who sent invitations in the quarter: 1,400
Of those, with at least one signup from an invitation: 655
Of those 655, with all their referrals flagged as fraudulent: 15 (removed)
Brought in 4 or more referrals: each counted once

Referrers = 655 − 15 = **640**
397.importance: **It shows the breadth of the base** the program rests on. When there are few referrers but many referrals, the flow depends on a handful of people, and losing any of them noticeably hurts acquisition. The number goes into the denominator of [[Average Referrals per Referrer→referalnaya_programma/referalov_na_rekomendatelya]], and inflating it with people whose invitations produced no signups blurs the picture of activity.
397.essence_note: the more people bring in friends, the wider the program's reach

398.name: Referral Time to First Purchase
398.formula: Median time from a referral's signup to their first purchase
398.description: How much time typically passes from a referral's signup to their first purchase.
398.nuances:
The calculation includes **only referrals** who have already bought. Those who haven't bought would push the result up indefinitely, and they can be accounted for only by limiting the cohort to a fixed observation window.
**The observation window must** have ended for the whole cohort: if it includes people who signed up last week, the result is understated, because slow buyers haven't had time to buy yet.
**It's calculated as the median** rather than the arithmetic mean: a few referrals who bought six months later raise the mean so that it no longer reflects the typical time to purchase.
398.example:
Cohort: 900 referrals who signed up in January
Observation window: 90 days, ended for everyone
Bought within the window: 540
Bought on the first day: 216
On days 2–14: 194
After day 14: 130

Median time to first purchase = **3 days**
Arithmetic mean = 14 days: it was pulled up by those who bought closer to the end of the window.
398.importance: **It sets how long the welcome** bonus stays valid and when to remind the invitee. If the typical purchase happens on the third day, a promo code valid for a week looks reasonable, while one valid for a day cuts off half the cohort. When the time to first purchase grows, it means the program is bringing in people who don't need the product right now, and the reward stops paying off.
398.not_needed: Skip it when the invitee's reward is available **only at the moment** of the first purchase and the purchase happens right at signup: there's no spread worth measuring.
398.synonyms: Referral Time to Convert, Days to First Referral Purchase
398.essence_note: before a referred person buys, the reward has already been paid out and no money has come in

399.name: Referral Program Costs
399.formula: Sum of rewards paid + platform and program management costs
399.description: How much the company spent on the referral program: rewards to both sides, the platform and the work of the people who run the program.
399.nuances:
The referrer reward and the invitee reward are two separate line items with different mechanics: the first is tied to the referral's purchase, the second to their signup or first order. Counting **only payouts to referrers** understates costs, and the more generous the invitee reward, the larger the gap.
A cost **is assigned to the period** of the purchase the reward was credited for rather than to the date the money was transferred: payouts come with a lag, and assigning costs by transfer date makes a recent period look cheaper than it is.
**Rewards in the form of** bonus points and promo codes become a cost when they're redeemed rather than when they're issued: unredeemed bonuses haven't turned into money.
**The invitee's discount**, which has already reduced revenue, doesn't go into costs a second time.
Platform, anti-fraud and moderation costs **are included in the total**: without them, acquisition cost is understated.
399.example:
Rewards to referrers in the quarter: $16,200
Rewards to invitees: $10,800
Platform and anti-fraud: $3,600
Moderator labor: $1,800
Bonuses issued but not redeemed: $4,800 (not counted)

Referral Program Costs = **$32,400**
399.importance: It goes into both the acquisition cost and the program's return, so undercounting it makes both metrics look good at once. This total is used to decide whether the company can afford the current reward size and whether it's time to move the payout to the referral's second purchase. **It also shows** the size of the program's obligations: bonuses issued but not yet spent will be claimed one day.
399.synonyms: Referral Program Spend, Referral Marketing Costs
399.essence_note: every dollar of rewards is subtracted from what referred customers will bring in

400.name: Referral Invitation Acceptance Rate
400.description: The share of sent invitations for which the invitee met the program's requirement, usually by signing up. It counts invitations: one participant can send many, and each one counts separately.
400.nuances:
The denominator is available **only when** the invitation goes out through the program itself: an invitation form on the website, an email to the recipient, a personal link issued for a specific recipient. The company doesn't see a copied link that the participant sent out on their own, and that link doesn't go into the denominator.
An invitation counts as accepted **based on the** event set by the program terms: a signup, a first order or another qualifying action. The event is chosen once and kept the same between periods: if the acceptance point moves from signup to purchase, the percentage drops even though people's behavior hasn't changed.
Repeat invitations to the same recipient **count as separate sends**, while the acceptance is credited once, to the first invitation: otherwise the numerator is duplicated.
An invitation **is assigned to the period** by its send date, and the acceptance is attributed to that period. For a recent period, the rate is understated: some invitations are accepted later.
400.example:
Invitations sent through the program in the quarter: 2,400
Copied links that participants sent out on their own: not in the denominator
Acceptance means signup
Signed up through these invitations: 900
Of those, repeat invitations to the same person: 60 (acceptance counted once)

Acceptance rate = 900 / 2,400 × 100 = **37.5%**
400.importance: **It guides changes** to the invitation text and to what the invitee sees on the landing page. A low rate with a high volume of sends means participants send links indiscriminately and the offer to the invitee is weak. It's also an early signal: invitations drop off before [[Referral Revenue→referalnaya_programma/vyruchka_ot_referalov]] sags.
400.not_needed: Skip it when there's no way to track that an invitation was sent: the participant copies the link and sends it out on their own, and the company learns about the invitation **only at the moment** of a signup through it. In that case there's no denominator, and the signup itself becomes the first measurable point.
400.synonyms: Invitation Acceptance Rate, Invite Conversion Rate
400.essence_note: the more invitations are accepted, the more customers the same base of referrers brings in

401.name: Average Referrals per Referrer
401.description: How many referrals one referrer brings in on average.
401.nuances:
The numerator and the denominator **cover the same** period and use the same definitions: referrals are signups from invitations, and referrers are people who brought in at least one such signup.
**Customers** who sent invitations but got no signups don't go into the denominator; otherwise the average falls and mixes activity with results.
**The arithmetic mean is strongly** pulled up by a few people with very large numbers of referrals. The median shows the typical referrer; the mean is needed for volume planning.
401.example:
Referrals in the quarter: 900
Referrers: 640

Average Referrals per Referrer = 900 / 640 = **1.4**
Median = 1: the typical person brings in one, and the average is raised by the few who bring in dozens.
401.importance: It shows what drives the program's growth: new participants or repeat invitations from those already engaged. A value around one means people invite one acquaintance and forget about the program, so growth has to come from reach rather than motivation. The forecast of the referral flow is built on this number: without it, acquisition can be planned **only from the actuals** of the previous month.
401.not_needed: **Skip it in** programs with a per-person invitation limit: the average hits the cap and reflects the rule rather than willingness to recommend.
401.synonyms: Referrals per Referrer, Referrals per Advocate
401.essence_note: the more friends one customer brings in, the less each new one costs

402.name: Referred Customers
402.formula: Number of referrals who completed the qualifying action
402.description: The number of people who came through an invitation and completed the program's qualifying action: a first purchase, a subscription signup, an account activation.
402.nuances:
**It's counted per unique** person: several actions by one person count once.
The qualifying action **is set by the program terms** and kept the same between periods: moving it from signup to purchase changes the number more than the flow of referrals itself does.
A person **is assigned to the period** by the date of the qualifying action rather than the signup date: attributing them to the signup date retroactively rewrites closed periods.
**The action counts as completed** once it's confirmed: the order is paid, the subscription is active. An action canceled before fulfillment removes the person from the count.
People whose signup is flagged as fraudulent **are excluded** from the count, even if their action went through.
402.example:
Qualifying action: first purchase
Referrals who paid for their first order in the quarter: 561
Of those, with the order canceled before shipping: 12 (removed)
Signup flagged as fraudulent: 9 (removed)
Placed a second and third order: counted once

Referred Customers = 561 − 12 − 9 = **540**
402.importance: This is the program result that gets compared with paid channels: people who reached the goal rather than signups. The number goes into the denominator of the acquisition cost, so an error in it distorts both CAC and the program's return. When you look **only at signups**, the program seems stronger than it is.
402.essence_note: these are new customers acquired without paying an ad platform

403.name: Referral Fraud Rate
403.description: The share of referrals identified as fraudulent. A fraudulent referral is a signup created for the reward rather than for a purchase, including self-referrals and fake signups with other people's data.
403.nuances:
The numerator and the denominator **count signups** from invitations, the same as the Fraudulent Referrals count.
**Signups are flagged as fraudulent** by automated rules: the same device, the same address, the email or phone number of an existing account, self-referral, exceeding the invitation limit. The signup is still created, gets a flag and goes into the denominator too.
The flag is sometimes removed after the person contacts support: a rule flagged them, but they turned out to be genuine. **Such signups are removed from the numerator**, so the rate for a past period settles slightly lower.
403.example:
Referrals in the quarter: 900
Flagged by automated rules: 78
Flag removed after contacting support: 6 (back among genuine signups)

Fraudulent referrals = 78 − 6 = 72
Rate = 72 / 900 × 100 = **8%**
403.importance: It determines how many rewards are wasted and whether it's time to tighten the rules: an invitation limit per person, device checks, payouts **only after a paid** order. A sharp rise in the rate usually means someone has worked out how to game the program terms and is handing out links en masse. Without this number, the reward budget grows while the number of referred customers doesn't.
403.not_needed: **Skip it** when there's no way to flag fraudulent signups: the program has no rules, signups have no flag, and there's nowhere to get the numerator from.
403.synonyms: Fraudulent Referral Rate, Referral Fraud Percentage
403.essence_note: the company pays rewards for fake signups and gets no customers

404.name: Fraudulent Referrals
404.description: The number of signups from invitations flagged as fraudulent: self-referrals, multiple accounts belonging to the same person, fake signups made to get the reward.
404.nuances:
**It's counted per signup**, rather than per person or per blocked reward: one fraudster can produce many signups.
A signup **is assigned to the period** in which it happened rather than to the date the rule fired: otherwise late flags inflate the current month.
**Flags are set by automated** rules based on a matching device, address, email or phone number. Support can remove a flag when the person contacts them, and then the signup is removed from the count.
404.example:
Signups from invitations in the quarter: 900
Flagged by automated rules: 78
Flag removed after contacting support: 6 (removed)
Flagged this quarter but signed up in the previous one: 9 (go to the previous period)

Fraudulent Referrals = 78 − 6 = **72**
404.importance: **It tallies money** that missed its target: each such signup has either already resulted in a reward payout or would have if the rule hadn't fired. A sharp jump means a workaround has been posted publicly and the rules need to change urgently. Without this count, all the program's other numbers are inflated, and the decision to expand it is based on a referral flow that doesn't exist.
404.not_needed: **Skip it** when there's no way to flag fraudulent signups: the program has no rules, signups have no flag, and there's nothing to count.
404.synonyms: Fake Referrals, Flagged Referrals, Referral Fraud
404.essence_note: these are rewards paid out without a single real customer

405.name: Average Delivery Time
405.formula: Total Delivery Time for All Orders / Number of Deliveries
405.description: How much time passes, on average, from handing an order over for delivery until it arrives at the pickup location or is handed to the customer by a courier.
405.nuances:
The clock **starts at handover** to the carrier: including picking and order processing gives a different metric, the full order-to-delivery time, which is longer by the time the order spends at the warehouse.
**The end point for courier delivery** is handing the order to the customer. For delivery to a pickup point or parcel locker, it's the order's arrival at the location rather than the moment the customer picks it up. How long the order waits there depends on the customer, and including that time takes the metric out of your control: delivery got a day faster, but the number didn't move because customers started picking up later.
**The time an order sits** at a pickup point is measured separately: it's needed to plan shelf space and pickup reminder emails, but it has nothing to do with delivery speed.
The unit is chosen **to match delivery speed**: hours for same-day delivery, days for intercity delivery. What matters is that it's the same in all periods.
The calculation includes **only completed deliveries**: unfinished ones would pull the average down.
The basis for assigning orders to a period is chosen **once** for the whole map: delivery date or order date.
405.example:
Deliveries completed: 5
Time from handover to the carrier to arrival at the pickup point: 2, 3, 3, 4, 8 days

Average = (2 + 3 + 3 + 4 + 8) / 5 = **4 days**

Counting until the customer picked up the order gives 7 days: the number includes the three days the parcel sat on the shelf, and route improvements won't show up in it.
405.importance: **It sets the delivery time** you can show on the product page without risking late deliveries. If the actual average is longer than the promised time, the average delivery is late by definition, and no amount of support work will fix that.
405.synonyms: Average Transit Time, Delivery Lead Time
405.essence_note: the longer an order takes to arrive, the more often it's refused and the less often the customer comes back for the next one

406.name: Average Distance per Delivery
406.formula: Total Delivery Route Mileage (miles) / Number of Deliveries
406.description: How many miles, on average, a courier drives to deliver one order.
406.nuances:
**Actual route mileage is counted** rather than straight-line distance: the street network makes the route longer than a straight line, and fuel is burned on the actual route.
Mileage covers **the entire shift route**, from leaving the warehouse to returning: splitting the recorded mileage into productive and return miles makes no sense, since fuel and vehicle wear are the same throughout the route. Without the return leg, distant zones look as cheap as nearby ones, although it's the way back that makes them expensive.
Undelivered orders **stay in the denominator**: the courier drove to them and put the miles on the vehicle.
406.example:
Routes for the day: 8
Total mileage including the return to the warehouse: 461 miles
Deliveries on these routes: 196

Average distance = 461 / 196 = **2.4 miles per delivery**
406.importance: Multiplied by **the cost per mile**, it gives the transportation component of delivery cost directly. A rise shows that the delivery zone has expanded or route planning has become less efficient: such changes are easy to miss until someone compares the number with the previous quarter.
406.not_needed: **Skip it when** a contractor delivers for a per-shipment fee: there's no route data, and the rate doesn't depend on mileage.
406.synonyms: Average Delivery Distance, Miles per Delivery
406.essence_note: the longer the route, the more each delivery costs

407.name: Vehicle Fill Rate
407.description: How full a vehicle is during transport relative to its maximum capacity.
407.nuances:
Fill **is calculated by the** constraint that's hit first: bulky, light cargo fills the vehicle by volume while weight capacity is still left over; heavy cargo does the opposite. Calculating by the other constraint makes a vehicle that can't take any more look underloaded.
The calculation **is done per** trip, and the average for the period is weighted across trips: a simple average of percentages gives a trip in a small vehicle the same weight as a trip in a large one.
Capacity **is the usable capacity**, which excludes space for securing the load and for aisles.
407.example:
