Trip in a van with a capacity of 560 cubic feet
Loaded: 392 cubic feet at a weight of 1,980 pounds
Payload capacity: 3,300 pounds

By volume = 392 / 560 × 100 = **70%**
By weight it would be 60%, but volume is the constraint that's hit first, so 70% is the number to use.
407.importance: It suggests whether to put a smaller vehicle on a route and whether to combine trips. Hauling air is expensive: a trip at 40% fill costs **the same** as a full one, so the unused space goes straight into the cost of delivering each order.
407.not_needed: **Skip it** when all transport is outsourced and paid per shipment: you pay for each shipment carried, and filling the vehicle is the carrier's concern.
407.synonyms: Truck Fill Rate, Load Factor, Vehicle Utilization
407.essence_note: the fuller the vehicle, the less it costs to deliver each order

408.name: Delivery CSAT
408.formula: (Delivery Ratings of 4 and 5 / Number of Ratings Received) × 100
408.description: The share of positive ratings among all delivery ratings customers left.
408.nuances:
**Divide by** the number of ratings received rather than by all deliveries: not every customer leaves a rating, and dividing by all deliveries lowers the number in proportion to the response rate and turns it into the share of all customers who responded positively.
**Ratings of 4 and 5** on a five-point scale count as positive: this is the industry standard for CSAT.
The rating **comes from a question** about delivery itself: a product rating measures something else and isn't included.
Each delivery counts once: if it's rated again, **the latest rating is used**.
Orders are assigned to the period by their delivery date or by their order date. By delivery date, the number is ready right away, but orders placed at the end of a month arrive in the next one, and a spike in problems gets spread across periods. By order date, you see the service quality for the orders placed in the period, but the period closes **only after** the last order arrives.
408.example:
Deliveries in the month: 940
Customers who rated the delivery: 75
Of those, ratings of 4 and 5: 61

Delivery CSAT = 61 / 75 × 100 = **81%**
Response rate = 75 / 940 × 100 = 8%

Dividing 61 by all 940 gives 6.5%: that's the share of all customers who responded positively rather than satisfaction.
408.importance: **It shows** how the process looks from the customer's side rather than from internal logs: a delivery can arrive on time even if the courier is rude or fails to call ahead. A drop in ratings while delivery times are normal points to problems that don't appear in any carrier report.
408.not_needed: **Skip it** when no delivery survey is sent: without a dedicated question about delivery, there's nowhere to get ratings from, and product reviews don't replace it.
408.synonyms: Delivery Satisfaction Score, Customer Delivery Satisfaction Rate
408.essence_note: delivery leaves the final impression of a purchase, and customers use it to decide whether to come back

409.name: Delivery Damage Rate
409.formula: (Damaged Deliveries / Deliveries That Left the Warehouse) × 100
409.description: The share of deliveries in which the product was damaged.
409.nuances:
**Damage counts regardless** of who found it: the courier in transit, the customer at delivery, or the customer within the claims window. An order returned to the warehouse because of damage goes into the numerator just like a delivered one.
Denominator: all deliveries that left the warehouse rather than **only delivered ones**. Otherwise, orders sent back drop out of the calculation, even though the product is ruined and the money is lost.
**Set a claims window**: without it, damage reports keep coming in long after the period ends, and the number for a closed period keeps growing.
Wrong and missing items **don't count** as damage: they're picking errors rather than transport errors.
A delivery with several broken items **counts as one** damaged delivery.
The basis for assigning orders to a period is chosen **once** for the whole map: delivery date or order date.
409.example:
Deliveries that left the warehouse in the month: 1,060
Courier found damage in transit, order returned to the warehouse: 7
Damage recorded at delivery: 17
Customer claims within 14 days: 12
Wrong item: 6 (not counted)

Damage rate = (7 + 17 + 12) / 1,060 × 100 = **3.4%**

Dividing only by the 922 delivered orders and leaving out damage found in transit gives 3.1%: the most serious cases drop out of the metric.
409.importance: **It answers** whether to change the packaging and whether to file a claim with the carrier. A rise is a reason to check whether the transfer process or the packaging has changed. Every damaged delivery means a return, a reshipment and time spent dealing with the customer, so it costs more than the product itself.
409.not_needed: **Skip it for** a product range that isn't fragile or bulky, such as clothing or consumables: damage is rare there, and the number gives no signal.
409.synonyms: Transit Damage Rate, Shipping Damage Rate, Damaged Shipment Rate
409.essence_note: damaged products come back, and the company pays for both the delivery and the replacement

410.name: Delivery Success Rate
410.description: The share of deliveries completed without a failure: the order was delivered on time, intact and with the product that was ordered. Undelivered and lost orders also count as failed.
410.nuances:
Completed deliveries: delivered orders plus orders closed as undelivered (refused, unclaimed or lost). [[Orders in Transit→dostavka_zakazov/zakazy_v_puti]] **aren't counted**: they can still arrive on time.
A delivery **counts as failed based on a fixed** list of events: not delivered, delivered late, product damaged, lost, wrong product delivered. Without a fixed list, the metric can't be calculated at all, because a “problem” isn't stored anywhere as a field.
A delivery with two failures **counts as one** failed delivery.
Orders are assigned to the period by their delivery date or by their order date. By delivery date, the number is ready right away, but orders placed at the end of a month arrive in the next one, and a spike in problems gets spread across periods. By order date, you see the service quality for the orders placed in the period, but the period closes **only after** the last order arrives.
410.example:
Deliveries completed in the month: 940
Not delivered: 18
Delivered late: 76
Damaged: 12
Wrong item: 5
Overlaps (late + damaged): 4

Failed = 18 + 76 + 12 + 5 − 4 = 107
Success rate = (940 − 107) / 940 × 100 = **89%**
410.importance: It combines all types of failures **into one number** that the head of logistics reports on and is measured against. Separate metrics for late and damaged deliveries can each look tolerable, while together they add up to a problem in one delivery out of ten: without a combined metric, you don't see it.
410.not_needed: **Skip it** until failure reasons are tagged in the system: without tags, the number has to be compiled by hand, and it goes out of date before it's ready.
410.synonyms: Successful Delivery Rate, Perfect Delivery Rate
410.essence_note: a successful delivery is an order that arrived intact and on time

411.name: Delivery Density
411.description: How many deliveries there are per square mile of territory.
411.nuances:
The denominator **is the area of the service zone** rather than only the part where deliveries took place: measured only over the area with deliveries, density always comes out high and becomes useless for comparison.
**The length of the period** sets the scale of the number directly: deliveries per day and per month differ by a factor of about thirty, so the window is always stated with the number.
411.example:
Service zone: 93 square miles
Deliveries in the week: 1,320

Density = 1,320 / 93 = **14.2 deliveries per square mile per week**
411.importance: It determines **whether deliveries fit** into compact routes or the courier spends a long time driving between stops. At low density, in-house delivery doesn't pay off: the metric is used to decide whether to raise the free shipping threshold or stop using in-house couriers.
411.not_needed: Skip it when a contractor or a marketplace handles **all** delivery: you don't plan routes and have no way to influence density.
411.synonyms: Stops per Square Mile, Drop Density, Stop Density
411.essence_note: the closer the addresses are to each other, the more orders one courier delivers per shift

412.name: First-Attempt Delivery Success Rate
412.description: The share of courier deliveries handed to the customer on the first trip.
412.nuances:
The metric covers courier delivery only: pickup points and parcel lockers involve no trip to the customer, and they **aren't included**.
An attempt **is counted each time an order** is given to a courier for delivery. If the customer didn't answer the phone, didn't open the door or asked to reschedule, the attempt still counts, and the order goes out for redelivery.
**The denominator includes** all courier deliveries with a final outcome, including orders never delivered: they had attempts that cost money, and excluding them inflates the percentage.
412.example:
Courier deliveries completed: 600
Delivered on the first trip: 486
Delivered on the second or a later trip: 99
Not delivered at all: 15

First-attempt rate = 486 / 600 × 100 = **81%**
412.importance: **Every repeat attempt** means another paid trip, so the metric is used to decide whether to require customers to confirm the delivery time the day before and whether couriers should call ahead. A low value eats directly into margin: two trips instead of one double the last-mile cost.
412.not_needed: **Skip it** when all deliveries go to parcel lockers and pickup points with no courier leg: there's no trip that could be wasted.
412.synonyms: First-Attempt Delivery Rate, First-Time Delivery Rate
412.essence_note: the company pays for every repeat courier trip

413.name: On-Time Delivery Rate
413.description: The share of deliveries that reached the customer no later than the date promised at checkout.
413.nuances:
Completed deliveries: delivered orders plus orders closed as undelivered (refused, unclaimed or lost). [[Orders in Transit→dostavka_zakazov/zakazy_v_puti]] **aren't counted**: they can still arrive on time.
**The date used is** the one the customer saw at checkout.
**Rescheduling at the request** of the customer moves the promised date. Rescheduling initiated by the company doesn't: the original date stays.
Orders are assigned to the period by their delivery date or by their order date. By delivery date, the number is ready right away, but orders placed at the end of a month arrive in the next one, and a spike in problems gets spread across periods. By order date, you see the service quality for the orders placed in the period, but the period closes **only after** the last order arrives.
413.example:
Deliveries completed in the month: 940
Of those, delivered no later than the promised date: 846
Still in transit at the end of the month: 120

On-time rate = 846 / 940 × 100 = **90%**

Adding the 120 orders in transit to the denominator gives 80%: orders that couldn't be late yet are counted as late.
413.importance: **It sets the delivery time** you can show on the website and answers whether to promise an exact date instead of a range. Comparing with other companies' numbers is pointless: the metric depends on what delivery dates you chose to promise. Watch for dips: they're followed by more tickets about delivery times and by refusals at the door when the customer no longer needs the product.
413.not_needed: Skip it for **customer pickup** from your own location: the customer comes whenever it's convenient, and there's no delivery date. It's also useless for digital goods delivered instantly.
413.essence_note: the customer was given a date and notices a delay right away

414.name: Orders Delivered on Time
414.formula: Number of orders delivered no later than the promised date
414.description: The number of orders delivered to the customer no later than the promised date during the period.
414.nuances:
The date given to the customer at checkout **counts as the promised date**; if the customer asks to reschedule, the new date is used.
An order shipped in several parcels **counts as delivered on time** only if all its parts arrived on time.
The basis for assigning orders to a period is chosen **once** for the whole map: delivery date or order date.
414.example:
Orders delivered in the month: 940
Of those, no later than the promised date: 846

Orders delivered on time = **846**

The 90% figure is a different metric: the On-Time Delivery Rate.
414.importance: The absolute number is needed when the discussion is about volume: 90% looks **the same** with ten late orders and with a thousand, while the compensation budget and the support workload depend on the count. It's also what you reconcile with the carrier when reviewing the SLA.
414.not_needed: **Skip it where** customers aren't given a delivery date: there's nothing to compare the delivery against.
414.essence_note: these are orders where the promise to the customer was kept

415.name: Orders in Transit
415.formula: Total number of orders in transit
415.description: The number of orders in transit at the time of measurement.
415.nuances:
It's **a snapshot at the time of measurement**: adding it up across days counts the same orders many times.
**An order is included** from the moment the carrier accepts it: a picked order that hasn't been handed over is still at the warehouse.
An order that has reached a pickup point moves out of “in transit”: in the standard industry status scheme, it becomes “ready for pickup.” Such orders are counted **separately**: they're no longer moving but haven't been handed to the customer yet.
415.example:
Snapshot on Monday morning:
Handed over to the carrier and moving: 145 orders
Picked but still at the warehouse: 40 (not counted)
Waiting at pickup points for customers: 62 (not counted)

Orders in Transit = **145**

Adding up the snapshots for every day of the week gives about 1,000: the same order is counted as many times as the number of days it was in transit. To compare periods, take the daily average rather than the sum.
415.importance: Orders in transit show **how much money is tied up** in products that have already left but haven't been accepted by the customer yet. A sharp rise while shipments stay the same means a bottleneck on the carrier's side: orders go out, but there are no deliveries, and support then starts getting questions about delivery times.
415.not_needed: Skip it for **same-day delivery**: an order doesn't spend measurable time in transit, and the count is always close to zero.
415.synonyms: In-Transit Orders, Shipments in Transit, Open Shipments
415.essence_note: a count of zero means there's nothing to deliver, while a count that rises with no change in shipments means a bottleneck at the carrier

416.name: Shipping Cost per Order
416.formula: Total Shipping Cost / Number of Orders with Shipping
416.description: How much delivering one order costs the company on average, including all its shipments.
416.nuances:
Denominator: orders rather than shipments. An order shipped in two boxes means paying for two shipments, and both **belong to one** order: dividing by shipments understates the cost of an order by the same factor as the average number of shipments per order.
The cost per shipment is calculated **separately**: it's needed to reconcile with the carrier's invoice, which is priced per shipment rather than per order.
**The denominator includes** all orders with shipping costs incurred, including undelivered ones: the carrier was paid for a refused order all the same.
Costs and orders **cover the same** period; otherwise, the metric jumps because of shipments paid for in the following month.
Customer pickup **isn't in the denominator**: such orders have no shipping costs.
416.example:
[[Total Shipping Cost→dostavka_zakazov/rashody_na_dostavku]] for the month: $16,880
Orders with shipping: 1,060
Shipments (some orders were shipped in two parcels): 1,210

Shipping cost per order = 16,880 / 1,060 = **$15.92**

Dividing by shipments would give 16,880 / 1,210 = $13.95. That's the cost per shipment, and it's too low for setting the free shipping threshold: the customer sees one cart, while the company ships it in two boxes and pays for both.
416.importance: **The number from which** the free shipping threshold and order margin are calculated: the decision is made per order, because the customer builds one cart and sees one total. If the threshold is based on the cost per shipment, free shipping will cost more than planned by exactly what the second and third boxes cost.
416.not_needed: **Skip it** when the customer pays the carrier for delivery directly: the cost doesn't pass through the company.
416.synonyms: Average Shipping Cost per Order, Delivery Cost per Order
416.essence_note: every dollar spent on delivery comes out of the order's profit

417.name: Total Shipping Cost
417.formula: Σ (Carrier Payments + In-House Courier Payroll + Fuel and Upkeep of Company Vehicles + Shipping Packaging + Cargo Insurance)
417.description: The total of all costs of delivering orders to customers during the period.
417.nuances:
In-house delivery is counted at full cost: **courier wages alone**, without fuel, depreciation and vehicle maintenance, understate costs so much that comparing them with a carrier's rate becomes meaningless.
Reverse logistics for returns and refusals **isn't included** here: those are return costs, and they're counted separately.
Warehouse handling costs before handover for delivery **belong to the warehouse** rather than to delivery.
417.example:
Carrier payments: $9,800
In-house courier payroll: $4,600
Fuel and vehicle upkeep: $1,450
Shipping packaging: $790
Cargo insurance: $240
Reverse logistics for returns: $2,000 (not counted)

Total Shipping Cost = **$16,880**
417.importance: The basis for choosing between in-house couriers and a contractor, and for calculating the free shipping threshold. As long as **only carrier payments** show up in the costs, in-house delivery looks cheap: its full cost can turn out higher than the market rate, and that becomes clear only after the vehicles are bought.
417.not_needed: **Skip it** when the customer pays the carrier for delivery directly: the money doesn't pass through the company and doesn't show up in costs.
417.synonyms: Delivery Costs, Shipping Expenses, Outbound Logistics Costs
417.essence_note: this is the full cost of getting orders to customers, and it comes out of profit

418.name: Orders Delivered
418.description: The number of orders delivered to customers during the period.
418.nuances:
The delivery date used **is the actual one** rather than the date the order was closed in the accounting system: closing can happen in batches at the end of the week and moves orders into another period.
A return after delivery doesn't reduce the count: the delivery took place, and the return **is counted separately**.
An order split into several shipments **counts as delivered** when the last one is delivered.
The basis for assigning orders to a period is chosen **once** for the whole map: delivery date or order date.
418.example:
Delivered to customers in March: 940 orders
Of those, 60 delivered March 30–31 and closed in the system on April 2
Of the March deliveries, customers returned 45 in April

Orders Delivered in March = **940**

By system closing date, the count would be 880: deliveries from the last days moved to April. Returns don't reduce the count: the delivery took place.
418.importance: The workload used to plan couriers and vehicles for the next period. If it **doesn't match the number** of shipments you paid the carrier for, some orders got lost somewhere or were paid for twice.
418.essence_note: the money for an order stays with the company for good only after delivery

419.name: Orders Dispatched for Last-Mile Delivery
419.formula: Total number of orders handed over for delivery
419.description: The number of orders handed over to a carrier or to your own couriers for last-mile delivery during the period.
419.nuances:
The handover time **is when the carrier records acceptance** of the order: a picked and packed order waiting for the truck isn't included yet.
**It's counted cumulatively over** the period, unlike the number of orders in transit at the time of measurement.
An order split into several shipments **is counted once**, when the last part is handed over, just as it counts as delivered when the last part is delivered. Counting by the first shipment puts one order into different periods in the counts of orders handed over and orders delivered.
419.example:
Handed over to carriers in March: 1,060 orders
Picked and packed, to be picked up by the truck on April 1: 85 (not counted)
Order shipped in two parcels, with the second box leaving on April 2: 1 (counted in April)

Orders Dispatched for Last-Mile Delivery = **1,060**
419.importance: **It shows** how many orders the warehouse actually released for delivery. A gap between this count and the number of picked orders means orders get stuck between picking and handover: at that point, the customer already sees that the order has been picked and thinks the product is on its way.
419.not_needed: Skip it for **customer pickup and digital goods**: there's no last-mile stage.
419.synonyms: Orders Dispatched, Orders Handed Over to Carriers
419.essence_note: the more orders go out, the more of them will be delivered and paid for

420.name: Refused or Unclaimed Orders
420.formula: Total number of refused or unclaimed orders
420.description: The number of orders the customer didn't accept: refused at delivery or never picked up from the pickup point.
420.nuances:
Both situations **are counted together**: a refusal at the door and an order left unclaimed after the hold period ends. In both cases, the product goes back, and the money is lost the same way.
Refusing part of an order **doesn't count** as refusing the whole order: it goes into partial returns; otherwise the metric is inflated by orders that were mostly kept.
**It's counted in orders** rather than in units.
An order not delivered **because of a logistics failure** (lost, or canceled after a missed deadline) doesn't count as a refusal: the customer didn't refuse it.
The basis for assigning orders to a period is chosen **once** for the whole map: delivery date or order date.
420.example:
Refused when the courier arrived: 6
Not picked up from the pickup point before the hold period ended: 9
Refused some items and took the rest: 12 (not counted)

Refused or Unclaimed Orders = 6 + 9 = **15**
420.importance: **Every refusal costs** shipping both ways and ties up the product until it's back at the warehouse. The trend is used to decide whether to introduce prepayment or partial prepayment.
420.not_needed: **Skip it for** digital goods and services with no physical delivery: there's nothing to refuse.
420.synonyms: Delivery Refusals, Refused Packages, Unclaimed Packages
420.essence_note: for such an order, the company pays for shipping both ways and gets no money

421.name: Late Deliveries
421.formula: Number of delivered orders with a delivery date later than the promised date
421.description: The number of orders delivered to the customer after the promised date.
421.nuances:
**It's counted directly** as late deliveries rather than by subtracting on-time deliveries from the total: subtraction puts orders still in transit, lost orders and refused orders, which weren't late, into the late count.
Orders are assigned to the period by their delivery date or by their order date. By delivery date, the number is ready right away, but orders placed at the end of a month arrive in the next one, and a spike in problems gets spread across periods. By order date, you see the service quality for the orders placed in the period, but the period closes **only after** the last order arrives.
**If you count by delivery date**, a late order is assigned to the period by its actual delivery date rather than by the date the promised deadline passed.
Rescheduling at the customer's request **doesn't count** as a late delivery.
421.example:
Deliveries completed in the month: 940
Of those, delivered after the promised date: 76

Late Deliveries = **76**

The subtraction trap: 1,060 orders handed over for delivery in total, 846 delivered on time, a difference of 214. Only 76 of them were late; the rest are 120 orders still in transit and 18 undelivered orders that weren't late.
421.importance: **The absolute number of late deliveries**: it's the support workload and the amount of compensation you'll have to pay. It's used to calculate the damage from a carrier's failure and to file a claim: a percentage doesn't work in negotiations, while “you were late on 76 orders in March” does.
421.not_needed: **Skip it where** no date is promised to the customer: for preorders with no fixed delivery date, there's no promise to break.
421.essence_note: every late delivery is an unhappy customer and a likely refusal

422.name: Average Delivery Delay
422.formula: Total Delay Time / Number of Late Deliveries
422.description: The average delay for deliveries that arrived after the promised date.
422.nuances:
The denominator includes **only [[Late Deliveries→dostavka_zakazov/prosrochennye_dostavki]]**: adding on-time deliveries with zero delay turns the metric into the average delay across all orders and understates it, and the smaller the share of late deliveries, the bigger the gap.
The delay **is measured from the originally** promised date: a renegotiated date wipes out a delay the customer has already experienced.
The unit is **the same for the whole calculation**: mixing hours and days in one sum gives a meaningless average.
The basis for assigning orders to a period is chosen **once** for the whole map: delivery date or order date.
422.example:
Late deliveries in the month: 76
Total delay: 137 days

Average delay = 137 / 76 = **1.8 days**

One parcel that was lost, then found and delivered 21 days late adds a quarter of a day to the average: the median for the same month is 1 day.
422.importance: **It answers the question** of how long the delays behind the percentage are: a customer will barely notice a short delay, while a long one leads to a refusal and a refund. It's used to set the delay at which compensation kicks in automatically.
422.not_needed: **Skip it** when there are only a handful of late deliveries: an average of three cases jumps from month to month, and no decisions are based on it.
422.synonyms: Average Days Late, Average Delay Time
422.essence_note: the longer the delay, the higher the chance the customer refuses the order

423.name: Late Delivery Rate
423.description: The share of deliveries handed to the customer after the promised date.
423.nuances:
Completed deliveries: delivered orders plus orders closed as undelivered (refused, unclaimed or lost). [[Orders in Transit→dostavka_zakazov/zakazy_v_puti]] **aren't counted**: they can still arrive on time.
A delivery **counts as late when it's made after** the promised date: if the customer was given a range, it's measured from the end of the range.
The numerator includes **only delivered orders**: undelivered orders never arrived, so they can't be late.
Rescheduling at the customer's request **doesn't count** as a late delivery.
The basis for assigning orders to a period is chosen **once** for the whole map: delivery date or order date.
423.example:
Deliveries completed in the month: 940
Of those, delivered late: 76

Late rate = 76 / 940 × 100 = **8.1%**
423.importance: **It answers whether** to build a buffer of a day or two into the promised date. A late delivery costs more than it seems: on top of the compensation, the customer stops trusting the promised date and next time builds in a buffer of their own.
423.not_needed: **Skip it where** no delivery date is given to the customer at all: for example, preorders for products with no fixed arrival date.
423.synonyms: Late Order Rate, Delayed Delivery Rate
423.essence_note: a late delivery is a broken promise, followed by tickets and refusals

424.name: Average Delivery Attempts
424.formula: Total Number of Delivery Attempts / Total Number of Deliveries
424.description: How many courier trips, on average, it takes for an order to reach the customer.
424.nuances:
An attempt **is counted each time an order** is given to a courier for delivery. An unanswered call, a closed door and rescheduling at the customer's request count as an attempt just like a completed trip: the courier has already gone out with the parcel.
The denominator includes **all deliveries with a final outcome**, including orders never delivered: they had attempts that cost money, and excluding them understates the average.
**Orders** still in progress aren't counted: they may still need more attempts.
424.example:
Completed courier deliveries: 600
Of those, delivered: 585, not delivered: 15
Total courier trips: 738

Average attempts = 738 / 600 = **1.23**

Removing the 15 undelivered orders from the denominator gives 738 / 585 = 1.26: the trips for these orders stayed in the numerator, even though the orders themselves dropped out of the calculation.
424.importance: **A direct multiplier** of last-mile cost: at 1.4 attempts per order, you pay for 40% more trips than orders. It's used to decide how much to pay a courier service per shipment and whether to introduce fixed delivery slots.
424.not_needed: Skip it for **delivery to pickup points** and parcel lockers: there's no trip to an address, and the number of attempts always equals one.
424.synonyms: Delivery Attempts per Order, Attempts per Delivery
424.essence_note: the company pays for every extra courier trip

425.name: Losses from Refused or Unclaimed Orders
425.formula: Σ (Outbound Shipping Cost + Return Shipping Cost + Return Storage and Handling + Value Lost on Marked-Down Products)
425.description: The money lost on orders the customer refused or never picked up.
425.nuances:
The cost of the product **isn't included** in losses if it came back to the warehouse in sellable condition: it remains an asset rather than a loss.
If the product **can no longer be sold as new** or is perishable, the losses include the difference between its cost and the marked-down sale price.
Lost revenue **isn't counted**: it's forgone profit rather than costs incurred, and mixing the two inflates the losses.
The basis for assigning orders to a period is chosen **once** for the whole map: delivery date or order date.
425.example:
Refused or unclaimed orders in the month: 15
Outbound shipping: 15 × $11.20 = $168
Return to the warehouse: 15 × $8.60 = $129
Receiving and storing the returns: $45
Marked down because they could no longer be sold as new: 2 orders, a loss of $96

Losses = 168 + 129 + 45 + 96 = **$438**

The cost of the other 13 orders isn't included in losses: the products are back on sale.
425.importance: It converts refused and unclaimed orders from a count into dollars, and this is the number that settles the debate about switching to prepayment. As long as **only the refusal rate** is tracked, the issue looks like a low priority: with expensive shipping, a low refusal rate can cost more than the entire discount program for a quarter.
425.not_needed: **Skip it for** digital goods and services: there's no reverse logistics, and a refusal costs nothing except the cost of the refund itself.
425.essence_note: this is money lost directly on orders nobody accepted or picked up

426.name: On-Time Shipment Rate
426.description: The share of shipments handed over to the carrier on schedule.
426.nuances:
Shipment time **is the handover to the carrier**, when the carrier records acceptance, rather than the truck physically leaving the warehouse: there can be idle time between the two, and using the truck's departure time gives a higher percentage.
The planned time **comes from the shipping schedule** rather than from the date promised to the customer: the customer's date also includes transit time, and measured against it, a shipment looks on time even when the schedule was missed.
The denominator includes **all shipments in the period**, including late ones.
426.example:
Shipments in the week: 310
Handed over to the carrier within the scheduled window: 291
Handed over after the window: 19

On-Time Shipment Rate = 291 / 310 × 100 = **94%**
426.importance: **It shows** whether the warehouse or the carrier missed the deadline: if the shipment left on time and the delivery was late, the issue is with the carrier rather than the warehouse. Without it, the warehouse and logistics keep shifting blame onto each other, and each side is half right.
426.not_needed: **Skip it for** same-day delivery by your own couriers: there's no handover to a carrier, and the whole delivery time comes down to one stage.
426.synonyms: On-Time Shipping Rate, On-Time Dispatch Rate
426.essence_note: a late shipment pushes back the whole delivery and the date promised to the customer

427.name: Days Sales of Inventory (DSI)
427.description: How many days, on average, it takes to sell the current inventory.
427.nuances:
The number of days in the numerator **matches the window** over which turnover was calculated: 365 for annual turnover, 90 for quarterly, 30 for monthly.
Dividing 365 by monthly turnover overstates the time twelvefold. The calculation inherits all of turnover's assumptions, including the choice of measure: in dollars, it's based on the cost of goods sold and average inventory value; in units, on units sold and average inventory in units. In both cases, average inventory **is calculated from several** snapshots within the period.
**The costing method** changes the result through turnover.
427.example:
Cost of goods sold for the year: $3,150,000
[[Average Inventory Value→upravlenie_zapasami/srednyaya_stoimost_zapasov]]: $1,050,000
Turnover = 3,150,000 / 1,050,000 = 3 times a year

DSI = 365 / 3 = **122 days**

If you take monthly turnover (0.25) and divide 365 by it, you get 1,460 days: the numerator doesn't match the turnover window.
427.importance: **It turns abstract turnover into** days you can compare with the supplier's payment terms. When the time to sell is longer than the payment terms, the company finances the difference with its own money, and a cash shortfall arises from the size of the inventory rather than from weak sales.
427.not_needed: **Skip it when** you order goods only after a customer buys them and have no warehouse of your own: there's no inventory to sell through.
427.synonyms: Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO), Days in Inventory, Inventory Days
427.essence_note: the longer inventory takes to sell, the longer money sits in goods instead of circulating

428.name: Average Inventory Value
428.formula: Σ Inventory Value at Each Snapshot Date / Number of Snapshots
428.description: The average monetary value of inventory over the period.
428.nuances:
The number of snapshots determines the result: an average of two points works **only with steady** inventory movement; with seasonality or large batches it drifts away from a calculation based on monthly snapshots, and the stronger the seasonality and the larger the batches, the wider the gap. Snapshots are taken at equal intervals: with monthly deliveries, snapshots on the 1st and 15th fall into different phases of the delivery cycle and skew the average.
Valuation is at cost, with the same costing method as in the rest of the accounts. Goods in transit **are included in a snapshot** only if they're included in the inventory value on those dates; otherwise the average won't reconcile with the balance sheet.
428.example:
Inventory on January 1: $920,000
Inventory on December 31: $1,180,000
Average of two points = (920,000 + 1,180,000) / 2 = $1,050,000

Sum of values from 12 monthly snapshots: $12,600,000
Average of 12 snapshots = 12,600,000 / 12 = **$1,050,000**

The match here is a coincidence: with a December stock-up for the holidays, the two-point estimate would give $1.2 million instead of $1.05 million, and turnover would fall from 3 to 2.6.
428.importance: **It's the denominator of turnover**, time to sell and GMROI: an error in it spreads across three calculations at once. Companies that use the December 31 balance often catch it at its low point after the holiday sales and live with overstated turnover all year.
428.not_needed: **Skip it when** you order goods only after a customer buys them and have no warehouse of your own: inventory value is zero on any snapshot date.
428.essence_note: too little money in goods means shortages; too much means working capital is sitting in the warehouse

429.name: Average Supplier Lead Time
429.formula: Σ Lead Times / Number of Deliveries
429.description: The average time from placing an order with a supplier to the goods arriving at the warehouse.
429.nuances:
**It's counted in calendar** days, not business days: an order placed on a Friday still has to wait out the weekend.
**The starting point** is the date the order was placed, not the date the supplier confirmed it: with some suppliers, time passes between the two, and that time drops out of the calculation.
**The end point** is when the goods are ready for sale after receiving, not when the truck pulls into the yard.
The average hides variation: a few fast deliveries and one long one give a decent average, and an order timed by it will arrive late exactly when the supplier is delayed again. **The maximum lead time is also calculated**, and it goes into the safety stock calculation.
Canceled and open orders **aren't included**: their lead times haven't ended and would inflate the average.
429.example:
Deliveries in the quarter: 12
Lead times in calendar days: 14, 18, 21, 16, 19, 45, 17, 20, 22, 15, 23, 22
Sum of lead times: 252 days

Average lead time = 252 / 12 = **21 days**
Maximum lead time = 45 days; this is the value that goes into the safety stock calculation.
429.importance: **It determines** how many days before stock hits zero you need to place an order. When the lead time grows but the reorder point isn't raised, the company starts running into shortages regularly, and the cause looks like poor planning, even though it's the supplier that changed.
429.not_needed: **Skip it when** you buy off the shelf from a local wholesaler on the same day: there's no lead time to measure.
429.synonyms: Supplier Lead Time, Vendor Lead Time, Procurement Lead Time
429.essence_note: the longer goods take to arrive, the more stock you need to hold to cover that time

430.name: Dead Stock Rate
430.formula: Dead Stock Units / Total Units in Stock × 100
430.description: The share of dead stock units in total inventory.
430.nuances:
The numerator and denominator **are measured in units** of goods as of the same snapshot date.
The dead stock threshold **is set as a number**: no sales for N days in a row, or enough stock for more than N days at current demand. Moving the threshold from 90 to 180 days noticeably lowers the result, and the slower the assortment turns over, the bigger the drop.
**Seasonal goods in** the off-season formally cross the threshold, so for them the day counter is either stopped out of season, or the share grows every summer with no real problem behind it.
Goods in transit **aren't included** in the denominator: they aren't in storage yet and can't sit idle.
**Calculating the share in** dollars instead of units is possible, but it's a different figure: cheap slow-moving goods give a large percentage in units and barely register in dollars.
430.example:
Total in the warehouse: 42,000 units
No sales for over 180 days: 3,360 units
Goods in transit: 2,500 (not included)

Dead Stock Rate = 3,360 / 42,000 × 100 = **8%**
430.importance: **It shows** how much space and money are tied up in goods that don't move, and when it's time to start a clearance sale. A growing share means purchasing keeps bringing in goods that don't sell, and eventually the warehouse hits its capacity while the rest of the assortment is still selling.
430.not_needed: **Skip it for** perishable goods that turn over in a few days: there, goods don't have time to sit; they're written off when they expire.
430.synonyms: Dead Stock Percentage, Obsolete Inventory Rate
430.essence_note: dead stock takes up space and ties up money, and it can no longer be sold at the regular price

431.name: Demand Forecast Accuracy
431.description: How closely the demand forecast matched actual sales. Accuracy shows the size of the miss, and bias shows its direction: whether more or less was ordered than needed.
431.nuances:
The error **is taken as an absolute value**: without it, underforecasting and overforecasting cancel each other out, and overall accuracy looks perfect with misses in both directions. But the absolute value removes the sign, and misses in different directions have different costs: overforecasting means cash tied up in inventory and a risk of dead stock; underforecasting means an empty shelf and lost sales. That's why bias is calculated alongside accuracy, with the same formula without the absolute value: a positive value means the forecast is too high, and a negative value means it is too low.
**Bias is averaged across** items with its sign and shows the model's systematic error: consistently positive bias means purchasing keeps bringing in too much, while consistently negative bias means it regularly underorders.
**The result can go** negative when the error exceeds the actual value: a forecast of 300 against an actual of 100 gives −100%.
Clipping negative values to zero hides the worst misses. The evaluation is done for each item **separately** and then averaged: calculating on the total cancels out misses in opposite directions across items and inflates accuracy.
The actual **is based on demand**, not sales: days when the item was out of stock understate the actual and make the forecast look like an overforecast.
The forecast **is locked before the start** of the period and compared in the same unit of measure as the actual: a forecast in dollars can't be compared with an actual in units.
431.example:
Item A: forecast 2,000 units, actual 1,750
Deviation = |2,000 − 1,750| = 250
Accuracy = (1 − 250 / 1,750) × 100 = **85.7%**
Bias = (2,000 − 1,750) / 1,750 × 100 = **+14.3%**, the forecast is too high

Item B: forecast 1,000 units, actual 1,250
Accuracy = (1 − 250 / 1,250) × 100 = **80%**
Bias = (1,000 − 1,250) / 1,250 × 100 = **−20%**, the forecast is too low

Adding up both items (3,000 against 3,000) would give 100% accuracy with two misses. Average accuracy across items is 82.9% and average bias is −2.9%: there's no systematic skew, and the errors go in opposite directions.
431.importance: **It shows** whether purchasing decisions can be based on the forecast or whether it's simpler to hold a larger [[Safety Stock→upravlenie_zapasami/strahovoy_zapas]]. When the forecast error is comparable to the safety stock, calculating the reorder point from the forecast turns into guesswork, and the money is better invested in delivery speed than in the model. Bias answers the second question: if misses go in the same direction month after month, the cause is the model itself rather than chance, and correcting it costs less than extra inventory.
431.not_needed: **Skip it when** you purchase against confirmed customer orders: the volume is known in advance, and there's nothing to forecast.
431.essence_note: the more accurate the forecast, the less inventory you need to hold just in case

432.name: Economic Order Quantity (EOQ)
432.description: The purchase batch size at which the total cost of placing orders and holding inventory is lowest.
432.nuances:
All three values **cover the same** window: annual demand requires an annual holding cost per unit, and mixing annual demand with monthly costs inflates the result.
Holding cost is entered per unit for the period, not as the warehouse total. Ordering cost **is calculated per** order placed and doesn't depend on batch size: it includes the buyer's work, paperwork, receiving and the fixed part of shipping.
Variable costs that grow with volume **aren't included** in this value; otherwise the formula stops working.
The formula assumes steady demand and instant delivery: with pronounced seasonality the result drifts away from a reasonable value, and it has to be capped **manually**.
**Rounding to a multiple** of the supplier's pack size changes the final order quantity: the calculated number rarely divides evenly by the case size, and the batch is set to the nearest multiple up or down.
432.example:
Annual demand: 120,000 units
Cost of placing one order: $580
Holding cost per unit per year: $16

EOQ = √((2 × 120,000 × 580) / 16) = √(139,200,000 / 16) = √8,700,000 ≈ **2,950 units**

The supplier ships in cases of 500 units, so the order is rounded to 3,000.
432.importance: **It gives a starting point in** the dispute between purchasing, which wants a bigger volume discount, and the warehouse, which has nowhere to put the pallets. An order twice the calculated size doesn't double the savings; it increases holding time and the risk that part of the batch turns into dead stock.
432.not_needed: **Skip it when** you buy from a supplier with a strict minimum order quantity: the batch size is dictated by the contract rather than by the calculation.
432.synonyms: Optimal Order Quantity, Economic Lot Size
432.essence_note: small batches make you pay for every order placed, while large ones increase holding time

433.name: Gross Margin Return on Investment (GMROI)
433.description: How many dollars of gross profit each dollar invested in inventory brings in.
433.nuances:
Gross profit **is calculated as revenue** minus the cost of goods sold: using total revenue turns the metric into a different one and inflates it by the entire cost.
**The numerator covers the period**, and the denominator is [[Average Inventory Value→upravlenie_zapasami/srednyaya_stoimost_zapasov]] for the same period. With different windows, the result loses its meaning.
Average inventory value **is calculated from several** snapshots within the period: calculating from the stock on the last day after a large delivery understates the result.
**The value depends on** the length of the period, just like turnover: annual GMROI is four times quarterly GMROI for the same business, so the period is stated next to the number.
**The costing method** moves both parts of the calculation: under FIFO with rising prices, gross profit is higher, and so is the value of the stock.
433.example:
Revenue for the year: $5,250,000
Cost of goods sold: $3,150,000
[[Average Inventory Value→upravlenie_zapasami/srednyaya_stoimost_zapasov]]: $1,050,000

Gross profit = 5,250,000 − 3,150,000 = $2,100,000
GMROI = 2,100,000 / 1,050,000 = **$2 of profit per $1 of inventory per year**
433.importance: It combines **markup and sales speed** in one number and shows which goods are worth putting money into. An item with a 15% markup and eight turns is more profitable than an item with a 100% markup and one turn, and without this calculation purchasing gravitates toward high margins, tying up working capital.
433.not_needed: **Skip it** when inventory is held for continuity rather than for sale: raw materials and spare parts for your own production don't bring in profit directly.
433.synonyms: Gross Margin Return on Inventory, GMROII
433.essence_note: the more profit a dollar invested in goods brings, the more worthwhile it is to hold this inventory

434.name: Holding Cost per Unit
434.description: How much it costs to store one unit of goods for the period.
434.nuances:
The numerator and denominator cover **the same window**: annual costs are divided by the average number of units for the year, not by the stock at the end of the period.
The number of units **is the average of** several snapshots; otherwise a snapshot right after a large delivery understates the cost of storing a unit.
**Goods of different sizes** get the same cost even though they take up different amounts of space: if the assortment is mixed, calculating per cubic foot gives a different picture than per unit.
Holding costs for goods sold by the piece and by weight **are calculated separately**: dividing total costs by a sum of units and pounds is meaningless.
The cost of the goods themselves **isn't included** in the numerator.
434.example:
Holding costs for the year: $672,000
Average number of units from 12 snapshots: 42,000

Holding cost per unit = 672,000 / 42,000 = **$16 per year**

The same value goes into the economic order quantity calculation.
434.importance: **It shows what's at stake when** choosing between a large discounted batch and frequent deliveries: the volume discount is calculated in dollars and compared with the cost of extra months of storage. Without this figure, purchasing agrees to a larger volume for the sake of a discount and loses more on storage than it gained.
434.not_needed: **Skip it for** a mixed assortment where a unit can be an earring or a refrigerator: the average is not meaningful.
434.synonyms: Carrying Cost per Unit, Storage Cost per Unit
434.essence_note: every dollar of storage comes out of the product's margin

435.name: Inventory Accuracy Rate
435.description: How closely the stock in the system matches what's actually in the warehouse.
435.nuances:
An item **counts as accurate only** when the quantity matches exactly: a discrepancy of one unit makes it inaccurate; otherwise the metric turns into a “roughly matches” estimate.
The discrepancy tolerance **is set separately and** changes the result a lot: a ±2% tolerance turns 88% accuracy into 96%.
**It's counted by item**, not in units or in dollars: this way the metric answers the question “For how many items can't the stock figure be trusted?” The price of this approach is that the size of the discrepancy is lost: a three-unit discrepancy on a stock of ten is an accounting failure, while the same discrepancy on a stock of ten thousand is counting noise, and in items they count the same.
**That's why, alongside** the share of items, you look at the discrepancy in dollars or units: the share shows how wrong the system is overall, and the discrepancy amount shows what it costs.
The base **includes only counted** items, not the whole assortment: with a cycle count of 200 items out of 1,200, the denominator is 200.
Positive and negative discrepancies **count the same**: a surplus is as much an accounting error as a shortage, and offsetting different items against each other inflates accuracy.
**Inventory movements are suspended during** the count; otherwise a shipment made during counting creates a discrepancy out of nothing.
435.example:
Items counted: 200
Exact match: 176
Shortage: 18
Surplus: 6

Inventory accuracy = 176 / 200 × 100 = **88%**

With a ±2% tolerance, 192 items count as accurate and accuracy comes out at 96%: the same count, a different figure.
435.importance: **It determines** whether you can trust the stock figure when selling and planning purchases. Every inaccurate item is a product shown to the customer as available and not found during picking: the order gets canceled after it has already been paid for.
435.not_needed: **Skip it when** you use a marketplace's fulfillment service: the marketplace keeps the stock records, and the seller doesn't run physical counts and can't check its system against the shelf.
435.essence_note: if the system's stock can't be trusted, goods are promised to customers and then not found during picking

436.name: Inventory Age
436.description: How many days a unit of goods has been in the warehouse since it was received.
436.nuances:
**The costing method determines** which batch is considered to be in the warehouse: under FIFO, older receipts are sold first and the remaining stock stays relatively new; under weighted average, batches lose their identity and the receipt date has to be taken from the latest receipt, which understates age.
The receipt date **is when goods are actually** received at the warehouse, not the supplier's shipment date: time in transit doesn't count as storage age.
**A customer return** either gets a new receipt date or keeps the original one: in the first case, an item that sat for a long time and came back from a canceled order resets the counter and drops out of dead stock.
When a batch is partly sold, the age of the remaining stock **is calculated from the receipt date** of the batch it physically comes from; otherwise mixing receipts gives an average age instead of the real one.
436.example:
Batch received at the warehouse: January 12
Shipped by the supplier: December 28 (not counted)
Calculation date: August 6

Age = August 6 − January 12 = **206 days**

Counting from the supplier's shipment date gives 221 days: that's the time since payment rather than the storage time.
436.importance: Age is used to pick items for markdown and to decide what ships first when the same product sits in several batches. **Without it, goods that are** nearing expiration sit in the back row until they become a write-off.
436.not_needed: **Skip it for** undifferentiated bulk goods without batch tracking: bulk solids and liquids physically mix in one container, and there's no way to assign a receipt date to a specific unit.
436.essence_note: the longer goods sit, the more money is tied up in them and the closer they are to being written off

437.name: Inventory Holding Cost
437.description: The sum of all costs of holding inventory for the period: warehouse rent, warehouse staff payroll, utilities, insurance.
437.nuances:
The cost of the goods themselves **isn't included** in holding costs; only the costs of storing them are included.
**You decide** whether to include the cost of money tied up in inventory: a financial calculation includes it; an operating warehouse budget doesn't. The higher the interest rate and the larger the inventory, the more it changes the result.
[[Depreciation and Amortization (D&A)→finansy/amortizaciya]] of racks and warehouse equipment **is shown as its own expense line** rather than here: in the Map Library, depreciation isn't allocated across expense items.
Holding costs for owned and rented warehouses are calculated **differently**: for an owned one, instead of rent you have upkeep and property tax.
Receiving and shipping **are not included** in holding costs: these are costs of moving goods, and they change with the number of operations rather than the volume stored.
437.example:
Warehouse rent: $20,000
Warehouse staff payroll, including payroll taxes: $26,000
Utilities, cleaning and security: $6,500
Inventory insurance: $1,250
Depreciation of racks and equipment: $3,750 (not counted: depreciation is its own expense line)
Receiving and shipping handling: $10,000 (not included: this is order processing)

Inventory Holding Cost = 20,000 + 26,000 + 6,500 + 1,250 = **$53,750 per month**
437.importance: It answers **which is cheaper**: holding a large inventory and ordering less often, or cutting batch sizes and paying for delivery more often. Without this amount, the decision to expand the warehouse is made blindly, and the company rents extra square footage for goods that don't pay for their own storage.
437.not_needed: Skip it when you use a fulfillment provider with per-operation pricing: the contractor bills receiving, storage and shipping as one item, and warehouse upkeep costs aren't broken out **separately**.
437.synonyms: Inventory Carrying Cost, Carrying Costs, Storage Costs
437.essence_note: the warehouse costs money every day the goods sit in it

438.name: Replenishment Frequency
438.description: How many times during the period replenishments arrived at the warehouse.
438.nuances:
**The result depends mechanically on** the length of the window, so the time unit is stated next to the number: 24 times a year and 2 times a month are the same frequency, and 24 on its own, without a period, can't be interpreted.
A replenishment **is counted as a receipt** at the warehouse, not as an order placement: an order that arrived in three trucks on different days is either three replenishments or one, and the choice changes the figure by a multiple.
One delivery under one order **counts as one replenishment** regardless of the number of trips.
Internal transfers between storage zones **don't count** as replenishment; the goods were already in inventory.
Customer returns **don't count** as replenishment. Frequency is directly linked to batch size: doubling the frequency at the same sales volume means batches have been halved, and this affects ordering and holding costs.
438.example:
Receipts at the warehouse in the year: 24
Of those, one order delivered in three trips: 3 trips counted as 1 replenishment
Internal transfers: 40 (not counted)
Customer returns: 210 (not counted)

Replenishment frequency = 24 / 12 months = **2 times a month**
438.importance: **It links the receiving workload** to batch size: two deliveries a month of 5,000 units and eight of 1,250 require different numbers of receiving staff and different amounts of storage space. A sharp rise in frequency usually means purchasing is covering shortages with rush reorders, and for each such delivery the company pays the full cost of placing an order for a small batch.
438.not_needed: **Skip it for** continuous scheduled deliveries: goods arrive daily in a fixed flow, and the frequency is set by the contract rather than by purchasing decisions.
438.essence_note: infrequent large deliveries tie up cash and space, while frequent small ones cost the full price of placing an order every time

439.name: Inventory Shrinkage Rate
439.description: The share of inventory value lost to theft, damage and accounting errors.
439.nuances:
Losses **are valued at cost** rather than at selling price, and the denominator is at cost too.
**The costing method** changes both parts: under FIFO, a lost unit is valued at the old purchase price and under weighted average at the average cost, and the faster purchase prices rise, the wider the gap.
Losses **include only unexplained** shortages found in the physical count and spoilage: planned write-offs for expiration don't belong here.
The denominator **is the average** inventory value for the period rather than the stock on the last day; otherwise a physical count right after a large delivery would understate the percentage.
SKU mix-ups are offset before the calculation: a shortage of one item against a surplus of a similar item at the same price **doesn't count** as a loss.
439.example:
[[Average Inventory Value→upravlenie_zapasami/srednyaya_stoimost_zapasov]] for the quarter: $1,050,000
Shortage found in the physical count: $6,300
Damage during transfers: $4,200
Written off at expiration: $15,000 (not included)

Losses = 6,300 + 4,200 = $10,500
Shrinkage rate = 10,500 / 1,050,000 × 100 = **1%**
439.importance: **It's what you look at** when deciding whether to install video surveillance, change access to the storage area or revisit the contract with the warehouse contractor. Multiplying the rate by your inventory value gives the loss in dollars, and that's money already spent: the goods are paid for, but no one will sell them.
439.not_needed: **Skip it when** you use a marketplace's fulfillment service or a third-party logistics provider: the contractor is responsible for safekeeping, and losses are reimbursed under the contract rather than tracked as a share of inventory.
439.essence_note: these are paid-for goods that disappeared and won't be sold

440.name: Inventory Turnover
440.formula: Cost of Goods Sold / Average Inventory Value
440.alt_formula: Units Sold / Average Inventory in Units
440.description: How many times during the period the inventory sold out completely and was replenished. It's calculated either in dollars or in units: these are two versions of the same metric, and the one you use is stated next to the number.
440.nuances:
You can calculate it in dollars or in units, but the numerator and denominator **are expressed in the same** units. In dollars, the result depends on purchase prices and the costing method; in units, it shows the physical movement of goods more cleanly, but adding up units across a mixed assortment is meaningless.
**The result depends mechanically** on the length of the window: the same data give a monthly figure one-twelfth the size of the annual one, so the period is stated next to the number.
**The numerator is the cost** of goods sold, not revenue: using revenue inflates the result by exactly the markup and makes comparison with other companies' figures meaningless.
[[Average Inventory Value→upravlenie_zapasami/srednyaya_stoimost_zapasov]] **is calculated from several** snapshots within the period, at least monthly ones: a snapshot taken right after a large delivery inflates the denominator and understates turnover.
**The costing method** changes the numerator: when purchase prices are rising, FIFO gives a lower [[Cost of Goods Sold (COGS)→finansy/sebestoimost_prodazh]] and lower turnover than weighted average.
**Written-off and dead** stock stays in the denominator as long as it sits in the warehouse: excluding dead stock inflates the result and hides cash tied up in inventory.
440.example:
In dollars:
Cost of goods sold for the year: $3,150,000
[[Average Inventory Value→upravlenie_zapasami/srednyaya_stoimost_zapasov]] from 12 monthly snapshots: $1,050,000
Turnover = 3,150,000 / 1,050,000 = **3 times a year**

In units:
Sold in the year: 126,000 units
Average inventory: 42,000 units
Turnover = 126,000 / 42,000 = **3 times a year**

The same calculation for a month gives 0.25: without the period, the figure can't be compared with anything.
440.importance: **It shows** how quickly the money put into goods comes back. The number of turns translates into how long a dollar spent on purchasing stays tied up, and any growth in purchasing within that time has to be financed with credit rather than from sales.
440.not_needed: **Skip it when** you order goods only after a customer buys them and have no warehouse of your own: goods go straight from the supplier to the customer, no inventory builds up, and there's nothing to replenish.
440.synonyms: Inventory Turnover Ratio, Inventory Turns, Stock Turnover
440.essence_note: the faster inventory sells and is replenished, the less money sits on shelves instead of circulating

441.name: Inventory Write-Off Rate
441.formula: Value of Written-Off Inventory / Average Inventory Value × 100
441.description: The share of inventory value written off during the period due to defects, expiration and obsolescence.
441.nuances:
**Write-offs are recorded at cost**, and the costing method determines the amount: FIFO uses the oldest purchase prices, weighted average uses their average, and when purchase prices fluctuate, the numbers diverge.
**The denominator is the average** inventory value for the same period, not the ending stock: a one-off delivery before the reporting date inflates the base and understates the percentage.
A markdown is different from a write-off: goods sold at 70% off still count as sales, and **only what** is physically taken out of stock is written off.
The reporting period for a write-off **is determined by the date on the write-off** record, not by the date the goods actually spoiled.
441.example:
[[Average Inventory Value→upravlenie_zapasami/srednyaya_stoimost_zapasov]] for the quarter: $1,050,000
Written off at expiration: $15,000
Written off as defective: $5,250
Sold at a markdown: $45,000 (not included)

Write-offs = $20,250
Write-off rate = 20,250 / 1,050,000 × 100 = **1.9%**
441.importance: **It shows** how much money purchasing put into goods that never reached the register. When write-offs start to outweigh the volume discount, it's cheaper to cut batch sizes and order more often: the savings on the wholesale price no longer pay for what gets thrown away. The threshold is calculated from your own numbers by comparing the two in dollars.
441.not_needed: **Skip it** when goods go back to the supplier under a buyback agreement: unsold goods are shipped back instead of being written off.
441.essence_note: written-off goods are paid for, and no money will come in for them

442.name: Lost Sales Due to Stockouts
442.formula:
Lost Units = Average Daily Demand × Days Out of Stock − Substitute Purchases
Lost Sales Due to Stockouts = Lost Units × Average Selling Price
442.description: An estimate of the revenue not received because an item was out of stock. Lost units can't be observed; they're calculated as how many units would have sold during the days out of stock if the item had been available.
442.nuances:
Lost units are an estimate rather than a fact: demand during the days without stock isn't recorded anywhere and is reconstructed from average daily demand before the item ran out. The result **changes noticeably** depending on the base period chosen for this average.
Average demand **is calculated for the period before** the item ran out, and days out of stock are counted for each item separately: you can't add up days across the whole assortment and multiply them by total demand.
**The average selling price** after discounts is closer to reality than the list price, and the gap is wider for promoted items.
Customers switching to another product inflate the result: if a customer bought a similar item, the revenue isn't lost, and such substitutions **are subtracted** from the calculation.
**Calculating lost** profit instead of revenue gives lower figures: revenue shows the scale of the problem; profit shows the actual loss.
442.example:
Average daily demand for the item before it ran out: 64 units
Days out of stock: 6
Substitutes bought by customers during those days: 96 units
Average selling price: $43.75

Lost units = 64 × 6 − 96 = 384 − 96 = **288 units**
Lost Sales Due to Stockouts = 288 × 43.75 = **$12,600**

At a unit cost of $25, the actual lost profit is 288 × 18.75 = $5,400.
442.importance: It puts a dollar figure on shortages and makes the purchasing conversation concrete: lost revenue is compared with the cost of holding the stock that would have prevented it, and the safety stock level **is calculated** rather than debated. Without this figure, shortages stay invisible, because by definition they don't appear in the sales report.
442.not_needed: **Skip it when** you order goods only after a customer buys them and an item missing from the warehouse doesn't block the sale: the order is placed and passed on to the supplier.
442.essence_note: this is revenue lost only because the item wasn't in the warehouse

443.name: Dead Stock Units
443.description: The number of units that can't be sold at the regular price: outdated models, items that are no longer presentable, items that have sat in stock longer than the set limit.
443.nuances:
The dead stock threshold **is set as a number of days** without sales or as days of supply above target. The size of the threshold changes the result a lot: the shorter the threshold, the more items count as dead stock, and the more of them will still sell.
**It's counted in units** of goods, not in SKUs: one slow item with 500 units in stock and one with 3 units contribute differently.
Goods sold by the piece and by weight **are counted separately**; you can't add units to pounds. Out of season, seasonal items cross the threshold automatically, so for them the day counter is either paused, or every off-season produces a spike with no real problem behind it.
Goods set aside for warranty replacements or kitting **are excluded from dead stock**: they aren't sold as such, but they're needed.
443.example:
Items with no sales for over 180 days: 84 SKUs
Units of those items: 3,480
Of those, set aside for warranty replacements: 120 (not counted)

Dead Stock Units = 3,480 − 120 = **3,360 units**
443.importance: **It sizes the markdown or disposal decision** in units rather than percentages: a promotion and a channel for it are planned around a specific number of units. Until this figure is calculated, the goods keep occupying bins the company pays rent for every month.
443.not_needed: **Skip it for** perishable goods that turn over in a few days: unsold goods are written off when they expire instead of turning into dead stock.
443.synonyms: Dead Stock, Obsolete Stock, Dead Inventory
443.essence_note: each such unit has been paid for, takes up a bin and won't sell at the regular price

444.name: Reorder Point (ROP)
444.formula:
Reorder Point = Lead Time Demand + Safety Stock
Compared with available stock:
Available Stock = Stock on Hand − Reserved for Paid Orders + Goods in Transit
444.description: The stock level at which a new order is placed with the supplier. It's compared with available stock rather than total stock: net of reserves and including batches already on the way.
444.nuances:
Both terms **are calculated using the same** lead time and the same demand observation window; otherwise the reorder point won't match actual needs.
Goods in transit are added to available stock: without this, the system gives a signal every day while the batch is on the way, and purchasing duplicates the order. **This works differently here** than in the Understock Rate, where goods on the way don't count toward stock: there, the metric shows that the shelf is emptying right now; here, you decide whether to place another order.
**The point is recalculated when** demand or lead time changes: a value calculated before the season and left for the whole year leads to shortages at the peak and overstock after the season.
Goods reserved for paid orders **are subtracted from available stock**: they're physically in the warehouse but can't be sold, and otherwise the signal would come too late.
444.example:
[[Lead Time Demand→upravlenie_zapasami/spros_za_period_postavki]]: 1,344 units
[[Safety Stock→upravlenie_zapasami/strahovoy_zapas]]: 2,931 units

Reorder point = 1,344 + 2,931 = **4,275 units**

Stock in the warehouse: 4,600
Of that, reserved for paid orders: 500
Ordered from the supplier and on the way: 0
Available stock = 4,600 − 500 + 0 = 4,100

4,100 is below the reorder point of 4,275, so the order is placed today. If 2,000 units were already on the way, available stock would come out at 6,100, and there would be no signal.
444.importance: **It replaces manual stock reviews with** a rule that triggers on its own. Until the point is set as a number, orders go out either too early, tying up cash, or too late, and the item runs out just when a customer comes for it.
444.not_needed: **Skip it when** you purchase for a specific customer order: the supplier order is placed when the deal is made rather than based on the stock level.
444.essence_note: set too low, it leaves the shelf empty while goods are on the way; set too high, it ties up cash too early

445.name: Safety Stock
445.formula: (Max Daily Usage × Max Lead Time) − (Average Daily Usage × Average Lead Time)
445.description: Extra inventory held on top of normal needs in case of a demand spike or a delivery delay.
445.nuances:
The maximum **is a high level that recurred** in the observations, rather than a single record day: one abnormal spike inflates safety stock to a volume that will later turn into dead stock.
**The observation window determines the result**: the maximum over a year and over a quarter differ, and for seasonal goods the calculation is done within the season rather than over the whole year.
Lead time **is measured in calendar** days, the same as in the reorder point calculation; otherwise the two metrics will diverge.
Days out of stock **are excluded** from the calculation of average usage: zeros understate both the average and the safety stock.
The formula builds in the full worst case, peak demand and the maximum delay at the same time, even though the two **rarely coincide**. So the calculated number is an upper bound rather than a recommendation: for expensive goods it's weighed against the cost of cash tied up in inventory and lowered; for cheap and critical goods it's kept as is.
**The formula ignores holding** costs entirely, which is another reason not to take the result literally.
445.example:
Average daily usage: 64 units
Maximum sustained daily usage: 95 units
[[Average Supplier Lead Time→upravlenie_zapasami/sredniy_srok_postavki]]: 21 days
Maximum lead time: 45 days

Safety stock = (95 × 45) − (64 × 21) = 4,275 − 1,344 = **2,931 units**

A one-off peak of 210 units a day isn't included: with it, safety stock would come out at 8,106 units, and most of it would sit until the end of the season.
445.importance: **It puts a dollar price on insurance against** shortages: the calculated volume is multiplied by unit cost, and the inventory size becomes a deliberate choice rather than a habit. Without it, shortages are covered by building up all inventory across the board, including items that never run out.
445.not_needed: **Skip it for** goods with a short shelf life: stock held just in case will spoil before it's needed.
445.essence_note: too little won't cover even the first delivery delay, while too much ties up cash and turns into dead stock

446.name: Inventory Out-of-Stock Rate
446.formula: SKUs with No Available Stock at the Snapshot / Total SKUs × 100
446.alt_formula: SKUs That Hit Zero at Least Once in the Period / Total SKUs × 100
446.description: The share of SKUs unavailable for sale, either at the moment of the snapshot or at least once during the period. These are two different ways of counting the same metric, and the one you use is stated next to the number.
446.nuances:
**A point-in-time snapshot shows** what's missing right now; the period calculation shows how many items ran out at any point. The second method always gives a higher figure that's closer to the truth: an item can repeatedly hit zero between snapshots and be back in stock exactly on the snapshot day.
For a point-in-time snapshot, **the same time** of day is used every time: a snapshot in the morning before shipping and one in the evening after it give different numbers.
The denominator includes **only active SKUs**; delisted items inflate the base.
Goods reserved for a paid order are physically in the warehouse but can't be sold to another customer: if reserved units aren't subtracted from stock, the item **counts as available** even though a new customer can't buy it.
Goods in transit don't count as available: they **don't change** the fact that the shelf is empty.
446.example:
Active SKUs: 1,200

Point-in-time snapshot:
With zero stock: 36
With all stock reserved: 12
Unavailable for sale = 36 + 12 = 48
Out-of-stock rate = 48 / 1,200 × 100 = **4%**

For the month:
Hit zero at least once: 168
Out-of-stock rate for the period = 168 / 1,200 × 100 = **14%**

The difference is 120 items that were back in stock by the time of the snapshot.
446.importance: **It directly links the warehouse's work** to lost sales: every out-of-stock item is traffic that arrived and then left for a competitor. The point-in-time snapshot is needed to react today, and the period calculation is needed to see the scale of the problem: it reveals items that run out regularly and are restocked by the reporting date. Until the rate is calculated, purchasing learns about out-of-stock product pages from complaints rather than from a report.
446.not_needed: **Skip it for** make-to-order production, where finished goods aren't stored in the warehouse and availability isn't expected.
446.essence_note: what's not in stock won't be bought, and the customer goes to a competitor

447.name: Total Inventory Value
447.description: The monetary value of all goods in the warehouse at purchase prices at the time of the snapshot.
447.nuances:
**Valuation is at cost**, not at selling price: using retail prices inflates inventory value by the entire markup and distorts all derived calculations.
**The costing method determines** which purchase price is applied to the stock: FIFO leaves the latest, more expensive purchases on the balance sheet, while weighted average uses the average cost of all receipts.
**When purchase prices rise**, the gap between the methods widens, and the faster they rise, the wider the gap.
Unit cost either **includes shipping and** customs duties or doesn't: including them raises inventory value and defers recognition of these costs until the goods are sold.
**Goods in transit** aren't in the warehouse, but ownership of them may already have passed: whether they're included depends on the delivery terms, and for large batches this changes the amount noticeably.
Goods reserved for paid orders **aren't subtracted from inventory** until they ship.
447.example:
Units in the warehouse: 42,000
Average unit cost including shipping: $25
Goods in transit: 2,500 units (ownership hasn't passed, not counted)

Inventory value = 42,000 × 25 = **$1,050,000**
447.importance: **It's the company's money** sitting on shelves instead of in its bank account. It's used to calculate working capital needs and to decide whether your own funds will cover a seasonal purchase or a loan will be needed.
447.not_needed: **Skip it when** you order goods only after a customer buys them and have no warehouse of your own: no inventory is recorded on the balance sheet, and inventory value is zero for the whole period.
447.essence_note: a small inventory turns into shortages, while a large one is money sitting on shelves instead of in the bank

448.name: Total Units in Stock
448.formula: Sum of units across all SKUs
448.description: The total number of units of goods in the warehouse at the time of the snapshot.
448.nuances:
**Units of goods are counted**, not SKUs: 1,200 items in the assortment and 42,000 units in the warehouse are different numbers, and they mustn't be confused.
Goods sold by the piece and by weight **aren't added together**: units and pounds give a meaningless sum, so separate totals are maintained for them.
The unit **is defined before the calculation**: a case of 12 bottles is either one unit or twelve, and the total differs by an order of magnitude depending on the choice.
Goods reserved for paid but unshipped orders are physically in the warehouse and **are included** in stock.
Goods in transit **aren't included**; they haven't been received yet.
**Defective goods awaiting** write-off stay in stock until the date of the write-off record.
448.example:
Sellable goods: 39,400 units
Reserved for paid orders: 1,240
Defective goods awaiting a write-off record: 1,360
Goods in transit: 2,500 (not counted)

Stock in the warehouse = 39,400 + 1,240 + 1,360 = **42,000 units**
448.importance: **It's the basis for calculating** warehouse utilization and the cost of storing one unit. If this figure differs from what's actually on the shelves, the system shows the sales team goods that aren't there, and the order gets canceled after it has already been paid for.
448.not_needed: **Skip it for** goods sold by weight or volume without unit packaging: inventory is measured by weight or volume, and there's no such thing as a unit of goods.
448.synonyms: Stock on Hand, Units on Hand, On-Hand Inventory
448.essence_note: too few units, and the shelf goes empty; too many, and they take up paid-for square footage

449.name: Understock Rate
449.description: The share of SKUs whose stock has fallen below the set threshold, including items that have hit zero.
449.nuances:
**It's counted in SKUs**, not in units of goods: an item with two units left and an item with two hundred weigh the same.
