The threshold **is set by the reorder** point of each item rather than a single unit count for all SKUs: an item selling 100 units a day and an item selling one unit a week become understocked at different stock levels.
Zero-stock items **are included in the numerator** along with the rest: a stockout is the most severe form of understock, and keeping such items only in the denominator understates the share exactly where the problem is most acute. The metric overlaps with the Inventory Out-of-Stock Rate on purpose: that one shows what's already gone from the shelf, and this one shows for how many items it's time to act.
The denominator **includes only active** SKUs: delisted items with zero stock inflate the base and understate the percentage.
**Goods in transit** don't count toward stock: otherwise an item with a batch already on the way stops counting as understocked, and the signal disappears before the goods reach the shelf.
449.example:
Active SKUs in the assortment: 1,200
Stock below the reorder point but above zero: 96
Zero stock: 36
Delisted SKUs: 140 (not in the base)

Understock Rate = (96 + 36) / 1,200 × 100 = **11%**

Without zero-stock items it would be 8%: the share would fall because of the items that have already run out.
449.importance: **It answers whether** purchasing reacts in time, before the shelf goes empty. The share shows for how many items an order decision is needed now: some of them will hit zero within the lead time, and some are already there. Until it's calculated, shortages are discovered from complaints by sales staff rather than from stock levels.
449.not_needed: **Skip it for** one-of-a-kind goods, where each item exists as a single unit and there's nothing to set a minimum stock threshold for.
449.essence_note: for these items the shelf is about to go empty, and their sales will stop

450.name: Vendor Fill Rate
450.description: The share of ordered units that arrived sellable. Defective and wrong items are subtracted from the quantity received: only goods that can be sold fill the order.
450.nuances:
**It's counted in units** of goods, not by number of orders: a delivery short by half the batch cuts the metric in half rather than zeroing it, as an “order filled or not” count would.
**Goods sold by the piece and by weight** aren't summed in one metric; the rate is calculated separately for each.
A follow-up shipment isn't added to the original delivery: if the supplier delivers the shortfall later and it's credited to the first delivery, the metric rises to 100%, and the timing problem disappears from the figure. A follow-up shipment **counts as a separate receipt**.
Wrong and defective items **are subtracted from the quantity received**: a batch with 4% breakage fills 96% of the order, not 100%. Otherwise the metric counts what was delivered rather than what's sellable.
If more arrived than was ordered, **the result is capped** at 100%; otherwise an excess of one item masks a shortage of another.
450.example:
Ordered from the supplier: 5,000 units
Arrived per the packing slip: 4,700
Of those, found defective during receiving: 100

Sellable units received = 4,700 − 100 = 4,600
Fill rate = 4,600 / 5,000 × 100 = **92%**

If defective units aren't subtracted, you get 94%: that's the share of what was delivered rather than the share that's sellable.
450.importance: **It's used to decide** whether to renew a supplier contract and how much extra stock to hold against its shortfalls. A consistent shortfall means you need to order extra to cover the difference; otherwise the shelf will be empty even though an order was formally placed.
450.not_needed: **Skip it when** you order goods only after a customer buys them and have no warehouse of your own: goods go straight from the supplier to the customer, and a shortage shows up immediately in that customer's order.
450.synonyms: Supplier Fill Rate, Supplier Order Fill Rate
450.essence_note: the more of what was ordered actually arrives and is sellable, the fewer gaps on the shelf

451.name: Units Received
451.description: The number of units of goods received at the warehouse during the period.
451.nuances:
The unit of measure **matches the one** used in stock records: if stock is kept in bottles, a receipt of 200 cases of 12 is 2,400 units, not 200.
Goods sold by the piece and by weight **are counted separately**. The date of receiving at the warehouse determines the period, not the supplier's shipment date or the payment date.
Defective goods found during receiving and returned to the supplier **are subtracted from units received**; otherwise receipts won't reconcile with stock.
Customer returns **don't count** as receipts; these goods were already purchased.
451.example:
Received per packing slips in the month: 11,200 units
Rejected at receiving and returned to the supplier: 240
Customer returns: 380 (not counted)
Shipped by the supplier on the 30th, arriving on the 2nd: 1,500 (goes into next month)

Units Received = 11,200 − 240 = **10,960 units**
451.importance: **It's a check that warehouse records reconcile**: receipts minus sales and write-offs should give the stock, and a discrepancy points to unrecorded movement before a physical count finds it. The same figure is used to plan the receiving workload and the number of shifts.
451.not_needed: **Skip it when** you order goods only after a customer buys them and have no warehouse of your own: goods don't go through receiving and travel from the supplier straight to the customer.
451.essence_note: you can only sell what the warehouse has received

452.name: Units Shipped
452.description: The number of units shipped to customers during the period.
452.nuances:
The unit of measure **matches the one** used for stock; otherwise sales won't reconcile with receipts.
Goods sold by the piece and by weight **are counted separately**. A sale is recorded on the date it ships from the warehouse, not the order date: goods that are paid for but reserved for an order haven't left the warehouse.
Customer returns **are subtracted from sales** in the period when they came back, not the period of the sale: otherwise a closed month would have to be recalculated retroactively.
**Shipments without a sale (samples**, warranty replacements, transfers) don't count as sales; they're removed from stock under their own reason code.
452.example:
Shipped to customers in the month: 10,600 units
Returned by customers: 420
Samples and warranty replacements shipped: 180 (not counted)
Paid for but reserved for orders: 1,240 (will count in the month they ship)

Units Shipped = 10,600 − 420 = **10,180 units**
452.importance: **It's the basis for calculating** daily demand, the reorder point and safety stock: an error here carries through to every purchasing calculation at once. If you count by order date instead of shipment date, demand shifts by the time goods stay reserved before shipping, and purchasing places orders at the wrong time.
452.essence_note: these are actual sales in units: the more shipped, the more revenue

453.name: Written-Off Units
453.description: The number of units taken out of stock during the period due to defects, spoilage, expiration or obsolescence.
453.nuances:
The unit of measure is the same as for stock. A write-off **is recorded on the date** of its write-off record, not the date the spoilage was found: there can be a gap between the two, and the item stays in stock all that time.
Goods sold at a markdown **aren't written off**: they went through the register.
Defective goods returned to the supplier under a claim **are excluded from write-offs**, since the supplier bears the loss.
**A shortage** found during a physical count is recorded under a separate reason: mixing it with write-offs hides the difference between spoiled goods and missing ones.
453.example:
Write-off records for the quarter: 1,640 units
Of those, expired: 1,210
Defects and spoilage: 430
Returned to the supplier under a claim: 260 (not counted)
Shortage found in the physical count: 310 (separate reason)

Written-Off Units = **1,640 units**
453.importance: **A breakdown by reason shows** what exactly to fix: expiration write-offs mean overpurchasing, while spoilage write-offs mean a problem with storage conditions or with moving goods. A single total without this split doesn't point to any action.
453.not_needed: **Skip it** when goods go back to the supplier under a buyback agreement: unsold goods are returned rather than written off.
453.essence_note: these are goods that were paid for and taken out of stock without a single sale

454.name: Lead Time Demand
454.formula:
Average Daily Demand = Sales for the Period / (Days in the Period − Days Out of Stock)
Lead Time Demand = Average Daily Demand × Lead Time
454.description: How many units will leave the warehouse while a new order from the supplier is on the way.
454.nuances:
**Both factors are in** the same time units: daily demand is multiplied by lead time in days, and using weekly demand with a lead time in days gives a result seven times larger.
Lead time **is counted in full**, from placing the order until the goods are ready for sale: the supplier's order processing, shipping and receiving at the warehouse.
Leaving out receiving understates the need by the demand that falls during receiving. Average daily demand **is calculated from sales**, not from all types of shipments: warranty replacements and transfers don't create demand.
Days when the item was out of stock **are excluded** from the average demand calculation; otherwise the zeros understate demand and the reorder point drops below what's needed.
For seasonal goods, **demand for the expected** lead time period is used rather than the annual average: an order that arrives at the season's peak but was calculated from the annual average will be smaller than needed, and the sharper the peak, the bigger the shortfall.
454.example:
Sold over 90 days: 5,400 units
Days the item was out of stock: 6

Average daily demand = 5,400 / (90 − 6) ≈ 64 units a day
Lead time including receiving: 21 days
Lead Time Demand = 64 × 21 = **1,344 units**
454.importance: **It sets the minimum stock level** below which it's too late to order. Underestimate it by a week of demand, and the shelf stays empty for exactly that week before the truck arrives, so customers go to whoever has the item in stock.
454.not_needed: **Skip it when** you purchase against confirmed customer orders: the volume is known in advance, and there's no need to estimate usage during the lead time.
454.essence_note: a small value means demand is falling; a large one means more money has to be held in goods to cover the time in transit

455.name: Storage Utilization Rate
455.formula: Occupied Storage Locations / Total Storage Locations × 100
455.alt_formula: Volume Occupied by Goods / Usable Storage Volume × 100
455.description: What share of the warehouse's capacity is occupied by goods. The simplest way is to count storage locations: how many bins or pallet positions are occupied out of those available.
455.nuances:
Counting storage locations is simpler and more reliable: the warehouse knows the number of bins and pallet positions from its layout, and there's nothing to calculate. A half-filled location **counts as occupied**: you can't put another product there anyway.
Counting by volume shows more accurately how much space is wasted, but it requires product dimensions and the warehouse's usable volume. Both values are then in cubic feet: using area instead of volume understates the result in warehouses with tall racks, and the volume of goods **is measured by the packaging**, including the pallet, because the empty space inside boxes physically takes up room.
The method is chosen **once** and used consistently: the two versions give different numbers and aren't comparable with each other.
**Utilization measured on a single** date fluctuates with the delivery schedule: calculating from several snapshots within the period gives a usable figure, while a snapshot on the day after receiving overstates utilization.
455.example:
By storage locations:
Total pallet positions: 1,400
Occupied: 1,050
Storage utilization = 1,050 / 1,400 × 100 = **75%**

By volume:
Usable storage volume: 300,000 cu ft
Volume of goods with packaging and pallets: 225,000 cu ft
Storage utilization = 225,000 / 300,000 × 100 = **75%**

A company finds its own ceiling from the data: it's where growing utilization starts to coincide with growing order picking time.
455.importance: **It answers the question** of whether a second warehouse is needed or rearranging the racks will do. Working at full capacity slows shipping and increases picking errors, while chronic underuse means the company pays rent for unused space.
455.not_needed: **Skip it when** you store goods in a contractor's space and pay per pallet position: the volume inside a position isn't the seller's concern.
455.synonyms: Warehouse Utilization, Space Utilization, Warehouse Capacity Utilization
455.essence_note: a warehouse packed to the limit slows shipping, while a half-empty one means rent is paid for unused space

456.name: Total Warehouse Space
456.formula: Total warehouse area under the lease
456.alt_formula: Storage area excluding aisles and support areas
456.description: Warehouse area in square feet. Either the entire area under the lease is counted, or only the storage area without aisles and support areas: the method is chosen once and used consistently.
456.nuances:
**The simple method** is to take the area from the lease: the figure is at hand, nothing needs to be measured, and it's enough for comparing months.
It's more accurate to use the storage area, subtracting aisles, receiving, shipping and support areas: a smaller part of the warehouse is set aside for goods, and the cost per square foot of storage comes out higher. **This calculation makes sense** when the areas are on the floor plan; it isn't worth taking measurements just for it.
Whichever you choose, don't change the method between periods: switching from the total area to the storage area will raise the cost per square foot, even though nothing in warehouse operations **changes**.
Multi-level racking isn't measured by area: with it, the metric no longer reflects capacity and **is replaced by storage volume**.
456.example:
Warehouse area under the lease: 30,000 sq ft

Simple method = **30,000 sq ft**

If there's a floor plan:
Receiving and shipping area: 4,000 sq ft
Aisles between racks: 5,000 sq ft
Support areas and staff facilities: 1,000 sq ft
Storage area = 30,000 − 4,000 − 5,000 − 1,000 = **20,000 sq ft**
456.importance: This is the basis for calculating **the cost per square foot** of storage and for checking whether purchasing growth runs up against physical capacity. The difference between the two methods shows what share of the leased space is actually used for storage: if you plan inventory by the area in the lease, a batch arrives at a warehouse with nowhere to put it.
456.not_needed: **Skip it when** you use a marketplace's fulfillment service or a third-party logistics provider: you pay by volume or per operation, and the contractor manages the space.
456.essence_note: too little space means there's nowhere to put a batch, and extra space is rent paid for unused space

457.name: Search Ads Spend
457.description: How much money the ad platform charged while the ads were running in the period. Throughout this map, spend means the amount charged rather than the amount planned: it's what gets divided to calculate the cost per click, per thousand impressions and per conversion.
457.nuances:
Spend **includes only the charges** from the ad platform for clicks and impressions. The agency fee, a contractor's management fee and creative production costs aren't included: these are separate expense lines; otherwise the cost per click and per conversion will stop matching the ad account data.
Account top-ups and the planned amount for the period **don't count** as spend here: money can remain as an unspent balance, and the daily limit in the account sets a ceiling rather than actual spend. What's counted is what was charged.
**Promotional credits and promo codes** granted by the platform are spent like money but don't create real costs for the company.
457.example:
Account topped up in March: $12,000
Charged by the platform for March: $9,450
Of that, covered by promotional credits: $600
Remaining account balance: $3,150
Contractor's management fee: $1,800 (not counted)

Search Ads Spend = **$9,450**

The company's out-of-pocket spend for March: $8,850
457.importance: It's the basis for all cost metrics on the map: an error in spend carries over into the cost per click, the cost per conversion and the return on ad spend **in full**. If spend is counted from account top-ups, the month's spend is overstated or understated by the account balance, and the decision to scale is based on the wrong number.
457.synonyms: Ad Spend, Paid Search Spend, PPC Spend
457.essence_note: every advertising dollar is subtracted from the profit it brings in

458.name: Top Impression Rate
458.description: The share of the ad's impressions that appeared in the block above the search results. Calculated from all of the ad's impressions.
458.nuances:
The top block **includes all ad** spots above the organic results rather than only the first position within it. An ad in the third spot of the top block goes into the numerator.
Impressions in the bottom and side blocks **don't go** into the numerator but stay in the denominator. Impressions on display network sites are removed from the calculation entirely: they have no search results blocks, and including them in the denominator understates the rate. If a report combines search and the network, split them before calculating.
458.example:
Total impressions: 84,000
Of those, in the top block: 29,400
In the bottom block: 41,200
In the side block: 13,400

Top-block share = 29,400 / 84,000 × 100 = **35%**
458.importance: **It explains** why there are few clicks despite a healthy volume of impressions: at the bottom of the page, the ad is seen less often and clicked less than at the top. When the share drops while the bid hasn't changed, competitors have raised theirs or ad quality has dropped, and that's what needs fixing rather than the ad text.
458.not_needed: Skip it when ads run **only on display network sites**: there are no search results blocks there.
458.essence_note: an ad above the search results is seen by far more people than one below them

459.name: Average Daily Budget
459.formula: Monthly Budget / Average Number of Days in a Month
459.description: How much to spend per day on average to stay within the monthly budget. A benchmark for setting the daily limit in the ad account.
459.nuances:
This is a planned value, unlike Search Ads Spend on this map, which **counts what was charged**: here you set a limit for the day, while how much the platform actually charges depends on demand.
Ad platforms allow overspending on some days when demand is high and spend less on others: **the monthly total** matches the budget, rather than each day's spend.
**The daily limit cuts impressions** when the money runs out: ads stop in the middle of the day and miss evening demand, so an even split doesn't suit every business.
**The number of days in** a month varies, and dividing by 30.4 instead of the actual number shifts the result by about 2% in a 31-day month and by about 8% in February.
459.example:
Monthly budget: $9,450
Days in the month: 31

Average Daily Budget = 9,450 / 31 = **$304.84**

Actually charged on Friday: $413; on Tuesday: $214. The platform balances the total over the month.
459.importance: **It turns the approved budget into** a setting you can enter in the ad account. A limit that's too low stops ads before the end of the day and hands evening inquiries to competitors; one that's too high uses up the monthly budget early and leaves the end of the month without any ads.
459.not_needed: **Skip it** when the budget has no upper limit and campaigns run as long as [[Search Ads Cost per Conversion→poiskovaya_reklama/stoimost_konversii]] stays within target values.
459.essence_note: a low limit is used up before the evening peak and leaves demand uncaptured, while a high one eats up the monthly budget early in the month

460.name: Search Ads Clicks
460.description: How many times users clicked the ad in the period. A click is counted at the moment it happens, so there are almost always more clicks than sessions in the analytics system.
460.nuances:
**Clicks and website sessions** diverge: some people close the page before the analytics tag loads, so there's always a small gap. It stays steady from period to period, and when it grows, that means a slow website or broken tag code.
**Repeat clicks by one** person within a short time are merged into one click by the ad platform, yet the merging algorithm isn't disclosed and differs between platforms.
**The platform filters out invalid** clicks and refunds the money for them, and because of that the number in reports for past days can go down retroactively.
460.example:
Clicks recorded: 3,970
Filtered out as invalid: 190

Search Ads Clicks = **3,780**

Sessions in the analytics system: 3,260
Gap of 14%: people left before the page loaded
460.importance: **It's the volume of traffic** you paid for, and the basis for the cost per click and the conversion rate. A noticeable gap between clicks and sessions most often means money lost to slow loading: the click is paid for, but the person never reached the website.
460.synonyms: Paid Search Clicks, PPC Clicks, Ad Clicks
460.essence_note: every click is a person brought to the website

461.name: Search Ads CTR
461.description: The share of impressions that ended in a click on the ad. It's calculated from impressions rather than people: one person can see the ad several times.
461.nuances:
The numerator and denominator **are taken from the same** set of placements. Dividing search-only clicks by impressions that include the display network understates CTR, because the network has far more impressions and people click there less often.
**Invalid clicks filtered out by the platform** are removed from the numerator, while their impressions stay in the denominator: because of this, the recalculated CTR for a past period comes out lower than what was visible at the time of the impressions.
461.example:
Impressions: 84,000
Clicks counted: 3,780
Filtered out as invalid: 190 (already excluded)

CTR = 3,780 / 84,000 × 100 = **4.5%**
461.importance: The first signal that the ad **doesn't match the query**: people see it and scroll past. It reacts earlier than the cost per conversion, because enough impressions for a conclusion pile up much sooner than enough inquiries. Ad platforms factor CTR into ad quality, so a drop in CTR raises the cost per click at the same bid.
461.not_needed: **Skip it in campaigns** that pay for impressions rather than clicks: display formats work for reach, and a low CTR there isn't a sign of a problem.
461.essence_note: the more impressions end in a click, the cheaper each click

462.name: Conversion Lag
462.formula: Average time from click to conversion
462.description: How much time passes on average from an ad click to the conversion. Shows how long people take to decide.
462.nuances:
**Only completed conversions count**: people who are still thinking it over or will never buy aren't in the average, so the real decision cycle is longer than the calculated one.
**The [[Conversion Window→poiskovaya_reklama/okno_konversiy]] cuts off** later conversions: with a 7-day window, the average can't exceed a week, even if half the buyers purchase in the third week.
**The average is sensitive to** a few deals that take a long time to close, and the median is usually noticeably lower: with an average of 9 days, half of purchases may happen within the first day.
462.example:
[[Conversion Window→poiskovaya_reklama/okno_konversiy]] widened to 30 days to capture late conversions
Conversions for March with this window: 247
Of those, within the first day: 104
On days 2–7: 61
On days 8–30: 82
Total time to conversion: 2,223 days

Conversion Lag = 2,223 / 247 = **9 days**

The median here is 1 day: the deals that took a long time pulled the average up. With a 7-day window, the same clicks would have given 199 conversions, and the lag couldn't have exceeded a week.
462.importance: **It sets** how long the [[Conversion Window→poiskovaya_reklama/okno_konversiy]] should be and how many days must pass before a campaign's results can be judged at all. If conclusions about a launch are drawn on day three while the lag is nine days, not all inquiries have come in yet, and an effective campaign gets turned off as unprofitable.
462.not_needed: **Skip it for** impulse purchases, where the decision is made in the same session: the lag is measured in minutes and doesn't affect the settings.
462.synonyms: Days to Conversion, Time to Conversion, Time Lag
462.essence_note: the longer people delay their decision after the click, the more of them change their minds and never convert

463.name: Search Ads Conversion Rate
463.description: The share of ad clicks that ended in a conversion. The denominator is clicks, so the rate relates directly to the cost per click.
463.nuances:
Conversions in the numerator **are counted with the same** attribution model as in [[Search Ads Conversions→poiskovaya_reklama/konversii]]: changing the model changes only the numerator, and the result jumps even though traffic stayed the same.
**A click and a session** aren't the same thing: if the numerator comes from session-based data in the analytics system and the denominator from clicks in the ad account, the result is understated by the gap between them.
**If you count all conversions** rather than unique ones, the result can exceed 100% when one person submits several inquiries in a single session.
463.example:
Clicks: 3,780
Conversions: 199

Search Ads Conversion Rate = 199 / 3,780 × 100 = **5.3%**

Using sessions (3,260) as the denominator gives 6.1%: a nicer number, but it doesn't describe the traffic you paid for.
463.importance: **It separates two different problems**: poor traffic and a poor website. With a normal CTR and a low conversion rate, the money is lost on the landing page, and changing the ads won't help. This rate links the cost of a click to the cost of a conversion, so it's used to work out the maximum bid the business can afford.
463.not_needed: **Skip it** when the conversion happens off the website: a call without call tracking, an office visit, an order through an intermediary. There's no way to capture those conversions.
463.synonyms: Conv. Rate, Paid Search Conversion Rate, Click-to-Conversion Rate
463.essence_note: the more clicks end in a conversion, the less each result costs

464.name: Conversion Value per Cost
464.description: How much money conversions brought in for each dollar of ad spend. A value of 1 means the ads returned exactly what was spent.
464.nuances:
The metric compares revenue with spend rather than profit with spend: the cost of goods and other expenses **aren't included**, so a return of 2 at a 30% margin means a loss.
Value and spend **should cover the same** window: value keeps being added to the click date for several more days, and recent periods always look worse than they will once that value comes in.
Value and spend **come from the same** set of campaigns; otherwise the return is overstated.
**The attribution model shifts** revenue between channels: under last-click attribution, search loses some of the orders that started with it.
464.example:
[[Total Conversion Value→poiskovaya_reklama/cennost_konversiy]]: $74,400
Spend: $9,450

Conversion Value per Cost = 74,400 / 9,450 = **7.9**

At a 25% margin, gross profit = $18,600, which covers the spend almost twice over.

At a 10% margin, profit would be $7,440: the ads would be in the red.
464.importance: The only metric on the map that answers the owner's question: did we earn money or just spend it? It's used to allocate money across campaigns and channels, because a cheap inquiry for a cheap product returns less than an expensive inquiry for an expensive one. The break-even point **is calculated from the margin**, and without that adjustment a good-looking number hides a loss.
464.not_needed: **Skip it** when [[Total Conversion Value→poiskovaya_reklama/cennost_konversiy]] isn't reported or the revenue per conversion is the same for every conversion: the cost per conversion is enough then.
464.synonyms: ROAS, Return on Ad Spend, Conv. Value / Cost
464.essence_note: the more money each ad dollar brings in, the more profitable the advertising

465.name: Conversion Window
465.description: How many days after a click the ad platform keeps crediting conversions to that click. It's an account setting rather than a calculated result.
465.nuances:
**The width of the window directly** sets the number of conversions: with a 7-day window, some purchases with a long decision process won't make it into the report at all; with a 90-day window, the report will include purchases the ads had almost nothing to do with.
**The window should be** wider than the actual conversion lag; otherwise the cost and return metrics systematically understate the contribution of advertising.
Changing the window affects more than **just future numbers**: it also changes how a comparison with the past looks, so two periods with different windows can't be compared.
465.example:
Average [[Conversion Lag→poiskovaya_reklama/cikl_konversiy]]: 9 days
Window set: 7 days
Conversions credited for March: 199

Conversions credited for March with a 30-day window: 247

The difference of 48 conversions: purchases that happened more than a week after the click
465.importance: **It determines** how much of the result gets credited to the ads at all. A narrow window with a long decision cycle makes search unprofitable on paper, campaigns get turned off, and then sales drop in other channels too, because the top of the funnel was removed.
465.not_needed: **No need to adjust it** when the decision is made in the same session and the [[Conversion Lag→poiskovaya_reklama/cikl_konversiy]] is measured in minutes: any window longer than a day gives the same result.
465.synonyms: Lookback Window, Click-Through Conversion Window, Attribution Window
465.essence_note: a short window undercounts sales with a long decision process, while a long one credits the ads with purchases that happened for other reasons

466.name: Search Ads Conversions
466.description: How many conversions were completed by users who came from ads. A conversion is whatever was set up in advance as a conversion action: an inquiry, a call, a purchase, a signup.
466.nuances:
The longer the customer's path to an inquiry, the more the conversion count depends on the attribution model. Under last-click attribution, the inquiry is credited to the last ad the person clicked; under first-click attribution, to the ad through which they first learned about the company. Search looks stronger under first click and weaker under last click, and you can compare **only numbers from** the same model.
**Decide** whether to count repeat conversions by the same person: if you count all conversions, one person's three purchases count as three; if you count unique ones, they count as one. For inquiries, all conversions are usually counted; for signups, unique ones.
A conversion **is assigned to the date** of the click rather than the date of the action itself, so yesterday's numbers keep growing for several more days.
466.example:
Clicks in March: 3,780
Form inquiries: 148
Calls from the website: 51
Repeat inquiries from the same people: 22

Conversions (all) = 148 + 51 = **199**
Conversions (unique) = 199 − 22 = 177
466.importance: **The result** you buy the traffic for, and the denominator of the cost per conversion. Without one attribution model across all channels, search ads either take credit for other channels' sales or give away their own, and the budget gets reallocated to whichever channel simply happened to be closer to the purchase.
466.not_needed: Skip it when the deal closes **only offline** and the data isn't sent back to the ad platform: there's no conversion on the website, and you'll have to judge by calls and revenue.
466.synonyms: Conversions, Paid Search Conversions, PPC Conversions
466.essence_note: these are the actions the ads were launched for

467.name: Search Ads CPC
467.description: How much one ad click cost on average. It's the actual price after the auctions rather than the bid set in the account.
467.nuances:
Clicks **are the same ones** as in [[Search Ads Clicks→poiskovaya_reklama/kliki]]: invalid clicks are excluded along with the money refunded for them; otherwise the average price is overstated.
**If spend is divided** by website sessions rather than by clicks from the ad account, the average price is inflated by the full gap between the two, although the clicks cost the same.
Spend **excludes the agency fee** and ad production costs: with them, it becomes the company's traffic cost rather than the price of a click.
467.example:
Spend: $9,450
Clicks: 3,780

CPC = 9,450 / 3,780 = **$2.50**

The maximum bid here is $3.60: the auction charges less than the ceiling.

Dividing by sessions (3,260) gives $2.90: overstated because the denominator changed from clicks to sessions.
467.importance: **It shows** what the auction actually cost, and together with the conversion rate it fully determines the cost per conversion. A rising average cost per click at an unchanged bid means competitors raised theirs or ad quality dropped, and this becomes visible before inquiries get more expensive.
467.synonyms: Avg. CPC, Average Cost per Click, Paid Search CPC
467.essence_note: the cheaper the click, the more people the same budget brings in

468.name: Search Ads CPM
468.description: How much a thousand ad impressions cost. Shows the price of reaching the audience whether or not people clicked the ad.
468.nuances:
Spend and impressions **are taken from the same** set of placements. Dividing search-only spend by impressions that include the display network understates CPM, because the network has far more impressions for the same spend.
In search advertising you pay for clicks, so this value is calculated: it **changes with both** the cost per click and CTR, and a rise can mean either a more expensive auction or a better ad.
Spend **is the same** as in Search Ads Spend: without the agency fee or ad production costs.
468.example:
Spend: $9,450
Search impressions: 84,000

CPM = 9,450 / 84,000 × 1,000 = **$112.50**

Adding 610,000 display network impressions to the denominator gives $13.62: that's the cost of impressions in a different channel.
468.importance: **The only value** that lets you compare search with display placements and social media ads, where you pay for impressions. Within search, it works as an early sign of overheating: a rising cost per thousand impressions at an unchanged CTR means the auction has become more expensive, and the bid decision gets made before this shows up in the cost per inquiry.
468.not_needed: **Skip it** when the campaign's goal is to capture existing demand. You pay for clicks there, and decisions are based on their cost rather than the cost of impressions.
468.synonyms: Cost per Mille, Cost per Thousand Impressions, Avg. CPM
468.essence_note: the cheaper a thousand impressions, the more attention the same budget buys

469.name: First Page Bid Estimate
469.description: The bid at which the ad platform forecasts that the ad will make it onto the first page of search results. The minimum threshold for getting impressions.
469.nuances:
**It's a visibility threshold** rather than a position threshold: at this bid, the ad will be on the first page, most often in the block below the organic results.
**A bid below the threshold** means no impressions rather than cheap clicks: the ad is active in the account but doesn't win the auction.
**The forecast depends on** ad quality and is recalculated from recent auctions.
469.example:
First page bid estimate: $1.35
Current keyword bid: $0.90
Impressions for the keyword over the week: 0

First Page Bid Estimate = **$1.35**

The bid is $0.45 below the threshold, so ads for this keyword don't show at all.
469.importance: **It explains keywords with no impressions**: they're active in the account, yet their ads never show, and without this threshold, people look for the cause in ad review or targeting. It's also used to calculate the minimum cost of entry in a topic, to decide whether the business can afford search ads for this query at all.
469.not_needed: **Skip it with** automated bidding strategies and in niches without competition, where any bid wins the auction.
469.synonyms: First Page Bid, First Page CPC
469.essence_note: the lower the price of getting onto the first page, the cheaper it is for an ad to show up in the results at all

470.name: First Position Bid Estimate
470.description: The bid at which the ad platform forecasts that the ad will show in the very top ad spot. A platform forecast rather than a guarantee.
470.nuances:
The forecast is based on recent auction history and **changes along with** competitors' bids, so the value goes stale quickly.
**The estimate factors in ad quality**, so two advertisers on the same keyword see different numbers: a higher-quality ad gets the same position for less.
**Setting the recommended bid** doesn't give you the first position on every impression: the forecast describes a typical auction rather than each one.
470.example:
First position bid estimate: $6.25
Current maximum bid: $3.60
Current absolute top share: 14%

First Position Bid Estimate = **$6.25**

After the bid was set to $6.25, the absolute top share rose to 58% rather than to 100%.
470.importance: **It turns the goal of being first** into a specific price and lets you check it with a calculator before spending money. If at this bid the cost per conversion comes out above the margin per sale, the question is settled without an experiment, and the budget isn't burned on testing the obvious.
470.not_needed: Skip it with automated bidding strategies: the platform sets the bids, and you can't enter the recommended number **manually**.
470.essence_note: the cheaper the top spot, the more clicks the same budget brings

471.name: Frequency Cap
471.description: A limit on how many times an ad is shown to one person in a period. An account setting that keeps ads from being shown to the same people too often.
471.nuances:
**The cap works at** the level of a browser ID or a signed-in account: a person who uses both a phone and a computer gets the full cap on each device.
**Lowering the cap reduces** impressions and increases reach on the same budget: the money goes to new people instead of repeat impressions. Raising it does the opposite and drives up frequency among the same audience.
A frequency cap **applies to impressions** on the display network: on search, the ad shows in response to a query, and a person who searches ten times will see the ad ten times.
471.example:
Display network impressions without a cap: 610,000
Reach: 92,000
Average frequency: 6.6

Cap set: **3 impressions per day**

After setting the cap, with the same budget: 540,000 impressions, reach 178,000, average frequency 3.0
471.importance: **It controls** whether money goes to expanding the audience or to repeatedly targeting people who've already seen the ad. At high frequency, people stop noticing the ads, CTR drops, and the cost per click rises as ad quality falls. At too low a frequency, people don't get the repeat exposure they need to decide in a long decision cycle.
471.not_needed: Skip it in **search-only** campaigns: there an impression is triggered by the user's query, and a frequency cap can't limit it.
471.essence_note: a person doesn't notice a single impression, but after several repeats the ad starts to annoy them

472.name: Search Ads Impressions
472.description: How many times the ad was displayed to users in the period. Impressions are counted rather than people: if one person was shown the ad ten times, that's ten impressions.
472.nuances:
**An impression is counted** when the ad loads on the page, whether or not the person scrolled down to it: ads in the bottom block collect impressions no one saw.
**Impressions on search** and on display network sites are looked at separately. They behave differently: on search, the person typed the query themselves; on the network, the ad reaches them on third-party websites, so there are far more impressions there and CTR is lower. Combined in one report, they produce a blended average that says nothing about either. Some platforms keep search and the network in separate campaigns; in others, the network is enabled within a search campaign through a setting, and then the split has to be made at the report level.
472.example:
Search impressions: 84,000
Display network impressions: 610,000

Impressions (search only) = **84,000**
Impressions (including the network) = 694,000

CTR on search is 4.5%, with the network 0.6%: these are different placements rather than a drop in the ad's performance.
472.importance: **The denominator of CTR** and of the cost per thousand impressions, so mixing search with the network distorts several metrics on the map at once. On its own, the number speaks to the volume of demand: a drop in impressions at an unchanged bid means there are fewer searches or competitors have raised the auction price.
472.synonyms: Impr., Paid Search Impressions, Ad Impressions
472.essence_note: without an impression, the ad can't work at all

473.name: Search Ads Keywords
473.description: How many keywords are used in search ads. Counts the keywords added to campaigns rather than the queries users typed.
473.nuances:
The same keyword with different match types **counts as separate keywords**: broad, phrase and exact match behave differently in the auction.
Paused keywords and keywords disapproved in ad review are usually excluded: **they don't generate** impressions, while in the total count they create an illusion of coverage.
**A keyword and an actual** search query are different things. For one broad match keyword, the platform shows the ad for many different phrasings, so the number of keywords says nothing about query coverage.
473.example:
Total keywords in the account: 640
Of those, paused manually: 95
Disapproved in ad review: 28

Search Ads Keywords = 640 − 95 − 28 = **517**

Unique search queries that triggered impressions: 4,200
473.importance: It determines how manageable a campaign is: no one checks a long keyword list **manually**, and many keywords keep spending money without a single inquiry. A sharp rise in the number of keywords without a rise in conversions means the keyword list was expanded for reach rather than for sales.
473.not_needed: Skip it in campaigns without a manual keyword list: in dynamic search ads and shopping campaigns, the platform matches queries itself based on the feed or website content, and there's no keyword list to count. Automated bidding strategies don't do away with keywords by themselves: they manage bids, while the keyword list stays manual and **is counted as usual**.
473.essence_note: too narrow a list limits impressions, while too broad a list brings irrelevant clicks for the same money

474.name: Maximum CPC Bid
474.description: The maximum amount an advertiser is willing to pay for one click. Set manually, it caps what the ad can bid in the auction.
474.nuances:
**The actual cost per click** is almost always lower than the maximum bid: the auction charges the amount needed to beat the next competitor rather than the stated ceiling.
The bid **is set at different** levels, and the one set at the most granular level applies: a keyword-level bid overrides the ad group's bid.
Bid adjustments for devices, time and audiences **apply on top of the bid** and change it at auction time, so the real ceiling differs from the number entered.
474.example:
Maximum bid set: $3.60
Mobile adjustment: +30%
Real ceiling on mobile: $4.68
Actually charged on average: $2.50

Maximum CPC Bid = **$3.60**
474.importance: **The only lever** that directly controls volume under manual bidding: raise the ceiling, and you get more top impressions and more expensive clicks. A typo with one extra digit burns through the daily budget quickly, and the money can't be recovered.
474.not_needed: **Don't set it with** automated bidding strategies, where the platform is given a target [[Search Ads Cost per Conversion→poiskovaya_reklama/stoimost_konversii]] or return on ad spend and manages bids on its own.
474.synonyms: Max CPC, Max. CPC Bid, Max Bid
474.essence_note: a low ceiling leaves the ad without impressions, while a high one lets the platform overpay for clicks

475.name: Negative Keywords
475.description: How many negative keywords have been added to campaigns so the ad doesn't show for irrelevant queries. Counts the words and phrases added rather than the queries blocked.
475.nuances:
Negative keywords work at different levels: those set for a campaign block impressions in all its ad groups, those set for an ad group only within that group. The same word added at both levels **counts twice**.
Match type applies to negative keywords too: a broad negative can cut off whole swaths of relevant queries, while an exact one blocks **only that specific query**.
Shared lists attached to several campaigns are usually counted **separately** from the campaign's own negative keywords; otherwise one list inflates the count across the whole account.
475.example:
Negative keywords at the campaign level: 340
Negative keywords within ad groups: 210
Negative keywords in the attached shared list: 1,500 (counted separately)

Negative Keywords = 340 + 210 = **550**
475.importance: **A measure of how** thoroughly junk traffic is filtered out of the campaign. An empty list means money goes to queries about freebies, reviews and jobs, and in reports this looks like expensive clicks and a low conversion rate. The opposite mistake also costs money: an overgrown list with broad negatives chokes impressions, and volume drops for no visible reason.
475.not_needed: **Skip it where** no negative keyword list is kept: there's nothing to count. In campaigns without a manual keyword list, on the other hand, negative keywords remain the main way to cut off irrelevant impressions, and the metric is needed there just as much.
475.essence_note: without negative keywords, the budget goes to irrelevant queries, and with too many, the ad stops showing to the right people

476.name: Top of Page Bid Estimate
476.description: The bid at which the ad platform forecasts that the ad will show in the block above the search results. A platform forecast rather than a guarantee.
476.nuances:
The estimate is lower than the one for the first position because it covers getting into the block **as a whole**, including the second and third positions.
Ad quality **is factored in**: a weak ad gets a higher estimate for the same position.
**The value is recalculated from** recent auction history and quickly goes out of date.
476.example:
Top of page bid estimate: $4.35
[[First Position Bid Estimate→poiskovaya_reklama/ocenka_stavki_dlya_pervoy_pozicii]]: $6.25
Current bid: $3.60

Top of Page Bid Estimate = **$4.35**

The $1.90 difference is the price of moving from any spot in the block to the very top.
476.importance: It gives a middle-ground benchmark between the expensive top and the cheap bottom of the page. The gap between this estimate and the first position estimate shows what it costs to aim for the very top: a spot in the top block **can cost much less**, while the difference in click volume may be small.
476.not_needed: **Skip it with** automated bidding strategies, where the platform manages bids.
476.synonyms: Top of Page Bid, Top of Page CPC
476.essence_note: the less it costs to get into the top block, the more affordable a prominent position on the same budget

477.name: Search Ads Reach
477.description: How many different people saw the ad at least once in the period. Each person is counted once, however many impressions they got.
477.nuances:
Unique users **are identified by their** browser IDs or signed-in accounts on the platform. One person on a phone and on a work computer counts as two, and two family members on one browser count as one.
**Reach doesn't add up** across periods or campaigns: the sum of reach for two separate weeks is greater than the reach for the two weeks together, because some people saw the ads in both weeks.
Overlaps are removed **only by the ad platform** itself.
477.example:
Impressions: 84,000
Unique users: 31,500

Search Ads Reach = **31,500**

Average frequency = 84,000 / 31,500 = 2.7 impressions per person

Reach of 12,000 in the first week and 14,000 in the second doesn't add up to 26,000 for the two weeks: some of the people are the same.
477.importance: **It answers** how many people learned about the offer at all, rather than how many times the ad ran. Without reach, you can't tell which of two things is behind a rise in impressions: new people were reached, or the same people were shown the ad more often. In the second case, the budget grows while the audience stays the same.
477.not_needed: **Skip it** when the campaign's goal is to capture existing demand from narrow commercial queries. What matters there is the cost per inquiry, and the size of the audience is set by the number of searches rather than by the ads.
477.essence_note: the more different people saw the ad, the wider the audience the offer reached

478.name: Absolute Top Impression Rate
478.description: The share of the ad's impressions that appeared in the very top ad spot on the page. Calculated from all of the ad's impressions.
478.nuances:
**The first position** is the top row above the organic results, so this share is always less than or equal to the Top Impression Rate.
**Impressions on display** network sites are removed from the calculation: they have no search result positions, and including them in the denominator understates the rate. If a report combines search and the network, split them before calculating.
478.example:
Total impressions: 84,000
Impressions in the top block: 29,400
Of those, in the very top row: 11,800

Absolute top share = 11,800 / 84,000 × 100 = **14%**

Dividing by top-block impressions gives 40%: that's the first-position share within the top block rather than of all impressions.
478.importance: **It shows** what the advertiser actually pays for in the most expensive position. The first row gets the most clicks for a query, so this share is used to decide whether to catch up with competitors through bids or move to cheaper queries where the top spot doesn't require overpaying.
478.not_needed: Skip it when ads run **only on the display** network and when working with low-volume queries without competition: there the ad is almost always at the top anyway.
478.essence_note: the top spot gets noticeably more clicks at the same bid

479.name: Average Monthly Searches
479.formula: Total Searches for the Period / Number of Months
479.description: How many times a month, on average, users search for a keyword. A demand estimate from the ad platform based on search history.
479.nuances:
**The value is averaged over** several months, so a seasonal peak gets smoothed out: for Christmas ornaments, the annual average tells you nothing about December.
The estimate **is based on the wording** of the keyword rather than its match type. With broad match, there will be more impressions than the estimate; with exact match, fewer.
**Demand for a keyword** isn't the same as eligible impressions: some searches come from regions and devices that aren't in the campaign settings.
479.example:
Searches for the keyword over 12 months: 96,000
Of those, in December: 34,000

Average per month = 96,000 / 12 = **8,000**

In December, demand is 4 times the average, and planning the budget around 8,000 means missing the seasonal peak.
479.importance: The basis for planning before launch: it shows whether a keyword has enough volume to be worth writing ads and building a landing page for. A mistake here comes to light **only after the campaign has been running** for a while, when the campaign is already built, the money for preparation is spent, and there are almost no impressions.
479.not_needed: **Skip it when** you already have historical performance data from your own campaigns: actual impressions are more accurate than any outside estimate.
479.synonyms: Search Volume, Monthly Search Volume, Avg. Monthly Searches
479.essence_note: the more often a query is entered, the more people it can bring in

480.name: Search Ads Cost per Conversion
480.description: How much one conversion cost on average. It links the money spent to the result you bought the traffic for.
480.nuances:
Conversions **are counted using the same** attribution model as in [[Search Ads Conversions→poiskovaya_reklama/konversii]]: with the same spend, search shows cheaper inquiries under first-click attribution and more expensive ones under last-click.
Spend and conversions should cover the same window: conversions are credited to the click date and keep coming in for several days, so the cost for a **just-closed** month looks inflated in the first days and then goes down.
Spend **excludes the agency fee** and ad production costs.
**If the denominator** counts all conversions rather than unique ones, the cost comes out lower: repeat inquiries from one person share the same spend.
480.example:
Spend: $9,450
Conversions: 199

Search Ads Cost per Conversion = 9,450 / 199 = **$47.49**

With unique conversions (177), it comes to $53.39.

On the third day after the month closed, there were 172 conversions and a cost per conversion of $54.94: the number settled within a week.
480.importance: **The main measure for deciding** whether to turn a campaign off or add money: it's compared with the margin the business earns per deal. Without it, a cheap click is taken for success, even though an inquiry from that traffic can cost much more than one from a more expensive source.
480.not_needed: **Skip it** when conversions aren't tracked or there are only a handful in the period: with a few inquiries, the average cost depends on one or two random deals, and you can't make decisions based on it.
480.synonyms: CPA, Cost / Conv., Cost per Acquisition
480.essence_note: the cheaper each conversion, the more conversions the same spend brings

481.name: Total Conversion Value
481.formula: Sum of the values of all conversions
481.description: How much money the conversions credited to the ads brought in, in total. The values of all conversions in the period are added up.
481.nuances:
Value is either the actual order amount or a number assigned manually to each conversion action. With assigned values, the total reflects the marketer's estimate rather than money actually received, and when the estimate is revised, the total **changes on its own**, with no new sales.
Canceled orders and returns **are subtracted** only if the data is sent back to the ad platform; otherwise the total stays above actual revenue by the full value of canceled orders and returns.
Value **is tied to the date** of the click and keeps being added for several days, so the total for a recent period grows retroactively.
481.example:
Orders with a reported value: 199
Order total: $74,400
Cancellations reported to the platform: 0

Total Conversion Value = **$74,400**

A week later, the total grew to $77,700: conversions from March clicks were added.
481.importance: **The numerator of Conversion Value per Cost** and of Value per Conversion, so an error here carries over into both. Automated bidding strategies that maximize conversion value learn from exactly this data: if value isn't reported for every order, the platform optimizes on incomplete data and turns off what actually brings in money.
481.not_needed: Skip it in businesses where the deal amount becomes known only after negotiations and isn't sent back to the ad platform: the inquiry remains the conversion, and the money **is counted outside the ad account**.
481.synonyms: Conversion Value, Conv. Value, Attributed Revenue
481.essence_note: this is the money the ads brought in over the period

482.name: Value per Conversion
482.description: How much money one conversion brings in on average. Calculated by dividing the total value by the number of conversions that value was assigned to.
482.nuances:
The numerator and denominator **are taken from the same** set of conversion actions: if value is reported only for purchases while the denominator also includes inquiries, the average comes out too low.
Value is either actual, when the order amount is sent to the platform, or assigned manually, when each inquiry gets a fixed number. Actual value reflects real money; assigned value shows only what the marketer put in, and when the estimate changes, the number **changes on its own**, while sales have no effect on it.
Value **is taken from** [[Total Conversion Value→poiskovaya_reklama/cennost_konversiy]] and follows the same rules; otherwise the average won't match the return on ad spend, which relies on the same number.
Cancellations and returns usually **aren't subtracted automatically**: unless the data is sent back, the average stays inflated.
482.example:
[[Total Conversion Value→poiskovaya_reklama/cennost_konversiy]]: $74,400
Conversions with a reported value: 199

Value per Conversion = 74,400 / 199 = **$373.87**

Adding 340 inquiries without a value to the denominator gives $138.03: that's the average across all conversion actions rather than the value of a conversion.
482.importance: **It sets the ceiling for an acceptable cost** per conversion: as long as a conversion costs less than its average value adjusted for margin, the campaign can be scaled up. Automated bidding strategies learn from this number, and an understated value makes the platform hold back and lose high-value orders.
482.not_needed: **Skip it** when [[Total Conversion Value→poiskovaya_reklama/cennost_konversiy]] isn't sent to the ad platform: there's nothing to divide.
482.essence_note: the more valuable each conversion, the more money the same ads bring in

483.name: Impression Share
483.description: What part of the eligible auctions the ad actually won. Shows how many impressions it received out of those it had a chance to compete for.
483.nuances:
**Eligible impressions** are the ad platform's estimate of how many times the ad could have shown with the current targeting settings. It's an estimated value, and platforms use different methods to calculate it.
**Losses are split by cause**: the budget ran short, or the bid and ad quality fell short. Without this split, the number shows the problem but not its source.
Auctions the ad didn't enter because of targeting settings **aren't included** in the denominator: narrowing the targeting raises the share even though impressions go down.
483.example:
Impressions received: 84,000
Estimated eligible impressions: 210,000

Impression Share = 84,000 / 210,000 × 100 = **40%**

Lost to budget: 35%
Lost to bid and quality: 25%
483.importance: It answers whether there's room to grow without new queries and new campaigns. At a 40% share, less than half of the demand is captured, and growth is possible by adding money rather than by reworking the ads. When the share is high, you've hit the ceiling of demand, and a bigger budget will bring **only expensive clicks**.
483.not_needed: **Skip it** when the ad platform doesn't report estimated eligible impressions: a numerator without a denominator is meaningless.
483.synonyms: Search Impression Share, Search IS, Impr. Share
483.essence_note: every lost auction is an impression a competitor took

484.name: Backlinks
484.description: The number of external links from other websites pointing to your website.
484.nuances:
**Links that pass link equity are counted**: links with nofollow, sponsored and ugc attributes are reported on a separate line; otherwise, links bought on link marketplaces and links in comments inflate the number without affecting rankings.
Several links from one referring domain **are counted separately**: one site with a sitewide block gives many links, so the number of links alone doesn't show reach.
**Stick to one data source**: backlink tools build their databases with their own crawlers, and the databases differ, so you can compare periods only within one tool, never across tools.
The number **is cumulative as of the check date** rather than growth over the period: some old links drop off, and the cumulative total can fall on its own.
484.example:
Backlink tool as of March 1
Total links found: 14,800
Of those, with nofollow and similar attributes: 5,100 (reported separately)
Passing link equity: 9,700
Of those, 6,200 come from one referring domain with a sitewide block in the footer

Backlinks = **9,700**

Without a breakdown by referring domain, the number looks strong, even though two-thirds came from one site.
484.importance: **It shows the size of the accumulated** link profile and the pace of link buying: a sharp jump within a week looks unnatural to a search engine and leads to penalties, while a collapse in the number usually means the contractor stopped renewing rented links. On its own, without a breakdown by referring domain, the number is easy to fake, so decisions are made by looking at it alongside [[Referring Domain Count→seo/ssylayuschiesya_domeny]].
484.not_needed: Skip it when no link-building work is being done: without link buying and outreach to linking sites, the number **changes with random** mentions, and no decisions are made based on it.
484.essence_note: links bring people and lift the website in search results

485.name: Organic Impressions
485.formula: Number of impressions in organic search results
485.description: The number of times the website's pages appeared in organic search results.
485.nuances:
An impression counts when the user opened the page of results where the website appears. A result in 87th place is on the ninth page, and it gets impressions **only when someone** scrolls that far, not on every search.
Impressions on the first page and on later pages work differently: on the first page, almost every search produces them; on later pages, **only searches** where the user kept paging. These groups have different CTRs, so look at impressions by position range rather than as a single number.
Impressions from each search engine **are counted separately and** aren't added together: the engines have different audiences with different results, and one person can see the website in both engines.
Impressions in related blocks (images, videos, product carousels) **aren't included**, so that the composition matches organic clicks; otherwise, [[Organic CTR→seo/organicheskiy_ctr]] is calculated over different sets.
485.example:
Period: March, one search engine
Total impressions: 1,240,000
Of those, in positions 1–10: 310,000
In positions 11–100: 930,000
Impressions in image results: 240,000 (not counted)

Organic Impressions = **1,240,000**

Impressions in low-ranking positions come from searches where users paged past the first page of results. Their CTR is lower than for the first ten results, so the overall click-through rate across all impressions reflects the distribution of positions rather than snippet quality.
485.importance: **Responds earlier than clicks**: growth in impressions with unchanged clicks means the website has started appearing in search results for new queries, but only in low-ranking positions so far. The opposite picture, when impressions fall while clicks hold, usually points to lost reach in the long tail of low-volume queries, and it shows up before traffic drops.
485.essence_note: without appearing in search results, the website gets no clicks from search

486.name: Organic CTR
486.description: The share of impressions in organic search results that ended in a click to the website.
486.nuances:
The numerator and denominator **are taken for the same** search engine, the same period and the same mix of search results: if impressions include images and product listings while clicks don't, the percentage comes out artificially low.
**It's calculated for a specific** page or query rather than for the website as a whole: the aggregate CTR is dragged down by a tail of impressions in low-ranking positions that nobody looked at, and the total number doesn't tell you what to fix.
Branded queries are broken out **separately**: their CTR is higher, and in the total they hide the result for other queries.
Position **is held fixed when comparing**: CTR falls along with position on its own, so a snippet change is evaluated only on queries where the position stayed the same.
486.example:
One query, steadily in 3rd position for the whole period
Impressions: 24,000
Clicks: 1,680

CTR = 1,680 / 24,000 × 100 = **7%**

For the whole website, the same calculation gives 3.7%, because the denominator includes impressions in positions beyond 10: that reflects the distribution of positions rather than snippet effectiveness.
486.importance: **The only metric** that shows the quality of the title and description in search results: the position is the same, impressions are the same, and people click more or less often. A CTR drop at an unchanged position usually means a competitor rewrote their snippet or a new search result block appeared above the organic results. It's used to decide whether to rewrite the title and whether to add structured data with price and rating.
486.not_needed: Skip it when the website ranks **beyond the first page** for most queries: there are plenty of impressions and hardly any clicks, and the low percentage reflects rankings rather than snippet quality.
486.essence_note: the more often people click on the snippet, the more users the website gets from the same positions

487.name: Keyword Rankings
487.formula: Position in organic search results for a keyword
487.description: The website's place in organic search results for a specific query. The lower the number, the higher the website appears in the results.
487.nuances:
Position is recorded **based on organic results**, not counting ads and special search result blocks; otherwise, the same place gives different numbers depending on whether they're present.
Region, device and search engine **are fixed**: results for the same query differ between New York and Chicago, and between mobile and desktop.
Rankings are checked **anonymously**, without browsing history or being signed in: personalized results push up websites the user has already visited.
If the website **isn't in the top 100** results, the position is recorded as "outside the top 100" rather than as a number: substituting 100 or 101 creates the appearance of a measured value and distorts any average.
Rankings **change during** the day, so how the number was obtained matters. A third-party rank tracker gives the position at the moment of the check, and it's run at the same time of day; otherwise, numbers for different days aren't comparable. Search Console shows an average position for the period, weighted by impressions, rather than an instantaneous one: a position where the website was shown more often carries more weight, so the values aren't whole numbers. The two methods give different numbers, and they mustn't be mixed in one report.
487.example:
Query: "buy treadmill"
Region: New York, device: mobile, checked at 10:00 a.m.
Results from top to bottom: 2 ad blocks, then organic results
The website is the fourth organic result

Position = **4**

Counting the ads would give 6: numbers for different periods would no longer be comparable, because the number of ads in search results changes.
487.importance: The fastest signal: rankings respond to changes sooner than traffic, which **changes noticeably later**. They're used to catch the effects of edits and algorithm updates before revenue shows them, and to identify queries sitting at the edge of the first page that need only a small push to reach the top 10.
487.not_needed: **Skip it for** queries with heavily personalized or location-dependent results, where every user sees their own top ten: the measured value doesn't reflect what people see.
487.essence_note: the lower the number, the higher the website's listing in search results and the more clicks it gets

488.name: Pages with Indexing Errors
488.formula: Number of pages with indexing issues
488.description: The number of pages that the search engine couldn't properly crawl or index.
488.nuances:
**Pages are counted**, not issue types: five types of errors can affect three pages or thirty thousand, and the scale isn't visible from the number of types.
Pages intentionally blocked from indexing **are excluded** from the count: Search Console lists them under Not indexed together with the errors, though that's the result of a setting rather than a problem.
A page with several errors **counts once**; otherwise, the count exceeds the number of pages on the website.
Pages with errors **are counted separately** for each search engine: each engine's webmaster tools have their own sets and names of issues, and they can't be combined into one number.
488.example:
Search Console, Page indexing report as of March 1
Pages in the Not indexed section: 5,400
Of those, intentionally blocked via robots.txt and noindex: 4,100 (not counted)
Canonicalized duplicates: 900 (not counted, consolidation works)
Server error (5xx) during crawling: 260
Page not found, although it's in the sitemap: 140

Pages with Indexing Errors = 260 + 140 = **400** pages
488.importance: Gives a ready-made list of what to fix when the indexing percentage has dropped: it shows both **how many pages** were lost and the reason. Server errors during crawling are especially urgent, because the search engine lowers the crawl rate for the whole website, and getting the affected pages reindexed after that takes time.
488.not_needed: Skip it for websites **with a dozen or so pages**: indexing problems there are visible in the page list in Search Console, and a separate number isn't needed.
488.essence_note: a page with an error won't appear in search results and won't bring a single user

489.name: Average Position
489.formula:
By keyword set (own rank tracking): Sum of Keyword Positions / Number of Keywords
By impressions (Search Console): Sum of Positions across All Impressions / Number of Impressions
489.description: The website's average place in organic search results across a set of tracked queries. The lower the value, the higher the website ranks on average.
489.nuances:
The two versions give different numbers. In the first, each query carries **equal** weight, and you see movement across the selected set. In the second, the weight depends on the number of impressions, and the result reflects the mix of search demand rather than the SEO work. Each version is compared only with itself over time.
Search Console shows **only queries** where the website has already appeared. Phrases for which the website isn't in the results won't be there, and they're what the work is aimed at, so the set for your own rank tracking is taken from [[Target Keyword Count→seo/klyuchevye_slova]].
The keyword set and checking rules **match those of** [[Keyword Rankings→seo/pozicii_po_klyuchevym_slovam]]: the same region, device and search engine. The set is fixed: adding low-volume queries worsens the average, even though nothing changed on the website.
Keywords outside the top 100 **are excluded** from the calculation, and their number is shown alongside: substituting 100 ties the average to the tracking cutoff, while dropping them without a note improves the metric when rankings collapse.
489.example:
Set: 250 keywords, New York, mobile, one search engine
Keywords ranking in the top 100: 209
Sum of their positions: 4,807
Keywords outside the top 100: 41 (excluded from the calculation, shown alongside)

Average position for the set = 4,807 / 209 = **23.0** with 41 keywords outside the top 100

Search Console will show 12.4 for the same period: there the average is calculated over impressions, and about ten high-volume queries in the top 5 pull the average toward their own positions.
489.importance: It rolls the movement of the whole query set into one number: individual positions jump around, and the average smooths out the noise. The trap is that moving from 60th place to 40th shifts it more than moving from 11th to 9th, although **only the latter** brings in money, so decisions are made by looking at it alongside the Share of Keywords in Top 10.
489.not_needed: Skip it when the queries in the set **vary widely in search volume**: one average across high-volume and long-tail queries describes neither.
489.essence_note: the lower the average place, the higher the website ranks for its queries and the more clicks it gets

490.name: Organic Click Share
490.formula: (Website Clicks on Tracked Keywords / All Clicks on These Keywords) × 100
490.description: The share of all clicks on tracked keywords in search results that goes to the website. An estimate of how much search demand the website captures and how much goes to competitors.
490.nuances:
The denominator can't be taken from Google Search Console: it shows **only your own website's clicks**.
All clicks for a query **come from a paid third-party** service and are estimated from the query's search volume and a model of how clicks are distributed across positions rather than from the search engine's actual data.
The metric is useful for comparing periods with each other but not as an exact value. The numerator and denominator **are calculated using the same** keyword set from [[Target Keyword Count→seo/klyuchevye_slova]]: when the set grows, the share changes even though rankings stay the same.
Region and device type **are fixed**, because search results and the click distribution differ.
490.example:
Tracked keywords: 120
Website clicks on them in the month (Search Console): 8,400
Estimated total clicks on these 120 keywords (third-party service): 56,000

Organic Click Share = 8,400 / 56,000 × 100 = **15%**

The denominator here is modeled: it's calculated from search volume and a CTR curve by position, so another service would get a different number for the same keywords.
490.importance: It shows the website's position **relative to competitors** when absolute traffic is misleading: clicks can grow along with seasonal demand while market share falls. It's used to decide whether the current strategy is enough to win demand from competitors or whether the website needs to move into new topics.
490.not_needed: **Skip it** when there's no budget for a third-party search analytics service: without the denominator, the metric can't be calculated. It's also meaningless for websites in narrow niches, where few queries are tracked and search volume estimates are too rough.
490.synonyms: Search Visibility, Organic Share of Voice
490.essence_note: the larger the website's share of clicks on its queries, the more people come from search

491.name: Interaction to Next Paint (INP)
491.formula: INP = 75th percentile of interaction latency across page visits
491.description: How quickly a page responds to user actions: clicks, taps, keyboard input. It's the value not exceeded in 75% of page visits, meaning that for three quarters of users, the response took no longer than this.
491.nuances:
**It's calculated from field** data from real users rather than a lab test: a test from one location on one device gives a different number, because it doesn't account for low-end phones and slow networks.
INP **is calculated separately** for mobile and desktop page visits: the value is worse on mobile, and a combined number turns into a meaningless average.
Ready-made data **comes from Search** Console, which always uses a rolling 28-day window that can't be changed. Low-traffic pages don't make it into the report: data appears only once enough visits accumulate.
Break the value down by template type (catalog, product page, blog) rather than looking at the website **as a whole**: different templates have different code, and the overall number hides the problematic section. Search Console groups similar pages by template automatically.
The percentile **is calculated over page visits** rather than individual taps: within one page visit, the slowest interaction counts, and those values are then ranked across all page visits.
491.example:
URL group: product pages, mobile page visits
Source: Search Console, rolling 28-day window
Page visits with a measured interaction: 40,000
In each page visit, the slowest interaction was taken
These values were sorted from best to worst
Value at position 30,000 (75% of 40,000): 240 ms

INP = **240 ms**

A quarter of page visits had a response slower than 240 ms. The average for the same sample would be 130 ms and would hide the problem.
491.importance: It catches **what analytics doesn't show**: the user tapped a button, nothing happened, and they tapped again or left. A delay above 200 ms feels like a sluggish interface, and on mobile it can kill add-to-cart conversion. The value for the website is part of the page experience assessment in search engines.
491.not_needed: Skip it for **static websites** with no interactive elements (simple brochure landing pages, documentation pages): there are no interactions besides scrolling, and the metric isn't collected.
491.essence_note: while the page doesn't respond to a tap, the person thinks it's broken and leaves

492.name: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP)
492.formula: LCP = 75th percentile of time to render the largest element across page visits
492.description: The time until the largest visible element of a page appears: the main image, heading or banner. It's the value not exceeded in 75% of page visits, meaning that for three quarters of users, loading was no slower than this.
492.nuances:
**It's calculated from field** data from real users rather than a lab test: a check from one location on a fast connection gives a better value than the real one.
LCP **is calculated separately** for mobile and desktop page visits: they have different connections and device performance, and a combined value describes neither group.
Ready-made data **comes from Search** Console, which always uses a rolling 28-day window that can't be changed. Low-traffic pages don't make it into the report: data appears only once enough visits accumulate.
Break the value down **by template type**, because the home page, catalog and product page have different largest elements that load differently. Search Console groups similar pages by template automatically.
**The largest element on** the same page can be a different object for different users: it depends on screen size, and on a narrow screen a different part of the page falls within the visible area.
492.example:
URL group: product pages, mobile page visits
Source: Search Console, rolling 28-day window
Page visits to product pages: 52,000
LCP times sorted from best to worst
Value at position 39,000 (75% of 52,000): 3.1 s

LCP = **3.1 s**

The same template on desktop gives 1.6 s, and a lab test gives 1.2 s. The decision is based on 3.1 s, because that's how long real people on phones wait.
