492.importance: It determines whether the user waits for the page to load at all: the longer the wait, the more users close the tab, and those sessions never make it into the funnel. The value **is part of the assessment** of page experience in search engines, so it affects rankings too, but what matters first is that a click you paid for, from ads or search, is lost before the above-the-fold content loads.
492.not_needed: Skip it for low-traffic pages: Search Console shows the value only once **enough visits accumulate**, and rarely visited sections simply have no data.
492.essence_note: people leave before they see the content, and search engines factor speed into rankings

493.name: Organic Clicks
493.formula: Number of clicks from organic search results
493.description: The number of clicks to the website from unpaid search results.
493.nuances:
Clicks from each search engine **are counted separately and** aren't added together: the engines define a click and filter out bots differently, and the same user can click in both engines.
**Branded queries** are reported on a separate line: they come from people who already know the company, and their growth masks a decline in commercial queries.
Clicks from the search engine's related services (images, videos, maps, product listings) **aren't included** in organic search: a different mechanism decides what appears there.
Data arrives with a delay, so the period is closed **only after** the numbers have stabilized; otherwise, the last day's numbers always look artificially low.
493.example:
Period: March 1–31, data pulled on April 4
Clicks from main search: 46,200
Of those, branded: 12,400 (shown separately)
Clicks from image results: 3,800 (not counted)
Clicks from a second search engine: 18,900 (kept on a separate line)

Organic Clicks = **46,200**, of which 33,800 are non-branded
493.importance: **The end result** of all search work: rankings, impressions and indexing matter only to the extent that they turn into clicks. A drop with unchanged rankings points to a change in the search results rather than in the website: an answer box or a product carousel has appeared and captures clicks before users reach the organic results.
493.essence_note: these are clicks you didn't pay a single cent for

494.name: Clicks per Keyword
494.description: The average number of organic clicks that one keyword from the target set brings.
494.nuances:
The denominator **includes all keywords** in the set, including those that got no clicks: if you count only keywords that bring clicks, the metric will grow when clicks for some queries fall to zero. The numerator is limited to clicks on these same keywords rather than all of the website's organic traffic; otherwise, the average picks up a tail of queries that aren't in the set.
Branded queries **are counted separately**: they bring more clicks per keyword, and in the overall average they completely mask the result for commercial queries.
The numerator and denominator **are taken for the same** period and the same search engine.
494.example:
Target keyword set: 250
Of those, branded: 10 (counted separately)
Non-branded keywords: 240
Clicks on non-branded keywords in the month: 12,000
Keywords with zero clicks: 90 (stay in the denominator)

Clicks per Keyword = 12,000 / 240 = **50**

Dropping the zero-click keywords would give 80 clicks per keyword, with the same traffic.
494.importance: It shows **the return on expanding the keyword set**: when hundreds of queries are added to the set and clicks don't grow, the average falls, and you can see that keywords were added just to make the list bigger. It's used to decide whether to focus more effort on existing queries or keep expanding the list.
494.not_needed: Skip it when the keywords in the set **vary widely in search volume**: one average across "buy refrigerator" and a query for a specific model means nothing, and it's more useful to look at the distribution.
494.synonyms: Clicks per Query, Traffic per Keyword
494.essence_note: the more clicks one query brings, the fewer queries you need to push to the top

495.name: Target Keyword Count
495.description: The number of queries the website deliberately targets.
495.nuances:
The set **includes only queries selected** manually, not every query the website ranks for at any position: random impressions for irrelevant phrases pile up and don't reflect the work.
**Unique queries are counted** after merging word forms, typos and word-order variants: the search engine treats them as one query, and counting them separately inflates the set.
The set is revised on a fixed date, because the Share of Keywords in Top 10, [[Average Position→seo/srednyaya_poziciya]] and Clicks per Keyword **change mechanically** with its size, even when rankings haven't moved.
495.example:
Queries collected from a keyword research tool: 1,400
Manually selected as relevant: 312
Of those, word forms and typos of main phrases: 62 (merged)

Target Keyword Count = 312 − 62 = **250**

Queries the website appears for by chance (about 3,000) aren't in the set.
495.importance: **It sets the boundaries of the whole map**: the denominators of several SEO metrics depend on the size of the set, and when the list grows, the Share of Keywords in Top 10 and [[Average Position→seo/srednyaya_poziciya]] get worse, even though nothing changed on the website. It also shows demand coverage: a narrow set means the website is competing for a small part of the market, however good its top 10 percentage looks.
495.essence_note: the more queries the website targets, the wider its search reach

496.name: Direct Traffic
496.description: The number of sessions for which the analytics system couldn't determine the traffic source.
496.nuances:
Besides typed-in addresses and bookmarks, this includes clicks from messaging apps, email clients, documents and apps, as well as sessions that lost the referrer when going from HTTPS to HTTP: they can't be separated within the metric, so the number is always higher than the real volume of direct visits. **Sessions are counted**, not users: one person can visit three times a day and generate three sessions.
Employees' internal visits **are filtered out by** IP address or a separate parameter; otherwise, on a small website they make up a noticeable share.
Sessions from links with UTM tags don't go into direct traffic, even if the user typed the address **manually**: the tags override source detection.
496.example:
Period: March
Sessions with an undetermined source: 9,400
Of those, from internal office IPs: 600 (excluded)

Direct Traffic = 9,400 − 600 = **8,800 sessions**

Unique users in the same group: 5,200. The number of sessions and the number of people must not be confused.
496.importance: **An indirect sign of brand awareness**: people who type the address themselves already know the company, and growth in this group after media coverage or an ad campaign shows a delayed effect that isn't visible in channel attribution. A sharp spike usually means broken link tagging rather than brand growth, and that's what to check first.
496.not_needed: Skip it for **new websites** with no brand awareness and for projects with a large share of traffic from messaging apps: the share of sessions with an undetermined source is high in those cases and says nothing about the brand.
496.essence_note: these are sessions nobody paid for and whose source wasn't determined: visits driven by brand awareness and return visits end up here too

497.name: Duplicate Pages
497.description: The number of website pages with identical or nearly identical content.
497.nuances:
The text similarity threshold **is fixed before measuring**, for example, at a 90% content match: at a 70% threshold, ordinary product pages of the same kind count as duplicates, and at 98%, almost nothing does.
Pages whose code specifies a canonical version (a rel="canonical" tag pointing to the main URL) **are excluded** from the count: the search engine shows only the main one in search results, and the duplicate is already resolved by the setting.
Technical duplicates of one page at different URLs (with and without a trailing slash, with UTM tags, HTTP and HTTPS) **are counted** if they haven't been consolidated.
**Extra copies are counted**, not groups: three identical pages give two duplicates, not three and not one.
497.example:
Similarity threshold: 90%
The crawler grouped similar pages: 46 groups
Total pages in these groups: 119
In each group, one page is the original and the rest are copies
Originals: 46, extra copies: 119 − 46 = 73
Of those, with a canonical version specified: 31 (not counted, the duplicate is resolved)

Duplicate Pages = 73 − 31 = **42** extra copies
497.importance: It explains why, for the same query, search results show one page of the website at one time and a different one at another, and **the ranking never settles**. Copies split link equity and behavioral signals between them, and the crawler spends its crawl budget recrawling the same content. It's most noticeable in catalogs with filters, where parameters multiply URLs.
497.essence_note: identical pages compete with each other in search results, and the search engine shows the wrong one

498.name: Broken Links
498.description: The number of links on the website that point to pages that fail to load.
498.nuances:
Broken links **include links** to URLs that return 404 or 410, as well as to URLs with 5xx server errors: in both cases the page is unavailable to the user.
**Unique destination URLs are counted**, not every occurrence of the link: one link in a sitewide menu across 3,000 pages gives 3,000 occurrences and turns the counter into the number of pages on the website.
Internal and external broken links **are counted separately**: you fix internal ones yourself, while external ones depend on someone else's website.
Redirect chains **aren't counted** as broken links: the final page opens.
498.example:
The crawler scanned the website and found broken links:
Internal unique URLs with 404: 37
Internal unique URLs with 500: 4
Occurrences of these links on pages: 1,812 (not counted)
External broken links to other websites: 23 (counted separately)

Internal broken links = 37 + 4 = **41**
498.importance: It shows **where the link equity** of internal linking leaks and where the user hits a dead end. The crawler spends crawl budget on nonexistent URLs, and a shopper who lands on a 404 from a product page may leave the website altogether instead of going back to the catalog. The number of broken links grows especially fast after products are removed and after a move to a new URL structure.
498.essence_note: the person hits a page that doesn't work and leaves, and the search engine trusts the website less

499.name: Referring Domain Count
499.description: The number of different websites that have at least one link to your website. Each referring domain counts once, regardless of how many links come from it.
499.nuances:
**Domains are counted** if their link is live on the check date: backlink tools keep history in their databases, and sites whose links are gone stay in the export.
Subdomains are rolled up to the main domain and **counted as one** referring domain; otherwise, a site with regional subdomains counts as many referring domains instead of one.
**Stick to one data source**: backlink tools crawl the web with their own crawlers and find different numbers of referring domains, so comparing across tools is meaningless.
The number is cumulative as of the check date: old links get removed, so the total can fall on its own, and growth **is calculated as the difference** between two snapshots.
499.example:
Backlink tool as of March 1
Unique domains in the export: 640
Of those, with the link already removed: 95 (not counted)
Subdomains of one site: 34 (rolled up into 1 domain)

Referring Domain Count = 640 − 95 − 33 = **512**

Backlinks on the same date: 9,700. One site with a sitewide block gives many links but remains one domain.
499.importance: **Gives a more honest picture** of the link profile than the total number of links: 10,000 links from 20 sites look like manipulation, while 500 links from 400 different websites look like natural mentions. It's used to plan work with linking sites and to assess the gap with competitors, because growing the number of referring domains is harder and more expensive than growing the number of links.
499.not_needed: Skip it when no link-building work is being done: the set of referring domains **changes on its** own, and there's nothing to base plans on.
499.essence_note: a link from a new website carries more weight than one more link from the same website

500.name: Share of Indexed Pages
500.description: The share of the website's pages that are in the search engine's index. Shows how many of the existing pages the search engine knows about and can show in search results.
500.nuances:
The denominator **is taken from the same** source as for Website Pages: the sitemap, a crawl and the CMS give three different numbers, and if they don't match, the percentage loses its meaning.
Pages intentionally blocked from indexing (noindex, robots.txt, canonicalized duplicates) **are excluded** from the denominator; otherwise, 100% is unreachable and the metric always shows a failure.
Indexed pages **are counted separately** for each search engine: the engines' indexes differ, and the sum of indexed pages across two engines means nothing.
The snapshot is taken on a fixed date, because the number of indexed pages **changes from day to** day.
500.example:
Page source: sitemap as of March 1
Total in the sitemap: 4,200 pages
Of those, blocked from indexing (pagination, filters): 700
Calculation base: 4,200 − 700 = 3,500
In the search engine's index on March 1: 2,940

Share of Indexed Pages = 2,940 / 3,500 × 100 = **84%**

Calculating from all 4,200 would give 70%: the difference comes only from pages that aren't supposed to be in the index anyway.
500.importance: Explains why part of the content **brings no traffic** at all. A page outside the index doesn't appear in search results for any query, so an indexing problem devalues any investment in content and links. A drop in the percentage after a release usually means that a new template or robots.txt blocked more than it should.
500.not_needed: Skip it for websites **with a dozen or so pages**, where it's easier to check indexing manually against the page list than to calculate a share.
500.essence_note: a page outside the index won't appear in search results for any query

501.name: Share of Keywords in Top 10
501.description: The share of target keywords for which the website is on the first page of organic search results.
501.nuances:
The top 10 **is based on organic** positions: ads and special search result blocks aren't included in the numbering; otherwise, the same place would be eighth one time and twelfth another.
The denominator **matches the set** in Target Keyword Count: any expansion of the list lowers the share without any change in rankings.
Region and device type **are fixed**: mobile and desktop results differ in composition and in the number of organic spots.
Rankings jump around daily, so for the period, each keyword's position **is averaged over** daily checks rather than taken on one random date.
501.example:
Target keywords in the set: 250
Rank checks: New York, mobile, daily in March
Keywords with an average position of 1–10 in March: 78
Keywords outside the top 100: 41 (stay in the denominator)

Share in the top 10 = 78 / 250 × 100 = **31%**

Dropping the 41 keywords with no position from the denominator would give 37%: the metric would improve precisely because rankings for some queries dropped.
501.importance: The only ranking metric **directly tied to money**: clicks fall off steeply beyond the first page, so moving a keyword from 11th place to 9th changes traffic more than moving from 40th to 20th. It's used to decide whether to push near-miss queries to the top or take on new topics.
501.essence_note: searchers rarely go on to the second page of results

502.name: Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS)
502.formula: CLS = 75th percentile of the total layout shift across page visits
502.description: How much the page layout shifts while loading: when an image finishes loading and pushes text or a button. It's the value not exceeded in 75% of page visits, meaning that for three quarters of users, shifts were no larger than this.
502.nuances:
CLS is a **unitless score** of 0 or higher rather than a count of items: it's calculated as the share of the screen area that shifted multiplied by the distance of the shift.
**It's calculated from field** data from real users rather than a lab test: a test misses shifts from banners, pop-ups and content loaded on scroll, which real visits capture.
CLS **is calculated separately** for mobile and desktop page visits: on a narrow screen, a shift affects a larger share of the area and gives a worse result with the same code.
Ready-made data **comes from Search** Console, which always uses a rolling 28-day window that can't be changed. Low-traffic pages don't make it into the report: data appears only once enough visits accumulate.
Break the value down by template type: shifts are caused by a specific template's layout, and for the website **as a whole** the problematic section isn't visible. Search Console groups similar pages by template automatically.
502.example:
URL group: blog pages, mobile page visits
Source: Search Console, rolling 28-day window
Page visits to blog pages: 31,000
CLS values sorted from best to worst
Value at position 23,250 (75% of 31,000): 0.18

CLS = **0.18**

The threshold for a good value is 0.1, while a quarter of users get layout shifts even larger than the result. The lab test showed 0.02, because the ad block didn't load during the test.
502.importance: It explains accidental taps and abandoned forms: the user aims at a button, a banner finishes loading at that moment, and the finger hits the neighboring link. On mobile, this feels like a broken website, and trust in it drops instantly. The value **is part of the assessment** of page experience in search engines, alongside loading speed.
502.not_needed: Skip it for pages where **nothing loads on top of** the finished layout: with no banners, pop-ups or content loaded on scroll, there's nothing to shift.
502.essence_note: when the layout jumps during loading, the person misses the button and leaves

503.name: Website Pages
503.formula: Number of pages on the website
503.description: The number of website pages available to users via a direct link.
503.nuances:
**Use a single source, the same** one used for [[Share of Indexed Pages→seo/proindeksirovannyh_stranic]]: the sitemap, a crawl and the CMS give three different numbers, and a crawl usually finds the most URLs because of filters and pagination.
Drafts and unpublished content **aren't counted**: they don't open via a link. Utility pages, pagination and filter pages are either included or not, but the decision is the same for both metrics in the pair: if you drop them here and keep them in the indexed pages, the indexing percentage will exceed 100%.
The snapshot is taken on a **fixed date**.
503.example:
Source: sitemap as of March 1
URLs in the sitemap: 4,200
Pages in the CMS: 3,850 (the gap comes from pagination)
URLs found by the crawler: 9,600 (filters and sorting)
Drafts: 140 (not counted; they didn't get into the sitemap anyway)

Website Pages = **4,200** per the sitemap

This same number is the basis for the denominator of the Share of Indexed Pages.
503.importance: **The reference number** for calculating indexing and for planning crawling: until it's clear how many pages there are in total, you can't tell whether many of them are lost. A sharp increase between measurements usually means filters generating additional URLs rather than new content, and it's the first sign of future problems with duplicates.
503.not_needed: Skip it for websites with just a few pages, such as a landing page or a simple brochure site. The number is known anyway, and all metrics that need it as a denominator **aren't calculated** there either.
503.essence_note: with too few pages, there's nothing to show in search, and with too many, they compete with each other and dilute the website's authority

504.name: Pageviews
504.description: The number of times website pages were opened during the period. Each pageview counts separately, including repeat views of the same page and reloads.
504.nuances:
If the website is built so that moving between sections doesn't reload the page, the tag counts only the initial page load: after that the URL **changes**, but the page stays the same. Pageviews on such a website are counted only when the developer sends an event on every navigation. It's easy to check: if the website has dozens of sections and pageviews are almost equal to sessions, the event isn't set up.
Loading content as the user scrolls and switching tabs within a page count as pageviews if an event is set up for them. This decision **changes the count for the same** traffic, so it's fixed and not revisited between periods.
**Reloading the page from the keyboard** and going back with the back button produce new pageviews.
504.example:
Pages opened in the month: 112,400
Reloads and returns to pages already opened: 7,600

Pageviews = 112,400 + 7,600 = **120,000**

Sessions in the same month: 40,000, so there are 3 pageviews per session.
504.importance: **It shows** how much work the website actually does: if pageviews grow while sessions don't, people are browsing sections longer. This changes hosting requirements before the server starts returning errors, and shows which pages put more load on the server than others.
504.essence_note: the more pages people open, the more of the website's content reaches them

505.name: Cost per Session
505.description: The average marketing spend per acquired session.
505.nuances:
The denominator **has to match** the numerator: the ad budget is divided by sessions from paid sources rather than by all [[Website Sessions→voronki_prodazh_h4/vizity_sayta]].
The value is never higher than the cost per user, because one user can have several sessions. The two values can't be compared with each other: they're **measured in different** units.
What counts as spend **is set once**: only placement payments, or also agency work, creatives and salaries.
505.example:
Ad spend for the month: $25,050
Sessions from paid sources: 16,700

Cost per Session = $25,050 / 16,700 = **$1.50**

[[Cost per User→voronki_prodazh_h4/stoimost_posetitelya]] for the same spend is $1.94: a paid user visited 1.3 times on average, so the price per session is lower.
505.importance: **The value closest to what the ad** account shows: it's used to catch a rising auction price and to compare bids across sources. A noticeable gap from the cost per click in the ad account points to lost tagging or to slow loading of the landing page.
505.not_needed: **Skip it** when there's no paid traffic at all and all traffic comes from search, recommendations and direct visits.
505.essence_note: the more expensive a session, the more each inquiry from the website costs

506.name: Paid Sessions
506.formula: Number of sessions from paid sources
506.description: The number of website sessions from paid placements: search and display ads, paid social, and placements with publishers and creators.
506.nuances:
**The definition of a paid session** rests on link tagging. Traffic from an untagged link lands in direct or organic, so paid traffic is undercounted and the analytics number is always lower than the ad account's.
The number of sessions in analytics doesn't equal clicks in the ad account. **A click is counted** on the click itself, and a session when the page loads and the tag fires; some people leave between these two moments.
**Placements without direct** payment per click are paid too: barter deals, sponsored posts, working with creators in exchange for products. Tag them the same way as ads; otherwise, they drift into organic and inflate it.
506.example:
Sessions in the month: 40,000
From search ads: 11,200
From paid social: 4,300
From creator placements: 1,200
Clicks reported by the ad accounts: 19,400

Paid Sessions = 11,200 + 4,300 + 1,200 = **16,700**

The gap between clicks and sessions is 2,700: some people closed the page before the tag loaded.
506.importance: **The denominator for the cost** per session and the basis for deciding how much more traffic to buy to meet the target. If paid sessions grow faster than orders, the auction is getting more expensive or the ads are attracting the wrong audience, and the budget needs to be shifted before the end of the month rather than after it.
506.not_needed: **Skip it for websites** with no paid traffic: internal portals, services accessed by link, projects that rely on search and recommendations.
506.essence_note: this is paid traffic: the more of it you get for the same money, the more people see the website

507.name: Organic Sessions
507.formula: Number of sessions from unpaid sources
507.description: The number of sessions from sources where placement wasn't paid for. The company decides which sources to include: anything from organic search results alone to all unpaid sources.
507.nuances:
**Decide** whether direct visits and email referrals are included. A narrow definition keeps only organic search results; a broad one adds direct, referral and email sessions. The gap between them grows with the share of direct, referral and email traffic, so the definition is set once.
**Some paid sessions** lose their tracking tags and get counted as organic: a click on an ad link copied from the address bar, or tags lost during a redirect. When that happens, organic grows with no real change behind it.
**Branded search traffic** is formally organic, but it's driven by advertising and media mentions. If you don't separate it, the effect of paid channels gets credited to unpaid ones.
507.example:
Sessions in the month: 40,000
From search engines, excluding ads: 14,800
Direct visits: 6,100
Referrals from other websites: 2,400
From ads: 16,700 (not counted)

Organic Sessions = 14,800 + 6,100 + 2,400 = **23,300**

With the narrow definition, search only, the result is 14,800.
507.importance: **It shows** what part of demand comes without paying per click, and how much the website's traffic would drop if ads were turned off tomorrow. Growth here is the only way to lower the average acquisition cost without cutting traffic volume.
507.essence_note: this traffic comes without paying per click, so it lowers the average acquisition cost

508.name: Landing Page Views
508.description: The number of views of preselected landing pages in the period. It counts views, not people: one user can open a page several times in one session.
508.nuances:
The list of landing pages **is fixed**. Expanding the list raises the number, and comparison with past months stops working.
Analytics can count pages with the same content but different URL parameters separately: without merging URLs, one page splits into multiple rows, while the total **doesn't change**.
508.example:
Service page views in March: 3,400
Pricing page views: 1,600
“Thank you for your inquiry” page views: 420 (not in the set)

Landing Page Views = 3,400 + 1,600 = **5,000**
508.importance: **How much interest there is in what** the company sells, unlike overall traffic, which the blog and random users inflate. When overall traffic grows and this number stays flat, acquisition is spinning its wheels: the people coming are readers rather than buyers.
508.not_needed: **Skip it** if the site has no designated landing pages: without a list, the metric turns into total pageviews.
508.essence_note: these are the pages where a person decides whether to submit an inquiry

509.name: Leads
509.description: The number of inquiries from potential customers in the period: form submissions, calls, emails and messaging app messages.
509.nuances:
A lead **is assigned to the period** by the date of the inquiry.
Duplicates are merged: the same inquiry that came in both as a call and as a form **counts as one lead**; otherwise the flow is inflated and Cost per Lead (CPL) comes out understated.
Spam and test inquiries **are excluded**: without cleanup, the numbers look good while the sales team complains about an empty pipeline.
Repeat inquiries from existing customers **don't count as leads** if the metric is meant to measure the inflow of new ones.
509.example:
Form submissions in March: 310
Calls from call tracking: 145
Messaging app inquiries: 35
Duplicates across channels: 40 (subtracted)
Spam and tests: 30 (subtracted)

Leads = 310 + 145 + 35 − 40 − 30 = **420**
509.importance: The upper limit for everything that happens next: you can sell **only to those** who reached out. If the flow drops, sales will dip one sales cycle later, and this is the only place to see it in advance. Without a lead count, ads are judged by revenue with a long delay, when the money has already been spent.
509.not_needed: **Skip it in** retail and on marketplaces, where there's no inquiry before the purchase: people come in and pay right away, and there's no intermediate step.
509.essence_note: every inquiry is a person ready to talk about buying

510.name: Cost per Lead (CPL)
510.description: How much it costs on average to get one lead.
510.nuances:
Spend includes ad budgets, platform fees and payments for promotional services. Pay for the sales reps who handle inquiries **isn't included**.
The denominator **is the same as** Leads: inquiries with duplicates and spam removed. Without cleanup, the cost per lead comes out understated, and the campaign looks more profitable than it is.
Spend and leads **cover the same** period. When ads are prepaid, use the amount actually spent in the period rather than the account top-up amount.
510.example:
Acquisition spend in March: $17,640
Leads in March: 420

Cost per Lead (CPL) = 17,640 / 420 = **$42**

Without subtracting the 70 duplicates and spam inquiries, it would be $36, and the campaign would look cheaper than it is.
510.importance: The first number used to compare acquisition methods with each other, and the first to respond to bid changes. Relying **only on it** is risky: a cheap unqualified lead can end up costing more per deal.
510.not_needed: **Skip it with** free traffic: without acquisition spend, the numerator is zero.
510.essence_note: the cheaper a lead, the more of them the same budget brings

511.name: Visitor-to-Lead Rate
511.description: The share of site users who submitted an inquiry. A person who reached out twice counts once.
511.nuances:
**The numerator counts unique people who reached out** rather than inquiries: a person who submitted two inquiries counts as one lead. Otherwise active customers inflate the numerator, and the result can exceed 100% and stop being a share.
The numerator and denominator **are taken for the same** period and on the same basis: people who reached out through the site are divided by site users. Adding offline inquiries and calls without call tracking overstates the rate.
A user **is identified by browser**, so one person on a phone and a laptop counts as two users in the denominator, and the rate is understated.
511.example:
Users in March: 12,000
Inquiries from the site: 420
Of those, repeat inquiries from the same people: 45
Inquiries from a physical location: 60 (not counted)

Visitor-to-Lead Rate = (420 − 45) / 12,000 × 100 = **3.1%**

Counting all inquiries, it would be 3.5%: the difference is that some people reached out twice.
511.importance: The main lever you can **move without a bigger** budget: double the rate and you get twice as many inquiries for the same money. Until it's measured, any dip in inquiries gets blamed on traffic and more ads are bought, even though the cause may be a broken form or a new version of the page.
511.not_needed: **Skip it in** retail and ecommerce, where people buy right away: there's no inquiry stage on the path, and the conversion rate is based on orders.
511.synonyms: Visit-to-Lead Rate, Website Lead Conversion Rate
511.essence_note: the more users submit an inquiry, the less each customer costs

512.name: Landing Page View Rate
512.formula: (Users Who Viewed a Landing Page / Users) × 100
512.description: The share of users who reached a landing page.
512.nuances:
The numerator **counts users**, not views. If you divide total views by users, the result can easily exceed 100%: one person opens a page several times.
Users who entered the site on a landing page **are included in the numerator**: they got to it from an ad rather than through internal navigation.
512.example:
Users in March: 12,000
Landing page views: 5,000
Users who opened a landing page at least once: 3,100

Landing Page View Rate = 3,100 / 12,000 × 100 = **25.8%**

Counting views, it would be 41.7%: that's the average number of views per user rather than a share of people.
512.importance: **It separates two different failures**: users aren't brought to the page, or the page doesn't sell. If a meaningful share of traffic gets here but inquiries are few, fix the page itself. If almost no one gets here, the problem is upstream, in navigation and ad links, and changes to the page won't help.
512.not_needed: Skip it on single-page sites, where the landing page **is the entry page** and the metric always equals 100%.
512.essence_note: a user who doesn't reach a landing page won't see the offer or submit an inquiry

513.name: Time on Landing Page
513.formula: Total Time on Landing Pages / Landing Page Views
513.description: The average time a user spends on a landing page per view.
513.nuances:
The list of pages that count as landing pages **is set in advance**. Adding utility pages such as “Thank you for your inquiry” drags the average down: people spend almost no time there.
The result depends on how the system measures time. Where duration **is calculated from the gap** between events, the last view in a session gets zero: the person read the page and closed the tab, and their five minutes didn't make it into the calculation. Where active tab time is measured, such views count in full, and the number comes out noticeably higher.
**Tracking scrolls** and other on-page events extends the measured time, so turning it on raises the number with no change in how people behave.
513.example:
Landing page views in the month: 5,000
Total time on them: 9,500 minutes

Time on Landing Page = 9,500 / 5,000 = **1.9 minutes**

Of the 5,000 views, 1,400 were the last in their session. If the system gives them zero, they pull the average down: for the rest, it comes to 2.6 minutes.
513.importance: **It's used to judge** whether people read the page or close it without scrolling past the first screen. A sharp drop after a copy edit or an offer change means the new version doesn't hold attention, and it's better to roll it back before inquiries dip: time responds earlier than conversion.
513.not_needed: **Skip it on pages** where a short time is normal: inquiry confirmations, redirects, pages with a single button.
513.synonyms: Landing Page Dwell Time, Average Time on Landing Page
513.essence_note: too little means the page was closed without being read, and too much means the person can't figure it out and find the form

514.name: Time to Conversion
514.formula: Total Time from First Session to Key Event / Key Events
514.description: The average time from a user's first session to a key event.
514.nuances:
**The clock starts at** the user's first session rather than at the start of the session in which the key event happens. Otherwise the metric turns into time within one session and shrinks to minutes.
**The attribution window cuts off** long paths: users whose first session was before the window are included with only part of their time to conversion, and the average is understated.
**The average is pulled up by rare** long paths, so calculate the median alongside it: when the two differ several-fold, go by the median.
514.example:
Key events in the month: 685
Total time from first session to key event: 5,823 days

Time to Conversion = 5,823 / 685 = **8.5 days**

For 612 users the path took 2 days, for 73 about 63: the median is 2 days and the average 8.5.
514.importance: **It determines** how many days after an ad launch you can judge the result at all. If people need three weeks to decide and the campaign is turned off on day seven, it's turned off before the inquiries have had time to arrive. It also sets the attribution window length and how long an email sequence should run.
514.not_needed: **Skip it with** impulse purchases, where the path fits into one session and the metric reduces to session length.
514.essence_note: the longer a person thinks it over, the higher the chance they won't come back

515.name: Sessions to Conversion
515.formula: Total Sessions up to the Key Event / Key Events
515.description: The average number of sessions per key event. Shows on which visit to the site people convert.
515.nuances:
The numerator includes **only the sessions of** users who completed a key event. If you add up all site sessions, including those of users who left without converting, the number inflates and stops answering the metric's question.
The session in which the key event happens **is included**: a path of three sessions with an inquiry in the third gives 3, not 2.
**The attribution window length** changes the result mechanically: with a 30-day window, earlier sessions drop out of the path, and the average is understated.
515.example:
Key events in the month: 685
Total sessions of these users up to and including the key event: 1,781

Sessions to Conversion = 1,781 / 685 = **2.6**
515.importance: **It determines** whether you need nurturing between the first touch and the inquiry. With an average close to 1, people decide right away, and it makes sense to invest in the above-the-fold section. With a high average, traffic will leak away without retargeting and messaging campaigns, and the spend will look unprofitable on a last-click basis.
515.not_needed: **Skip it** if the site doesn't link one person's sessions together: without cross-session identification, every session looks new, and the metric will always show 1.
515.essence_note: the more sessions it takes, the more each action costs and the more people drop off along the way

516.name: Landing Page Views per Session
516.description: The average number of landing page views per session.
516.nuances: The denominator includes all site sessions, including those where no landing page was opened. Dividing **only by sessions** with a landing page view turns the metric into the average number of landing page views in those sessions, and it will never be below 1.
516.example:
Sessions in March: 16,000
Landing page views: 5,000

Landing Page Views per Session = 5,000 / 16,000 = **0.31**
516.importance: **It shows** whether the site leads people to the right pages or they wander through random sections. Growth after a menu redesign means the new navigation works, and you can see it right away, before inquiry data builds up.
516.not_needed: **Skip it on** single-page sites: there, every session is a landing page view, and the value is always around 1.
516.essence_note: the more landing pages viewed per session, the higher the interest in the offer

517.name: First-Session Key Event Rate
517.formula: (First Sessions with a Key Event / First Sessions) × 100
517.description: The share of first sessions in which the user completed at least one key event. The metric counts sessions rather than people: one session with three key events goes into the numerator once.
517.nuances:
**A session counts as a first session** when the device has no previous sessions. Clearing cookies, switching browsers or moving from a phone to a computer creates a new “first” session, so their number is always higher than the real number of new people.
The set of key events **that goes into the calculation** is defined in advance: if micro-conversions such as scrolls or phone clicks are turned on in the analytics system, the rate rises sharply compared with counting inquiries only.
517.example:
First sessions in the month: 8,400
Of those, with at least one key event: 630
Total key events in these sessions: 810

First-Session Key Event Rate = 630 / 8,400 × 100 = **7.5%**

The numerator is 630, not 810: a session with two key events counts once.
517.importance: It answers whether the landing page works on cold traffic. If a person leaves the first session without acting, you can bring them back **only by paying**, through retargeting or a messaging campaign. A drop in this rate while the total lead count is normal means inquiries come from repeat sessions and new traffic is simply wasted.
517.not_needed: **Skip it with** a long sales cycle, where users need a long time to decide and the first session realistically can't end in an inquiry. It's also useless if the site has no analytics system with key events configured: first sessions can't be reconstructed after the fact.
517.synonyms: First-Visit Conversion Rate, First-Session Conversion Rate
517.essence_note: the more people take the desired action right away, the fewer you need to bring back with ads

518.name: Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)
518.formula: Contribution Margin Ratio × Monthly Revenue per Customer × [[Average Customer Lifetime→saas_produkty/sredniy_srok_zhizni_klienta]] in Months
518.description: How much money a customer brings in on average for as long as they keep buying from the company or paying for a subscription.
518.nuances:
For subscriptions, the monthly revenue per customer is the Average Revenue per Account (ARPA): **it's based on MRR** rather than total revenue, because one-time payments and implementation fees don't recur every month and overstate LTV. For one-time purchases, monthly revenue equals [[Average Order Value (AOV)→zakazy/sredniy_chek_aov]] multiplied by the number of orders per month over the customer's lifetime.
Decide whether to calculate it **on a margin or a revenue basis**. Margin is more accurate: it removes **all variable costs**, as defined by the Contribution Margin Ratio, rather than only the cost of goods: with [[Gross Margin→finansy/rentabelnost_valovoy_pribyli]], LTV is overstated by shipping, returns, payment processing and support. A revenue basis is simpler, but it lets you compare segments only if their margins are the same: a channel with discounts and returns looks better on a revenue basis than on a margin basis. At a 30% margin, the two figures differ roughly threefold: switching methods between periods changes LTV with no change in the business, and revenue-based LTV inflates the [[LTV-to-CAC Ratio→saas_produkty/sootnoshenie_ltv_k_cac]], making unprofitable acquisition look profitable.
For one-time purchases, the average order value, the number of orders per month and the [[Average Customer Lifetime→saas_produkty/sredniy_srok_zhizni_klienta]] are calculated **for the same customers using the same churn threshold**: their product equals the revenue per customer over the lifetime. Raising the threshold lengthens the lifetime and lowers the number of orders per month by the same factor, so LTV doesn't change; with different thresholds, it ends up overstated or understated. The order value is calculated across all kept orders of these customers: the first order's value is usually lower and understates LTV. [[Orders per Customer→crm/zakazov_na_klienta]] is a different number: it divides orders by the customers who bought during the period, leaving out months without an order, and using it overstates LTV.
The lifetime is calculated **across all customers**: both those still buying and those who bought once. [[Customer Lifespan→crm/srok_zhizni_klienta]] can't be used here: it measures the time from the first to the last purchase, only for churned customers who bought twice or more, and that's a different number.
Revenue per customer and lifetime are expressed in **the same unit of time**: monthly revenue is multiplied by the lifetime in months. Multiplying monthly revenue by a lifetime in days overstates the result by a factor of 30.
Decide whether to calculate it **from actuals or as a forecast**. Calculated from actuals, the lifetime comes from the history of mature cohorts in which most customers have already churned, and you can apply that figure to the current cohort only if the business model hasn't changed: otherwise new customers will have a different revenue per customer and lifetime.
A forecast based on current churn **is capped at the planning horizon**: the lifetime is the sum of monthly retention rates over the horizon, which with constant churn is (1 − (1 − churn)^H) / churn. With 2% churn and a 36-month horizon, that's 25.8 months rather than 50 or 36.
The formula assumes that a customer **brings in today's average revenue for their entire lifetime**: where customers add seats and [[Net Revenue Retention (NRR)→saas_produkty/chistoe_uderzhanie_vyruchki_nrr]] is above 100%, LTV is understated; where they move to cheaper plans, it's overstated. In that case, a more accurate figure is the cohort's contribution margin over the horizon divided by the number of its customers.
The formula **doesn't discount future cash flows**: at a 20% annual rate, a dollar three years from now is worth $0.58 today, while acquisition is paid for today. Discounted at the company's rate, LTV is lower, and the longer the horizon, the bigger the difference.
518.example:
One-time purchases:
Average order value: $70
Orders per month over the customer's lifetime: 0.3
Average Customer Lifetime: 8 months
Contribution Margin Ratio: 30%
Monthly revenue per customer = 70 × 0.3 = $21

Margin-based LTV = 0.3 × 21 × 8 = **$50.40**
Revenue-based LTV = 21 × 8 = **$168**

Subscription:
MRR on March 31: $84,000
Paying accounts on March 31: 1,218
ARPA = 84,000 / 1,218 = $68.97 per month
Churn: 6% per month, 36-month horizon → lifetime (1 − 0.94^36) / 0.06 = 14.9 months
Contribution Margin Ratio: 78%

LTV = 0.78 × 68.97 × 14.9 = **$801.57**

Without the horizon, the lifetime would be 1 / 0.06 = 16.7 months, and LTV = 0.78 × 68.97 × 16.7 = $898.40, 12% higher.
Only the margin-based figure can be compared with the cost of acquisition: on a revenue basis, a channel looks profitable even while it pays more for a customer than it earns from them.
If the lifetime for one-time purchases is entered in days (240), the result is $1,512: the revenue is monthly, but the lifetime is in days.
518.importance: It sets the ceiling on what you can pay for a customer, and so it directly controls the ad budget. An overstated LTV keeps justifying unprofitable acquisition: the costs are visible right away, while the revenue shortfall only becomes clear later. The same number decides which customer segment deserves **a dedicated retention program** and which would cost more than it brings in.
518.not_needed: Skip it **when the customer base is new** and no cohort has been around long enough to measure its lifetime: use [[X-Day LTV→crm/ltv_za_x_dney]] instead. Also skip it where a customer buys **only once**, as with wedding rings or a wedding dress: LTV equals the contribution margin of the first order.
518.essence_note: the more a customer brings in over their lifetime, the more you can pay to acquire them

519.name: CRM LTV-to-CAC Ratio
519.description: How many dollars of lifetime revenue come in per dollar spent on acquiring a customer.
519.nuances:
LTV and CAC are taken for **the same cohort**: the revenue of customers who came in during the period is divided by the cost of acquiring exactly these customers, rather than taking the average [[Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)→crm/pozhiznennaya_cennost_klienta_ltv]] of the whole base. Otherwise an expensive channel hides behind old loyal customers.
The LTV window **is fixed and stated next to** the result: the ratios over 90 days and 180 days are different numbers, and without a note, two calculations side by side can't be compared.
If LTV is calculated on revenue **rather than on margin**, the payback threshold shifts: at a [[Gross Margin→finansy/rentabelnost_valovoy_pribyli]] of 30%, a ratio of 3 to 1 means acquisition barely broke even.
519.example:
March cohort: 1,200 [[New Customers→crm/novye_klienty]]
Acquisition costs: $37,000
CAC = 37,000 / 1,200 = $30.83
This cohort's 90-day LTV: $140

LTV/CAC = 140 / 30.83 = **4.5**

At a 30% margin, the same LTV gives $42, and the ratio comes to 1.4: acquisition barely pays off, although on a revenue basis it looked like it paid for itself several times over.
519.importance:
It's the one number that shows whether **the company makes money on acquisition** or buys revenue at a loss. A ratio below 1 means a direct loss on every new customer; around 3 is considered a working benchmark for retail; above 5 more often points to **underinvestment in growth** than to efficiency: the channel could bring in more, but the budget hit a ceiling.
It's used to decide **whether to increase spending** on advertising and which channel to switch off.
519.not_needed: Skip it when customers come **without paid acquisition**: word of mouth, mall foot traffic, government contracts. CAC is close to zero, the ratio goes to infinity and measures nothing.
519.essence_note: the more revenue a customer brings in per acquisition dollar, the more money the company keeps

520.name: LTV-Based ROAS
520.description: How much revenue acquired customers bring in over their lifetime per dollar of ad spend.
520.nuances:
**The company decides** what goes into ad spend: at a minimum, paid placements; beyond that, agency fees, creative production and marketing salaries can be added. The fuller the denominator, the closer the result is to the real return: with paid placements alone, the metric looks better than it is. The composition **is fixed and doesn't change** between periods; otherwise, the trend shows a change in the rule rather than how advertising performs.
[[New Customers→crm/novye_klienty]] and spend are taken for **the same period**, and LTV for that same cohort. Customers who came from March ads but bought in April belong to March: otherwise one month's ad spend is divided by another month's customers.
Only **customers acquired through advertising** count, rather than all new customers in the period. In retail, without a promo code or a dedicated landing page, there's no way to separate customers brought in by ads from passersby, and then the metric is systematically overstated because it also counts customers who came organically.
The LTV window **is fixed and stated next to** the result, as in [[CRM LTV-to-CAC Ratio→crm/ltv_cac]]: the figure depends strongly on the window.
520.example:
Ad spend in March: $18,000
New customers from ads (by promo code and UTM tags): 400
90-day cohort LTV: $140

LTV-Based ROAS = (400 × 140) / 18,000 = **3.1**

There were 1,200 [[New Customers→crm/novye_klienty]] in March in total: taking all of them gives 9.3, but 800 of them didn't come from ads.
520.importance:
Regular ROAS counts **only the first purchase** and so shuts down channels that bring in customers with a long payback cycle.
Calculating it on [[Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)→crm/pozhiznennaya_cennost_klienta_ltv]] shows which channel brings in **customers who come back again**: it can be the channel that's most expensive on the first order and looks unprofitable by regular ROAS. A mistake here means cutting a channel that drives growth.
520.not_needed: Skip it **without paid advertising** or without a way to link a customer to a source: if a brick-and-mortar store doesn't use promo codes and cards that record the channel, attribution is impossible, and an eyeball estimate gives a number you can't act on.
520.essence_note: the more lifetime revenue per ad dollar, the more profitable the ad buying

521.name: X-Day LTV
521.formula: ARPU per Time Unit × Number of Such Units in the Window
521.alt_formula: Cohort Revenue for the Window / Number of Customers in the Cohort
521.description: The revenue a customer brings in over a set window from their first purchase: 30, 90 or 180 days.
521.nuances:
It's calculated **on a revenue or a margin basis**, like [[Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)→crm/pozhiznennaya_cennost_klienta_ltv]]. For comparison with acquisition cost, margin is used: on a revenue basis, payback looks better than it is.
**The time units of ARPU and the window** **must match**: monthly ARPU is multiplied by the number of months rather than the number of days. Multiplying monthly ARPU by 90 days overstates the result by a factor of 30.
**It's calculated by cohort**: it includes customers whose first purchase was in the same month, and each one's window is counted from their own first purchase. A calendar window instead of a cohort window mixes customers with different tenure and understates the result for recent arrivals.
The window **must have fully closed**: only cohorts at least X days past their first purchase qualify. Cohorts whose window hasn't closed pull the average down.
[[Sales Returns→finansy/vozvraty]] **are subtracted from the revenue of the customer** who returned the item. The higher the return rate in a category, the bigger the gap between gross and net revenue.
521.example:
Cohort: 500 customers with a first purchase in January
Their revenue over 90 days from the first purchase date: $75,000
Returns within the window: $5,000

90-day LTV = (75,000 − 5,000) / 500 = **$140**

Via ARPU: the cohort's monthly ARPU of $46.67 × 3 months ≈ $140. Multiplying it by 90 days would give about $4,200.
521.importance: It gives a number you can rely on when planning the acquisition budget right now, without waiting until the customer stops buying. It rests on **money already received** rather than on an assumption about how much the customer will bring in someday: it's harder to overpay for acquisition with such a number. Comparing cohorts over the same window shows **whether the quality of acquired customers is improving** from month to month.
521.not_needed: **Skip it** when the repeat purchase cycle is longer than any reasonable window: furniture, cars, large appliances. The second purchase doesn't fall into the window at any reasonable X, and the metric reduces to the average value of the first order.
521.essence_note: the more a customer brings in over this window, the sooner their acquisition cost is recovered

522.name: Referral Reward Redemption Rate
522.description: The share of issued rewards that recipients actually spent. It counts individual rewards rather than people: one participant can receive several promo codes or bonuses.
522.nuances:
Issued **rewards are those** credited to the participant's account or released as a promo code, rather than those accrued for a future payout.
**A reward counts** as redeemed when it's applied to a paid order: bonuses that were applied but returned with a canceled order count as unredeemed again.
**For rewards with an** expiration date, expired ones stay in the denominator: without them, the percentage is inflated and hides that bonuses expire unused.
**A two-sided program produces** two streams of rewards: to the referrer and to the invitee. They're redeemed differently, so a combined percentage for both streams hides a failure in one of them.
522.example:
Rewards issued in the quarter: 1,200
Applied to orders: 700
Of those, returned to the owner after canceled orders: 40 (removed)
Expired: 180 (stay in the denominator)

Redemption rate = (700 − 40) / 1,200 × 100 = **55%**

Removing expired rewards from the denominator gives 65%: the number looks better, and the 180 expired bonuses disappear from view.
522.importance: **It shows** whether the reward works as a motivator or the program hands out bonuses nobody spends. A low percentage means money held in reserve is tied up for nothing: how to earn the reward is clear, but how to spend it isn't.
522.not_needed: Skip it when the reward is paid as cash to a bank card or as an automatic discount on the next order: there, redemption **coincides with issuance** and always equals 100%.
522.synonyms: Reward Redemption Rate, Referral Reward Usage Rate
522.essence_note: an unredeemed reward doesn't motivate anyone to keep referring

523.name: Lead Value
523.description: The total monetary value assigned to the leads received.
523.nuances:
The valuation method determines the result **entirely**. Valuing leads by deals that were actually paid gives a reliable but lagging figure: some leads are still in the pipeline, so recent periods are always understated.
**A forecast-based valuation** (average deal size × lead-to-sale rate) gives a number right away, but when the lead-to-sale rate changes, the whole amount shifts even though lead quality hasn't changed.
Lead value **uses the same leads** as the lead count: if the number of leads includes duplicates and junk while value is assigned only to valid leads, the average value per lead stops adding up.
523.example:
Leads in the period: 375
Average deal size: $4,200
Lead-to-sale rate: 12%

Forecast value = 375 × 4,200 × 0.12 = **$189,000**

Actually paid by the end of the period: 26 deals worth $110,000
The remaining leads are still in the pipeline, so the actual figure catches up with the forecast with a lag of one sales cycle.
523.importance: **The only way to compare** ad spend with the money it brings in when the sale doesn't happen right away or online: without it, you can't tell whether a channel with a long sales cycle pays off. It reveals cases where a channel with expensive leads earns more than a cheap one because it brings in customers with larger deals.
523.not_needed: Skip it where no leads are collected or where the sale **is recorded immediately and** its amount is known exactly: then you use actual revenue.
523.essence_note: the more valuable the leads, the more money the same ads will bring in

524.name: Cost per In-Platform Purchase
524.description: The average amount spent per purchase within the ad platform.
524.nuances:
The denominator **uses the same** basis as the purchase count: counting placed orders instead of paid ones understates the cost by the share of cancellations.
The attribution **model and window** carry over from the purchase metric: the wider the window, the more orders get into the denominator and the cheaper a purchase looks.
524.example:
Spend: $25,200
Orders placed: 480
Paid: 435

Cost per purchase using placed orders = 25,200 / 480 = **$52.50**
Using paid orders = 25,200 / 435 = **$57.93**
524.importance: **It's compared with the average** order value and the markup: if acquiring a purchase costs more than the gross profit from it, every sale deepens the loss. It quickly shows whether the in-platform shop pays off, without waiting for an export from accounting.
524.not_needed: **Skip it** when orders are placed outside the platform.
524.synonyms: Cost per Purchase, Cost per Onsite Purchase
524.essence_note: the more the ads spend per purchase, the less you earn on it

525.name: B2B Sales Qualified Leads (SQLs)
525.description: How many leads passed qualification during the period: need, budget and access to the decision-maker are confirmed.
525.nuances:
**The company sets** the qualification criteria: the set of attributes directly determines the final number.
A lead is assigned to the period by its **arrival date** rather than its qualification date: the count describes that month's flow of leads, and the share of qualified leads is calculated from the same flow. Qualification counts only within **the same window from each lead's arrival** as in the rest of the funnel; otherwise the count won't match the numerator of the share.
**Unit of count**: an inquiry, as in [[B2B Leads→b2b_prodazhi/lidy]]. Two inquiries from one company about different needs are two leads and are qualified separately.
525.example:
Leads in March: 340 (repeat inquiries and spam already excluded)
March leads qualified, including those reviewed in April: 96

Qualified leads for March = **96**
525.importance: This is **the real workload** the sales team receives and the input to the whole funnel: reps' workload is planned around it, and it's used to work out whether the flow is enough for the deal quota. If there are half as many qualified leads as needed, **no amount of effort will meet the quota**, and you can see it at the start of the month rather than at the end.
525.not_needed: Skip it when **there's no qualification stage** and every incoming inquiry gets worked.
525.essence_note: these are the only inquiries that can turn into deals, and the more of them there are, the higher the sales ceiling

526.name: Deals Won
526.formula: Number of deals closed as won
526.description: How many deals were closed as won during the period.
526.nuances:
Decide which **event counts as closing** a deal, and fix the rule for the whole map: contract signing, shipment of goods, completion of project work, or receipt of payment. With deferred payment and long projects, these dates can be far apart, and the same deal would land in different periods.
**Lost deals don't count**.
A repeat deal with the same customer counts **as a separate deal**.
A deal canceled after closing **is subtracted from the period** in which it was closed: otherwise the deal count for the past period stays overstated forever.
526.example:
A deal counts as closed on the contract signing date
Contracts signed in March: 18
Of those, canceled after signing: 1 (subtracted)

Deals Won = 18 − 1 = **17 for March**

By lead cohort: 340 March leads × a Lead-to-Close Rate of 5% = 17 deals from them by the end of the counting window. The number is the same, but the deals are different: some will be signed in April and May, and the March contracts include some February leads.
526.importance:
**A direct measure of the team's results** and the denominator for [[Average Deal Size→b2b_prodazhi/srednyaya_vyruchka_sdelki]] and [[Cost per Deal Won→b2b_prodazhi/stoimost_sdelki]].
The later the chosen event, the **closer the metric is to the actual money**, but the longer you wait for the result: with signing, the team sees the outcome right away; with deferred payment, March's work shows up only when the payment arrives.
526.synonyms: Closed-Won Deals, Won Deals, Deals Closed
526.essence_note: this is the team's output in units: the more deals, the more money

527.name: Proposals Sent
527.description: How many proposals were sent to customers during the period.
527.nuances:
What counts is **sending the proposal** rather than its delivery or the customer opening the email.
A revised version of the same proposal **doesn't count separately**: it's the same document after edits. A proposal for a different need from the same customer counts separately.
A price quoted verbally without a document **doesn't count**.
527.example:
Emails with proposals sent in March: 41
Of those, revised versions for the same projects: 12
Price quoted verbally without a document: 5 (not counted)

Proposals Sent = 41 − 12 = **29**
527.importance: It shows how many deals are actually **at the final stage**: it lets you see ahead of time what results to expect by the end of the period. If meetings are being held ([[Meetings Held→b2b_prodazhi/vstrechi]]) but almost no proposals go out, **the work is stalled**: there are conversations, but they never get to pricing.
527.not_needed: Skip it when **no proposals are prepared**: customers buy from the price list or through a bidding platform.
527.essence_note: a proposal is a deal that has reached the pricing stage, and the more of them there are, the more will close

528.name: Share of Category A Leads
528.description: What share of qualified leads is assigned top priority: these are the most promising customers, and they get worked first.
528.nuances:
**The company sets** the criteria for category A: usually the potential contract value and how soon the purchase is expected, and the cutoff threshold directly changes the number in the numerator.
Use the category assigned **at the moment qualification is completed**.
**Denominator**: all [[B2B Sales Qualified Leads (SQLs)→b2b_prodazhi/kvalificirovannye_lidy]] in the cohort, including those that weren't assigned a category.
528.example:
Qualified leads for the month: 100
Category A: 20
Category B: 50
Category C: 24
No category: 6

Share of Category A Leads = 20 / 100 × 100 = **20%**
528.importance:
It's used to plan workload: Category A leads require **in-person meetings and the involvement of the head of sales**, and if their share doubles, the team can't handle them with the same headcount.
A falling share of Category A leads with the same overall flow is **an early signal** that advertising is bringing in smaller customers, before it shows up in revenue.
528.not_needed: Skip it when leads **aren't prioritized** and all of them are worked in the order they come in.
528.synonyms: A Lead Percentage, Hot Lead Percentage
528.essence_note: a large customer brings in more for the same amount of team effort

529.name: Share of Category B Leads
529.description: What share of qualified leads is assigned medium priority: a purchase is possible but takes longer or brings a smaller deal than with top-priority leads.
529.nuances:
**The company sets** the line between top and medium priority: where it's drawn directly changes the number in the numerator.
Use the category assigned **at the moment qualification is completed**.
**Denominator**: all [[B2B Sales Qualified Leads (SQLs)→b2b_prodazhi/kvalificirovannye_lidy]] in the cohort, including those that weren't assigned a category. That's why the A, B and C shares add up to less than 100% by exactly the share of uncategorized leads.
529.example:
Qualified leads for the month: 100
Category B: 50

Share of Category B Leads = 50 / 100 × 100 = **50%**

Together with A (20%) and C (24%), that's 94%: the missing 6% are leads that weren't assigned a category.
529.importance:
Category B makes up **the bulk of the team's work**, and its share is used to calculate how many rank-and-file reps are needed.
If B leads **are shifting into C** while A isn't growing, fewer deals will close a sales cycle later, even though the number of leads looks normal.
529.not_needed: Skip it when leads **aren't prioritized** or only two groups are used: leads to work and leads to skip.
529.synonyms: B Lead Percentage, Warm Lead Percentage
529.essence_note: this is the main flow of leads the team handles: if it grows at the expense of large customers, customers are getting smaller, and if it shrinks, a sales cycle later there will be no one to work with

530.name: Share of Category C Leads
530.description: What share of qualified leads is assigned the lowest priority: a purchase is unlikely or the deal is too small to be worth a rep's time.
530.nuances:
**The company sets** the cutoff: usually a minimum deal value or the lack of a decision timeline, and the number in the numerator depends on it.
Use the category assigned **at the moment qualification is completed**.
**Denominator**: all [[B2B Sales Qualified Leads (SQLs)→b2b_prodazhi/kvalificirovannye_lidy]] in the cohort, including those that weren't assigned a category.
Category C leads **stay in the denominators of conversion rates** even if no one works them: excluding them inflates conversion and hides the cost of the decision not to work them.
530.example:
Qualified leads for the month: 100
Category C: 24

Share of Category C Leads = 24 / 100 × 100 = **24%**
530.importance: It shows how much effort goes into leads known in advance to be weak. The larger the C share, the more it pays **to automate follow-up for these leads** with messaging campaigns and a standard price list rather than having reps call them one by one. It also explains a drop in conversion to deals: it falls **because of the lead mix** rather than because of the team's work.
530.not_needed: Skip it when leads **aren't prioritized** and all of them are handled the same way.
530.synonyms: C Lead Percentage, Cold Lead Percentage
530.essence_note: these leads take up reps' time and bring in almost no money

531.name: Deal Quota Attainment
531.description: How the actual number of deals compares with the quota for the period.
531.nuances:
Actuals include only deals **closed as won**, as in [[Deals Won→b2b_prodazhi/sdelki]]; lost deals don't count.
The closing event is the same as in [[Deals Won→b2b_prodazhi/sdelki]], and **the same for quota and actuals**.
**Decide** what to do with overachievement: if a month's quota is rewritten to match actuals after the month closes, the surplus deals don't carry over to the following periods.
531.example:
Quota for the month: 40 deals
Closed as won: 31
Lost: 12

Attainment = 31 / 40 × 100 = **78%**

Adding the lost deals to actuals would give 108%, even though the quota wasn't met.
531.importance: It shows whether the team keeps up **the flow of deals it needs** rather than hitting the quota with a couple of large contracts. A gap with [[Revenue Quota Attainment→b2b_prodazhi/vypolneniya_plana_po_vyruchke]] tells you directly what's going on: **few deals but the money is there** means revenue depends on a few customers, and losing one would sink the quarter. Many deals but no money means the average deal size has dropped.
531.not_needed: Skip it for **project sales** with two or three deals per period: one contract makes the percentage jump from 50 to 150, and it tells you nothing.
531.synonyms: Deal Target Attainment, Unit Quota Attainment
531.essence_note: a shortfall means fewer customers are coming through than planned, and there will be nothing to close next quarter

532.name: Revenue Quota Attainment
532.description: How actual revenue compares with the quota for the period. It can be calculated during the period or after it ends.
532.nuances:
Quota and actuals use **the same revenue recognition event**, the one used in [[Deals Won→b2b_prodazhi/sdelki]]. If the quota is based on one date and actuals on another, the percentage compares different things.
Decide what to do with **overachievement**. Some companies rewrite a month's quota to match actuals after the month closes: attainment becomes exactly 100%, and the extra money doesn't count toward the quarterly total. If the quota isn't rewritten, the overachievement stays in the running total and covers shortfalls in the following months.
532.example:
Quota for the quarter: $240,000, by payment
Received in the quarter: $192,000

Attainment = 192,000 / 240,000 × 100 = **80%**

March: quota $80,000, received $96,000, which is 120%.
If the March quota was rewritten to $96,000, the quarterly quota grows to $256,000, and attainment for the quarter = 192,000 / 256,000 = 75%.
If the March quota stayed at $80,000, the extra $16,000 counts toward the quarter: attainment = 192,000 / 240,000 = 80%.
532.importance: It determines whether **to push deals to close** before the period ends, whether to reschedule shipments, and whether to pay bonuses. While the period is still in progress, it shows **whether the current pace is enough**: if attainment is far behind by mid-quarter, the rest of the quota can no longer be met with the usual workload, and it takes either a large deal or a revised quota. Without it, the gap shows up only at the very end of the period, when nothing can be done.
532.not_needed: Skip it when **there's no revenue quota**: sales come from inbound demand, and targets are set by the number of deals or by margin.
532.synonyms: Quota Attainment, Percent to Quota, Revenue Attainment
532.essence_note: the closer to quota, the more money has actually come in

533.name: Average Deal Size
533.formula: Total Value of Closed Deals / Number of Closed Deals
533.description: How much money one deal brings in on average.
533.nuances:
The numerator and denominator come from **the same cohort**: the value of deals closed in the period is divided by the count of the same deals in [[Deals Won→b2b_prodazhi/sdelki]].
The numerator includes **the full contract value** regardless of how [[B2B Revenue→b2b_prodazhi/vyruchka]] is recognized: a partial payment doesn't make the deal smaller. That's why the average deal size multiplied by the number of deals doesn't have to match the period's [[B2B Revenue→b2b_prodazhi/vyruchka]].
The closing event **is the same** as in [[Deals Won→b2b_prodazhi/sdelki]].
533.example:
Total value of deals closed in the month: $510,000
Deals closed: 17

Average Deal Size = 510,000 / 17 = **$30,000**
533.importance: It shows whether the team should focus on closing more deals or increasing deal size. If the average deal size falls while the number of deals stays the same, the team **is sliding toward smaller customers**, and the reps' workload doesn't go down: a small contract takes about as much work as a large one. It also sets **the break-even threshold**: if the margin per deal is below the acquisition cost per deal, every sale loses money.
533.not_needed: Skip it when deal sizes **differ by orders of magnitude** and one deal outweighs all the others: the average doesn't describe any real deal, so look at the median instead.
533.synonyms: Average Deal Value, Average Contract Value
533.essence_note: with the same number of deals, a larger deal size means more money

534.name: B2B Revenue
534.formula: Total value of deals for the period
534.description: How much money deals brought in during the period.
534.nuances:
Revenue is recognized at **the same event** that counts as a deal closing in [[Deals Won→b2b_prodazhi/sdelki]]. Revenue doesn't get a separate rule; otherwise the deal count and the money from those deals would fall into different periods.
When revenue is recognized on payment, a partial payment adds only **the amount received** to revenue: a 30% advance on a $100,000 contract adds $30,000. With any other recognition event, the deal goes into revenue in full.
For funnel analysis, revenue **is allocated separately**: the money goes to the month the lead came in, so it lines up with cohort conversion rates. This is a supporting calculation rather than a replacement for the main one.
**Refunds and canceled** payments are subtracted from the period in which the money was returned.
534.example:
Lead arrived in January, deal closed in March for $100,000
Payment: 30% advance in March, the balance in May
Separately, an $80,000 payment for a February deal arrived in March

By lead arrival date: $100,000 goes to **January**
By closing date: $100,000 goes to **March**
By payment date: March gets 30,000 + 80,000 = **$110,000**, and the remaining $70,000 goes to May

The same deals, three different answers to the question "how much did we earn in March?"
534.importance: The main number used to calculate **quota attainment and bonuses**. Counting money received rather than signed contracts shows the real situation: with deferred payment terms, the team can close $400,000 in contracts while $120,000 reaches the bank account in the same period, and **payroll is paid out of that $120,000**.
534.essence_note: this is the money earned that pays for everything else

535.name: Deal Quota
535.description: The target number of deals to close during the period.
535.nuances: The event that marks a deal as closed is the same as in [[Deals Won→b2b_prodazhi/sdelki]]: signing, shipment, completion of work, or payment. Quota and actuals must be based **on the same event**.
535.example:
Quarterly team quota: 40 deals
Uses the same closing event as Deals Won: contract signing
Lost deals don't count toward the quota

Deal Quota = **40**

Together with the $240,000 revenue quota, that's an average deal size of $6,000: if the actual average is lower, one of the two quotas can't be met.
535.importance:
It guards against the situation where the revenue quota is met with **one large contract** while the flow of new customers has dried up: revenue looks fine, but there's nothing to close next quarter.
It gives reps **a clear daily rhythm**: a given number of deals per month translates into a number of meetings and calls per week.
535.not_needed: Don't set it for **project sales** with two or three large deals per period: a quota in units doesn't set any real standard for the work.
535.essence_note: a quota set too low doesn't set a standard for the work, and one set too high pushes reps to split deals to pad the count

536.name: Revenue Quota
536.description: The target revenue to bring in during the period.
536.nuances: The quota is based **on the same event** at which [[B2B Revenue→b2b_prodazhi/vyruchka]] is recognized: that event is defined by [[Deals Won→b2b_prodazhi/sdelki]], and it's the same for the quota.
536.example:
Quarterly team quota: $240,000
Uses the same recognition event as revenue: contract signing
Individual quotas of six reps combined: $210,000

Revenue Quota = **$240,000**

The $30,000 difference is the head of sales' buffer for shortfalls, so you can't add up individual quotas to get the team quota.
536.importance: **The reference point** for the whole incentive system: bonuses are calculated from it, and hiring and advertising budget decisions are based on it. **A quota set too low** pays bonuses for weak results; **one set too high** devalues the team's work and leads strong reps to leave after they miss it quarter after quarter.
536.not_needed: Don't set it when sales depend entirely **on outside demand** that the company can't influence: the quota turns into a forecast and doesn't motivate anyone.
536.synonyms: Sales Quota, Revenue Target, Sales Target
536.essence_note: a quota set too low doesn't push anyone, and one set too high soon stops being taken seriously

537.name: SQL-to-Close Rate
537.formula: (Qualified Leads with a Won Deal / [[B2B Sales Qualified Leads (SQLs)→b2b_prodazhi/kvalificirovannye_lidy]]) × 100
537.description: What share of qualified leads eventually converted to won deals. The end-to-end conversion rate of the whole sales funnel.
537.nuances:
The cohort is defined by **the lead's arrival date**, as in [[B2B Leads→b2b_prodazhi/lidy]]: check how many leads from that flow converted to a won deal ([[Deals Won→b2b_prodazhi/sdelki]]), even if it closed months later.
The product of the step conversion rates matches the end-to-end rate **only if** every step uses leads from the same cohort and treats leads that don't have an outcome yet the same way.
537.example:
March leads qualified (in March and April): 96
Of those, converted to a won deal by the end of the counting window: 17

SQL-to-Close Rate = 17 / 96 × 100 = **18%**
537.importance: The bottom-line number for planning: with it, you can work **backward** to how many leads the deal quota requires and compare that with how many marketing actually brings in. A gap here means **the quota can't be met on the math alone**, however well the team works. It's the basis for calculating an acceptable [[Cost per SQL→b2b_prodazhi/stoimost_kval_lida]].
537.not_needed: Skip it when **there's no qualification stage**.
537.synonyms: SQL-to-Win Rate, SQL Close Rate, SQL-to-Customer Rate
537.essence_note: the higher the rate, the fewer leads you need to buy for the same revenue

538.name: SQL-to-Attended-Meeting Rate
538.formula: (Qualified Leads That Attended a Meeting / [[B2B Sales Qualified Leads (SQLs)→b2b_prodazhi/kvalificirovannye_lidy]]) × 100
538.description: What share of qualified leads attended a meeting.
538.nuances:
The numerator counts leads that had **at least one meeting**, rather than the number of [[Meetings Held→b2b_prodazhi/vstrechi]]: repeat meetings with the same customer don't count; otherwise the rate could exceed 100%.
