The cohort is defined by **the lead's arrival date**, as in [[B2B Leads→b2b_prodazhi/lidy]]: check whether leads from that cohort attended a meeting, even if the meeting took place later. A meeting counts only within **the same window from each lead's arrival** as in the rest of the funnel: only then does the product of the step conversion rates match the end-to-end Lead-to-Close Rate.
538.example:
March leads qualified (in March and April): 96
Attended a meeting: 58 leads
Total meetings with them, including repeat ones: 79

SQL-to-Attended-Meeting Rate = 58 / 96 × 100 = **60%**

Putting the 79 meetings in the numerator gives 82%: leads with repeat meetings would be counted more than once.
538.importance: **The first break in the funnel**: the customer was qualified, but the conversation never happened. It's used to decide which part of the process leaks money: **response speed**, first-call scripts, or the quality of qualification itself. If the rate is low, marketing is paying for leads that **sales never gets around to**.
538.not_needed: Skip it when **the sales process has no meetings**.
538.essence_note: every lead that never gets to a conversation has already been paid for and won't bring in any money

539.name: Meetings Held
539.formula: Number of meetings held with customers
539.description: How many meetings with customers were held during the period.
539.nuances:
Count **meetings that took place** in any format: in-person meetings, video calls and phone calls.
Canceled meetings and no-shows **don't count**.
Each meeting counts **separately**: three meetings with one customer give 3 rather than 1.
**Internal meetings without** a customer don't count.
539.example:
Meetings booked in March: 91
Customer didn't show up or canceled: 12
Internal meetings without a customer: 8 (not counted)

Meetings Held = 91 − 12 = **79**

These 79 meetings were with 58 leads: some customers had two meetings.
539.importance:
A measure of **the team's workload** that shows whether there's enough activity to meet the quota.
When revenue falls, there are usually two explanations: **fewer meetings** means the problem is at the top of the funnel; **the same number of meetings** means the problem is in what happens at the meetings themselves. Without this count, both cases look the same.
539.not_needed: Skip it when deals close **without negotiations**: customers order from the price list or through a bidding platform.
539.synonyms: Sales Meetings, Meetings Completed, Completed Meetings
539.essence_note: a deal rarely closes without a meeting, so the more meetings, the more sales

540.name: Meeting-to-Proposal Rate
540.formula: (Leads with a Proposal Sent / Leads That Attended a Meeting) × 100
540.description: What share of leads that attended a meeting received a proposal.
540.nuances:
Unit of count: a lead, as in [[B2B Leads→b2b_prodazhi/lidy]] and the rest of the funnel. Several meetings with one lead count as **one unit** in the denominator, and revised versions of the proposal for that lead as one unit in the numerator.
If two proposals go out for the same need, for example for two stages of work, it's still **one lead**: the funnel counts leads rather than deals. A different need from the same customer counts as a different lead, as in the lead count.
**It's calculated by cohort, based on the lead's arrival date**, as in the rest of the funnel: take leads that came in during the period and attended a meeting, and check whether a proposal went out to them. The meeting and the proposal count only within **the same window from each lead's arrival** as in the rest of the funnel: only then does the product of the step conversion rates match the end-to-end Lead-to-Close Rate. A recent period is still maturing: the final rate is calculated after an interval comparable to the sales cycle.
540.example:
March leads that attended a meeting: 58
Total meetings with them: 79 (some leads had two meetings)
Leads that received a proposal: 29

Meeting-to-Proposal Rate = 29 / 58 × 100 = **50%**

Dividing by the 79 meetings gives 37%: repeat conversations with the same lead would look like meetings that ended without a proposal.
540.importance: It shows whether reps **move the conversation to pricing** or hold meetings that go nowhere. If few meetings lead to a proposal, the problem is **upstream**: customers who aren't ready are getting to meetings, and qualification needs to be tightened rather than putting pressure on the team. A consistently high rate with a low Proposal-to-Close Rate means the opposite: **proposals go out to everyone**, including those who definitely won't buy.
540.not_needed: Skip it when the proposal is prepared **before the meeting** or not at all.
540.essence_note: the more meetings lead to a proposal, the more deals come out of the same number of meetings

541.name: Proposal-to-Close Rate
541.formula: (Leads with a Won Deal / Leads with a Proposal Sent) × 100
541.description: What share of leads that received a proposal resulted in a won deal.
541.nuances:
**Unit of count**: a lead, as in [[B2B Leads→b2b_prodazhi/lidy]] and the rest of the funnel. Revised versions of a proposal for the same lead count as one unit: otherwise a won deal with three versions would give a conversion rate of 33% instead of 100%.
The denominator includes **all leads with a proposal sent**: a customer who is still thinking it over or has gone silent by the end of the counting window doesn't count as a win. Otherwise, proposals that stall without an explicit refusal would inflate the rate. That's why the rate for a recent period is understated: compare only cohorts whose counting window has ended.
**It's calculated by cohort, based on the lead's arrival date**, as in the rest of the funnel: take the period's leads that got a proposal and check whether they converted to a won deal. The proposal and the won deal count only within **the same window from each lead's arrival** as in the rest of the funnel: only then does the product of the step conversion rates match the end-to-end Lead-to-Close Rate. So a late proposal, sent after a long wait for a meeting or a lengthy pricing process, leaves the customer less time to decide before the window ends, and such proposals convert less often even when the customer is just as interested.
541.example:
March leads that received a proposal: 29
Total proposals sent, including revised versions: 41
By the end of the counting window, deals were won for 17 leads; for the other 12, the customer declined or never replied

Proposal-to-Close Rate = 17 / 29 × 100 = **59%**

Dividing by the 41 proposals sent gives 41%: revised versions would look like lost proposals.
541.importance: The last step of the funnel, where **price and terms** decide the outcome: a low rate here means proposals don't match the market or go to the wrong person. It's used to decide whether to change the discount policy and whether to require **presenting the proposal in a meeting** instead of sending it by email.
541.not_needed: Skip it when **no proposals are prepared**: customers buy from the price list or through formal bids.
541.synonyms: Proposal Win Rate, Proposal Acceptance Rate, Proposal Close Rate
541.essence_note: the more often proposals are accepted, the more deals come out of the same work

542.name: Average Sales Cycle Length
542.formula: Σ for each won deal (Close Date − Lead Created Date) / Number of Won Deals
542.description: How much time passes on average from lead creation to the close of a won deal.
542.nuances:
The clock starts at **the moment the lead is created** in the system ([[B2B Leads→b2b_prodazhi/lidy]]): it's the only point recorded for every deal.
**The end point** is the deal closing event, the same as in [[Deals Won→b2b_prodazhi/sdelki]]. If the end point is signing, the metric measures the sales team's work; if it's completion of work or payment, the cycle also includes production and accounting, and the number grows.
Deals that haven't closed **aren't included**, so during a period of rapid growth the metric is understated: fast deals have already closed, while slow ones are still in progress.
The unit is chosen **to fit the cycle length** in the industry: days, weeks or months, counted as business or calendar time. What matters is that it's the same in all periods.
542.example:
Each won deal gets its own duration:
Deal A: lead on January 12, contract signed April 3 = 81 days
Deal B: lead on January 20, contract signed March 14 = 53 days
Deal C: lead on February 8, contract signed April 22 = 73 days
…and so on for all 51 won deals from January–March leads

Sum of durations: 3,570 days
Average Sales Cycle Length = 3,570 / 51 = **70 days**

Counting to completion of work instead of signing gives 165 days for the same deals: the cycle picks up three more months of production.
542.importance: It determines how far ahead of the target date a lead needs to come in for the money to arrive on time: with a three-month cycle, the leads behind December's deals arrive in September, and by November it's too late to affect the annual result. It's also used to calculate how many deals need to be **in progress** at the same time to keep the flow of deals uninterrupted.
542.not_needed: Skip it for **quick deals** closed in one or two calls: a cycle that short has nothing in it to manage, and it doesn't affect decisions.
542.synonyms: Sales Cycle Length, Average Sales Cycle, Time to Close
542.essence_note: the faster a deal closes, the sooner the money comes in and the more deals a rep can handle

543.name: B2B Leads
543.description: How many inquiries showing interest in buying came in during the period.
543.nuances:
A lead is **an inquiry showing interest in buying**: a website form submission, an inbound call, a contact from a trade show. Spam and supplier pitches that come through the same form are screened out.
An exported list of companies for cold calling **doesn't count as leads**: no interest has been shown, and including such lists inflates the number. But if a company shows interest during a cold call, it becomes a lead as of the date of that conversation.
Unit of count: **the inquiry rather than the company**. One customer can reach out twice about different needs, and that's two leads. A repeat inquiry about the same need doesn't count as a new lead; otherwise a persistent customer inflates the flow.
543.example:
Website form submissions: 221
Inbound calls: 77
Emails and chat messages: 60
Duplicates and spam: 18 (not counted)

B2B Leads = 221 + 77 + 60 − 18 = **340 for March**
543.importance: **The top of the funnel**, from which everything else is calculated, and the first place to show that the flow has dried up. A drop in leads shows up **a sales cycle ahead** of a drop in revenue, while there's still time to add budget or start calling the customer base. Without it, a revenue shortfall is discovered only after the fact, when the funnel is already empty.
543.not_needed: Skip it where **there are no inbound inquiries** and reps work only cold lists.
543.synonyms: Inbound Leads, Lead Volume, Sales Inquiries
543.essence_note: the more inquiries showing interest in buying, the more deals the same team can close

544.name: B2B Lead-to-SQL Rate
544.description: What share of incoming leads turned out to be worth pursuing: need, budget and access to the decision-maker were confirmed.
544.nuances:
**The company sets** the qualification criteria: the set of attributes (budget, access to a decision-maker, confirmed need, company size) directly determines the number in the numerator.
A lead is assigned to the period by its **arrival date** rather than its qualification date: the metric evaluates the leads that came in that month, and the result is attributed to that month even if a lead was reviewed later. So the rate for a recent month keeps changing after the month ends. Qualification counts only within **the same window from each lead's arrival** as in the rest of the funnel: only then does the product of the step conversion rates match the end-to-end Lead-to-Close Rate.
The numerator and denominator both count **inquiries**: the unit must be the same as in [[B2B Leads→b2b_prodazhi/lidy]].
544.example:
Leads in March: 340
Of those, qualified by the end of March: 78
Another 18 March leads qualified in April

Lead-to-SQL rate for March = (78 + 18) / 340 × 100 = **28%**

February leads qualified in March aren't part of this calculation: they belong to the February cohort.
544.importance: It shows whether marketing brings in people **you can sell to at all**. If only a small share of inquiries pass qualification, the sales team **spends its time sorting through junk leads** instead of working on deals. It's used to decide whether **to turn off a channel**, change the ad message, or tighten the inquiry form.
544.not_needed: Skip it when sales come **only from the existing customer base** and cold-calling lists: there are no inbound leads, so there's nothing to qualify.
544.essence_note: the higher the rate, the less time reps spend sorting through unqualified inquiries

545.name: Time to First Meeting
545.formula: Total Time from Lead Creation to First Meeting / Number of Leads That Attended a First Meeting
545.description: How much time passes on average from the moment a lead is created to the first meeting with that lead.
545.nuances:
**The denominator is the number of leads** that attended a first meeting rather than the total count of meetings ([[Meetings Held→b2b_prodazhi/vstrechi]]): repeat meetings with the same customer aren't included.
Leads that had no meeting **drop out of the calculation**, so the longer stuck leads go without a meeting, the better the average looks.
A lead is assigned to the period by its **arrival date** rather than the meeting date, and a meeting counts if it took place within **the same window from each lead's arrival** as in the rest of the funnel: then the calculation includes the same leads as the numerator of [[SQL-to-Attended-Meeting Rate→b2b_prodazhi/konversiya_kval_lid_vstrecha]]. If you take meetings by the date they were held, the time to meeting will describe different leads from the ones the conversion rate is calculated on.
The time unit is chosen **to fit the cycle length** in the industry: hours, days or weeks, counted as business or calendar time. What matters is that it's the same in all periods.
545.example:
March leads qualified (in March and April): 96
Attended a first meeting: 58
Total time from lead creation to first meeting: 348 days
Total meetings held, including repeat ones: 79

Time to First Meeting = 348 / 58 = **6 days**

Dividing by the 79 meetings gives 4.4 days: the metric improves by about a quarter, even though nothing changed in the work.
545.importance: In B2B, the deal more often goes to **whoever meets with the customer first**, while the request is still current. It's used to decide whether a dedicated person is needed for initial lead handling and what response-time standard to set. If the average stretches out, only the customers **who didn't find a supplier sooner** make it to a meeting.
545.not_needed: Skip it when selling happens **without meetings**: through written messages, through a bidding platform, or straight from the price list.
545.essence_note: the longer the customer waits, the more likely they are to go to whoever responded first

546.name: Sales Rep Share of Revenue
546.description: What share of total revenue a specific sales rep brought in.
546.nuances:
Decide how to count a deal handled by two reps: credit it in full to the main owner or **split the amount** between them. **You can't credit the full amount to each of them**: the shares would add up to more than 100%.
Revenue is recognized **at the same event** as in total [[B2B Revenue→b2b_prodazhi/vyruchka]]: if the total is counted by payment, the rep's revenue is counted by payment too.
546.example:
Total revenue for the quarter: $800,000
Peterson's revenue: $184,000

Share = 184,000 / 800,000 × 100 = **23%**
546.importance: It shows **dependence on one person**: if a rep brings in 40% of revenue, the company loses that 40% along with the customer contacts when the rep leaves. It's used to decide whom **to back up with a second owner** on key accounts and how to redistribute the customer base. Without it, the risk surfaces only when the resignation letter arrives.
546.not_needed: Skip it when **one person or the owner** does all the selling: the share is always 100%.
546.synonyms: Rep Revenue Contribution, Revenue Contribution by Rep
546.essence_note: revenue concentrated in one person means a risk of losing a large part of it when they leave, and a share near zero means the rep isn't paying for themselves

547.name: Revenue per Sales Rep
547.description: How much revenue one sales rep brings in on average during the period.
547.nuances:
Decide how to count the denominator. **The headcount at the end of the period** is simpler, but hiring or departures within the period skew the result: a new hire who worked one month out of three weighs as much as someone who worked the whole quarter. The average for the period removes the skew but requires tracking headcount month by month.
Decide whether to count **people or FTEs**: by headcount, a half-time employee counts in the denominator as a whole person, double their actual share of the work.
**Decide** who goes into the denominator: only reps with an individual quota, or the whole department, including the head of sales and trainees. This determines what to compare the result with: a rep's productivity target or the cost of running the whole department.
547.example:
Revenue for the quarter: $800,000
At the start of the quarter: 8 reps, one of them half-time
Joined mid-quarter: 2

Headcount at the end of the quarter (10): 800,000 / 10 = **$80,000**
FTEs at the end of the quarter (9.5): 800,000 / 9.5 = **$84,211**
Quarterly average in FTEs (8.5): 800,000 / 8.5 = **$94,118**

A spread of $14,118 on the same data: periods can be compared only when the metric is calculated the same way.
547.importance: It shows **whether expanding the team pays off** and how many people next year's quota requires: if the quota grew by 30% and revenue per rep stays flat, you'll have to hire proportionally. A decline in the metric while total [[B2B Revenue→b2b_prodazhi/vyruchka]] grows means the team is growing faster than its results, and new people aren't paying for themselves.
547.not_needed: Skip it when sales are handled by **one person** or the owner: the metric equals total revenue.
547.synonyms: Revenue per Rep, Sales Productivity per Rep
547.essence_note: the more one person brings in, the less the same revenue costs the company

548.name: Proposal Turnaround Time
548.formula: Σ (First Proposal Version Sent Date − First Meeting Date) / Leads with a Proposal Sent and a Recorded Meeting
548.description: How much time passes on average from the first meeting with the customer to sending the first version of the proposal.
548.nuances:
The clock starts at **the first meeting** rather than when the task is assigned: the customer has been waiting for a number since the end of the conversation, and the time the task sat unclaimed is part of their wait too. Proposals without a recorded meeting aren't included; show their share next to the number.
Waiting for pricing from a supplier **counts toward turnaround time**: for the customer, it's part of the wait, and excluding it would leave the main cause of delays out of the metric.
Count **the first version**: revisions after the customer responds are part of negotiation, so the time spent on them is excluded and they don't count as separate proposals. If two proposals go out for the same need, for example for two stages of work, the first one counts: the second goes out once the deal has moved forward, and its timing reflects the deal's progress rather than the customer's wait.
A lead is assigned to the period by its **arrival date** rather than the date the proposal was sent, and a proposal counts if its first version went out within **the same window from each lead's arrival** as in the rest of the funnel: then the calculation includes proposals for the same leads as the denominator of [[Proposal-to-Close Rate→b2b_prodazhi/konversiya_kp_sdelka]]. If you take proposals by send date, the turnaround time will describe a different set of proposals from the one used to count deals.
The unit is chosen **to fit the cycle length**: hours, days or weeks, counted as business or calendar time. What matters is that it's the same in all periods.
548.example:
March leads that received a proposal: 29, all with a recorded first meeting
Total time from the first meeting to sending the first version: 116 business days

Proposal Turnaround Time = 116 / 29 = **4 business days**
548.importance: It shows **how long the customer waits for a number** after showing interest: while waiting, the customer has time to get a competitor's proposal. It's used to decide whether to introduce standard templates and a pricing calculator, whether a dedicated person is needed for pricing, and where **the bottleneck** is: in price approval or in pricing from the supplier.
548.not_needed: Skip it when prices are **standard** and the proposal is generated automatically from the price list: turnaround takes almost no time and doesn't affect the deal.
548.synonyms: Quote Turnaround Time, Time to Proposal, Proposal Response Time
548.essence_note: while the price is being worked out, the customer has time to get a competitor's proposal

549.name: Cost per Deal Won
549.description: How much acquisition costs per won deal.
549.nuances:
Acquisition spend includes the same items as in [[Cost per SQL→b2b_prodazhi/stoimost_kval_lida]]: ad budgets, trade shows, contractors, and pay for marketing and first-contact staff. Pay for the reps who run the deal **isn't included**: that's work with a lead already acquired rather than acquisition.
Spend is **lagged by** the [[Average Sales Cycle Length→b2b_prodazhi/sredniy_cikl_sdelki]]: deals closed in the period are matched with spend from the months when the leads behind them came in.
549.example:
Acquisition spend for December–February: $57,600
Deals closed as won in March: 18

Cost per Deal Won = 57,600 / 18 = **$3,200**
549.importance: It's compared with **the margin per deal** and shows whether acquisition pays off: if a deal brings in $6,000 of margin and costs $3,200, the channel works; if it costs $7,000, it doesn't. It differs from the full cost of acquiring a customer in that it **doesn't include the sales team's work**: to assess the economics as a whole, sales payroll is added to this number separately.
549.not_needed: Skip it when deals come in **with no acquisition spend**: through referrals or from regular customers.
549.synonyms: Cost per Closed Deal, Cost per Won Deal
549.essence_note: this comes straight out of the margin on every sale

550.name: Cost per SQL
550.description: How much it costs to get one lead that passed qualification.
550.nuances:
Spend includes the costs of acquiring leads **before they're handed over to sales**: ad budgets, trade show participation, contractor work, and pay for marketing and first-contact staff. Pay for the reps who run the deal **isn't included**: that's work with a lead already acquired.
Spend and leads come from **the same cohort**: March spend is divided by the leads that arrived in March and passed qualification, even if qualification happened in April. Dividing March spend by the leads qualified in March mixes two different cohorts.
550.example:
Acquisition spend in March: $19,200
Leads that arrived in March: 340
Of those, qualified (in March and April): 96

Cost per SQL = 19,200 / 96 = **$200**

The cost per lead would be $56.47: the difference shows how much you pay for screening out unqualified leads.
550.importance: It gives **the price of a qualified contact** rather than the price of an inquiry: a cheap inquiry can turn into an expensive qualified lead, and the cost per inquiry doesn't show it. If the cost per qualified lead approaches **the margin per deal multiplied by the SQL-to-Close Rate**, acquisition stops paying off regardless of how the team works.
550.not_needed: Skip it when **no money is spent** on acquisition: customers come through referrals and from the existing base.
550.synonyms: Cost per Sales Qualified Lead, SQL Acquisition Cost
550.essence_note: every dollar here comes out of the profit on a future deal

581.name: Budgeted Headcount
581.description: How many positions are approved in the headcount plan.
581.nuances:
The number **is taken from the current** headcount plan on a specific date, the same date used for actual headcount in the fill rate.
**It's counted in FTEs**, so a 0.5 FTE position counts as 0.5. When counting positions, two half-time positions count as two, and the fill rate is understated.
Vacant positions **are included**, including those frozen for budget reasons: as long as they're in the headcount plan, they're part of the planned staffing need. If it's decided not to fill a position, it's removed from the plan rather than ignored in the count.
The position of an employee on parental leave **remains one position**, and their temporary replacement is a separate budgeted position for the duration of the replacement. If they're counted as one, there will be no room in the plan for the replacement.
581.example:
Headcount plan on December 1
Full-time positions: 220
Half-time (0.5 FTE) positions: 8 → 4 FTEs
Vacant, including frozen: 20 (part of the 220)
Temporary positions to cover parental leave: 6

Budgeted Headcount = 220 + 4 + 6 = **230 FTEs**

Counting positions rather than FTEs would give 234, and the fill rate would come out lower than it really is.
581.importance: It's **the planning baseline** against which the fill rate is measured and the personnel budget is planned: the number of budgeted FTEs multiplied by the pay ranges for each role gives the maximum payroll for the year. When the headcount plan isn't revised for years, it turns into a list of positions nobody intends to fill, and the fill rate stays permanently below 100% with no real shortage of people.
581.not_needed: It isn't kept in companies **without a headcount plan**, where people are hired for specific tasks rather than for approved positions.
581.synonyms: Approved Headcount, Authorized Headcount, Planned Headcount
581.essence_note: an inflated plan keeps the company permanently understaffed on paper, and an understated one leaves no room for hiring

582.name: Revenue per Employee
582.description: How much revenue there is per employee for the period.
582.nuances:
The numerator and denominator cover **the same period**: monthly revenue is divided by that month's headcount. Annualizing monthly revenue gives a value with a different meaning, and the two can't be mixed in one series.
Headcount **is the average for** the period rather than on a date: the month's revenue was earned partly by people who left mid-month, and end-of-period headcount doesn't count them. When headcount grows, end-of-period headcount understates the metric; when it shrinks, it inflates it.
**Decide** whether to count people or FTEs. People are easier to count, but with many part-time employees, revenue per person looks understated; FTEs make departments with different work schedules comparable. One choice for the whole map: if FTEs are used here, then [[Cost per Employee→hr/zatraty_na_sotrudnika]] and the [[Headcount Fill Rate→hr/ukomplektovannost]] use FTEs too.
**Decide** whether part-timers whose main job is elsewhere, contractor firms' workers and independent contractors are included. If they do the work but aren't in the denominator, revenue per employee grows with no change in real productivity.
582.example:
Revenue for July: $3,600,000
Headcount on July 1: 60 people
Headcount on July 31: 64 people
Average headcount for July: 62 people
Contractors on a project: 5 (not included in the denominator)

Revenue per Employee = 3,600,000 / 62 = **$58,065**

With end-of-month headcount, it would come to $56,250: hiring at the end of the month would lower the metric even though the new people haven't had time to work yet.
582.importance: It answers whether the business grows by adding people or by how well it operates. When revenue and headcount grow **at the same rate**, the company scales linearly and will hit a hiring ceiling. The metric is a basis for defending the budget for new positions: a 20% increase in headcount should be backed by the revenue plan.
582.not_needed: **It works poorly where** revenue is recognized in large, uneven chunks: a project-based company with one delivery a quarter will see jumps unrelated to people.
582.synonyms: Sales per Employee, Revenue per Head
582.essence_note: the more revenue there is per working person, the fewer people are needed for the same revenue

583.name: Cost per Employee
583.formula: Personnel Costs / Average Headcount for the Period
583.description: How much one employee costs the company over the period, including all related costs.
583.nuances:
The numerator is broader than in Average Gross Pay: besides pay, it **includes payroll taxes**, health insurance, training and other costs of keeping employees. The difference between the two metrics is the cost of everything beyond pay.
Headcount **is the average for** the period. With headcount on a single date, the costs of someone who left mid-month stay in the numerator while the person drops out of the denominator, and the metric is inflated.
Whether to count people or FTEs **is decided the same way** as in the other metrics on the map: when you count people, part-time employees pull the average cost down; when you count FTEs, the result is comparable across departments.
If contractor costs are included in the numerator, the contractors **are also included in** the denominator.
583.example:
[[Personnel Costs→hr/zatraty_na_personal]] for October: $496,750
Headcount on October 1: 64
Headcount on October 31: 60 (four people left mid-month)
Average headcount: 62

Cost per Employee = 496,750 / 62 = **$8,012**

With end-of-month headcount, it would come to $8,279: the pay of those who left stayed in the numerator, while they themselves dropped out of the denominator.
583.importance: **It's the number used** in hiring decisions: a position costs this much rather than its base salary. It's also needed for a fair comparison of an employee with a contractor: the contractor's rate looks higher than a salary, but it should be compared with the full cost of your own employee, which adds payroll taxes, workstation costs and everything else on top of base salary. It's also used to calculate the payback of automation: how much money is freed up, rather than how many hours.
583.not_needed: It means little when **positions vary widely**: an average across a company with both warehouse loaders and top management describes neither.
583.synonyms: Fully Loaded Cost per Employee, Total Cost per Employee
583.essence_note: the more one person costs, the higher the fixed costs for the same amount of work

584.name: Personnel Cost Share of Total Costs
584.description: What share of all the company's costs goes to people.
584.nuances:
The numerator **is the same** as in Personnel Costs: payroll plus [[Other Personnel Costs→hr/prochie_rashody_na_personal]] plus recruiting costs. If the numerator is calculated using one method here and another in the Personnel Costs card, the two metrics stop matching.
**Decide** what goes into total costs. With all costs, including purchases of goods, a trading company's share is low and moves month to month with purchasing rather than with headcount. If you take only [[Operating Expenses→finansy/operacionnye_rashody]] without the cost of goods sold, the metric shows the structure of the company's operating costs and responds to personnel decisions. The second option is closer to what the metric is for, but the definition of total costs has to be fixed once and kept: switching it changes the result sharply.
584.example:
[[Personnel Costs→hr/zatraty_na_personal]] for the quarter: $1,350,000
Cost of goods sold: $6,200,000
Rent, software, logistics, advertising: $1,650,000

As a share of operating expenses: 1,350,000 / (1,350,000 + 1,650,000) × 100 = **45%**
As a share of all costs: 1,350,000 / 9,200,000 × 100 = 14.7%

Both numbers are correct, but they answer different questions. Until the definition of total costs is fixed, comparing months makes no sense.
584.importance: It answers **how much** the company pays for its own people's work compared with everything else. A sharp rise in the share while revenue is stable signals that headcount grew for tasks that didn't pay off. The metric is used when deciding what's cheaper: hiring or outsourcing.
584.not_needed: Skip it when **only the owner** works in the company: what the owner pays themselves can't be separated from profit, and the personnel cost share depends on how much they decided to pay themselves rather than on the cost structure.
584.synonyms: Labor Cost Percentage, Workforce Cost Ratio
584.essence_note: with the same results, a smaller share of spending on people means more productive work

585.name: Key Employee Retention Rate
585.formula: ((Key Employees at the Start of the Period − Key Employees from That Group Who Left) / Key Employees at the Start of the Period) × 100
585.description: The share of key employees who were with the company at the start of the period and were still there at its end.
585.nuances:
**Base**: the list of key employees at the start of the period. If you take the count at the end, those who left have already dropped out of the denominator, and the metric systematically shows retention above the actual level, up to 100% despite real departures.
Key employees hired during the period **aren't in the base or** the numerator: the metric measures how well the people you already had were retained. Otherwise active hiring masks the losses.
The list of key employees is approved before the period starts and **doesn't change** during it. Revising the list after the fact makes it possible to drop someone who has already left from the base, and the metric stops meaning anything.
The criteria for a "key" employee **are written down**: unique expertise, a process that depends on the person, impact on revenue. Both the base and the result depend on how broad the criteria are.
585.example:
Key employee list on January 1: 24 people
Of those, left during the year: 3
New key employees hired during the year: 5 (not included in the calculation)
Key employees on December 31: 26

Key Employee Retention Rate = (24 − 3) / 24 × 100 = **87.5%**

With the year-end count as the base: (26 − 3) / 26 × 100 = 88.5%. With ten departures and twenty new key hires, the gap would be much more visible, 58% versus 71%: the metric would show a healthy picture while almost half of the original team had left.
585.importance: Overall turnover can look normal because it's driven by frontline employees, while the company is losing the people key processes depend on. This metric shows those losses **separately**. It's used for decisions on individual retention packages, successors, and which knowledge held by a single person urgently needs to be documented.
585.not_needed: **Skip it** when there's no approved list of key employees: without criteria, the number is put together from scratch every period, and there's nothing to compare.
585.synonyms: Key Talent Retention Rate, Critical Talent Retention Rate
585.essence_note: losing a person a process depends on costs the company more than any frontline turnover

586.name: Employee Satisfaction Score
586.formula: Sum of Scores from All Responses / Number of Respondents
586.description: How satisfied employees are with working at the company, according to a survey.
586.nuances:
The scale **is fixed once** (for example, 1 to 5), and so is the set of questions: changing the scale or the wording breaks comparability with past surveys.
The average score **is calculated over respondents** rather than total headcount: people who didn't respond don't count as zero points.
With participation below half the staff, the result is skewed: the people who respond are either the satisfied ones or, on the contrary, those with complaints to voice. The participation rate **is recorded along with** the score; otherwise a rise in the score can't be told apart from a drop in turnout.
**Anonymity affects the number**: non-anonymous surveys give noticeably higher scores, and switching between formats makes surveys incomparable.
586.example:
Staff: 210 people
Responded: 148 (70% participation)
Scale: 1 to 5
Sum of scores: 561

Employee Satisfaction Score = 561 / 148 = **3.8 out of 5**

Dividing the sum by all 210 gives 2.7: that spreads the respondents' points over people who didn't respond, and it no longer measures satisfaction.
586.importance: It's the only metric on the map where the data comes **from employees themselves** rather than from record-keeping systems. A drop in a department's score comes before a rise in separations, and that lead time is the window in which something can still be changed. Individual survey questions point to where to look: pay, manager, workload, conditions.
586.not_needed: **It makes no sense** in teams of a few people: anonymity can't be ensured, answers will be cautious, and the score won't show anything.
586.synonyms: Employee Satisfaction Index, Job Satisfaction Score
586.essence_note: satisfied employees leave less often, and a drop in the score comes before a rise in separations

587.name: Headcount Fill Rate
587.description: The share of approved budgeted positions filled by employees.
587.nuances:
Both values **are counted in the same** units: if the headcount plan is kept in FTEs, actual headcount is converted to FTEs too. Comparing people with FTEs gives a percentage that's bound to be wrong wherever there's part-time work.
Both values **are taken on the same** date. Average actual headcount for the period against the headcount plan at month-end gives an inconsistent result, especially if the plan changed during the period.
An employee on parental leave occupies a budgeted position and **isn't counted** in actual headcount while not working: otherwise the position looks filled although no one is doing the work. Their temporary replacement counts as a separate actual FTE in the same position.
**Vacant positions frozen for budget reasons** stay in budgeted headcount until they're removed from the headcount plan, and they lower the fill rate.
A rate **above 100% is possible** when people were hired beyond the plan: it's a signal that the headcount plan has drifted from reality rather than a calculation error.
587.example:
Budgeted FTEs on December 1: 230
Actually working: 210
Of those, 4 are half-time; converted to FTEs: 208
On parental leave: 6 (they occupy budgeted positions and aren't counted in actual headcount)
Temporary replacements for parental leave: 4 (counted)

Headcount Fill Rate = 208 / 230 × 100 = **90.4%**

Counting heads, it would be 210 / 230 = 91.3%: at this scale, half-time positions barely show, but in a small department the difference will be noticeable.
587.importance: **It shows the gap between what** the company has and what it planned. A steady 85% means the revenue plan was calculated for full staffing, but it will be delivered with 85% of the people, and the gap will be covered by overtime. The metric also catches the opposite situation: a headcount plan that hasn't been revised for years and no longer describes the real need.
587.not_needed: Skip it where **there's no headcount plan** and people are hired for tasks: the denominator would have to be made up.
587.essence_note: the closer to full staffing, the less work depends on overtime

588.name: Actual Headcount
588.formula: Number of active employees on a date
588.description: How many employees work at the company.
588.nuances:
Headcount on a date and the average for the period are **different values**, and the metric provides both: headcount on a date for the fill rate and HR workload, the period average for metrics whose numerator accumulates over the month, such as Revenue per Employee and Cost per Employee. When headcount grows or shrinks, end-of-period headcount distorts such metrics in either direction.
**Decide** whether to count people or FTEs. Counting people is simpler and matches HR records; FTEs are comparable across departments with different work schedules and are correct for the fill rate if the headcount plan is kept in FTEs. One choice is fixed for the whole map.
**Decide whether** contractor firms' workers and independent contractors are included. If they do the work but aren't in headcount, [[Revenue per Employee→hr/vyruchka_na_sotrudnika]] is inflated and [[Cost per Employee→hr/zatraty_na_sotrudnika]] is understated; if they are included, their pay must also go into [[Personnel Costs→hr/zatraty_na_personal]].
Employees on parental leave and long unpaid leave **aren't counted** in active headcount: they're not working, although they're still on the books. People on regular sick leave or vacation are counted.
588.example:
Employees on the books on July 31: 72
On parental leave: 6 (not counted)
On long unpaid leave: 2 (not counted)
On sick leave: 3 (counted)
Contractor firms' workers and independent contractors: 5 (not counted)

Headcount on July 31 = **64**
On July 1, it was 60
Average headcount for July = (60 + 64) / 2 = **62**
588.importance: It's **the denominator for half the map**: revenue per employee and [[Cost per Employee→hr/zatraty_na_sotrudnika]], turnover, fill rate and HR workload all depend on it. An error here distorts all these metrics at once and isn't visible in them: the discrepancy is usually discovered when two systems give different numbers at the same meeting.
588.synonyms: Headcount, Employee Count, Number of Employees
588.essence_note: when there aren't enough people, work doesn't get done, and when there are too many, payroll eats up profit

589.name: Employee Separations
589.description: How many employees left the company during the period.
589.nuances:
A separation **is assigned to the period by the last** day worked rather than the date the termination paperwork is signed: the paperwork can be signed in advance, and then the person lands in the wrong month.
**All reasons are counted**: voluntary resignation, mutual agreement, layoff, end of a temporary contract, not passing the probationary period, retirement.
Going on parental leave **isn't a separation**: the employment continues, and the person stays on staff.
A transfer between legal entities of the same group **isn't counted as a separation**, even though it's formally processed as one: the employee doesn't leave the company. If such transfers are included in the count, turnover will rise with reorganizations even though nobody left the company.
Part-timers whose main job is elsewhere and contractors are treated the same way as in actual headcount: if they **are in the denominator** of turnover, their departures are counted here too.
589.example:
Last day worked in June
Voluntary resignation: 8
Layoff: 2
End of a temporary contract: 1
Paperwork signed June 28, last day July 3: 1 (counted in July)
Went on parental leave: 2 (not counted)
Transferred to another legal entity in the group: 3 (not counted)

Employee Separations = **11**
589.importance: It's the count that turnover and replacement planning depend on. The number itself is needed for hiring: eleven people leaving means eleven positions to fill on top of new ones, and without this number the recruiting plan is put together as an afterthought. A spike in a particular month usually **matches an event**: a change of manager, seasonal overtime, delayed pay.
589.essence_note: every departure is a position to fill again and knowledge that leaves with the person

590.name: Employee Turnover Rate
590.formula: (Employee Separations / Average Headcount for the Period) × 100
590.description: The share of employees who left the company during the period.
590.nuances:
Average headcount **is calculated by one** method all year: either the average of the headcounts at the start and end of the period, or the average of daily headcounts. When people join and leave within a month, these methods give different results, and switching between them breaks the comparison of periods.
The numerator **matches what** [[Employee Separations→hr/uvolivshiesya_sotrudniki]] counts: the same date rule and the same types of separations.
**All separations are counted**, including layoffs and the end of temporary contracts. Separately, voluntary turnover is calculated with the same formula from voluntary resignations: it answers a different question, because a layoff is the company's decision, while a resignation is the employee's.
Monthly turnover **isn't annualized** by multiplying by 12: seasonal months would give unrealistic values. For an annual figure, take the separations for the year and the average headcount for the year.
590.example:
Headcount on June 1: 210
Headcount on June 30: 202
Average headcount: 206
Left in June: 11 (8 voluntary resignations, 2 layoffs, 1 end of a temporary contract)

Employee Turnover Rate = 11 / 206 × 100 = **5.3%**
Voluntary turnover = 8 / 206 × 100 = 3.9%

You can't multiply 5.3% by 12: June had seasonal hiring and departures, and February looks different.
590.importance: It's **the earliest financial signal** about personnel: every separation costs a replacement hire plus the time until the new person reaches full productivity. A spike in one department while the rest of the company is stable usually points to the manager rather than the market. If turnover isn't tracked, the problem gets noticed when the people leaving are the ones who can't be replaced.
590.not_needed: It adds little with **a staff of a few people**: one person leaving out of five gives 20%, and the swings reflect individual events rather than processes.
590.essence_note: every person who leaves means a new opening and the time until the replacement reaches full productivity

591.name: HR Headcount
591.description: How many people in the company work in HR.
591.nuances:
**Count those** whose main function is HR work: recruiters, HR administrators, training staff and the head of HR. A line manager who interviews their own candidates isn't counted: otherwise the number turns into a count of everyone who ever took part in hiring.
**Decide** whether to count people or FTEs. Counted by head, a half-time HR person equals a full specialist, and their workload in the Employee-to-HR Ratio looks half as high as it really is; FTEs give a more accurate picture but require data on work hours. For a small HR team, the difference is fundamental.
An outsourced recruiter **isn't included** in headcount: they aren't an employee, and their work shows up in recruiting costs.
The number **is taken on the same** date or for the same period as headcount in the [[Employee-to-HR Ratio→hr/sotrudnikov_na_odnogo_hr]].
591.example:
HR director: 1
Recruiters: 2
HR administrator at 0.5 FTE: 1 person, 0.5 FTE
Warehouse manager who hires loaders themselves: not counted
Recruiting agency: not counted

Counting heads: 1 + 2 + 1 = 4
In FTEs: 1 + 2 + 0.5 = **3.5**
591.importance: It's **the denominator for assessing** HR workload and the entry point to a discussion of the HR budget. By itself, the number shows whether there's anyone at all to handle hiring and onboarding: with zero dedicated HR staff, all these tasks fall on managers and get done with whatever time is left, which later shows up in time to fill and turnover.
591.not_needed: There's nothing to count in a company without a single dedicated HR person: this also **applies to organizations** that have fully outsourced HR.
591.synonyms: HR Staff Count, HR Team Size
591.essence_note: without dedicated specialists, hiring and onboarding fall on managers, and a bloated HR team costs money when the staff is small

592.name: Employee-to-HR Ratio
592.description: How many employees there are per HR specialist.
592.nuances:
Both values **are taken on the same** date, or both as averages for the period, but not mixed.
Whether to count people or FTEs **is decided the same way in** the numerator and the denominator. Counted by head, one HR person at 0.5 FTE becomes a whole one, and their workload comes out at half the actual level; in FTEs, you divide by 0.5, and the result doubles.
The numerator includes the company's entire headcount rather than **only those** an HR specialist covers in their own area: the metric assesses the staffing of the HR function as a whole.
HR employees themselves **are in the numerator**, since they're part of actual headcount.
592.example:
Actual headcount on December 1: 210 people
HR team: HR director, 2 recruiters, an HR administrator at 0.5 FTE

In FTEs: 210 / 3.5 = **60 employees per HR staff member**
Counting heads: 210 / 4 = 53

The difference of 7 people per specialist comes from a single half-time position: with a small HR team, the counting method changes the conclusion about workload.
592.importance: It's **an argument** in discussions about expanding or cutting the HR team. When there are twice as many people per specialist as is standard in the industry, what isn't urgent suffers: onboarding, training, work with departing employees, and the consequences show up later in turnover. The metric also shows the opposite situation: a bloated HR team in a company with a small staff.
592.not_needed: It's meaningless **without dedicated HR staff**: there's nothing to divide by.
592.essence_note: when HR is overloaded, what isn't urgent suffers: onboarding and work with departing employees, and when it has too little work, the HR team costs more than it delivers

593.name: Applicant-to-Hire Rate
593.description: The share of applicants who made it to their first day of work.
593.nuances:
The numerator counts **people rather than openings**: one opening can be for twenty hires, and dividing filled openings by candidates gives a meaningless number.
A hire **is someone** who started work rather than someone who accepted an offer: declines after an offer should lower the metric.
Candidates and hires **are taken as a cohort**: count those who applied in the period and the hires from those same applications, even if the hire happened later. If the numerator includes starts by people who applied in earlier months while the denominator has the current month's applications, the metric mixes two different flows and drops for no reason in a month with a job ad campaign.
The denominator **matches what** [[Job Applications→hr/otkliknuvshiesya_kandidaty]] counts: if two applications from one person count as two there, they do here too.
593.example:
Applied in May: 320 candidates
Of those, received an offer: 14
Of those, started work: 11 (three declined after the offer)
Started in May from April applications: 8 (not counted; they're in the April cohort)

Applicant-to-Hire Rate = 11 / 320 × 100 = **3.4%**

Openings filled in May: 4. Dividing 4 by 320 gives 1.3%: that's a share of openings rather than candidates.
593.importance: It shows whether the flow of applications is **usable at all**. A rate of a fraction of a percent means the opening attracts irrelevant people and the recruiter spends time sorting through junk: the fix is the posting text and the job board rather than tougher selection. A rate that's too high is a signal too: there's almost no one to choose from.
593.not_needed: Skip it when hiring **only through direct** sourcing and referrals: there are no applications as such, and there's nothing to put in the denominator.
593.essence_note: when the rate is too low, applications come from the wrong people, and when it's too high, the company hires everyone who applies

594.name: Time to Fill
594.formula: Sum of Fill Times / Positions Filled
594.description: How much time passes on average from publishing a job posting to the new hire's first day of work.
594.nuances:
The clock runs **until the employee actually starts** rather than until the offer is accepted: between the two is usually the customary two weeks' notice at the previous job, and the metric differs by that time.
**It's counted in calendar** days.
**An opening goes into** the period in which it was filled, with its entire duration, even if it opened three months earlier. Because of this, filling a long-open position sharply raises the month's average.
Openings canceled without a hire aren't included: their duration isn't complete. Those filled by an internal transfer **are included** if an internal transfer counts as a fill in [[Positions Filled→hr/zakrytye_vakansii]].
If an opening was put on hold, **decide** whether the pause is subtracted from the duration: without subtracting it, the metric measures calendar time; with it, the recruiter's working time. On positions that stay open a long time, the difference can be large.
594.example:
Openings reviewed for June: 4
Sales manager: posted May 5, started June 12: 38 days
Warehouse clerk: May 20, started June 9: 20 days
Accountant: March 3, started June 22: 111 days
Analyst: June 1, offer accepted June 27, start July 14: doesn't count for June

Time to Fill = (38 + 20 + 111) / 3 = **56 days**

Without the accountant, the average would be 29 days: with so few openings, one long one nearly doubles the result.
594.importance: This duration determines when the business can plan to launch a new line of business and how many months a department works understaffed. If hiring takes two months and a manager requests the opening two weeks before the date it's needed, the gap is covered by overtime from current employees. **Only together with** the stage pass-through rates does the metric show which funnel stage the time goes to.
594.not_needed: It tells you little with **one-off hiring** during a year, when the average over one or two openings simply equals their duration.
594.synonyms: Days to Fill, Time to Start
594.essence_note: while an opening is unfilled, the work gets done through other people's overtime

595.name: Recruiting Costs
595.description: How much the company spent on recruiting during the period.
595.nuances:
What's included is fixed **once**: paid job postings, resume database access, staffing agency fees, employee referral bonuses, job ads, candidate assessments and background checks.
**Decide** whether recruiter salaries are included. With them, the total is noticeably higher for companies with in-house recruiting and becomes comparable to agency spending; without them, in-house hiring looks almost free. The chosen option must match what's used in [[Cost per Hire→hr/stoimost_nayma]].
Hiring managers' time **isn't included** in costs: it isn't paid for separately and can only be estimated roughly.
An expense **is assigned to the month** of payment. Tying it to the month an opening is filled requires splitting a single payment for job postings across several future hires, and the amounts stop matching the books.
In [[Personnel Costs→hr/zatraty_na_personal]], this amount **is included as a separate component**, alongside payroll and other personnel costs. Recruiter salaries are counted once: they're already in payroll, so they're subtracted from recruiting costs in the total.
595.example:
Job board posting package, paid in September: $4,000
Agency fee for hiring a manager: $22,000
Employee referral bonus: $2,000
Recruiter salary for September: $7,000 (this company includes it)
Manager's time on 12 interviews: not counted

Recruiting Costs = 4,000 + 22,000 + 2,000 + 7,000 = **$35,000**
595.importance: It determines whether the chosen recruiting approach pays off. An agency at $22,000 per position is justified for a rare specialist and ruinous for frontline hiring, and you can see this **only by adding up all** channels' costs into one amount. Without tracking, the costs get lost in marketing and administrative line items, and nobody knows what it really costs to staff the company.
595.not_needed: Don't collect it when hiring happens only **through the manager's personal connections** and no money is spent.
595.synonyms: Recruitment Spend, Hiring Costs, Talent Acquisition Costs
595.essence_note: every dollar spent on recruiting is subtracted from profit and produces nothing by itself

596.name: Applications per Job Posting
596.description: How many applications one job posting gets on average.
596.nuances:
The denominator **is the number** of postings active in the period rather than only those published in it: applications also come in for postings that have been up since last month, and without them the average shoots up.
The numerator **matches what** [[Job Applications→hr/otkliknuvshiesya_kandidaty]] counts, with the same duplicate rule and the same date rule.
An application **is tied to the posting** it came in for. One person who applied to two postings counts as two applications: the metric measures application volume per posting rather than the number of people.
Applications from all channels **are added together**, including messaging apps and referrals, if they're logged as applications to a specific posting.
One posting published on several job boards **still counts as one**: otherwise the denominator grows while the applications stay the same.
596.example:
Active postings in November: 9 (4 of them opened in October)
Each published on three job boards: count 9, not 27
Applications in November: 414

Applications per Job Posting = 414 / 9 = **46**

Dividing only by the 5 postings opened in November gives 83: the applications to the older postings didn't go anywhere, but the denominator lost those postings.
596.importance: It's **the first signal** that people don't see the posting or don't want the job. Few applications for a frontline position mean the problem is the pay, the description or the job board, and it needs to be sorted out before time to fill stretches out. On the other hand, a very large number of applications is a load on the recruiter that keeps good candidates waiting a long time for a reply.
596.not_needed: Skip it when **hiring is done through direct sourcing**: the recruiter reaches out to candidates, and there are no applications to a posting.
596.synonyms: Applicants per Opening, Applications per Opening
596.essence_note: few applications mean people don't see the posting or don't want the job, and more applications than the recruiter can physically review don't improve selection

597.name: Job Postings
597.description: How many job postings the company had up during the period.
597.nuances:
**Count the postings** active in the period rather than only those published in it: a posting that's been up for five months continues to collect applications and stays in the count. Otherwise the denominator in [[Applications per Job Posting→hr/zayavok_na_vakansiyu]] loses some postings while the applications to them remain.
One opening published on several job boards **is counted once**, since job boards are channels rather than separate positions.
An opening for several people **counts as one posting**, although it will produce as many fills as people who started. Because of this, filled positions for a period can outnumber postings.
A position that's open but not published **isn't included**: the metric measures what's been advertised to candidates.
597.example:
New postings published in November: 5
Still up from October and earlier: 4
One of them duplicated on 3 job boards: count 1
Positions approved in the headcount plan but not published: 2 (not counted)

Job Postings = 5 + 4 = **9**
597.importance: It shows the recruiting workload and serves as the denominator for Applications per Job Posting. A gap between postings and fills that grows month after month means positions that can't be filled are piling up: departments work short-staffed, and **the number of filled positions alone** doesn't show it.
597.not_needed: **Skip it when** recruiting is done only through direct sourcing and referrals: openings aren't published, so there's nothing to post.
597.essence_note: when there are no open positions, the company isn't growing, and when there are many, departments work short-staffed

598.name: Job Applications
598.description: How many job applications the company received during the period.
598.nuances:
**All applications received are counted** before screening: filtering for fit with the requirements turns the count into a measure of the recruiter's work and makes the hire rate incomparable across months.
**Obvious spam** and applications without a resume are filtered out if the funnel conversion rates are set up the same way: one rule for the whole funnel.
Unit of count: an application rather than a person. One candidate who applied to two openings counts as two applications; a repeat application to the same opening **is counted once**.
An application **is assigned to the period by the date** it was received rather than the date the recruiter opened it: otherwise a spike in applications shifts into the next month along with the review queue.
598.example:
Applications received in November: 471
Of those, obvious spam and empty applications: 56 (not counted)
One candidate applied to 2 different openings: 2 applications
Another applied to one opening twice: 1 application
Applications received November 30 and reviewed December 2: 18 (counted in November)

Job Applications = **414**
598.importance: It's the top of the hiring funnel: without it, you can't calculate either the conversion rates or the application volume per posting. The number itself shows whether the company has anyone to choose from: when the flow drops, hiring slows down later, and **only here** can you see it in advance.
598.not_needed: **Don't collect it when** recruiting is done only through direct sourcing and referrals, where candidates are approached with an offer rather than applying.
598.essence_note: the more applications, the more candidates to choose from and the faster an opening gets filled

599.name: Candidate Pass-Through Rate
599.formula: (Candidates Who Moved to the Next Stage / Candidates at the Previous Stage) × 100
599.description: The share of candidates who move from one hiring stage to the next.
599.nuances:
The metric gives **a set of numbers rather than one**: a value for each pair of adjacent stages in the funnel.
The set of stages differs across openings: developers get a skills test and warehouse clerks don't, and a hiring manager interview isn't part of every process. Within one opening, the list **is fixed in advance and** doesn't change, and comparisons across openings use only the stages they share: application, screening, interview, offer, start.
**It's calculated by cohort**: take the candidates who reached a stage in the period and track whether they move on, even if that happens the next month. Counting by calendar month compares different groups of people and, in a month with a spike in applications, shows a false drop in the pass-through rate.
A candidate **sent back to a previous stage** stays in their cohort and is counted at the furthest stage reached.
A candidate **moved to another opening** is excluded from the original funnel: it's neither a rejection nor a move forward.
599.example:
Funnel for a manager opening, cohort of February applications
Applications: 180
Passed screening: 54
Reached the hiring manager interview: 21
Received an offer: 6
Started work: 4

Application → screening = 54 / 180 × 100 = **30%**
Screening → interview = 21 / 54 × 100 = **39%**
Interview → offer = 6 / 21 × 100 = **29%**
Offer → start = 4 / 6 × 100 = **67%**

Two of the four hires started work in March but stay in the February cohort.
599.importance: **It shows exactly at which** step candidates are lost, and that's what sets it apart from the overall hire rate. A drop between offer and start is fixed with better terms and faster decisions, a drop at screening by rewriting the job posting, and a drop after the hiring manager interview usually means the requirements at screening and at the interview differ. Without a breakdown by stage, all you see is "we're not hiring enough," and the cause stays hidden.
599.not_needed: Skip it where selection **is a single step**: an interview followed by a start date doesn't make a funnel.
599.synonyms: Stage Conversion Rate, Pass-Through Rate, Pipeline Conversion Rate
599.essence_note: at 0%, nobody makes it to a hire; at 100%, the stage screens out nobody and does no selecting

600.name: Positions Filled
600.description: How many openings were filled with a hire during the period.
600.nuances:
An opening **counts as filled when** the employee starts work, rather than when the offer is signed: until the start, the hire can still fall through. The same definition is used in [[Cost per Hire→hr/stoimost_nayma]] and [[Time to Fill→hr/vremya_nayma]].
The unit of count is **a position rather than a job posting**: hiring three warehouse clerks gives three fills, even if there was one job posting. Otherwise the metric won't match the number of people hired.
An opening canceled without a hire **doesn't count as filled**.
**Decide** whether a fill by an internal candidate counts. If it does, the metric measures how well the business's needs are covered; if not, it measures only external hiring. An internal transfer usually leaves a vacated position that becomes a new opening, and that one is counted separately.
600.example:
Started work in August: 6 people, 3 of them loaders hired from one job posting
Accepted an offer in August, starting in September: 2 (not counted)
Position filled by a transfer from another department: 1 (counted)
Opening canceled, position no longer needed: 1 (not counted)

Positions Filled = 6 + 1 = **7**
600.importance: It's **the base count** that the cost and speed of hiring rely on. By itself, it answers whether recruiting keeps up with the stated need: if 15 openings were opened and 7 filled, by the end of the quarter half the departments are working short-staffed, and this is visible before project deadlines start slipping.
600.not_needed: Skip it with **one-off hiring**, when one or two positions are filled a year: the count just repeats the list of names and doesn't summarize anything.
600.synonyms: Hires, Number of Hires, Filled Requisitions
600.essence_note: every filled position is a department that's no longer short-staffed

601.name: Cost per Hire
601.description: How much it costs the company to fill one opening.
601.nuances:
The numerator **includes the same cost items** as [[Recruiting Costs→hr/zatraty_na_naym]], including the decision on recruiter salaries: with them, the cost per fill for a company with in-house recruiting rises noticeably.
An opening **counts as filled** when the employee starts work rather than when they accept the offer: the same as in the count of filled positions.
An opening for several people gives **as many fills** as people who started, so high-volume hiring lowers the cost per fill with spending unchanged.
The numerator and denominator **cover the same** period, even though costs and fills don't line up in time: the posting is paid for in April, and the person starts in June. Over a short window, this creates jumps, even months with costs but no fills; calculating over a quarter or a year smooths them out.
601.example:
[[Recruiting Costs→hr/zatraty_na_naym]] for September: $35,000
Positions filled in September: 7 (including 3 loaders from one job posting)

Cost per Hire = 35,000 / 7 = **$5,000**

The $22,000 agency fee was for one manager but got spread across seven hires. Over the quarter, the number is steadier: 96,000 / 19 = $5,053.
601.importance: It's **the only way** to tell what's cheaper: paying an agency, investing in job postings or training up an in-house recruiter. The cost of retention is also compared with this number: if filling a position costs three months' pay, the conversation about retaining an employee looks different. It also sets next year's recruiting budget through the hiring plan.
601.not_needed: Skip it with **one-off hiring**: with one opening a year, the "average cost" is simply the total spent on it.
601.synonyms: Recruiting Cost per Hire, Hiring Cost per Employee
601.essence_note: every filled position comes with recruiting costs, and that money produces nothing by itself

602.name: Personnel Costs
602.formula: Total Payroll + Other Personnel Costs + Recruiting Costs
602.description: How much the company spends on personnel in total: pay to current employees plus everything else spent on keeping them and on bringing in new ones.
602.nuances:
Payroll **is calculated as the sum of actual** gross pay from the payroll register.
[[Recruiting Costs→hr/zatraty_na_naym]] **are included as a separate component** rather than in other personnel costs: other costs are for keeping current employees, and recruiting is for bringing in new ones. They are added together here.
Recruiter salaries **are counted once**. If they're included in [[Recruiting Costs→hr/zatraty_na_naym]], they aren't subtracted from payroll; instead, they're taken out of recruiting costs when the terms are added up: otherwise they'd enter the total twice.
**Decide** where employer payroll taxes go: inside payroll or in other personnel costs. This doesn't affect the total as long as they land in exactly one place, but it does affect the [[Bonus Share of Payroll→hr/bonusov_v_fot]] and the [[Payroll-to-Revenue Ratio→hr/fot_v_vyruchke]].
Training, health insurance, meals, stipends and other personnel costs **are assigned to the month** of payment, the same as in the Other Personnel Costs card.
602.example:
Gross pay on the October payroll register: $382,500
Employer payroll taxes: $38,250 (counted in payroll)
Health insurance, meals, training: $48,000
[[Recruiting Costs→hr/zatraty_na_naym]] for October: $35,000, including $7,000 for the recruiter's salary

Personnel Costs = 382,500 + 38,250 + 48,000 + (35,000 − 7,000) = **$496,750**

The recruiter's salary is already on the payroll register, so it's subtracted from recruiting costs when the terms are added up: otherwise the same $7,000 would be counted twice.
602.importance: It's the full cost of the workforce, used to calculate the break-even point and the maximum personnel spending the business can sustain. When companies budget from base salaries alone, they miss the payroll taxes and benefits, and then **the budget doesn't add up**. It's the starting point when deciding whether to hire an employee or outsource to a contractor.
602.synonyms: Labor Costs, Workforce Costs, People Costs
602.essence_note: this is the full cost of the workforce, subtracted from profit every month

603.name: Total Payroll
603.formula: Sum of actual gross pay on the payroll register for the period
603.description: The gross pay accrued to employees for the period, per the payroll register.
603.nuances:
**Actual gross pay is used** rather than [[Average Gross Pay→hr/srednyaya_zarplata]] multiplied by headcount: when people join or leave mid-month, the register shows amounts for the time actually worked, and average times headcount doesn't reproduce them. Besides, average gross pay is itself calculated from payroll, so such a formula makes the two metrics depend on each other in a loop.
Gross pay **includes base salaries**, differentials and allowances, bonuses and incentive pay, vacation pay and employer-paid sick leave.
The amount **is taken before** income tax and other withholdings: it's what was accrued, rather than take-home pay.
Pay to contractor firms and independent contractors **isn't included** in payroll: it's paid under other contracts and doesn't go through the payroll register.
**Decide** whether employer payroll taxes are included. With them, the total is higher by the amount of payroll taxes and closer to the real cost; without them, payroll stays what's owed to people. The decision is made once: the Payroll-to-Revenue Ratio, the Bonus Share of Payroll and [[Personnel Costs→hr/zatraty_na_personal]] depend on it.
603.example:
Base pay, differentials and other pay for April: $270,000
KPI bonuses and quarterly bonus: $90,000
Vacation pay and employer-paid sick leave: $0
Independent contractor agreements: $25,500 (not part of payroll)

Total Payroll without payroll taxes = **$360,000**
With payroll taxes at 10%: $396,000

If you calculated it from an average base salary of $4,700 × 60 people + bonuses, you'd get $372,000: five people started and three left mid-month, and they weren't paid a full month's salary.
603.importance: It's **one of the largest and** most rigid cost items: it can't be cut within a month, so it's the basis for calculating the safety margin and the minimum revenue the company can live on. The Payroll-to-Revenue Ratio and [[Average Gross Pay→hr/srednyaya_zarplata]] are derived from it, so an error in what it includes carries through all the financial metrics on the map.
603.not_needed: Skip it when there are no employees and all work is done under contracts with contractor firms and independent contractors: there's no payroll register, and payments against invoices **count as services** rather than labor costs.
603.synonyms: Gross Payroll, Payroll Costs, Wage Bill
603.essence_note: this is one of the largest and most rigid cost items, subtracted from profit every month

604.name: Average Gross Pay
604.formula: Total Payroll / Average Headcount for the Period
604.description: How much gross pay was accrued per employee on average for the period.
604.nuances:
Payroll **is calculated as the sum of actual** gross pay from the payroll register; otherwise average gross pay and payroll are defined through each other, and neither can be calculated.
Bonuses **are included**: on the register they're accrued together with base salary, so in months with quarterly bonuses the average is higher with no change in base salaries.
The amount **is taken before** income tax and other withholdings: it's what the company accrued, and the same amount is used in all the other financial metrics on the map.
Employer payroll taxes **aren't included**: the employer pays them on top of gross pay, and the employee doesn't receive that money. With payroll taxes, the result stops being pay and is inflated by the amount of payroll taxes, and it can no longer be compared with market offers. The full cost of a person including payroll taxes is shown by [[Cost per Employee→hr/zatraty_na_sotrudnika]].
Headcount **is the average for** the period. When you count people, part-time employees pull the average down; when you convert to FTEs, you get the average for full-time work. These are different values, and one method is fixed for the whole map.
604.example:
Gross pay on the April payroll register (without payroll taxes): $360,000
Average headcount for April: 60 people, 4 of them half-time
In FTEs: 58

Counting heads: 360,000 / 60 = **$6,000**
In FTEs: 360,000 / 58 = $6,207

A quarterly bonus of $37,500 was accrued in April, so the average is higher than in March with the same base salaries.
604.importance: It's the number **you take to the job market**: it shows whether the company fits within the pay range that candidates will consider at all. If the average lags the market, first time to fill grows, then turnover, and both effects cost more than a raise. Inside the company, the average gives a quick check of whether the base salaries of new and long-standing employees have drifted apart.
604.not_needed: It's of little use when pay **varies widely** across roles: an average across the warehouse and top management doesn't describe any real salary, so look at the median or averages by pay grade instead.
604.synonyms: Average Salary, Average Pay, Average Earnings
604.essence_note: when pay is below the market, time to fill and turnover grow; when it's above the market, payroll outpaces revenue, and pay doesn't come back down

605.name: Payroll-to-Revenue Ratio
605.description: What share of revenue the company spends on pay.
605.nuances:
Payroll **is calculated as the sum** of actual gross pay from the payroll register for the period, rather than as [[Average Gross Pay→hr/srednyaya_zarplata]] multiplied by headcount.
**Decide** whether employer payroll taxes are included in payroll: with them, the ratio is higher in proportion to the payroll tax rate. Payroll taxes are included or excluded the same way in all metrics on the map; otherwise the [[Payroll-to-Revenue Ratio→hr/fot_v_vyruchke]] and the [[Bonus Share of Payroll→hr/bonusov_v_fot]] will be calculated from different amounts.
Both numbers cover **the same period**: a month's gross pay is matched with the same month's revenue, even if someone worked half the month, because the register already shows their actual amount.
605.example:
Gross pay on the March payroll register: $315,000
Employer payroll taxes (not included in payroll): $31,500
Revenue for March: $1,575,000

Payroll-to-Revenue Ratio = 315,000 / 1,575,000 × 100 = **20%**

With payroll taxes included, it's 346,500 / 1,575,000 = 22%. It's the same month and the same revenue; the only difference is what payroll includes.
605.importance: **It shows whether** revenue can support the current headcount. When the ratio creeps up while revenue stays flat, the company has added people faster than sales have grown, and this shows up before profit drops. It's used to decide whether to freeze hiring or revise the pay structure.
605.not_needed: It says little for companies where most of the work **is outsourced to contractor firms** and independent contractors: their pay isn't part of payroll, so the ratio looks low while spending on people is high.
605.synonyms: Payroll as a Percentage of Revenue, Payroll Ratio
605.essence_note: the bigger the share of revenue that pay eats up, the less is left for the company

606.name: Bonus Share of Payroll
606.description: What share of pay to employees is variable pay rather than base salary.
606.nuances:
Bonuses **are in both** the numerator and the denominator, which is the entire payroll on the register, variable pay included. So the result is always below 100%.
**A fixed list defines** what counts as a bonus: KPI bonuses, quarterly and annual bonuses, sales commissions, holiday bonuses. One-time payments such as milestone birthday gifts and hardship payments aren't bonuses.
A bonus is included **in full** in the month it's accrued on the payroll register. If a quarterly bonus is spread over three months, bonuses in the accrual month stop matching that month's payroll. Because of this, the share jumps in months with quarterly and annual payouts: it makes sense to compare comparable months or the whole period.
606.example:
Gross pay on the April payroll register: $360,000
Of that, base pay and differentials: $267,000
KPI bonuses: $52,500
Quarterly bonus: $37,500
Hardship payment to an employee: $3,000 (not counted as a bonus)

Bonuses = 52,500 + 37,500 = $90,000
Bonus Share of Payroll = 90,000 / 360,000 × 100 = **25%**
606.importance: It determines how much personnel spending shrinks in a bad month. With bonuses at 5% of payroll, payroll is practically fixed, and a drop in revenue hits profit **in full**; at 30%, part of the blow is absorbed on its own. The metric is reviewed when the incentive system is redesigned and when calculating the minimum revenue the company can survive on.
606.not_needed: There's nothing to calculate where all pay is **base salary** and there are no bonuses by design: the result will be zero every month.
606.synonyms: Variable Pay Ratio, Variable Pay Percentage
