606.essence_note: when payroll is almost all base salary, a drop in revenue hits profit in full, and when the variable part is too large, people leave for jobs with a higher base salary

607.name: Absenteeism Rate
607.formula: (Hours of Unplanned Absence / Scheduled Work Hours) × 100
607.description: The share of work time lost to unplanned employee absences.
607.nuances:
**Only unplanned absences are counted**: sick days, no-shows, late arrivals, and time off first reported that day. Paid vacation, public holidays and time off approved in advance aren't included. Including vacation inflates the rate and makes it meaningless: vacation is planned in advance and doesn't disrupt work.
Educational leave and time off to donate blood **aren't unplanned**: they're arranged in advance.
Denominator: scheduled hours from the work calendar for the entire headcount for the period, rather than hours actually worked. With hours actually worked, absence hours **are subtracted from the denominator**, and the rate is inflated.
The denominator **is calculated over all** employees rather than only those who were absent: otherwise you get the average length of an absence rather than the share of lost time.
607.example:
Employees: 50
Scheduled work hours in March: 168 per person
Total scheduled hours = 50 × 168 = 8,400 hours
Sick days: 240 hours
No-shows and late arrivals: 32 hours
Annual vacation: 336 hours (not counted)

Absenteeism Rate = (240 + 32) / 8,400 × 100 = **3.2%**

With vacation, it would be 7.2%: the number would more than double because of planned time the company itself approved.
607.importance: An unplanned absence means work that **nobody did** that day, and it's either shifted onto colleagues or lost. A rise in the rate in one department while the company is stable usually means burnout or a conflict with the manager, and it shows up before a spike in separations. In shift-based operations, it's used to size the backup staff pool.
607.not_needed: Skip it where work time isn't tracked and results are measured by tasks rather than presence: such teams simply **don't record** absence hours.
607.essence_note: this is paid work time in which nobody did the work

608.name: Other Personnel Costs
608.description: Spending on employees beyond what's paid through the payroll register.
608.nuances:
The line items **are set as a fixed list**; otherwise the total is put together differently every month. The list typically includes training and conferences, health insurance and medical checkups, meals, phone, commuting and housing stipends, company events, gifts, workstation equipment and workplace safety.
[[Recruiting Costs→hr/zatraty_na_naym]] **aren't included** here: they're about bringing in new people rather than keeping current employees, and they have their own metric.
Employer payroll taxes go either here or into payroll, but **in exactly one place**, and the decision is the same as in [[Personnel Costs→hr/zatraty_na_personal]].
An expense **is assigned to the month** of payment. An annual health insurance policy paid upfront lands entirely in the month it's paid and creates a spike: in month-to-month comparisons, such one-time payments are shown on a separate line.
608.example:
Health insurance for the year, paid in January: $360,000
Training and conferences: $16,000
Meals and office coffee: $7,000
Phone stipends: $3,000
Holiday party: $34,000
[[Recruiting Costs→hr/zatraty_na_naym]] for January: $23,000 (not counted; it's a separate metric)

Other Personnel Costs = **$420,000**

Of that, $360,000 is an annual payment, so January can't be compared with February directly.
608.importance: It's the part of personnel spending that usually **isn't collected in one place** and comes up when the budget is cut. It's used for decisions about the benefits package: you can see what health insurance costs per person and what dropping it would save. Without this amount, [[Personnel Costs→hr/zatraty_na_personal]] are understated, and the cost of one employee looks lower than it really is.
608.not_needed: **Skip it** when nothing is spent on employees beyond pay: with no health insurance, training, meals or stipends, the metric is always zero, and [[Personnel Costs→hr/zatraty_na_personal]] come down to payroll.
608.synonyms: Non-Wage Labor Costs, Employee Benefits Costs
608.essence_note: this is spending beyond pay that is subtracted from profit

609.name: Customer Retention Rate
609.formula: (Customers at the Start of the Period Who Kept Their Subscription Through the End / Customers at the Start of the Period) × 100
609.description: The share of customers who were there at the start of the period and were still paying at its end.
609.nuances:
**It's calculated only for** the customers at the start of the period: new customers go into neither the numerator nor the denominator.
Taking the end-of-period total without subtracting new customers **gives more than 100%** in months when more customers came than left, while retention by definition can't exceed 100%.
**Paying customers are counted** rather than all registered users: without payment, there's nothing to retain.
A customer who left and came back within the period **counts as retained** if the subscription is active at the end of the period.
In B2B, the unit **is the company account** rather than an employee: one employee leaving doesn't mean losing the customer.
609.example:
Paying customers on March 1: 1,200
Of those, subscription active on March 31: 1,128
New customers in March: 90 (not counted)
Total paying customers on March 31: 1,218

Customer Retention Rate = 1,128 / 1,200 × 100 = **94%**

The formula (1,218 − 90) / 1,200 gives the same 94%. Without subtracting new customers, in a month with 200 new and 72 churned customers, the end-of-month total gives (1,200 + 200 − 72) / 1,200 × 100 = 110.7%, and retention can't be above 100%.
609.importance: **It sets the ceiling on growth**: every month part of the base leaves, and the bigger the base, the more customers are lost in absolute numbers. Sooner or later, the losses catch up with the inflow, and the base stops growing even if acquisition works as before. There are two ways to raise the ceiling: bring in more customers or retain them better. This is the number used to decide whether to move budget from advertising to the product and support.
609.not_needed: Skip it for **one-time sales** with no ongoing relationship with the customer.
609.essence_note: the fewer customers leave, the bigger the base at the end of the period with the same acquisition

610.name: Sessions
610.formula: Number of sessions in the product during the period
610.description: The number of user sessions in the product during the period. A session ends after a set period of inactivity; the default in analytics tools is 30 minutes.
610.nuances:
The inactivity threshold is tuned to how the product is used: where people work in short visits, 30 minutes merges two visits into one session; where people spend a long time studying a report, it splits one task into several sessions. The chosen value **is fixed**; otherwise, comparisons between periods break.
**Sessions inside** the product are counted rather than visits to the website: marketing pages and the blog aren't included.
**Background tab activity** and auto-refresh don't create a new session: otherwise the count measures browser activity.
610.example:
Session timeout: 30 minutes of inactivity (the default)
Product sessions in March: 61,000
Visits to the marketing website: 24,000 (not counted)
A user worked in the morning and in the evening with a 4-hour break: 2 sessions

Sessions = **61,000**
610.importance: It shows the intensity of use **separately** from audience size: MAU can stay flat while sessions grow, which means the product is being opened more often, and that usually precedes growth in retention. It's also the basis for calculating infrastructure load.
610.not_needed: **Skip it for products** that run in the background without human involvement: integrations, scheduled services, automated exports. There are no user sessions there.
610.essence_note: the more often the product is opened, the more deeply it's woven into people's work and the harder it is to give up

612.name: Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)
612.formula: Marketing and Sales Costs for the Period / New Paying Customers for the Period
612.description: How much it costs on average to acquire one new paying customer.
612.nuances:
Costs **include ad spend**, marketing and sales salaries with payroll taxes, sales commissions and bonuses, subscriptions to advertising and CRM tools, content production and agency fees. Ad spend alone, without staff costs, understates CAC.
The denominator includes **all new paying** customers, including those who came without advertising: this is the company-wide average cost.
Paid-channel acquisition cost is calculated separately: there, the numerator is **only ad spend**, and the denominator only customers from ads. This metric isn't on the map: it's calculated separately and compared across channels, without being confused with the company-wide cost.
**The lag** between spending and a customer's arrival is handled by shifting the cost window: if the sales cycle is two months, January costs are matched with March customers. Without the shift, CAC jumps around following the ad budget.
Customers **are counted in the same** unit as in [[Paying Customers→saas_produkty/platyaschie_polzovateli]]. In B2B, that's a company account rather than an individual employee.
612.example:
Marketing and sales costs for January: $24,300
Of which: ads $14,200, salaries $8,100, tools $2,000
Sales cycle: 2 months → matched with March customers
New paying customers in March: 90

CAC = 24,300 / 90 = **$270**

Without salaries and tools, it would come out to $157.78: a nicer number, but it doesn't cover the real cost of acquisition.
612.importance: **The line** beyond which growth stops paying off: comparing it with LTV directly answers whether the company makes money on a new customer or loses money on them. An understated CAC is the most expensive mistake in SaaS: budgets grow on the strength of a flattering number, and the loss surfaces later, when customers don't stay long enough to pay back.
612.not_needed: Skip it when there's no paid acquisition or dedicated sales team, and customers come **only through referrals**.
612.essence_note: every dollar spent on acquisition is subtracted from what the customer will bring in

613.name: Cost per Signup
613.formula: Marketing Costs for the Period / Signups for the Same Period
613.description: How much it costs on average to acquire one signup.
613.nuances:
Costs include **only marketing spend**, without sales costs: the sales team usually isn't involved before signup, and including it inflates the cost of a step it isn't responsible for. This is how the numerator differs from CAC.
The denominator includes **all signups**, organic ones too: this is the company-wide average cost.
Paid-channel cost per signup is calculated separately: there, the numerator is **only ad spend**, and the denominator only signups from ads. This metric isn't on the map: it's calculated separately and compared across channels rather than with the company-wide cost.
Signups **are counted with the same** exclusion rules as in the signup count: if unconfirmed addresses are dropped there, they're dropped here too.
A window shift between spending and signup **isn't needed**: people respond to ads in the same days the money is spent, unlike with paying customers.
613.example:
Marketing costs for March: $16,000
Sales salaries and bonuses: $5,400 (not included)
Signups in March: 800

Cost per Signup = 16,000 / 800 = **$20**
613.importance: The first metric to show that traffic buying is becoming less efficient: it reacts quickly, while CAC becomes clear **only after a full** sales cycle. A rising cost per signup with unchanged conversion further down the funnel means the channel has exhausted its cheap audience.
613.not_needed: **Skip it** when the website has no signup and the sales team grants access after negotiations.
613.essence_note: the more a signup costs, the more each future paying customer costs

614.name: Trial Start Rate
614.formula: (Signups That Led to a Trial / Signups) × 100
614.description: The share of registered users who started a trial.
614.nuances:
**It's calculated by the signup cohort**: both the numerator and the denominator are grouped by signup month; otherwise, the rate can exceed 100%.
Trials with and without a card on file **are counted the same way**, since the event is the same: access to paid features is granted.
614.example:
Signed up in March: 800
Of those, started a trial: 464
Started a trial in March but signed up earlier: 60 (not counted)

Trial Start Rate = 464 / 800 × 100 = **58%**
614.importance: **It shows** whether the product's value is clear before people get into it. The more signups stop short of a trial, the more likely the problem is in how the product is presented: people don't understand what they'll get, or they hit the card requirement. With a low rate, expensive paid traffic is wasted before it reaches the product.
614.not_needed: **Skip it** when the trial starts automatically with signup: the value is always 100%.
614.synonyms: Signup-to-Trial Conversion Rate, Trial Opt-In Rate
614.essence_note: the more registered users get to a trial, the more potential paying customers

615.name: Time to Value (TTV)
615.formula: Sum of Signup-to-Activation Intervals for Activated Users / Number of Activated Users
615.description: How much time passes on average from signup to activation: the first action after which a person gets real value from the product.
615.nuances:
**It's calculated only for** those who activated: users who didn't activate have no interval, and including them as zero or as the maximum distorts the result either way.
With a wide spread, use **the median** rather than the mean: a few activations after six months pull the mean up and make the number unrealistic for most users.
**Use the same time unit for** all calculations: hours for products with activation on the first day, days for the rest.
Outliers are cut off **at the observation horizon**: if activations are counted for up to a year after signup, recent cohorts will look faster simply because they've had less time.
615.example:
March signup cohort, 30-day horizon
Activated: 296 people
Intervals: 40% within 1 day, 30% in 2–5 days, 30% in 6–30 days
The middle value of the sorted list: 2 days

Time to Value (TTV) = **2 days (median)**

The mean of the same data gives 6.4 days: the result of a few activations on days 28–30.
615.importance: **It determines** when to trigger emails, calls and in-product tips: if half of users activate within two days, a reminder on day seven reaches people who have already left. An increasing time to value is a sign that an unnecessary step was added to the start of the user journey.
615.not_needed: **Skip it** when activation happens during signup itself and the interval is always close to zero.
615.synonyms: Time to Activation, Time to First Value
615.essence_note: the longer a person goes without getting value, the higher the chance they won't come back

616.name: Onboarding Completion Rate
616.description: The share of registered users who completed all the steps of the onboarding flow: filling out the profile, completing setup and inviting colleagues. Onboarding is complete when the last step of the flow is done, whether or not the person got value from the product.
616.nuances:
Onboarding and activation are related but **aren't the same**. Activation can be one of the steps of the flow, if the flow makes the user take an action that delivers real value, or it can lie outside the flow and happen later. So a person can finish onboarding without activating, or activate without completing the flow.
**It's calculated by the signup cohort**: both the numerator and the denominator are grouped by signup month. Users who signed up at the very end of the period haven't had time to complete the flow yet: until the cohort matures, the rate is understated.
The overall rate shows how well the flow works **as a whole** but doesn't show where it breaks. If there are several steps, the transitions between them are calculated too: that shows the step where the most people drop off.
616.example:
Signed up in March: 800
Required onboarding steps: 4
Completed all 4: 412

Onboarding Completion Rate = 412 / 800 × 100 = **51.5%**

By step: step 1 completed by 720, step 2 by 640, step 3 by 557, step 4 by 412. The biggest drop is at the last step: from 557 to 412, where 145 people are lost.
616.importance: **It answers the question** of whether getting into the product takes too long. You can see exactly which step people drop off at, and that step can be removed or postponed: without this metric, the team fixes the interface blindly while people leave during setup before reaching the product itself.
616.not_needed: **Skip it** when the product has no step-by-step flow and the user goes straight to the main product interface.
616.essence_note: the more people get through setup to the end, the more of them reach the product itself

617.name: Daily Active Users (DAU)
617.description: The number of unique users who took a meaningful action in the product during a calendar day.
617.nuances:
**Activity** is a meaningful action in the product rather than opening the login page. It differs from the activation action in that it repeats: activation happens once, while activity covers regular work with the product. The definition is the same for DAU and MAU, otherwise their ratio is meaningless.
Uniqueness **is determined by the user** account rather than by device or browser: one person on a phone and a laptop is one unit.
In B2B, **decide** what counts as a unit: the company account or an employee within it. Counted by account, the number is steadier; counted by employee, it shows real engagement but dips more on weekends.
Day boundaries **are set in the same** time zone for all users, otherwise the same activity lands on different days when recalculated.
617.example:
Unit of count: employee, UTC time zone
Sessions with a meaningful action on March 12: 1,940
Unique users among them: 1,210
Opened the login page and left: 260 (not counted)
Technical integration accounts: 15 (not counted)

DAU = **1,210**
617.importance: **It gives the fastest feedback** on a release or an outage: a drop is visible the next day, while in revenue it shows up only later. Without DAU, a weekend outage is discovered through support tickets.
617.not_needed: Skip it for products with infrequent use: payroll or month-end close tools are opened a few days a month, and the daily number reflects **only the date** on the calendar.
617.essence_note: the more people open the product every day, the stronger the habit and the lower the churn

618.name: Activated Users
618.formula: Number of users who signed up during the period and completed the activation action
618.description: The number of users in a cohort who got real value from the product for the first time: for example, connected a data source and saw their first report. The product defines the list of such actions in advance.
618.nuances:
**It's calculated by the signup cohort**: a user goes into the period when they signed up rather than when they activated. Otherwise the monthly number mixes fresh signups with earlier signups that have only now activated, and you can't tell from it which signup cohort performed well.
**The cohort needs time to mature**: if the typical path to activation takes a week, the month's latest signups haven't had time to activate yet, and the number will keep growing after the period closes.
Activation counts **once** over the user's entire lifetime: repeating the same action doesn't make a new activation.
The list of activation actions **is the same as the one** used by [[Activation Rate→saas_produkty/aktivirovannyh_polzovateley]], [[Time to Value (TTV)→saas_produkty/vremya_do_aktivacii]] and [[Activated-to-Paid Conversion Rate→saas_produkty/konversiya_v_platnuyu_podpisku]]. This metric is the numerator of the Activation Rate, so they share the same cohort.
618.example:
Activation = connected a store and saw the first report
Signed up in February: 100, of those activated: 50
Signed up in March: 200, of those activated: 50
Repeat connections of a second store: 85 (not counted)

Activated Users = **50** for the February cohort and **50** for the March cohort

The same activation counts with different cohort sizes: the February cohort's activation rate was twice as high. If the same activations were counted by activation month, they would merge into one number, and the difference between the cohorts would be invisible.
618.importance: **The real number of engaged users the product gains**, unlike signups, many of whom never come back. A breakdown by cohort shows which cohorts performed well: the same number of activations with a different number of signups means the channels differ in quality.
618.not_needed: **Skip it** when the product has no activation step and value comes right after login.
618.essence_note: these are the people who got value from the product, and only they come back and pay

619.name: Trials Started
619.formula: Number of users who started a trial
619.description: The number of users who started a trial during the period.
619.nuances:
**People are counted** rather than start events: this way the metric reconciles with the trial start rate, which also counts people.
Extending a trial that's already running **doesn't count** as a new start: access wasn't granted again.
**A start counts at** the moment access to paid features is granted, regardless of whether a card is on file.
619.example:
Got access to the trial version in March: 535 people
Extended a current trial: 45 (not counted, access wasn't granted again)

Trials Started = 535 − 45 = **490 people**
619.importance: **It drives the volume of future payments**: with a known trial-to-paid conversion rate, this count, allowing for the lag, translates directly into next month's paying customers. A drop here is visible before the drop in revenue.
619.not_needed: **Skip it** when the product has no trial.
619.essence_note: every trial user is a potential paying customer next month

620.name: Activated-to-Paid Conversion Rate
620.formula: (Activated Users Who Bought a Paid Subscription / [[Activated Users→saas_produkty/aktivirovannye_polzovateli]]) × 100
620.description: The share of activated users who bought a paid subscription. Activation is the first action after which a person gets real value from the product.
620.nuances:
**It's calculated by cohort**: the numerator includes only users from the same activation cohort as the denominator.
If you put **all paying customers for the month** in the numerator, it will include people who activated a year ago, and the rate can exceed 100%.
**A person becomes a paying customer** at the first successful charge rather than when a contract is signed or a trial ends.
Give the cohort **time to mature**, for a period comparable to the trial length: those who activated at the end of the month haven't had time to pay yet.
The denominator is activated users rather than all registered users; conversion from signups is shown by other metrics in the chain. Users who paid for a subscription without activating **aren't included**: the metric answers whether people who reached value go on to pay. If there are many such payments, count them separately; otherwise, part of the revenue isn't visible in any metric in the chain.
620.example:
Activated in the month: 3,100
Of those, paid for a subscription: 620

Activated-to-Paid Conversion Rate = 620 / 3,100 × 100 = **20%**
620.importance: It separates a product problem from a pricing problem: if people reach value but don't pay, the issue is in the plans, the limits of the free version or the moment you ask for a card. Low conversion with high activation means the free version can get the job done **completely**.
620.not_needed: Skip it when the product has only one type of access. If users **must pay before getting access** and only paying users can activate, the rate is always 100%. If the product is entirely free, there's no paid subscription, and the rate is always 0%.
620.essence_note: the more users who reached value go on to pay, the more revenue the same traffic brings in

621.name: Trial-to-Paid Conversion Rate
621.formula: (Users Who Started a Trial and Bought a Paid Subscription / Users Who Started a Trial) × 100
621.description: The share of users who started a trial and then bought a paid subscription.
621.nuances:
The numerator is a subset of the denominator: it includes **only those** who had a trial. The total number of paying customers doesn't go into the numerator: it would include those who bought directly, and the rate could exceed 100%.
**It's calculated by trial-start cohort**: a user goes into the month they started the trial, regardless of when they paid.
Trials still running at the end of the month **are excluded from the denominator until they** end: otherwise the most recent month's conversion is always understated.
**Payment counts at** the first successful charge rather than when a card is added.
621.example:
Started a trial in March: 464
Trial still running on March 31: 90 (excluded)
Base for the calculation: 374
Of those, paid after the trial ended: 116
Paid in March without a trial (bought right away): 30 (not counted)

Trial-to-Paid Conversion Rate = 116 / 374 × 100 = **31%**
621.importance: The main point where product usage turns into revenue: raising it **adds revenue from the same traffic**, and it costs less than increasing the ad budget. It's used to decide whether to change the trial length and what to make available for free.
621.not_needed: **Skip it** when there's no trial and payment happens right away.
621.synonyms: Trial Conversion Rate, Free Trial Conversion Rate
621.essence_note: this is the point where product usage turns into revenue: the higher the rate, the more paying customers from the same number of trials

622.name: Average Revenue per User (ARPU)
622.formula: Revenue for the Period / Active Users for the Same Period
622.description: How much revenue there is on average per active user over the period, including those who don't pay anything.
622.nuances:
The numerator is **all revenue for the period**, including one-time payments: this is how ARPU differs from MRR-based calculations.
**The denominator** is active users for the same period, by the same definition of activity as in MAU: using all registered users instead understates the result, and the more inactive accounts there are, the bigger the understatement.
The unit of count is the same across all metrics on the map: in B2B, **company accounts are counted** rather than employees. If the product is sold to both companies and individual users, the segments are calculated separately: a company pays for many seats at once, and individual users get lost in the overall average.
622.example:
Revenue for the month: $120,000
Active users for the month: 20,000
Of those, paying: 6,000

ARPU = 120,000 / 20,000 = **$6**

Per paying user, it's $20: the gap shows how much of the load falls on those who don't pay.
622.importance: It shows how much one active person in the product is worth to the business, **including non-paying users**. Comparing it with ARPPU immediately gives the cost of the free plan: the wider the gap between them, the larger the share of the load carried by non-paying users.
622.not_needed: Skip it when the product has only one type of access. With subscription-only access, all active users pay, and ARPU **equals ARPPU**. In a completely free product there's no revenue, and ARPU is always zero.
622.essence_note: the more revenue per active user, the better the whole audience pays off, free users included

623.name: Gross MRR Churn
623.formula: Churned MRR + Contraction MRR from Remaining Customers
623.description: How much monthly recurring revenue the company lost during the period because of churned customers and plan downgrades.
623.nuances:
**It's counted on a monthly** basis: for a churned annual contract, its monthly share goes into churn rather than the annual amount.
Churned and downgraded customers don't overlap: for a churned customer, the whole amount is counted; for one who stayed, **only the difference between** the old and the new plan.
A customer who downgraded and then left in the same month is counted **only among churned customers**, for the full amount.
The loss **is assigned to the date** the paid period ends rather than the cancellation date. New customers and expansion aren't included: this is the gross loss rather than the net balance.
623.example:
Customers who left had MRR of $3,600
Among them, an annual contract for $24,000 → $2,000 goes into churn
Downgraded: was $5,200, now $3,800 → $1,400
New customers in March worth $6,000 (not subtracted from the losses)

Gross MRR Churn = 3,600 + 1,400 = **$5,000**
623.importance: It translates customer churn into money and changes priorities: 10 small customers leaving and 10 large ones leaving give the same number of cancellations but different Gross MRR Churn. It's used to calculate how many new sales you need **just to** stay in place.
623.synonyms: Revenue Churn, MRR Churn, Lost MRR
623.essence_note: this is money that left the base and has to be won back through sales to new customers

624.name: Net Revenue Retention (NRR)
624.formula: ((Starting MRR + Expansion MRR − Churned MRR − Contraction MRR) / Starting MRR) × 100
624.description: What share of recurring revenue from existing customers was retained over the month, including plan upgrades and expansion. A value above 100% means the base grew on its own, without new customers.
624.nuances:
MRR from new customers acquired during the period **isn't included** in the calculation: including it is the main mistake in calculating NRR, and it turns the metric into a revenue growth rate and inflates it.
All terms are monthly amounts: for annual contracts, **the monthly share is taken**. Expansion is counted as the increase rather than the full amount of the new plan.
Churn and downgrades don't overlap: for a customer who left, the whole amount is subtracted; for one who stayed, **only the difference between plans**. The base and the comparison period are the same in all calculations: month over month or year over year.
A year-over-year comparison **gives higher values**, because more expansion accumulates over 12 months.
624.example:
MRR on March 1: $80,000
Expansion from existing customers: $3,000
Churned customers: $3,600
Downgrades: $1,400
New customers in March: $6,000 (not included)

NRR = (80,000 + 3,000 − 3,600 − 1,400) / 80,000 × 100 = **97.5%**

With new customers, it would come out to 105%: that's revenue growth rather than retention.
624.importance: **It answers the main question** about the health of a SaaS business: does revenue grow on its own? With NRR above 100%, the company grows revenue even if sales stop completely; at 90%, it has to replace a tenth of its recurring revenue every year just to stand still. This is the number investors look at when valuing the company.
624.not_needed: Skip it **without a subscription model** or without a way to expand a plan.
624.synonyms: Net Dollar Retention (NDR), Net Revenue Retention Rate
624.essence_note: above one hundred percent, the base grows on its own, and sales to new customers add to that growth instead of replacing what was lost

625.name: Average Customer Lifetime
625.formula: Σ over months from the cohort's first month (Cohort Members Who Were Customers That Month / Cohort Size)
625.description: How many months a customer stays with the company on average, counting from the first payment or first order.
625.nuances:
Who counts as **a customer in that month** depends on the model. For subscriptions, it's someone who paid for the month. For one-time purchases, it's a customer whose last kept order was less than K months ago, and K months in a row without an order mean churn. The company sets K, longer than the typical gap between orders; everyone stays a customer for the first K months after the first order, so the larger K is, the longer the lifetime. A customer who left and came back is a customer again from the month of the new order or payment, and the months of the gap don't count toward the lifetime.
A cohort is the customers who **started in the same month**: for subscriptions, the month of their first payment; for one-time purchases, the month of their first kept order.
An order without an identified customer doesn't extend that customer's lifetime, and two accounts belonging to the same person, including ones created to get a new trial, give two short lifetimes instead of one: the lifetime is understated. In the same way, after a database migration or a billing system change, old customers look new until their histories are merged.
The sum runs **up to the horizon** or for as long as the cohort has existed: lifetime over 12 months and lifetime over 24 months are different numbers.
**1 / Monthly Customer Churn** gives the same sum without a horizon when churn is constant: if the same share of the remaining customers leaves every month, the sum of the shares equals one divided by that share. With a horizon of H months, the sum equals (1 − (1 − churn)^H) / churn: with 2% churn, you get 50 months without a horizon and 25.8 over 36 months, and using the horizon itself, 36, in place of the sum overstates the lifetime by a factor of 1.4.
**Monthly customer churn** for subscriptions equals one minus the [[Customer Retention Rate→saas_produkty/koefficient_uderzhaniya_klientov]] for the same month. For one-time purchases, it's the share of customers at the start of the month who reached K months without an order that month. The unit of the result **is set by the churn window**: monthly churn gives months, annual churn gives years. Don't mix windows.
The churn-based estimate works only when churn is stable: if it jumps from month to month, take **the average over the last 6–12 months**. For subscriptions, the mix of the customer base also shifts the estimate: in growth months, newcomers, who leave more often, push churn up, and the lifetime comes out shorter; when the share of annual subscriptions grows, churn is understated, because annual subscribers can leave only in their renewal month, and the lifetime comes out longer. The cohort sum has neither error.
For one-time purchases, the churn-based estimate **doesn't reconcile with the cohort sum**: a customer who came back leaves again, churn counts both departures, and 1 / churn shows the length of one stretch, from an order to churn. A customer can't churn during the first K months after an order, so in growth months newcomers push churn down, and the lifetime comes out longer.
**Use customer churn** (account churn in B2B) rather than revenue churn: revenue churn gives the lifetime of the revenue rather than of the customer. It's shorter when customers move to cheaper plans and longer when they add seats.
[[Customer Lifespan→crm/srok_zhizni_klienta]] is **a different number**: the time from the first to the last purchase, and only for churned customers with two or more purchases. Here, all customers in the cohort go into the calculation, including those with one purchase, and the K months after the last order count toward the lifetime, while gaps of K months or longer don't.
625.example:
Subscription. Cohort: 200 accounts that first paid for a subscription in January of last year
Paying accounts in months 1 through 12: 200, 150, 138, 130, 124, 119, 114, 110, 106, 102, 99, 96
Total paid account-months: 1,488

Average Customer Lifetime over the first 12 months = 1 + 0.75 + 0.69 + … + 0.48 = 1,488 / 200 = **7.44 months**

One-time purchases, K = 3 months. Cohort: 1,000 customers with a first kept order in January two years ago
Bought once: 700, each stays a customer for 3 months, 2,100 months in total
Churned repeat customers: 260, with no 3-month gaps between orders and an average of 9 months from the first to the last order, so each was a customer for an average of 9 + 3 = 12 months, 3,120 months in total
Repeat customers retained for all 24 months: 40, for a total of 960 months

Average Customer Lifetime over the first 24 months = (2,100 + 3,120 + 960) / 1,000 = **6.18 months**

Customer Lifespan for the same cohort would give 9 months: it counts only the 260 churned repeat customers, without the 700 one-time buyers and without the K months after the last order.
625.importance: It's a multiplier in LTV, so an error here shifts LTV, and with it the economics of acquisition as a whole, by the same factor. Separately, it shows **how soon a customer has to pay back their acquisition cost**: if a customer stays 16 months and pays back in 12, the buffer is only four months, and any increase in churn makes acquisition unprofitable. For one-time purchases, the customer no longer orders during the last K months of the lifetime, so the buffer is K months shorter: with K = 3, one of the four months remains.
625.not_needed: Skip it in the business's first year: the cohort sum stops at the months observed so far, and with **unstable churn**, the churn-based estimate turns a random month into a multi-year forecast. It also doesn't fit one-time purchases where a repeat order **isn't part of the model**: every customer stays a customer for exactly K months, and the lifetime shows the chosen K rather than customer behavior.
625.essence_note: the longer a customer stays with the company, the more money acquiring that customer brings in

626.name: Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR)
626.formula: Sum of monthly payments for active subscriptions as of the calculation date
626.description: The total value of all active subscriptions as of a specific date, expressed as a monthly amount. Shows how much the company will receive in the coming month if nothing changes.
626.nuances:
One-time payments, implementation, training and add-on services **aren't included** in MRR: they won't recur next month.
An annual contract is divided by 12 and goes into the MRR of each of the 12 months rather than **all at once** into the month of payment.
**The value is taken as of** the end of the month rather than averaged over days: MRR is a snapshot of the subscription base on a given date, while a daily average blends the base at different points in time and doesn't reconcile with ARR, GRR and NRR.
Discounts are taken into account: MRR includes the amount the customer actually pays rather than the list price. Customers on a trial **aren't included**, even with a card on file: the subscription hasn't been paid for yet.
626.example:
Active on March 31:
900 monthly subscriptions at $65 = $58,500
40 annual contracts at $6,600 → 6,600 / 12 × 40 = $22,000
1 contract with a 30% discount: list price $5,000/month → $3,500
Implementation payments in March: $14,000 (not included)
Trials with a card on file: 210 (not included)

MRR = 58,500 + 22,000 + 3,500 = **$84,000**
626.importance: The one number that shows the real state of the subscription base: monthly revenue can jump because of one-time implementation fees while MRR is falling, and hiring gets planned around money that won't come in again. **ARR is calculated from it**, along with GRR, NRR and LTV, so an error here distorts much of the map at once.
626.not_needed: **Skip it when** you sell perpetual licenses or one-off work: the payments have no recurring component.
626.essence_note: this is the money that will come in next month if the base stays the same

627.name: Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR)
627.formula: MRR at the End of the Period × 12
627.description: Recurring subscription revenue on an annual basis as of a specific date.
627.nuances:
**MRR is taken for the last** day of the period rather than averaged over the year: it's an annualized snapshot of the current subscription base rather than the sum of revenue for the past 12 months.
One-time payments, implementation and add-on services **aren't included**, because they aren't included in MRR.
Annual contracts **are already converted to a monthly amount** within MRR and aren't multiplied by 12 again.
627.example:
MRR on March 31: $84,000
Implementation payments in March: $14,000 (not included)

ARR = 84,000 × 12 = **$1,008,000**

The sum of actual receipts over 12 months would give a different number: it includes one-time payments and leaves out future renewals.
627.importance: The language investors and acquirers use when talking about a SaaS business: the company's valuation **is calculated as a multiple of** ARR. Inside the company, it's used to compare annual spending on the team and infrastructure with the current subscription base.
627.not_needed: Skip it for a product **without recurring payments**: there's nothing to multiply.
627.essence_note: the higher the annualized recurring revenue, the more money the year will bring in with the same set of customers

629.name: LTV-to-CAC Ratio
629.description: The ratio of the money earned from a customer over their whole lifetime to the cost of acquiring them.
629.nuances:
LTV is calculated **on a margin basis**: all variable costs are subtracted from revenue rather than only the cost of goods. On a revenue basis, the lower the contribution margin, the more the ratio is overstated, and unprofitable acquisition looks profitable. Both values **are taken as of the same** calculation date: LTV depends on the current revenue per account and current churn, and CAC on the costs and customers of the same period. A common benchmark is 3:1 or higher.
A value around 1 means breaking even before development and other fixed costs; a value above 5 usually points to underinvestment in marketing rather than success. Both values **are taken in the same** currency.
629.example:
Revenue per account: $68.97 per month
Contribution Margin Ratio: 78%
[[Average Customer Lifetime→saas_produkty/sredniy_srok_zhizni_klienta]] with 6% monthly churn and a 36-month horizon: 14.9 months
LTV = 0.78 × 68.97 × 14.9 = $801.57
CAC for the same period: $270

LTV / CAC = 801.57 / 270 = **3.0**

Revenue-based LTV, 68.97 × 14.9 = $1,027.65, would give 3.8: acquisition would look 28% more efficient than it is.
629.importance: **It determines** whether you can put more money into marketing. At 3:1 or higher, a bigger budget is justified; at around 1, acquiring each new customer costs as much as they bring in, and scaling speeds up losses instead of growth.
629.not_needed: Skip it when customers come **only through referrals** and there are no direct acquisition costs: there's nothing to divide by.
629.essence_note: the more a customer pays over their lifetime per dollar spent acquiring them, the more profitable the subscription

630.name: CAC Payback Period
630.formula: [[Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)→saas_produkty/stoimost_privlecheniya_klienta_cac]] / (Average Revenue per Account (ARPA) of New Customers × Contribution Margin Ratio)
630.description: How many months it takes for the money earned from a new customer to cover the cost of acquiring them.
630.nuances:
CAC and revenue **cover the same** period: the period's costs are divided by the revenue of customers acquired in that same period.
Revenue per account (**ARPA**) is calculated for these same customers: their MRR at the end of the month divided by their number. The average across the whole base doesn't work: long-standing customers have different plans and add-ons, and the payback based on it will be wrong.
Multiplying by the contribution margin ratio **is required**: without it, the payback comes out shorter than it really is, because part of the payment goes to infrastructure and third-party services, support and customer success. The margin is the same as in [[Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)→saas_produkty/pozhiznennaya_cennost_klienta_ltv]].
In SaaS, payback is often calculated using **gross margin**. It equals the contribution margin ratio when all these costs are included in the cost of revenue; if some aren't, gross-margin payback comes out shorter.
The result is in months because the revenue **is taken monthly**: using an annual figure gives years.
630.example:
CAC for March: $270
Acquired in March: 120 paying accounts, their MRR on March 31: $8,276.40 → ARPA $68.97 per month
Contribution Margin Ratio: 78%
Contribution margin per account per month = 68.97 × 0.78 = $53.80

CAC Payback Period = 270 / 53.80 = **5 months**

Without the margin, it would come out to 3.9 months: on paper, the customer pays back a month earlier than in cash.
630.importance: **It determines** how much cash the company needs to keep on hand to grow: with a 5-month payback, each new customer is cash-negative for almost half a year, and aggressive customer acquisition leads to a cash shortfall even with unit economics that are profitable on paper. A common SaaS benchmark is 12 months or less.
630.not_needed: **Skip it** when customers pay for the product a year in advance and the money arrives at once: payback happens at the first payment.
630.synonyms: Payback Period, Months to Recover CAC
630.essence_note: the longer a customer takes to pay back, the longer the money spent acquiring them is tied up

631.name: Paying Customers
631.formula: Number of customers with an active paid subscription at the end of the period
631.description: The number of customers with an active paid subscription at the end of the period.
631.nuances:
The count is taken **as of the end of the period** rather than as “active for at least one day”: the second approach inflates the count with those who arrived and left within the month and doesn't reconcile with MRR for the same date.
A trial **isn't a paid subscription**, even with a card on file. A customer with a paused subscription who keeps access counts as paying if the payment for the period was charged, and doesn't count if there were no charges.
In B2B, the unit **is the company account**, the same unit as in customer retention and CAC: otherwise one customer with 50 employees turns into 50 units and drags down the calculated ARPPU.
631.example:
Paying customers at the start of the month: 5,600
Paid for the first time: 620, returned after a pause: 80
Canceled: 300
On a trial: 4,200 (not counted, no charge yet)

Paying Customers = 5,600 + 620 + 80 − 300 = **6,000 at the end of the month**
631.importance: **The denominator for ARPPU**, CAC and retention, so a discrepancy in the definition here breaks many of the financial calculations. On its own, the number answers whether the customer base is growing: one large contract can pull MRR up while the number of customers shrinks.
631.not_needed: Skip it for a **free product** with no paid plans.
631.essence_note: they're the ones who bring in money, and the more of them there are, the more stable the revenue

632.name: Activation Rate
632.description: The share of registered users who reached activation. Activation is the first action after which a person gets real value from the product, for example connecting a data source and seeing their first report. The product team defines the list of such actions in advance.
632.nuances:
The base is chosen once and **doesn't change**: registered users or installs. Based on registered users, the metric shows the quality of onboarding inside the product; based on installs, the whole path, including users lost at signup. The second figure is always lower, and you can't substitute one for the other: they answer different questions and call for different fixes.
The list of actions that **count as activation** is set once and is the same in all activation metrics.
**It's calculated by the signup cohort**: a person is assigned to both the numerator and the denominator by signup month rather than activation month. Otherwise the rate can exceed 100%.
**The cohort needs time to mature**: if the typical path to activation takes a week, signups from the most recent week understate the rate.
**Unique users are counted** rather than installs: reinstalling with the same account doesn't add another user to the count, and a repeat activation by the same user isn't counted again.
632.example:
Activation in the product = connected a store and saw the first report
Signed up in March: 800
Of those, activated (in March or later): 296
Activated in March but signed up in February: 120 (not in the March calculation)

Activation Rate = 296 / 800 × 100 = **37%**
632.importance: **It determines** where the product loses people: before first value or after it. If the rate is low, improvements to the paid features are pointless: almost no one gets there, and the acquisition budget is spent on users who never actually saw the product.
632.not_needed: **Skip it** when the product delivers value from the first screen and has no separate activation step: calculators, reference tools, reading apps without an account.
632.essence_note: the more people reach first value, the more of them will stay and pay

633.name: SaaS Revenue
633.formula: Total Payments for the Period − Refunds and Disputed Payments
633.description: The money received from customers during the period: subscriptions, one-time payments, implementation and add-on services.
633.nuances:
Refunds and chargebacks **are subtracted in the period** in which they occurred.
An annual payment **is allocated to the periods** it covers rather than entirely to the month it was charged: otherwise months with large annual contracts show spikes that don't reflect the actual business.
The payment processor's fee **isn't subtracted**: it's an expense rather than a reduction in revenue.
633.example:
Received in March: $116,400
Refunds in March: $2,400
Annual contract for $24,000 paid on March 1 → $2,000 goes to March, and the remaining $22,000 is spread over the next 11 months

SaaS Revenue for March = 116,400 − 2,400 − 22,000 = **$92,000**
633.importance: **The basis for all financial calculations**: profit, ARPU and payback on spending are calculated from it. Unlike MRR, it shows all the money received, including one-time payments: a product's revenue can grow through implementation fees while it loses its subscription base.
633.essence_note: this is all the money received from customers during the period

634.name: Trial Length
634.description: The set length of free trial access to the product.
634.nuances:
This is a product setting rather than a calculated value. When plans have different trial lengths, no average is derived: the value is given for each plan **separately**, otherwise the number doesn't match any real trial.
Manual extensions of trial access don't change the set value: they **affect the actual** length rather than the set one.
634.example:
Start plan: 14 days
Pro plan: 30 days
Enterprise plan: no trial
The sales team extended trials for some customers to 45 days: doesn't affect the set value

Trial Length = **14 days (Start), 30 days (Pro)**
634.importance: It sets the horizon over which all trial conversions are measured: with 14 days, a cohort's result is known after two weeks; with 30, **only after a month**, and decisions are made half as often. A trial shorter than the time to activation guarantees low conversion: the person simply doesn't have time to see the value.
634.not_needed: **Skip it** when there's no trial: the product is sold right away or offers a free plan with no time limit.
634.essence_note: a trial that's too short doesn't let people see the value, and one that's too long delays both payment and decisions about the cohort

635.name: Net New Paying Customers
635.formula: New Paying Customers for the Period − Cancellations for the Period
635.description: How much the number of paying customers grew or shrank during the period: the difference between new and churned customers.
635.nuances:
Both values **are about paying customers**: mixing new signups with paid subscription cancellations compares different sets and gives a number that means nothing.
**The result is in customers** rather than percentages: dividing by the base at the start of the period gives the growth rate, which is a different metric.
The value can be negative: that's exactly what the metric is about. A churned customer who comes back **counts as a new paying customer** if the subscription wasn't active between leaving and returning.
**The unit is the same** as in [[Paying Customers→saas_produkty/platyaschie_polzovateli]]: in B2B, a company account.
635.example:
Paying customers at the start of the month: 5,600
Paid for the first time: 620
Returned after a pause: 80
Canceled: 300

Net New Paying Customers = 620 + 80 − 300 = **400 for the month**

The base grew to 6,000, an increase of 7.1%
635.importance: **A single number** that shows whether the base is growing or being eaten away: strong sales and strong churn make reports look busy while the base doesn't move. When net growth goes negative, raising the ad budget doesn't help, because more customers leak out than come in.
635.not_needed: Skip it for **one-time sales** without a subscription: customers have no subscription to cancel.
635.synonyms: Net New Customers, Net Customer Growth
635.essence_note: this is the actual growth of the base: how many customers were added after all departures

636.name: Churned Subscriptions
636.formula: Number of subscriptions that ended during the period
636.description: The number of customers whose paid subscription ended during the period.
636.nuances:
A customer is assigned to a period **by the end date** of their paid access rather than the date they clicked “Cancel”: the two can fall in different months, and a subscription canceled in March can stay active into April.
A non-renewal due to a failed payment **counts the same** as a deliberate cancellation: access ended and the money didn't come in.
The split into voluntary and involuntary churn is done with a breakdown rather than with separate metrics. A move to the free plan **counts as churn**: the paid subscription ended.
A plan downgrade **doesn't count** as churn: it's a downgrade.
636.example:
Paid access ended in March and wasn't renewed: 72 customers
Of those, the card failed: 19 (counted)
Clicked “Cancel” in March, access until April 12: 15 (counted in April)
Downgraded: 36 (not counted)

Churned Subscriptions = **72**
636.importance: **It gives a named list of customers who left** rather than a rate: with it, you can analyze the reasons for leaving, which retention percentages don't allow. The gap between cancellations and revenue churn immediately shows who is leaving: small customers or large ones.
636.not_needed: Skip it for products with **perpetual licenses**: there's no subscription to end.
636.essence_note: every churned subscription is revenue that won't be there next month

637.name: Stickiness
637.description: What share of the monthly audience uses the product on an average day. Shows how much the product has become part of daily work.
637.nuances:
The numerator is **the average DAU** for the same month rather than a single day's value: a single day's figure jumps around because of weekends and holidays and makes comparing months meaningless.
DAU and MAU **are taken for the same** month and with the same definition of activity, otherwise the ratio is meaningless.
Calendar days **are all counted**: excluding weekends inflates the result for B2B products and makes it incomparable with other periods.
637.example:
Sum of DAU over the 31 days of March: 38,100
Average DAU = 38,100 / 31 = 1,229
MAU for March: 5,400

Stickiness = 1,229 / 5,400 × 100 = **22.8%**

The peak on March 12 gave a DAU of 1,940 and a ratio of 36%: that's one day rather than the month.
637.importance: **It separates a product people use out of habit** from one they open once a month when they have to. The value tells you what to expect from retention: with low stickiness, the customer doesn't think about the product between charges and cancels easily, so a drop in this metric warns of churn in advance.
637.not_needed: **Skip it for** products built for infrequent use: month-end close or regulatory filing doesn't involve logging in daily, and a low value means nothing here.
637.essence_note: the more often a person opens the product, the less likely they are to cancel the subscription

638.name: Monthly Active Users (MAU)
638.description: The number of unique users who took a meaningful action in the product during the month.
638.nuances:
The definition of activity and the way unique users are identified are the same as in DAU. Within a month, a user **is counted once** regardless of the number of visits: the sum of DAU over 30 days gives the number of visits rather than MAU and overstates the result, and the more often users come back, the bigger the overstatement.
The window **is fixed**: a calendar month or a rolling 30 days. A calendar month is easier to reconcile with revenue, but February and March have different numbers of days; a rolling window is comparable across periods but doesn't match the reporting month.
638.example:
Unique active users in March: 5,400
Sum of DAU over the 31 days of March: 38,100 (these are visits, not MAU)
Logged in every day: 620 people, counted once in MAU

MAU = **5,400**
638.importance: **The basis for comparing** audience size with revenue and infrastructure costs. It shows whether the product is actually growing: signups can increase while MAU stays flat, which means new users leave as fast as they arrive.
638.not_needed: **Don't use it for** products with infrequent use: regulatory filing, annual planning, services for a specific event. Using them once a quarter is normal there, and the monthly number doesn't describe engagement.
638.essence_note: this is the size of the active audience that paying customers come from

639.name: Expansion MRR
639.formula: Sum of MRR increases from customers whose payment went up during the period
639.description: How much monthly recurring revenue grew because existing customers started paying on more expensive terms.
639.nuances:
**The increase is counted** rather than the full amount of the new plan: when a customer moves from $200 to $600 a month, $400 goes to expansion.
The full amount of the new plan overstates the result and won't reconcile with NRR. Expansion within a plan **counts too**: added seats, licenses and overage charges give the same MRR increase as a plan change.
**Only customers** who were there at the start of the period are counted. A new customer's first purchase goes to new MRR rather than to expansion.
The increase **is taken on a monthly** basis: for an annual contract, the increase is divided by 12.
639.example:
Customer A: from $200 to $600/month → $400
Customer B: added 15 seats at $18 → $270
Customer C: annual contract grew from $12,000 to $16,800 → 4,800 / 12 = $400
New customer D bought a $1,000 plan (not counted, this is new MRR)

Expansion MRR = **$1,070**
639.importance: **It shows** how much revenue came from working with the existing base, and directly answers whether that work pays off. If expansion consistently exceeds [[Gross MRR Churn→saas_produkty/ottok_dohoda]], the product grows even if marketing stops.
639.not_needed: Skip it when there's **only one plan** with no way to expand.
639.essence_note: this is money from customers you already have, with no acquisition cost

640.name: Renewal Rate
640.formula: (Renewed Subscriptions / Subscriptions with a Renewal Date in the Period) × 100
640.description: The share of subscriptions renewed for the next term among those whose renewal date fell within the period.
640.nuances:
**The denominator counts subscriptions** rather than customers: the metric shows subscription renewals rather than the retention of people.
Annual and monthly subscriptions **are counted separately**: lumped together, monthly subscriptions, which renew 12 times a year, drown out the annual ones, and the number loses its meaning.
A failed card payment **doesn't count as a non-renewal** until the payment retries are used up: the subscription stays pending and is counted in the period in which the payment is resolved.
640.example:
Monthly subscriptions with a charge date in March: 940
Charged successfully: 872
Canceled before the date: 51
Card declined, retries still in progress: 17 (not counted in March)

Renewal Rate = 872 / (940 − 17) × 100 = **94.5%**
640.importance: **It shows** what share of subscriptions make it to the next term. It catches both cancellations and payment failures: if renewals dropped while cancellations didn't increase, customers were unable to pay rather than choosing to leave, and billing is what needs fixing.
640.not_needed: Skip it for a **perpetual license** or a one-time purchase: there's nothing to renew.
640.essence_note: every renewed subscription is next period's revenue without a new sale

641.name: Gross Revenue Retention (GRR)
641.formula: ((Starting MRR − Churned MRR − Contraction MRR) / Starting MRR) × 100
641.description: What share of recurring revenue from existing customers was retained over the month, excluding plan upgrades. The value doesn't exceed 100%.
641.nuances:
**It's calculated only for** customers who were there at the start of the period: MRR from new customers goes into neither the numerator nor the denominator; otherwise, the metric is no longer about retention.
**Expansion isn't added**: this is how it differs from NRR, and that's why GRR is always ≤ 100%. Churn and downgrades don't overlap: for a customer who left, the whole amount goes to churn; for one who stayed, the reduction in MRR goes to downgrades.
A customer who downgraded and then left goes only into churn, for the full amount. Starting MRR **is taken on the first** day of the month and equals MRR on the last day of the previous month.
The loss is counted **by the end date** of the paid period rather than the date the customer clicked the “Cancel” button.
641.example:
MRR on March 1: $80,000
Customers who left, total MRR: $3,600
Downgraded: was $5,200, now $3,800 → loss of $1,400
Expansion from remaining customers: $3,000 (not counted in GRR)
New customers in March: $6,000 (not counted)

GRR = (80,000 − 3,600 − 1,400) / 80,000 × 100 = **93.8%**
641.importance: It shows product quality in its purest form: how much money leaks out before expansion gets any credit. NRR above 100% with GRR around 80% means a few large customers are carrying the growth while the rest of the base is eroding, and that's visible **only here**.
641.not_needed: Skip it **without a subscription model**: without recurring payments, there's no base to retain.
641.synonyms: Gross Dollar Retention (GDR), Gross Revenue Retention Rate
641.essence_note: the less money leaks from the existing base, the less you need to sell to new customers just to stay in place

642.name: Upgrade Rate
642.formula: (Customers Who Moved to a More Expensive Plan / Paying Customers at the Start of the Period) × 100
642.description: The share of paying customers who moved to a more expensive plan during the period.
642.nuances:
**The numerator counts customers** rather than money: the money gained from upgrades is counted by [[Expansion MRR→saas_produkty/rost_vyruchki_ot_apselov]].
The denominator **is taken at the start** of the period: new paying customers arrived during the period and haven't had time to upgrade, so including them in the base understates the rate.
A customer who upgraded twice during the period **counts once**. Switching from a monthly to an annual plan isn't an upgrade by itself: the amounts are compared on a monthly basis.
642.example:
Paying customers on March 1: 5,600
Moved to a more expensive plan: 252 customers
Two of them upgraded twice: counted as 252, not 254
New paying customers in March: 620 (not in the denominator)

Upgrade Rate = 252 / 5,600 × 100 = **4.5%**
642.importance: It shows whether expansion within the base is working. If there are almost no upgrades, growth relies **only on new** customers: every dollar of revenue has to be bought through new acquisition, and the plan lineup doesn't let the product grow along with the customer.
642.not_needed: Skip it when there's **only one plan** or pricing is strictly usage-based, with no other plan to move to.
642.essence_note: a move to a more expensive plan is revenue growth with no acquisition cost

643.name: Active Free Users
643.formula: Active Users − Active Users with a Paid Subscription
643.description: The number of users who used the product during the period but didn't have a paid subscription.
643.nuances:
**Subtract only the** paying users who are among the active users for the same period and counted in the same unit: if you subtract all paying users indiscriminately, the result can go negative.
Users on a trial **count as non-paying**, even with a card on file: no money has been charged for them yet.
**The definition of activity is the same** as in DAU and MAU.
643.example:
Active in March: 5,400
Of those, with a paid subscription: 1,130
Paying users who didn't log in during March: 70 (not subtracted)
On a trial: 210 (stay among non-paying users)

Active Free Users = 5,400 − 1,130 = **4,270**
643.importance: This is **room for revenue growth**: these people are already in the product, and there's no need to acquire them again. At the same time, it's a bill for infrastructure and support that nobody pays, so this number is used to decide where to draw the line for the free plan.
643.not_needed: Skip it when the product has only one type of access. If access is paid only, there are no active non-paying users. If the product is entirely free, the metric **equals the number** of active users and repeats DAU and MAU.
643.synonyms: Free Active Users, Non-Paying Active Users
643.essence_note: this is both a pool of future sales and an infrastructure load that nobody pays for

644.name: Downgrade Rate
644.formula: (Customers Who Moved to a Cheaper Plan / Paying Customers at the Start of the Period) × 100
644.description: The share of paying customers who moved to a cheaper plan during the period.
644.nuances:
The numerator counts customers; the revenue lost to downgrades is measured by [[Gross MRR Churn→saas_produkty/ottok_dohoda]]. A full subscription cancellation **isn't included** here: it's churn, and otherwise the same departure ends up in two metrics.
**The denominator is taken at the start of the period**, the same as in [[Upgrade Rate→saas_produkty/apgreydov]]: otherwise the two rates can't be compared.
Cutting the number of seats or licenses within the same plan **counts as a downgrade** if the monthly payment went down.
644.example:
Paying customers on March 1: 5,600
Moved to a cheaper plan: 140
Cut licenses from 20 to 12: 28 (counted)
Canceled the subscription entirely: 300 (not counted, this is churn)

Downgrade Rate = (140 + 28) / 5,600 × 100 = **3%**
644.importance: **An early sign of churn**: a customer first downgrades their plan and cancels the subscription later. A rise in downgrades is used to decide whether the top plan is overpriced and whether customers are paying for features they don't use.
644.not_needed: Skip it when there's **only one plan** and no way to move to a lower one.
644.essence_note: every move to a cheaper plan is a direct loss of part of the recurring revenue

645.name: Share of Paying Users
645.formula: (Active Users with an Active Paid Subscription / All Active Users) × 100
645.description: The share of paying users among active users for the period.
645.nuances:
The numerator includes only paying users who **are among the active** users for the same period: a paying user who didn't log in all month isn't counted at all. Otherwise the share can exceed 100%.
**Active** means someone who took a meaningful action in the product rather than just opening the login page. The definition of activity is the same as in DAU and MAU.
Users on a trial **count as non-paying**, even with a card on file. The unit of count is the same in the numerator and the denominator: in B2B, either accounts everywhere or employees everywhere.
645.example:
Active users in March: 5,400
Of those, with an active paid subscription: 1,130
Paying users who didn't log in during March: 70 (counted in neither)

Share of Paying Users = 1,130 / 5,400 × 100 = **20.9%**
645.importance: **It shows** whether the free part of the product pays for itself. If the share falls while active users keep growing, the company is adding load on infrastructure and support without revenue: this number is used to decide what to put behind the paywall.
645.not_needed: Skip it when the product has only one type of access. If there's no free option and the product is used only by subscription, the share is always 100%. If the product is entirely free and is funded by advertising or a grant, the share is always 0%. In both cases the number **never changes and doesn't inform** any decisions.
645.synonyms: Paying User Ratio, Percentage of Paying Users
645.essence_note: the more paying users among active ones, the more money the same audience brings in

646.name: Qualified Leads
646.formula: Number of leads that passed qualification
646.description: The number of leads that passed a check against the company's criteria: there's a need, the budget fits, and the person has the authority to decide.
646.nuances:
A lead **is assigned to the period** by its arrival date, not its qualification date. A lead from March 30 reviewed on April 2 counts as a March lead, so the count for a completed month keeps growing after the month ends.
Qualification criteria **are put in writing and** don't change within the period: without a list of conditions, sales reps label the people they find more pleasant to work with as qualified, and the number stops being comparable across months.
**Duplicates are merged into** one lead: a repeat inquiry from the same person about the same need doesn't produce a second qualified lead.
Unreviewed leads **don't count as qualified**: until it's reviewed, a lead stays in the general pool of leads.
646.example:
Leads in March: 420
Passed qualification: 147
Screened out as unqualified: 243
Not reviewed at the time of calculation: 30 (not counted as qualified)

Qualified Leads = **147**
646.importance: **This is the real workload** for the sales team, and it's used to work out whether there are enough people and whether to hire. The total number of leads doesn't work for planning: many of them are screened out quickly, and a workload forecast based on them overstates the real one.
646.not_needed: **Skip it** when inquiries aren't screened and sales follows up on every one: in retail, in-store pickup and low-cost services, separating qualified from unqualified leads is unnecessary.
646.essence_note: no amount of work will turn an unqualified lead into a sale

647.name: Lead Qualification Rate
647.description: The share of leads that meet the company's qualification criteria.
647.nuances:
**Only reviewed leads count**: an unreviewed inquiry hasn't been rejected yet, and some of these will turn out to be qualified after review. If you leave them in the denominator, the rate drops simply because the incoming leads haven't been reviewed yet, and the more leads come in, the bigger the drop.
A lead enters the calculation by its arrival date rather than its review date: a lead that came in at the end of the month and was qualified at the start of the next **belongs to the month** it arrived. So the numerator and denominator for a completed month keep growing as the remaining leads are reviewed.
Look at the share of unreviewed leads next to it: if it's large, the rate is based on only part of the leads and **changes every day**.
647.example:
Leads in March: 420
Reviewed at the time of calculation: 390
Of those, qualified: 147
Screened out as unqualified: 243
Not reviewed: 30 (not in the calculation)

Lead Qualification Rate = 147 / 390 × 100 = **37.7%**

Once the remaining 30 are reviewed, both parts will change: the numerator and the denominator.
647.importance: It shows where to act when sales fall short: on traffic or on the sales team. A low rate with a high lead count means ads bring in the wrong people, and increasing the budget **will only multiply the junk**. A high rate with a low lead count shifts the conversation toward buying more traffic.
647.not_needed: **Skip it where** there's no qualification: in retail and small online stores, an inquiry goes straight into processing, and leads aren't sorted into qualified and unqualified.
647.essence_note: the higher the share of qualified leads, the less time sales spends sorting through junk

648.name: Cost per Qualified Lead
648.description: How much it costs on average to get one qualified lead.
648.nuances:
Spend includes **only the costs of** acquisition: ad budgets, platform fees, contractor fees and payments for promotional services.
Sales rep salaries **aren't included**: they are lead handling costs. The denominator is counted the same way as [[Qualified Leads→voronki_prodazh_h4/kvalificirovannye_lidy]]: by the lead's arrival date.
Use spend **from the** same period; otherwise a budget increase at the end of the month is assigned to leads that arrive in the next one.
**Because qualification is still in progress, the value** for a recent month starts out overstated and goes down as the remaining leads are reviewed.
648.example:
Acquisition spend in March: $17,640
Qualified leads in March: 147

Cost per Qualified Lead = 17,640 / 147 = **$120**

Across all 420 leads, it would be $42: that's the cost of an inquiry rather than the cost of a potential buyer.
648.importance: **The true cost of entry** into the funnel, unlike Cost per Lead (CPL), which is easy to improve by buying cheap, irrelevant traffic. The bid ceiling is the average profit per deal multiplied by the share of qualified leads that convert to sales: above it, the company pays more for each sale than it earns on it.
648.not_needed: **Skip it where** there's no qualification and sales follows up on every inquiry. Also skip it with free traffic: with no spend, there's nothing in the numerator.
648.synonyms: Cost per SQL, Cost per MQL
648.essence_note: every dollar comes out of the profit on a future deal

649.name: Number of Sales
649.formula: Number of orders for which the sale event occurred
649.description: The number of sales completed during the period.
649.nuances:
The company chooses the event that **counts as a sale**: receipt of payment, contract signing or shipment. The choice is made once and doesn't change: with deferred payment, shipment and payment can be far apart, and depending on the event, the same order lands in different months.
The same event **is used in all** metrics that involve sales: Lead-to-Sale Rate, Cost per Sale and Revenue from Leads. Otherwise the numbers across the map don't add up.
An order **counts once**. If payment is the chosen event, a partial payment or an advance doesn't count as a sale: the sale counts when the order is paid in full.
Returns and cancellations **are subtracted from sales for the** period in which the order was counted.
649.example:
Sale event: full payment
Orders paid in March: 68
Orders with an advance but not paid in full: 12 (not counted)
Returns on March orders: 5 (subtracted)

Number of Sales = 68 − 5 = **63**

By shipment, March would show 74: some orders were shipped to customers on deferred payment terms, and the money for them will arrive in April.
649.importance: The point where interest turns into money, and the denominator for Cost per Sale and, through it, for judging whether ads pay off. Choose the sale event based on what the company actually controls: if issued invoices count, the plan includes deals that will never be paid, and the gap surfaces **only during reconciliation** with bank statements.
649.essence_note: this is the whole funnel's result, counted in sales

650.name: Lead-to-Sale Rate
650.description: The share of leads that converted to sales.
650.nuances:
A sale **is assigned to the period** of the lead it came from rather than to the month of payment. Otherwise the numerator and denominator come from different lead cohorts: March deals from February leads divided by March leads, and when traffic grows, the rate drops artificially.
Because of this, the rate for a completed month **keeps updating as** deals close, and its final value is known only after a typical sales cycle has passed.
The numerator **is counted in deals**, and the denominator in leads. If one lead brought two orders, the second order doesn't go into the numerator; otherwise the result can exceed 100%.
650.example:
Leads in March: 420
Of those, ended in payment: 63
Payments in March from February leads: 40 (not counted)

Lead-to-Sale Rate = 63 / 420 × 100 = **15%**
650.importance: **It translates leads into money**: with this rate and the average deal size, you can calculate how many leads you need to buy to meet the sales plan. A drop while lead quality stays stable usually means the problem is in lead handling rather than in advertising, and increasing the budget is pointless.
650.not_needed: **Skip it where** the inquiry is the sale itself: payment happens at the moment of contact, and there's no gap between the lead and the deal.
650.essence_note: the more often a lead turns into a sale, the fewer leads you need to buy for the same revenue

651.name: Cost per Sale
651.description: How much it costs on average to get one sale.
651.nuances:
**Use the sales** that came from leads received during the period being analyzed, and spend for the same period. If you divide the March budget by March payments, the denominator picks up deals from February leads, and when the budget grows, the number is distorted.
**Because of the sales cycle, the value** for a recent month starts out overstated: some deals haven't closed yet. The final value is known after the typical time to close has passed.
Spend **includes only the costs** of acquisition, without sales team payroll.
651.example:
Acquisition spend in March: $17,640
Sales from March leads: 63

Cost per Sale = 17,640 / 63 = **$280**
651.importance: **It's compared directly with** the profit per deal and answers whether the company makes money on acquisition or loses money on every customer. The gap between this and the per-lead figure shows where money is lost: cheap leads with a high cost per sale mean the budget goes to people who don't buy.
651.not_needed: **Skip it with** free traffic, and with a long sales cycle where closing takes more than six months: by the time the number is in, ad buying conditions have completely changed.
651.synonyms: Cost per Acquisition (CPA), Cost per Closed Deal
651.essence_note: this comes straight out of the margin on every sale

652.name: Revenue from Leads
652.description: The money received from sales that came from leads during the period.
652.nuances:
Choose one basis and keep it constant: on a shipment basis, revenue is recognized when the goods are delivered or the customer signs off on the services; on a payment basis, when the money arrives. **With deferred payments and prepayments**, the two bases give different amounts for the same month.
Returns and canceled orders **are subtracted from revenue for the period** of the original sale; otherwise the month a promotion launches looks successful and the returns land in the next one.
**Discounts reduce revenue**; they aren't shown as a separate expense line.
652.example:
Shipped in March: $124,000
Returned from March shipments: $6,000

Revenue from Leads = 124,000 − 6,000 = **$118,000**
