652.importance: The basis **for calculating the cost-to-revenue ratio**, return on ad spend and profitability. An error here carries over into every derived metric at once, and it's hard to track down later because each report shows its own version of the truth.
652.essence_note: this is all the money from sales during the period

653.name: Lost Leads
653.formula: Leads − Leads with a Sale − Leads in Progress
653.description: The number of leads that didn't result in a sale.
653.nuances:
A lead counts as lost **only after** work on it has ended. Open deals don't count; otherwise all recently received leads are counted as lost, and the more leads come in, the worse the number looks.
**Because of this, the monthly number** grows as deals close and becomes final after a typical sales cycle has passed.
If one lead brought several orders, **the total is reduced by** one lead rather than by the number of orders.
653.example:
Leads in March: 420
Leads that ended in payment: 63
Deals still in progress: 55 (not counted as lost)

Lost Leads = 420 − 63 − 55 = **302**
653.importance: **This is the pool for win-back**: these people have already shown interest and cost money, and winning them back is cheaper than acquiring new ones. Until lost leads are counted in one place with their reasons, the contact list goes to waste, and you pay to acquire the same person through ads again.
653.not_needed: **Skip it** when leads aren't assigned a final status in the system: unworked leads stay in progress indefinitely, and you can't tell a lost lead from a stalled one.
653.essence_note: money and time have already been spent on these leads, and there will be no sale from them

654.name: Product List View Rate
654.formula: (Sessions with Product List Views / All Sessions) × 100
654.description: The share of sessions in which the user reached a product list. The first step of the funnel: shows what share of sessions got to the assortment at all.
654.nuances:
The numerator and denominator **are measured in sessions**: you can't mix sessions with unique users, or the share comes out inflated.
What **counts as a product list** is set once for the whole funnel: category pages, search results and the homepage collection are included; the “Similar products” block on a product page isn't.
A session goes into the numerator **once**, no matter how many lists were opened in it.
654.example:
Sessions in the month: 50,000
Sessions with at least one product list view, that is, [[Sessions with Product List Views→voronki_prodazh_h4/prosmotr_kataloga]]: 34,000

Product List View Rate = 34,000 / 50,000 × 100 = **68%**
654.importance: **It shows** whether the homepage leads users to products. If the rate is low while traffic is expensive, you're paying for sessions that end on the entry page: the reason is usually a mismatch between the ad's promise and the landing page, or unclear navigation. This is the earliest point in the funnel where a traffic quality problem shows up.
654.not_needed: **Skip it** when ads lead straight to product pages and users rarely go through the product list as a separate step.
654.essence_note: without a product list, the shopper won't get to a product page

655.name: Product List-to-Product Page Conversion Rate
655.formula: (Sessions with Product List and Product Page Views / Sessions with Product List Views) × 100
655.description: The share of sessions with a product list view that reached a product page. The second step of the funnel: shows whether the user finds something in the list worth opening.
655.nuances:
**Numerator**: sessions that had both a product list and a product page, in any order. A session that started from a direct link to a product gets into the numerator if a product list was opened later in it: it's also in the denominator, so the two sets stay aligned.
Sessions where the product page was opened from a messaging campaign or a direct link and no product list was opened at all **aren't counted anywhere**: they aren't in the denominator, so they have no place in the numerator.
Both quantities are measured in sessions: a session with five product pages opened **counts once**.
The denominator **matches the metric** [[Sessions with Product List Views→voronki_prodazh_h4/prosmotr_kataloga]], so this rate multiplied by the [[Product List View Rate→voronki_prodazh_h4/cr_v_prosmotr_kataloga]] gives the share of all sessions that reached a product page through a product list.
655.example:
Sessions with a product list view: 34,000
Of those, with a product page view: 12,300
Sessions where the product page was opened from a direct link with no product list visit: 3,300 (counted in neither the numerator nor the denominator)

Product List-to-Product Page Conversion Rate = 12,300 / 34,000 × 100 = **36%**

Adding the 3,300 direct visits to the numerator gives 46%: the numerator would include sessions that aren't in the denominator.
655.importance: **It shows** whether the product listings work: if users who open a list leave without opening a single product, that points to issues with the assortment, sorting and prices rather than traffic. Together with the Product List View Rate, it gives the full path from visit to product page and shows at which step more users are lost.
655.not_needed: **Skip it where** there's no separate product page: quick view and adding to the cart, as counted in [[Sessions with Cart Additions→voronki_prodazh_h4/dobavlenie_v_korzinu]], happen right in the list.
655.synonyms: PLP-to-PDP Conversion Rate, Product Detail View Rate
655.essence_note: choosing a product starts with opening its product page

656.name: Interactions per Product Page View
656.formula: Σ(Interactions on the Product Page) / Product Page Views
656.description: The average number of actions a user takes on a product page. Shows whether users study the product page or close it without going below the fold.
656.nuances:
**A fixed list of interactions**: switching photos in the gallery, opening a photo full screen, playing a video, switching to the specifications tab, switching to the reviews tab, expanding the description, choosing a size or color, opening the size chart, opening the delivery and payment block.
Anything outside the list **doesn't go into the numerator**; otherwise the metric for two periods can no longer be compared.
Scrolling **doesn't count as an interaction**: it happens on every product page and erases the difference between engaged and casual views.
Adding to the cart, as counted in [[Sessions with Cart Additions→voronki_prodazh_h4/dobavlenie_v_korzinu]], and adding to the wishlist **don't count**: these are funnel results with their own metrics.
Denominator: product page views rather than sessions with a view. Dividing events by sessions multiplies the average by **exactly the average number** of product pages opened per session.
656.example:
Product page views in the month: 40,600
Gallery photo changes: 36,500
Specifications tab opens: 17,800
Reviews tab opens: 12,100
Size or color selections: 16,400
Total interactions: 82,800

Interactions per Product Page View = 82,800 / 40,600 = **2.04 interactions per view**

Dividing by 15,600 sessions with a view gives 5.3: the figure is inflated by the number of product pages opened per session.
656.importance: **It separates product pages** that users study from those they close right away. If interactions per view grow while the View-to-Cart Rate stays flat, the user is looking for an answer and either doesn't find it, or finds it and leaves. In the first case, the product page lacks a size chart, in-room photos or return terms; in the second, the answer is there and doesn't suit them: delivery time, materials, final price. Which blocks of the product page users reach helps tell the two apart: if they open delivery and then close the page, missing information isn't the issue.
656.not_needed: Skip it on product pages **without interactive elements**: if the page has one photo and a paragraph of text, there's nothing to count.
656.essence_note: when there are few interactions, the product page wasn't studied; when there are many, the user can't find what they need right away

657.name: Zero-Result Search Rate
657.formula: (Search Sessions with No Results / All Search Sessions) × 100
657.description: The share of search sessions in which a search query returned no products. Shows how often users search for a product and get no results.
657.nuances:
Denominator: only sessions with at least one search rather than all site sessions. A session **counts as having no results** if at least one results page was empty: a session with two queries where the second one worked still goes into the numerator.
A results page with zero products and one that shows only “Similar” or “We recommend” products **count as equally empty**: there's no result for the query itself.
657.example:
Sessions in the week: 40,000
Of those, with search: 9,200
Sessions where at least one query returned an empty results page: 1,104

Zero-Result Search Rate = 1,104 / 9,200 × 100 = **12%**

Dividing by all 40,000 sessions gives 2.8%: that's the share of all traffic with a failed search rather than search quality.
657.importance: It points directly **to gaps in the assortment** and in the search engine: the list of zero-result queries shows which products people ask for and can't find, and where the engine stumbles over typos and synonyms. An empty results page often ends the session, so growth in the metric eats into conversion before it becomes visible in orders.
657.not_needed: Skip it for storefronts without a search bar: one-page landing pages and catalogs of 20–30 items where users navigate **only through the menu**.
657.synonyms: No Results Rate, Null Search Rate
657.essence_note: the person searched for a product and got nothing, so they leave without buying

658.name: Share of Sessions with Search, Filters, or Sorting
658.formula: (Sessions with Search, Filters, or Sorting Applied / All Sessions) × 100
658.description: The share of sessions in which the user used search, a filter or sorting. Shows how often users look for a product in the catalog deliberately rather than scrolling through everything.
658.nuances:
A session goes into the numerator **once**, no matter how many tools were used or how many times.
Filters and sort settings applied automatically through a banner or messaging campaign link **don't count**: the user didn't apply them.
The default sort order when the catalog opens **doesn't count as applied** until the user changes it.
658.example:
Sessions in the month: 50,000
Sessions with search: 9,000
Sessions with a filter: 7,500
Sessions with sorting: 3,000
Sessions with at least one of the three (no double counting): 13,400

Share of Sessions with Search, Filters, or Sorting = 13,400 / 50,000 × 100 = **26.8%**

The sum 9,000 + 7,500 + 3,000 = 19,500 would give 39%: the same sessions are counted two or three times.
658.importance: **It splits the audience into those** who came for a specific product and those who are choosing. What to invest in depends on this proportion: the search engine and filters, or curated collections and recommendations on the storefront. Sessions with search, filters or sorting convert better, so a low share usually means the tools simply aren't visible on the page.
658.not_needed: **Skip it in catalogs** with nothing to filter: when the catalog is small enough, the user sees the whole assortment on one screen.
658.essence_note: users who search and filter came for a specific product and buy more often

659.name: Wishlist-to-Cart Rate
659.formula: (Products Added to the Cart from the Wishlist / Products Added to the Wishlist) × 100
659.description: The share of wishlisted products that later ended up in the cart. Shows whether the saved list turns into purchases.
659.nuances:
The unit of count here is a product rather than a session: **the items in** the wishlist are counted, not sessions. The numerator counts a product added to the cart, the same action as in [[Sessions with Cart Additions→voronki_prodazh_h4/dobavlenie_v_korzinu]], if it was in that user's wishlist at the time, no matter which page the button was clicked on.
If you count **only button clicks** in the wishlist section, the metric ends up measuring how usable one screen is and comes out far too low.
The numerator and denominator **come from the same** cohort: products saved during the period and their cart additions within a fixed window after saving.
**Items stay in a wishlist for a long time**, and without a window, the numerator for the period fills up with products saved long before the period began.
A product that was saved and bought several times **counts once for each** save.
659.example:
Products saved to the wishlist in May: 12,000
Of those, added to the cart within 30 days of saving: 2,640
Products saved in March and added to the cart in May: 800 (not in the calculation)

Wishlist-to-Cart Rate = 2,640 / 12,000 × 100 = **22%**
659.importance: **It shows whether all the** wishlist features pay off: price-drop emails, back-in-stock reminders, the “You saved” block. If the rate stays very low, the wishlist is just a place where wishes pile up, and there's no point investing in wishlist re-engagement.
659.not_needed: Skip it if the wishlist isn't tied to a user and is stored **only in the browser**: there's no way to link a saved product to a later purchase.
659.essence_note: a saved product brings in money only when it reaches the cart

688.name: Sales per Employee
688.description: How much revenue there is per store employee for the period.
688.nuances:
The denominator includes **all store employees**, including those who don't work the register: receiving and stocking shelves support sales just as much, and counting only sales staff overstates the result, especially when a large share of the store's work happens off the sales floor.
Employees are counted **at the end of the period**.
688.example:
[[In-Store Revenue→riteyl/vyruchka]] for the month: $150,000
[[Store Headcount→riteyl/kolichestvo_sotrudnikov]] at the end of the month: 20
Of those, not working on the sales floor (receiving, stockroom): 5 (counted anyway)

Sales per Employee = 150,000 / 20 = **$7,500 per employee per month**
688.importance: It links the store's main expense line to what it brings in, and so underlies the decision **to hire or cut staff**. A drop while [[In-Store Revenue→riteyl/vyruchka]] grows means people **were hired faster than sales grew**, and payroll is absorbing the growth. It's dangerous on its own: you can cut staff to the bone and get a perfect figure **exactly once**.
688.not_needed: Skip it for locations **without permanent staff** and where one employee serves several locations: the denominator can't be tied to a specific store.
688.synonyms: Sales per Associate, Sales per Head
688.essence_note: the more revenue per person, the better the payroll pays for itself

689.name: Transactions
689.description: The number of completed transactions for the period. One transaction is one purchase at the register, regardless of how many items it contains or how many people came in together.
689.nuances:
Canceled and voided transactions **aren't counted**: the register records them, but no sale took place.
Return transactions **are subtracted from the total** rather than added to it: otherwise growth in returns would look like growth in purchases.
Non-sale register operations **don't count as transactions**, even though the register records them.
A transaction is assigned to the **date the register shift was closed** rather than the calendar date: in a 24-hour store the shift runs past midnight, and without a single rule the same day's count comes out differently.
689.example:
Visitors for the month: 32,000
Store Conversion Rate: 25%
Register records: 8,210, including 105 canceled and 105 non-sale operations (not counted)

Transactions = 32,000 × 25% = **8,000**
689.importance:
It's **the primary count of purchases**, the denominator for [[Average Transaction Value (ATV)→riteyl/sredniy_chek]] and the numerator for [[Store Conversion Rate→riteyl/konversiya_v_pokupku]].
Confusing **transactions with people** is the costliest mistake here: a family of four makes one transaction, and if you count transactions as [[Store Visitors→riteyl/posetiteli]], the store's conversion rate will show a figure **well above the real one**.
689.synonyms: Transaction Count, Receipt Count, Ticket Count
689.essence_note: every transaction is a purchase, and the more there are, the higher the revenue

690.name: Passerby Traffic
690.description: The number of people who passed through the exterior counter's field of view: both those who entered the store and those who walked past.
690.nuances:
The measurement zone is set by **the width of the field of view** of the exterior counter and determines the figure entirely: a sensor covering 15 feet along the window and a sensor covering the full width of the walkway give different numbers.
People who entered the store **aren't subtracted from the traffic**: they're part of it, and the Capture Rate is calculated from exactly this base. Subtracting them leaves you without a denominator.
A person who walked past several times counts **once per visit** to the mall; otherwise employees of neighboring stores inflate the traffic.
690.example:
Crossings recorded by the counter at the entrance for the day: 45,000
Repeat passes by the same people: 8,000 (merged)

Passerby Traffic = 45,000 − 8,000 = **37,000**

Of those, 12,000 entered the store: they stay in the traffic count as the base for [[Capture Rate→riteyl/konversiya_vhoda]].
690.importance:
It sets **the ceiling** the store can't rise above, and separates a location problem from a performance problem.
When [[Store Visitors→riteyl/posetiteli]] drop while traffic past the store stays the same, the problem is **with the window display or the sign**. When the traffic itself sags, there's nothing to change inside the store: **the location's passerby traffic** has changed, and that's an argument in lease negotiations.
690.not_needed: Skip it for **standalone** stores and locations people travel to on purpose: nobody happens to walk past them.
690.synonyms: Pedestrian Traffic, Passersby Count, Outside Traffic
690.essence_note: the more people walk past, the more of them can come in

691.name: Average Daily Passerby Traffic
691.formula: Passerby Traffic / Number of Days in the Period
691.description: How many people pass through the exterior counter's field of view on an average day in the period.
691.nuances:
Only **days the store is open** go into the denominator: including days when the store is closed understates the result, even though traffic past the store wasn't measured on those days.
Holiday and sale periods **distort the average** the most: a sale week raises the average for the whole month, and months become impossible to compare without a note.
It's calculated using **the same rules** as [[Passerby Traffic→riteyl/vneshniy_potok]], including merging repeat passes and counting those who entered as part of the traffic.
691.example:
[[Passerby Traffic→riteyl/vneshniy_potok]] for the month: 1,110,000 people
Calendar days: 31
Store closed: 1 day (excluded)

Average Daily Passerby Traffic = 1,110,000 / 30 = **37,000 people a day**
691.importance:
It puts **months of different lengths** on a common basis: otherwise February with its 28 days and a month with several public holidays can't be compared.
It shows **whether traffic past the store is itself changing**: when it falls while the store operates as before, the problem is **the location**, and that's an argument in lease negotiations.
691.not_needed: Skip it **without an exterior counter** and for locations customers travel to on purpose.
691.synonyms: Daily Pedestrian Traffic, Average Daily Footfall
691.essence_note: the more people walk past on an average day, the higher the store's sales ceiling

692.name: Store Visitors
692.description: The number of people who entered the store during the period. One person in one visit counts once, regardless of whether they bought anything.
692.nuances:
**Staff are subtracted**: sales associates and cashiers use the same entrance as customers and, in a small store, account for a noticeable share of counter triggers.
Exits through the same doorway **are filtered out**: a bidirectional sensor counts crossings, and without separating directions the number doubles.
A repeat entry during a visit, for example after stepping out for a forgotten card, **is merged into one visit**.
**The counter type changes the figure**: an infrared beam can't tell apart people walking close together and undercounts traffic at peak hours compared with a video counter.
692.example:
Counter triggers for the month: 73,000
Exits (opposite direction): 34,100
Staff passes: 6,100
Repeat entries within one visit: 800

Store Visitors = 73,000 − 34,100 − 6,100 − 800 = **32,000 for the month**

Across 8 stores, that's 4,000 visitors per store.
692.importance:
It's the denominator for [[Store Conversion Rate→riteyl/konversiya_v_pokupku]] and the point where **the sales funnel breaks** if there's simply no traffic.
Without a counter, the store sees only those who **made it to the register** and can't tell a slow day from a day when everyone came but nobody bought.
692.not_needed: Skip it for formats without a sales floor: at an order pickup counter, a pickup location or a vending machine, the person who enters and the buyer are the same, so traffic adds no separate measure.
692.synonyms: Store Traffic, Foot Traffic, Door Count
692.essence_note: without people walking in, there are no sales at all

693.name: Capture Rate
693.description: What share of the people walking past the store come inside.
693.nuances:
The denominator includes everyone in the counter's field of view, **including those who went in**: dividing only by those who walked past drops the visitors from the base and inflates the percentage.
The exterior counter's coverage area **determines the figure entirely**: the narrower the zone in front of the entrance, the higher the capture rate, so two stores' figures are comparable only with the same counter settings.
Staff **are subtracted from both the numerator and the denominator**; otherwise in a small store employees make up a noticeable share of entries.
693.example:
[[Passerby Traffic→riteyl/vneshniy_potok]] for the day: 37,000
Entered the store: 12,000
Walked past without entering: 25,000

Capture Rate = 12,000 / 37,000 × 100 = **32%**

Dividing only by the 25,000 who walked past gives 48%: the denominator excludes those who entered.
693.importance:
It evaluates everything **outside the store**: the sign, the window display, the entrance, outdoor promotion. It's the only metric where the effect of a new window display shows up **first**, before the change reaches [[In-Store Revenue→riteyl/vyruchka]].
A dip here means the store **is paying rent for traffic** that doesn't notice it.
693.not_needed: Skip it **without an exterior counter** and for standalone buildings where nobody happens to walk past.
693.synonyms: Entry Rate, Walk-In Rate, Passerby Conversion
693.essence_note: the more passersby come in, the more customers the same foot traffic brings

694.name: Store Conversion Rate
694.description: How many purchases there are per hundred visitors who enter. Transactions and visitors are counted in different units: a family of four counts as four people at the door counter but makes one transaction at the register.
694.nuances:
Because of the difference in units, conversion in stores with family traffic **always understates the store's real performance**. Stores are compared **within the same format**, keeping in mind that with family traffic conversion is lower for the same sales floor performance.
Staff **are subtracted from the visitor count**: without that, conversion is understated, and the smaller the store, the more so.
Both counts cover **the same time interval**; otherwise evening-shift transactions get divided by the daytime count of [[Store Visitors→riteyl/posetiteli]].
694.example:
Visitors for the month: 32,000 (staff already subtracted)
Completed transactions: 8,000

Store Conversion Rate = 8,000 / 32,000 × 100 = **25%**

If you count groups of shoppers as single transactions rather than as people at the entrance, the figure comes out higher than the real one: a family of three makes one transaction.
694.importance:
It separates two very different problems: people don't come in, or people come in and leave empty-handed. The first is fixed with signage and advertising; the second, with **assortment, pricing and sales staff performance**.
Without conversion data, a drop in sales gets blamed on traffic, and budget goes to bringing in more people when the leak is **in the store itself**.
694.not_needed: Skip it for formats where people come in to pick up an order they've already paid for: at an order pickup counter or a pickup location, conversion stays close to 100% and tells you nothing.
694.synonyms: Retail Conversion Rate, Traffic Conversion Rate, Shopper Conversion
694.essence_note: a larger share of visitors making purchases means more revenue from the same traffic

695.name: Average Transaction Value (ATV)
695.description: The average amount of one transaction.
695.nuances:
The numerator and denominator follow **the same rule** as their source metrics: if [[Sales Returns→finansy/vozvraty]] are subtracted from revenue, return transactions are also subtracted from [[Transactions→riteyl/kolichestvo_chekov]]; otherwise the average transaction value is understated.
Large one-off purchases **pull the average up** and make it unrepresentative: either exclude them or look at the median next to the average.
695.example:
Revenue for the month: $400,000
Transactions: 8,000 (return transactions already subtracted)

Average Transaction Value (ATV) = 400,000 / 8,000 = **$50**

Check with the second method: an average unit price of $20 × 2.5 units per transaction = $50.
695.importance:
It's the other driver of [[In-Store Revenue→riteyl/vyruchka]] besides the number of purchases, and usually **the easier one to manage**: raising the transaction value through add-on sales and rearranged displays is cheaper than bringing in new traffic.
The trend in transaction value shows **earlier than revenue** that customers have started cutting back: they still come in but buy less and choose cheaper items.
695.synonyms: Average Ticket, Average Sale, Average Basket Value
695.essence_note: with the same number of purchases, a higher transaction value translates directly into more money

696.name: Line Items per Transaction
696.description: The average number of different line items in one transaction. Two pens and a pencil are two line items, however many units are bought.
696.nuances:
**Line items are counted rather than units**: two pens and a pencil are two line items and three units, which is what [[Units per Transaction (UPT)→riteyl/kolichestvo_edinic_tovara_v_cheke]] counts. Line items show the breadth of the basket; units show its depth. Each grows in response to different decisions.
A line item is counted by **unique SKU**, and **the store decides** how granular its product catalog is: flavors, colors and sizes are sometimes separate SKUs and sometimes variants within a single product record. The figure depends on this, so it's compared only with its own history and only as long as the catalog hasn't been restructured.
An item rung up on two lines because of a cashier's correction **collapses into one line item**; otherwise register errors look like a broader basket.
Return transactions **don't go into the denominator**, and their line items don't go into the numerator.
696.example:
[[Transactions→riteyl/kolichestvo_chekov]] for the month: 8,000
Unique line items across all transactions: 14,400
Total units in them: 20,000, that is, 2.5 units per transaction ([[Units per Transaction (UPT)→riteyl/kolichestvo_edinic_tovara_v_cheke]], a different metric)

Line Items per Transaction = 14,400 / 8,000 = **1.8 line items**

The gap from units per transaction (2.5) shows that customers buy the same item in multiples.
696.importance: It measures **the breadth of the basket**, and it's the only metric that shows whether add-on selling and cross-merchandising work: they add **a different product** to the transaction rather than one more unit of the same one. Comparing it with [[Units per Transaction (UPT)→riteyl/kolichestvo_edinic_tovara_v_cheke]] shows what exactly is happening: customers **pick up a variety of items** or take several units of the same one, and the two cases call for opposite merchandising decisions.
696.not_needed: Skip it where a purchase almost always has **a single line item**: major appliances, furniture, services.
696.essence_note: the more different items customers take at once, the higher the transaction value without any discounts

697.name: In-Store Average Unit Retail (AUR)
697.description: The average price at which one unit of merchandise sold, after all discounts. For items sold by the piece it's the price per piece; for goods sold by weight, the price per pound.
697.nuances:
It's calculated at the **actual selling price** rather than the shelf price: the gap is larger the higher the promo share of sales.
The numerator and denominator are calculated **on the same basis**: if [[Sales Returns→finansy/vozvraty]] are subtracted from revenue, returned units are subtracted from units.
Items sold by the piece and goods sold by weight are counted **on separate lines**: the former give a price per piece, the latter a price per pound. It's the same metric in different units; they can't be combined into one average, and both need to be watched.
Zero-price promotional items **are included in the denominator** and pull the average price down, which is the real effect of the promotion on the selling price.
697.example:
Revenue for the month: $400,000
Units sold: 20,000

In-Store Average Unit Retail (AUR) = 400,000 / 20,000 = **$20**
697.importance:
It separates **the price component** of growth from the volume component and shows how much the store actually gives away in discounts.
The gap between this figure and the average shelf price is **the cost of the promotional policy**, which isn't visible as a single number anywhere else.
697.not_needed: Skip it with a **broad assortment** of categories at very different prices, where bread and home appliances get averaged into one meaningless number.
697.synonyms: Average Selling Price, Average Unit Price
697.essence_note: the higher the price a unit sells at, the more money the same sale brings in

698.name: Units per Transaction (UPT)
698.description: The average number of physical units of merchandise in one transaction. All units count, however many different products the transaction contains: two pens and a pencil are three units. For items sold by the piece it's measured in pieces; for goods sold by weight, in pounds.
698.nuances:
Units and line items are **different quantities**: two pens and a pencil are three units but two line items, which is what [[Line Items per Transaction→riteyl/kolichestvo_tovarov_v_cheke]] counts. Units show the depth of the basket; line items show its breadth. Each grows in response to different decisions.
Items sold by the piece and goods sold by weight are counted **on separate lines**: pieces per transaction and pounds per transaction. They can't be added into one number, but both are meaningful and are looked at side by side.
Returned units **are subtracted from the numerator**, and return transactions from the denominator; otherwise the metric drifts upward.
Zero-price promotional items **count toward units**: the customer physically took them home.
698.example:
Units sold in the month: 20,000
Transactions: 8,000

Units per Transaction (UPT) = 20,000 / 8,000 = **2.5**
698.importance:
It shows whether customers buy **to stock up** or strictly one unit at a time. It grows with **volume promotions**: “three for the price of two,” a discount on the second unit, larger pack sizes.
When [[Average Transaction Value (ATV)→riteyl/sredniy_chek]] grows only because of price while units stay flat, the growth depends **on inflation** and will end with it.
698.not_needed: Skip it where a transaction **almost always has one unit**: major home appliances, furniture, jewelry.
698.essence_note: more units per transaction means more revenue from the same customer

699.name: Net Units Sold
699.formula: Σ Units Rung Up − Returned Units
699.description: The number of units of merchandise sold during the period: items sold by the piece are counted in pieces, goods sold by weight in pounds. Three identical packs in one transaction count as three units (see [[Transactions→riteyl/kolichestvo_chekov]]).
699.nuances:
Returns are subtracted in the period **when they're processed**: without subtracting them, the metric shows what left the shelf rather than actual sales.
Items sold by the piece and goods sold by weight are counted **on separate lines**: the former in pieces, the latter in pounds. A combined figure of “units” across a mixed assortment is meaningless: half a pound of cheese and a carton of milk aren't two units of the same thing.
Promotional items with a zero price **are included in units sold**: they physically left the shelf and must be deducted from inventory.
699.example:
Items sold by the piece, rung up in the month: 7,800 pcs
Promotional items at a zero price: 180 pcs (included in the 7,800)
Returned by customers: 300 pcs

Net Units Sold, items sold by the piece = 7,800 − 300 = **7,500 pcs**

Goods sold by weight in the same month: 5,300 lb, counted on a separate line and not added to the piece count.
699.importance:
It's the only sales metric that **price doesn't affect**, so it shows real demand separately from inflation and discounts.
When [[In-Store Revenue→riteyl/vyruchka]] grows while units fall, the store is selling **less merchandise at higher prices**, and the growth will end as soon as customers notice the price.
699.essence_note: unit counts show demand without the price distortion that revenue carries

700.name: Dwell Time
700.formula: Σ Time in Store / Store Visitors
700.description: The average time a visitor spends inside the store, from entry to exit.
700.nuances:
Staff **are excluded from the calculation**: an employee spends the whole shift on the sales floor and single-handedly pulls the average up.
An **upper limit on visit length** is set: without it, sessions that hang open because someone left a phone behind or lingered at the window outside produce outliers.
Time at the registers **is part of dwell time**, so growth isn't always good news: it can mean a longer line rather than more careful browsing.
700.example:
[[Store Visitors→riteyl/posetiteli]] for the day: 12,000
Total time on the sales floor: 174,000 minutes
Sessions longer than 3 hours: 60, capped at the limit
Staff tracking: excluded

Dwell Time = 174,000 / 12,000 = **14.5 minutes**
700.importance:
Time on the sales floor and [[Average Transaction Value (ATV)→riteyl/sredniy_chek]] **move together**: the longer a person walks around, the more they put in the basket.
That's why this figure is used to evaluate **floor layout changes** and wayfinding, and a drop with unchanged traffic means customers don't find a reason to stay.
700.not_needed: Skip it for formats built on **a quick, planned purchase**: kiosks near the checkout lanes, stores people stop at on their way somewhere, gas station convenience stores, where a short visit is normal rather than a problem.
700.synonyms: Time in Store, Visit Duration, Average Visit Length
700.essence_note: a visit that's too short means the person didn't choose anything, and one that's too long means they're waiting in line or can't find the product

701.name: Zones Visited per Visitor
701.description: The average number of sales floor zones a visitor covers during one visit.
701.nuances:
A zone counts **once per visit**, even if the visitor came back to it twice: without merging, the metric starts measuring how chaotic the route is rather than how much of the floor is covered.
A **minimum time in the zone** is set: without a threshold, passing through a zone on the way to the register counts as a visit and inflates the result.
The number of zones in the floor layout sets **the metric's ceiling**: the same path gives twice as many zones visited when the floor is split into 20 zones instead of 10.
701.example:
[[Store Visitors→riteyl/posetiteli]] for the day: 12,000
Zones in the floor layout: 12
Zone visits recorded: 50,400
Repeat entries into the same zone: 12,000 (merged)
Passes shorter than 5 seconds: 4,800 (not counted)

Zones Visited per Visitor = (50,400 − 12,000 − 4,800) / 12,000 = **2.8 zones**
701.importance:
It shows **what part of the assortment** customers see at all. If visitors cover three of twelve zones, nine categories sell only to those who came for them **on purpose**.
This is the basis for decisions on **moving anchor categories** deeper into the store and on placing wayfinding signage.
701.not_needed: Skip it for formats where **the whole sales floor is one zone**: small stores, mall kiosks, stands.
701.essence_note: the more zones a customer covers, the more merchandise they see

702.name: Store Penetration Rate
702.formula: Visitors Who Went Past the Entrance Zone / Store Visitors × 100
702.description: The share of visitors who entered and went past the entrance zone into the main sales floor.
702.nuances:
The boundary of the entrance zone is set by **a line of sensors**, and the figure depends directly on it: the closer the line is to the doors, the higher the percentage.
A visitor is counted **once**, even if they crossed the line several times during the visit. Without merging repeat crossings, the result goes above 100%.
Staff **are subtracted from both the numerator and the denominator**: a sales associate crosses the line many times per shift.
702.example:
[[Store Visitors→riteyl/posetiteli]] for the day: 12,000
Crossings of the line onto the main sales floor: 9,400
Of those, repeat crossings by the same people: 1,300
Line crossings by staff: 500

Visitors who went past the entrance zone = 9,400 − 1,300 − 500 = 7,600
Store Penetration Rate = 7,600 / 12,000 × 100 = **63%**
702.importance:
It answers whether **the entrance zone draws people in** or cuts them off. A low percentage means a person walks in, runs into a promo stand or the line at the registers, and **turns around** without ever seeing the main assortment.
Without this figure, a drop in sales looks like **an assortment problem**, even though customers simply never got to the assortment.
702.not_needed: Skip it in **small spaces** where the whole floor is visible from the doors: splitting it into an entrance zone and the main sales floor makes no sense.
702.essence_note: anyone who didn't reach the main sales floor didn't see the assortment and didn't buy

703.name: In-Store Out-of-Stock Rate
703.formula: SKUs with an Empty Shelf / SKUs in the Active Assortment × 100
703.alt_formula: SKUs with Zero Stock in the Store / SKUs in the Active Assortment × 100
703.description: The share of items unavailable for sale out of all items in the active assortment. Unavailability means either an empty shelf or the product being absent from the store entirely: these are two different measurements of the same metric, and the chosen one is stated next to the figure.
703.nuances:
The criterion for unavailability is chosen **once** and kept constant. With the shelf measurement, unavailability is **an empty spot on the shelf**, even if the product is in the store's stockroom: customers won't buy what they can't see. With the stock measurement, it's **zero stock** anywhere in the store, and a product that isn't on the shelf doesn't count as out of stock. The shelf measurement gives a higher figure, and the two measurements aren't compared with each other.
The shelf measurement catches **merchandising** problems; the stock measurement catches **supply** problems. The difference between them is the amount of merchandise that sits in the store's stockroom and hasn't made it to the sales floor.
Only items in **the active assortment** go into the denominator. Delisted SKUs left in the denominator inflate the base and understate the percentage.
The stock measurement comes from the inventory system and can be calculated across the whole assortment as often as daily. The shelf measurement requires walking the floor, so it's done **using a sample**: promotional items, top categories, shelves near the entrance. The denominator is then the audited sample rather than the whole assortment, and this is stated next to the figure.
703.example:
SKUs in the active assortment: 2,400
Delisted: 180 (not in the denominator)

Stock measurement, whole assortment from the inventory system:
SKUs with zero stock: 122
Stock-based out-of-stock rate = 122 / 2,400 × 100 = **5.1%**

Shelf measurement, audit of the promo zone and a top category:
SKUs checked: 300
SKUs with an empty shelf: 42, of which 20 are in the store's stockroom
Shelf-based out-of-stock rate = 42 / 300 × 100 = **14%**

The figures aren't compared with each other: they have different denominators and different meanings. Those 20 items that are in the stockroom but not on the shelf are the part merchandising has to fix.
703.importance: Every empty shelf is **a lost sale**, and some customers leave the store altogether rather than switching to a substitute. The stock measurement shows **where supply breaks down**: the supplier order, receiving, delivery lead times. The shelf measurement shows **whether merchandise makes it** from the back room to the sales floor. Without these figures, a drop in a category's sales is blamed on demand, even though the product simply wasn't there.
703.not_needed: Skip it where **there's no assortment plan** and the store fills the shelf with whatever arrives: there's nothing to compare the actual shelf with.
703.essence_note: what isn't on the shelf won't be bought, and some customers leave the store altogether

704.name: Planogram Compliance Rate
704.description: The share of audited sales floor zones where the display matches the planogram. Calculated from audit results.
704.nuances:
A zone counts as compliant **only as a whole**: if one of ten items in it doesn't match the planogram, the zone is classified as noncompliant. Awarding partial credit within a zone raises the result and hides errors: a zone with one violation scores as nearly compliant.
Zones that weren't audited **are excluded from the denominator**; otherwise the metric turns into a measure of how complete the audit was.
A product missing because of a supply shortage **doesn't count as a display violation**: that's a separate supply problem.
704.example:
Zones on the sales floor: 40
Audited: 32
Zones with empty shelves due to supply shortages: 2 (excluded from the calculation, there was nothing to display)
Fully compliant with the planogram: 24
Zones with at least one noncompliant item: 6

Planogram Compliance Rate = 24 / 30 × 100 = **80%**

If the zones with shortages stay in the denominator, you get 75%: the merchandiser gets a violation recorded where the product simply wasn't there.
704.importance:
A planogram is built around **specific sales logic**: priority items at eye level, complementary items next to anchor ones.
When compliance falls, sales of promotional items **sag for no visible reason**, and the drop is easy to blame on demand, even though the product simply wasn't where customers look for it.
704.not_needed: Skip it when **there's no planogram** and the staff choose how to arrange the displays: there's nothing to compare with.
704.synonyms: Planogram Compliance, Merchandising Compliance, Planogram Integrity
704.essence_note: a product placed where customers don't look for it simply doesn't get bought

705.name: In-Store Inventory Turnover
705.formula: Net Units Sold / Average Inventory for the Period
705.description: How many times inventory was fully sold and replaced during the period. A value of 4 means the stock was sold through and replenished four times.
705.nuances:
The result depends on **the length of the window**: annual turnover is roughly twelve times the monthly figure, so a figure without its period can't be interpreted.
Average inventory is calculated from **several counts** within the period rather than from the ending stock: stock after a clearance sale is low, and turnover comes out overstated.
The numerator and denominator use **the same units**: either pieces or dollars. Mixing pieces in the numerator with dollars of purchase cost in the denominator gives a number that means nothing.
Goods in transit **aren't part of the store's inventory**: they can't be sold off the shelf.
705.example:
Period: month
[[Net Units Sold→riteyl/prodannye_edinicy]]: 7,500
Stock counts: 2,400, 2,700, 2,500, 2,400 pcs
Average inventory = (2,400 + 2,700 + 2,500 + 2,400) / 4 = 2,500 pcs

Turnover = 7,500 / 2,500 = **3 times a month**

Taking only the end-of-month stock (2,400) gives 3.1: the difference adds up when you compare periods.
705.importance: It shows **how much money is tied up** in merchandise that isn't selling. Slow turnover means **a specific sum sitting on the shelves** instead of in the bank account, plus the risk of write-offs for expired goods. It's the basis for cutting purchases, removing items from the assortment and negotiating **frequent small deliveries** with suppliers instead of infrequent large ones.
705.not_needed: Skip it where there's **no inventory**: services, special-order sales, drop shipping from the supplier.
705.synonyms: Stock Turn, Inventory Turns, Stock Turnover
705.essence_note: the faster stock sells through and is replenished, the less money sits on the shelves instead of circulating in the business

706.name: Transaction Time
706.description: The average time a cashier spends on one transaction, from scanning the first item to handing the receipt to the customer.
706.nuances:
Register idle time between transactions **isn't included in the total**: otherwise service would look slow during quiet hours with an empty store.
Processing a return and voiding a transaction are counted **separately**: they take noticeably longer than a regular sale and skew the average.
706.example:
[[Transactions→riteyl/kolichestvo_chekov]] per shift: 3,000
Total service time: 4,500 minutes
Returns and voids: 40 operations, 120 minutes (not included)
Idle time between transactions: not counted

Transaction Time = 4,500 / 3,000 = **1.5 minutes per transaction**
706.importance:
**It determines how many transactions** can physically go through a register at peak hours, and so bears directly on the decision to open an additional register.
The heavier the flow of customers, the faster extra seconds per transaction add up to cashier hours. A slowdown can be the first sign that the staff haven't gotten used to **new equipment** yet.
706.not_needed: Skip it for **self-checkout** and formats without a cashier: there's no one providing the service.
706.essence_note: the longer a cashier takes to ring up a transaction, the fewer purchases go through the register at peak hours

707.name: Average Queue Length
707.formula: Σ People in Line Across All Counts / Number of Counts
707.description: The average number of people waiting in line at checkout, based on counts taken during the period.
707.nuances:
Counts are taken at **equal intervals**: counting only when a line forms captures just the peaks and overstates the average.
A person being served **isn't part of the line**; only those waiting are counted: otherwise the queue length would never be zero, even when no one is waiting at the registers.
Hours when the registers are closed **are excluded from the counts**; otherwise the average falls because of time when a line couldn't form at all.
707.example:
Counts every 10 minutes over 12 business hours: 72 counts
Total people in line across all counts: 122
Customers being served at the register: not counted

Average Queue Length = 122 / 72 = **1.7 people**

If you count only when the line is noticeable, the average comes out at about 4 people: that's the average line length at peaks rather than the average line.
707.importance:
It shows **the visual threshold** past which customers turn around on their way to the register without trying to get in line.
The average length reacts to a shortage of cashiers **faster than wait time** does, because the line grows before anyone's wait has time to grow. This is the basis for decisions on how many registers to open during each hour.
707.not_needed: Skip it where **lines don't form**: showrooms, appointment-based locations, stores with a handful of sales.
707.essence_note: customers see a long line from afar and turn around before reaching the register

708.name: Store Headcount
708.formula: Σ Employees at the End of the Period
708.description: The number of store employees at the end of the period. People are counted rather than FTEs.
708.nuances:
Part-time employees count **as one person each**: converting to FTEs gives a different number, and metrics based on it stop matching the actual shift staffing.
Employees on long-term leave **are excluded**: they're on the books but not working, and including them inflates the denominator in derived metrics.
Contract workers, including security and cleaning staff, **aren't included**: they don't affect sales and don't report to the store.
708.example:
On the staff roster at the end of the month: 26 people
On parental leave or long-term sick leave: 4 (excluded)
Contracted security and cleaning: 2 (not included)
Working half-time: 3 (counted as 3 people)

Store Headcount = **20**
708.importance:
It's **the starting point for all of the store's economics**: payroll, workload per person, the hiring plan.
An error here is **hard to notice and costly**: if you include employees on parental leave, you get an understated [[Sales per Employee→riteyl/prodazhi_na_sotrudnika]] and conclude that the staff perform worse than they do.
708.not_needed: Skip it for locations **without permanent staff**: vending machines, self-service kiosks, locations with an employee who comes in on a schedule.
708.synonyms: Store Staff Count, Employee Count, Number of Employees
708.essence_note: too few people, and there's no one to serve customers at peak hours; too many, and wages eat the store's profit

709.name: Transactions per Employee
709.description: How many transactions there are per store employee for the period.
709.nuances: Transactions are counted using **the same rules** as in the Transactions metric: return transactions are subtracted and canceled transactions are excluded.
709.example:
[[Transactions→riteyl/kolichestvo_chekov]] for the month: 3,000
[[Store Headcount→riteyl/kolichestvo_sotrudnikov]] at the end of the month: 20

Transactions per Employee = 3,000 / 20 = **150 transactions per employee per month**
709.importance:
It measures **workload in transactions** rather than dollars, so price changes don't distort it: when prices go up, [[Sales per Employee→riteyl/prodazhi_na_sotrudnika]] grows on its own, while transactions per person show **whether there's really more work**.
A divergence between the trends of these two figures is exactly what exposes **inflation-driven growth**.
709.not_needed: Skip it where **a transaction doesn't reflect the amount of work**: salons with long consultations, major appliance stores, where one transaction takes far more time than at a regular checkout.
709.essence_note: the more purchases one person handles, the lower the labor cost per transaction

710.name: Sales per Square Foot
710.description: How much revenue one square foot of sales floor brings in. Shows how intensively the space is used.
710.nuances:
Only the **selling area** counts: the stockroom, back rooms, the checkout area beyond the registers and service corridors are excluded. Using the total floor area of the premises understates the result, especially in stores with large stockrooms and back rooms, and makes stores impossible to compare with one another.
Fitting rooms and seating areas **are part of the sales floor area**, since they help make sales.
The calculation uses the area **as of the end of the period**: if the floor was expanded mid-month, using the old area inflates sales per square foot without any real increase in sales density.
710.example:
[[In-Store Revenue→riteyl/vyruchka]] for the month: $150,000
Total floor area of the premises: 4,200 sq ft
Stockroom and back rooms: 1,200 sq ft (excluded)
Sales floor area: 3,000 sq ft

Sales per Square Foot = 150,000 / 3,000 = **$50 per sq ft per month**
710.importance: It's the only way to **compare stores of different sizes** with one another and see whether the sales floor covers its rent. It's the basis for deciding whether to **reduce the space** when the lease is renewed and whether to give floor space to a slow-moving category. A store with higher [[In-Store Revenue→riteyl/vyruchka]] may well have lower sales per square foot than a small one, and you can't see that without this metric.
710.not_needed: Skip it for formats **without their own sales floor**: mall kiosks, order pickup counters, sales from a display case inside another business, where the space isn't the store's to manage.
710.synonyms: Sales Density, Revenue per Square Foot
710.essence_note: the more each square foot brings in, the better the sales floor covers its rent

711.name: Share of Promotional Sales
711.description: The share of [[In-Store Revenue→riteyl/vyruchka]] from goods sold at a discount or as part of a promotion.
711.nuances:
It's calculated at the **actual selling price** rather than the price before the discount: otherwise the promo share is inflated by the size of the discount itself.
A loyalty card discount counts as promo **only if the company classifies it that way**. The difference is significant: including the card discount raises the promo share, and the wider the program's reach, the bigger the increase.
“Buy one, get one free” and “three for the price of two” deals **count as promo in full**, including the zero-price item; otherwise the [[In-Store Revenue→riteyl/vyruchka]] attributed to the promotion comes out lower than it really is.
711.example:
[[In-Store Revenue→riteyl/vyruchka]] for the month: $400,000
Revenue from promotional items at actual prices: $120,000
The same items at regular prices would have brought in $160,000 (not used in the calculation)

Share of Promotional Sales = 120,000 / 400,000 × 100 = **30%**
711.importance:
It shows **what sales depend on**: demand or discounts. As the share grows, customers **learn to wait for promotions** and stop buying at the regular price, and margin falls faster than [[In-Store Revenue→riteyl/vyruchka]] grows.
This figure is used to decide whether to **reduce discount depth** and whether to space promotions out over time.
711.not_needed: Skip it for formats with **a single fixed price** and for hard discounters, where the business model doesn't use promotional discounts.
711.essence_note: every promotional sale gives away part of the margin the company would have kept at full price

712.name: In-Store Return Rate
712.description: The share of units sold that customers returned. Calculated in units rather than in dollars.
712.nuances:
A return is assigned to the **date it was processed** rather than the date of the original purchase: otherwise closed periods would have to be recalculated after the fact.
An exchange for a different size or color counts as a return only if it's **processed at the register** as a return and a new sale.
Returns of defective items and warranty returns **are included in the total**: the item came back and the money was refunded. Return reasons are analyzed with the Return Reason breakdown rather than by excluding those returns from the numerator; otherwise the metric stops matching the returns actually received.
712.example:
[[Net Units Sold→riteyl/prodannye_edinicy]] for the month: 7,500
Returned by customers: 300
Of those, defective and warranty returns: 45 (included in the count, analyzed by return reason)

In-Store Return Rate = 300 / 7,500 × 100 = **4%**
712.importance:
Growth shows that customers take home **something other than what they wanted**: an error in the size chart, weak advice on the sales floor, a product that looks different at the register than it did on display.
A return eats into [[In-Store Revenue→riteyl/vyruchka]] **twice**, through the refund and through the labor of processing it, so it's used to decide what to change in merchandising and sales staff training. The breakdown by reason shows where to look: at **supplier defects** or at how the store itself serves customers.
712.not_needed: Skip it for formats where a return is **physically impossible**: food, prepared meals, products dispensed from a tap.
712.synonyms: Store Return Rate, Product Return Rate
712.essence_note: a return reduces revenue and adds processing costs

713.name: In-Store Revenue
713.description: The total of all sales for the period. Calculated from the completed transactions counted in [[Transactions→riteyl/kolichestvo_chekov]].
713.nuances:
A return reduces revenue in the period **in which it's processed**, rather than the period of the original sale: the sale is treated as canceled and reversed as of the current date. Closed periods aren't revised, since reports have already been filed for them and percentage rent has already been charged.
Revenue is recognized on the **transaction completion date**, regardless of when the money reaches the bank account: card payments are deposited later, and using the deposit date puts revenue in the wrong month.
Money from gift card sales **doesn't become revenue**: it's a prepayment, the store's obligation to hand over goods. Revenue is recognized when the gift card is redeemed. The difference shows up when gift cards are bought as presents in December and redeemed in January.
713.example:
Completed transactions for the month: $154,000
Of that, gift card sales: $4,000 (a prepayment, not counted as revenue)
Returns processed this month: 0

In-Store Revenue = 154,000 − 4,000 = **$150,000**

That $4,000 becomes revenue in the month when the gift cards are used to pay for goods.
713.importance:
It's the **top line** that everything else is calculated from: percentage rent, bonuses, payback on the store.
An error in this starting figure **carries through** to every derived metric, and the discrepancy then has to be traced after the fact in each of them.
713.synonyms: Store Sales, Brick-and-Mortar Sales, Offline Revenue
713.essence_note: this is all the money the store took in during the period

714.name: Queue Wait Time
714.description: The average time a customer spends in line, from the moment they join it until service starts at the register.
714.nuances:
The wait ends **when the cashier starts scanning**: if service itself is added, the metric starts duplicating [[Transaction Time→riteyl/vremya_obsluzhivaniya]].
Customers who left the line **aren't included in the average**, because their wait was cut short. This understates the result exactly when the line is longest, so they're counted as a separate number.
An all-day average **hides peaks**: the same figure comes from a steady line all day and from a half-hour backup in the evening.
714.example:
Customers served for the day: 3,000
Total wait time: 3,600 minutes
Left the line before being served: 45 people (not in the average, counted separately)

Queue Wait Time = 3,600 / 3,000 = **1.2 minutes**
714.importance: The checkout line, measured by [[Average Queue Length→riteyl/srednyaya_dlina_ocheredi]], is **the last point** where the store loses an already filled basket, and the loss happens after all the spending on traffic and merchandising. Customers' patience threshold differs by format and shows up in the store's own data: it's where rising wait time starts to coincide with more baskets abandoned in the store. The figure feeds straight into **the shift schedule**: it shows the hours when there aren't enough registers rather than how many people came in.
714.not_needed: Skip it where **lines don't form** because of the format: appointment-based salons, showrooms, locations with a handful of sales a day.
714.synonyms: Checkout Wait Time, Line Wait Time
714.essence_note: in line, customers abandon an already filled basket and leave

715.name: Active Staff per Shift
715.formula: Σ Employees on Shifts / Number of Shifts
715.description: The average number of employees from [[Store Headcount→riteyl/kolichestvo_sotrudnikov]] working at the same time during one shift.
715.nuances:
The calculation includes **those who actually showed up** rather than those on the schedule: no-shows and substitutions create exactly the difference the metric is calculated for.
An employee working half a shift is counted by **hours worked**; otherwise short fill-ins look like a full extra person on the shift.
Administrative staff **are excluded from the calculation**: the metric answers whether there's someone to help the customer.
715.example:
Shifts in the month: 60
Employee shifts worked in total: 480
Half shifts worked: 8, counted as 4 full-shift equivalents
Administrative staff off the sales floor: not counted

Active Staff per Shift = 480 / 60 = **8 people**
715.importance:
The shift schedule decides whether there will be someone to serve customers at peak hours, and here **the cost of a mistake is asymmetric**: an extra person in a quiet hour costs their wages, while being one person short at peak means **abandoned baskets**.
The figure is needed to check actual coverage against **the traffic curve**.
715.not_needed: Skip it when **staffing levels are constant** and the same number of people come in every day: the average will equal the headcount.
715.synonyms: Staff per Shift, Floor Staffing Level
715.essence_note: an extra person in a quiet hour costs their wages, while being one person short at peak means abandoned baskets

716.name: Course Costs
716.formula: Σ Course Creation and Delivery Costs
716.description: Total spending on creating and running the course over the period: filming and recording materials, fees for authors and experts, mentor pay, the platform, and student support.
716.nuances:
Costs are split into one-time and recurring: course production is paid for **once**, while mentors and support are paid for in every cohort. Writing off the entire recording against the first cohort makes it unprofitable and the following ones free of production costs.
**Production costs are spread over** the planned life of the course or the planned number of cohorts: if a $240,000 recording is planned for 6 cohorts, each cohort carries $40,000.
**Decide** whether to include the salaries of in-house instructional designers and producers: without them, the course cost is understated, and the price is set below the real cost of production.
When the founder teaches the course, the costs don't disappear: the platform subscription, filming, and editing remain, and the founder's own time is counted at the rate you would have to pay a guest expert. **Without this, the course looks** almost free, and its price is set below its real cost.
716.example:
Course recording cost $240,000, planned for 6 cohorts: $40,000 per cohort
Mentor pay per cohort: $85,000
Student support: $18,000
Platform and video hosting: $9,000
Guest expert fee: $12,000

Course Costs = 40,000 + 85,000 + 18,000 + 9,000 + 12,000 = **$164,000**
716.importance: It determines the price and cohort size at which the course makes sense to run at all. Schools regularly count **only mentor pay** and forget to amortize the recording: as a result, the product looks profitable until it's time to reshoot outdated lessons.
716.synonyms: Course Delivery Costs, Cost of Delivery
716.essence_note: this is the cost of running the course, subtracted from its revenue

717.name: Course Starts
717.formula: Σ Students Who Opened the First Lesson
717.description: The number of students who started the course: paid for it and opened at least the first lesson. Counted by the cohort in which students started.
717.nuances:
Those who paid but never logged in to the platform **aren't counted** as starters: they belong to sales rather than to learning. Including them in the base understates all derived rates and hides an onboarding problem.
A student **counts once**, even if they bought the course twice or logged back in after a pause. The unit of count here is a person, not a payment.
Students transferred from the previous cohort **belong to their** original cohort: counting them again in the new cohort inflates the base and distorts the completion calculation for both cohorts.
717.example:
Paid for the course by the start of the February cohort: 268 people
Opened the first lesson: 240
Paid but never logged in: 28 (not counted)
Transferred from the January cohort: 15 (stay in January)

Course Starts = **240**
717.importance: The denominator of almost every rate in the course: **completion is calculated from it**, along with activity and mentor workload. The gap between this number and the number of payments is a diagnosis in itself: if one in ten buyers never logs in, money is being lost at a stage where nothing beyond an email with a link is needed.
717.essence_note: the more of those who paid actually start, the more of them will reach the end and come back

718.name: Course Completions
718.formula: Σ Students Who Met the Course Completion Criterion
718.description: The number of students who reached the end of the program and received confirmation of completion. Counted by cohort: a graduate belongs to the cohort in which they started.
718.nuances:
**The completion criterion is chosen** to fit the program and kept the same for all measurements: submitting the final project where there is one, going through the whole program where there's no final project. It must match the criterion in the Course Completion Rate: otherwise the rate and the count will be counting different people.
A graduate **belongs to the cohort they started in**, not to the month the certificate was issued. Otherwise the cohort report will include people from previous cohorts.
Students who reached the end after transferring to the next cohort **are counted in their** original cohort once: double counting inflates the result of both cohorts.
718.example:
Completion criterion for this course: final project submitted

February cohort: 240 starters
Submitted the final project: 106
Watched all the lessons but didn't submit the project: 34 (not counted under this criterion)
Transferred to the April cohort and finished there: 9 (counted in the February cohort)
January graduates who received their certificate in March: 88 (not part of the February cohort)

Course Completions = **106**
718.importance: The absolute number of graduates sets the scale of everything that happens after the course: reviews, case studies, and buyers of the next level all come from them. At the same time, a graduate isn't the same as a satisfied graduate: how many of them will leave a review and come back for a second course is shown by Course NPS and the Alumni Repeat Purchase Rate, while this number speaks **only to the size** of the pool they can come from. If the pool is small, the next launch will have to be built on promises rather than student stories.
718.essence_note: graduates leave reviews, become case studies, and buy the next course

719.name: Course Completion Rate
719.description: The share of students who reached the end of the program among those who started the course.
719.nuances:
The numerator and the denominator **are taken from the same** cohort: a student who finished is assigned to the period when they started, not when they finished. Otherwise graduates of past cohorts end up in the numerator, and the rate can exceed 100%.
Immature cohorts **aren't counted**: until a cohort has had the full program length plus a buffer for those who fall behind, the number will be understated. A fresh cohort is shown separately with a note that it hasn't matured yet, or not shown at all.
The completion criterion is chosen to fit the program and isn't changed afterward. Where there's a final project, completion usually means submitting it: the student has shown a result rather than **just gotten through the materials**. On courses without a final project, completion means going through the whole program. The softer the criterion, the higher the rate, so rates calculated under different criteria aren't compared with each other, and when the criterion changes, past cohorts are recalculated.
719.example:
Completion criterion for this course: final project submitted

Cohort started on February 1: 240 students
The program is designed for 12 weeks; the deadline passed on April 26
Submitted the final project: 106
Watched all the lessons but didn't submit the project: 34 (not counted under this criterion)
Graduated in April from the January cohort: 88 (assigned to January)

Course Completion Rate = 106 / 240 × 100 = **44%**

If the course counted going through the whole program as completion, those 34 would also be in the numerator, and the rate would be 58%. Same cohort, different criterion.
719.importance: **It shows** whether the program keeps students going to the end. The drop usually happens at a specific point in the course, and it shows where students get stuck: a sharp jump in difficulty, a long module without practice, a gap in mentor support. Finishing the course doesn't guarantee a result, while a student who doesn't finish certainly won't get one, so material that students never reach can safely be reworked.
719.not_needed: **Skip it for** courses with open-ended access and no fixed finish: there's no moment when a student can be declared finished, and the cohort never matures.
719.essence_note: a student who reaches the end leaves a review, becomes a case study, and buys the next level

720.name: Course NPS
720.description: How willing students are to recommend the course to friends, based on answers on a scale from 0 to 10. Promoters give 9–10 and detractors 0–6; scores of 7–8 count only toward the denominator.
720.nuances:
**The denominator includes all** responses received, including passives at 7–8. Excluding them inflates the result because it removes from the base people who don't recommend the course.
**Non-respondents aren't** counted: the survey describes the opinion of those who responded. The lower the response rate, the more the result leans toward people with strong opinions, so the response rate is shown next to the score.
The timing of the survey changes the number: right after the course ends, a student rates their impression of it; some time later, what it gave them, and these are different questions. The timing **is kept the same for** all measurements; otherwise the trend will show a change in timing rather than in graduates' attitude.
**The result falls in** the range from −100 to +100 and is written as a number without a percent sign: despite multiplying by 100 in the formula, it's an index rather than a share.
720.example:
Graduates surveyed: 106
Responded: 68
Scores of 9–10: 39
Scores of 7–8: 17
Scores of 0–6: 12

Course NPS = (39 − 12) / 68 × 100 = **+40**

Without the passives, it would come out to (39 − 12) / 51 × 100 = +53, inflated because part of the base was thrown out.
720.importance: **Word of mouth in** online education brings in students more cheaply than any advertising, and this number shows whether it will work. A negative value means there are more detractors than promoters: each new cohort will have to be filled with more expensive advertising, because graduates talk people out of the course instead of bringing them in.
720.not_needed: **Skip it for** cohorts of fewer than 30 students: with about ten responses, one unhappy student moves the index by tens of points, and random swings can't be told apart from real changes.
720.essence_note: graduates who recommend the course bring in students more cheaply than any advertising

721.name: Student Satisfaction Score
721.formula: Σ Satisfaction Scores / Number of Responses
721.description: The average score students give the course as a whole after completing it. Shows how much students liked the course once the program is finished.
721.nuances:
Unit of count: one rating by one student. The survey is run **once** at the end of the course, and if the same person answers again, the repeat response doesn't go into the base.
**Only those who responded are counted**: non-respondents don't go into the base, and with a low response rate the result leans toward those who have an opinion. The response rate is shown next to the score.
**Decide** whom to ask: only those who reached the end or everyone who started. A survey of graduates rates the course through the eyes of those it suited, and that score comes out higher. Dropouts respond less often, yet their answers are exactly what explains why they left.
**A single scale is fixed for** all measurements; otherwise you can't build trends across cohorts.
The timing of the survey **is fixed**: right after the course ends, a student rates their impression of it; some time later, what it gave them, and these are different questions.
**Ratings given during** the course aren't mixed in here: they belong to the Average Course Component Rating. Mixed into one number, element-level and end-of-course ratings answer no question at all.
721.example:
February cohort: 240 starters, 106 reached the end
Survey sent to all 240 after the program ended

Responded: 87
Sum of scores on a ten-point scale: 679

Student Satisfaction Score = 679 / 87 = **7.8** with a 36% response rate

Among those who reached the end, the average was 8.4: those who dropped out give lower scores, and judging by graduates alone, the course looks better than it is for the cohort as a whole.
721.importance: **The overall attitude toward the course**, which you rely on when deciding what to change for the next cohort and what to say on the landing page. This number sits next to Course NPS and explains it: a person may rate the course highly yet not recommend it to friends, and the gap between the two numbers shows that students enjoyed the course but didn't get enough of a result to recommend it.
721.not_needed: **Skip it** when no end-of-course survey is run or only a handful of students respond: with only a few ratings, the average depends on whoever happened to answer.
721.essence_note: a satisfied graduate comes back for the next course and doesn't ask for a refund

722.name: Assignment Completion Rate
722.description: The share of assignments students submitted out of all assignments available to them in the program. It's calculated over assignments rather than students: each student counts once for every assignment open to them.
722.nuances:
The denominator includes only assignments open to the student at the time of measurement. If the program is released week by week, assignments from future modules **are not included** in the base; otherwise the rate is artificially understated for students who are on schedule.
**An assignment counts as completed** once the work is submitted, not once a mentor accepts it. Review speed is tracked by the [[Feedback Turnaround Time→onlayn_obuchenie/vremya_proverki_zadaniya]] metric, and mixing the two counts the mentors' review speed against the student's result.
Optional assignments are either **excluded from the base** entirely or included for everyone: including them only partly shifts the number in a way that has nothing to do with student behavior.
722.example:
[[Students per Cohort→onlayn_obuchenie/studentov_na_potok]]: 80
Assignments open to each student: 12
Total available assignments: 960
Work submitted: 780
Of those, sent back for revision: 41 (counted as completed, since the work was submitted)

Assignment Completion Rate = 780 / 960 × 100 = **81%**
722.importance: It shows exactly which assignment students stop at: the drop is visible at a specific assignment rather than across the course **as a whole**. This gives grounds to rewrite the wording or split the assignment in two instead of guessing from the overall completion rate. The signal comes while the cohort is still running, when it's still possible to step in, rather than after it ends.
722.not_needed: **Skip it for** courses without required practical work: in a lecture format with no homework, both the numerator and the denominator are zero.
722.synonyms: Homework Completion Rate, Assignment Submission Rate
722.essence_note: practice is what the course was bought for, and the more assignments students submit, the closer they get to the result

723.name: Average Course Component Rating
723.formula: Σ Ratings Given / Number of Ratings
723.description: The average score students give to parts of the course as they go: lessons, modules, homework assignments. It's made up of all ratings across the program and shows the course part by part rather than as one impression at the end.
723.nuances:
Unit of count: one rating by one student of one course element. Over the whole program, one student contributes **as many ratings** as there are lessons and assignments they rated.
**A single scale is fixed for** all elements and all measurements: 4.2 on a five-point scale and 4.2 on a ten-point scale mean different things and can't be compared.
The average for the whole course is needed for trends across cohorts, but decisions come from the breakdown: the rating of each lesson and assignment **separately**. The overall number shows that something got worse; the breakdown shows what exactly to fix.
Ratings aren't collected equally across elements: a lesson at the start of the course is rated by many, the last module **only by those who got that far**. So the course average leans toward the beginning of the program, and it's worth comparing the same elements across cohorts.
**Only those who responded are counted**. The lower the response rate, the more the average is skewed: unhappy students are more likely to leave without responding.
**The average hides polarization**: 4.0 can come from straight 4s or from a mix of 5s and 2s. The distribution of ratings shows this; the average doesn't.
723.example:
Cohort: 240 students, 12 lessons and 12 assignments with ratings
Scale: five-point

Ratings collected for the course: 3,180
Sum of scores: 14,187

Average Course Component Rating = 14,187 / 3,180 = **4.46**

The breakdown by element shows what's behind the overall number: the ninth lesson got 3.1, while the rest stay above 4.4. That's the lesson to rework; the overall average alone wouldn't lead to this decision.
723.importance: **It shows the course part by part** while the cohort is still running: when the rating of a specific lesson or assignment drops, you see it early rather than in the final survey, when there's nothing left to fix. Outdated material, a disrupted live session, or unclear assignment wording surface here earlier than in refunds and completion rates.
723.not_needed: Skip it when ratings aren't collected during the course and the survey is run **only at the end**: then there's only end-of-course satisfaction, and element-level ratings don't exist.
723.essence_note: low ratings of lessons and assignments end in student drop-off and refunds

724.name: Course Cohorts
724.description: The number of course cohorts run during the period. One cohort is one group of students that started on a shared schedule.
724.nuances:
