A cohort **is assigned to the period** by its start date: a cohort that started in December and ended in March counts as a December cohort.
**Only cohorts that actually started are counted**: those announced and then canceled because too few students signed up don't count.
Two cohorts running in parallel on different schedules **count as two**, even if they share the material.
724.example:
Cohorts started in the year: 6
Of those, two ran in parallel in September: both counted
Announced and canceled because too few signed up: 1 (not counted)
Started in December, finished in March: counted in December

Course Cohorts = **6**
724.importance: **It sets the pace of all operations**: the number of cohorts determines how many times a year you need to budget for ads, hire mentors, and update materials. Starting too often leaves the previous cohort no time to wrap up and piles one cohort's reviews on top of another's; starting too rarely lets the audience cool off between launches.
724.not_needed: **Skip it with** continuous enrollment, when a student can start on any day: there are no groups starting on a schedule, and there's nothing to split into cohorts.
724.essence_note: each new cohort is sold using material that has already been recorded

725.name: Students per Cohort
725.description: How many students on average start the course in one cohort.
725.nuances:
**The numerator is [[Course Starts→onlayn_obuchenie/nachavshie_obuchenie]]**, not those who paid: otherwise the cohort average includes people who never made it to the platform.
The numerator and the denominator **are taken for the same** window, and cohorts are counted by start date. A cohort that started at the end of the period brings all its students with it, and you can't divide them by the number of cohorts from the previous window.
Cohorts canceled because too few students signed up **aren't included** in the denominator: including them understates the average and hides the real fill rate of the cohorts that did run.
725.example:
Course starts for the year: 1,380
Cohorts started: 6
Canceled because too few signed up: 1 (not in the denominator)

Students per Cohort = 1,380 / 6 = **230**
725.importance: **How full a cohort is determines** whether it covers its fixed costs: the expert's fee, the producer's work, and the amortization of the recording are split among everyone who enrolled. Below the break-even point, it's better not to launch the cohort and to move its students to the next cohort instead: this number gives grounds for that decision in advance.
725.not_needed: **Skip it with** continuous enrollment without groups: students start every day, and there are no cohorts as such.
725.essence_note: a cohort's fixed costs are split among everyone who enrolled, so the more students there are, the less each one costs

726.name: Course Completion Time
726.formula: Σ Time from Start to Completion for Students Who Finished / Number of Students Who Finished
726.description: How much calendar time passes on average from the start of the course to its completion for those who reached the end.
726.nuances:
**Only those who finished** go into the calculation: dropouts have no finish date, and the only way to include them is to make one up. That's exactly why the number is always more optimistic than reality: the students who would have taken the longest are the ones who most often just drop out and never make it into the base.
Immature cohorts skew the result downward: if you calculate for a cohort whose deadline hasn't passed yet, **only fast students** make it into the base. Wait until the whole cohort's term is over.
Pauses and access freezes are either **subtracted for everyone** or for no one: a selective approach makes the numbers for different cohorts incomparable.
726.example:
February cohort, deadline passed: 106 students finished
Total time from start to finish: 10,070 days
Of those, two froze their access for 30 days (freeze days are subtracted for everyone who froze)
The 134 students who dropped out aren't included

Course Completion Time = 10,070 / 106 = **95 days** compared with the stated 84
726.importance: **Missing the promised** timeline erodes trust faster than the course content does: a student planned for three months, and the course stretched to five. This number is used to decide whether to cut the program's scope and when to open enrollment for the next cohort so that mentors don't run two cohorts at once.
726.not_needed: **Skip it with** open-ended access and no deadlines: students keep returning to the course with no end date, and the average describes the spread of study habits rather than the program.
726.synonyms: Time to Complete, Time to Completion
726.essence_note: a stretched-out course diverges from the promised timeline, and one finished too fast means the program was skimmed without practice

727.name: Active Student Rate
727.description: The share of students who keep studying during the period among all who started the course. The course itself defines what counts as studying: an opened lesson, a submitted assignment, attendance at a live session. Shows what share of buyers actually use the course.
727.nuances:
**The activity criterion is chosen** to fit the course format and isn't changed afterward: an opened lesson where students learn from platform materials, a submitted assignment on courses with practice, attendance where there are live sessions. The stricter the criterion, the lower the rate, so it's tied to what moving forward means for the course: a student who opens lessons but doesn't submit work is active by one criterion and inactive by the other.
A single activity window **is fixed for** all measurements: with a weekly window, the rate will be lower than with a monthly one for the same students.
727.example:
Started the course: 240 students
Activity criterion for this course: at least one lesson opened in the month

Logged in and opened lessons: 156
Logged in but didn't open any materials: 18 (not counted)

Active Student Rate = 156 / 240 × 100 = **65%**

If the same course counted as active only those who submitted an assignment in the month, there would be 98 of them, and the rate would come out to 41%. The cohort is the same and only the criterion differs, so the two numbers can't be compared with each other.
727.importance: **It's the first to sag** when something is wrong with the course: the number drops before the fall in completion and the spike in refunds become visible. It's used to decide whom to follow up with through emails and mentor calls before the student drops out for good.
727.not_needed: **Skip it for** short two- to three-day intensive courses: all participants are active by definition there, and dropouts are visible right away from live session attendance.
727.synonyms: Student Engagement Rate, Active Learner Rate
727.essence_note: a student who keeps studying will reach the end and won't ask for a refund

728.name: Login Frequency
728.formula: Σ Platform Logins / Students with at Least One Session
728.description: How many times on average a student logs in to the platform over the period. It's calculated per student who logged in: the total number of logins is divided by the number of those students.
728.nuances:
A login **is a new session** after a break, not every page opened. Without a 30-minute inactivity threshold, a single study session in which the student moves between lessons will count as multiple logins.
**The denominator is the number of students** with at least one session, not everyone who started: dividing by everyone mixes frequency with the active student rate and gives a number that answers no question.
Logins from a phone and a computer at the same time aren't doubled: one student logging in from two devices back to back **counts as one session**.
728.example:
Students with at least one session in the month: 156
Sessions started: 1,092
Page views within sessions: 8,400 (not counted as logins)

Login Frequency = 1,092 / 156 = **7 times a month**
728.importance: **Regularity drives results more** than total time does: seven short visits do more than one long marathon at the end of a module. Falling frequency while time holds steady means students have switched to catch-up mode, and one missed deadline is all that separates them from dropping out.
728.not_needed: **Skip it** when learning happens off the platform: visits to get materials don't reflect real participation in the course.
728.essence_note: regular visits keep a student in the program better than occasional long ones

729.name: Time on Platform
729.formula: Σ Session Time on the Platform / Students with at Least One Session
729.description: How much time a student spends on the platform on average over the period. Calculated per student: the total time of all sessions is divided by the number of students who had at least one session.
729.nuances:
A session closes after an inactivity timeout; otherwise a forgotten open tab gets recorded as the student's study time. The threshold is set once for all measurements; when watching video, **playback itself counts** as activity.
The denominator **is the number of students** with at least one session, not everyone who started. Dividing by everyone gives a mix of average time and the active student rate, and the number no longer answers the question about time.
The mobile app and the web **are counted together**: counting them separately understates the result for those who watch lessons on their phone on the go.
729.example:
Students with at least one session in the month: 156
Total session time: 1,248 hours
Discarded due to the inactivity timeout: 214 hours

Time on Platform = 1,248 / 156 = **8 hours per student**
729.importance: **It shows** whether the course fits into a student's life. The stated workload in hours per week is on the landing page, and a gap between that and the actual time means the program is overloaded: first the deadlines slip, then students drop out. A sharp increase is also a signal: students get stuck where the material is unclear and rewatch the same thing.
729.not_needed: Skip it when most of the learning happens off the platform: live sessions on a third-party service, work in a chat, or offline practice leave no trace in the system, and the number describes **only viewing the lesson notes**.
729.essence_note: too little means the student isn't studying, and too much means the course is overloaded and the student is getting stuck

730.name: Live Session Attendance Rate
730.formula: (Σ Attendances / (Number of Live Sessions × Students in the Cohort)) × 100
730.description: The share of actual attendances at live sessions out of the number possible: how many students could have come and how many did. Unit of count: one student's attendance at one session.
730.nuances:
The denominator **is calculated as the number** of sessions multiplied by the number of students, not as the number of sessions. Dividing attendances by sessions alone gives the average number of attendees per session rather than a share, and the result easily exceeds 100%.
A student **counts as attending only if present longer than** a threshold the school sets itself and doesn't change afterward. A brief drop-in doesn't count; otherwise the number describes curiosity rather than participation. The threshold is chosen to fit the format: for a lecture, most of the session is appropriate; for a Q&A session, the segment the student came for is enough.
Watching the recording **doesn't count** as attendance: it's a separate behavior, and mixing it with live turnout hides real engagement in live sessions.
730.example:
Sessions in the cohort: 12
Students: 80
Possible attendances: 12 × 80 = 960
Present for more than half the session: 442
Joined for less than 15 minutes: 61 (not counted)
Watched recordings: 380 views (not counted)

Live Session Attendance Rate = 442 / 960 × 100 = **46%**
730.importance: **It answers the question** of whether live sessions are needed at all: with low turnout, the format is expensive and requires a fixed schedule while only a handful of students benefit from it. This number is used to decide whether to change session times, reduce their number, or switch the course to recordings with Q&A sessions.
730.not_needed: **Skip it for** fully pre-recorded courses: there are no live sessions, and the denominator is zero.
730.synonyms: Webinar Attendance Rate, Live Class Attendance Rate
730.essence_note: a live session is expensive and requires a fixed schedule, so the more students attend, the more the format is justified

731.name: First-Attempt Pass Rate
731.formula: (Assignments Accepted on the First Attempt / Reviewed Assignments) × 100
731.description: The share of assignments a mentor accepted after the first submission, out of all reviewed assignments. The unit of count is a specific student's assignment, not a student.
731.nuances:
The denominator includes only assignments whose review is complete. Work under review and work sent back for revision with no final verdict **are not included** in the base until a decision is made.
An attempt **is a submission of work** to the mentor, not saving a draft in the interface. For auto-graded tests, an attempt is a run with a recorded result.
Assignments without review (automatic credit for watching, optional exercises) **are excluded** from the base: they're credited immediately, and the question of attempts doesn't apply to them.
Work reviewed by a person and auto-graded tests are counted separately. For tests with unlimited attempts, the first-attempt rate shows which questions trip students up and what the theory lessons should explain better; for work reviewed by a mentor, it shows **whether the requirements match** the way the assignment is explained. Mixed into one number, they answer neither question.
731.example:
Submitted for review during the cohort: 780 assignments
Review completed: 720
Accepted right away: 497
Sent back for revision at least once: 223
Still under review: 60 (not counted)

First-Attempt Pass Rate = 497 / 720 × 100 = **69%**
731.importance: **The gap between the difficulty** of the material and the requirements for the work shows up right here. A low rate means either the grading asks for more than the assignment explains, or mentors nitpick: both multiply review rounds and the team's workload. A rate that's too high says the review is a formality and the feedback adds nothing.
731.not_needed: Skip it where the course rules allow only one attempt: there are no resubmissions, and the rate **matches the overall share** of assignments passed.
731.synonyms: First-Time Pass Rate, First-Submission Acceptance Rate
731.essence_note: a low rate means the grading asks for more than the assignment explains, and a rate that's too high means the review is a formality

732.name: Attempts per Assignment
732.formula: Σ Attempts on Assignments / Number of Assignments with a Completed Review
732.description: How many submissions it takes on average for an assignment to be accepted. The unit of count is a specific student's assignment, not an assignment in the program.
732.nuances:
The denominator includes **only assignments with** a completed review: work still awaiting review adds an unfinished attempt and understates the average.
An attempt **is a submission of work** to the mentor or a test run with a recorded result, not saving a draft.
Assignments with no limit on attempts are counted **separately** from those reviewed by a person: with unlimited attempts, the average is higher because of how the assignment works rather than the difficulty of the material. The number of attempts on a test is still useful on its own: it shows which questions trip up the cohort and what the theory lessons should explain better.
732.example:
Assignments with a completed review: 720
Submissions for them: 1,034
Accepted on the first attempt: 497
One assignment was submitted 6 times

Attempts per Assignment = 1,034 / 720 = **1.44**
732.importance: **Every extra attempt** is a separate review paid for with a mentor's time. So a growing average increases the team's workload with the same students and without any growth in sales: planning mentor staffing by the number of students without looking at this number means regularly coming up short on people. It also points to assignments where the requirements for the work diverge from how the assignment is explained.
732.not_needed: **Skip it where** the course rules allow one attempt: the result always equals one.
732.essence_note: every extra attempt is one more review paid for with a mentor's time

733.name: Feedback Turnaround Time
733.formula: Σ Time from Submission to Review Decision / Number of Reviews
733.description: How much time passes on average between a student submitting work and the mentor's decision on it. The unit of count is one review, so a resubmission after revision adds another one.
733.nuances:
Time **is counted in calendar hours**, from submission to decision. You can subtract weekends and nights, but then the number no longer reflects the student's wait: the student's wait runs on calendar time, not on the mentors' schedule.
**Open reviews aren't** included in the calculation: they don't have a decision yet, and therefore no final waiting time. While work is pending, its wait keeps growing but doesn't get into the average, so the number based on closed reviews is lower than students' actual wait. The number of submissions still awaiting a decision and the longest wait among them are shown alongside.
**The average hides the tail**: work that sat for a long time gets lost among the fast reviews. The median and the share of reviews that went past the time promised to students show the situation more honestly.
733.example:
Reviews completed in the month: 720
Total wait time for a decision: 18,000 hours
Submissions waiting for a decision for over a week: 23 (not included)

Feedback Turnaround Time = 18,000 / 720 = **25 hours**

A resubmission after revision adds another review with its own wait time.
733.importance: It shows whether the school delivers what it promised in the offer: the review time is usually stated when the course is sold, and students notice any gap right away. Where the next step is locked until the mentor's decision, the wait stops learning **entirely**; where it isn't, feedback arrives on work the student has already forgotten about and loses its point. This number is used to decide whether to hire more mentors or change the promise to one that can be kept.
733.not_needed: **Skip it with** fully automatic grading: the result comes instantly, and there's nothing to measure.
733.essence_note: while work waits for a decision, the student is stuck and loses momentum

734.name: Students per Mentor
734.description: How many students there are per mentor. Shows the actual workload of those running the cohort.
734.nuances:
**The numerator is [[Course Starts→onlayn_obuchenie/nachavshie_obuchenie]]**, not everyone who paid: a student who never logged in to the platform creates no workload and inflates the mentor's estimated load.
Mentors **are counted in FTEs**, not headcount: five half-time mentors make 2.5 FTEs, and without the conversion the workload looks half as high.
**It's calculated as of** the cohort start: by the finish, fewer students are still active, and a calculation based on them shows a workload that didn't exist at the peak of reviews.
734.example:
Course starts: 240
Mentors in FTEs: 8.5
Paid but never logged in: 28 (not included)

Students per Mentor = 240 / 8.5 = **28 students**
734.importance: **It determines** whether the team can handle the enrolled cohort. Going over the workload target immediately drags out review time, followed by student drop-off and refunds: saving on mentors comes back as spending under another line item. This number is used to calculate how many seats can be sold for the next cohort.
734.not_needed: **Skip it for** courses without mentor support: there are no mentors and nothing to divide by.
734.essence_note: overload drags out reviews and drives students away, and a light load means a mentor is paid but has little work

735.name: Mentors
735.description: The number of people who review work and guide students in a cohort.
735.nuances:
**Mentors are counted** if they worked during the period, not if they're listed in the database: those who didn't pick up a single assignment have no workload and aren't counted.
**With part-time work, count** in FTEs rather than headcount: four mentors each working a quarter of a full-time load make one FTE, and without this conversion the workload per mentor looks four times lower than it really is.
A course author who answers questions in the chat **isn't counted** as a mentor if they don't review work.
735.example:
Listed in the mentor database: 14
Reviewed work in the cohort: 11
Of those, six full-time and five half-time

Mentors = 6 + 5 × 0.5 = **8.5 FTEs**
735.importance: **The main recurring cost** item in every cohort and, at the same time, the limit on cohort size. If you enroll more students than the mentors can handle, reviews will drag out, refunds will pour in, and completion will fall: sales will hit a ceiling set by the reviewers rather than by demand.
735.not_needed: **Skip it for** pre-recorded courses without mentor support: no one reviews work, and the number is always zero.
735.essence_note: with too few mentors, reviews drag out and refunds pour in; with too many, they eat up the cohort's profit

736.name: Refund Requests
736.description: The number of requests for a course refund submitted during the period, regardless of the decision on them.
736.nuances:
A request **is assigned to the date** it was submitted, not the date of the decision: the metric describes the flow of requests in the period.
A repeat request from the same student about the same purchase **counts as one request**: otherwise one person's persistence looks like a spike in dissatisfaction.
Support questions about refund terms **don't count** as requests until a formal request is submitted: questions about the terms outnumber the requests themselves, and counting them inflates the metric.
736.example:
Refund requests submitted in April: 46
Of those, with repeat contacts about the same purchase: 7 (each counted once)
Support questions about refund terms: 63 (not counted)
Decisions made in May on 12 requests submitted in April (they stay in April)

Refund Requests = **46**
736.importance: **The signal comes before the money**: requests pile up before refunds show up in revenue. A spike right after launch points to a gap between the promise and the product; a spike in the middle of the cohort, to problems with mentors or the pace of the program.
736.not_needed: **Skip it in** free and corporate programs: there was no payment, and refund requests don't come up.
736.essence_note: every request is money that may go back out

737.name: Refund Rate
737.description: The share of sales for which the money was returned to the student, out of all sales in the period. Shows what share of payments the school didn't keep.
737.nuances:
A refund **is assigned to the period** of the original sale, not to the date the money was returned. Otherwise one number mixes payments from different months, and the rate is distorted in either direction.
**Refunds for recent periods are undercounted**: students have time to cancel, and some refunds on recent sales haven't been requested yet. The latest month's figure keeps growing after the month ends.
Partial refunds (part of the amount returned for unused modules) **count as one** refund if the metric counts refunds rather than dollars. To look at the money, calculate a separate metric based on refund amounts.
**Read the rate together** with the number of refunds: in a small cohort a couple of cases move the percentage by several points. You can't compare cohorts of different sizes by the rate alone.
737.example:
Sales in March: 420
Of those, refunded: 29
Refunds in March on February sales: 11 (assigned to February)

Refund Rate = 29 / 420 × 100 = **6.9%**
737.importance: It directly cuts revenue and shows the gap between the promise in the ads and the course content. A jump after a change to the offer or landing page means sales grew thanks to people the course didn't suit. **Without this number, gross** sales look healthy right up until the money goes back out.
737.not_needed: **Skip it in** free and corporate programs where students don't pay themselves: there's nothing to refund.
737.essence_note: a refund takes back money already received, while the costs of acquisition and teaching remain

738.name: Refund Approval Rate
738.description: The share of refund requests decided in the student's favor out of all requests submitted during the period. Shows how often the company agrees to return the money.
738.nuances:
A request **is assigned to the period** in which it was submitted, and the decision is attributed to that same period. Counting by decision date mixes different batches of requests in one number.
Requests still in progress, with no decision yet, **are excluded from the denominator until** they're closed. While they sit in the database as not approved, the rate is understated.
Mandatory refunds (canceling within a set period after payment if the student hasn't started the course) are approved automatically and are usually **counted separately from** disputed cases: mixing them into one number hides the real approval rate for the decisions the company actually makes.
738.example:
Requests in April: 46
Approved: 34
Denied: 8
Under review: 4 (excluded from the base)

Refund Approval Rate = 34 / (34 + 8) × 100 = **81%**
738.importance:
**A metric to monitor** rather than a target: it has no correct value, since the level is up to the company. The point is to analyze changes, so it's tracked over time and across courses and cohorts: if it rose in a specific cohort, something happened there with the product or with the promise in the ads.
**Read it** together with the number of requests: with only a few requests, a single case moves the rate by tens of percentage points, and 100% may mean one approved request.
738.not_needed: **Skip it where** no real decision is made on requests: either a refund is approved automatically whenever it's requested, or it's never given except where mandatory. In both cases the rate sits at an extreme and describes the rule rather than how requests are handled.
738.essence_note: approving everything makes payment optional, and denying everything brings public complaints and chargebacks

739.name: Course Revenue
739.alt_formula: Number of Sales × Average Course Price (excluding the school's own installment plans)
739.description: The amount of money received from selling courses over the period.
739.nuances:
Refunded payments **are subtracted from the revenue** of the period in which the sale took place, not the one in which the money was returned.
Installments through a bank or a buy now, pay later service are recognized immediately and in full: the school receives the entire amount from the bank at the time of purchase, and it's the student who then pays the bank in installments. Revenue from the school's own installment plan, where the student pays the school directly, is recognized as payments come in: otherwise the month's revenue includes money that hasn't arrived yet and **doesn't match the cash received**.
Payment processing fees and affiliate commissions **are not subtracted** from revenue: they're expenses, and they belong in costs.
739.example:
Payments received in March: $627,350
Refunds on March sales: $41,800
Balance still due on the school's own installment plans: $189,000 (not recognized in March; the money hasn't arrived yet)

Course Revenue = 627,350 − 41,800 = **$585,550**

Purchases on bank installment plans are already included in this amount in full: the bank transferred the entire amount at once.
739.importance: The top line of the school's finances: **profit is calculated from it**, along with ad payback and the ceiling on mentor costs. An error in how it's calculated flows into every derived number, and the decision to launch the next cohort gets made on bad data.
739.essence_note: this is all the money received for courses

740.name: Average Course Price
740.formula: Total Value of Courses Sold / Number of Sales
740.description: How much one buyer pays for a course on average. It's calculated per sale: the total value of courses sold is divided by the number of sales.
740.nuances:
A sale on an installment plan **counts once**, at the time of purchase, not for each payment: counting by payments multiplies the number of sales by the number of installments and drags the average price down. A sale on the school's own installment plan is included **at the full amount** in the period of sale, not as payments come in: otherwise it counts in full in the denominator but only partly in the numerator, and the price is understated.
**Refunded sales are removed** from the numerator and the denominator at the same time: subtracting the money while leaving the sale in the count understates the price.
Sales with promo codes and presales **are included** at the amount actually paid, not the list price: otherwise the metric shows the intended price rather than the money paid.
740.example:
Payments received for courses sold: $585,550
Not yet received on the school's own installment plans: $189,000 (added)
Total value of courses sold = 585,550 + 189,000 = $774,550
Courses paid for: 391
Refunded: 29 sales (removed from both the total and the count)
Of the courses sold, 118 were bought with a promo code for 30% off (counted at the amount actually paid)

Average Course Price = 774,550 / 391 = **$1,981**

Revenue alone would give 585,550 / 391 = $1,498: sales on the school's installment plans are in the denominator in full but only partly in the numerator.
740.importance: It shows what's happening with discounts: a falling average price with rising sales means volume is being bought with lower prices rather than driven by demand. This amount is **the basis for the allowable cost** of acquiring a student, and when it drops, advertising that used to pay off starts losing money right away.
740.not_needed: **Skip it when** there's a single course with one fixed price and no discounts or installments: the average always equals the list price.
740.synonyms: Average Selling Price, Average Sale Value
740.essence_note: with the same number of sales, a higher average price directly means more money

741.name: Alumni Repeat Purchase Rate
741.description: The share of graduates who bought another course after completing their studies, out of all graduates. Counted by person: several purchases by one student count as one unit in the numerator.
741.nuances:
A graduate **is assigned to a cohort** by completion date, and a repeat purchase is counted within a fixed window after it, for example 6 or 12 months. Without a common window, recent graduates will always look worse than earlier ones simply because they've had less time for a second purchase.
An upgrade within the same course (switching to a plan with personal feedback) **doesn't count** as a repeat purchase: it's an extra payment for the current course rather than a new sale.
**The numerator is limited to those** in the denominator: a purchase by someone who didn't finish the course isn't counted.
741.example:
Graduated in the first quarter: 310 students
Observation window: 12 months after graduation
Bought another course during that time: 74 people
Of those, bought two courses: 12 (counted as 12 people, not 24)
Paid extra for the upgraded plan of their current course: 19 (not counted)

Alumni Repeat Purchase Rate = 74 / 310 × 100 = **23.9%**
741.importance: **It answers the question** of whether the school has a product line or has to buy every new cohort with advertising from scratch. The higher the number, the more you can pay for a first-time student: the cost of acquiring them is recovered through a chain of purchases rather than a single payment. A low value with good completion means the next level simply doesn't exist or students aren't told about it.
741.not_needed: Skip it for schools with a single course: there's nothing to buy again, and a low percentage speaks **only to the lack** of a product line.
741.synonyms: Alumni Repurchase Rate, Graduate Repeat Purchase Rate
741.essence_note: a repeat purchase is revenue without acquisition costs

742.name: Course Profit
742.description: How much money the school keeps after subtracting the costs of acquiring students and running the course.
742.nuances:
All three figures **are taken for the same** period and on the same recognition basis: if revenue is recognized as payments come in, costs are also assigned to the period in which they were actually incurred, not to the date the invoice was paid.
Course production **is charged to costs** in allocated shares rather than all at once in the period when the course was filmed: otherwise the first cohort shows a loss and the following ones an inflated profit.
**Refunds are subtracted from** the revenue of the period in which the sale took place, not the period of the refund.
Administrative costs that aren't directly tied to courses **are not included**: with them, you'd get the operating profit of the whole company rather than the course's result.
742.example:
Course Revenue: $585,550
[[Course Costs→onlayn_obuchenie/zatraty_na_obuchenie]]: $164,000
[[Marketing Spend→onlayn_obuchenie/zatraty_na_marketing]]: $200,700

Course Profit = 585,550 − 164,000 − 200,700 = **$220,850**

If the entire course recording ($240,000) were written off in this period instead of $40,000, profit would drop to $20,850, even though nothing in the cohort's economics changed.
742.importance: **The only number** that tells you whether launching the cohort was worth it. Revenue grows along with the ad budget, and without subtracting costs, higher sales can easily mean a bigger loss. It's used to decide whether to raise the price, cut back on mentoring, or discontinue the line of courses.
742.not_needed: **Skip it for** free programs run to build an audience or to recruit employees: there's no revenue, and the result is judged by something other than money.
742.essence_note: this is what the school keeps after the costs of acquiring students and running the course

743.name: Marketing Spend
743.description: Total spending on acquiring students over the period: advertising, work with influencers, affiliate payouts, and marketing team salaries.
743.nuances:
Costs **are assigned to the period** in which the ads ran, not to the invoice payment date. A quarterly prepayment assigned entirely to the month of payment distorts the payback of all three months.
Affiliate fees and commissions for referred students **belong here** rather than being subtracted from revenue.
**Decide** whether to include your own team's salaries and contractor fees: with them, the number shows the full cost of acquisition; without them, only the ad budgets. Stick with that choice; otherwise payback can't be compared across periods.
743.example:
Ad account spend for March: $96,000
Influencer placements: $46,500
Affiliate payouts for referred students: $22,200
Marketing salaries: $33,000
Annual analytics subscription paid in March: $36,000 ($3,000 assigned to March)

Marketing Spend = 96,000 + 46,500 + 22,200 + 33,000 + 3,000 = **$200,700**
743.importance: **Without this amount, you can't** tell whether the school earns money on the cohort or pays extra for every student. Understating it by leaving out salaries and affiliate payouts makes acquisition look like it pays off: ad buying gets scaled on that basis, and the school loses money at a larger scale.
743.not_needed: Skip it if students come **only from your own** organic audience and nothing is spent on acquisition.
743.essence_note: every dollar spent on acquisition comes out of the cohort's profit

744.name: Return Experience Satisfaction Score
744.formula: Sum of Scores / Number of Responses
744.description: The average score customers give the product return process after it's complete.
744.nuances:
**Count only completed** returns: a rating in the middle of the process reflects the wait rather than the result.
The calculation includes **only the responses received**. The lower the response rate, the more the result leans toward people who had a reason to speak up, so the response rate is shown next to the score.
The scale **is fixed and doesn't** change between periods: switching from a five-point to a ten-point scale doubles the score even though nothing in the process changed.
744.example:
Returns completed in the month: 640
Rated: 190
Sum of scores on a five-point scale: 741

Average score = 741 / 190 = **3.9**
744.importance: **A return is usually the last** interaction a customer has with the company, and this score is used to decide whether to invest in simplifying the procedure. A low score with a normal support CSAT means the problem lies in refund times or packaging requirements, outside the agents' work.
744.not_needed: **Skip it in** services and subscriptions, where there are no product returns.
744.essence_note: a customer happy with the return comes back for the next purchase

745.name: Post-Return Purchase Rate
745.formula: (Customers Who Bought After a Return / All Customers with Returns) × 100
745.description: The share of customers who placed a new order after returning a product. Shows whether the company keeps a customer after an unsuccessful purchase.
745.nuances:
**An observation window is set** after the return, and it must be the same for all customers in the calculation. A customer who returned a product last week can't be compared with one whose return was six months ago: the second had more time to come back.
**Exchanges and** refunds are kept apart: with an exchange, the customer actually keeps the purchase, and counting it as a new purchase inflates the metric.
The denominator **counts unique** customers, not returns: a customer with three returns in the period counts once.
745.example:
Customers who made a return in January: 640
Of those, bought again within 90 days: 179
Chose an exchange instead of a return: 85 (not in the denominator)

Post-Return Purchase Rate = 179 / 640 × 100 = **28%**
745.importance: **It determines** how much money it makes sense to put into making returns easier. If a meaningful share of customers come back after a return, free return shipping pays off; if almost none do, the return marks the end of the customer relationship, and what needs fixing is the product description rather than logistics.
745.not_needed: **Skip it in** services and subscriptions, where there are no product returns.
745.synonyms: Post-Return Repurchase Rate, Post-Return Retention Rate
745.essence_note: a customer who comes back after a return stayed with the company when they could have left for good

919.name: Average Subscription Price
919.formula: Sum of Monthly List Prices of Paying Customers' Subscriptions on a Date / [[Paying Customers→vyruchka/platyaschie_polzovateli]] on the Same Date
919.description: The average price at which a subscription was bought, before discounts and promotions.
919.nuances:
It's calculated **as a weighted average across customers** rather than across the price list: with plans at $30, $42 and $60, the simple average of the price list is always $44, while the weighted average price drops toward $30 when almost everyone is on the cheapest plan.
In B2B, the paying unit is **the company account** rather than its employees: the account has one subscription. With per-seat pricing, its list price equals the seat price multiplied by the number of paid seats. Modules and add-ons billed monthly are included at their list prices.
**The list price** is used rather than the actual payment: the gap between this price and the Average Revenue per Account (ARPA) is exactly the total of discounts and promotions, including the annual billing discount. Prices are taken **excluding taxes**, like revenue per account: with tax included, the tax ends up in the gap and reads as a discount.
For customers who stayed on old prices, **their plan's price** is used rather than the current price list: otherwise a price increase for new customers is recorded as a discount for existing ones, and the subscription price rises the same day even though nobody started paying more. For an account without a public price, use the internal price list that the contract discount is calculated from.
Annual subscriptions are taken **at the monthly list price of the same plan**: the annual billing discount stays a discount and goes into the Effective Discount Rate. Otherwise it hides in the price, and the price after the discount stops matching revenue per account. A plan sold only annually is taken at its annual list price divided by twelve.
The price after the Effective Discount Rate is applied equals revenue per account only if the discount is calculated for the same subscriptions on the same date: 1 − MRR / sum of monthly list prices.
919.example:
Paying accounts on March 31, list prices excluding taxes:
Basic plan, $30: 2,000 accounts
Pro plan, $42: 2,000 accounts, of which 500 on annual billing at $420 a year
Team plan, $60: 2,000 accounts

Average Subscription Price = 264,000 / 6,000 = **$44**

Annual Pro accounts are counted at the monthly list price of $42. Taking their payment, 420 / 12 = $35, gives $43.42: the annual billing discount hides in the price.
Revenue per account is $40: the $4 difference goes to discounts and promotions, of which $0.58 is the annual billing discount.
919.importance: When revenue per account falls, the question is always the same: did the subscription get cheaper at list prices, or did discounts grow? This metric answers the first part, and a subscription can get cheaper without any new prices: new customers choose entry-level plans, customers on higher-tier plans leave, and existing ones move to cheaper plans. The answer determines what to do: revise the price list and steer customers to higher-tier plans, or cut discounts.
919.not_needed: Skip it where there's **a single plan** and no discounts: the price matches revenue per account. Also skip it where each contract's price is negotiated separately and there's no price list: there's no reference price to split revenue into price and discount.
919.essence_note: the more a subscription sells for, the more revenue from the same number of customers

920.name: Lead-to-Close Rate
920.description: What share of incoming leads resulted in a won deal. The end-to-end conversion rate of the whole funnel: it includes both losses at qualification and losses while pursuing qualified leads.
920.nuances:
The cohort is defined by **the lead's arrival date**, as in [[B2B Leads→vyruchka/lidy]]: check how many of the month's leads converted to a won deal ([[Deals Won→vyruchka/sdelki]]), even if the deal closed months later.
It combines **two different failures**: leads screened out at qualification and qualified leads lost later in the funnel. The overall number doesn't tell them apart, so when it drops, look at each one separately.
A recent period is **always undercounted**: leads from the last few weeks are still being worked, and they have no deals yet. The final rate is calculated after a **counting window** comparable in length to the sales cycle: it's measured from each lead's arrival and is the same for all funnel steps; otherwise the product of the step conversion rates won't match the end-to-end rate.
The numerator includes leads with **at least one won** deal: a second deal from the same lead doesn't change the number; otherwise the result could exceed 100%. Lost and open deals aren't included.
The rate counts leads rather than deals: if one lead can produce several deals, leads × rate gives fewer deals than there actually are.
920.example:
B2B leads in March: 340
Of those, converted to a won deal by the end of the counting window: 17

Lead-to-Close Rate = 17 / 340 × 100 = **5%**
920.importance: It lets you plan backward: work out how many leads the deal quota requires and compare that with how many marketing actually brings in. A gap means **the quota can't be met on the math alone**, however well the team works. It's also the basis for the acceptable cost per lead: above that limit, acquisition doesn't pay off.
920.essence_note: the more often an inquiry turns into a deal, the fewer leads you need to buy for the same revenue

926.name: Units per Order
926.description: How many physical units of goods the customer keeps per paid order on average. Every unit counts, however many different products are in the order: two T-shirts and a cap are three units. Goods sold by the piece are measured in units, goods sold by weight in pounds.
926.nuances:
Units and line items **are different quantities**: three identical T-shirts are three units but one line item, which is what [[Line Items per Order→assortiment/srednee_kolichestvo_tovarov_v_zakaze]] counts.
Goods sold by the piece and by weight are counted **separately**: adding them up gives a number that describes no order.
The numerator includes only units **from paid orders**: sales are counted across all channels, including store registers, but not every channel creates an order.
The numerator and denominator are adjusted for returns **differently**: returned units are subtracted from the numerator, and only fully returned orders are removed from the denominator.
Bundles and multipacks are counted by **one rule across all periods**: a six-can pack under one SKU is one unit; six loose cans are six.
An item at zero price in a promotion **counts as a unit**, while shipping and packaging lines aren't included: they aren't goods.
926.example:
Paid orders in March: 4,800
Units of goods in these orders: 12,000

Units per order = 12,000 / 4,800 = **2.5 units**

Units Sold for the same March is 12,400: the difference went through store registers, where no order is created. Using the full Units Sold figure gives 2.58 units per order: a number about a different population.
926.importance: **The second half** of [[Average Order Value (AOV)→zakazy/sredniy_chek_aov]]: until this second factor is calculated, every movement in order value gets attributed to price. It shows whether “three for the price of two,” a discount on the second unit and in-cart recommendations work. A bundle or multipack under one SKU won't help here: it raises order value but **counts as one unit** and pulls the metric down. If units grew while order value stayed the same, **basket depth was bought with discounts**: each extra unit added picking and shipping work without adding revenue.
926.not_needed: Skip it where an order **almost always has one unit**: furniture, major appliances, jewelry, sets sold under one SKU. Brick-and-mortar retail has no orders, and basket depth there is measured by [[Units per Transaction (UPT)→riteyl/kolichestvo_edinic_tovara_v_cheke]].
926.synonyms: Average Units per Order, Basket Size
926.essence_note: at an unchanged unit price, each extra unit in an order raises order value

927.name: Units per Line Item
927.formula: (Units in Paid Orders − Units Returned from Them) / Product Lines in the Same Orders Excluding Lines Returned in Full
927.description: The average number of units the customer kept per order line: two identical T-shirts are one line and two units. The value starts at one and grows when customers buy several units of the same product at a time.
927.nuances:
The denominator is lines rather than orders: [[Line Items per Order→assortiment/srednee_kolichestvo_tovarov_v_zakaze]] divides by orders and measures **basket breadth**, while this metric divides by lines and measures **line depth**. The product of the two gives [[Units per Order→assortiment/srednee_kolichestvo_edinic_v_zakaze]] for goods sold by the piece, and neither breadth nor depth is visible in it separately anymore.
An order line is an SKU: two sizes of one model make two lines, as in Line Items per Order. Lines of one SKU in an order **count as one line**: the register and the accounting system often split an SKU into separate lines, one per unit-level tracking code, or by price in a “buy one, get one” promotion, including a zero-price line. Without this, depth stays stuck at 1.0, and a successful “buy two” promotion shows up as basket breadth.
The numerator and the denominator are taken **from the same orders**: units are counted within the same paid orders whose lines are in the denominator. [[Units Sold→assortiment/kolichestvo_prodannyh_edinic]] doesn't work as the numerator: **some sales didn't go through orders**, and they have no order lines.
**Goods sold by weight** are removed from both parts: pounds per line and units per line are different quantities, and an average that mixes them describes neither kind of line. A fractional quantity in a line means goods sold by weight got into the calculation: in online grocery, they're ordered by the piece, but the receipt shows them in pounds.
**Returned units** are subtracted from the numerator: units the customer kept are counted. A line returned in full is removed from both parts, and an order returned in full is removed with all its lines: the orders are the same as in [[Average Order Value (AOV)→zakazy/sredniy_chek_aov]]. A return entered in the order as a separate negative line **isn't counted as a line**: otherwise, the denominator grows by a line the customer never bought, and its units are subtracted from the numerator twice.
**A bundle under one SKU** is one unit: six cans in a multipack give 1 per line, while the same six cans bought individually give 6. Moving best-sellers to multipacks lowers the metric even though the customer takes home just as much; when a marketplace sells a multipack as a separate listing, the same purchase gives a line with one unit rather than six.
**Shipping, packaging and service fee lines** are removed from both parts: there's no product in them, and each such line adds exactly one unit and pulls the result toward 1.0.
Bulk purchases by businesses and resellers shift the monthly average: one order for 500 units of one product raises 1.39 to 1.45. They're excluded using a units-per-line threshold that's the same in all periods.
An order **is assigned to the period by its order date**, as in Line Items per Order, even though only paid orders go into the calculation. The monthly number is final after the return window closes: if one of two identical units is returned, depth goes down; if a one-unit line is returned in full, it goes up.
927.example:
Lines in orders for the month (unique products), excluding lines returned in full: 8,640
Units in these lines minus returned units: 12,000
Partially returned from these lines: 300 units (not counted)
Paid orders, excluding orders returned in full: 4,800
No goods sold by weight and no service lines in this month's calculation

Units per Line Item = 12,000 / 8,640 = **1.39 units**

Units per order: 12,000 / 4,800 = 2.5; the same by multiplication: 1.8 line items × 1.39 = 2.5

Without subtracting returned units, it comes to 12,300 / 8,640 = 1.42: units the customer returned get into line depth.
Taking the units-sold counter, 12,400 units, as the numerator gives 1.44: in the example, the 400-unit difference is sales outside orders. With real data, a date shift adds to the gap: the counter assigns a unit to the sale date, while here it goes by order date.
927.importance: [[Average Order Value (AOV)→zakazy/sredniy_chek_aov]] breaks down into three factors: how many different products are in the order, how many units of each, and the price per unit. This metric is the second factor, and it has its own levers: multipacks, a discount on the second unit, larger pack sizes, a quantity threshold in a promotion. [[Line Items per Order→assortiment/srednee_kolichestvo_tovarov_v_zakaze]] counts items and **doesn't see the difference between one cap and two identical ones**, yet that difference shows up in revenue. When order value grows while line depth stays flat, “buy two” **brought no noticeable lift** across the store, and the growth came from price or from new items in the cart; whether the promotion itself worked shows in line depth for its products.
927.not_needed: Skip it where an item **is inherently bought one at a time**: furniture, major appliances, jewelry. A value stuck at 1.0–1.1 that doesn't move after second-unit promotions isn't a lever: line depth is set by the nature of the product rather than by merchandising. Where sales happen without an order, there are no order lines at all, and purchase depth is calculated from receipts. Also skip it for marketplace data: the seller sees shipments rather than the customer's cart, and on some marketplaces each unit ships as a separate order.
927.synonyms: Units per Line, Average Line Quantity
927.essence_note: at the same unit price, every extra unit in a line raises order value, with no need to find a new product for it

928.name: Average List Price
928.formula: Value of Units Sold at Pre-Discount Prices / [[Units Sold→assortiment/kolichestvo_prodannyh_edinic]]
928.description: The average catalog price of one unit sold, before promo codes, promotions, coupons and points. It changes for two reasons: the store changed its prices, or customers started buying more expensive products.
928.nuances:
The pre-discount price is **the unit's price in the store's catalog** at the time of the order or the in-store sale. It's taken from the order line or the price history: using the current catalog price instead of the price on the order date rewrites past months with every repricing. The manufacturer's suggested retail price (MSRP) isn't used here: the store sells above or below it, and an average based on it describes someone else's price list. A unit sold on a marketplace has its own pre-discount price, from the seller's price list on that marketplace.
In a sale, the crossed-out price counts as the pre-discount price **if the product sold at it before the promotion** for at least 30 days, and the difference from the sale price goes into the discount. An end-of-season markdown of leftover stock also remains a discount from the previous price: the product sold at that price all season. Only a price revision after which the product keeps selling at its regular price sets a new pre-discount price; a crossed-out price at which nobody bought doesn't: otherwise, the metric describes the storefront, and the discount is overstated.
Goods sold by weight are counted **the same way as in the denominator**: separately per pound, or in units through a fixed pack size. The value of goods sold by the pound divided by a unit count overstates the unit price.
Returned units **aren't included in either part**: they're already out of the denominator, and they're removed from the numerator at the same pre-discount price. [[Gross Merchandise Value (GMV)→assortiment/valovyy_oborot_gmv]] doesn't work as the numerator: returned units remain in it. The monthly number is final after the return window closes: until then, both parts include units that will still be returned, and if expensive items are returned, the average goes down.
**The price excludes taxes**, as revenue does: where the displayed price includes tax, not deducting it overstates the average price by the tax rate.
A bundle under one SKU **is one unit at the bundle price**, as in [[Units per Order→assortiment/srednee_kolichestvo_edinic_v_zakaze]]: six cans in a multipack make one unit, or six if bought individually, and moving best-sellers to multipacks raises the average price without a single new price tag.
[[Units Sold→assortiment/kolichestvo_prodannyh_edinic]] also includes units sold without an order, in physical stores and on marketplaces. Each channel has its own price list and its own product mix, and a shift in their shares moves the average even though the order basket is unchanged. Multiplying it by the other AOV factors gives the AOV of orders only when it's calculated on units from the same orders.
928.example:
Units sold in the month, excluding returns: 12,000
Their value at pre-discount catalog prices, excluding taxes: $252,000
Returned: 400 units, $8,400 at pre-discount prices (not counted)

Average List Price = 252,000 / 12,000 = **$21.00**

Taking GMV, $260,400, as the numerator gives 260,400 / 12,000 = $21.70: returned units remain in GMV but are no longer in the denominator.
928.importance: When AOV dips, it shows whether the items going into the cart got cheaper, or the price list held and discounts grew: the answer tells you whether to work on assortment and prices or on promotions. A shift of purchases toward expensive models raises it without a single new price tag: growth with an unchanged price list means customers are choosing pricier items. Seasonality and promotions on cheap items, which pull unit sales toward them, also move it.
928.not_needed: Skip it when products always sell at list price, without promotions, promo codes or points: the metric matches the [[Average Selling Price (ASP)→assortiment/srednyaya_cena_tovara]].
928.synonyms: Average Regular Price, Average Full Price
928.essence_note: at the same discount, a more expensive unit brings in more money

929.name: Effective Discount Rate
929.formula: (1 − Revenue After Discounts / Value of the Same Sales at Pre-Discount Prices) × 100
929.description: The share of the full price of everything sold that customers didn't pay because of discounts: promo codes, promotions, coupons, points, an annual-billing discount on a subscription. Sales without a discount are also included, so the metric shows the discount across everything sold rather than the depth of individual promotions.
929.nuances:
The pre-discount price is the same one used in the Average List Price: **the catalog price at the time of the order**. A crossed-out price at which nothing sold doesn't count as the pre-discount price: otherwise, a markdown from a price nobody paid counts as a discount.
**Anything counts as a discount** if it lowered the selling price relative to the pre-discount price: promo codes, promotions, coupons, individual prices, points redeemed as payment, an annual-billing discount on a subscription. A product given away free in a “buy one, get one” promotion is included in the pre-discount value at its full price and counts entirely as a discount: the customer put it in the cart themselves. A free gift with the order and samples the customer didn't choose aren't included, nor is free shipping: they add to costs rather than lowering the product's price.
Revenue includes **only money for sales that have a pre-discount price**: shipping and other service fees, and for subscriptions one-time payments and overage charges, aren't included, even though shipping fees are part of [[Revenue→vyruchka/vyruchka]]. This money has no pre-discount price, and including it in revenue would understate the discount.
Points redeemed as payment and member-card discounts **are subtracted from revenue**, even if accounting books them as an expense, as in [[Loyalty Program Costs→kommercheskie-rashody/zatraty_na_programmu_loyalnosti]]: otherwise, the discount is understated by their amount. In an order, points and gift cards are usually recorded as payment methods, like money, and they're subtracted from the order total separately. A gift card given away for free is also a discount, while a purchased one isn't: it was paid for when it was bought.
**Returned goods aren't included** in either part. If a return is subtracted from revenue but left in the pre-discount value, it counts as a discount, and the discount is overstated. For the same reason, the metric can't be derived from the total of [[Discounts→finansy/skidki]]: that total still includes the discount on goods that were later returned.
**Both parts exclude taxes**: revenue without tax against a displayed price that includes tax turns the tax itself into a discount.
For subscriptions, the pre-discount price is **the plan's monthly list price on the terms the customer subscribed under**: a customer who kept the old price after a price increase is counted at the old price, as in [[Average Subscription Price→vyruchka/srednyaya_cena_podpiski]]. At the new list price, the discount would jump in the month of the increase even though nobody gave any new discounts. An enterprise plan without a public price list is compared with the internal price list from which the contract discount is calculated.
For subscriptions, it's calculated **from paying accounts' subscriptions as of one date**, like [[Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR)→saas_produkty/ezhemesyachnyy_regulyarnyy_dohod_mrr]]: each subscription contributes its monthly payment after discounts and its monthly list price. If you calculate it from the month's payments, an annual payment goes entirely into the month of payment and causes a spike, and the subscription price net of the discount stops reconciling with Average Revenue per Account (ARPA).
An annual payment **is compared with the monthly list price × 12**: if you compare it with the annual list price, the annual-billing discount disappears. A plan sold only annually is compared with its own annual list price.
A month at a token price, for example the first month for $1, is included and counts almost entirely as a discount, while a free trial month isn't included: it isn't paid. So the discount changes with **the inflow of new customers**: every new customer gets a welcome promo code or an introductory price, and in a month of strong acquisition the discount grows even though the promotions are the same.
A discount that the marketplace gives the customer at its own expense **isn't included in the seller's calculation**: the seller receives its full price, and its revenue didn't decrease. A discount later reimbursed by the supplier is included in full: revenue from the sale decreased, and the reimbursement comes separately.
A sale is assigned **to the month of the order** rather than the month of receipt: otherwise, a sale event in the last days of the month goes into the next month as a discount. Until the return window for the month's sales has passed, the number is preliminary: the calculation includes goods that will still be returned, and the discount will shift depending on whether they were bought at a discount.
929.example:
A store's sales for the month, excluding returns and taxes:
Value of goods sold at pre-discount prices: $252,000
Revenue from goods sold after discounts, promo codes and points: $214,200
Shipping fees paid by customers: $7,000 (not counted)
Returned: $8,400 at pre-discount prices (not counted)

Effective Discount Rate = (1 − 214,200 / 252,000) × 100 = **15%**

Keeping shipping fees in revenue gives (1 − 221,200 / 252,000) × 100 = 12.2%: these fees have no pre-discount price, and the discount is understated.

A subscription service as of April 1: 1,600 paying accounts on monthly billing at a list price of $20 and 400 on annual billing at $192 a year, that is, $16 a month
Value at the monthly list price: 2,000 × 20 = $40,000
Monthly payments after discounts: $31,000 from monthly accounts after promo codes and 400 × 16 = $6,400 from annual ones, $37,400 in total

Effective Discount Rate = (1 − 37,400 / 40,000) × 100 = **6.5%**

Comparing annual billing with the annual list price rather than the monthly price × 12 gives a pre-discount base of $38,400 and a discount of 2.6%: $1,600 in annual-billing discounts drops out of the calculation.
929.importance: It brings promo codes, promotions, points and annual-billing discounts into one number: different people set them up, but they all come out of the same revenue. The [[Average Discount Rate→zakazy/sredniy_skidki]] doesn't give such a number: it averages the announced promotions and ignores how much was sold under them. It's used to decide where to cut promotions and how much discounting the business can afford given its margin. Growth with unchanged price lists means customers buy at a discount more often or discounts got deeper; the [[Share of Promotional Sales→vyruchka/promo_prodazh]] shows which.
929.not_needed: Skip it when you sell strictly at list price, without promotions, promo codes, points or annual-billing discounts: the metric is always zero. Also skip it where there's no price list and each contract's price is negotiated separately, as with enterprise plans priced on request: there's nothing to compare with.
929.essence_note: every percentage point of discount reduces revenue from the same sale

930.name: Contribution Margin Ratio
930.description: The share of revenue the company keeps after variable costs: those that grow with each sale or each customer served. Unlike [[Gross Margin→finansy/rentabelnost_valovoy_pribyli]], it subtracts from revenue everything it costs to fulfill sales and serve customers rather than only the cost of goods. Fixed costs and customer acquisition costs, which [[Operating Margin→finansy/rentabelnost_operacionnoy_pribyli]] subtracts, aren't subtracted here.
930.nuances:
For one-time purchases, variable costs include the cost of goods sold, picking and packing, shipping net of what customers pay for it, payment processing, the costs of returns and refused or unclaimed orders (return shipping, receiving, markdowns and write-offs), messaging campaigns and ads aimed at existing customers, and, when selling through a marketplace, its commission and logistics fees. For subscriptions, they include cloud capacity and third-party services, payment processing and the app store commission. Support, customer success and the company's own servers are included if the company decides to treat them as variable.
**Acquiring new customers** isn't a variable cost, even though it grows with sales, and neither are the costs of trials and the free plan: they're the price of acquiring paying customers. The margin goes into LTV, and LTV is divided by the cost of acquisition: deducting acquisition costs here would count them twice. **Retention** isn't part of the cost of acquisition and so is subtracted here: messaging campaigns to existing customers and the services behind them, ads aimed at existing customers. Discounts and points are already subtracted from revenue and aren't subtracted a second time.
Support, customer success and the company's own servers grow in steps rather than with each sale: people are hired as the customer base grows, and capacity is added as load grows. Decide **whether to treat them as variable**. As variable costs, they show the full cost of serving a customer, and the margin is lower. As fixed costs, the margin is higher, and so are LTV and the acceptable cost of acquisition. The longer the time frame of the decision, the closer they are to variable costs: over the horizon for which LTV is calculated, headcount and capacity grow with the customer base. Moving a line item from one group to the other between periods shifts the margin by that item's share of revenue, even though nothing has changed in the business.
Revenue and costs are taken **for the same sales and the same months**: the cost of goods only for what was sold and not returned, an annual subscription payment at one twelfth per month, and likewise costs paid a year in advance: licenses, capacity, the processing fee on an annual payment. An annual payment booked in full in the month it's paid overstates that month's margin and understates the other eleven.
For one-time purchases, **the margin for the most recent month is overstated**: returns and refused or unclaimed orders are still to come for its orders, part of the revenue will be reversed, and their costs haven't been recorded yet. The month's figure is final once the return window has expired for its orders.
**Shipping fees paid by customers aren't included in revenue here**, even though [[Revenue→vyruchka/vyruchka]] includes them: they're already subtracted from shipping costs, and otherwise the same money would be counted twice. Money refunded to customers reduces revenue and doesn't go into costs. Marketplace revenue is taken as the sales total from the marketplace's report rather than the payout amount: the payout already has the commission and logistics fees deducted. For subscriptions, one-time payments for implementation and training are included in revenue only together with their costs.
Revenue is taken **excluding taxes**: with tax included, the margin comes out overstated. Costs are taken excluding any tax the company gets back as a credit or refund.
**Decide** whether to subtract a tax charged on revenue, such as a state gross receipts tax. It grows with each sale, like variable costs, but it's a tax, and gross and operating margins are calculated before taxes. Subtracted, it lowers the margin by its rate.
If new customers get a first-order discount or free shipping, or, for subscriptions, kickoff meetings, an inflow of new customers lowers the margin even though prices haven't changed.
[[Marketplace Net Margin→marketpleysy/marzhinalnost]] is a different number: net profit as a share of gross merchandise value, after all costs, including fixed costs and advertising.
930.example:
Subscription, one month; the company treats support and customer success as variable:
Subscription revenue excluding taxes: $60,000
Cloud capacity and third-party services: $4,800
Support: $3,600
Payment processing: $1,200
Customer success: $2,400
Variable costs = 4,800 + 3,600 + 1,200 + 2,400 = $12,000
Contribution Margin Ratio = (60,000 − 12,000) / 60,000 × 100 = **80%**

One-time purchases, one month; the company treats support as variable:
Revenue excluding taxes, after returns and without shipping fees paid by customers: $100,000
Cost of goods sold: $55,000
Picking and packing: $3,000
Shipping net of customer fees: $4,000
Payment processing: $2,000
Returns and refused or unclaimed orders: $3,000
Messaging campaigns and ads aimed at existing customers: $1,000
Support: $1,000
Variable costs = 55,000 + 3,000 + 4,000 + 2,000 + 3,000 + 1,000 + 1,000 = $69,000
Contribution Margin Ratio = (100,000 − 69,000) / 100,000 × 100 = **31%**

Subtracting only the cost of goods gives 45%: that's the gross margin, and LTV based on it would be overstated by a factor of 1.45.
930.importance: Decisions on prices, discounts and the acceptable cost of acquisition are based on it: at a 30% margin, a 10% discount takes a third of the contribution margin per sale, and sales have to grow 1.5 times to bring back the previous contribution margin. Revenue doesn't show this: sales grow, while each new order or customer may bring in less and less as shipping, servers, support and returns get more expensive.
930.essence_note: each additional percentage point leaves more money from every sale for acquisition, fixed costs and profit

931.name: Infrastructure and Third-Party Service Cost per Account
931.formula: Infrastructure and Third-Party Service Costs for the Month / [[Paying Customers→saas_produkty/platyaschie_polzovateli]] at the End of the Month
931.description: The average monthly cost of the servers, cloud and third-party services the product runs on for one paying account. An account is a subscription customer: a company in B2B, a person in B2C.
931.nuances:
It includes servers, cloud, data storage, third-party services and licenses **without which the product doesn't work for the customer**: transactional SMS and emails (login codes, notifications), maps, speech recognition, language models. Messaging campaigns for retention and sales aren't included: they're part of working with customers rather than of running the product. The company website, internal systems, and development and testing environments aren't included either: they don't grow with the number of customers. Website hosting, software for employees and IT contractors are counted in [[IT and Telecom Costs→finansy/it_i_infrastruktura]]. Salaries of the engineers who keep the product running aren't included: only vendor bills count here.
**Trials and the free plan** aren't included: the cost of their servers and services belongs to acquiring paying customers. They aren't in [[Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)→saas_produkty/stoimost_privlecheniya_klienta_cac]] either, which covers only marketing and sales, and without separate tracking these costs drop out of the customer payback calculation.
The cloud bills by resource rather than by customer. Pay-per-use services are assigned to accounts from the call log, and shared servers by an allocation key: the share of requests, compute or storage. **The key is chosen once**: a different key gives non-paying accounts a different share of the bill. If the bill is split evenly across paying accounts, the load from non-paying ones stays in the metric, and breakdowns by plan, size and cohort show the same number.
**Part of the bill doesn't grow with each account**: the minimum set of servers, the database server license. As the base grows, cost per account falls without any savings, and with churn it rises without any new load, and a subscription price floor calculated from the average comes out overstated.
The denominator includes **all paying accounts at the end of the month**, including those that didn't log in to the product, as in the Average Revenue per Account (ARPA): otherwise cost and revenue per account are divided by different bases. An annual account is in the denominator every month, even though it paid once. Accounts that run the product on their own servers aren't in the denominator: they cost almost nothing, and with them the metric is understated.
Annual licenses and capacity paid in advance **are spread across months**: otherwise cost per account spikes in the month of payment and is understated in the other eleven. Cloud and services paid in arrears are assigned **to the month of consumption**: the March bill arrives in April, and by bill date, March's costs are understated and April's overstated. Cloud credits don't reduce costs: costs are taken at the price without credits. Otherwise they drop to zero during the credit months and jump afterward.
931.example:
Cloud bill for March: $15,800
Of that, trials and the free plan by share of requests: $2,000 (not counted)
Of that, development and testing environments: $1,800 (not counted)
Third-party services for paying accounts (transactional SMS and emails, maps, speech recognition): $4,800
Annual database license $24,000, for March: $2,000
Paying accounts on March 31: 2,400, of which 400 are on annual billing

Costs = 15,800 − 2,000 − 1,800 + 4,800 + 2,000 = $18,800
Infrastructure and Third-Party Service Cost per Account = 18,800 / 2,400 = **$7.83**

Dividing only by the 2,000 accounts that paid in March gives $9.40: annual accounts paid for March in advance and use the product the same way.
931.importance: The cloud bill grows with load without anyone deciding to spend more, and in dollars its growth looks like a natural result of a growing base. Per account, you can see whether each customer is getting more expensive: features built on language models, where every request is paid for, can raise cost per account faster than the subscription price grows. It's used to decide which capacity to turn off and when to prepay for capacity at a discount.
931.not_needed: Skip it when the product **is installed on the customer's servers**: the customer pays for servers and cloud, and the company has almost no cost per account left.
931.synonyms: Hosting Cost per Customer, Cloud Cost per Customer
931.essence_note: servers and services are paid for out of the customer's fee, and at the same price every dollar saved on them stays as contribution margin

932.name: Support Cost per Account
932.formula: Support Costs for the Month / [[Paying Customers→saas_produkty/platyaschie_polzovateli]] at the End of the Month
932.description: The average monthly cost of supporting one paying account: answering its tickets via chat, email and phone. An account is a subscription customer: a company in B2B, a person in B2C.
932.nuances:
**Planned work initiated by the company** isn't included: meetings, training and reviews of how the account uses the product belong to customer success. Support includes only responses to tickets: the customer writes in, the company answers. The costs of an employee who does both are split by share of time.
**The cost components** are the same as in [[Total Support Cost→podderzhka_klientov/rashody_na_podderzhku_klientov]]: salaries with payroll taxes, contractors, licenses for the ticketing system, telephony and the bot; the cost of an employee who answers tickets between other tasks is included by share of time. **Decide** whether to allocate rent and other overhead here. With allocation, cost per account can be compared with a contractor's price, which already includes the contractor's rent, but the number depends on the key used to split rent between departments. Without allocation, the number changes only with the support team's own costs.
**Tickets from trials and the free plan** aren't included: they're the price of acquiring paying customers, as are questions from users before signup about pricing, integrations and terms. Their part of the costs is subtracted by their share of tickets or, if the system logs time spent answering, by their share of that time; tickets not linked to an account are split in the same proportion as linked ones. [[Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)→saas_produkty/stoimost_privlecheniya_klienta_cac]] doesn't include support, only marketing and sales, and without separate tracking these costs drop out of the customer payback calculation.
The denominator includes **all paying accounts at the end of the month**, whether or not they contacted support, as in the Average Revenue per Account (ARPA): otherwise cost and revenue per account are divided by different bases. An annual account is in the denominator every month, even though it paid once.
[[Cost per Ticket→podderzhka_klientov/stoimost_obrascheniya]] multiplied by [[Tickets per Customer→podderzhka_klientov/obrascheniy_na_klienta]] gives the cost per account that contacted support rather than per paying account: Tickets per Customer divides only by customers with tickets, and the product comes out higher by the ratio of paying accounts to those that contacted support.
New accounts contact support more often while they learn the product, and in large accounts many employees write in: an inflow of new or large accounts raises cost per account even though support works the same way.
932.example:
Support costs for March: $26,000
Tickets in March: 1,300, of which from trials and the free plan: 260
Attributable to non-paying accounts: 26,000 × 260 / 1,300 = $5,200 (not counted)
Paying accounts on March 31: 2,600

Support Cost per Account = (26,000 − 5,200) / 2,600 = **$8**

The same result calculated using cost per ticket and ticket volume: $20 per ticket × 0.4 tickets per paying account = $8
Keeping trial tickets gives $10: acquisition costs fall on paying accounts, and their margin comes out understated.
932.importance: It's used to calculate the payback of a knowledge base, in-product tips and a tier 1 bot: an investment has paid off if cost per account fell by more than the investment itself costs per account; the bot license is already part of the costs and isn't added a second time. Growth per account means one of three things: the product started generating more questions; answers got more expensive after a release, an interface change or a change of contractor; or the mix of the base changed.
