Cutting support raises the margin right away, while customers who didn't get an answer leave at the next renewal, annual ones months later, and the monthly report no longer shows the connection.
932.essence_note: the less it costs to answer tickets, the more of the customer's fee the company keeps

933.name: Customer Success Cost per Account
933.formula: Customer Success Costs for the Month / [[Paying Customers→saas_produkty/platyaschie_polzovateli]] at the End of the Month
933.description: The average monthly cost of planned, company-initiated work with one paying account: meetings, reviews of how the account uses the product, help with setup. An account is a subscription customer: a company in B2B, a person in B2C.
933.nuances:
It includes work that helps existing customers and retains them, including contract renewals, even if renewals carry a bonus, as sales do. **Expansion sales** (more seats, a pricier plan) belong to [[Sales Team Costs→kommercheskie-rashody/zatraty_na_otdel_prodazh]]: for a manager who both retains customers and sells expansions, costs are split by share of time, and where time isn't tracked, by a rule chosen once, for example by bonuses.
[[Customer Service Costs→finansy/rashody_na_klientskiy_servis]] is a different total: support, warranty repairs and the loyalty program. Customer success isn't part of it.
The boundary with support: if the customer writes and the company answers, the work belongs to support; if the company reaches out on its own as planned, to customer success. Moving the same work across this boundary changes both metrics even though the work itself hasn't changed.
In mass-market B2C subscriptions, there's no one-on-one work: customer success comes down to retention emails and push notifications and the team that runs them.
**Work with accounts on a trial or in pilots** isn't included: that's acquisition. It isn't in [[Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)→saas_produkty/stoimost_privlecheniya_klienta_cac]] either, which covers only marketing and sales, and without separate tracking these costs drop out of the customer payback calculation. A paid pilot is excluded entirely, both the costs and the account in the denominator, until the customer signs the main contract.
**Implementation the customer pays for separately** isn't included: its own fee covers it, and with it, cost per account comes out overstated.
Retention concessions, such as a discount, a free month or compensation for an outage, aren't included: they reduce revenue and show up in the Effective Discount Rate.
New accounts require more customer success work: kickoff meetings, help with setup, training. An inflow of new accounts raises cost per account even though the work with each one hasn't changed. The average mixes accounts with and without a dedicated manager, and a shift in their shares moves the number with no change in the work with each.
The denominator includes **all paying accounts at the end of the month**, including those nobody met with that month, as in the Average Revenue per Account (ARPA): otherwise cost and revenue per account are divided by different bases. An annual account is in the denominator every month, even though it paid once.
933.example:
Pay for 6 customer success managers, including payroll taxes: $45,000
Customer success platform: $1,200
A third of two managers' time goes to expansion sales: 2 × 7,500 / 3 = $5,000 (not counted)
Managers' time on pilot projects with trial accounts: $2,500 (not counted)
Paying accounts at the end of the month: 1,800

Customer success costs = 45,000 + 1,200 − 5,000 − 2,500 = $38,700
Customer Success Cost per Account = 38,700 / 1,800 = **$21.50**

Keeping expansion sales gives $24.28: the customer's margin comes out understated, and expansion revenue looks free.
933.importance: Together with revenue per account, it's used to decide who gets a dedicated manager and for whom group sessions and automated emails are enough: a manager costing $7,500 a month and handling 60 accounts costs $125 per account, and with revenue of $80 per account, this level of customer success loses money however long the customer stays. Customer success pays off through retention rather than the month's margin: rising cost per account with the same retention and the same inflow of new accounts means each retained customer costs more.
933.essence_note: with the same retention, every dollar saved on customer success stays with the company

934.name: Average Revenue per Account (ARPA)
934.formula: [[Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR)→saas_produkty/ezhemesyachnyy_regulyarnyy_dohod_mrr]] / [[Paying Customers→saas_produkty/platyaschie_polzovateli]] on the Same Date
934.description: How much one paying account pays on average for a month of subscription after all discounts. An account is a subscription customer: a company in B2B, a person in B2C.
934.nuances:
MRR and paying accounts are taken **on the same date**: MRR on March 31 divided by paying accounts on March 1 mixes two different bases, and revenue per account comes out overstated or understated because of the accounts that joined and left during the month.
The numerator includes **only recurring subscription fees**: the plan, added seats and modules after discounts and excluding taxes, with annual payments at one twelfth per month. One-time payments for implementation and training and usage fees above the plan's allowance aren't included: they have their own levers, and with them, revenue per account would jump from month to month with no change in plans. This is what sets the metric apart from [[Average Revenue per Paying User (ARPPU)→vyruchka/sredniy_dohod_na_platyaschego_polzovatelya]], which uses all revenue.
The denominator includes **only paying accounts**: trials and the free plan aren't included. This sets the metric apart from [[Average Revenue per User (ARPU)→saas_produkty/sredniy_dohod_na_polzovatelya_arpu]], where all revenue is divided by all active users, including non-paying ones, although in subscription practice this calculation is also called ARPU, especially in B2C, where each account represents one person. In B2B, the paying unit is the company account: the seats it pays for are already in the numerator, and dividing by employees gives revenue per seat, a different measure.
Subscriptions set up by different departments of the same customer **are merged into one account**: kept separate, they understate revenue per account and overstate the number of accounts. The merging rule is the same for all per-account calculations.
Revenue per account also changes **with the mix of the customer base**: small accounts leaving raise it while MRR falls, and an inflow of new accounts on entry-level plans and discounts lowers it, even though no customer has started paying differently.
934.example:
Monthly subscriptions after discounts: 1,500 accounts, $81,000
Annual subscriptions: 300 accounts, $216,000 a year, $18,000 per month
Implementation and training in March: $12,000 (not counted)
Usage fees above the plan's allowance: $3,000 (not counted)
On a trial: 700 accounts (not counted)
MRR on March 31 excluding taxes = 81,000 + 18,000 = $99,000
Paying accounts on March 31: 1,800

ARPA = 99,000 / 1,800 = **$55**

With implementation and usage fees above the allowance, it would come out to $63.33, and in April, with no implementations, revenue per account would drop even though no customer started paying less.
The same result calculated using price and discount: average subscription price $62.50, effective discount rate 12%, 62.50 × 0.88 = $55.
934.importance: It determines which sales and service model the product can sustain: at low revenue per account, customers buy and figure things out on their own, while at high revenue per account, a salesperson and a dedicated account manager pay off. Multiplied by the margin, it's also used to calculate the [[CAC Payback Period→saas_produkty/srok_okupaemosti_klienta]]: a one-fifth drop in revenue per account stretches the payback period by a quarter, even if MRR keeps growing.
934.not_needed: Skip it with **purely usage-based pricing** and no subscription fee: there's no recurring part, and MRR-based revenue per account is zero.
934.essence_note: with the same customer base, growth in revenue per account raises MRR by the same proportion with no new acquisition costs

935.name: Paying Customer Activation Rate
935.formula: New Paying Accounts That Completed the Key Action Within N Days of the First Payment / New Paying Accounts × 100
935.description: The share of new paying customers who completed the key action within N days of their first payment: the first action after which the product delivered value to them, for example connecting a data source and seeing the first report.
935.nuances:
**The account is counted rather than its employees**: in B2B, a company is activated when the key action happened in its account, no matter which of the customer's employees did it. The rate by employee is lower and falls with every invited colleague who hasn't used the product yet.
**The N days are counted from the first payment**, that is, from the start of the first paid period: with invoice payment, the money arrives after access is granted, and counting from the day the money arrives would stretch the window by those days. An action taken earlier, during a trial or on the free plan, counts. A window counted from signup would record as not activated a customer who spent months on the free plan and reached value right before paying.
An action before payment counts only if **the same account** in which the product was tried is the one paid for: when a new account is created for the purchase, or an app store purchase isn't linked to the user, the customer ends up among the non-activated, and the rate is understated.
What counts is what **the customer did or saw themselves**. A data source connected by the company's manager on the customer's behalf, demo data and a report the product built and sent out on its own produce the event without the customer getting any value: help with setup then raises the rate even if the customer never logged in to the product.
The rate is **inherently higher** than the [[Activation Rate→saas_produkty/aktivirovannyh_polzovateley]]: those who decide to pay are mostly people who have already reached value, while the base there is everyone who signed up. Industry activation benchmarks are also calculated against all signups, and compared with them, this rate always looks high.
**The path to the first payment** shifts the rate without any help with setup. Those who choose to pay after a trial are more likely to have already reached value. An automatic charge to a card on file at the end of the trial, a first month for $1 and payment under a contract before setup turn people who haven't used the product yet into paying customers. When the length or terms of the trial change, or the share of customers who bought through the sales team grows, the activation rate shifts even though nothing happened with setup.
**A new account** is one paying for the first time. If a customer returning after a long break is also counted as new, they come in already activated: they reached value last time, and a win-back campaign raises the rate without a single new activation. A customer refunded within the first N days stays in the denominator: refunds are requested more often by those who didn't reach value, and without them the rate is overstated.
**The larger N, the higher the rate**: with 14 and 30 days, they're different measures. With monthly billing and N longer than a month, the rate becomes known only after the first renewal. Setup takes large customers longer, and with a common N their rate is lower, even though they get no less help.
Accounts whose **N days haven't passed yet** aren't included for now, even those that reached value during the trial: with all such accounts, the rate is understated, since some of them have yet to complete the key action; with only those that reached it, the rate is overstated. So the rate for a month is final only N days after the month ends.
935.example:
Key action: connected a data source and saw the first report
Window: 14 days from the first payment, calculation date April 4
Paid for a subscription for the first time in March: 420 accounts
Paid after March 20, so 14 days haven't passed yet: 95 (not included for now; the March rate is final on April 15)
In the calculation: 325
Completed the key action by day 14 after payment: 247, of which 182 during the trial (counted)

Paying Customer Activation Rate = 247 / 325 × 100 = **76%**

Counting only actions after payment gives 65 / 325 × 100 = 20%: most reached value during the trial, before paying.
935.importance: This rate shows how many customers already pay but still haven't gotten value from the product: the [[Activation Rate→saas_produkty/aktivirovannyh_polzovateley]] divides by everyone who signed up, and a gap among paying customers gets lost there among the free users. It's used to decide whether new customers need **help with setup**: a customer success call, a walkthrough of the first steps, a welcome email sequence.
935.not_needed: Skip it when value comes **with the first login** and there's no separate key action in the product, and where you can pay **only after the key action**: such a rate is always 100%. It also doesn't fit where there are **only a handful** of new customers a month, as in enterprise sales: one customer moves the rate by around ten points, and each customer's onboarding is tracked individually.
935.essence_note: a customer who has reached value renews more often

936.name: Active Days per Account per Month
936.formula: Active Days of Paying Accounts in Their Paid Month / Paying Accounts Whose Paid Month Started in the Reporting Month
936.description: How many days per month a paying account uses the product on average.
936.nuances:
The denominator includes **all paying accounts**, including those that didn't take a single meaningful action during the month: they have zero days. If you divide by accounts with activity, accounts that pay but don't use the product drop out of the calculation, and the average doesn't show that there are more of them.
An active day is a day when **a meaningful action** was taken in the account, as in [[Daily Active Users (DAU)→saas_produkty/dau]]. Integration requests and scheduled exports don't make a day active: otherwise an account with a connected integration looks active every day even if no one logs in to the product. Actions by the company's own employees in the customer's account, such as support logging in as the customer or setup by the implementation team, don't make a day active either: otherwise an account the team is trying to save looks active exactly on the days it's being saved.
For an account with several employees, a day **counts once**: five people working on March 12 give one day rather than five. Days are counted in one time zone for everyone, as in DAU. Separately paid workspaces of one company are merged into one account, as in the Average Revenue per Account (ARPA): kept separate, each of them has fewer days.
That's why for an account with dozens of seats, the number of days **sits near the ceiling**: if 50 employees each log in on two random working days out of 21, the account is active almost every working day, and losing half of them lowers the figure only from 20.9 to 19.3 days. When people in large accounts stop using the product, it shows up in the share of active seats rather than in days. The average across the base grows with the share of large accounts and the share of long-standing ones that survived churn, with no change in behavior.
Each account's month is counted **from its payment date** rather than by the calendar: an account that started paying on March 25 would collect no more than seven days in calendar March, and in months of strong inflow the average would dip with no change in behavior. The March report includes accounts whose paid month started in March, and March is closed when the last of those months has ended: until then, recent accounts are still accumulating days, and the average is understated.
The ceiling is set by the length of the month, 28 days or 31, and in a B2B product by **the number of working days**: the metric dips on its own in a month that includes the year-end holidays.
936.example:
Accounts whose paid month started in March: 800
Of those, without a single meaningful action in the month: 120 (in the denominator, zero days)
Days with a meaningful action for the other 680 in their paid month: 7,520
Days when the account had only integration exports: 1,150 (not counted)

Active Days per Account per Month = 7,520 / 800 = **9.4 days**

Dividing only by the 680 accounts with activity gives 11.1 days: the 120 accounts that pay but don't use the product disappear from the calculation.
936.importance: It falls before cancellations arrive, when an account first logs in less often and only later fails to renew. A drop in it is used to decide whether to launch digests and reminders that bring users back to the product, and it also shows whether logins recovered after them. [[Stickiness→saas_produkty/regulyarnost_ispolzovaniya_dau_mau]] doesn't give this signal: it divides by those who logged in, and a paying account **that stopped opening the product drops out of it**.
936.not_needed: Skip it for products with **an infrequent use case**, where two or three days a month is normal: month-end close, regulatory filings, budget planning. It also doesn't fit services that **run without people involved**: backups, monitoring, payment processing. They deliver value while nobody logs in, and zero days says nothing about churn there.
936.essence_note: a product people use every day is harder to give up

937.name: Core Features Used per Account
937.formula: Sum over Paying Accounts of the Number of Core Features Each Account Used in Its Paid Month / Paying Accounts Whose Paid Month Started in the Reporting Month
937.description: How many features from the core feature list one paying account uses per month on average.
937.nuances:
The list excludes actions that **everyone who logs in takes**: login, profile settings, the home page. They add one to every account and hide the difference between those who have adopted the product and those who only log in.
A feature added to the list **raises the average from the very first month**, even though customers behave as before: growth between months with the old and the new list says nothing about adoption until the series is recalculated with the new list. The level can be read only together with the length of the list: 2.8 out of 6 and 2.8 out of 10 mean different breadth of use.
Use means **a meaningful action** in the feature: a report built, an export. An opened screen without an action doesn't count: otherwise accidental clicks from the menu get into the average. The threshold depends on how often the feature is normally used: a monthly report needs one action, while daily work counts after several days with an action. Otherwise an in-product tip raises the average with one-off tries. **The threshold is chosen once**: with a different threshold, the series breaks.
A feature that runs on its own after setup, such as an automation, counts in every month in which it fired. Actions by the company's own employees in the customer's account, such as support logging in as the customer, don't count.
A feature counts for an account **once**, however many employees use it: five people working in reports count as one feature. That's why large accounts sit near the ceiling, while new ones are still adopting features in their first months: a growing share of large accounts raises the average, an inflow of new ones lowers it, and long-standing cohorts that survived churn keep it higher, even though nobody started using the product differently.
If some core features are available **only on higher-tier plans**, customers moving to a lower-tier plan lower the average: those features are out of their reach.
Each account's month is counted **from its payment date**, as in Active Days per Account per Month: an account that started paying on March 25 would have time to try fewer features in calendar March. The March report includes accounts whose paid month started in March.
The denominator includes **all paying accounts**, including those with zero features: dividing by those that used at least one overstates the average, and the more accounts pay without using the product, the greater the overstatement. In Pendo, this average (Adoption in the Product Engagement Score) is divided by accounts with any activity, and it's higher.
937.example:
Core features on the list: 6
Accounts whose paid month started in March: 500
Of those, didn't use any core feature: 60 (in the denominator, zero)
Sum of core features used by the accounts in their paid month: 1,400
Logged in to the product at least once: 470 accounts

Core Features Used per Account = 1,400 / 500 = **2.8 features**

Adding login to the list gives (1,400 + 470) / 500 = 3.74: the average grew by almost one, yet nobody started using the product more broadly.
937.importance: It's the basis for deciding whether tips for unused features, training webinars and adoption flows pay off: whether breadth of use grows after them. Which feature to promote is shown by the share of accounts that used each one. Without it, new features are released blind: you see that the product is used, but not that only one part of it is used while the rest is paid for and sits idle. At the same time, the average **hides a split**: a base where everyone uses three features and a base where half use one and half use five both give 3.
937.not_needed: Skip it for **single-feature** products: e-signatures, file converters, link shorteners. There are no other features to use, and the average sits at one.
937.synonyms: Feature Adoption Breadth, Breadth of Adoption
937.essence_note: each adopted feature adds value for the customer and makes switching to a competitor more costly

938.name: Product CSAT
938.formula: Respondents Who Answered 4 or 5 / All Respondents × 100
938.description: The share of paying customers responding to a regular survey who are satisfied with the product: they rated it 4 or 5 on a scale of 1 to 5.
938.nuances:
The survey is **regular and covers all paying customers** or a random sample of them, and its question is about the product. A post-ticket survey measures support, and only among those who contacted it: that's how [[Customer Satisfaction Score (CSAT)→podderzhka_klientov/indeks_udovletvorennosti_klientov_csat]] is calculated. A question that pops up right after a successful action in the product overstates the rate: it asks at the best moment. Reviews of individual items don't count here: a review is left by someone who has something to say, and it's about one item rather than the product as a whole; the share of good reviews is measured by the [[Share of Positive Reviews→assortiment/polozhitelnyh_otzyvov]].
The denominator is **respondents only**. Dividing by everyone surveyed gives the share of positive respondents rather than satisfaction. Non-respondents skew the rate one way: an in-product survey is seen only by those who log in, so accounts that pay but don't use the product are missing from the responses, yet they're the ones who churn most, and the share of satisfied customers is overstated. An email reaches everyone, but it gets fewer responses. The channel, question and scale are chosen once: after a change, new figures can't be compared with old ones.
The mix of those surveyed moves the monthly rate: if you survey one segment at a time, the rate depends on who was asked, and new accounts in their first weeks rate their expectations rather than the product. So new customers are surveyed after a month or two of using the product, and the survey sends are spread evenly across months.
Only paying customers are surveyed, so **dissatisfied customers leaving raises the share** of satisfied ones with no change in the product, and in long-standing cohorts it's higher on its own.
In B2B, the customer's employees respond, and **each response counts rather than each account**: an account with forty respondents weighs forty times as much as an account with one. Surveying one contact per account, such as the admin or the contract owner, puts customers on an equal footing. Regular users respond more often, while a manager makes the renewal decision, and their ratings can differ.
Even with hundreds of responses, the rate is noisy: with 360 responses and 70% satisfied, a difference of up to 6–7 percentage points between two months can be random.
938.example:
Survey in March: “How satisfied are you with the product?”, scale of 1 to 5
Surveys sent to paying customers: 1,200
Responded: 360
Ratings of 4 and 5: 252
Rating of 3: 60 (not in the numerator)
Ratings of 1 and 2: 48

Product CSAT = 252 / 360 × 100 = **70%**

Dividing by all 1,200 surveys sent gives 21%: that's the share of those who answered 4 or 5 among everyone rather than satisfaction.
938.importance: It shows whether the product got worse after a release, a plan change or an outage, and it's used to decide whether to focus retention efforts on the product itself. Willingness to recommend the company is measured by the [[Net Promoter Score (NPS)→podderzhka_klientov/indeks_loyalnosti_klientov_nps]], while here the question is about the product. But price and support drag this answer down too, so the reason for a drop is taken from the comments. Dissatisfaction shows up here earlier than in churn: an annual customer leaves only **on the renewal date** but stops being satisfied long before it.
938.not_needed: Skip it with a base of **a few dozen customers**: one response moves the rate by several percentage points, and its swings describe two or three respondents rather than the product.
938.essence_note: a customer satisfied with the product cancels the subscription less often

939.name: Month 1 to Month 2 Retention Rate
939.formula: Monthly Accounts That Paid for Month 2 / Monthly Accounts That Paid for Month 1 × 100
939.description: The share of customers on monthly billing who paid for a second month after their first paid month.
939.nuances:
Month 1 is **the first paid month**. A trial doesn't count: otherwise you're measuring the [[Trial-to-Paid Conversion Rate→saas_produkty/konversiya_iz_probnogo_perioda_v_oplatu]]. **Decide** where to put a token payment, for example a month for $1. If it counts as month 1, the cohort includes people who never intended to pay full price, and the rate is lower. If it counts as a trial, the first paid month is the first month at the plan price, even if discounted.
Repeat signups to get the introductory offer **are merged with the earlier account**, by card or phone number: otherwise the customer counts as not paying for month 2 in one cohort and enters the next one as a newcomer, and the rate is understated.
**Annual accounts aren't included**: their second month is paid in advance, there's no renewal decision in it, and they'd raise the rate without a single action. Accounts with a multi-month contract and monthly payments aren't included either: they have no renewal decision in month 2 either. Whether an account is monthly is determined by its payment for month 1: an account that switched to annual billing from month 2 has paid for month 2 and is in the numerator.
The numerator and denominator are taken **for the same cohort**: accounts that started paying in the same month. If you divide April's second payments by April's first payments, the fraction contains two different streams, and in months of growing acquisition the rate comes out understated.
Payment for month 2 means **the charge for the second billing period** rather than the account's second payment: an extra charge for an upgrade or added seats, or a retried charge of the same invoice after a failure, produces a second payment while still in month 1, and the account enters the numerator without reaching renewal.
An account whose charge for month 2 failed and **whose payment retries are still in progress** waits for the outcome: recording it as unpaid before the grace period ends understates the rate. An account that pays after the grace period counts as returning rather than renewing. For accounts paying by invoice, the outcome is awaited until the invoice due date.
A payment **refunded in full** doesn't count: an account refunded for month 2 doesn't go into the numerator, and one refunded for month 1 also drops out of the denominator. A refund comes after the charge, so a cohort's rate is final once the period in which the service issues refunds has expired.
An account that paused its subscription hasn't paid for month 2 but hasn't left either. **Decide** whether to wait for the pause to end, as you wait for the outcome of payment retries, or to count it as unpaid right away: in the first case, the pause delays the cohort's final rate by its length; in the second, the rate is lower.
The rate depends on who was acquired: customers who came in on a first-month discount or a promotion renew less often, and the rate for the cohort from a month with a big promotion dips with no change in the product.
For any two months, the same calculation is called the Month X to Month Y Retention Rate: for the step from month 1 to month 2, it gives the same number, because annual accounts and multi-month contracts have no renewal date in this window. The [[Renewal Rate→saas_produkty/prodleniy]] divides renewed subscriptions by all subscriptions of any age whose renewal date fell in the period; here, it's only the first renewal of monthly accounts from one cohort.
939.example:
Paid for a subscription for the first time in March: 520 accounts
Of those, annual: 120 (not counted: the second month is paid in advance)
Monthly: 400
Paid for the second month, including retries within the grace period: 332

Month 1 to Month 2 Retention Rate = 332 / 400 × 100 = **83%**

Keeping annual accounts gives (332 + 120) / 520 × 100 = 87%: annual accounts raised the rate without ever deciding whether to renew.
939.importance: It answers whether a **dedicated first-month program** is needed: reviewing new customers to see who hasn't reached value and what they don't use, and offering help before the second charge arrives. A loss here carries into every following month: a customer who leaves after the first month won't pay for the third or the twelfth. Average monthly churn across the whole base hides this loss: frequent churn among newcomers gets diluted by infrequent churn among long-standing customers.
939.not_needed: Skip it when almost all customers pay **a year in advance**: there are only a handful of monthly accounts, and the rate jumps with each one. It also doesn't fit where a contract requires paying **for several months in a row**: there's no renewal decision in the second month. Nor does it fit services that debit a prepaid balance daily: there's no paid month, and topping up the balance is the decision to continue.
939.essence_note: everyone who pays for the second month keeps bringing in revenue, and their acquisition has already been paid for

940.name: Month X to Month Y Retention Rate
940.formula: Accounts with a Renewal Date Between Months X and Y That Paid for Month Y / Accounts with a Renewal Date Between Months X and Y That Paid for Month X × 100
940.description: The share of customers who paid for month X and also paid for month Y. Months are counted from the customer's first payment rather than by the calendar.
940.nuances:
**The company chooses** X and Y; the step from the first month to the second is measured by the Month 1 to Month 2 Retention Rate.
The rate **falls with the length of the window** on its own: with 95% paying for each following month, the window from month 1 to month 3 gives 90%, and from month 3 to month 12 gives 63%, and the long window looks like the weakest stretch even though retention is no different.
The denominator includes accounts that **have a scheduled renewal date between X and Y**: all monthly accounts, annual ones only if the window includes their renewal date, and accounts with a multi-month contract and monthly payments only if the contract ends within the window. The numerator is taken from the same accounts. An annual account with no renewal in the window paid for month Y in advance and would raise the rate without a single decision, and a fixed-term contract has a charge but no renewal decision. Whether the account is monthly or annual is decided by its payment for month X.
At the step where annual accounts renew, **one rate combines a one-month decision and a one-year decision**: an annual account that doesn't renew takes away twelve months of payments at once, and the rate at this step is lower than at the neighboring ones, even if annual accounts are retained better than monthly ones. So it moves with the share of annual accounts in the cohort.
Selection is **by schedule rather than by actual payment**: an annual account that didn't renew stays in the denominator. If you look for annual accounts by their renewal payments, those that didn't renew won't be found at all, and the rate comes out close to 100%.
Only accounts for which **month Y has already started** and the charge for it has been resolved, including retries and the grace period, go into the calculation: for the rest, the outcome isn't known yet, and with them the rate comes out understated.
Payment for month Y means **the charge for that billing period** rather than any payment in the window: an extra charge for an upgrade or added seats doesn't put the account in the numerator. A charge refunded in full doesn't count as a renewal, so the outcome of month Y is final only after the period in which the service issues refunds.
A drop in the rate can result from success in earlier months: customers with a weaker need for the product who were retained in the first months survive to month X and renew less often than those who would have gotten there on their own.
The [[Renewal Rate→saas_produkty/prodleniy]] counts the renewals of a calendar month, first and later ones together, while here the window is counted from each customer's first payment: in the 12→13 window, it's the first renewal of annual accounts from one cohort.
940.example:
X = 12, Y = 13: for annual accounts, this step is the first renewal
Started paying in March of last year and paid for month 12: 300 accounts
Monthly among them: 180; paid for month 13: 171
Annual with a renewal in March: 120; renewed: 84
Annual accounts that didn't renew: 36 (stay in the denominator)

Month 12 to Month 13 Retention Rate = (171 + 84) / 300 × 100 = **85%**
Separately: monthly 171 / 180 × 100 = 95%, annual 84 / 120 × 100 = 70%

If annual accounts are found by renewal payments, the 36 that didn't renew won't be found, and the result is 255 / 264 × 100 = 96.6%: selecting by actual payment drops all churned annual accounts from the denominator, and every annual account looks renewed.
940.importance: It finds the stretch of the customer lifetime where **the most subscriptions are lost**: before the first annual renewal, in the third month, right after the introductory discount ends. That's where to put a retention program, for example a renewal campaign a month before the charge date. Overall monthly churn doesn't show this stretch: it mixes customers of all tenures.
940.not_needed: It doesn't fit services that debit a prepaid balance daily: there are no paid months, and topping up the balance is the decision to continue.
940.essence_note: the more customers keep paying through this stretch, the longer a customer pays on average

941.name: Involuntary Churn Rate
941.formula: Accounts Lost to Failed Payments in the Month / Paying Accounts at the Start of the Month × 100
941.description: The share of paying customers who left during the month only because a payment failed: the charge didn't go through and wasn't recovered, and the customer didn't cancel the subscription themselves.
941.nuances:
A loss is counted when **the grace period has expired** rather than on the day the charge failed: until the period ends, the payment can still be recovered, and a payment after the period no longer reverses the loss. That's why an account waiting for a retry on the first of the month is included among paying accounts at the start of the month: otherwise its loss would land in the numerator without being in the denominator.
**The length of the grace period** changes the figure: with three days, churn includes those who would have paid on the fifth; with thirty, the rate is lower, but the customer uses the product longer without paying. In the month the period is extended, some losses move to the next month, and the figure dips once.
A customer who **canceled the subscription themselves** after a payment failure left voluntarily: the decision was theirs rather than the bank's, and they're not in this rate. The same applies to a bank decline made at the customer's own request, when they turned off recurring charges or revoked authorization for them: such declines are separated by decline code. An email about a failed payment reminds customers of the subscription, and some of them cancel it: this rate then falls, while overall churn doesn't.
**The first charge after a trial** isn't included, even if it failed: the account hasn't paid yet, and this is a failed conversion to paid, measured by the [[Trial-to-Paid Conversion Rate→saas_produkty/konversiya_iz_probnogo_perioda_v_oplatu]]. Billing reports may also classify it as involuntary churn.
Annual accounts are charged once a year but sit in the denominator every month: **a growing share of annual accounts lowers the metric** even though billing works as before.
Total monthly subscriber churn equals 100% minus the [[Customer Retention Rate→saas_produkty/koefficient_uderzhaniya_klientov]], and this rate is part of it with one difference: a customer who comes back before the end of the month is retained there but lost here. The [[Customer Churn Rate→crm/ottok_klientov]] counts as churned someone who hasn't bought anything for longer than the window between purchases, and this rate isn't part of it.
The share of payments saved after a failure is measured for orders by the [[Payment Recovery Rate→zakazy/vosstanovlennyh_oplat]], with a 7-day window; here, it's lost accounts out of the whole paying base, and one rate can't be derived from the other.
941.example:
Grace period: 14 days
Paying accounts on April 1: 2,000, including 30 with retries in progress since late March
Accounts whose charge failed on the first attempt and whose grace period expired in April: 150
Of those, payment went through within the grace period: 104
Canceled the subscription themselves while retries were in progress: 6 (voluntary churn, not counted)
Charge failed on or after April 17; the grace period expires in May: 22 (awaiting the outcome)
Lost to failed payments: 150 − 104 − 6 = 40

Involuntary Churn Rate = 40 / 2,000 × 100 = **2%**

Counting all 150 as lost gives 150 / 2,000 × 100 = 7.5%: churn would include the 104 accounts that paid and stayed and the 6 that canceled the subscription themselves.
941.importance: It separates out the part of overall churn that **can be recovered without talking to the customer**: scheduled payment retries, an “update your card” email before the card expires, a backup payment method on the account, a grace period. It's used to decide how much to invest in billing and which of these measures to turn on. Without it, payment failures are indistinguishable from cancellations, and the product team looks for reasons for churn among customers who never meant to leave.
941.not_needed: Skip it when **there's no automatic charging**: the subscription is paid by invoice or manually each period, and nonpayment means the customer's decision or forgetfulness rather than a bank decline.
941.synonyms: Delinquent Churn, Passive Churn, Failed Payment Churn
941.essence_note: each such loss means losing the revenue of a customer who never refused to pay

942.name: COGS-to-Revenue Ratio
942.formula: Cost of Goods Sold / Revenue from the Same Sales × 100
942.description: The share of revenue that goes to the cost of goods sold: how many cents of every dollar of sales went to buying or making the goods themselves.
942.nuances:
**The numerator is the cost of the goods themselves**: the purchase price with inbound freight and duties, or the production cost. Storage, picking, packing and shipping to the customer aren't included: moving any of them into the cost of goods raises the share even though purchasing hasn't changed. Inbound freight and duties enter the share together with the goods if they were included in the goods' cost at receiving; if they're expensed in the month of the delivery, the share jumps with large deliveries. A supplier volume rebate either reduces the cost of the goods it was earned on, rather than the cost of the month it arrived in, or goes to [[Other Income→chistaya-pribyl/prochie_dohody]], and then the cost of goods, and with it the share, stays higher by the rebate amount.
**The costing method changes the share** when the same item is bought at different prices: with FIFO in a period of rising prices, the cost of goods is lower than with weighted average cost, and so is the share. The method is chosen once.
**Both parts are calculated for the same sales**: kept items after returns. A returned item leaves revenue, and its cost leaves the numerator, while refused or unclaimed orders aren't in either part. If a return is subtracted only from revenue, the share comes out overstated. If the money was refunded and the item stayed with the customer, or came back unsellable and was written off, its cost also leaves this metric and is counted in the Cost of Returns and Refused or Unclaimed Orders per Order as a write-off.
**Shipping fees paid by customers don't go into the denominator**, even though they're part of revenue in the books and in [[Revenue→vyruchka/vyruchka]]: they pay for transport rather than goods, and with them the share would fall when shipping gets more expensive while purchasing and prices stay the same.
The share **doesn't equal 100% minus** [[Gross Margin→finansy/rentabelnost_valovoy_pribyli]]: [[Cost of Goods Sold (COGS)→finansy/sebestoimost_prodazh]] also includes inventory storage, shrinkage and defects, and preparation for sale, while Revenue includes shipping fees. With the numbers from the example, that would give 62.5% instead of 60%.
Both parts are taken excluding taxes: order totals on the website include tax, while the cost of goods is recorded in the books without it, and revenue taken from orders understates the share.
942.example:
Merchandise revenue for the month after discounts and returns, excluding taxes: $160,000
Shipping fees paid by customers: $6,400 (not included: they pay for transport)
Cost of kept goods: $96,000
Warehouse storage: $8,000 (not included: it isn't the cost of the goods)

COGS-to-Revenue Ratio = 96,000 / 160,000 × 100 = **60%**

Leaving the cost of goods returned to the warehouse, $7,200, in the numerator gives 103,200 / 160,000 × 100 = 64.5%: the goods are back in the warehouse, but the share counts them as sold.
942.importance: It singles out the part of costs that purchasing is responsible for: the cost of the goods themselves, separate from the warehouse, shipping and returns. The share grows for three reasons: purchase costs went up, goods sell for less at the same purchase cost, or sales shifted toward low-markup goods. It determines whether to revisit purchase prices, the price list or the depth of promotions, and which of the three is at work shows up item by item: in the [[Average Unit Cost→assortiment/srednyaya_sebestoimost_tovara]], the Average List Price and the Effective Discount Rate. If all three are unchanged, the sales mix has shifted. A missed rise in the share looks like a successful sale: revenue grew, but the earnings on each sale fell.
942.not_needed: Skip it when goods are sold on commission as an agent: revenue is the commission, the seller doesn't own the goods, and there's no cost of goods.
942.synonyms: COGS Percentage, Cost of Sales Ratio
942.essence_note: the smaller the part of revenue the goods themselves take, the more is left for other costs and profit

943.name: Net Shipping Cost per Order
943.formula: (Shipping Costs of Kept Orders − Shipping Fees Paid by Customers for Those Orders) / Kept Orders
943.description: The average cost of shipping one kept order, net of what the customer paid for shipping.
943.nuances:
**Shipping fees paid by customers are subtracted here**, so in a profit calculation that uses this metric, revenue is taken without them: otherwise the same money is counted twice, as revenue and as a cost reduction, and profit is overstated by exactly those fees. [[Revenue→vyruchka/vyruchka]] includes shipping fees, and it's paired with shipping costs without the deduction.
[[Shipping Cost per Order→dostavka_zakazov/stoimost_dostavki_na_zakaz]] is calculated differently: customer fees aren't subtracted, customer pickup isn't in the denominator, and refused or unclaimed orders are. The difference between it and the [[Average Shipping Fee→zakazy/srednyaya_stoimost_dostavki]], the customer's fee per paid order, doesn't give this metric either: all three have different denominators. [[Total Shipping Cost→dostavka_zakazov/rashody_na_dostavku]] includes shipping packaging: if costs are taken from there, packaging is removed.
Costs are taken from carrier invoices rather than from the rate calculated at checkout: the carrier adds charges for actual weight and dimensions and for additional services.
**Costs and orders are assigned to the month of the order**, as in the Cost of Returns and Refused or Unclaimed Orders per Order: an order that is later returned in full drops out of kept orders together with its shipping costs. The month's number is final once all carrier invoices have arrived and the return window has expired.
**Shipping for orders that were refused, unclaimed or returned in full** isn't included here, and neither is their return trip: it's part of the Cost of Returns and Refused or Unclaimed Orders per Order. Otherwise one shipment would land in both metrics.
**Picking, packing and the fee for collecting payment on delivery** aren't included here, even when the carrier or warehouse bills them on the same invoice as shipping: picking and packing are counted in the [[Fulfillment Cost per Order→obrabotka_zakazov/stoimost_obrabotki_zakaza]], and the payment collection fee goes into the Effective Payment Processing Rate: it comes in the carrier's report rather than the bank's, and it's moved there separately. Left here, they'd be counted twice.
**Customer pickup orders** from a store or warehouse stay in the denominator with zero cost: if you remove them, cost per order comes out overstated, and multiplied by kept orders it gives more than was paid for shipping. That's why the number falls when the share of customer pickup grows, even though shipping hasn't gotten cheaper.
943.example:
Kept orders for the month: 4,000, of which customers picked up 400 themselves from a store
Shipping kept orders to customers: $25,600
Shipping fees paid by customers for these orders: $6,400
Shipping for refused, unclaimed and fully returned orders: $2,880 (not counted: these are costs of returns and refused or unclaimed orders)
Shipping packaging and the carrier's fee for collecting payment on delivery: $2,200 (not counted)

Costs net of customer fees = 25,600 − 6,400 = $19,200
Net Shipping Cost per Order = 19,200 / 4,000 = **$4.80**

Removing the 400 customer pickup orders from the denominator gives 19,200 / 3,600 = $5.33: that's the cost per delivered order rather than per kept order.
943.importance: It's used to decide how much to charge customers for shipping, above what cart value to ship for free and which delivery methods to offer; for the fee and the threshold, it's taken for orders that were shipped, excluding customer pickup. Shipping costs without the fee deducted don't show this: when customers are moved to free shipping, transport costs the same, while the fee the store used to collect disappears.
943.not_needed: Skip it when the customer pays the carrier directly for shipping and the store only hands over the package: the store has no shipping costs.
943.synonyms: Shipping Subsidy per Order, Net Shipping Cost
943.essence_note: every dollar shipping costs above the customer's fee reduces the profit per order

944.name: Effective Payment Processing Rate
944.formula: Payment Processing Fees / Revenue from the Same Payments × 100
944.description: The share of revenue that goes to banks, payment providers and delivery services for accepting payments from customers: card processing, instant bank payments, digital wallets, installment plans, payment on delivery. Unlike [[Payment Processing Fees→kommercheskie-rashody/komissiya_za_priem_platezhey]] in dollars, the share doesn't grow with prices: it changes with processing rates, payment methods and refunds.
944.nuances:
The fee on a payment that was later refunded **stays in the numerator** if the processor doesn't return it, while there's no revenue from that payment. So the more refunds there are, the further the rate rises above the processor's rate. Cancellations and refused or unclaimed orders raise it only if the money has already been charged: with two-step payment (authorization, then capture), the money is held until shipment or delivery, and releasing the hold costs no fee.
A refund is assigned to the month of the original payment, so **the rate for the most recent month is understated**: the fee has already been taken, while part of the revenue is still to be refunded. The month's figure is final once the refund window has expired for its payments.
Revenue is taken **excluding taxes**, while the processor takes its percentage of the full payment, tax included: where sales tax is collected on top of the price, the rate is therefore higher than the processor's rate even without refunds.
For subscriptions, both parts are taken **for the subscription only**: one-time payments for implementation and training aren't included in either the fees or the revenue. With them, the rate in implementation months depends on how they were paid, by card or by invoice, rather than on rates.
The fee on an annual payment **is spread over twelve months**, like the revenue from it: if it's booked by payment date, the rate spikes in months when annual subscriptions are sold and dips in the others. If an annual payment is refunded early, the unallocated remainder of the fee goes to the month of the refund. Chargeback fees are also included in the numerator.
For one-time purchases, it also includes **the delivery service's fee for collecting payment on delivery**: left in shipping costs, it understates the rate, and payment on delivery looks free.
The app store commission on a subscription paid in the app **isn't included here**: it's a platform fee, like a marketplace commission, and with it the in-app rate would jump even though accepting payments didn't get more expensive.
944.example:
Subscription, March:
Subscription revenue excluding taxes: $96,000
Fees on subscription payments, with annual payments at one twelfth: $1,920
Effective Payment Processing Rate = 1,920 / 96,000 × 100 = **2%**

One-time purchases, March, no tax in the payment amounts, money charged when the order is placed:
Paid by customers: $15,000
Refunded for cancellations, refused or unclaimed orders and returns: $3,000
Revenue: $12,000
Processor fees on all payments: $300; the processor didn't return them on the refunded money
Effective Payment Processing Rate = 300 / 12,000 × 100 = **2.5%**

Dividing the fees by all payments, $15,000, gives 2%: that's the processor's rate. On the $3,000 refunded, a $60 fee was paid, but there's no revenue from it.
944.importance: It's used to decide which payment methods to offer customers: instant bank payments cost noticeably less than cards, and installment plans cost more, so shifting some customers from one method to another moves the contribution margin ratio without a single price change. It's also used to decide whether to switch to two-step payment, under which cancellations and refused or unclaimed orders cost no fees. In dollars, fees grow with revenue, and their growth looks normal, while a rising rate means that payment processing itself has become more expensive or refunds have grown. For negotiations, the processor's rate comes from fees divided by all payments: this rate also reflects refunds and taxes, which the processor doesn't control.
944.not_needed: Skip it when customers pay **only by bank transfer against an invoice**: the bank charges no percentage for incoming transfers, and the rate is zero.
944.essence_note: everything paid to the processor for accepting payments is subtracted from every dollar of revenue on the way to contribution margin

945.name: Cost of Returns and Refused or Unclaimed Orders per Order
945.formula: Costs of Refused, Unclaimed and Returned Orders and Items / Kept Orders
945.description: The average cost of returns and refused or unclaimed orders per kept order: picking and shipping what the customer didn't keep, return shipping, receiving and the loss in the value of the goods.
945.nuances:
**Money refunded to the customer** isn't included: it reduces revenue rather than being a cost. Added to costs, it would reduce profit a second time.
**Markdowns and write-offs are calculated from the cost of goods.** An item written off in full is counted at its cost of goods. A markdown below cost goes here only if the item's inventory value was reduced by that amount at receiving. If the item is sold for less at its original cost, the loss shows up in the COGS-to-Revenue Ratio in the month of the sale, and it isn't counted here: otherwise profit would be reduced twice. The difference from the original selling price isn't included: when the item sells for less, it already reduces revenue. [[Total Cost of Returns→vozvraty_tovara/obschaya_stoimost_vozvratov]] calculates the loss from the selling price, and the total there comes out larger.
**Picking and shipping to the customer** for orders that were refused, unclaimed or returned in full go here rather than into the Net Shipping Cost per Order: without them, a refusal costs only the return trip, even though the store also paid for the trip to the customer. For a partially returned order, return shipping, receiving and markdowns of the returned items go here: the order itself was kept, and its shipping to the customer stays in the Net Shipping Cost per Order.
The refused and unclaimed part is close to [[Losses from Refused or Unclaimed Orders→dostavka_zakazov/poteri_iz_za_otkazov]], but that's a monthly total without picking, while here picking is included, and together with returns the total is divided by kept orders.
An order canceled after picking is counted here as an order that wasn't kept: money has already been spent on picking it, and after shipment it also travels back. The accounting system may close such orders with a canceled status, so they're selected by whether they were actually picked and shipped rather than by status. An order canceled before picking has no costs.
What the customer paid for return shipping, or what was withheld from their refund, is subtracted from costs, like the shipping fee in the Net Shipping Cost per Order, so in a profit calculation that uses this metric, revenue is taken without that money.
**Costs are assigned to the month of the original order**: a return that arrives in August for a July order is assigned to July, as is the order itself. So the cost per order for the latest month is understated until the return window has expired.
945.example:
Kept orders for the month: 4,000
Refused, unclaimed and fully returned orders: 600; another 300 items were returned from kept orders
Picking and shipping to the customer for refused, unclaimed and fully returned orders: 600 × 5.80 = $3,480
Return shipping: $4,320
Receiving and inspection: $1,800
Markdowns below cost and write-offs: $2,400
Refunded to customers: $24,000 (not included)

Costs of returns and refused or unclaimed orders = 3,480 + 4,320 + 1,800 + 2,400 = $12,000
Per kept order = 12,000 / 4,000 = **$3**

With refunded money included, it would come out to 36,000 / 4,000 = $9: that money has already been subtracted from revenue, and profit would be reduced by it a second time.
945.importance: It gives the cost of free returns and payment on delivery per kept order. It's used to decide whether to require prepayment or charge for returns, and whether to keep items in the assortment that come back more often than others. As a monthly total, these costs grow with sales, and whether each order is getting more expensive shows only per kept order.
945.not_needed: Skip it for digital goods and services: there's nothing to ship back or mark down, and refunded money isn't included.
945.synonyms: Return Cost per Order, Reverse Logistics Cost per Order
945.essence_note: this is money spent on orders and items that never brought in revenue

946.name: Support Cost per Order
946.formula: Costs of Handling Customer Tickets / Kept Orders
946.description: The average cost of answering customer tickets per kept order.
946.nuances:
**The numerator includes the costs of all customer tickets**: questions before purchase, about delivery, about refused, unclaimed and returned orders. The costs are divided only by kept orders: a kept order also carries the support for purchases that didn't happen. Order confirmation calls and taking orders by phone aren't included, even when the same agents or contractor handle them: such employees' costs are split by share of time.
**The cost components** are the same as in [[Total Support Cost→podderzhka_klientov/rashody_na_podderzhku_klientov]]: salaries with payroll taxes, contractors, licenses for the ticketing system, telephony and the bot; the cost of an employee who answers tickets between other tasks is included by share of time. **Decide** whether to allocate rent and other overhead here. With allocation, cost per order can be compared with a contractor's price, which already includes the contractor's rent, but the number depends on the key used to split rent between departments. Without allocation, the number changes only with the support team's own costs.
**In-house agent pay grows in steps rather than with each order**: staffing is set to cover support's operating hours. During a sales peak, the number falls, and the next month it rises: there are fewer orders, while questions and returns on peak orders are still coming in.
The first figure for a month is overstated: orders from the last days are still in transit and haven't been counted as kept.
946.example:
Pay for 2 agents, including payroll taxes: $8,800
Weekend contractor: $1,400
Ticketing system and telephony: $840
Share of office rent: $1,000 (not counted: the company doesn't allocate overhead to support)
Orders placed in the month: 4,600; kept: 4,000

Support costs = 8,800 + 1,400 + 840 = $11,040
Per kept order = 11,040 / 4,000 = **$2.76**
Tickets in the month: 1,200; per kept order: 1,200 / 4,000 = 0.3
Cost per Ticket = 11,040 / 1,200 = $9.20
Calculated using the two factors: 9.20 × 0.3 = $2.76

Dividing by all placed orders gives 11,040 / 4,600 = $2.40, and the profit calculation per kept order omits $1,440 in support costs: 2.40 × 4,000 = $9,600 instead of $11,040.
946.importance: It shows what customer questions cost each order, and many of them are generated by the order itself: where's my package, when will it arrive, how do I return it. It's used to decide what's cheaper: having agents answer or eliminating the cause of the question by sending delivery status updates, filling out the size chart, simplifying returns. Growth is broken down into two factors: tickets per kept order and [[Cost per Ticket→podderzhka_klientov/stoimost_obrascheniya]]. The first grows when customers ask more often or keep less of what they order; the second grows with salaries and vendor pricing, and, with the same headcount, also when there are fewer tickets.
946.essence_note: the less it costs to answer customers per order, the more is left from each sale

947.name: Orders per Customer per Lifetime Month
947.formula: Customers' Kept Orders / Customers' Lifetime Months, Including Months Without an Order
947.description: How many kept orders a customer places per month on average until they churn, counting months without an order.
947.nuances:
A customer is considered churned after K consecutive months without a kept order; the company chooses K, longer than the usual [[Time Between Orders→zakazy/intervaly_mezhdu_zakazami]]. A lifetime month is a calendar month in which less than K months have passed since the last kept order, so a customer with a single order contributes exactly K lifetime months.
The result depends on K mechanically: **with a larger K, the denominator has more empty months**, and the number is lower even though the orders are the same.
It differs from [[Orders per Customer→crm/zakazov_na_klienta]] in its denominator: there, it's customers who bought during the period; here, it's lifetime months including empty ones, and the more months without an order customers have, the lower the number.
Months after churn don't go into the denominator, so there are fewer lifetime months than months since the first purchase: if you count every month since the first purchase, as in a cohort table, churned customers stay in the denominator. A customer who comes back is no longer considered churned from the month of the new order.
In the monthly figure for the whole customer base, new customers move the result: each of them has an order in their first lifetime month, and the next K − 1 may be empty. An inflow of new customers raises the number in the month they arrive and lowers it in the following months, even though nobody started ordering more or less often. Seasonality works the same way: with K = 4, customers from the November sale with no repeat orders stay in the denominator through February.
An order is one purchase the customer confirmed, however many packages it ships in, and only a kept one counts: paid for, received and not returned in full. An order is assigned to the month it was placed, and the K months are counted from the same date: otherwise the order lands in the numerator of one month and the customer in the denominator of another. Until the return window has closed for the month's last orders, the number is preliminary: if orders that weren't canceled are treated as kept, it's overstated; if you wait for them to be kept, it's understated.
Two accounts belonging to the same person that aren't merged into one customer give more lifetime months than the person has, and the result is understated. It's also understated when some of the person's orders bypass identification, in a physical store or on a marketplace. Orders that couldn't be linked to a customer don't go into the numerator: their lifetime months aren't in the denominator, and with them the result is overstated.
Orders and lifetime months are first summed across all customers and only then divided: the average of individual customers' frequencies gives a different number, in which a customer with one order weighs as much as a regular one. Resellers, group-buy organizers and corporate buyers with dozens of orders a month are excluded using a threshold that's the same in all periods: otherwise a few people raise the average for the whole base.
947.example:
Customers not yet churned in March (K = 4 months): 12,000, which is 12,000 lifetime months
Of those, with a kept order in March: 3,100
Without an order in March: 8,900 (counted: these are lifetime months without an order)
Their kept orders in March: 3,600
Canceled, unclaimed and fully returned: 900 (not counted)
Orders not linked to a customer: 150 (not counted)

Orders per Customer per Lifetime Month = 3,600 / 12,000 = **0.30**

Dividing by the 3,100 customers with a kept order gives 1.16: the months without an order drop out.
With K = 6, there are 14,400 customers not yet churned in March, and the result is 0.25: the same orders, more lifetime months.
947.importance: Together with the [[Average Customer Lifetime→saas_produkty/sredniy_srok_zhizni_klienta]], it gives a customer's number of orders over their entire lifetime: orders per lifetime month multiplied by lifetime months. That's why [[Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)→crm/pozhiznennaya_cennost_klienta_ltv]] needs this metric specifically, alongside the [[Average Order Value (AOV)→zakazy/sredniy_chek_aov]]. If orders per customer who bought in the month are used there instead, LTV is overstated by the ratio of lifetime months to months with an order: the empty months are counted in the lifetime and thrown out of the frequency. Growth for the same customers with the same K means they've started ordering more often while they stay with you: it's used to check whether messaging campaigns, curated collections and reminders bring in orders.
947.not_needed: Skip it when a product is bought once in a lifetime: a wedding dress, wedding rings. Each customer contributes one order per K lifetime months, and the result is almost exactly 1 / K: it shows the chosen window rather than customer behavior. Also skip it where orders follow a recurring delivery schedule: the schedule sets the frequency rather than the customer's decision.
947.essence_note: each extra order per lifetime month adds revenue with no new acquisition costs

948.name: Sessions per Customer per Lifetime Month
948.formula: Customers' Identified Sessions in Their Lifetime Months / Customers' Lifetime Months, Including Months Without Sessions
948.description: How many times per month a customer visits the website or the app on average until they churn, counting months without sessions. Only sessions in which the customer was recognized count.
948.nuances:
A customer is considered churned after K consecutive months without a kept order; the company chooses K, longer than the usual gap between orders. A lifetime month is a calendar month in which less than K months have passed since the last kept order. A customer who comes back is no longer considered churned from the month of the new kept order, and their sessions in that month go into the calculation.
The result depends on K: with a larger K, the calculation includes months when the customer hasn't ordered for a long time and rarely visits, and the number is usually lower.
The denominator includes **all lifetime months, including those without sessions**: dividing by those who visited, as in [[Sessions per User→voronki_prodazh_h4/sessiy_na_posetitelya]], throws out the months without sessions. Sessions of churned customers who kept nothing that month don't count, and neither do sessions of identified people who haven't kept any order yet, such as newsletter subscribers: they have no lifetime months.
An identified session: the customer logged in to their account on the website or in the app, arrived via a link from an email or a push notification, or was recognized by a cookie from an earlier identification. Unidentified sessions are lost, and the metric is lower than the true visit frequency, so its level can't be compared with other stores. A click-through from an email or a push and a logged-in session in the app are always identified, while the same visit made directly, from another device, may not be: the contribution of messaging campaigns and the app is overstated here.
**The share of identified sessions changes with no change in behavior.** In Safari, cookies set by a script last no longer than 7 days, and a customer who visits from an iPhone less than once a week isn't recognized between visits; launching an app, requiring login or adding a new tracker, on the contrary, identifies more customers. If the share of identified sessions shifted in the same month as the metric, that's the cause.
A session ends after 30 minutes of inactivity, the same on the website and in the app: a longer timeout merges visits, and there are fewer sessions. Mobile analytics tools have their own defaults: in some of them, a new session starts if the app was in the background for more than 10 seconds, and a customer who switches to a banking app to pay produces two sessions. Such sessions added to website sessions overstate the metric. Background sessions in which the customer didn't open the app don't count as sessions.
In the month of the first order, there are always sessions: a newcomer had to visit to buy, and a session with an order is almost always identified. So across the whole base, the metric grows with an inflow of new customers with no change among the rest; for cohorts at the same age since the first order, there's no such shift.
Sessions also include visits about an order already placed: checking its status, starting a return. They grow when orders are late or get returned, and the metric grows from problems rather than from interest in the store.
A few accounts with hundreds of sessions a month shift the average: employees' test accounts, resellers, scripts that track prices from a customer's account. Email security scanners on corporate mailboxes follow links in an email before the recipient does, and such a click is identified as the customer's session at the time of the send.
The number for the latest month is preliminary: for a newcomer or a returning customer, the lifetime month exists only because of an order from that same month, and if the order is refused, goes unclaimed or is returned in full, the customer drops out of the month along with their sessions. Two accounts of one person that aren't merged into one customer add extra lifetime months and split the sessions, and the result is understated.
948.example:
Customers not yet churned in March (K = 4 months): 12,000, which is 12,000 lifetime months
Among them, 900 March newcomers and 150 who came back after churning: March is a lifetime month for them too
Their identified sessions in March: 18,000
Sessions of churned customers who kept nothing in March: 1,100 (not counted)
Sessions of subscribers and registered users who haven't kept any order yet: 2,400 (not counted)
Visited at least once in March: 6,800

Sessions per Customer per Lifetime Month = 18,000 / 12,000 = **1.5**

Dividing by the 6,800 who visited gives 2.6: the months without sessions drop out.
With K = 6, there are 14,400 customers not yet churned in March, with 18,700 identified sessions, and the result is 1.30: lifetime months grew more than sessions.
948.importance: It shows how often a customer visits the store while they're with you, with or without an order. This is where you see first whether messaging campaigns, push notifications and the app bring them back: an email with a reason to visit produces a session the same day, even if no order follows. It's used to decide whether customers have enough reasons to come back between orders: curated collections, replenishment reminders, promotions for existing customers.
948.not_needed: Skip it where customers mostly order outside the store's own website and app: in a physical store with a loyalty card, by phone, via messaging apps, through auto-replenishment, on marketplaces. Their lifetime months sit in the denominator with no sessions, and the number shows the share of customers who visit online rather than how often a customer comes back.
948.essence_note: every visit by a customer is another chance for an order

949.name: Session-to-Placed-Order Rate
949.description: How many placed orders there are per hundred sessions on the website or in the app.
949.nuances:
**An order isn't tied to a specific session**: orders placed on the website and in the app are divided by all sessions in the same period. Orders by phone, through a sales rep and auto-reorders don't go into the numerator: they have no session, and with them the rate would grow with no change on the website. Sessions come from the tracker and orders from the store's database: sessions hidden by ad blockers drop out of the denominator only, and the rate is overstated.
Both parts are taken for the same people: if the denominator has only customers' identified sessions, the numerator has those same customers' orders; if it has all sessions, then all orders.
Calculated on identified sessions, **the rate is overstated**: a session with an order is almost always identified, because at checkout the customer logs in or enters a phone number, while a session without an order is identified only if the customer logged in or was recognized by a cookie. The effect is strongest for new customers: almost all of their sessions before the first order are unidentified, and an inflow of new customers raises the rate with no change on the website. The more sessions without an order are identified, the lower the number: login by phone number lowers it, and cookies cleared by the browser raise it. If customers hardly ever log in, the identified sessions are mostly those with an order, and the number loses its meaning.
A placed order is the same as in the Placed-to-Kept Order Rate: the customer clicked “Place order,” even if the payment later failed or the agent couldn't reach them by phone to confirm. Orders later canceled or left unclaimed aren't removed from the numerator, while duplicates, test orders and an order recreated after a payment failure are removed: they don't reflect a customer's decision.
The [[Ecommerce Conversion Rate→zakazy/konversiya_v_zakaz]] is calculated differently: it divides orders paid during the session by all website sessions, and with payment on delivery it's noticeably lower. The conversion rate in GA4 is another number too: it's the share of sessions in which the purchase key event fired, and all sessions are counted rather than only identified ones.
A session is the same as in Sessions per Customer per Lifetime Month: **it ends after 30 minutes of inactivity, on the website and in the app alike**. With 60 minutes, there are fewer sessions, and the rate is higher without any changes on the website. In some mobile analytics tools, an app session ends by default after 10 seconds in the background: with such sessions, the same visits produce more app sessions, and as the app's share grows, the rate falls with no change in behavior.
949.example:
Identified customer sessions in March: 18,000
Orders placed by the same customers on the website and in the app: 4,500, of which 750 were later canceled or left unclaimed
Orders by the same customers by phone: 200 (not counted)

Session-to-Placed-Order Rate = 4,500 / 18,000 × 100 = **25%**

Dividing by all 140,000 website sessions gives 3.2%: the denominator has everyone's sessions, including people who haven't bought yet and unidentified ones, while the numerator has orders of identified customers only.
949.importance: When orders per customer decline, it shows where the loss is: customers visit less often, or they visit and leave without ordering. In the second case, the cause is on the website or in the assortment: search doesn't find what customers want, the product they need is out of stock, checkout is too long. It's also used to check changes to the catalog and the cart: in regular customers' sessions, the change shows up earlier than in revenue.
949.not_needed: Skip it when most orders are placed outside the website and the app: by phone, through a sales rep, as auto-reorders. The rate then describes a small part of sales.
949.synonyms: Orders per 100 Sessions, Session Conversion Rate
949.essence_note: with the same number of customer visits, the store gets more orders

950.name: Placed-to-Kept Order Rate
950.description: The share of placed orders that were kept: the customer paid for the order, received it and didn't return it in full. Canceled, unpaid, unclaimed and fully returned orders don't count as kept.
950.nuances:
Orders are counted rather than units, and an order **returned in full after receipt isn't kept**. The [[Marketplace Kept Order Rate→marketpleysy/vykupa]] follows different rules: it counts units, leaves orders canceled before shipment out of the base, and a return after receipt still counts as kept.
An order in which the customer kept at least one item is kept: rejecting part of it reduces the order's revenue rather than the number of kept orders. An order in which only the paid shipping remains, with no products, doesn't count as kept. In apparel and footwear, when customers order two sizes and keep one, the order-level rate is high, and the losses show only when you count units.
A canceled order isn't kept, whoever canceled it: the customer changed their mind, or the store couldn't find the item in the warehouse. An order that was never paid and that the system closed when the payment window ran out isn't kept either, even though it usually isn't classified as canceled. Orders canceled before shipping are in the denominator, so the rate is lower than in the carrier's report, which sees only shipped orders.
An order is placed when the customer clicks “Place order,” even if the payment later fails or the agent can't reach them by phone to confirm. Duplicates, test orders and an order recreated after a payment failure are removed from both numbers. A size exchange processed as a return and a new order is counted as one kept order.
Full returns are counted through every path: via a pickup point, a courier or a physical store. A return accepted in a store and not linked to the order leaves the order counted as kept, and the rate is overstated.
Both numbers are assigned to periods by order date: an order placed in March and received in April counts toward March's kept orders. If kept orders are assigned by date of receipt, the rate depends on delivery speed: in the month after a sale, it's overstated and can exceed 100%.
**The rate for a recent period is understated**: orders still in transit or waiting at a pickup point are already in the denominator but not in the numerator. If such orders are excluded, the rate is overstated instead: an order that gets picked up closes quickly, while an unclaimed one closes only after the holding period ends. So the period is closed after a lag that's the same for all periods: delivery, the holding period at the pickup point and the return window for non-defective goods. The closed period isn't recalculated for returns of defective items after that lag.
The rate also changes with the order mix: a growing share of orders with payment on delivery, with pickup-point delivery, from remote regions or from new customers lowers it, even though the kept rate within each group is unchanged. Requiring prepayment raises the rate even when the number of kept orders falls: some customers stop placing orders. A confirmation call turns future unclaimed orders into cancellations, and the rate barely changes, even though the cost of refused and unclaimed orders goes down.
950.example:
Orders placed in March: 4,500
Canceled by the customer or the store: 220
Not paid and closed when the payment window ran out: 80
Unclaimed: 450
Returned in full: 150
Returned in part: 90 (still kept)
Kept = 4,500 − 220 − 80 − 450 − 150 = 3,600

Placed-to-Kept Order Rate = 3,600 / 4,500 × 100 = **80%**

Counting fully returned orders as kept, for example by the delivery status “Delivered,” gives 83%: the customer returned everything, but the order is counted.
