950.importance: An order that isn't kept may already have been picked, shipped and brought back, and the store gets no money for it: at an 80% rate, one placed order in five brings in nothing. It's used to decide whether to send reminders about an order waiting at a pickup point, and in which delivery methods, with which carriers and in which categories to look for losses. A drop in the kept rate lowers orders per customer even when customers visit and place orders just as often.
950.not_needed: Skip it for digital goods and services delivered instantly and for purchases at a store register: the customer pays for and receives the purchase at the same time, and keeping the order coincides with payment. Skip it for sales through marketplaces: the seller doesn't see the customer's whole order, and on some marketplaces each unit ships as a separate order. There, the rate is counted in units: that's the [[Marketplace Kept Order Rate→marketpleysy/vykupa]].
950.essence_note: only orders the customer received and kept bring the store money

951.name: Contactable Customer Rate
951.formula: Customers with Active Marketing Consent and Valid Contact Details in at Least One Channel / Customers × 100
951.description: The share of customers who haven't churned yet and can receive the store's messaging campaigns: the customer gave consent in at least one channel, hasn't unsubscribed, and messages reach them.
951.nuances:
Customers in both parts are those who haven't churned yet, that is, whose last kept order was less than K months ago. The company sets K itself, making it longer than the usual gap between orders. With churned customers included, the rate would depend on the age of the base: for those who stopped buying years ago, contact details go stale and consent is withdrawn more often.
Consent is usually requested with the first order, while unsubscribes and dead addresses accumulate over time. So **an inflow of new customers raises the rate**, and a slowdown in it lowers the rate, even though consent is handled the same way.
Only customers go into the numerator: **subscribers and people who allowed push notifications without a single kept order aren't counted**. If you take the whole subscriber base from [[Total Subscribers→e_mail_marketing/vsego_podpischikov]], the rate is overstated and can exceed 100%.
It's calculated as of a date: consent is active if the customer gave it and hadn't withdrawn it by that day. Consent counts only if the customer **gave it separately and actively**: checked an empty box or confirmed the subscription. Consent buried in the terms of sale and a pre-checked box aren't valid opt-ins, and with them the rate is overstated: nearly every customer with contact details ends up in the numerator. A change in the consent form makes the rate jump for new customers.
For push notifications, **permission for notifications on the phone isn't the same as marketing consent**: on Android versions before 13, notifications are on without asking, and using permission instead of consent makes the rate higher.
Contact details must be valid: emails don't hard bounce, push notifications reach the device, the phone number is in service. Consent for an address that messages don't reach is useless, and counting it overstates the rate. Customers who haven't opened emails in a long time stay in the numerator: messages still reach them. Without them, the rate describes those who read the campaigns rather than everyone you can message. You can verify contact details only by sending a message: an address you haven't emailed in a long time counts as valid until a message bounces, and the rate is overstated. The same goes for addresses the store itself suppressed from campaigns for inactivity: their consent remains, but there's no way to check the address.
**Transactional order notifications don't count as consent**: every customer receives them, and they don't give permission to send marketing through that channel.
A customer is counted once, however many channels they have. Consent is linked to the customer by contact details: a subscription with a different address, or push consent the customer gave before logging in to the app, won't be linked to them, and the rate is understated.
951.example:
Customers not churned as of March 31: 12,000
Churned customers whose consent is still active: 3,100 (not counted)
Subscribers and people who allowed push notifications without a single kept order: 9,800 (not counted)
Of the 12,000, gave separate consent to marketing by email or push: 8,400
Unsubscribed from everything: 700 (not counted)
Of the rest, emails hard bounce and there's no push channel: 500 (not counted)
With active consent and valid contact details: 7,200

Contactable Customer Rate = 7,200 / 12,000 × 100 = **60%**

Adding up active consents with valid contact details by channel, 5,900 for email and 4,100 for push, gives 83%: customers with two channels are counted twice.
951.importance: It determines how many customers the store can bring back on its own: the post-purchase series, the repeat-purchase reminder and product picks reach only this share. At 60%, they can reach six customers in ten, and the rest have to be brought back with paid ads targeting the store's own customer base. It's used to decide whether to keep the signup bonus, the consent request at checkout and the push permission prompt in the app.
951.not_needed: Skip it when you sell only through marketplaces: the marketplace doesn't give the seller customer contacts, and there's no one to reach with your own messaging campaigns.
951.essence_note: the store can message a customer with consent on its own, without paying for impressions

952.name: Second Order Rate
952.formula: Customers Who Placed a Second Kept Order Within K Months of the First / Customers with a First Kept Order × 100
952.description: The share of new customers who place a second kept order within K months of the first. Those who don't come back within that time are considered churned.
952.nuances:
Customers are grouped by the month in which their first kept order was placed, and only those whose K window has already closed are included. **Newcomers with an open window understate the rate**: many of them haven't placed their second order yet. If the accounting system dates a sale by shipment or delivery, an order placed in late November becomes a December sale, and the customer lands in the wrong cohort.
The K window is the same one after which a customer with no orders is considered churned; the company sets it itself, making it longer than the usual gap between orders. Each customer's window is counted from the date of their first order. The rate depends on K mechanically: for the same customers, it's higher with a 6-month window than with a 3-month one.
It differs from the [[Repeat Purchase Rate→crm/koefficient_uderzhaniya]] in its base and window: there, the base is everyone who bought during the period, new and existing customers, and both purchases must fall within the period; here, only new customers count, and the window is counted from each customer's first order. A customer with orders on December 20 and January 10 won't get into the numerator there for either December or January, but here they will. An influx of newcomers pulls that rate down: those who arrive at the end of the period don't have time to come back.
The first order is the first kept order: if a customer left their very first order unclaimed or returned it in full, the count starts from the next one. A customer is a newcomer only if they had no earlier kept orders, so the full history is needed: if the orders in the database start with a migration to a new system, existing customers look like newcomers in the first months after it, come back more often than real newcomers, and the rate for those months is overstated.
A customer must be recognized in all of their orders. A second order under a different phone number or email, not merged with the first, turns a returning customer into two newcomers: the first order's cohort gets no second order, the second order's cohort has an extra newcomer, and the rate is understated in both. A second order is also lost where the customer can't be recognized: a customer who came back through a marketplace didn't come back as far as the website is concerned, and the more sales move to marketplaces, the lower the website's rate.
The second order must also be kept, so the rate for a month's newcomers becomes final once the orders at the end of the window have been delivered, unclaimed ones have come back from pickup points, and the return window for received ones has expired: with K = 4, November's newcomers give a final number only in May. The return window is the one the store offers for non-defective goods; returns of defective items that arrive later no longer change the number.
An order the store split into several shipments remains one order. **Orders placed on the same day as the first are merged with it**: a follow-up order for a forgotten item doesn't count as a second order, since the customer hasn't come back yet. If it's counted, the rate grows without a single customer coming back, most of all where a second-order coupon can be used right away: the customer splits the cart into two orders.
A second order isn't always the customer coming back. Auto-reorders and product subscriptions place it on a schedule, and the rate grows with the share of customers who set them up with their first order. In apparel and footwear, it can be a size exchange: the item from the first order was returned and the same model was ordered in a different size.
Cohorts differ in composition: newcomers who came for a first-order discount come back for a second order less often, and their share in a month moves the rate even when you engage newcomers the same way.
952.example:
First kept order in November: 2,000 customers, K = 4 months
All windows closed by the end of March, March orders have been delivered, and their return window has expired
Second kept order within 4 months of each customer's first order: 560
Second order after each customer's 4-month window, including in March for those who first bought in early November: 60 (not counted)
Only a follow-up order on the day of the first order, no other orders in the window: 45 (not counted)

Second Order Rate = 560 / 2,000 × 100 = **28%**

Adding 2,300 February newcomers with an open window and their 400 second orders gives 22%: many of them haven't placed their second order yet.
952.importance: The second order is the turning point for a customer: without it, the acquisition cost has to be paid back by a single order, unless the customer comes back later. It's used to decide whether the welcome series, the second-order coupon and product picks based on the first purchase work, by comparing newcomers who were sent them with newcomers from the same month who weren't. At a 28% rate, almost three newcomers in four leave after their very first order.
952.not_needed: Skip it for products bought once every few years: furniture, major appliances. K has to be set in years, and the rate describes customers who arrived years ago rather than how you engage newcomers now. Also skip it where the product itself rules out a second purchase: a wedding dress, a prom suit. The rate is close to zero no matter how you engage newcomers.
952.synonyms: Second Purchase Rate, Second Order Conversion Rate
952.essence_note: the second order comes from a customer whose acquisition has already been paid for

953.name: Repeat Customer Churn Rate
953.formula: Repeat Customers Who Churned in the Month / Repeat Customers Not Churned by the Start of the Month × 100
953.description: The share of repeat customers, those with at least two kept orders, who churn in a month. A customer is considered churned after K consecutive months without a kept order.
953.nuances:
Not churned by the start of the month: repeat customers whose last kept order was less than K months before the end of the previous month. Churned in the month: those of them who reached K consecutive months without a kept order in this month.
Customers with one order aren't included: their churn is shown by the Second Order Rate. With them, churn comes out higher: newcomers who don't come back after their first order push it up and obscure the churn of regular customers.
A customer becomes a repeat customer **with a second kept order placed on a different day from the first**: a same-day follow-up order is merged with the first order, as in the Second Order Rate.
It differs from the [[Customer Churn Rate→crm/ottok_klientov]] in its base: there, the denominator is customers who bought in the previous period; here, it's all repeat customers who haven't churned yet, including those who ordered nothing last month. That's why monthly churn here can be calculated with any K, even six months: the numerator includes only those whose window expired in this particular month.
The company sets K itself, making it longer than the usual gap between orders. Churn depends on it mechanically: **the larger K, the lower the monthly churn**, because more customers manage to come back before they're counted as churned. If K is shorter than the actual gap between orders, churn is overstated: a customer who buys once a year for the season churns and comes back every year when K is less than 12 months.
Churn is recorded **K months after the last order**: with K = 4, March churn describes customers who stopped ordering in November, and seasonality shows up in churn with a lag of K months. A customer who placed a second order enters the denominator from the next month and can't churn until K months have passed without an order: after a strong season, churn first falls and then jumps K months later, even though customers are handled the same way.
An order is assigned to the month it was placed. A month's churn stays preliminary until delivery and the return window are over for its orders: if you wait for orders to be kept, a customer with an order in transit may be counted as churned, and churn is overstated; if you treat orders that weren't canceled as kept, an order that later goes unclaimed or is returned in full keeps the customer among those not churned, and churn is understated.
Orders not linked to the customer are lost: a second account, a guest order with a different email, a purchase in a physical store or on a marketplace. A customer who keeps buying this way is counted as churned, so **churn is overstated**, and the gap grows with the number of orders that go unidentified. Two unmerged accounts of one person split their orders, and some repeat customers fall into the group with one order.
A customer who comes back after churning is back among those not churned from the month of the new order, and their past churn isn't removed from the calculation.
953.example:
Repeat customers not churned by March 1: 5,000, K = 4 months
Reached 4 consecutive months without a kept order in March: 350
Became repeat customers in March: 400 (not in March's denominator)

Repeat Customer Churn Rate = 350 / 5,000 × 100 = **7%**

Adding 7,000 customers with one order and the 1,440 of them who churned gives 15%: newcomers' churn obscures the churn of regular customers.
953.importance: It sets the lifetime of the regular customer base: with monthly churn averaging 7% over the year, a repeat customer stays with the store about 14 months; at 5%, about 20. A two-percentage-point decrease makes regular customers stay almost one and a half times longer, and [[Customer Lifetime Value (LTV)→crm/pozhiznennaya_cennost_klienta_ltv]] grows along with it. It shows whether repeat customers' churn changes after purchase-cycle reminders and personalized picks sent before the customer reaches K months without an order.
953.not_needed: Skip it where purchases are infrequent by nature, as with furniture and major appliances: K is measured in years there, and churn is recorded years after the last purchase.
953.synonyms: Repeat Buyer Churn Rate, Repeat Customer Attrition Rate
953.essence_note: every regular customer who churns takes away the orders they would have continued to place

954.name: Order CSAT
954.formula: Order Ratings of 4 and 5 / All Order Ratings Received × 100
954.description: The share of positive ratings among all ratings customers gave to orders they received. A rating on a 1-to-5 scale is requested after every order received.
954.nuances:
Positive means a rating of 4 or 5 on a five-point scale; a 3 doesn't go into the numerator. A change of scale or question starts the series over: a binary “liked it or not” scale has no neutral option, and the share of satisfied customers is higher for the same orders. The average star rating moves differently: ratings shifting from 5 to 4 lower it but don't change the share.
The denominator includes only ratings received. Dividing by all orders received gives the share of orders with a good rating rather than satisfaction. The response rate also moves the result: customers with a strong impression, good or bad, are more willing to respond, and a new survey channel, a reminder or points for responding shift the percentage for the same orders.
**Unit of count: an order rating** rather than a customer. A customer who received four orders in a month and rated each one gives four ratings, and frequent buyers carry more weight than infrequent ones. If the survey is frequency-capped, for example no more than once a month per customer, frequent buyers carry less weight, and changing this rule shifts the number for the same orders.
**An order has one rating, the first.** A rating changed after a call or email from the store measures the call rather than the order: if you take the latest one, the metric grows faster the harder customers are pressed to change it. An order that arrived in several shipments is rated once, after the last one. A batch of ratings for one order in the same second comes from an email program that opens every link in the message rather than from the customer: such ratings aren't counted.
First orders are usually rated lower than repeat ones: second orders come from those who liked the first. So the overall number rises with the share of repeat orders and dips in a month of heavy advertising, even though the products and delivery are the same.
The order is rated as a whole: product, delivery, packaging. An answer to a separate question about delivery belongs to [[Delivery CSAT→dostavka_zakazov/udovletvorennost_dostavkoy]], stars in a product review belong to the [[Share of Positive Reviews→assortiment/polozhitelnyh_otzyvov]], and they don't go here. Nor do ratings after support tickets, even if the ticket was about this order: they rate the conversation with support and are counted by the [[Customer Satisfaction Score (CSAT)→podderzhka_klientov/indeks_udovletvorennosti_klientov_csat]].
Orders that didn't reach the customer **get no survey**: those canceled because of a delay, left unclaimed at a pickup point, or lost. Yet these orders belong to the most dissatisfied customers, and in a month of delivery failures, satisfaction can hold steady while the share of orders that never arrived grows.
The timing of the survey changes the result: right after receipt, customers rate delivery and packaging; later on, the product itself. The survey goes out a set time after delivery, the same in every month: if it's timed from shipment, some customers rate an order that hasn't arrived yet, and the longer delivery takes, the more such ratings. A rating is assigned to the month the order was received, and the month's number stays preliminary until the survey response window has expired.
954.example:
Orders received in March: 3,750
Rated: 600
Of those, 4 or 5: 492
Rated 3: 48 (not in the numerator)
Ratings after support tickets about these orders: 85 (not counted)

Order CSAT = 492 / 600 × 100 = **82%**
Response rate = 600 / 3,750 × 100 = 16%

Dividing by all 3,750 orders received gives 13%: customers who didn't respond are counted as dissatisfied, and the number will grow with every survey reminder rather than with order quality.
954.importance: It's the first signal that customers may not come back: a bad rating arrives in the first days after the order is received, while churn becomes visible only after months without orders. It's used to decide which cause of dissatisfaction to fix first, such as a product that doesn't match the photo, a delay or damaged packaging, and to check whether the fix helped.
954.not_needed: Skip it when there are fewer than a hundred ratings a month: random variation in the rate then exceeds ±7 percentage points, and a real change can't be told apart from a random one.
954.essence_note: a customer satisfied with an order is more willing to come back for the next one

955.name: Loyalty Program Enrollment Rate
955.formula: Customers Registered in the Loyalty Program / Customers × 100
955.description: The share of customers who haven't churned yet and are registered in the loyalty program.
955.nuances:
Customers in both parts are those who haven't churned yet, that is, whose last kept order was less than K months ago. The company sets K itself, making it longer than the usual gap between orders. Churned customers stay in the program long after they stop buying, and with them the rate describes the base's whole history rather than current customers. The rate depends on K: with a short K, mostly frequent buyers remain, there are more members among them, and the rate is higher.
A member is someone who registered in the program, that is, linked a card or an app profile to a phone number or email. A cardholder without registration isn't a member: points build up on the card, but who's behind it is unknown, and it can't be matched to orders. Whether the member has earned points recently doesn't matter for the rate.
Only members who are customers themselves go into the numerator: **those who registered without a single kept order aren't counted**. If you take all [[Loyalty Members→programma_loyalnosti/uchastniki_programmy]], the rate can exceed 100%.
**A customer is identified by the account or contact details in the order rather than through the program itself.** Anyone visible only through a card or a phone number given at the register to earn points always turns out to be a member, and with such customers the rate is overstated. In a chain with physical stores, the rate is calculated for customers with orders on the website and in the app.
A member and a customer are matched as one person by phone number or email rather than by the card in the order: a person can have several cards, and a card from a store may not be linked to the website account. An unmatched person is counted twice, as a customer outside the program and as a member without purchases, and the rate comes out understated.
If customers **are enrolled when they create an account**, the rate equals the share of customers with an account: it moves with whether you can order without registering rather than with the program's terms. A “Join” checkbox checked by default works the same way. Switching on such enrollment breaks the series.
People are counted rather than orders. In retail, “member share” and program “penetration” often refer to the share of receipts or revenue with a loyalty card: that's a different number, and it's usually higher because members order more often.
An inflow of new customers lowers the rate: a newcomer was invited to join once, with the first order, while an existing customer was invited with every order. After a big promotion for new customers, the rate drops for up to K months, even though nothing changed in the program.
It's calculated as of a date: a member is someone who is in the program on that day. Deleted and blocked profiles aren't counted. Past dates need the registration date: with the current “member” flag, people who joined later get into past months, and the rate for the past is overstated. The join date is the registration date rather than the date the card was issued.
955.example:
Customers not churned as of March 31 (K = 6 months): 12,000
Of those, registered in the program: 5,400
Program members without a single kept order: 2,100 (not counted)
Members who churned as customers: 6,500 (not counted)

Loyalty Program Enrollment Rate = 5,400 / 12,000 × 100 = **45%**

Dividing all 14,000 program members by 12,000 customers gives 117%: the numerator has people who aren't in the denominator.
955.importance: It's used to decide whether to build program enrollment into the first order and how much to simplify the rules for points and tiers. The rate shows what share of customers the program budget, personalized offers and member promotions reach at all: at 45%, more than half of customers don't get them.
955.not_needed: Skip it when everyone who places an order is enrolled automatically: the rate is always 100% and doesn't tell any groups apart. Skip it for physical stores where a customer is recognized only by a card or a phone number at the register: purchases outside the program are anonymous, and for the same reason the rate is close to 100%. In stores, the program's reach is shown by the share of receipts with a card. Skip it for invitation-only programs that people are invited to based on purchase volume or a company decision: the rate is set by the threshold rather than by customers' wishes.
955.synonyms: Loyalty Program Participation Rate, Member Enrollment Rate
955.essence_note: a member benefits from buying at this store specifically, and switching to another store costs them more; default enrollment raises the rate by adding people who don't know about the program

956.name: Repeat Customer Purchase Rate
956.formula: Regular Customers Not Churned by the Start of the Period Who Placed a Kept Order in the Period / Regular Customers Not Churned by the Start of the Period × 100
956.description: The share of regular customers who hadn't churned by the start of the period and placed a kept order during the period. A customer becomes regular with their second kept order and is considered churned after K consecutive months without a kept order.
956.nuances:
The base is the same as in the [[Repeat Customer Churn Rate→ltv/ottok_povtornyh_pokupateley]]: “repeat” there means “bought more than once,” as “regular” does here.
The denominator includes regular customers whose last kept order was less than K months before the start of the period. A customer who becomes regular during the period enters the denominator from the next period, and one who churns during the period stays in this period's denominator.
A customer becomes regular **with a second kept order placed on a different day from the first**: a same-day follow-up order for a forgotten item is merged with the first order. If it's counted, the denominator picks up newcomers who haven't come back yet. They buy less often than regular customers, and the rate is understated.
The rate depends on K mechanically: **the larger K, the lower the rate**, because customers who haven't ordered for many months stay in the denominator longer.
**The length of the period changes the rate mechanically**: more regular customers manage to buy in a quarter than in a month. With a period of K or longer, a regular customer who didn't buy during the period has already churned by its end, and the rate no longer shows inactivity before churn.
An order is assigned to the period by its order date. A period's rate stays preliminary until delivery and the return window are over for its orders: if you wait for orders to be kept, a customer with an order in transit doesn't get into the numerator, and the rate is understated; if you treat orders that weren't canceled as kept, an order that later goes unclaimed or is returned in full keeps the customer in the numerator, and the rate is overstated.
Orders under a second account, as a guest with a different email, in a store without a card or on a marketplace aren't linked to the customer. A regular customer who buys this way is counted as not having bought, while their second account is counted as a newcomer and isn't in the denominator: **the rate is understated**, and the gap grows with the number of orders that can't be linked to a customer.
The rate also grows with no change in how you engage regular customers when infrequent buyers churn: those who buy more often remain in the denominator.
956.example:
Regular customers not churned by March 1: 5,000, K = 4 months
Placed a kept order in March: 3,000
Didn't buy in March: 2,000; of those, 350 reached 4 months without an order in March (they hadn't churned by March 1 and stay in the denominator)
Became regular in March: 400 (not in March's denominator)

Repeat Customer Purchase Rate = 3,000 / 5,000 × 100 = **60%**

3,000 regular customers, 150 newcomers who came back for a second order and 450 customers who came back after churning make up March's 3,600 Repeat Customers.
956.importance: It shows regular customers going inactive in the same month, while the [[Repeat Customer Churn Rate→ltv/ottok_povtornyh_pokupateley]] records churn only after K months without an order. It's used to check purchase prompts for regular customers who are still within their usual cycle, such as purchase-cycle reminders and product picks: it shows whether they work sooner than churn does. Without it, growth in [[Repeat Customers→crm/povtornye_klienty]] driven by returning newcomers and churned customers hides that regular customers have started buying less often.
956.not_needed: Skip it for products bought once every few years, such as furniture and major appliances: K is measured in years, and only a small share of regular customers buys in a month or a quarter no matter how you engage them.
956.essence_note: every regular customer who buys brings in revenue for the period and pushes their churn back another K months

957.name: Sessions per Customer
957.formula: Identified Sessions of Active Customers on the Website and in the App for the Period / [[Active Customers→crm/aktivnye_klienty]] for the Period
957.description: How many identified sessions on the website and in the app there are on average per customer who bought during the period.
957.nuances:
The denominator includes **everyone who bought during the period**, including those who bought only in a physical store with a card or ordered by phone: they have no sessions. The larger the share of such customers, the lower the number, even if everyone else visits just as often.
The numerator includes only sessions of customers in the denominator: sessions of people who bought nothing during the period don't count, even if the person is identified.
A purchase means an order the customer kept, as in [[Orders per Customer→crm/zakazov_na_klienta]]: a customer whose orders for the period were all fully returned or left unclaimed isn't in the denominator, and their sessions aren't in the numerator.
Only **identified** sessions count: the customer logged in to their account, provided a phone number or was recognized by a cookie. Login by phone number raises the number, and cookies cleared by the browser lower it, even though customers visit just as often. If the analytics system attributes sessions before login to the customer, there are more sessions than without such attribution. Without attribution, new customers' sessions are most likely to be missed: before the first order, almost all of them are unidentified, and an inflow of new customers lowers the number.
A session **ends after 30 minutes of inactivity on both the website and the app**, as in [[Session-to-Placed-Order Rate→ltv/konversiya_vizita_v_oformlennyy_zakaz]]. In some mobile analytics tools, an app session ends by default after 10 seconds in the background: with such sessions, the same visits produce more sessions, and as the app's share grows, the number grows with no change in behavior.
Sessions hidden by ad blockers don't reach the tracker, and the number is understated.
**The length of the period changes the result mechanically**: there are more sessions per customer over a quarter than over a month.
957.example:
Active customers in March: 4,800
Identified sessions of these customers on the website and in the app in March: 30,000
Customers who bought in March only in a store with a card or by phone: they have no sessions but stay in the denominator
Sessions of identified shoppers who didn't buy in March: not counted

Sessions per Customer = 30,000 / 4,800 = **6.25**

Cross-check with Orders per Customer: these customers' 30,000 sessions produced 7,500 placed orders and 6,000 kept orders
Kept orders from the website and the app per customer = 6,000 / 4,800 = 1.25
Another 800 orders without a session, by phone and in store, give 800 / 4,800 = 0.17 per customer, 1.42 in total.
In the metric tree, this number is calculated for returning customers: sessions, placed orders and kept orders are taken for the same customers, those who bought in March and had bought before. If the conversion and kept-order rates are calculated across everyone who has ever bought, they include sessions of people who didn't buy in March, and the product comes out lower even though behavior didn't change.
957.importance: It separates two reasons why a customer started ordering less often: they visit less often, or they visit but don't order. If sessions per customer are down while the [[Session-to-Placed-Order Rate→ltv/konversiya_vizita_v_oformlennyy_zakaz]] is unchanged, look at what prompts customers to visit: messaging campaigns, push notifications, reminders timed to the purchase cycle. Changes to the catalog and the cart won't stop such a decline.
957.not_needed: Skip it when the store has no website or app, or almost all sales happen in physical stores or by phone: most customers have no sessions, and the number describes only a small share of customers. Also skip it where customers almost never log in to their account: there are few identified sessions, and the number is understated at any visit frequency.
957.essence_note: every new visit gives the store another chance to sell to the customer

958.name: Customer Reactivation Rate
958.formula: Customers Churned by the Start of the Period Who Placed a Kept Order in the Period / Customers Churned by the Start of the Period × 100
958.description: The share of customers who had churned by the start of the period and came back to place a kept order during the period. A customer is considered churned after K consecutive months without a kept order, however many orders they had before.
958.nuances:
It differs from [[Lost Customers→crm/poteryannye_klienty]] in who counts as churned. There, churned customers are those who bought in the period before the inactivity window and didn't buy during the window, and a customer who bought once long ago isn't counted as lost. Here, a churned customer is anyone who has reached K consecutive months without a kept order, including customers with a single order, no matter how long ago they churned. If you take the ready-made Lost Customers count as the denominator, one-time buyers and customers who churned long ago drop out of it, and the rate comes out higher.
The denominator **isn't limited** by how long ago customers churned: otherwise, a customer who churned long ago and comes back gets into neither the numerator nor the denominator. As a result, churned customers keep accumulating, and **the rate falls as the base ages and as the share of one-time buyers in it grows**: those who bought once during a promotion in past years rarely come back. Two stores that engage churned customers the same way get different rates if one has an older base.
The smaller K, the sooner a customer is counted as churned: the denominator has more customers who stopped buying recently, and they come back more often than those who churned long ago, so **the rate is higher**. K is the same as in the [[Second Order Rate→ltv/konversiya_vo_vtoroy_zakaz]] and the [[Repeat Customer Churn Rate→ltv/ottok_povtornyh_pokupateley]].
An order is assigned to the period by its order date. A period's rate stays preliminary until delivery and the return window are over for its orders: if you wait for orders to be kept, a returning customer with an order in transit doesn't get into the numerator, and **the rate is understated**; if you treat orders that weren't canceled as kept, a returning customer who later leaves the order unclaimed or returns it in full stays in the numerator, and **the rate is overstated**.
The full order history is needed. If it starts with a migration to a new system, customers who churned before the migration don't get into the denominator, and those of them who come back look like newcomers. The customers who churned longest ago drop out, and they come back least often, so the rate is overstated.
A customer who comes back under a new phone number or email and isn't merged with their past orders counts as a newcomer, and one who comes back through a marketplace hasn't come back at all as far as the store is concerned: **the rate is understated**.
**The length of the period changes the rate mechanically**: more churned customers manage to come back in a quarter than in a month.
958.example:
Customers churned by March 1: 18,000, K = 4 months
Placed a kept order in March: 450

Customer Reactivation Rate = 450 / 18,000 × 100 = **2.5%**

By April 1, the 450 returning customers will leave the denominator, and 350 regular customers who churned in March will enter it, along with newcomers who reached 4 months without a second order in March.
450 customers who came back after churning, 3,000 regular customers who bought in March and 150 newcomers who came back for a second order make up March's 3,600 Repeat Customers.
958.importance: It's used to evaluate campaigns to bring customers back: emails and offers to churned customers, reminders about points in their accounts. Churned customers whom the campaign reached are compared with similar churned customers it didn't reach. Without this rate, reactivated customers get mixed with regular ones in [[Repeat Customers→crm/povtornye_klienty]], and growth after a campaign to bring customers back can't be told apart from regular customers' usual purchases.
958.not_needed: Skip it for products that by nature are bought once: a wedding dress, a prom suit. Almost all churned customers there are one-time buyers, and the rate is close to zero no matter how you engage them.
958.essence_note: every customer who comes back brings back revenue the store had already written off along with them

960.name: Lead Contact Rate
960.description: What share of leads got as far as a conversation: someone spoke by phone with the person who submitted the inquiry, or that person replied in writing.
960.nuances:
**Only a live conversation between an employee and the person who submitted the inquiry counts as contact.** A customer's reply to an automated message confirming receipt of the inquiry doesn't count: no employee has entered the conversation yet. In a written conversation the customer started, contact begins with the customer's reply to an employee: the customer's first message is the inquiry itself, and if it counted, every inquiry from chat, messaging apps and email would count as contacted.
**An attempt without a response doesn't count as contact**: an unanswered call, an auto-reply, an email or message left unanswered. A call doesn't count either if it was answered by a call-screening assistant, by a receptionist who didn't put the call through to the person who submitted the inquiry, or by someone who didn't submit it. The CRM status "In progress" or "Processed" is also set after an attempt without a response, and the phone system's "call answered" flag is set even when someone other than the inquirer picked up: a share based on these flags will be inflated.
The denominator includes all of the period's [[B2B Leads→b2b_prodazhi/lidy]], **including inquiries no one called or wrote to**: such an inquiry is also lost at this step. If an inquiry is entered into the CRM only after a conversation, the CRM has no leads that couldn't be reached, and the share calculated from it comes out around 100%: then the denominator is counted from all leads from website forms, chats and messaging apps, calls and email rather than from the CRM. Spam and duplicates have already been screened out of leads: if you divide by all incoming requests, spam inquiries that no one intended to respond to will understate the share.
Count **inquiries rather than calls**: three calls before the first answer give one contacted inquiry. The call answer rate, the share of calls answered, is counted by calls: for the same three calls, the call answer rate is 33%, while the lead contact rate is 100%.
A lead that reached later steps counts as contacted **even if the CRM didn't record the contact**: the steps go in order, and a missing record understates the share. This rule will also count inquiries handed over to sales without a conversation as contacted and inflate the share, but then the product of this share and the [[Contacted-to-SQL Rate→konversiya-lid-sdelka/dolya_kvalificirovannyh_sredi_lidov_s_kotorymi_svyazalis]] will match the [[B2B Lead-to-SQL Rate→b2b_prodazhi/kval_lidov]]. Whether to remove such inquiries from both shares **is up to the company**: without them the shares are more accurate, but their product won't match the B2B Lead-to-SQL Rate.
A lead is assigned to the period by its **arrival date** rather than the date of the conversation: the metric evaluates that month's flow of leads, and the result is credited to that month even if contact happened later. So the share for a recent month keeps changing while the team is still trying to reach leads from the month's last days.
A conversation or a written reply counts within **the same window from the inquiry's arrival** as qualification. The window runs from each inquiry's arrival rather than stopping at the end of the reporting month: otherwise inquiries from the last days of the month have almost no time left for contact, and the share will be understated even once the month's number is final. With a longer window the share is higher, and with different windows the product of this share and the Contacted-to-SQL Rate won't match the B2B Lead-to-SQL Rate.
960.example:
Leads in March: 340 (duplicates and spam already excluded)
Leads with a phone conversation or a written reply (in March and April): 240
Leads called or written to, with no response or only an auto-reply: 85
Leads no one got around to calling or writing to: 15

Lead Contact Rate = 240 / 340 × 100 = **71%**

Counting by the CRM status "In progress," which is also set after an attempt without a response, gives (240 + 85) / 340 × 100 = 96%: that's the share of inquiries the team started working on rather than the share of leads it spoke with.
Dividing only by inquiries with a contact attempt gives 240 / 325 × 100 = 74%: the 15 inquiries no one got around to contacting drop out of the calculation.
960.importance: It separates **leads the team never got to or couldn't reach** from unsuitable ones. Some contact attempts fail because the inquiry has a wrong number or someone else's number, while lead handling accounts for inquiries with no attempt at all and those abandoned after one or two attempts. Without this share, failed contact hides inside the [[B2B Lead-to-SQL Rate→b2b_prodazhi/kval_lidov]], and marketing turns off a channel where customers simply **weren't called back in time**. It's the basis for the rules of initial lead handling: within how many minutes to respond to an inquiry, how many times and at what hours to call back, whether to write via a messaging app or email after an unanswered call, and whether to validate the phone number right in the form.
960.not_needed: Skip it when inquiries are received by **a partner or dealer** who passes on to the company only the leads they've already spoken with: the company has no data on failed contact attempts, and the share always comes out around 100%.
960.essence_note: without a conversation, an inquiry won't become either a qualified lead or a deal

961.name: Contacted-to-SQL Rate
961.description: What share of contacted leads passed qualification: the customer meets the company's criteria, and the inquiry was handed over to sales as qualified.
961.nuances:
**The company sets** the qualification criteria: the set of attributes (company size, the need, budget, access to the person who makes the decision) directly determines the number in the numerator. The share also moves with the handoff threshold, that is, how many of these criteria must be met for the lead to be handed over: **the stricter the threshold, the lower the share**, and when it changes, the share jumps even with the same flow of inquiries.
**Every qualified lead is also included in the denominator**, even if the CRM didn't record the contact; otherwise the share will be inflated and could exceed 100%. If some inquiries go to sales without a conversation, for example from large companies straight to a key account manager or from existing customers to their account manager, whether to keep them in the calculation **is up to the company**. If they stay, they count as contacted, and both this share and the [[Lead Contact Rate→konversiya-lid-sdelka/dolya_lidov_s_kotorymi_svyazalis]] will be inflated, but the product of the two shares will match the [[B2B Lead-to-SQL Rate→b2b_prodazhi/kval_lidov]]. If they're removed from both shares, the shares become more accurate, but their product won't match the B2B Lead-to-SQL Rate.
"Contacted" in the denominator is counted the same way as in the Lead Contact Rate: an attempt without a response doesn't count. If you use the CRM status "In progress," which is also set after an unanswered call, **unanswered calls will swell the denominator**, and the share will be understated.
A lead is assigned to the period by its **arrival date** rather than its qualification date: the metric evaluates that month's flow of leads, and the result is credited to that month even if the lead was reviewed later. So the share for a recent month keeps changing after the month ends.
Contacted and qualified leads are counted within **the same window from the inquiry's arrival**: if qualified leads are counted over a longer period, the share will be inflated, and its product with the Lead Contact Rate won't match the B2B Lead-to-SQL Rate. The window runs from each inquiry's arrival rather than stopping at the end of the reporting month: otherwise leads contacted in the last days of the month don't get qualified in time, and the share will be understated even once the month's number is final.
961.example:
Leads in March: 340
Contacted (in March and April): 240
Of those, qualified and handed over to sales by the end of March: 78
Another 18 of them qualified and handed over to sales in April

Contacted-to-SQL Rate = (78 + 18) / 240 × 100 = **40%**

Dividing by all 340 leads gives 28%: that's already the B2B Lead-to-SQL Rate, and its denominator also includes 100 inquiries that weren't contacted.
The B2B Lead-to-SQL Rate equals the product of the two shares: 71% × 40% ≈ 28%.
961.importance: It shows whether marketing brings in the right customers and how strictly they're screened at qualification, **without failed contact mixed in**: in the [[B2B Lead-to-SQL Rate→b2b_prodazhi/kval_lidov]], an unsuitable customer and a customer who couldn't be reached look the same. Marketing uses it to choose which sources and audiences to spend the budget on, what to promise in ads, what questions to ask in the inquiry form, and whether to show the price on the website. It shows the head of sales what the handoff threshold costs: a looser threshold raises the share, but sales gets customers who **are less likely to attend a meeting or receive a proposal**.
961.not_needed: Skip it when **there's no qualification stage** and all inquiries are worked. Also skip it where inquiries are handed over to sales based on a questionnaire, **before any conversation**: the metric assumes the conversation comes before qualification. Nor is it worth tracking separately where almost everyone who submitted an inquiry gets contacted: the share then differs little from the [[B2B Lead-to-SQL Rate→b2b_prodazhi/kval_lidov]].
961.essence_note: the more suitable customers there are among those already spoken with, the more deals the same flow of inquiries can produce

962.name: SQL-to-Booked-Meeting Rate
962.formula: (Qualified Leads with a Booked Meeting / [[B2B Sales Qualified Leads (SQLs)→b2b_prodazhi/kvalificirovannye_lidy]]) × 100
962.description: What share of qualified leads were booked for a meeting: the day and time of the first meeting were agreed on with the customer, even if the meeting later fell through.
962.nuances:
A lead counts as booked when **the day and time of the meeting have been agreed on**. Agreement without a date ("let's talk next week," "send us the materials and we'll set something up") doesn't go into the numerator: if it counted, the share would grow from meetings that aren't on the calendar, and the [[Meeting Show Rate→konversiya-lid-sdelka/dohodimost_do_pervoy_vstrechi]] would be understated.
Any meeting format counts, as in [[Meetings Held→b2b_prodazhi/vstrechi]]: in person, by video or by phone. However, **the call on which the lead was qualified doesn't count as a meeting**: otherwise everyone who passed qualification would have a meeting, and the share would approach 100%. If that call moved straight to a demo, or the rep or specialist who will handle the deal joined it, the meeting counts as both booked and held.
**Count leads rather than calendar entries**: a rescheduled meeting remains the same meeting, and the second and later meetings with the same customer aren't included. If you count entries, reschedules and repeat meetings will swell the numerator, and the share could exceed 100%.
The steps go in order: **a lead whose meeting took place counts as booked** even if the CRM didn't record the booking. Conversely, a lead **still counts as booked if the meeting later falls through**. If you count by the current CRM stage and such a lead was moved back to the previous stage, the meetings that fell through show up in this share instead of the Meeting Show Rate: this share will be understated, the show rate inflated, and the product of the two won't change.
The denominator includes all [[B2B Sales Qualified Leads (SQLs)→b2b_prodazhi/kvalificirovannye_lidy]], **including those the rep never managed to reach after the handoff**: they answered neither calls nor emails. Such a lead passed qualification and was lost at exactly this step: removing it inflates the share.
A lead is assigned to the period by its **arrival date** rather than the booking date: the metric evaluates that month's flow of leads, and the result is credited to that month even if the meeting was booked later. So the share for a recent month keeps changing: some of its leads are qualified only the following month and booked for a meeting even later.
A booking counts within **the same window from the lead's arrival** as qualification and the meeting itself. The window runs from each lead's arrival rather than stopping at the end of the reporting month: otherwise leads from the last days of the month have almost no time left to be booked, and the share will be understated even once the month's number is final. With a longer window the share is higher, and with different windows the product of this share and the Meeting Show Rate won't match the SQL-to-Attended-Meeting Rate.
962.example:
March leads qualified and handed over to sales (in March and April): 96
Booked for a first meeting, day and time agreed on: 68; for 10 of them the meeting later fell through
Not booked: 28 (declined a meeting, put off the conversation without a date, or stopped responding to the rep after the handoff)

SQL-to-Booked-Meeting Rate = 68 / 96 × 100 = **71%**

If booked leads are counted by the current CRM stage and the 10 leads whose meeting fell through were moved back to the previous stage, the result is 58 / 96 × 100 = 60%, and the Meeting Show Rate shows 100%: a meeting that fell through would look like a refusal to book.
962.importance: It answers **whether a suitable customer has a reason to meet**. It's used to change the invitation itself: what we offer as the reason to meet (a review of the customer's problem, a cost estimate, a demo on the customer's own data), how long the meeting lasts, and whether we put it on the calendar right on the call. Without it, a refusal to meet and a no-show merge into a single loss inside the SQL-to-Attended-Meeting Rate, and the team works on reminders instead of the invitation. If the people who book meetings are paid for booked meetings, the share grows **by booking everyone indiscriminately**, while the [[Meeting Show Rate→konversiya-lid-sdelka/dohodimost_do_pervoy_vstrechi]] and the Meeting-to-Proposal Rate fall: judged by this share alone, such growth looks like success.
962.not_needed: Skip it when a lead becomes qualified **only when a meeting is booked**: the customer is qualified at the meeting itself, only leads booked for a meeting are marked as qualified, or all customers book the meeting themselves through a website form before qualification. The share then comes out around 100% by design.
962.synonyms: Meeting Booking Rate, Meetings Booked Rate
962.essence_note: the more suitable customers are booked for a meeting, the more meetings and deals the team can get from the same flow of leads

963.name: Meeting Show Rate
963.formula: (Qualified Leads That Attended a Meeting / Qualified Leads with a Booked Meeting) × 100
963.description: What share of qualified leads booked for a first meeting attended it. It's calculated from leads with a booked meeting rather than from all qualified leads: those who weren't booked aren't in the calculation.
963.nuances:
The denominator includes leads with whom **the day and time of the meeting have been agreed on**. Agreement without a date ("let's talk next week") doesn't go into the denominator: if it counted, the calculation would include meetings that aren't on the calendar, the share would be understated, and the [[SQL-to-Booked-Meeting Rate→konversiya-lid-sdelka/konversiya_kval_lid_naznachennaya_vstrecha]] inflated.
Any meeting format counts, as in [[Meetings Held→b2b_prodazhi/vstrechi]]: in person, by video or by phone. However, **the call on which the lead was qualified doesn't count as a meeting**: otherwise every qualified lead would have a meeting before being booked, and the share would approach 100%.
A meeting **took place even if the person who makes the decision on the customer's side wasn't there**: not counting such a meeting understates the share.
The steps go in order: **every lead with a meeting that took place is also included in the denominator**; otherwise the share could exceed 100%. This applies both to leads whose booking the CRM didn't record and to those whose qualification call moved straight to a demo or was joined by the rep or specialist who will handle the deal: such a meeting counts as both booked and held.
**A rescheduled meeting remains the same meeting**: if it took place within the window from the lead's arrival after one or more reschedules, the lead attended it, whether the customer or the rep did the rescheduling. The same applies if the customer first canceled the meeting and then booked again. A lead **didn't attend if the meeting never took place within that window**: the customer didn't show up, or canceled and never rebooked; the meeting kept being rescheduled until the window ran out; or the rep canceled it and never set a new one. If only no-shows count as meetings that fell through and leads with canceled meetings are removed from the denominator, the share will be inflated. A lead whose meeting fell through **stays in the denominator** even if the CRM moved it back to the previous stage: otherwise meetings that fell through drop out of the calculation, and the share approaches 100%.
**Count leads and their first meeting rather than calendar meetings**: the second and later meetings with the same customer aren't included. Dividing held meetings by booked ones from the calendar, the way Meetings Held counts them, gives a different number: there each meeting counts separately, repeat ones included, and is assigned to the period by meeting date rather than lead arrival date.
A lead is assigned to the period by its **arrival date** rather than the meeting date: the metric evaluates that month's flow of leads, and the result is credited to that month even if the meeting took place later. So the share for a recent month keeps changing: meetings booked in the month's last days haven't happened yet, and the share is understated.
A meeting counts within **the same window from the lead's arrival** as its booking: a meeting booked at the end of the window that took place after it doesn't go into the numerator. The window runs from each lead's arrival rather than stopping at the end of the reporting month: otherwise meetings of leads from the last days of the month don't have time to take place, and the share will be understated even once the month's number is final. With a longer window the share is higher, and with different windows the product of the SQL-to-Booked-Meeting Rate and this share won't match the SQL-to-Attended-Meeting Rate.
963.example:
Of 96 March leads qualified in March and April, booked for a first meeting: 68
Meeting took place, including after rescheduling: 58
Didn't take place: 10 (5 customers didn't show up, 3 canceled and never rebooked, 2 meetings kept being rescheduled until the window from the lead's arrival ran out)

Meeting Show Rate = 58 / 68 × 100 = **85%**

Dividing by all 96 qualified leads gives 60%: that's already the SQL-to-Attended-Meeting Rate, and its denominator also includes 28 leads that weren't booked for a meeting.
The SQL-to-Attended-Meeting Rate equals the product of the SQL-to-Booked-Meeting Rate and this share: 71% × 85% ≈ 60%.
963.importance: It's used to tune everything that happens **between booking and the meeting**: the calendar invitation, reminders the day before and an hour before, a date within the next few days instead of "in two weeks," and an offer to reschedule instead of canceling. Every meeting that falls through leaves an empty slot in the rep's calendar, and a lead that has already been acquired, qualified and booked gets stuck one step short of a conversation about a deal. Without this share, a meeting that fell through looks the same as a refusal to meet in the SQL-to-Attended-Meeting Rate, and the team rewrites the invitation when the customer **simply wasn't reminded**.
963.not_needed: Skip it when the customer is qualified **at the meeting itself**: then only customers who attended a meeting end up qualified, and the share is 100% by design. The same applies when the meeting with every qualified lead happens **right on the qualification call**, without booking.
963.synonyms: Show Rate, Meeting Attendance Rate, Show-Up Rate
963.essence_note: the more customers with a booked meeting show up, the more deal conversations the team gets without new leads

964.name: Share of First Meetings with a Decision-Maker
964.formula: (Leads with a Decision-Maker at the First Meeting / Leads That Attended a Meeting) × 100
964.description: What share of leads that attended a meeting had the customer's decision-maker at the first meeting: the person who signs the contract or approves the budget for this purchase.
964.nuances:
If the customer has several decision-makers, for example the CEO signs the contract and the CFO approves the budget, it's enough for **at least one** of them to be at the meeting. Members of a buying committee or working group **without the authority to sign or approve the budget** don't count as decision-makers, however many of them attend. Requiring all decision-makers understates the share for customers where several people decide, and counting any committee member inflates it.
The numerator includes a lead whose decision-maker **was among the attendees** of the first meeting, even for part of the conversation. A decision-maker who was invited but didn't attend doesn't count, nor does a contact with the decision-maker role in the customer record: if access to the decision-maker is checked during qualification, almost every lead has such a contact, and the share would approach 100%.
Whether the decision-maker was at the meeting is determined from **the first meeting's outcome record**, even if the outcome was entered on a later day, but no later than the proposal was sent: if you take only records made on the day of the meeting, the share will depend on how quickly the team fills in the CRM. A decision-maker role assigned to a contact **when the deal moves to the proposal stage or later** doesn't count: it's added once the deal is already moving, and if the CRM won't let a deal reach the proposal stage without a decision-maker, the role goes to whatever contact is there. Counting such roles raises the share only through leads that received a proposal, whoever attended their meeting. If the first meeting's outcome was never entered, the lead doesn't go into the numerator, and the share of such leads is shown next to the number: when the CRM requires the outcome only to move to the proposal stage, it stays empty for leads that went silent after the meeting, even though a decision-maker might have been there.
Only **the first meeting** is considered: if the decision-maker was only at the second or a later one, the lead doesn't go into the numerator. Counting any meeting within the window gives leads with several meetings a better chance of getting into the numerator, and the share will be inflated.
A meeting **without a decision-maker still took place**: the lead stays in the denominator even if the CRM moved it back to the booking stage afterward to invite the decision-maker to the next meeting. Not counting such a meeting inflates the share and understates the [[Meeting Show Rate→konversiya-lid-sdelka/dohodimost_do_pervoy_vstrechi]].
A lead is assigned to the period by its **arrival date** rather than the meeting date, and a meeting counts within **the same window from each lead's arrival** as in the rest of the funnel: then the denominator matches the denominator of the [[Meeting-to-Proposal Rate→b2b_prodazhi/konversiya_vstrecha_kp]]. If you take meetings by the date they were held or with a window of their own, the share will describe a different set of meetings from the one used to calculate the Meeting-to-Proposal Rate.
964.example:
Leads that arrived in March and attended a meeting: 58
Total meetings with them: 79; only each lead's first meeting goes into the calculation
Decision-maker recorded in the first meeting's outcome: 35
Not recorded: 23
Of those, a first-meeting attendee was given the decision-maker role when the deal moved to the proposal stage: 6 (not included in the numerator)

Share of First Meetings with a Decision-Maker = 35 / 58 × 100 = **60%**

Taking first-meeting attendees' roles as they stand in the CRM today gives (35 + 6) / 58 × 100 = 71%: the increase comes only from leads that received a proposal.
964.importance: At a meeting without a decision-maker, **no one can say "send us a proposal"**: the person across the table first has to get approval internally, so the request for a proposal stalls on the customer's side. This share is used to decide how to book meetings: whether to ask who makes the decision, whether to invite that person right away, and whether to find out in advance from public sources who decides at the company. If the [[Meeting-to-Proposal Rate→b2b_prodazhi/konversiya_vstrecha_kp]] sags together with this share for companies of the same size and leads in the same category from the same source, the problem is **who was at the meeting** rather than how the rep ran it. Some growth comes without any work by the team: in small companies the owner is more often the one who decides, so the more small companies there are among leads, the higher the share.
964.not_needed: Skip it when meetings are booked **only with a decision-maker attending**: the share then comes out around 100% by design. Also skip it where, under the sales playbook, the first meeting **with any customer is held without a decision-maker**, with working-level staff or a working group, and the decision-maker joins only to discuss the proposal: the share is then around zero by design.
964.essence_note: the more often the person who decides for the customer is at the first meeting, the more often the conversation gets to a proposal

965.name: Share of First Meetings with Poor-Fit Customers
965.formula: (Leads That Attended a Meeting, Were Judged a Poor Fit and Received No Proposal / Leads That Attended a Meeting) × 100
965.description: What share of leads that attended a meeting turned out to be a poor fit: only after qualification did it become clear that the company doesn't sell to such customers, and no proposal was prepared for them.
965.nuances:
A customer is **a poor fit** if the rep judged them unsuitable and gave a reason from **the list of profile criteria** the company has set: industry, size, a need outside its offering, geography. Without a reason from the list, it's easy to apply this flag to a meeting that didn't work out for other reasons as well, and the share will be inflated.
A refusal from a customer **who fits the company's profile** isn't included: "no budget right now," "let's revisit in six months," "we don't need it." A customer handed over to another business line of the company isn't included either: the company does sell to them, just a different product, and counting them would inflate the share in the business line they were handed over from. Nor is a lead judged unsuitable only because **there was no decision-maker** at the meeting: that isn't a profile field, and the [[Share of First Meetings with a Decision-Maker→konversiya-lid-sdelka/dolya_pervyh_vstrech_s_lpr]] covers such a meeting; otherwise the same meeting would count as bad in both shares, and this one would be inflated. A poor-fit customer is included even if there was no decision-maker at the meeting.
A customer counts if they were judged a poor fit **before the proposal was sent**: at the first meeting, at a later one, or while the proposal was being prepared, within the window from the lead's arrival. If you count only poor-fit flags in the first meeting's outcome record, the share will depend on how quickly the rep records them. If the customer was judged unsuitable after the proposal was sent, or was sent a proposal anyway, the lead isn't included: it's among those who received a proposal, and the loss is reflected in the [[Proposal-to-Close Rate→b2b_prodazhi/konversiya_kp_sdelka]]. Otherwise one lead would be both among those who received a proposal and among those for whom none was prepared.
A meeting the rep **canceled in advance** after checking the company and realizing it was a poor fit isn't included: the lead never made it to the meeting, and it counts as a meeting that fell through in the [[Meeting Show Rate→konversiya-lid-sdelka/dohodimost_do_pervoy_vstrechi]]. Counting it here would bring a meeting that never happened into the calculation, and the share would be inflated.
The steps go in order: a lead whose first meeting took place **stays in the denominator** even if the CRM later moved it back to the previous stage or closed the deal. If you count by the current CRM stage, leads judged a poor fit can drop out of the leads that attended a meeting, along with their flag, and the share will be understated, potentially down to zero.
A lead is assigned to the period by its **arrival date**, and the meeting and the poor-fit flag count within **the same window from each lead's arrival** as in the rest of the funnel: then the denominator matches the denominator of the [[Meeting-to-Proposal Rate→b2b_prodazhi/konversiya_vstrecha_kp]]. The share for a recent month **keeps changing**: the flag is also set after the first meeting, and until the window has ended, the month's share is understated. The window runs from each lead's arrival rather than stopping at the end of the reporting month: otherwise leads from the last days of the month don't get flagged in time, and the share will be understated even once the month's number is final.
965.example:
Leads that arrived in March and attended a meeting: 58
Received a proposal: 29
Judged a poor fit, no proposal prepared: 7 (5 at the first meeting, 2 at a later meeting or while the proposal was being prepared)
Left without a proposal for other reasons: 22
Of those, the rep marked "customer isn't a fit" without specifying a profile criterion: 4 (not counted)

Share of First Meetings with Poor-Fit Customers = 7 / 58 × 100 = **12%**

Counting every "customer isn't a fit" flag gives (7 + 4) / 58 × 100 = 19%: the share would include meetings that didn't work out for other reasons.
965.importance: Such a meeting points to **a qualification error found too late**: a customer the company doesn't sell to passed screening and got as far as a conversation about a deal. But some mismatches only show up at the meeting, when a specialist works through the customer's problem, and **zero isn't the goal here**: pushing for zero drags out qualification and screens out some suitable customers, and the loss moves into the [[Contacted-to-SQL Rate→konversiya-lid-sdelka/dolya_kvalificirovannyh_sredi_lidov_s_kotorymi_svyazalis]]. This share is used to adjust qualification: what profile questions to ask on the first call, which projects the company doesn't take on, and how strict the handoff threshold should be. Without it, such meetings get lost among unsuccessful conversations in the [[Meeting-to-Proposal Rate→b2b_prodazhi/konversiya_vstrecha_kp]], and the training goes to the reps who ran the meeting rather than to those who did the qualifying. The share also falls when reps check the company before the meeting and cancel the poor-fit ones: screening has become cheaper, but qualification hasn't improved, and the losses have moved into the [[Meeting Show Rate→konversiya-lid-sdelka/dohodimost_do_pervoy_vstrechi]]. And when the people who book meetings are paid for each booked meeting, the share grows: everyone gets invited to a meeting.
965.not_needed: Skip it when the process sends a proposal **to every customer the team meets with**, for example a standard or automated one: then no poor-fit customers are left without a proposal, and the share is around zero by design.
965.synonyms: Non-ICP Meeting Rate, Bad-Fit Meeting Rate
965.essence_note: each such meeting takes up rep time that could have gone to a customer able to buy

966.name: Proposal Follow-Up Rate
966.formula: (Leads the Team Followed Up With After the Proposal Was Sent / Leads with a Proposal Sent) × 100
966.description: What share of sent proposals were followed up on: in the first days after sending, the team itself spoke with the customer by phone, met with them, or got a reply from them to an individually written email or message.
966.nuances:
**Only a conversation counts as a follow-up here**: by phone, at a meeting, or in writing when the customer replied to an individually written email or message. A meeting or call where the proposal was presented to the customer is also a follow-up, even if the proposal file was sent after it: the conversation about the proposal took place. An automated email or message from the CRM and a messaging campaign don't count as a follow-up, even if they went out from the rep's number or mailbox and the customer replied: no one entered into a conversation with the customer.
**An attempt without a response doesn't count as a follow-up**: an unanswered call, an email or message with no reply or only an auto-reply, a meeting that didn't take place. So the share also depends on the customer: if they don't pick up and don't reply, the proposal is left without a follow-up no matter how many times they were called or written to. Counting attempts would make the share show the sales team's effort rather than a conversation with the customer, and it would rise because of unanswered calls and template messages. Nor does a call count if it was answered by voicemail or by a receptionist who didn't put the call through to the customer's contact person: the phone system sets the "call answered" flag in this case too, and a share based on such flags will be inflated.
A follow-up counts if the conversation was started by **any employee working on this deal**: the rep who sent the proposal, the head of sales, a colleague covering for the rep, or a technical specialist. Counting only conversations by the person who sent the proposal makes the share lower where a technical specialist calls the customer after the proposal, even though a conversation took place. A conversation **started by the customer** doesn't count as a follow-up: the customer called or wrote after the proposal on their own, including replying to the email or message with the proposal itself, and the rep answered or sent a revised version. So where customers frequently come back with questions on their own, the share is lower, even though there are just as many conversations after the proposal. Counting any conversation after the proposal would make the share rise with customer interest rather than with the sales team's work: a customer who's ready to buy calls on their own anyway.
A follow-up counts **whatever the conversation was about**, even if the customer said in it that they accept the proposal. A customer who declined right away, before anyone contacted them, stays in the denominator without a follow-up. If proposals whose outcome was decided before or during the follow-up are removed from the calculation, the share will be calculated on different proposals from the ones the [[Proposal-to-Close Rate→b2b_prodazhi/konversiya_kp_sdelka]] is calculated on.
A follow-up counts within the first **N days after the first version** of the proposal was sent. A later conversation doesn't count as a follow-up, even if it falls within the first days after a revised version: counting from any version gives proposals with long negotiations a better chance of getting into the numerator, and the share would grow with the number of revisions. The company chooses N, in business or calendar days: the larger N, the higher the share, and changing N or switching from business days to calendar days changes the share without any change in the work.
A follow-up is counted by **the date of the conversation, meeting or customer reply itself**, rather than by the CRM entry date or a closed "call after proposal" task. The task gets closed without a call, after an unanswered call, and after the customer called, so a share based on closed tasks will be inflated. By entry date, the share will depend on how quickly the rep fills in the CRM: a conversation that took place on day two but was entered into the CRM after day N drops out of the numerator.
A lead is assigned to the period by its **arrival date** rather than the date the proposal was sent, and a proposal counts if its first version went out within **the same window from each lead's arrival** as in the rest of the funnel: then the denominator matches the denominator of the proposal-to-close rate. If you take proposals by send date or with a window of their own, the share will cover a different set of proposals from the one used to calculate the proposal-to-close rate. A follow-up counts **for all N days after sending, even if they run past that window**: otherwise proposals sent in the last days of the window have almost no time left for a follow-up, and the share falls when the early funnel steps slow down, even though customers are contacted as before. So a month's number is final only N days after the window of its last lead has ended.
966.example:
Leads that arrived in March and received a proposal: 29
The company's follow-up window: 3 business days after the proposal is sent
The team contacted the customer within this window (a call, a meeting or the customer's reply to an individually written email): 22
The customer called with questions on their own, and the rep didn't reach out again: 3 (not counted)
The rep called and wrote, the customer didn't respond: 1 (not counted)
The "call after proposal" task was closed without a call: 2 (not counted)
The rep got through only on the fifth business day: 1 (not counted)

Proposal Follow-Up Rate = 22 / 29 × 100 = **76%**

Counting by closed "call after proposal" tasks gives (22 + 2 + 1 + 3) / 29 × 100 = 97%: the task was closed without a call, after an unanswered call, and after the customer called.
Counting conversations started by the customer as well gives (22 + 3) / 29 × 100 = 86%: the share would rise with customer interest rather than with the sales team's work.
966.importance: When a proposal receives no follow-up, the customer **decides alone**: no one has answered their questions about price and terms, and no one has agreed on the next step. This share is used to choose whether to create a call task right when the proposal is sent, how many days later to call, and whether to agree on the date of the next conversation while still at the meeting. Without it, it's easy to blame a drop in the [[Proposal-to-Close Rate→b2b_prodazhi/konversiya_kp_sdelka]] on price and respond with a bigger discount, even though in fact no one talked to the customer after the proposal. In the data, the link between this share and the proposal-to-close rate looks **stronger than it is**: follow-ups happen more often with customers who are already inclined to buy. They pick up and reply, reps are more willing to call them and talk to them even about a proposal they've already accepted, while those who declined right away or went silent are left without a follow-up. So if both rose together, that doesn't yet mean the calls brought in the deals.
966.not_needed: Skip it when proposals **are always presented at a meeting instead of being sent**: the conversation about the proposal happens as it's handed over, and the share is around 100% by design.
966.essence_note: a proposal discussed with the customer is less likely to go unanswered than one that was simply sent

967.name: Initial Proposal Discount Rate
967.formula: (Σ (List Price − First Proposal Version Price) / Σ List Price) × 100
967.description: How far below list price the first offer to the customer is: what share of the list price was conceded in the first version of the proposal, before any negotiation. Lost proposals and proposals without a discount are both included, so the metric shows the discount that was offered rather than the discount applied to completed sales, as the [[Effective Discount Rate→ltv/srednyaya_fakticheskaya_skidka]] does.
967.nuances:
Count **the first version** of the proposal: revisions after the customer responds count as negotiation, and discounts added in them aren't included. Taking the last version would include negotiation in the number, and the metric would show what was agreed rather than what was offered up front.
Proposals **without a discount count as zero**, and the discount is calculated **as a ratio of totals** across all proposals rather than as an average of percentages. Taking only proposals with a discount inflates the number, and it grows even when discounts become rarer but larger.
