Averaging percentages gives a small proposal with a 30% discount the same weight as a large one with a 3% discount. With a ratio of totals, large proposals move the number more than small ones.
**Anything counts as a discount** if it brought the proposal price below list price: a discount as a separate line, reduced item prices, items and work thrown in **free of charge**. A free item is included in the list-price total at its full list price, and that entire amount counts as a discount: otherwise, with a discount cap, concessions will be shifted into free items, and the number will fall even though the customer got the same concession. A service from the price list given away free also counts as a free item. A discount offered **subject to a condition**, for example for prepayment or for signing by a certain date, is also included: it was offered in the first version. If it's not counted, the metric won't see the discount for a quick decision. Deferred payment terms, an extended warranty, and free delivery or installation that aren't on the price list don't count as a discount: there's nothing to subtract them from, and the metric doesn't see such concessions.
An item priced **above its list price**, for example with a rush surcharge, goes into the calculation with a discount of 0 rather than a negative one: otherwise a surcharge on one item will hide a discount on another, and the number will be understated.
The list price is taken from the company's price list, **public or internal**, rather than from the "price before discount" column in the proposal: the rep can edit it by hand, and then the discount hides in the base price. Items **without a list price** aren't included in either total: if their proposal price is taken as the list price, they enter the calculation with no discount and understate it. Proposals where no item is on the price list aren't included; their share is shown next to the number. Removing an entire proposal from the calculation because it has at least one item without a list price also removes the discount on the items that are on the price list.
The list price is taken **as of the date the first version was sent**. With a price list from a different date, a change in the price list itself ends up in the discount: a price cut becomes a discount no one gave, and a price increase hides a discount that was given. If there are several price types, for example retail, wholesale and dealer, or the list price depends on volume, the discount is calculated from the price **the customer is entitled to under company rules** for that volume, and for a customer with a contract, from their contract prices. Calculating from the base price list turns the wholesale prices the customer is entitled to, volume discounts and contract terms into discounts, and the number will grow with the customer mix and order size even though reps gave up nothing in these proposals.
The list price and the proposal price are taken **on the same basis**: both excluding taxes and in the same currency; a price list in a foreign currency, or pegged to one, is converted at the same exchange rate as the proposal prices. If the price list includes tax and the proposal doesn't, the tax itself becomes a discount, and with different exchange rates the rate difference becomes a discount or a surcharge.
If the first version offers several options to choose from, the calculation uses **the option marked as primary in the proposal**. Proposals with options where none is marked as primary aren't included; their share is shown next to the number. Taking the most expensive or the cheapest option makes the number depend on which options are put in the proposal next to the intended one, for example an expensive one for comparison. The option the customer chose is known only for won proposals, so a number based on it would depend on the outcome, and adding up all options would give a proposal with three options three times the weight of a proposal with one.
A lead is assigned to the period by its **arrival date** rather than the date the proposal was sent, and a proposal counts if its first version went out within **the same window from each lead's arrival** as in the rest of the funnel: then the calculation includes proposals for the same leads as the denominator of the [[Proposal-to-Close Rate→b2b_prodazhi/konversiya_kp_sdelka]]. If you take proposals by send date or with a window of their own, the discount will cover a different set of proposals from the one used to calculate the proposal-to-close rate.
967.example:
Leads that arrived in March and received a proposal: 29
Every item has a list price, none is priced above its list price, and the proposals have no options to choose from
First versions at list prices, excluding taxes: $928,000
The same first versions at proposal prices: $844,480
Proposals without a discount: 11 of 29, worth $292,000 at list prices

Discount in the first versions = 928,000 − 844,480 = $83,520
Initial Proposal Discount Rate = 83,520 / 928,000 × 100 = **9%**

Counting only the 18 proposals with a discount gives 83,520 / (928,000 − 292,000) × 100 = 83,520 / 636,000 × 100 = 13%: the 11 proposals where the customer got no concession at all drop out of the calculation.
Taking the last versions, after negotiation, where the same items now cost $816,640, gives (928,000 − 816,640) / 928,000 × 100 = 12%: the number includes negotiation.
967.importance: The discount in the first version **goes to everyone who accepts the proposal**, including those who would have bought at list price, and if the customer negotiates, they start from the already reduced price. This metric is used to set a cap on the discount in the first offer, to decide who can approve a discount and up to what level, and whether to give a time-limited discount for a quick decision. If a cap is set but reps start giving the discount in the second version, in response to the customer's very first "too expensive," the metric will fall, but the final discount on deals won't change. A discount cuts both ways: it can raise the [[Proposal-to-Close Rate→b2b_prodazhi/konversiya_kp_sdelka]] but lowers the [[Average Deal Size→b2b_prodazhi/srednyaya_vyruchka_sdelki]], so a rise in conversion following a discount doesn't yet mean sales brought in more money. And comparing proposals with and without a discount by outcome is misleading: if discounts go mainly to difficult deals, proposals with a discount lose more often, and the discount will look useless even if it helped.
967.not_needed: Skip it when proposals are issued **strictly at list price, with no discounts**, including when the customer gets concessions only through fewer estimated hours while the hourly rate stays the same: the metric is always zero. Also skip it where **there's no price list** and each proposal is priced separately for the customer's needs: there's nothing to compare against.
967.synonyms: Proposal Discount Rate, Quote Discount Rate
967.essence_note: every percentage point of discount in the first offer is money the company won't collect on any deal that closes on that offer

4361.text: Are pages intentionally blocked from indexing counted as errors when Search Console shows them in the same list?

4362.text: Are pages that should be in search results blocked from indexing by mistake?

4436.text: How do duplicates break down: filter and sorting pages, the same product in several categories, product variants by color and size, or technical copies of a URL?

4438.text: For which queries do different pages of the website alternate in search results?

4384.text: How does the interaction delay change after third-party scripts are added, such as live chats, widgets and analytics tags, compared with before?

4446.text: Where do most broken links point: to removed products, to old URLs after a website restructure or to pages with a server error?

4447.text: Which broken links sit in the website's templates: the menu, the footer, recommendation blocks?

4448.text: How do sessions end when the user lands on a nonexistent page: do they leave the website or continue through the catalog and site search?

4449.text: Which broken links should we fix first: which ones are on the pages that get the most users?

4450.text: Which nonexistent pages should we redirect to live ones first: which of them do the most other websites link to?

4452.text: Do broken links include URLs that return an error only to the crawler, for example because of bot protection or rate limits?

4411.text: If clicks per keyword change, what drives it: clicks on keywords in the set or the keyword set behind Target Keyword Count?

4418.text: Does the numerator include clicks on queries that aren't in the set?

7709.text: If the rate is falling, what drives it: the B2B Lead-to-SQL Rate or the SQL-to-Close Rate?

7710.text: If Deals Won changes, what drives it: a change in B2B Leads in the arrival months of the leads behind those deals, or in those leads' conversion rate to a won deal?

7711.text: Which acquisition channels and sources have a noticeably lower lead-to-close rate?

7712.text: Which customer industries, sizes and types have a noticeably lower lead-to-close rate?

7713.text: Which reps have a noticeably lower lead-to-close rate when the lead mix is comparable by channel and customer size?

7714.text: If the rate is changing, is it because the share of incoming inquiries from existing customers has changed?

7715.text: How many leads does each team need to meet the Deal Quota if the lead-to-close rate stays the same, and how many come in now?

7716.text: How much can we pay for a lead in each channel, given its lead-to-close rate and the margin per deal?

7717.text: How many days after the period ends does the lead-to-close rate stop changing?

7718.text: Is each deal linked to the lead it grew out of, or are the month's deals divided by the same month's leads?

8115.text: If the B2B Lead-to-SQL Rate changed, what drove it: a change in the Lead Contact Rate or in the Contacted-to-SQL Rate?

8116.text: If the share of leads contacted is falling, what drives it: more inquiries with no attempt to call or write at all, or more attempts with no response?

8117.text: Which inquiries lead to a conversation noticeably less often: those submitted through a website form, in chat, by email, in a messaging app, or as a missed call?

8118.text: If the share of leads contacted changed, is it because the flow now has more or fewer inquiries with contact from the very start: answered inbound calls and conversations at a trade show booth?

8119.text: Which employees and teams have a noticeably lower contact rate on inquiries assigned on arrival than colleagues with inquiries from the same channels?

8120.text: How does the share of leads contacted change as the number of new inquiries per employee per day grows?

8121.text: If the share of leads contacted is falling in all channels and for all employees at once, is it because the company's outbound number isn't registered for branded caller ID or is labeled as spam on recipients' phones?

8122.text: Within how many minutes should we respond to an inquiry: how does the share of leads contacted change as the time from an inquiry's arrival to the first contact attempt grows, for inquiries that arrived at the same hours?

8123.text: How many times and at what hours should we call back after an unanswered call: after which attempt does contact almost never succeed, and at what hours do calls get through noticeably less often?

8124.text: Should we write via a messaging app or email after an unanswered call: how does the share of leads contacted differ between inquiries where someone wrote after the unanswered call and similar inquiries where they only called?

8125.text: Should we validate the phone number right in the inquiry form: how many inquiries go without a conversation because of a wrong number or someone else's number?

8126.text: Should we handle inquiries in the evening and on weekends: how does the share of leads contacted differ for inquiries that arrived during business hours, in the evening, at night and on weekends?

8127.text: Should we turn off an acquisition channel or source with a low B2B Lead-to-SQL Rate: how does the share of leads contacted there compare with the shares in other channels and sources?

8128.text: What marks a lead as contacted: a phone conversation with the inquirer or their written reply to an employee, or the CRM status, the phone system's answered-call flag and any customer reply, which also capture unanswered calls, call-screening assistants and replies to automated messages?

8129.text: Are leads counted as contacted when the conversation with them bypassed the CRM: a call from a rep's personal phone, a conversation in the rep's personal messaging app, or one with no contact record before qualification?

8130.text: Is the call answer rate from the phone system, where each call counts separately, being used in place of the share of leads contacted?

8131.text: Does the denominator include inquiries no one called or wrote to, or only inquiries with contact attempts?

8132.text: How many days after the period ends does the share of leads contacted stop changing?

8133.text: If the B2B Lead-to-SQL Rate changed, what drove it: a change in the Lead Contact Rate or in the Contacted-to-SQL Rate?

8134.text: How does the share of contacted leads that qualify change after a noticeable rise or fall in the Lead Contact Rate, compared with before?

8135.text: When the share of contacted leads that qualify falls, which rejection reasons move outside their usual range: company size, need, budget, or access to the person who makes the decision?

8136.text: For which employees and in which teams does a noticeably smaller share of leads go on to sales after a conversation than for colleagues with inquiries from the same channels, and how does the SQL-to-Attended-Meeting Rate differ for the leads they hand over?

8137.text: For which products are there noticeably fewer suitable customers among those contacted than for the rest?

8138.text: How does the share of contacted leads that qualify differ for businesses, sole proprietors and individuals?

8139.text: How does the share of contacted leads that qualify differ for new companies and for existing customers?

8140.text: Where should we move the ad budget: in which channels, sources and campaigns is the share of contacted leads that qualify noticeably higher and the Cost per SQL below average?

8141.text: Which audiences should we target with ads: in which industries and regions do customers meet the company's criteria noticeably less often after a conversation?

8142.text: Should we ask about company size and customer needs in the inquiry form and show the price on the website: how do the share of contacted leads that qualify and B2B Sales Qualified Leads (SQLs) change after that, compared with before?

8143.text: Where should we set the handoff threshold: how do the share of contacted leads that qualify and the SQL-to-Attended-Meeting Rate change after the threshold changes, compared with before?

8144.text: Are contacted leads counted the same way here and in the Lead Contact Rate, and are contacted and qualified leads counted within the same window from the inquiry's arrival?

8145.text: Does the denominator include qualified leads with no record of a conversation or written exchange in the CRM?

8146.text: Are industry, region, product and customer type filled in for leads that were contacted but not qualified, or are these fields required only for the handoff to sales?

8147.text: How many days after the period ends does the share of contacted leads that qualify stop changing?

8148.text: If the SQL-to-Attended-Meeting Rate changed, what drove it: a change in the SQL-to-Booked-Meeting Rate or in the Meeting Show Rate?

8149.text: When the SQL-to-booked-meeting rate falls, what moves outside its usual range: refusals to meet, conversations put off without a date, or leads the rep couldn't reach after the handoff?

8150.text: How does the SQL-to-booked-meeting rate change after a noticeable rise or fall in the Contacted-to-SQL Rate, compared with before?

8151.text: For which employees are qualified leads booked for a meeting noticeably less often than for colleagues with leads from the same channels and from companies of the same size?

8152.text: Which channels, sources and ad campaigns have a noticeably lower booking rate for qualified customers than the rest?

8153.text: How does the SQL-to-booked-meeting rate differ for companies of different sizes?

8154.text: Should we pay the people who book meetings for each booked meeting: how do the SQL-to-booked-meeting rate, the Meeting Show Rate, the Meeting-to-Proposal Rate and the Share of First Meetings with Poor-Fit Customers change after switching to this pay scheme, compared with before?

8155.text: Should we book the meeting right on the qualification call: how does the SQL-to-booked-meeting rate change as the time from qualification to the first attempt to set up a meeting grows?

8156.text: What should we invite customers to the meeting for: how does the SQL-to-booked-meeting rate change after a change in the invitation (a review of the customer's problem, a cost estimate, a demo on the customer's own data), compared with before?

8157.text: Should we offer a short first video meeting: how does the SQL-to-booked-meeting rate change after switching to it from a long or in-person meeting, compared with before?

8158.text: How many times should we try to set up a meeting with a lead who stopped responding after the handoff to sales: after which attempt does booking almost never succeed?

8159.text: Is the call on which the lead was qualified marked as a meeting in the CRM even when it didn't move to a demo and the rep or specialist who will handle the deal didn't join it?

8160.text: What record marks a lead as booked for a meeting: the funnel stage, a CRM task, a calendar invitation with the customer among the attendees, or a booking through a scheduling tool; and is it set when the team agrees with the customer to talk later but doesn't agree on a day and time for the meeting?

8161.text: Do leads whose meeting fell through remain counted as booked if the CRM moved them back to the previous stage, the meeting was deleted from the calendar, or it was arranged by phone or in a messaging app and never recorded in the CRM?

8162.text: Which employee is the share attributed to if a booked lead is handed over to the rep who will run the meeting: the one the lead was assigned to when the customer was invited to the meeting, or the current owner in the CRM?

8163.text: Is a lead that meets the criteria but declined a meeting marked as qualified, or do only leads booked for a meeting become qualified in the CRM?

8164.text: How many days after the period ends does the SQL-to-booked-meeting rate stop changing?

8165.text: If the SQL-to-Attended-Meeting Rate changed, what drove it: a change in the SQL-to-Booked-Meeting Rate or in the Meeting Show Rate?

8166.text: How does the show rate change after a noticeable rise or fall in the SQL-to-Booked-Meeting Rate, compared with before?

8167.text: When the show rate falls, what moves outside its usual range: no-shows, cancellations by the customer, meetings rescheduled until the window from the lead's arrival ran out, or cancellations by the rep without a new meeting?

8168.text: Which employees have a noticeably lower show rate among the leads they booked than colleagues with leads from the same channels and from companies of the same size?

8169.text: Which channels and sources have a noticeably lower show rate for customers with a booked meeting than the rest?

8170.text: How does the show rate differ by the format of the booked meeting: in person, by video and by phone?

8171.text: How does the show rate differ for companies of different sizes?

8172.text: If the show rate has grown, how does the Meeting-to-Proposal Rate change for the same monthly lead cohorts compared with cohorts from before the increase?

8173.text: How many days out should we schedule the first meeting: how does the show rate change as the time from booking to the meeting grows?

8174.text: Which days and hours should we offer for the meeting: how does the show rate differ by the day of the week and the hour, in the customer's time zone, that the meeting was set for at booking?

8175.text: Should we send the customer a calendar invitation right at booking and remind them about the meeting the day before and an hour before: how does the show rate change after each of these steps is introduced, compared with before?

8176.text: Should we offer rescheduling to a customer who wants to cancel the meeting: what share of rescheduled meetings eventually take place within the window from the lead's arrival?

8177.text: Is the call on which the lead was qualified marked as a meeting in the CRM even when it didn't move to a demo and the rep or specialist who will handle the deal didn't join it?

8178.text: Do leads whose meeting fell through remain counted as booked if the CRM moved them back to the previous stage, the meeting was deleted from the calendar, or it was arranged by phone or in a messaging app and never recorded in the CRM?

8179.text: How does the CRM record a rescheduled meeting: does it change the date on the same meeting, so the day and hour set at booking are lost, or cancel it and create a new one, so the canceled meeting counts as the lead's first meeting?

8180.text: Are leads counted as having attended when the meeting bypassed the CRM: a video call arranged through the rep's personal calendar, a call on the rep's personal phone, or a meeting with no record that it took place?

8181.text: How does the CRM tell a meeting that took place from a no-show: is any past meeting that wasn't deleted from the calendar counted as held, even if the customer didn't show up?

8182.text: Which employee is the share attributed to if a booked lead is handed over to the rep who will run the meeting: the one who booked the lead for the meeting, or the current owner in the CRM?

8183.text: How many days after the period ends does the show rate stop changing?

8184.text: If the Meeting-to-Proposal Rate changed, what drove it: a change in the Share of First Meetings with a Decision-Maker, in the Share of First Meetings with Poor-Fit Customers, or in how often good-fit customers get a proposal, with and without a decision-maker at the first meeting?

8185.text: How do the Meeting-to-Proposal Rate and the Proposal-to-Close Rate differ between leads that had a decision-maker at the first meeting and those that didn't?

8186.text: When the share of first meetings with a decision-maker falls, what moves outside its usual range: meetings where the decision-maker wasn't invited, was invited but didn't come, or was never identified at the customer?

8187.text: If the share of first meetings with a decision-maker changed noticeably, how much of the change came from more or fewer small companies among leads that attended a meeting, and how much from a change in the share within companies of each size?

8188.text: Which employees and teams have a noticeably lower share of first meetings with a decision-maker among the meetings they booked than colleagues with leads from the same channels and from companies of the same size?

8189.text: For leads from which channels, sources and ad campaigns does a decision-maker attend the first meeting noticeably less often than for other leads from companies of the same size?

8190.text: In which industries does a decision-maker attend the first meeting noticeably less often than at companies of the same size in other industries?

8191.text: For which products does a decision-maker attend the first meeting noticeably less often than for other products?

8192.text: Should we find out in advance who makes the decision at the customer's company: how does the share of first meetings with a decision-maker change after the team started identifying that person from the company's website and public business records before booking the meeting, compared with before?

8193.text: Should we ask who makes the decision when booking the meeting and invite that person right away: how do the share of first meetings with a decision-maker, the SQL-to-Booked-Meeting Rate and the Meeting Show Rate change after the team started doing this, compared with before?

8194.text: How is it determined who attended the first meeting on the customer's side: by the attendees the rep recorded after the meeting, by the calendar invitation, which also lists a decision-maker who didn't come, or by the deal's contacts, where a decision-maker is added even after the meeting; and for what share of first meetings are the attendees not recorded at all or recorded without their roles?

8195.text: Can the CRM change history show when a contact was given the decision-maker role, in the first meeting's outcome record or only when the deal moved to the proposal stage, or is the role taken as it stands now?

8196.text: Does the CRM require a decision-maker to move a deal to the proposal stage, and who gets that role if no decision-maker was at the meeting?

8197.text: What marks a contact as a decision-maker: job title, or whether the person signs the contract or approves the budget for this deal; and does any manager on the customer's side or any buying committee member without signing authority get this role?

8198.text: Do leads whose first meeting took place without a decision-maker remain counted as having attended a meeting if the CRM moved them back to the booking stage afterward to invite the decision-maker to the next meeting?

8199.text: How many days after the period ends does the share of first meetings with a decision-maker stop changing?

8200.text: If the Meeting-to-Proposal Rate changed, what drove it: a change in the Share of First Meetings with a Decision-Maker, in the Share of First Meetings with Poor-Fit Customers, or in how often good-fit customers get a proposal, with and without a decision-maker at the first meeting?

8201.text: If the share of first meetings with poor-fit customers fell, what drove it: poor-fit customers get through qualification less often; meetings with them started being canceled in advance, and the Meeting Show Rate fell for the same monthly lead cohorts; or they started being sent proposals, and the Proposal-to-Close Rate fell?

8202.text: How does the share of first meetings with poor-fit customers change after a noticeable rise or fall in the Contacted-to-SQL Rate, compared with before?

8203.text: How does the share of first meetings with poor-fit customers change in the first months after the company narrows or widens its customer profile, compared with before?

8204.text: Which employees and teams have a noticeably higher share of poor-fit customers among the leads they qualified and booked than colleagues with leads from the same channels?

8205.text: From which channels, sources and ad campaigns do leads turn out to be a poor fit at the meeting noticeably more often than the rest?

8206.text: For which products does a poor-fit customer get as far as a meeting noticeably more often than for the rest?

8207.text: Which profile questions should we add to qualification: on which profile criteria, and because of which projects the company doesn't take on, are customers who attended a meeting most often judged unsuitable, and does qualification ask about these?

8208.text: Should we pay the people who book meetings for each booked meeting: how do the SQL-to-Booked-Meeting Rate, the Meeting Show Rate, the Meeting-to-Proposal Rate and the share of first meetings with poor-fit customers change after switching to this pay scheme, compared with before?

8209.text: What share of "not a fit" flags have no profile criterion from the list: no reason was selected, the option for other reasons was chosen, the reason was typed in as free text, or the list of closing reasons has only a generic reason for poor-fit customers; and how many companies that are too small get recorded as refusals for lack of budget instead of a poor-fit flag?

8210.text: When is the poor-fit flag set: right after the meeting or only when the deal is closed; and for how many leads with poor-fit customers does the deal stay open beyond the window from the lead's arrival, so the lead misses the numerator?

8211.text: Is it checked whether a proposal went to a lead whose deal was closed with a poor-fit reason, or is the numerator taken from the closing reason alone, so it includes customers judged unsuitable only after the proposal; and what share of leads closed with a poor-fit reason did get a proposal after all, a standard or automated one?

8212.text: How is it determined that a lead flagged as a poor fit attended a meeting: by the stage history, by the current CRM stage, which the lead drops out of once the deal is closed, or by the loss reason alone, which also brings into the numerator a lead whose meeting the rep canceled in advance after checking the company?

8213.text: Which reps who ran the meeting judge customers a poor fit noticeably more often than colleagues with leads from the same channels, and do they apply this flag to meetings that didn't work out for other reasons?

8214.text: Which employee is the share attributed to if a booked lead is handed over to the rep who will run the meeting: the one who qualified the lead and booked the meeting, or the current owner in the CRM?

8215.text: How many days after the period ends does the share of first meetings with poor-fit customers stop changing?

8216.text: If the Proposal-to-Close Rate changed, what drove it: a change in the Proposal Follow-Up Rate, the Initial Proposal Discount Rate, the Proposal Turnaround Time, or in how often customers accept proposals while all three remain at their previous levels?

8217.text: How does the Proposal-to-Close Rate differ between proposals where someone tried to contact the customer within the follow-up window and proposals with no attempt at all, if you keep only proposals the customer didn't accept or decline on their own before the first attempt or, where there were no attempts, before the end of the follow-up window?

8218.text: When the proposal follow-up rate falls, what moves outside its usual range: proposals with no contact attempt, attempts the customer didn't respond to, conversations the customer started, or conversations after the follow-up window?

8219.text: If the proposal follow-up rate changed noticeably, how much of the change came from a change in the share of proposals sent to large customers, and how much from a change in the rate within each customer size group?

8220.text: For which reps and in which teams are proposals left without a follow-up noticeably more often than for colleagues who sent proposals for the same products to customers of the same size?

8221.text: How does the proposal follow-up rate change as the number of proposals a rep sends per week and the number of their open deals grow?

8222.text: For proposals sent on which days of the week and before which holidays does the team manage to contact the customer within the set window noticeably less often?

8223.text: For leads from which channels and sources are proposals left without a follow-up noticeably more often than for other leads from companies of the same size?

8224.text: Should we create a call task right when a proposal is sent: how has the proposal follow-up rate changed since the task started being created automatically, compared with before, and what share of these tasks are closed without a conversation with the customer?

8225.text: How many days after sending a proposal should we call the customer: how does the share of proposals followed by a conversation with the customer change depending on how many days after sending the first contact attempt was made?

8226.text: Should we agree on the date of the post-proposal conversation while still at the meeting: how has the proposal follow-up rate changed since the date of the next conversation started being recorded in the meeting outcome, compared with before, and what share of scheduled conversations fall after the follow-up window?

8227.text: What counts as a follow-up: a conversation with the customer in the phone system's call recording, a meeting on the calendar and a customer reply in writing, or a closed post-proposal call task and the phone system's answered-call flag, which also capture unanswered calls, voicemail and receptionists?

8228.text: How does the CRM tell a conversation started by an employee from one started by the customer, including a reply to the email or message with the proposal itself, and from a reply to messages the CRM sent automatically, even from the rep's number or mailbox: by call direction, by the author of the first message in the thread, or by a flag the rep sets?

8229.text: Are post-proposal conversations that bypassed the CRM counted as follow-ups: calls from the rep's personal phone, video meetings arranged through the rep's personal calendar, and messages in a personal messaging app where the customer replies about the proposal?

8230.text: Which follow-up date does the CRM store: the date of the conversation, meeting or customer reply itself, or the date the rep entered it; and how many days typically pass between them?

8231.text: From which date is the follow-up window measured: from sending the first version of the proposal, or from a send date that the CRM overwrites when a revised version goes out?

8232.text: Does the calculation include post-proposal conversations that the CRM logged to the customer's contact or company rather than to the deal with the proposal, or to another employee: the head of sales, a colleague covering for the rep, a technical specialist?

8233.text: How many days after the period ends does the proposal follow-up rate stop changing?

8234.text: If the Proposal-to-Close Rate changed, what drove it: a change in the Proposal Follow-Up Rate, the Initial Proposal Discount Rate, the Proposal Turnaround Time, or in how often customers accept proposals while all three remain at their previous levels?

8235.text: How do the Proposal-to-Close Rate and the Average Deal Size change after the company changes the first-version discount cap or the rules for approving it, compared with before, and what else changed in the same months: the price list, products, acquisition channels?

8236.text: How are proposals distributed by first-version discount percentage around the limit up to which a rep can give a discount without approval: how many are exactly at the limit, just below it and just above it?

8237.text: If the initial proposal discount changed noticeably, how much of the change came from a change in the share of proposals sent to large customers, and how much from a change in the discount within each customer size group?

8238.text: How does the first-version discount differ between proposals where a price objection from the customer, or a competitor the customer is comparing us with, was recorded at the meeting and other proposals to customers of the same size?

8239.text: If the initial proposal discount falls after the discount cap is lowered, is it because concessions are now given in ways the metric doesn't see: deferred payment terms, an extended warranty, free delivery and installation, items without a list price, free items recorded without a price, or a discount in later versions of the proposal?

8240.text: For which reps and in which teams is the first-version discount noticeably deeper than for colleagues sending proposals for the same products to customers of the same size?

8241.text: For leads from which channels and sources is the discount in the first version of the proposal noticeably deeper than for other leads from companies of the same size?

8242.text: What discount limit should reps have in the first version of the proposal without approval: what share of proposals require discount approval, how much longer is their Proposal Turnaround Time, and what share of requested discounts does the approver reduce or reject?

8243.text: Should we revise the price list: for which products do most proposals get a first-version discount, and for how many months in a row has this held?

8244.text: Should we give a time-limited discount for a quick decision: what share of proposals with such a discount were accepted before it expired, and what share later, after the discount was extended?

8245.text: Where is the first-version proposal price taken from: the saved file or the email used to send it to the customer, or the CRM, where the proposal is overwritten when revised; and for what share of proposals is the first version no longer available?

8246.text: Where is the list price taken from: the "price before discount" column in the proposal line, which the rep can edit, or the price list as of the date the first version was sent, for the price type the customer is entitled to; and have the prices as of that date been kept if the price list has changed since?

8247.text: How are free items and work recorded in the proposal: as a line with the list price and a zero amount due, as a line without a price, or only in words in the proposal text?

8248.text: What share of proposals is left out of the calculation because none of their items has a list price, and what share of the first-version total of the remaining proposals comes from items without a list price?

8249.text: What share of first proposal versions go out with several options to choose from, and how many of them have no option marked as primary?

8250.text: Does the CRM store who approved the discount in the first version of the proposal and what discount the rep requested, or is only the price sent to the customer visible?

8251.text: Which proposal amount is used to classify the customer as large, medium or small if size is based on deal value: the amount at list price, or at the first-version price, which puts a proposal with a deep discount in a smaller group?

8252.text: How many days after the period ends does the initial proposal discount stop changing?

7801.text: If the margin on one-time purchases falls, which line item grows per dollar of revenue: goods, picking and packing, shipping, returns, payments, the marketplace, retention or support?

7802.text: If the subscription margin falls, which line item grows per dollar of revenue: servers and services, payment processing, the app store, support or customer success?

7803.text: If the margin falls while prices stay the same, is it because there are more new customers with a first-order discount, free shipping or kickoff meetings?

7804.text: In which sales channels is a noticeably smaller share of revenue left after variable costs?

7805.text: Which products sell at a loss after variable costs once an order's shipping, picking and packing, and returns are allocated across its line items?

7806.text: Customers from which acquisition channels and sources bring in revenue with a noticeably lower contribution margin ratio?

7807.text: Which categories should we review first: where is the contribution margin ratio noticeably lower and revenue the largest?

7808.text: Is the decision on whether to treat support, customer success and the company's own servers as variable costs the same in all the periods you compare?

7809.text: Do variable costs include the costs of acquiring new customers, which are then subtracted a second time through the cost of acquisition?

7810.text: Does revenue include shipping fees paid by customers, which are already subtracted from shipping costs?

7811.text: How many days after the month ends does the contribution margin ratio stop changing?

7812.text: Are annual subscription payments and costs paid a year in advance allocated at one twelfth per month?

7843.text: If revenue per account changes, what drives it: the Average Subscription Price or the Effective Discount Rate?

7844.text: If revenue per account changes, what drives it: different payments from the same accounts or a change in the mix of the base, for example small accounts leaving or new ones joining on entry-level plans?

7845.text: How does a cohort's revenue per account change over its lifetime: do customers add seats and modules or move to cheaper plans?

7846.text: Which acquisition channels and sources bring in accounts with noticeably lower revenue?

7847.text: For which customer types and industries is revenue per account noticeably lower than for the rest?

7848.text: Who should get a dedicated account manager: on which plans and for which customer sizes does revenue per account not cover the Customer Success Cost per Account?

7849.text: Are MRR and paying accounts taken on the same date?

7850.text: Does the numerator include implementation, training and usage fees above the plan's allowance?

7851.text: Are subscriptions from different departments of one customer merged into one account by the same rule in all per-account calculations?

7852.text: Does the denominator include accounts on a trial or the free plan?

7974.text: If the frequency falls for the same customers, what drives it: Sessions per Customer per Lifetime Month, the Session-to-Placed-Order Rate, the Placed-to-Kept Order Rate or orders without a session?

7975.text: If the number for the whole base changes, what drives it: a change in frequency for cohorts at the same age since the first order, or the inflow of new customers?

7976.text: How does the number of orders per lifetime month differ between cohorts from different acquisition months at the same age since the first order?

7977.text: Which acquisition channels and sources bring in customers with noticeably fewer orders per lifetime month?

7978.text: Is the number of orders per lifetime month higher for customers who opted in to messaging campaigns than for similar customers who didn't?

7979.text: Which reasons for customers to come back to the site should we work on first: after which messaging campaigns and notifications do customers visit more often and place orders?

7980.text: Is Orders per Customer, which leaves out months without an order, used in the LTV calculation instead of this frequency?

7981.text: Are orders per month and the Average Customer Lifetime taken with the same K and for the same customers?

7982.text: Are orders and lifetime months summed across all customers first, rather than averaging individual customers' frequencies?

7983.text: Does the denominator include months after the customer churned, as in a cohort table?

7984.text: How many days after the month ends does the number of orders per lifetime month stop changing?

7929.text: If the share grows, what drives it: higher purchase costs, a lower pre-discount price or deeper discounts for the same goods, or more sales of goods with a high cost share?

7930.text: Which suppliers' goods cost noticeably more relative to the selling price than those of other suppliers in the same category?

7931.text: In which price tiers does the cost of goods take a noticeably larger part of revenue?

7932.text: In which categories should we revisit purchase prices, the price list or the depth of promotions: where are purchase costs rising, where is the pre-discount price falling, and where is the discount growing?

7933.text: Are inbound freight and duties included in the cost of goods at receiving, or are they expensed in the month of the delivery?

7934.text: Is 100% minus Gross Margin used instead of the share, even though its cost of goods includes storage and shrinkage and its revenue includes shipping fees?

7935.text: Does the denominator include shipping fees paid by customers, or the numerator storage, picking and packing, and shipping to the customer?

7936.text: Does the cost of goods returned to the warehouse leave the numerator together with their revenue?

7813.text: If cost per account grows, what drives it: a higher bill for servers and services, or fewer paying accounts to split its fixed part across?

7814.text: Which line items make up most of the cost per account, and which of them grow faster than the number of paying accounts: cloud, storage, third-party services or licenses?

7815.text: On which plans does cost per account grow faster than the Average Revenue per Account (ARPA)?

7816.text: How does cost per account change after launching features that use third-party services billed per request, compared with before?

7817.text: For which customer sizes does an account cost noticeably more per dollar of its fee, based on measured consumption?

7818.text: Which cloud and third-party service vendors are raising the price of the unit of consumption itself: a request, a gigabyte or a server hour?

7819.text: What part of capacity should we prepay at a discount: what load holds steady month after month?

7820.text: Do the costs include development and testing environments, the company website and retention messaging campaigns?

7821.text: Is the load from trials and the free plan subtracted using an allocation key, or is the whole bill split evenly across paying accounts?

7822.text: Where are the costs of trials, pilots and the free plan counted, if they're neither here nor in Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)?

7823.text: Is the cloud bill assigned to the month of consumption, and are annual licenses spread across months rather than booked by payment date?

7824.text: If support cost per account grows, what drives it: a higher Cost per Ticket or paying accounts contacting support more often?

7825.text: If paying accounts contact support more often, what drives it: more new and large accounts in the base, or long-standing accounts of the same size writing in more often?

7826.text: Which ticket topics are the most expensive for support per account?

7827.text: If support cost per account is cut, do accounts whose tickets waited longer than usual for an answer renew less often afterward?

7828.text: On which plans and for which customer sizes is support noticeably more expensive per dollar of revenue per account?

7829.text: Do the knowledge base and in-product tips pay off: after they're introduced, does cost per account fall by more than the investment costs per account?

7830.text: Does this include planned work initiated by the company, which belongs in the Customer Success Cost per Account?

7831.text: Where are the costs of trials, pilots and the free plan counted, if they're neither here nor in Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)?

7832.text: Is cost per account calculated as Cost per Ticket multiplied by Tickets per Customer, which gives the cost per account that contacted support rather than per paying account?

7833.text: Is the part of the costs for tickets from trials and the free plan subtracted here?

7937.text: If the net shipping cost per order grows, what drives it: more expensive shipping, lower customer fees or fewer customer pickup orders?

7938.text: For which regions, delivery methods and categories is the customer's shipping fee noticeably lower or higher than what the company pays the carrier?

7939.text: Which products are noticeably more expensive to ship at the store's expense when an order's shipping costs are allocated across its line items?

7940.text: Which threshold should we choose: at what value does the margin on additional items in the cart cover the cost of free shipping?

7941.text: Are costs taken from carrier invoices rather than from the rate calculated at checkout?

7942.text: Is shipping for refused, unclaimed and fully returned orders counted twice: here and in the Cost of Returns and Refused or Unclaimed Orders per Order?

7943.text: Has the carrier's fee for collecting payment on delivery stayed here, even though it belongs in the Effective Payment Processing Rate?

7944.text: Do customer pickup orders stay in the denominator with zero shipping cost?

7945.text: If the processing rate grows, what drives it: higher rates, a larger share of payment methods with high rates, or more refunds on which the fee wasn't returned?

7946.text: With which payment methods do fees take a noticeably larger share of revenue once the carrier's fee for collecting payment on delivery is included?

7947.text: Should we switch to two-step payment: how much do we pay in fees on canceled, refused and unclaimed orders for which the money had already been charged?

7948.text: Which payment method should we offer first on the site: where is the rate lower while the Order Payment Rate is no lower than for the others?

7949.text: Has the carrier's fee for collecting payment on delivery stayed in the Net Shipping Cost per Order, even though it belongs here?

7950.text: Does this include the app store commission on subscriptions paid in the app?

7951.text: Is the fee on an annual payment spread over twelve months together with the revenue from it?

7952.text: How many days after the month ends does the processing rate stop changing?

7834.text: Is the Customer Retention Rate higher for accounts with a dedicated manager than for similar accounts without one?

7835.text: If cost per account grows, what drives it: more expensive work with each account, or more new accounts and accounts with a dedicated manager in the base?

7836.text: Which line items make up most of the customer success cost per account, and which grow faster than the number of paying accounts?

7837.text: How does the customer success cost per account change from the first month of an account's lifetime to the following ones?

7838.text: Who should get a dedicated account manager: on which plans and for which customer sizes does the Average Revenue per Account (ARPA) not cover the customer success cost per account?

7839.text: Is managers' time spent on expansion sales, which belongs to sales team costs, separated out?

7840.text: Does this include answers to customer tickets, which belong in the Support Cost per Account?

7841.text: Where are the costs of trials, pilots and the free plan counted, if they're neither here nor in Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC)?

7842.text: Does this include implementation the customer pays for separately?

7953.text: If the cost per order grows, what drives it: picked orders being refused, left unclaimed or returned in full more often, items being returned from orders more often, or each case costing more?

7954.text: Which line item makes up most of the cost: picking and shipping of refused or unclaimed orders, return shipping, receiving, or markdowns and write-offs?

7955.text: Which return and refusal reasons account for most of the costs?

7956.text: Does the cost of returns and refused or unclaimed orders per order grow when Units per Order grows?

7957.text: How does the cost per order differ between customers' first orders and repeat orders?

7958.text: With which delivery methods do returns and refused or unclaimed orders cost noticeably more per order: courier, pickup point or parcel locker?

7959.text: Where should we introduce prepayment or partial prepayment: in which categories and regions do refusals of orders paid on delivery cost the most?

7960.text: Which categories and products need a different return policy, or should be dropped from the assortment: where do losses from returns eat up a noticeable part of gross profit?

7961.text: Does the calculation include money refunded to customers, so that one transaction reduces profit twice?

7962.text: Is shipping for refused, unclaimed and fully returned orders counted twice: here and in the Net Shipping Cost per Order?

7963.text: How many days after the month ends does the cost of returns and refused or unclaimed orders per order stop changing?

7964.text: Are orders canceled after picking selected by whether they were actually picked and shipped rather than by their canceled status?

7965.text: If cost per order grows, what drives it: more tickets per kept order or a higher Cost per Ticket?

7966.text: If there are more tickets per kept order, what drives it: customers asking more often, or a falling Placed-to-Kept Order Rate while questions about purchases that didn't happen remain?

7967.text: With which carriers is supporting an order noticeably more expensive for the same destinations?

7968.text: Which products' orders require noticeably more support than orders with similar products in the same category?

7969.text: How does the support cost per order differ between new and returning customers?

7970.text: Which causes of questions should we eliminate first: which topics, from delivery status to the return process, make up most of the cost per order?

7971.text: Does this include order confirmation calls and taking orders by phone?

7972.text: Are costs divided by kept orders rather than by all placed orders?

7973.text: How many days after the month ends does the support cost per order stop changing?

7700.text: If the Average Revenue per Account (ARPA) changes, what drives it: the average subscription price or the Effective Discount Rate?

7701.text: If the average subscription price falls, what drives it: lower list prices, new customers choosing entry-level plans, customers leaving higher-tier plans, or a growing Downgrade Rate?

7702.text: On which per-seat and per-module plans do accounts mostly take the minimum number of seats and modules?

7703.text: Through which sales channels and for which customer types are entry-level plans chosen noticeably more often?

7704.text: How much revenue does the company miss out on from customers who stayed on old prices, and on which plans is the gap larger?

7705.text: Which plans should we steer new customers to: on which higher-tier plans is the Customer Retention Rate no lower than on entry-level ones?

7706.text: For customers on old prices, is their plan's price used rather than the current price list?

7707.text: Are annual subscriptions counted at the monthly list price of the same plan rather than the annual payment divided by twelve?

7708.text: Does the Average Revenue per Account (ARPA) match the subscription price after the Effective Discount Rate is applied on the same date?

7768.text: With which promotion type do customers buy more units of a product in one order line: a discount on the second unit, two for the price of one, or a quantity threshold?

7769.text: If units per line fall while the Average List Price rises, is it because best-sellers were moved to multipacks?

7770.text: How do units per line differ between a customer's first order and repeat orders?

7771.text: In which categories and price tiers do customers buy several units of an item at a time, and in which only one?

7772.text: Which customer groups buy several units of the same item noticeably more often?

7773.text: For which products should we launch volume promotions: which of them are bought often, but one unit at a time?

7774.text: Which volume promotions should we cancel: for which of them do units per line for promoted products barely differ from their level in regular weeks?

7775.text: Are lines of one SKU that the register splits by tracking code or by different prices in a promotion merged into one line?

7776.text: Are goods sold by weight, shipping and packaging lines, and returns entered as separate negative lines removed from both parts?

7777.text: Are bulk purchases by businesses and resellers excluded using a units-per-line threshold that's the same in all periods?

7778.text: Is the units-sold counter, which includes sales outside orders, being used as the numerator?

7779.text: If the average list price falls, what drives it: the same products got cheaper in the catalog, or customers started buying cheaper items?

7780.text: Which categories pull the average list price down: where are unit sales growing while the unit price is below average?

7781.text: If Units per Line Item falls while the average list price rises, is it because best-sellers were moved to multipacks?

7782.text: If the average list price changes, is it because the shares of units sold through physical stores, the website and marketplaces have shifted?

7783.text: How does the average list price differ for new and returning customers in the same categories?

7784.text: Where should we revisit supplier costs, list prices or promotion depth: in which categories are supplier costs rising, in which is the pre-discount price falling, and in which is the discount growing?

7785.text: Is the price taken from the order line or the price history on the sale date rather than the current catalog price?

7786.text: Is a crossed-out price at which the product never sold being counted as the pre-discount price?

7787.text: Are returned units removed from both parts, and has Gross Merchandise Value (GMV) been kept out of the numerator?

7788.text: If the effective discount grows with unchanged price lists, what drives it: more sales at a discount, or deeper discounts themselves?

7789.text: Which tactics account for most of the effective discount: promo codes, promotions, points, individual prices or the annual-billing discount on subscriptions?

7790.text: If the effective discount grows with the same promotions, is it because the inflow of new customers with a welcome discount has grown?

7791.text: For which codes is the effective discount noticeably deeper than the code's stated discount: where does the code stack with a promotion or points?

7792.text: At which loyalty program tiers do members buy at a noticeably deeper discount?

7793.text: In which plans and for customers of which size is the discount from the list price noticeably deeper?

7794.text: Where should we revisit supplier costs, list prices or promotion depth: in which categories are supplier costs rising, in which is the pre-discount price falling, and in which is the discount growing?

7795.text: Are points and member-card discounts that accounting books as loyalty program expenses subtracted from revenue?

7796.text: Does revenue include shipping fees and one-time payments that have no pre-discount price?

7797.text: Is annual subscription billing compared with the monthly list price multiplied by twelve rather than with the annual list price?

7798.text: Is the effective discount being derived from the Discounts total, which still includes the discount on goods that were later returned?

7799.text: Does the discount include what the marketplace gives the customer at its own expense?

7800.text: How many days after the month ends does the effective discount stop changing?

7985.text: When sessions per lifetime month decline, which kind of session moves outside its usual range: sessions from messaging campaigns, push notifications, ads or direct visits?

7986.text: If the number for the whole base changes, what drives it: a change in visit frequency for cohorts at the same age since the first order, or the inflow of new customers?

7987.text: How do sessions per lifetime month differ between customers with one order and repeat customers?

7988.text: If sessions per lifetime month grow, is it because customers visit more often to check order status or start a return?

7989.text: Which reasons for customers to come back to the site should we work on first: after which messaging campaigns and notifications do customers visit more often and place orders?

7990.text: Does the change in sessions coincide with a shift in the share of identified sessions: login by phone number, required login, a new tracker or the cookie lifetime in Safari?

7991.text: Is the number inflated by employees' test accounts, resellers, price-tracking scripts and email scanners that open links in emails?

7992.text: Are sessions divided by all lifetime months rather than only the months when the customer visited?

7993.text: How many days after the month ends do sessions per lifetime month stop changing?

7994.text: If customers order less often on the website and in the app, what drives it: less frequent visits, a lower Session-to-Placed-Order Rate or a lower Placed-to-Kept Order Rate among the same customers?

7995.text: When the rate falls, what moves outside its usual range: the Zero-Result Search Rate, the In-Stock Rate or the Cart Abandonment Rate?

7996.text: If the rate grows, is it because of a larger inflow of new customers, whose sessions before the first order are hardly ever identified?

7997.text: How does the rate differ on the web and in the app for the same customers?

7998.text: Which acquisition channels bring in customers who place noticeably fewer orders with the same number of sessions?

7999.text: How does regular customers' session-to-placed-order rate change after changes to the catalog, search or cart, compared with the same length of time before them?

8000.text: Are sessions and orders taken for the same people: identified sessions with identified customers' orders, or all sessions with all orders?

8001.text: Is the rate overstated by orders placed by phone and through a sales rep, which have no website session?

8002.text: Does a session end the same way on the website and in the app, or are app sessions split after a few seconds in the background?

8003.text: Does the change in the rate coincide with a shift in the share of sessions without an order that get identified, for example from login by phone number or cleared cookies?

8004.text: If the kept rate falls, what drives it: more cancellations, more orders closed without payment, more unclaimed orders, or more orders returned in full?

8005.text: If the kept rate falls, what drives it: a lower kept rate within payment methods, delivery methods and regions, or a growing share of those where the kept rate is lower?

8006.text: In which categories and with which delivery methods is the kept rate noticeably lower than in the rest?

8007.text: Which products appear in orders that are kept noticeably less often than orders with other products in the same category?

8008.text: Which carriers have a noticeably lower kept rate for the same destinations and with the same delivery method?

8009.text: How does the kept rate differ between a customer's first order and their repeat orders with the same payment method?

8010.text: Which acquisition channels and sources bring in orders that are kept noticeably less often?

8011.text: How do the kept rate and the number of kept orders change after prepayment is introduced, compared with before?

8012.text: When should we send a reminder about an order waiting at a pickup point: by which day of the holding period have most orders that will eventually be picked up been collected?

8013.text: How many days after the period ends does the kept rate stop changing?

8014.text: Are kept orders assigned to the month the order was placed rather than the month it was received?

8015.text: Do fully returned orders stay counted as kept if the kept status is taken from the delivery status or if the return was accepted in a store without being linked to the order?

8016.text: If the rate falls, what drives it: fewer new customers giving consent, more unsubscribes, or a buildup of addresses that messages don't reach?

8017.text: If the rate changes, is it because the share of newcomers among customers has changed?

8018.text: In which messaging channels does a noticeably smaller share of customers have consent and valid contact details?

8019.text: Which sales channels and first-purchase stores bring in customers whom messaging campaigns reach noticeably less often?

8020.text: Is Orders per Customer per Lifetime Month higher for customers with messaging consent than for similar customers without it?

8021.text: Is the Second Order Rate higher for newcomers who gave messaging consent with their first order than for similar newcomers without it?

8022.text: Should we keep the consent request at checkout: how many consents does it add, and how many of them are still active a few months later?

8023.text: Does only consent given separately and by the customer themselves count, rather than consent buried in the terms of sale or a pre-checked box?

8024.text: Is permission for notifications on the phone being taken as consent to marketing push notifications?

8025.text: Are addresses that haven't been emailed in a long time, or that were suppressed from campaigns for inactivity, counted as valid?

8026.text: Are consents being added up by channel, so that a customer with email and push is counted twice?

7853.text: Is the Month 1 to Month 2 Retention Rate higher for customers who completed the key action within N days of payment than for those who didn't?

7854.text: If the rate changes, is it because the share of customers who started paying through an automatic charge after the trial, a month at a token price or a contract signed before setup has changed?

7855.text: Which acquisition channels bring in paying customers who complete the key action noticeably less often?

7856.text: On which plans do new paying customers complete the key action noticeably less often?

7857.text: How does the activation rate differ between customers who got help with setup and similar customers who didn't, counting only the customer's own actions?

7927.text: Is a loss counted when the grace period expires rather than on the day the charge failed?

2426.text: Which agents have noticeably more or fewer tickets than colleagues on the same topics and tier?

2427.text: How does the number of tickets per agent differ between senior and junior agents on the same topics?

2428.text: How does the number of tickets per agent differ across contact channels?

2429.text: How does the number of tickets per agent differ between tiers with similar topics?

2430.text: If tickets per agent increase, what drives it: growing Ticket Volume or fewer working agents?

2431.text: Does the Repeat Contact Rate of agents grow some time after their tickets per agent increase?

2432.text: What tickets-per-agent target should we set for each channel and each seniority level?

2433.text: Does the denominator include agents on vacation and new hires in training?

2434.text: Are agents who worked part of the period counted as a fraction?

2435.text: Does the numerator use incoming tickets rather than resolved ones?

2436.text: Do tickets closed by the bot without an agent inflate the number of tickets per agent?

2380.text: If Average Active Agents drops while the number of agents stays the same, what drives it: hiring and departures during the period, vacations, training, other tasks or the shift schedule?

2381.text: How many weeks does it take a new agent to reach the same Tickets per Agent level as experienced colleagues on the same tier?

2382.text: Does the number of agents cover Forecasted Ticket Volume for peak season at the current tickets-per-agent target?

2383.text: On which tiers are there more agents than the volume requires: where does the Agent Utilization Rate stay near the lower edge of the range all season?

2384.text: How is the team counted in all per-agent reports: in people or in FTEs?

2385.text: Does the number of agents include contractors and outsourced staff who handle tickets?

2386.text: Does the number of agents include managers and trainers who don't take tickets?

2387.text: Do per-agent metrics use the average number of agents for the period rather than the number at the end of the period?

2395.text: Is Employee Turnover Rate higher in the following months on tiers where team satisfaction is lower?

2396.text: For which tenure groups is satisfaction noticeably lower than for others?

2397.text: How does satisfaction differ between senior and junior agents?

2398.text: How does satisfaction differ between in-house and contracted agents?

2399.text: On which tiers is team satisfaction noticeably lower than on the rest?

2400.text: Is team satisfaction lower on tiers where the Agent Utilization Rate stays high for a long time?

2401.text: On which survey questions is the share of positive answers noticeably lower than on the rest?

2402.text: Is the Customer Satisfaction Score (CSAT) lower on tiers where team satisfaction is lower?

2403.text: Which tiers should we talk to first: where is satisfaction lowest and falling from survey to survey?

2404.text: Is the rate skewed because only a small share of agents responded on some tiers?

2405.text: Is the threshold for a positive rating the same in all surveys you compare?

2406.text: Are the surveys you compare equally anonymous?

2371.text: If costs grow, which line items drive it: labor, contractors, licenses or overhead?

2372.text: Is labor cost for in-house agents growing faster than their number, meaning each agent is getting more expensive?

2373.text: How does the hourly cost of an in-house agent compare with a contractor's on the same topics?

2374.text: Do support costs grow in months when Ticket Volume is higher, or do they stay the same?

2375.text: Does the bot pay off: how many agent hours do Automated Resolutions save, and does that cover the cost of the bot?

2376.text: Does labor cost include payroll taxes on top of take-home pay?

2377.text: Do costs include contractors, outsourcing and licenses for the system, telephony and the bot?

2378.text: Are rent and equipment allocated to support, and is it the same in all the periods you compare?

2379.text: Which month are costs recorded in: the month the work was done or the month the contractor and license invoices were paid?

research.name: Exploratory
research.hint: Help find where the metric goes off track and which neighboring metrics it is linked to.

decision.name: Decision
decision.hint: Questions about a decision this metric’s data can answer: what to change and where to put money and effort.

data.name: Data & calculation
data.hint: Check whether you can trust the number: data quality, calculation and accounting rules, and for bids and budgets, the settings too.

1.text: How much has the metric changed compared with the previous period and the same period last year?

2.text: Is the value within the usual range of fluctuation for this metric?

3.text: How does the value compare with the plan or the target range?

4.text: If the metric has changed, when did it start and how: as a jump or gradually?

5.text: If the metric has changed, did it change the same way in all segments, or is the change concentrated in one?

6.text: Are there gaps, duplicates or changes in accounting rules in the data for the period?
